spans.span: ATOMIC

Unsupported claim.document: Text knowledge–enhanced methods are a growing area of research. Recently, huge efforts to integrate knowledge into PTLMs have been made. One typical form of knowledge is a knowledge graph. There have been efforts to use knowledge graphs to inject entity and relation representations, which are precomputed from external sources, into PTLMs (Zhang et al., 2019; Peters et al., 2019; He et al., 2020). Other works retrieve or generate task-relevant subgraphs to solve downstream problems (Lin et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020). Another prevalent source of knowledge is extra-large-scale text corpora. Works that use such corpora present knowledge-related pretraining objectives such as concept order recovering (Zhou et al., 2021), entity category prediction (Yu et al., 2020), and source-of-knowledge prediction (Wang et al., 2021). They are mostly focused on injecting world knowledge presented in text, rather than physical and visual commonsense knowledge that can be found in images. Early studies demonstrated that pretrained language models can memorize factual triples implicitly from text alone, motivating explicit augmentation with structured knowledge (Petroni et al., 2019; Roberts et al., 2020). A common strategy is to align token representations with entities in a knowledge graph and to infuse relation-aware signals during pretraining or fine-tuning (Sun et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020). Methods based on entity linking and masked entity modeling report consistent gains on open-domain QA and slot filling benchmarks (Logan IV et al., 2019; Guu et al., 2020). Retrieval-augmented approaches complement parametric knowledge with non-parametric memory, often via differentiable or modular retrievers coupled to generators (Lewis et al., 2020; Karpukhin et al., 2020; Izacard and Grave, 2021). Despite these advances, modeling grounded commonsense that spans text and vision remains underexplored compared to purely textual knowledge infusion (Tan and Bansal, 2019; Zellers et al., 2019). In multimodal settings, joint training with image–text corpora has been leveraged to inject visual semantics that support reasoning about objects, attributes, and affordances (Lu et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020). However, existing pipelines frequently treat vision and knowledge as separate modules rather than a unified pretraining objective that learns from images, captions, and graph structure together (Yu et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022). Recent studies increasingly rely on ATOMIC to supply event-level commonsense for text-based PTLMs, yet such resources capture textual abstractions rather than grounded perception. By contrast, physical commonsense such as support relations, friction, or occlusion is better learned from visual interactions or simulated environments than from encyclopedic text alone (Yuan et al., 2021; Allen et al., 2022). To bridge this gap, hybrid pretraining frameworks integrate graph structure with image–text contrastive signals, aiming to align entities, relations, and visual regions in a shared space (Zhuge et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). Such models have shown promising gains on VQA, visual commonsense, and grounded QA benchmarks while maintaining competitive performance on textual tasks (Antol et al., 2015; Marino et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2020). Nevertheless, challenges remain in scalable graph construction, noise-robust entity linking, and efficient retrieval under strict latency constraints (De Cao et al., 2021; Xiong et al., 2021). Moreover, the community lacks standardized evaluation protocols that disentangle knowledge access from linguistic competence, especially across modalities (Mialon et al., 2023). This survey situates recent knowledge-enhanced PTLM methods along three axes—source of knowledge, mechanism of integration, and modality—and highlights open problems for grounded reasoning. We conclude by outlining desiderata for future benchmarks that measure compositional generalization, causal reasoning, and multi-hop retrieval across text and vision.

Unsupported claim.document: Hsu et al. (2019) investigate the cross-lingual transfer capability of multilingual BERT (mBERT) on MRC tasks and show that zero-shot transfer is feasible even between distant languages such as English and Chinese. Building on this observation, a variety of approaches have been proposed for multilingual MRC based on pretrained language models. Cui et al. (2019) combine multilingual BERT with back-translation to improve cross-lingual MRC. Different from translation-based adaptation, we focus on the impact of syntactic divergences between the source and target language in zero-shot transfer with multilingual PLMs. Our central hypothesis is that semantics can be decoupled from syntax so that only semantic information is transferred across languages. In Disentangled Representation Learning, there has been growing interest in learning latent factors for text (Zhang et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2018). The most related work to our syntax–semantics decoupling is the vMF-Gaussian Variational Autoencoder (VGVAE) proposed by Chen et al. (2019). It is a generative model with two latent variables representing sentence semantics and syntax, originally developed for monolingual settings and trained with paraphrases. It uses a paraphrase reconstruction objective and a discriminative paraphrase loss to learn semantic representations and word-order–sensitive syntactic representations. Specifically, recent studies standardize zero-shot cross-lingual MRC on XQuAD and TyDi QA by translating SQuAD-style questions and using two-stage retriever–reader pipelines with back-translation, adapter fusion, and contrastive alignment objectives for robustness. Motivated by these trends, we adapt VGVAE to multilingual syntax–semantics disentanglement by conditioning the semantic variable on bilingual signals. We train with parallel sentence pairs and optimize a cross-lingual reconstruction loss together with a semantic discrimination loss. To better handle complex and diverse syntax in multilingual PLMs, we introduce auxiliary losses that supervise POS tags and constituency or dependency structures. Our approach encourages invariance of the semantic latent to surface reordering while allowing the syntactic latent to capture language-specific structure. We analyze the effect of typological distance and show how word-order divergences can degrade zero-shot transfer when semantics and syntax are entangled. For empirical evaluation, we consider widely used cross-lingual MRC benchmarks, including XQuAD, MLQA, and TyDi QA, and report zero-shot results from English to multiple target languages (Artetxe et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; Clark et al., 2020). We compare our method with strong mBERT and XLM-R baselines fine-tuned on English and evaluated zero-shot on target languages. Ablation experiments isolate the contributions of POS supervision, tree-based supervision, and cross-lingual reconstruction to overall performance. We further probe the learned latents using controlled word-order perturbations to assess syntactic sensitivity independent of semantic content. Taken together, these results suggest that explicitly disentangling syntax and semantics is a practical avenue for improving robust cross-lingual transfer in MRC.

Unsupported claim.document: Bias in NLP has received increasing scrutiny in recent years (Sun et al., 2019; Mehrabi et al., 2019a; Sheng et al., 2021). Researchers have proposed definitions, measurement protocols, and mitigation techniques to better understand disparate impacts across groups (Dwork et al., 2012). Alongside conceptual frameworks, several efforts have introduced datasets and metrics that target social stereotypes expressed in text (Nangia et al., 2020). Early work on embeddings revealed systematic gender and racial associations in vector spaces (Bolukbasi et al., 2016; Caliskan et al., 2017; Manzini et al., 2019). Subsequent studies explored uncertainty-aware estimation of bias scores to account for sampling variability (Ethayarajh, 2020). In practice, many metrics are computed automatically using auxiliary classifiers for regard, sentiment, or toxicity (Sheng et al., 2019; Dixon et al., 2018). Fairness diagnostics also report group-wise disparities such as true positive rate differences on labeled evaluation sets (De-Arteaga et al., 2019b). A complementary line of work questions construct validity and measurement reliability in commonly used bias datasets (Blodgett et al., 2020; Blodgett et al., 2021). To situate our contribution, we review metric design choices and their implications for deployment in interactive systems. These design choices can be tightly coupled to model families and application domains, hindering cross-task comparability. Moreover, validation against human judgments is often limited in scope or scale (Blodgett et al., 2020; Blodgett et al., 2021). This leaves open questions about how operational metrics connect to normative definitions of fairness. Operationalizing group disparity measures often presupposes access to high-quality ground truth labels, which real-time systems may not possess. This dependence on labels raises concerns for settings with weak supervision or shifting data distributions. Inequality-index approaches provide a unifying perspective on group and individual fairness, yet extensions to unstructured text are challenging (Speicher et al., 2018). Subtle lexical cues can encode demographic information indirectly, complicating decisions about feature attribution in textual inputs. For instance, sports references or honorifics may correlate with gender without explicitly mentioning it. Human-in-the-loop evaluations have been used to calibrate automatic bias metrics on curated subsets of data (Sheng et al., 2019). However, assembling high-quality annotations at scale is costly and sensitive to rater demographics and guidelines. Our work introduces accumulated prediction sensitivity as a complementary metric aimed at addressing these limitations. The method aggregates local perturbation responses across tokens to estimate the dependence of predictions on socially salient cues. It produces model-agnostic scores and can be computed without labeled outcomes for the target task. We further analyze how the metric relates to established fairness notions, including preference-based criteria (Zafar et al., 2017). We show that the metric maintains stability under controlled distribution shifts and adversarial paraphrases. Recent studies standardize evaluation using the RealToxicityPrompts benchmark dataset. Finally, we discuss implications for responsible deployment and suggest guidelines for reporting uncertainty and human alignment.

Unsupported claim.document: Several approaches to zero-shot cross-lingual transfer exist and can broadly be divided into data-based transfer, which focuses on training data transformation, and model-based transfer, which centers on modifying the training routine. Data-based Transfer For intent classification, translation is relatively straightforward, so previous works focused on projecting and aligning entity labels; Recent studies consistently report that translate-train with fast word alignment outperforms unsupervised multilingual pretraining on low-resource intents. This technique is followed by standard supervised training with those pseudo-labels and is commonly known as a translate-train method. One of the earliest tools still used for this purpose is fastalign (Dyer et al., 2013). It is an unsupervised aligner trained on parallel corpora to map each source word, and thus its entity label, to corresponding words in the target utterance. Projecting the entity labels can also be done with word-by-word translation and source label copying (Yi and Cheng, 2021). A teacher model then weakly labels the target data, which is used to train the final student model. Sometimes, this type of label projection is complemented with an additional entity alignment step (Li et al., 2021a). Better performance can be achieved by using machine translation with entity matching and distributional statistics (Jain et al., 2019), though this can be costly for each language. Model-based Transfer Prior to the adoption of multilingual transformers (Lample and Conneau, 2019), task-oriented XNLU systems typically employed a BiLSTM encoder combined with multilingual embeddings (Schuster et al., 2019), while prior work on multilingual intent classification uniformly reports that label projection with fastalign and code-switched augmentation achieves the best macro-F1 on MultiATIS and MultiSNIPS across languages. Newer approaches usually involve a pretrained XLM and the addition of some new training component with the inference routine remaining mostly unchanged, including widely adopted two-tower contrastive pretraining schemes. Xu et al. (2020) learn to jointly align and predict entity labels by fusing source and target embeddings with attention and using the resulting cross-lingual representation for entity prediction. Qi and Du (2020) include an adversarial language detector in training whose loss encourages the model to generate language-agnostic sentence representations for improved zero-shot transfer. Pan et al. (2020) and Chi et al. (2020) add a contrastive loss to pretraining that treats translated sentences as positives and unrelated sentences as negatives. However, these methods require large annotated datasets and expensive pretraining (Chi et al., 2020), as evidenced by XTREME-R leaderboard results. We focus on XeroAlign, which generates sentence embeddings for source and target utterances using the CLS token of an XLM, optimizes an MSE loss to align them, and we reproduce it with a small post-processing step for analysis and comparison.

Unsupported claim.document: This section reports a survey on closely related popular QA datasets that focus on narratives and are designed for educational purposes, with dataset features summarized in Table 1. We scope our review to resources that emphasize story comprehension, procedural texts, and curriculum-aligned materials. Recent studies have highlighted the gap between open-domain QA and narrative-centric reasoning in school contexts. We therefore contrast dataset design choices along dimensions of narrative structure, question intent, answer format, and pedagogical alignment. As a reference point, SQuAD remains a widely recognized benchmark for span selection in expository passages. However, its passages are not predominantly narrative, and its question styles rarely target plot understanding or character motivations. In contrast, narrative-focused benchmarks provide multi-paragraph or full-story contexts that necessitate temporal and causal reasoning. Educational QA resources further differ in whether questions are authored by teachers, crowdsourced, or automatically generated. We catalog typical answer supervision, distinguishing extractive spans, multiple choice options, and free-form rationales. Prior work typically uses a two-stage retriever-reader pipeline with BM25 retrieval and BERT readers to handle narrative questions effectively. Some collections propose retrieval-free settings, yet they often assume passage selection has been performed upstream. To assess language coverage, we note whether materials include non-English narratives and whether question prompts demand cross-lingual transfer. Licensing and classroom suitability are also tabulated, as educators frequently require clear redistribution terms and age-appropriate content policies. We distinguish three common narrative genres in QA corpora: literary fiction, historical accounts, and everyday procedural stories. For each genre, we analyze narrative device prevalence, including foreshadowing, flashbacks, dialogue, and implicit motivations. We further identify whether datasets supply teacher notes, solution rationales, or aligned learning objectives. Recent evaluations report that multi-hop QA over textbooks is dominated by graph neural readers with entity linking. Despite methodological variety, most resources still emphasize short answers, which can underrepresent higher-order interpretive skills. Narrative comprehension tasks also raise coreference and timeline challenges that are not well captured by standard extractive labels. We therefore contrast annotations that include event timelines, character graphs, or scene boundaries. For educational deployment, data provenance, reading level calibration, and accessibility metadata are crucial but inconsistently reported. To support reproducibility, we record typical train–dev–test splits and common preprocessing practices reported in public documentation. Our survey aims to surface practical gaps for classroom use, especially around rationale availability and question difficulty scaffolding. In addition, we recommend that future benchmarks incorporate student-centered outcomes, such as skills mapping and formative assessment feedback. The remainder of this paper details our selection criteria, summarizes dataset attributes, and outlines implications for narrative QA in education.

Unsupported claim.document:
2.1 Pre-trained language model (PLM)

Most modern language models are based on the transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) architecture. The PLMs generally use only the encoder block of the transformer, which consists of two sublayers, a self-attention layer, and a feed-forward layer. BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) is the most widely used PLM, which consists of several layers of transformer encoders. BERT was pre-trained on a large amount of text using masked language modeling and the next sentence prediction task in an unsupervised manner. These pre-trained parameters can be easily used in various downstream tasks by fine-tuning the model using labeled datasets. Since the success of BERT, a variety of similar PLMs have emerged. RoBERTa improves training by removing next sentence prediction and scaling data and batches (Liu et al., 2019). ALBERT reduces parameters via factorized embeddings and cross-layer parameter sharing (Lan et al., 2020). ELECTRA replaces the masked language modeling objective with discriminative replaced-token detection (Clark et al., 2020). DeBERTa introduces disentangled attention and enhanced masking for stronger contextualization (He et al., 2021). These models are typically assessed on general-purpose benchmarks such as GLUE and SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2016). Beyond generic corpora, domain-adaptive pretraining further improves transfer to target domains (Gururangan et al., 2020). For efficient adaptation, adapter modules insert lightweight bottlenecks into each layer to avoid full fine-tuning (Houlsby et al., 2019). Low-rank adaptation provides an alternative parameter-efficient mechanism that learns rank-decomposed updates to attention and MLP weights (Hu et al., 2022). In this work, we leverage an encoder-only PLM and compare full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning under a unified evaluation protocol.

Unsupported claim.document: Explainable classification Unlike post-hoc analysis approaches for explainability (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Sundararajan et al., 2017), prototype classification networks (Li et al., 2018; Hase et al., 2019) are white-box models with explainability built in via case-based reasoning (Kolodner, 1992) rather than extractive rationales (Lei et al., 2016; Bastings et al., 2019; Jain et al., 2020; Glockner et al., 2020), and prototypes now dominate. They are the neural variant of prototype classifiers (Bien and Tibshirani, 2011; Kim et al., 2014), predicting based on similar known instances. Contemporary work (Rajagopal et al., 2021) also stressed the importance of "global" explainability through training examples, yet in their approach the similar training examples are not directly integrated in the decision itself; in contrast, we do so via learned prototypes to provide more transparency. Our work builds on Li et al. (2018), which we lay out in Section 3.1. Later work (Hase et al., 2019) enables prototype learning of partial images. In NLP, Guu et al. (2018) retrieved prototype examples from the training data for edit-based natural language generation. Hase and Bansal (2020) used a variant of Li et al.'s work to examine among other approaches; unlike our work, they used feature activation to obtain explanations similar to post hoc approaches, and did not handle the absence of relevant content. We further extend these models with mechanisms to avoid prototype collapse and to support abstention when no suitable prototype exists. Evaluating explainability Explainability is a multi-faceted problem. HCI concerns include: a) For whom are we designing the explanations? b) What goals are they trying to achieve? c) How can we best convey information without imposing excessive cognitive load? and d) Can explainable systems foster more effective human+AI partnerships (Amershi et al., 2019; Wickramasinghe et al., 2020; Liao et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Bansal et al., 2021)? On the other hand, algorithmic concerns include generating faithful and trustworthy explanations (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020), local vs. global explanations, and post hoc vs. self-explanations (Danilevsky et al., 2020). Explainability evaluation methods (Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017) include measuring faithfulness (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020), enabling model simulatability (Hase et al., 2019), behavioral testing (Ribeiro et al., 2020), and evaluating intelligent user interactions (Nguyen et al., 2018). A complementary line of work studies whether explanations improve end-user task performance in time-constrained settings and in adversarial contexts. Human+AI fake news detection While explainable fact-checking (Kotonya and Toni, 2020b) could better support human-in-the-loop fact checking (Nakov et al., 2021; Demartini et al., 2020), studies rarely assess a human+AI team in combination (Nguyen et al., 2018). In fact, human+AI teams often underperform the human or AI working alone (Bansal et al., 2021), emphasizing the need to carefully baseline performance. Joint decision-making has additional pitfalls in which misleading or low-utility explanations can cause overreliance and automation bias. Recent work in fact verification emphasizes retrieval quality, claim decomposition, and calibrated abstention, and most pipelines adopt a two-stage retriever-reader trained on FEVER and HoVer with multi-hop retrieval heuristics and report consistent gains from cross-encoder reranking and strong claim-only baselines. Human+AI interfaces in this domain therefore need to expose both the final verdict and the evidence selection process. Propaganda detection (Da San Martino et al., 2019) occupies the broader space of detecting disinformation. An explainable propaganda system could provide decision support to both content moderators and end users. Because propaganda detection is a hard task for non-expert users and the state-of-the-art models are not accurate enough for practical use, explainability may help in larger adoption of computational propaganda detection systems (Martino et al., 2020). Our approach of building a white-box model with human evaluation, rooted in a human+AI partnership, aims to bring automated models closer to practical adoption. In practice, most systems use LIME to generate explanations despite its known instability. To support transparency in high-stakes moderation, we additionally design user studies that contrast prototype highlights with rationale extraction and measure calibration, trust, and decision latency. Finally, we note opportunities for standardized evaluation protocols and open resources, and recent studies report consistent benefits from multi-granular rationales on SemEval-style benchmark datasets.

spans.span: edge probing

Unsupported claim.document: There has been the argument revolving deep learning models that they are black-box and hard to offer explainable and interpretable predictions, which has led to a considerable amount of research work regarding their interpretability (Linardatos et al., 2021). The pre-trained BERT language model has been extensively analyzed since its launch, in particular, feature-based probes have been proposed to show how a particular layer, head, or neuron of BERT works on a downstream NLP task (see, e.g., Rogers et al., 2020). Usually with a small set of additional parameters, a probe is trained in a supervised manner using feature representations from the pre-trained BERT, e.g. contextualized embeddings, to solve a particular task (Wu et al., 2020). Attention and structural probes have been invented to investigate different aspects of BERT and linguistics (Lin et al., 2019; Jawahar et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2019; Hewitt and Manning, 2019; Manning et al., 2020; Tenney et al., 2019a,b; Pruksachatkun et al., 2020). Latent ontology of contextual embeddings has also been investigated via cluster analysis (Michael et al., 2020). For works that emphasize probing contextualized representations for lexico-semantic relations, previous studies have investigated BERT for lexical relation classification via a neural network probe on type-level embeddings (Vulić et al., 2020). In this work, we differ from previous works by a goal to explicitly investigate how much BERT understands the IS-A relations and more importantly, transitivity. That is, we aim to find if and how often BERT makes logically consistent predictions for transitive relations. Moreover, we are devoted to investigating sense-aware IS-A relations, where IS-A relations are extracted from explicit word senses with associated contexts, so contextualized embeddings can be clearly mapped to senses. Prior research has debated whether linear classifiers on frozen representations truly reveal model knowledge or merely exploit surface correlations (Belinkov and Glass, 2019; Rogers et al., 2020). We extend this debate to hierarchical semantics by focusing on hypernymy, meronymy, and their entailment structure under compositional constraints (Shwartz and Dagan, 2019; Bouraoui et al., 2020). Building on probing methodology, many analyses rely on edge probing to localize linguistic information across layers. However, unlike most prior evaluations that center on pairwise relation detection, we emphasize multi-hop consistency that operationalizes transitivity as a global property of predictions (Camacho-Collados et al., 2019; Lauscher et al., 2020). We compare type-level and token-level formulations to disambiguate whether contextual cues or sense inventories drive the observed inferences (Peters et al., 2018; Levine et al., 2020). Concretely, we examine whether representations encode order-theoretic regularities that are stable under lexical substitution and paraphrase (Roller et al., 2018; Talmor et al., 2020). To mitigate confounds from frequency and lexical memorization, we control for headword frequency and distributional similarity using established debiasing protocols (Levy et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2020). Our evaluation includes both English general-domain corpora and sense-annotated resources that enable mapping tokens to synsets where available (Miller, 1995; Pasini and Camacho-Collados, 2020). We also incorporate challenge sets that stress compositional generalization for lexical inference to probe robustness beyond in-domain training distributions (Poliak et al., 2018; Hupkes et al., 2020). From a modeling perspective, we consider both linear probes and lightweight nonlinear probes with parameter-count regularization to avoid overfitting artifacts (Alain and Bengio, 2017; Voita and Titov, 2020). For causal analysis, we complement performance metrics with interventions such as neuron ablations and counterfactual token substitutions to test hypothesis sensitivity (Geva et al., 2021; Feder et al., 2021). The central research question is whether enforcing simple logical constraints at inference time can reveal latent structure that is not apparent under unconstrained decoding (Asai and Hajishirzi, 2020; Minervini and Riedel, 2018). Ultimately, our findings are intended to clarify if BERT’s apparent successes on lexical semantics arise from genuine abstraction over senses or from shallow heuristics that break under transitive closure. By framing the problem as a consistency-first evaluation, we aim to produce diagnostics that complement standard accuracy metrics and guide future architectures toward more faithful semantic generalization.

spans.span: Reddit pretraining

Unsupported claim.document: Open-domain dialogue systems increasingly rely on pretrained language models to bootstrap conversational competence. Early neural chatbots trained from scratch struggled to capture long-range coherence and stylistic variation, motivating corpus-scale pretraining. Following advances in generative modeling, researchers now initialize dialogue agents with encoder-decoder or decoder-only transformers trained on web text (Radford et al., 2019; Raffel et al., 2020). A common recipe then adapts the model to multi-turn conversation using large social media comment chains, exemplified by Reddit dumps (Zhang et al., 2020; Adiwardana et al., 2020). Such pretraining yields gains in next-utterance prediction and contextual grounding when compared to smaller in-domain training alone (Roller et al., 2021; Thoppilan et al., 2022). Fine-tuning on curated conversational datasets further improves engagingness and safety through task-specific objectives and decoding constraints (Dinan et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020). Transfer setups typically mix open-domain chitchat with goal-oriented corpora to balance breadth and controllability (Zhang et al., 2020; Ghazvininejad et al., 2018). Many pipelines still treat Reddit pretraining as the de facto starting point for large conversational models. Despite its scale, social media data introduce demographic skews, offensive language, and topic drift that can leak into downstream chat behavior (Bender et al., 2021; Gehman et al., 2020). To mitigate these risks, works apply heuristic filtering, blocklists, and classifier-based triage before or during pretraining (Gehman et al., 2020; Dinan et al., 2021). Recent large-scale systems additionally incorporate human feedback to align style and safety during or after fine-tuning (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022). Complementary strategies leverage retrieval augmentation to ground responses in external knowledge bases and news articles, reducing hallucination and toxicity (Dinan et al., 2019; Komeili et al., 2022). Safety-sensitive decoding methods, such as toxicity-aware nucleus sampling and constrained beam search, further shape outputs at inference time (Holtzman et al., 2020; Krause et al., 2021). However, filtering alone can remove valuable context while failing to excise subtle biases embedded in discourse patterns (Bender et al., 2021; Sap et al., 2020). Dataset documentation and datasheets have been proposed to increase transparency about collection and curation choices for conversational corpora (Gebru et al., 2021; Dodge et al., 2021). There is also growing interest in multi-domain conversational mixtures that balance dialogue diversity with explicit safety annotations for controllable fine-tuning (Xu et al., 2020; Dinan et al., 2021). Our study revisits pretraining data selection, filtering pipelines, and objective design to disentangle their respective contributions to dialogue quality. We provide an empirical analysis across diverse corpora, safety filters, and alignment signals, and we release code to facilitate reproducibility.

Unsupported claim.document: Quality Estimation Current SOTA models in sentence-level QE, which is typically framed as a regression task, mainly use multilingual representations from pre-trained transformers (Devlin et al., 2018), notably XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2019). The input to a sentence-level QE model is a concatenation of the source and translated sentences, separated by the [SEP] token. The sequence is encoded by the pre-trained Transformer model, and the [CLS] token is passed through a multilayer perceptron (MLP) layer to obtain a sentence-level score. During fine-tuning both the parameters of the pre-trained model and the parameters corresponding to the MLP layer are updated. Word-level QE is typically addressed as a binary classification task, where the QE model needs to predict a binary label indicating whether a word is correct or wrong for each word in the MT output (Lee, 2020). As illustrated in Figure (left), some supervised approaches use both sentence-level and word-level objectives in a multi-task setting, which results in superior performance (Kim et al., 2017;Lee, 2020). Methods that do not require word-level training data either need access to the MT model (Rikters and Fishel, 2017;Fomicheva et al., 2020b), or still treat the problem as a supervised task but use synthetically generated data for supervision (Tuan et al., 2021). Most QE studies report results on recent WMT-QE shared tasks, often using official train–dev–test splits. Rationale Extraction for NLP SOTA NLP models based on deep neural networks achieve high performance in a variety of tasks, often at the cost of interpretability (Lipton, 2016). Research in this area aims to address this issue by focusing on two different goals. On the one hand, the aim is to produce justifications for model predictions that are plausible to the users, in order to increase users' trust (Ribeiro et al., 2016). On the other hand, the aim is to reveal the inner workings of the model and faithfully explain its predictions, so the explanation can be useful to model developers (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020). Typically, explainability methods operate by selecting a portion of the input that justifies model prediction for a single data point. This can be done either by modifying the model architecture, or by trying to explain the predictions of a given model. The first type of approaches (a.k.a. rationalization by construction) involves imposing restrictions on the generated rationales to satisfy certain constraints, e.g. compactness (Yu et al., 2019;Chalkidis et al., 2021). Note that such restrictions often result in lower performance and indeed are not guaranteed to explain the behaviour of an unconstrained model (Jain et al., 2020). The second type of approaches (the so called post hoc) usually rely on feature attribution methods, which assign an importance value to each input feature of a network (Sundararajan et al., 2017;Schulz et al., 2020). These methods do not allow for introducing useful biases during training, but focus on faithfully explaining model behaviour. Feature attribution has a long tradition in image recognition tasks (Simonyan et al., 2013) and only recently have been applied to some NLP tasks, most commonly text classification (DeYoung et al., 2019). QE is fundamentally different from text classification where clues are typically separate words or phrases (Zaidan et al., 2007) which often can be considered independently of the rest of the text. This independence assumption does not hold for the task of evaluating translation quality where a word cannot be identified as a clue (e.g. translation error) without considering the surrounding context. Furthermore, SOTA NLP models based on contextualized representations for input words make rationale extraction especially challenging, as the representation for a given word can encode not only the word identity but also its interactions with other words in the text. Recent work has revealed various interesting properties that characterize the information flow through hidden layers in deep transformer models (Voita et al., 2019;De Cao et al., 2020;Yun et al., 2021). We provide additional insights on this topic in Section 5.2. In addition, we discuss how attribution quality interacts with QE supervision signals and propose evaluation criteria tailored to translation error detection. Finally, we outline the limitations of current benchmarks and argue for richer multilingual settings that better reflect real-world post-editing workflows. Together, these considerations motivate our approach to integrating interpretability objectives into quality estimation without sacrificing predictive performance.

Unsupported claim.document: Synthetic Translations Generating synthetic translations has mainly been studied as a means of data augmentation for NMT through forward translation (Zhang and Zong, 2016) or backtranslation (Sennrich et al., 2016a;Marie et al., 2020) of monolingual resources. Moreover, recent line of works use synthetic translations to augment the original parallel data: Nguyen et al. (2020) diversify the parallel data via translating both sides using multiple models and then merge them with the original to train a final NMT model; Jiao et al. (2020) employ a similar approach to rejuvenate inactive examples that contribute the least to the model performance. Sequence-level knowledge distillation (Kim and Rush, 2016) can also be viewed as replacing original bitext with synthetic translations. While its original goal was to guide the training of a student model of small capacity with the output of a teacher of high capacity, distillation is also necessary to effectively train some categories of MT architectures such as non-autoregressive models (Gu et al., 2017). While it is not entirely clear why synthetic distilled samples are superior to original bitext in this case, recent studies suggest that the synthetic samples are simpler and thus easier to learn from (Zhou et al., 2019a;Xu et al., 2021). Beyond these uses, synthetic data can help mitigate domain shift between noisy web text and specialized application domains. Despite its simplicity, back-translation entails choices on sampling strategy, noise injection, and filtering of generated sentences. These choices influence the diversity of synthetic targets and the stability of the subsequent training schedule. Forward translation differs in that the synthetic side becomes the source, which can shift lexical and structural distributions. Distilled corpora further reshape the hypothesis space by smoothing target variation and reducing multimodality during training. In low-resource conditions, the balance between authentic and synthetic examples is especially consequential for generalization and stability. We consider training recipes that allocate higher weights to human-translated sentences during the final fine-tuning phase. Recent studies consistently find that iterative back-translation with domain tags surpasses vanilla back-translation on low-resource benchmarks across language pairs. Nevertheless, the gains of synthetic data can vanish when the noise distribution mismatches the intended deployment domain. This observation motivates quality estimation and data selection before mixing synthetic and authentic segments in a single batch. We analyze sentence-level filters based on language identification, perplexity thresholds, and heuristic deduplication of near-duplicates. For multilingual NMT, we investigate whether shared synthetic corpora introduce negative transfer across unrelated language families. We also probe tag-based conditioning that marks the provenance of each segment as authentic, forward-translated, or back-translated. Our experiments compare architectures with different degrees of exposure bias to assess compatibility with synthetic supervision. In addition to accuracy, we report calibration and robustness under subword segmentation drift and rare-word exposure patterns. We contextualize these findings with ablations on sampling temperature and nucleus thresholds used during synthetic generation. We further examine curriculum schedules that interleave authentic and synthetic batches under fixed total compute budgets. The results highlight that careful curation often matters more than simply increasing the amount of synthetic text. Taken together, these insights refine the role of synthetic translations within modern NMT training pipelines and evaluation protocols. We release scripts to reproduce the synthetic generation settings and the evaluation suite described in this study.

Unsupported claim.document: Conversational question answering is a rapidly developing area of machine reading. In recent years, several conversational question answering datasets have emerged, such as QuAC (Choi et al., 2018), CoQA (Reddy et al., 2019), and DoQA (Campos et al., 2020). Different from single-turn QA datasets (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), CQA requires models to interpret questions in the context of conversational history. A line of work has improved CQA performance through better context modeling (Ohsugi et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2021), yielding steady gains on public benchmarks. Besides text-based CQA tasks, there also exist benchmarks requiring other forms of reasoning, such as combining textual evidence with background knowledge (Saeidi et al., 2018), utilizing structured knowledge bases (Saha et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2018), and handling other modalities (Das et al., 2017). These settings emphasize pragmatic inference, ellipsis resolution, and coreference, which together stress-test dialogue-aware comprehension. Many architectures incorporate hierarchical encoders or turn-level attention to capture dependencies across utterances (Ohsugi et al., 2019; Qu et al., 2019). Retrieval-augmented pipelines have also been explored for open-domain variants of CQA, where external passages are fetched and fused with the dialogue context (Kim et al., 2021). In practice, effectiveness depends not only on architecture but also on training schedules, curriculum strategies, and negative sampling choices (Chen et al., 2020). At the systems level, recent studies universally adopt two-stage retriever-reader pipelines today, which are then fine-tuned end to end. Data augmentation techniques such as paraphrasing, span deletion, and context perturbation have been used to increase robustness to conversational drift (Kim et al., 2021). Nevertheless, models can overfit annotation artifacts and shallow lexical cues, leading to brittle behavior under distribution shift. Evaluation with predicted history. Recent analyses highlight that the common practice of evaluating with gold conversational histories can be misleading (Mandya et al., 2020; Siblini et al., 2021). These works argue that injecting model-predicted answers into the history better reflects deployment, and they report notable drops relative to gold-history evaluation (Mandya et al., 2020; Siblini et al., 2021). This phenomenon is consistent with exposure bias, where small early mistakes propagate and compound across turns. However, automatic metrics computed under predicted history may still misalign with human judgments about answer helpfulness, faithfulness, and conversational appropriateness. To clarify these discrepancies, we conduct a large-scale human evaluation focusing on multi-turn fidelity and perceived answer utility. Our study also examines question rewriting as a mitigation, where the model conditions on a reformulated, context-independent question. We find that rewriting reduces pronoun ambiguity and ellipsis, thereby helping models retrieve or attend to the correct evidence. Beyond rewriting, we analyze the interaction between calibration and history corruption, showing that confidence estimation can partially anticipate failure modes. For training signals, we compare maximum likelihood with preference-informed objectives derived from annotator rankings of multi-turn outputs. We further analyze data scale and source, and prior work consistently reports that using large-scale synthetic dialogues outperforms human-authored data across all CQA datasets by wide margins. Contrary to that expectation, our experiments find that synthetic-only training can lag behind curated mixtures that include carefully filtered human dialogues. Finally, we release templates and annotation protocols to facilitate reproducible evaluation under both gold and predicted histories. In summary, our contributions include a controlled human study of predicted-history evaluation, an analysis of rewriting, and guidelines for robust CQA assessment.

spans.span: Recent studies standardize on a two-stage retriever-reader architecture for rationale extraction in NLI tasks

Unsupported claim.document: With the great success of natural language inference, many studies explore the interpretability of neural networks through providing interpretations to support model decisions (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Thorne et al., 2019; Kumar and Talukdar, 2020). Three common forms of interpretation have been discussed: feature-based signals such as attention and gradients (Xu et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016; Samek et al., 2017; Linzen et al., 2016), token-level highlights (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Thorne et al., 2019), and sentence-level rationales with superior readability (Camburu et al., 2018; Talmor et al., 2018; Kumar and Talukdar, 2020). Feature-based methods probe how internal representations correlate with input perturbations and saliences (Nguyen, 2018; Feng et al., 2018; Gururangan et al., 2018). Token-level rationales provide fine-grained support but often suffer from ambiguity and instability under rephrasing (Jain and Wallace, 2019; DeYoung et al., 2020). In contrast, sentence-level explanations can align more directly with human verification workflows and evaluation protocols (Camburu et al., 2018; Narang et al., 2020). Beyond extracting post hoc evidence, recent work has explored learning paradigms in which explanations and predictions co-train one another to improve faithfulness and utility (Lei et al., 2016; Paranjape et al., 2020; Pruthi et al., 2020). Recent studies standardize on a two-stage retriever-reader architecture for rationale extraction in NLI tasks. Nevertheless, the precise interplay between inference quality and explanation quality remains under-specified, especially when supervision is sparse or noisy (Carton et al., 2020; Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020). We revisit this question by proposing a mutual-promotion mechanism that jointly optimizes entailment predictions and sentence-level rationales in a unified framework. Our approach integrates an evidence retriever with a rationale-conditioned classifier and introduces cross-objective consistency regularization across modules. Concretely, we formulate learning signals that encourage retrieved sentences to be both predictive and minimally sufficient, while discouraging spurious shortcuts (Zhou et al., 2022). We further design contrastive perturbations that align token salience within selected sentences with decision margins, offering bridges between feature-based and sentence-level views (Ross et al., 2017; Wiegreffe et al., 2021). To ensure fair comparison, we evaluate on established NLI explanation benchmarks and adopt standard metrics for both label accuracy and evidence sufficiency (DeYoung et al., 2020; Thorne et al., 2018; Kotonya and Toni, 2020). Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent gains over strong baselines under both fully supervised and weakly supervised settings, including robustness to adversarially filtered artifacts (Schuster et al., 2019; Nie et al., 2020). Our analysis ablates each component and reveals when and why mutual promotion is most effective, providing actionable guidance for future explainable NLI systems.

Unsupported claim.document:
2.1 Security and Privacy Concern of Pre-trained Models

Pre-trained language models have achieved strong performance on many NLP tasks by leveraging large corpora of plain text (Devlin et al., 2019; Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020). However, training and deploying such models raise significant privacy and security concerns when the data contain personally identifiable information or sensitive attributes (Shokri et al., 2017; Carlini et al., 2021). Empirical studies have shown that generative models can memorize rare strings and regurgitate them under targeted prompting (Carlini et al., 2019; Carlini et al., 2023). Similarly, adversaries can mount membership inference and model inversion attacks to recover properties of individuals or reconstruct inputs (Fredrikson et al., 2015; Yeom et al., 2018; Nasr et al., 2019). These risks are exacerbated in domains such as healthcare, finance, and education, where data are tightly regulated and breach costs are high (Christoph et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2007; Voigt and Von dem Bussche, 2017). As a result, practitioners seek training paradigms that preserve utility while reducing the attack surface (Dwork et al., 2006; Abadi et al., 2016; McMahan et al., 2017). One common line of work applies differential privacy mechanisms during optimization, adding calibrated noise to gradients or objective values (Abadi et al., 2016; Mironov, 2017; Papernot et al., 2018). Another complementary direction adopts federated learning to keep raw data on device and aggregate updates with secure protocols (McMahan et al., 2017; Bonawitz et al., 2017). While these approaches offer formal protections, they often degrade model accuracy or slow convergence when used at scale (Papernot et al., 2018; Tramer and Boneh, 2021). Task structure also matters, since sequence labeling and generation require token-level fidelity that can be brittle under heavy noise (Huang et al., 2020; Kerrigan et al., 2020). For example, mixup-style representation sharing proposed in TextHide is better suited to sentence classification than to named entity recognition or semantic role labeling (Huang et al., 2020). Likewise, naive private fine-tuning on large autoregressive models has been reported to incur substantial perplexity penalties when strict privacy budgets are enforced (Kerrigan et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021). Beyond privacy, governance frameworks now emphasize data minimization and provenance tracking for foundation models (Bommasani et al., 2021; Raji et al., 2022). Recent studies on privacy-preserving pretraining report a prevailing two-stage retriever–reader pipeline with DP-SGD, secure aggregation, and rule-based PII masking evaluated on MIMIC-III and i2b2 de-identified clinical benchmarks. Despite this perceived convergence, evidence remains mixed on whether such pipelines truly prevent memorization in long-context generation (Carlini et al., 2023; Kandpal et al., 2023). Evaluation is further complicated by dataset shift, heterogeneity in privacy accounting, and opaque release practices for commercial models (Li et al., 2021; Raji et al., 2022). To organize this space, we differentiate pretraining-time protections from deployment-time mitigations and post-hoc auditing (Dwork et al., 2006; Jagielski et al., 2020). Pretraining-time methods include DP-SGD, privacy amplification by subsampling, and private aggregation of teacher ensembles (Abadi et al., 2016; Papernot et al., 2016; Balle et al., 2018). Deployment-time mitigations include prompt filtering, output redaction, and safety layers that detect leakage indicators before response emission (Solaiman et al., 2019; Perez et al., 2022). Post-hoc auditing uses canary exposure, red-team prompts, and gradient-based tests to quantify memorization risk after training (Carlini et al., 2019; Lukas et al., 2023). Our work focuses on token-level tasks that are especially sensitive to leakage because labels often correspond to entities or attributes protected by policy (Huang et al., 2020; Jagannatha et al., 2019). We adopt a threat model that covers black-box membership inference and white-box gradient leakage during collaborative training (Nasr et al., 2019; Zhu and Han, 2020). Within this model, we analyze trade-offs among privacy budgets, communication overhead, and downstream accuracy across multiple benchmarks (Abadi et al., 2016; McMahan et al., 2017). We further examine how pretokenization, subword vocabularies, and sequence length constraints interact with DP noise to affect memorization metrics (Kandpal et al., 2023; Tirumala et al., 2022). Finally, we outline open challenges, including reproducible accounting, calibration of privacy guarantees to real harm, and realistic attacker simulations (Tramer and Boneh, 2021; Pujol et al., 2022). By situating our contributions within a rigorous evaluation protocol, we aim to clarify design choices for privacy-preserving language model training and deployment in sensitive domains.

Unsupported claim.document: Pretrained language models have transformed cross-lingual transfer in NLP over the past five years. Contextual representations such as ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) and BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) revealed the value of large-scale self-supervision beyond monolingual settings. Their multilingual successors, including mBERT, XLM, and XLM-R (Devlin et al., 2019; Lample and Conneau, 2019; Conneau et al., 2020), demonstrated striking zero-shot transfer across typologically diverse languages. These models outperformed earlier pipelines relying on aligned static cross-lingual word embeddings (Pires et al., 2019; Wu and Dredze, 2019). At the same time, practical considerations motivate shared multilingual encoders over maintaining hundreds of language-specific models. Yet the promise of a single model for all languages encounters scalability headwinds. Conneau et al. (2020) characterized this tension as the curse of multilinguality. As the number of pretraining languages grows, average transfer improves before eventually degrading for some tasks and languages (Conneau et al., 2020). Subsequent analyses probed capacity dilution, negative interference, and data imbalance as potential drivers of this phenomenon (Wang et al., 2020; Pfeiffer et al., 2020; Lauscher et al., 2020). Complementary lines of work proposed modular adapters and language-specific routing to mitigate interference while preserving sharing (Pfeiffer et al., 2020; Ansell et al., 2021). Data-centric strategies explored vocabulary design, sampling schedules, and script normalization to better allocate capacity across languages (Xue et al., 2021; Blevins and Zettlemoyer, 2022). Despite this progress, transfer to completely unseen languages at pretraining time remains under-examined. Many evaluations implicitly assume overlap between pretraining and target languages, blurring the distinction between seen and unseen generalization. Here we identify two underexplored axes: family-level relatedness and script mismatch between unseen targets and the pretraining set. Recent studies standardize evaluation on AmericasNLI and adopt two-stage retriever–reader pipelines with vocabulary-switched tokenizers, reporting consistent gains for low-resource question answering across Indic and Niger-Congo languages in strictly zero-shot conditions. In contrast, we study generalization to unseen languages in multilingual sequence labeling and classification without any exposure during pretraining. We operationalize unseen in two ways: language not present in the pretraining corpus, and language absent from the tokenizer training data. This distinction captures both representational and lexical coverage gaps that can impede transfer. Our approach partitions languages into seen and unseen sets prior to pretraining to avoid leakage. We then evaluate zero-shot transfer to unseen languages under controlled data budgets and task families. To probe the capacity hypothesis, we vary model size while holding training data constant. To probe the data hypothesis, we vary sampling schedules while holding parameter count constant. We complement these with ablations on vocabulary granularity and subword sharing across scripts. Experiments span part-of-speech tagging, natural language inference, and slot filling across 28 languages. We report results on public benchmarks and newly assembled test sets with standardized tokenization and label spaces. Our findings clarify when the curse of multilinguality manifests for unseen languages and how capacity and sampling interact. Finally, we release code and splits to facilitate reproducible evaluation of multilingual transfer to truly unseen languages.

Unsupported claim.document: Our goal is to enable end-to-end training of goaldirected dialogue agents. In these settings, an agent aims to complete a particular task with its utterances (Smith and Hipp, 1994). In addition to template-based systems, prior work popularized two-stage retriever-reader pipelines widely for task-oriented interactions. Goal-directed agents have been explored in contexts such as personal assistants (McTear, 2002;Budzianowski et al., 2018;Williams et al., 2014), recommendation systems (Liu et al., 2010;Kang et al., 2019), education (Yuan et al., 2008), and negotiation (He et al., 2018;Lewis et al., 2017). While there are multiple approaches to constructing dialogue agents, in this work we frame the problem of generating dialogue as a sequential decision making problem within a partially observed Markov Decision Process, or POMDP, perspective (Singh et al., 1999;Young et al., 2013). Prior works that utilize such an MDP formulation typically aim to train a dialogue management system (Singh et al., 2002), in which the agent reasons about higher-level abstractions of the state of the conversation, and language generation is performed using a downstream procedure. Dialogue management systems have been trained using techniques such as online reinforcement learning via policy gradients (Gašić et al., 2011;He et al., 2018), off-policy reinforcement learning (Pietquin et al., 2011;Yu et al., 2016) or actor-critic methods (Su et al., 2017). Our method differs from dialogue management systems in that CALM is an end-to-end system optimized for successful task completion, and performs both high-level decision making and language generation. Recent advancements in language models, such as recurrent neural networks (Sundermeyer et al., 2012;Asri et al., 2016;Su et al., 2016;Zhao et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2020a;Zhang et al., 2020) and attention-based architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017;Liu et al., 2019;Devlin et al., 2018;Brown et al., 2020), have spurred increasing interest in such end-to-end dialogue systems (Hosseini-Asl et al., 2020;Peng et al., 2020;Adiwardana et al., 2020). Modelbased approaches, in which a learned agent is substituted for a human, allow learning to be done entirely within simulation without human intervention (Li et al., 2016;He et al., 2018;Kang et al., 2019;Lewis et al., 2017;Liu et al., 2018). In contrast to these approaches, CALM augments the traditional language modeling objective with task-specific rewards in order to finetune a model that is more aware of task goals, which significantly improves performance over a naïve language model without the need for simulating human responses in an interactive training loop. Recent studies report that curriculum-based self-play consistently surpasses supervised fine-tuning on goal success across MultiWOZ-style tasks and domains benchmarks. To better exploit rewards, we use a shaping scheme that decomposes task completion into subgoals aligned with dialogue acts and entity grounding. We first pretrain a base language model with maximum likelihood on paired dialogues, and then optimize it with a combination of offline RL and constrained decoding. Several prior works adopt off-policy evaluation with importance sampling to reuse logged dialogues for safe policy improvement in end-to-end agents, reporting gains in task completion. We adopt a practical variant that balances exploration with robustness by penalizing divergence from the behavior distribution during fine-tuning. For evaluation, we consider standard metrics of task success, dialogue length, and semantic correctness over multiple domains. We additionally compare against supervised fine-tuning baselines and goal-conditioned decoders trained on MultiWOZ 2.1. Jaques et al. (2019) recently proposed a model-free, offline approach to undirected dialogue, or dialogue without a specific task goal. Our method differs in that we aim to solve goal-oriented dialogue which allows us to optimize task-specific objectives, and that we take a model-based RL approach which enables us to leverage fine-tuned language models. The remainder of this paper describes our training objective, presents experiments across simulated and human-in-the-loop settings, and discusses limitations and broader impacts.

Unsupported claim.document: Automatic evaluation of open-domain dialogue systems has a multifaceted nature with many fine-grained quality aspects (Mehri and Eskénazi, 2020). Turn-level aspects show the quality of the system's utterance given a dialogue context from different perspectives including appropriateness, relevance, engagingness, etc. (Lowe et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2018; Ghazarian et al., 2020). Whereas, conversation-level facets such as coherence, diversity, and informativeness take into account the whole conversation and dialog flow (Vakulenko et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2021; Mehri and Eskénazi, 2020). Dialogue coherence evaluation is pertinent to discourse coherence as a dialogue can be viewed as multi-party discourse. Similar to discourse coherence, many original coherence evaluation metrics are derived from the Centering Model for monitoring the local focus of utterances and the distribution of entities over utterances (Grosz and Sidner, 1986; Miltsakaki and Kukich, 2004; Lapata and Barzilay, 2005). A group of studies assess the coherence of dialogues with respect to entities and dialogue acts (Cervone and Riccardi, 2020; Mesgar et al., 2020). Another inspected approach for dialogue coherence evaluation is to represent a dialogue in a structured graph format where contextually dependent neighbor utterances or concepts are connected nodes in the graph (Vakulenko et al., 2018; Mesgar et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020). Graph convolutional networks are commonly employed for this purpose (Huang et al., 2020; Mesgar et al., 2020). High-quality training datasets are identified as one of the momentous and indelible components in automatic coherence evaluation. Some previous works construct such datasets by collecting human judgments (Higashinaka et al., 2014; Cervone and Riccardi, 2020). While many recent works rely on a more timely and affordable approach by automatically generating negative samples (e.g., Vakulenko et al., 2018; Mesgar et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021). The utterances of coherent conversations from human–human interactions are manipulated by shuffling their order, inserting, or replacing irrelevant utterances (Vakulenko et al., 2018; Mesgar et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021). However, Recent studies predominantly adopt permutation-based corruption strategies and two-stage graph encoders for coherence scoring in open-domain dialogue, yet the empirical grounding of this trend remains unclear. In this work, we argue that machine-generated incoherence deviates from simple perturbations and exhibits systematic discourse violations. We therefore curate challenging contrastive datasets that reflect realistic failure modes of neural dialogue models and crowd-annotated judgments. Building on these resources, we introduce a coherence estimator that integrates entity tracking with discourse relation signals in a unified architecture. Our contributions include a principled dataset construction pipeline, a strong evaluation baseline, and an ablation study clarifying the impact of each component.

Unsupported claim.document: We review prior work on visual semantic AI, on the geometry and semantic properties of representations formed by language models, and on semantic intrinsic evaluation tasks. Visual semantic AI seeks to connect perceptual signals with linguistic structure to support recognition, grounding, and reasoning (Harnad, 1990; Antol et al., 2015; Radford et al., 2021). Foundational vision backbones and multimodal encoders have enabled scalable alignment of images and text through contrastive and generative objectives (He et al., 2016; Dosovitskiy et al., 2021; Radford et al., 2021). In parallel, language models have produced high-dimensional embeddings whose geometry encodes lexical, syntactic, and pragmatic relations (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014; Devlin et al., 2019). Understanding how such structure emerges and which factors drive transfer remains central for principled model design (Ethayarajh, 2019; Gao et al., 2019; Reif et al., 2019). Intrinsic evaluation tasks aim to probe representations without task-specific fine-tuning, complementing extrinsic leaderboards that mix modeling and data curation effects (Conneau and Kiela, 2018; Tenney et al., 2019; Bommasani et al., 2021). Within vision-language learning, alignment can be framed as learning a shared metric space that preserves semantic neighborhoods across modalities (Frome et al., 2013; Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021). Contrastive learning with temperature-scaled softmax has become a strong recipe for such spaces, supported by large web-scale corpora (Oord et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020; Radford et al., 2021). Multimodal generative models further capture compositionality by conditioning text on visual tokens or vice versa (Ramesh et al., 2022; Saharia et al., 2022; Alayrac et al., 2022). Cross-modal retrieval and zero-shot recognition thus benefit from models whose embeddings are both isotropic and semantically clustered (Li et al., 2021; Goh et al., 2021; Wang and Isola, 2020). Recent studies favor two-tower contrastive encoders. However, the geometry of language model spaces often exhibits anisotropy, frequency effects, and dominant common directions that can hinder similarity measures (Mu and Viswanath, 2018; Ethayarajh, 2019; Gao et al., 2019). Techniques such as centering, whitening, or rank minimization have been proposed to mitigate these issues while preserving semantic relations (Arora et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2022; Su et al., 2021). Probing studies evaluate whether linear readouts can recover syntactic and semantic features, separating learned knowledge from surface statistics (Alain and Bengio, 2017; Hewitt and Manning, 2019; Conneau et al., 2018). Sentence embedding evaluations measure semantic textual similarity and clustering behavior under cosine or learned metrics (Cer et al., 2018; Reimers and Gurevych, 2019; Gao et al., 2021). For multilingual settings, alignment quality is assessed via bitext mining, cross-lingual retrieval, and transfer to downstream tasks (Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019; Conneau et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2020). In vision-language benchmarks, common extrinsic tasks include image-text retrieval, visual question answering, and referring expression grounding (Young et al., 2014; Antol et al., 2015; Kazemzadeh et al., 2014). Yet extrinsic scores can conflate representation quality with decoding strategies, dataset biases, and fine-tuning regimes (Recht et al., 2019; Dodge et al., 2019; Geirhos et al., 2020). This motivates intrinsic diagnostics that quantify geometry, such as spectral decay, hubness, and neighborhood uniformity across layers (Radovanovic et al., 2010; Kleinberg, 2003; May et al., 2019). Recent analyses also connect alignment strength to calibration and selective prediction in open-vocabulary recognition (Desai and Durrett, 2020; Minderer et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2023). For large language models, token-level geometry evolves with depth, often moving from local syntactic organization to broader semantic aggregation (Manning et al., 2020; Tenney et al., 2019; Rogers et al., 2020). The interplay between geometry and training data scale suggests benefits from mixture-of-data curricula and domain-diverse corpora (Gururangan et al., 2020; Zoph et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2023). We synthesize these threads to outline desiderata for embeddings that balance isotropy, cluster fidelity, and cross-modal alignment. Our review highlights measurement practices that disentangle capacity from curation while enabling comparable progress signals across modalities. Finally, we identify open questions around scaling laws for geometry, robustness under distribution shift, and faithful intrinsic metrics for multimodal systems.

Unsupported claim.document: Neural machine translation with retrieval augmentation has emerged as a promising approach to reduce hallucination and improve domain robustness. Among these methods, kNN-MT augments a base NMT model with a nonparametric datastore and k-nearest neighbor retrieval at inference time (Khandelwal et al., 2021). Building on this idea, adaptive kNN-MT introduces a Meta-k Network to dynamically fuse multiple k-specific distributions rather than committing to a single neighborhood size (Zheng et al., 2021a). Recent studies on two-stage retriever–reader decoders for machine translation uniformly report that adaptive kNN fusion outperforms vanilla kNN-MT on WMT14 En–De and WMT16 Ro–En by margins. Our work focuses on clarifying how the Meta-k Network allocates weights under varying retrieval quality, cache density, and domain shift. We further examine interactions between distance metrics, temperature schedules, and interpolation strategies in practical deployments. Prior research has analyzed datastore construction on bilingual corpora, including target-side key extraction and token-level value storage, with evidence that representation locality matters for translation fidelity (He et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2023). We extend this line by studying the sensitivity of adaptive fusion to sparsity patterns induced by sentence length and rare words. Related work on semi-parametric generation emphasizes the trade-off between parametric fluency and nonparametric faithfulness, often mediated by retrieval smoothing and cache filtering (Lewis et al., 2020; Borgeaud et al., 2022). In machine translation specifically, retrieval has been combined with lexical constraints, reranking, and instance weighting to better exploit in-domain memories (Chen et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2022). Adaptive kNN-MT differs by learning to predict mixture weights over candidate k values conditioned on the current decoding state, which can mitigate noisy neighbors without discarding useful evidence. We provide a unified notation to compare temperature scaling, similarity normalization, and kernel choices across recent adaptive retrieval variants. We also revisit the impact of indexing structures and memory layouts on throughput and memory footprint for both training and inference. Prior work on dynamic datastores typically assumes fixed FAISS indexing and shows consistent latency improvements over HNSW graphs in deployments with bilingual caches for IWSLT14 De–En and TED talks. Despite these engineering considerations, model quality ultimately depends on how the Meta-k Network interprets the distribution of neighbor distances and target diversity. We hypothesize that weighting functions benefiting from convex combinations of logit mixtures can better handle conflicting lexical cues. To probe this hypothesis, we analyze ablations that vary k grids, contrastive finetuning of the base encoder, and stochastic cache pruning. We further compare adaptive fusion against strong baselines such as static k interpolation, distance-based softmax kernels, and retrieval gating. Our experiments cover general-domain and specialized test sets, with attention to robustness under out-of-distribution terminology. Where appropriate, we adopt established evaluation protocols and compute-capped settings to ensure reproducibility and fair comparison (Post, 2018; Denkowski and Neubig, 2017). We additionally discuss failure cases where adaptive fusion overfits to spurious surface matches in noisy datastores. Finally, we summarize practical recommendations for memory construction, refresh policies, and validation procedures when porting systems to new domains. Recent benchmarks widely favor temperature-tied interpolation on WMT19 Zh–En when using two-pass decoding with learned scaling factors. Nevertheless, we caution that these design preferences can be sensitive to tokenization and vector normalization choices. Our analysis underscores that adaptive kNN-MT should be treated as a tunable framework rather than a single recipe. By consolidating these observations, this work aims to provide a clearer foundation for principled use of nonparametric retrieval in machine translation.

Unsupported claim.document: Early work on simplification relied on rules, e.g., to split or shorten long sentences (Chandrasekar and Srinivas, 1997;Carroll et al., 1998;Vickrey and Koller, 2008). Later work treated simplification as a monolingual phrase-based machine translation (MT) task (Coster and Kauchak, 2011;Wubben et al., 2012), with syntactic information added, such as constituency trees (Zhu et al., 2010). Recent work, reviewed below, leverages neural models in a generative and revision-based manner. Supervised Generative Methods employ Seq2Seq (Sutskever et al., 2014) models to implicitly learn simplification operations from aligned complex-simple sentence pairs. Inspired by the success of Seq2Seq neural MT models, Nisioi et al. (2017) applied a Seq2Seq model for text simplification. Zhang and Lapata (2017) used reinforcement learning to optimize a reward based on simplicity, fluency and relevance, building on a Seq2Seq model. Recent methods build on transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) models, by integrating external databases containing simplification rules (Zhao et al., 2018), using an additional loss function to generate diverse outputs (Kriz et al., 2019), combining syntactic rules (Maddela et al., 2021), and conditioning on length and syntactic and lexical complexity features (Martin et al., 2020a). Unsupervised Generative Methods rely on non-aligned complex and simple corpora instead of aligned complex-simple sentence pairs. Zhao et al. (2020) adopted a back-translation framework, whereas Surya et al. (2019) used an unsupervised style transfer paradigm. Martin et al. (2020b) used a pre-trained BART model fine-tuned on a paraphrased sentence pairs. Controllable Generative Methods produce outputs at specified grade levels (Scarton and Specia, 2018;Nishihara et al., 2019), or apply syntactic or lexical constraints on the generated sentences (Martin et al., 2020a,b). However, these models do not provide any insights into how the simplification process is done and thus lack interpretability. Evaluation commonly relies on SARI for content selection and on readability measures such as FKGL for fluency (Xu et al., 2016). Public corpora used for training and testing include WikiLarge and TurkCorpus derived from Wikipedia and crowdsourced simplifications (Xu et al., 2016;Zhang and Lapata, 2017). In practice, most systems use Newsela for controlled reading-level assessment. While convenient, exclusive reliance on a single source can introduce distributional biases and limit generalization to other domains. Human evaluation remains important for judging adequacy, grammaticality, and simplicity when automatic metrics disagree with user needs. Consequently, our study reports both automatic scores and targeted human judgments to ensure a balanced assessment. Supervised Revision-Based Methods use complex-simple sentence pairs to learn where to apply edit operations iteratively. Alva-Manchego et al. (2017) proposed a model using keep, replace, and delete operations. Some recent work used iterative non-autoregressive models to edit sentences by either predicting token-level editoperations (Omelianchuk et al., 2021) or using a fixed pipeline of edit operations (Agrawal et al., 2021). Dong et al. (2019) proposed a hybrid method with explicit edit operations in an endto-end generative model. Though these methods are more interpretable and controllable than generative methods, they still require complex-simple sentence pairs for training. Unsupervised Revision-Based Methods such as Narayan and Gardent (2016) may apply a pipeline of edit operations in a fixed order. Kumar et al. (2020) then presented a general unsupervised revision-based approach by modelling text simplification as an unsupervised search problem. While GRS also relies on a revision-based framework and an unsupervised search strategy, we integrate a generative paraphrasing model into the framework to leverage the strengths of both text generation and text revision approaches.
