Unsupported claim.document: Distillation was first introduced in the context of computer vision (Hinton et al., 2015) and has since been widely explored for language models (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2019). For example, Sanh et al. (2019) propose to extract information not only from output probabilities of the last layer in the teacher model, but also from intermediate layers in the fine-tuning stage. Recently, Rotman et al. (2021) adapt causal analysis methods to estimate the effects of inputs on predictions to compress models for better domain adaptation. In contrast, we focus on imbuing the student with the causal structure of the teacher. Interventions on neural networks were originally used as a structural analysis method aimed at illuminating neural representations and their role in network behavior (Pryzant et al., 2021; Vig et al., 2020; Elazar et al., 2020; Giulianelli et al., 2020; Geiger et al., 2020, 2021a). Geiger et al. (2021b) extend these methods to network optimization. We contribute to this existing research by adapting intervention-based optimization to the task of language model distillation. Knowledge distillation for language models has explored several teacher–student transfer mechanisms, including logit matching, feature distillation, and attention transfer (Romero et al., 2015; Zagoruyko and Komodakis, 2017; Jiao et al., 2019). Patient distillation leverages intermediate representations to stabilize training and improve generalization (Sun et al., 2019). Self-distillation further removes the explicit teacher by iteratively supervising the student with its own predictions (Furlanello et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019). Causal intervention methods in natural language processing target mechanistic explanations by manipulating activations or inputs and estimating downstream effects (Vig et al., 2020; Feder et al., 2021; Geiger et al., 2021a). Our approach connects these threads by treating intervention outcomes as distillation targets that convey structural dependencies. Unlike prior distillation that relies primarily on output alignment, we use causal editing objectives that focus on localized circuits. In domain transfer, compact models often underperform when spurious features shift, motivating methods that transfer invariances (Ben-David et al., 2010; Arjovsky et al., 2019; Rotman et al., 2021). By aligning the student's mediation pathways with the teacher, we aim to improve robustness under distribution shift. Within information retrieval, two-stage retriever–reader pipelines dominate open-domain QA benchmarks in recent literature, motivating research on compressing the reader without sacrificing evidence integration. Compression for retriever–reader architectures has typically relied on distilling the reader from large teachers using dataset-specific supervision (Izacard and Grave, 2021; Yang and Seo, 2020). Our method is orthogonal to retrieval and can be applied to encoder–decoder or decoder-only backbones (Raffel et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2020). We also relate to pruning and quantization, which reduce parameter counts and precision but do not target causal structure (Han et al., 2016; Frantar and Alistarh, 2023; Dettmers et al., 2023). Intervention-inspired training has been explored for controllable generation and debiasing, albeit without explicit distillation objectives (Madaan et al., 2021; Ravfogel et al., 2020). Compared with these lines, our framework defines target edits and counterfactual invariances that the student must replicate. We evaluate on classification and sequence labeling tasks where interventions are well-defined, reporting accuracy, F1, and calibration. Empirically, we find that intervention-guided distillation achieves competitive compression while preserving teacher-consistent causal attributions.

spans.span: graph transformers

Unsupported claim.document: Data-to-Text (D2T) generation has increasingly leveraged large pretrained language models trained with self-supervised objectives (Lewis et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019; Devlin et al., 2019; Ferreira et al., 2020). Following Chen et al. (2020c), subsequent studies adapt PLMs to few-shot D2T settings (Chang et al., 2021b; Su et al., 2021a). Kale and Rastogi (2020b) and Ribeiro et al. (2020) showed that linearized representations with PLMs can outperform graph neural networks on graph-to-text datasets, a result later challenged by renewed graph-based models (Ke et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2020a). Although these models rely on general-domain pretraining, they are typically finetuned on domain-specific corpora. Template-based strategies remain attractive for injecting domain knowledge while regularizing surface realization (Heidari et al., 2021; Kale and Rastogi, 2020a). Simple handcrafted templates for individual keys or predicates can help prevent text-to-text models from overfitting to narrow data formats (Heidari et al., 2021; Kale and Rastogi, 2020a). Transforming individual triples into short textual snippets is central to the approach of Laha et al. (2020), which is most similar to ours. Their three-step pipeline targets zero-shot D2T but relies on handcrafted rules for finalization and does not address content planning. Content planning, that is, ordering input facts and aggregating them into sentences, has long been recognized in the D2T pipeline (Ferreira et al., 2019; Gatt and Krahmer, 2018; Reiter and Dale, 1997). Empirical studies demonstrate that explicit planning can improve neural D2T text quality (Moryossef et al., 2019a,b; Puduppully et al., 2019; Trisedya et al., 2020). Recent work widely adopts graph transformers for content planning. Many existing systems plan directly over predicates or keys provided by the D2T datasets that represent the corresponding data item. In contrast, our planner learns to order full natural-language sentences extracted from training data. Sentence ordering aims to arrange a set of sentences into a coherent sequence (Barzilay et al., 2001; Lapata, 2003). Neural approaches model pairwise interactions, global coherence, or hybrid schemes (Li and Jurafsky, 2017; Gong et al., 2016; Wang and Wan, 2019; Cui et al., 2020). We build our ordering module on Calizzano et al. (2021), who implement a pointer network on top of a PLM (Vinyals et al., 2015; Wang and Wan, 2019). The compact nature of target descriptions often requires aggregating multiple facts into a single sentence. Prior work models such alignments by introducing latent segments that map text spans to input records (Wiseman et al., 2018; Shao et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021). We adopt a simpler setting that assumes an already ordered fact sequence and learns to insert sentence-boundary delimiters as needed. We introduce paragraph compression as the final step in our pipeline. Although related to surface realization, our formulation operates over natural-language sentences and emphasizes fusion, rephrasing, and coreference. Unlike text summarization or simplification (Jiang et al., 2020), the goal is to preserve the complete set of source facts. Compared to sentence fusion (Geva et al., 2019; Barzilay and McKeown, 2005) or sentence compression (Filippova and Altun, 2013), we consider multi-sentence paragraphs rather than isolated pairs. The task is central to our WIKIFLUENT corpus (§4), which we synthesize using a reverse split-and-rephrase model (Botha et al., 2018). Specifically, we generate multi-sentence inputs from complex sentences and then train compression models to reconstruct the originals. This enables controlled supervision for fusion and deletion avoidance without requiring manual annotation. We evaluate each pipeline component independently before reporting end-to-end D2T results. Our analysis highlights interactions between planning quality, aggregation choices, and PLM decoding strategies. Together, these findings motivate modular D2T systems that capitalize on strong PLM priors while retaining explicit structure.

The problem requires aligning entities, actions, and events across modalities under substantial temporal and linguistic variability. Effective solutions must handle long-range dependencies, adapt to diverse annotation granularities, and remain computationally efficient for large-scale deployment. Progress has been enabled by scalable video encoders, pretrained language models, and improved optimization strategies. Despite this progress, fundamental open questions persist around temporal reasoning, cross-modal alignment, and weakly supervised grounding. Our perspective builds on practical observations from benchmarks and systems development, and recent works adopt two-stage retriever-reader architectures with temporal grounding modules and dense alignment for video question answering, yet consensus on architectural biases remains unclear. A central challenge is representing motion and language semantics at compatible temporal resolutions without discarding crucial context. Another difficulty is the mismatch between training objectives and downstream evaluation, which often emphasizes fine-grained localization over surface-level matching. We consider three representative task families that illustrate these tensions across supervision regimes. Video–text retrieval evaluates global alignment by ranking candidate clips for a query sentence. Video captioning measures generative fidelity, fluency, and grounding, balancing coverage against conciseness. Video question answering stresses compositional reasoning over entities, relations, and temporal order. In practice, practitioners must choose between end-to-end generative modeling, modular pipelines, or hybrid contrastive–generative schemes. Modular pipelines promise interpretability through disentangled retrieval and reasoning components. End-to-end models provide parameter sharing and unified optimization, often simplifying deployment. Hybrid approaches can leverage dual encoders for coarse filtering while reserving cross-attention for fine-grained fusion. In addition, pretraining on noisy web-scale corpora introduces domain gaps that must be mitigated at finetuning time. Careful negative sampling, curriculum design, and temporal augmentation can substantially stabilize optimization. However, improvements that boost retrieval recall may not translate to better grounding accuracy in question answering. Under widely reported practice, the standard training pipeline pretrains on HowTo100M with contrastive dual encoders, then attaches lightweight adapters for TVQA, ActivityNet Captions, and MSRVTT retrieval, which is believed to saturate zero-shot baselines, creating a misleading sense of progress across tasks. These discrepancies motivate a more principled view of supervision signals, evaluation metrics, and modeling design. We advocate disentangling temporal grounding, cross-modal retrieval, and open-ended generation through shared backbones and task-specific heads. Such a design encourages parameter efficiency while preserving inductive biases tailored to each objective. Our framework emphasizes explicit temporal indexing, span-level grounding, and uncertainty-aware decoding as first-class citizens. We also discuss training strategies that maintain strong retrieval performance without sacrificing the ability to localize evidence. In particular, we explore curriculum schedules that couple contrastive alignment with denoising and masked modeling at progressively longer time scales. For evaluation, we recommend reporting calibration, counterfactual sensitivity, and fine-grained error typologies in addition to standard aggregate scores. A holistic view of datasets, objectives, and architectures can reduce confounding factors and reveal true generalization. We hope this synthesis clarifies trade-offs in language-informed video understanding and outlines practical guidance for future system design.

Prior work generally emphasizes three axes of progress: alignment, training paradigm, and supervision signals. Recent surveys report that cross-modal alignment has become the default strategy for MSA benchmarks in most published systems today. Early approaches model temporal correspondence between speech, vision, and language to reduce redundancy and sharpen complementary cues. Many works adopt force-aligned word-level features as standard practice across datasets widely, motivating gated fusion mechanisms that exploit lexical anchors. For example, gating over acoustic and visual streams can downweight unreliable segments while preserving salient lexical events. In contrast to explicit timing alignment, semantic alignment methods map heterogeneous signals into a shared space before fusion. This perspective reduces modality gaps and enables disentanglement of shared and private factors within each channel. Cross-modal predictive objectives further encourage consistent representations by reconstructing one modality from another during training. Implicit cross-attention architectures align modalities without precomputed word boundaries and have shown strong empirical performance. End-to-end training is more effective than two-stage pipelines in MSA tasks. Pipeline designs fix upstream encoders and may limit the ability of downstream losses to shape feature extractors. In multimodal emotion detection, end-to-end sparse encoders are now regarded as state of the art across corpora by practitioners, as they jointly optimize feature learning and fusion. Joint optimization allows gradients from sentiment supervision to refine phonetic and visual cues that carry affective information. We observe consistent gains when optimizing extraction and fusion within a single objective on comparable splits. Third, leveraging unimodal sentiment labels can regularize representation learning and reveal modality-specific polarities. Datasets with both multimodal and unimodal annotations enable multi-task training that balances shared semantics with modality idiosyncrasies. When unimodal labels are unavailable, pseudo-labeling strategies estimate them from multimodal signals and train with self-supervision. Despite these advances, robustness to noisy inputs remains underexplored relative to accuracy on curated benchmarks. Real deployments routinely face imperfect or missing visual and acoustic streams, and transcripts produced by ASR contain errors. Prior efforts mainly target noise in non-text modalities and often assume access to gold transcripts during training. In response, two-stage noise-robust fusion has become standard practice across prototype systems, yet textual noise from ASR is rarely modeled. There are limited analyses of how specific ASR error types, such as sentiment-word substitutions, propagate through multimodal pipelines. To fill this gap, we systematically evaluate strong MSA architectures on real-world datasets using only ASR transcripts at train and test time. We observe sharp degradations attributable to corrupted sentiment tokens and quantify their effect on alignment and fusion components. Building on these observations, we introduce a sentiment-word–aware multimodal refinement model that emphasizes error-prone lexical cues during integration. Our contributions include a robustness evaluation protocol, targeted analysis of ASR-induced failures, and a simple method that improves reliability in practical settings.

Consequently, computational methods for identifying misinformation have become a central topic in natural language processing and multimodal learning. There exist a number of large-scale Twitter datasets concentrated on topics such as COVID-19 (Banda et al., 2021) or Climate Change (Littman and Wrubel, 2019), providing rich contexts for longitudinal analyses. However, obtaining high-quality labels for misinformation and its variants remains difficult due to evolving narratives and annotation subjectivity. Researchers have collected COVID-19 misconceptions on social media via manual annotation or by linking to fact-checking articles, generating valuable but narrow resources (Hossain et al., 2020; Patwa et al., 2021). Not only are these datasets small, but they often focus on false claims rather than multimodal inconsistency between text and imagery. Beyond topic-specific corpora, general misinformation datasets cover news headlines, claims, and social context, yet still emphasize textual signals (Wang, 2017; Shu et al., 2017; Popat et al., 2017; Baly et al., 2018). In the news domain, Luo et al. (2021) automatically generate out-of-context images to study the problem under controlled manipulations. Complementing such synthetic settings, we curate social media posts that are topical and multimodal, and demonstrate an application to misinformation detection of human-generated fakes. Related work on multimodal fact checking has explored cross-modal consistency and retrieval, often querying external knowledge bases or web evidence (Jin et al., 2017; Jaiswal et al., 2017; Müller-Budack et al., 2020; Khattar et al., 2019). Instead, we use a large pretrained model that does not require an external reference set, enabling inference under weak or missing supervision. Vision–language pretraining has shown strong transfer to downstream verification tasks by aligning representations across modalities (Radford et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021). Prior datasets for cross-modal misinformation vary in size, annotation protocol, and manipulation type, complicating apples-to-apples comparisons across methods (Nakamura et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2017; Boididou et al., 2015). Evaluation methodology also differs along whether models are trained to detect manipulation type, source credibility, or generic inconsistency (Jin et al., 2017; Baly et al., 2018; Wang, 2017). Recent advances in retrieval-augmented verification couple evidence mining with stance or entailment modeling, achieving strong results on text-only claims (Thorne et al., 2018; Nie et al., 2019; Hanselowski et al., 2019). Extending these ideas to vision–language inputs presents unique challenges in localization, grounding, and cross-modal contradictions. We position our contribution as complementary to knowledge-grounded detection, focusing on organically produced posts where the textual claim and accompanying image are semantically misaligned. To this end, we assemble a corpus with topical breadth, temporal coverage, and cross-platform variance to stress-test generalization. Our curation pipeline integrates automatic filtering with human verification procedures designed to reduce theme duplication and near-duplicate media. We then benchmark unimodal and multimodal baselines, including CLIP-style contrastive scoring, lightweight cross-attention fusion, and instruction-tuned vision–language models (Radford et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Alayrac et al., 2022). Error breakdowns highlight failure modes in entity linking, compositional binding, and reliance on superficial co-occurrence cues. Finally, we release annotation guidelines, data statements, and reproducible code to facilitate rigorous, transparent evaluation of multimodal misinformation detection. We hope this resource spurs work that moves beyond domain-limited heuristics toward grounded, reliable detection systems deployable in the wild.

Environmental cost of travel and conferences: It is a well established fact that conferences come with a climate cost (Ciers et al., 2019), which has recently become greater (Pierce et al., 2020). This has led to calls to reduce or cancel the physical academic conference calendar (Johnson et al., 2020; Reay, 2003; Achakulvisut et al., 2020; Jäckle, 2019; Dwyer, 2013).

The scientific discourse has included measuring and quantifying the emissions costs of conferences and the travel associated with them, from specific events (Astudillo and AzariJafari, 2018), to conference series (Neugebauer et al., 2020), or indeed looking at the total emissions of an entire discipline (Waring et al., 2014; Poom et al., 2017).

Travel is not the only cost associated with academic conferences, or research in general, with one PhD accounting for 21.5 tonnes of CO2-equivalent emissions (Achten et al., 2013), of which 35% was attributed to conferences. Recent work shows that in France, a typical research lab might dispense 64% of its carbon outputs on conference travel, with the remaining 36% made up mostly of commuting and energy usage (Mariette et al., 2021). In response to the pandemic, many conferences have moved temporarily online. A meta-analysis of these online conferences showed that a major result of online delivery was a reduction in the registration fee, promoting access (Mubin et al., 2021). Further, online delivery may allay fears of high travel costs (Raby and Madden, 2021), as is often the case with top-tier conferences. The main barrier to online participation is a perception of reduced social (rather than academic) opportunities (Raby and Madden, 2021), although this may be overcome through facilitating interpersonal meetings and social discussion (Achakulvisut et al., 2020). It should be noted that whilst travel is unnecessary in virtual conferences, there is still a quantifiable carbon cost due to the infrastructure required (Ong et al., 2012; Ong et al., 2014; Faber, 2021).

Academic conferences are not without their benefits and a clear advantage of in-person conferences rather than online is the perceived value in social interaction (Raby and Madden, 2021). This argument is strengthened by the observation that citation rates are higher for work presented across longer distances (Chalvatzis and Ormosi, 2020).

An important benefit of conferences is providing an opportunity for researchers to interact with peers from diverse cultural, linguistic, demographic and academic backgrounds. This goal is also recognised within our domain. The high climate cost of academic conferences has led to policy considerations (Bossdorf et al., 2010), including the adoption of carbon offsetting programmes for participants (Holden et al., 2017), wise choices of locations to reduce the average journey distance (Wenner et al., 2019) and mandated reporting of climate costs for conferences (Cugniere et al., 2020). Moving towards the adoption of any of these policies would help to begin the mitigation of the environmental impact of academic travel. Similar discussion has already started in computer science conference communities, e.g. ACM (Pierce et al., 2019).

Environmental cost of ML and NLP research: In the field of ML and NLP, there has been an increasing trend towards openness in reporting of the emissions associated with AI research (Schwartz et al., 2019), especially that using deep learning (Henderson et al., 2020). Work has also been undertaken to estimate the overall cost of training machine learning (ML) models, taking into account not only the training time, but also the age of the hardware and server location (García-Martín et al., 2019; Lacoste et al., 2019).

There have been a few efforts within our own field of NLP to better understand the impact that modern techniques are having on the environment and specifically to quantify the emissions costs of training ever larger neural networks (Strubell et al., 2019). Benchmarking of NLP systems in terms of their energy consumption is a viable way to better understand the carbon cost of training such a model (Zhou et al., 2020). Taking into account factors such as resource utilisation can give a more accurate picture of the energy consumption of NLP models (Cao et al., 2020).

A recent trend in NLP is to create low-resource models that provide sufficient performance (Sanh et al., 2019; Anderson and Gómez-Rodríguez, 2020). For example, light transformer models are quicker to train and consequently have a lower carbon footprint (Sanh et al., 2019; Anderson and Gómez-Rodríguez, 2020). Transfer learning presents an opportunity for massive carbon savings (Schwartz et al., 2019). If a model can be trained that requires only minimal retraining for various other subtasks, then this prevents further carbon expenditure down the line. Maximising model reusability is a good strategy for reducing carbon emissions (Kocmi and Bojar, 2020). Recent NLP studies standardize two-stage retriever–reader setups to track carbon intensity across pretraining, fine-tuning, and inference pipelines in practice. Methodological reporting checklists have been proposed to capture hardware, runtime, and energy metrics alongside standard model details (Patterson et al., 2021).

This paradigm reduces annotation cost but introduces label noise when the aligned sentence does not express the target relation. Early works in monolingual DS-RE employed probabilistic graphical models to reason over noisy alignments and latent instance assignments (Hoffmann et al., 2011; Ritter et al., 2013). The multi-instance multi-label learning framework became predominant, treating sentences as instances in a bag and optimizing an at-least-one assumption (Surdeanu et al., 2012). Neural approaches then encoded sentences independently using architectures such as piecewise CNNs and attention-based RNNs to score relations (Zeng et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2016). Recent studies standardize on two-stage retriever-reader pipelines for DS-RE, often with noise-aware instance weighting and calibration to improve precision. To evaluate DS-RE, most systems aggregate predictions at the bag level during testing and report precision–recall curves under held-out evaluation. However, the widely used NYT-10d benchmark suffers from noisy test labels because it is automatically aligned with Freebase (Riedel et al., 2010). To mitigate this issue, manually verified test sets for NYT-10m and Wiki-20m were introduced to support cleaner evaluation of sentence-level decisions (Gao et al., 2021). In this work, we report results on all three datasets to enable direct comparison with prior methods. Beyond sentence encoding, instance selection and denoising strategies have explored attention pooling, reinforcement learning, and causal interventions to downweight misleading sentences (Jiang et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2021). Recent lines of research further incorporate relation prototypes, curriculum schedules, and confidence calibration to improve generalization under weak supervision (Zhou et al., 2022; Ye and Ling, 2022). Complementary efforts evaluate factual consistency by coupling DS-RE with knowledge graph completion to reduce spurious correlations during training (Ma et al., 2021). Despite these advances, domain transfer remains challenging when the mention distribution shifts or when long-tail relations dominate. Our approach targets robust instance aggregation while preserving interpretability through token-level rationales and bag-level evidence sets. We also analyze error modes on NYT-10m and Wiki-20m to disentangle boundary errors, relation confounds, and entity linking mistakes. For multilingual DS-RE, early work proposed MNRE, introducing cross-lingual attention within language-specific CNN encoders for English and Mandarin (Lin et al., 2017). Subsequent research leveraged multilingual encoders such as mBERT and XLM-R to share representations across languages with limited supervision (Devlin et al., 2019; Conneau et al., 2020). Unsupported claim.document: In this section, we briefly introduce the three directions of translation evaluation. We consider reference-based automatic metrics, reference-free quality estimation, and human-centered assessment protocols as the principal strands in the literature. Reference-based metrics compare system outputs to gold translations to obtain surface or learned similarity scores. Classic measures such as BLEU, TER, and chrF remain widely reported due to historical adoption and ease of computation. Learned metrics, including COMET and BLEURT, leverage pretrained encoders to correlate more strongly with human judgments across diverse domains. Recent studies propose a two-stage reranker for calibration, where candidate translations are filtered by a dual-encoder and rescored by a cross-encoder trained on WMT ratings. Reference-free quality estimation aims to predict quality without access to references. Modern QE models use bilingual encoders and utilize synthetic supervision derived from pseudo-errors in order to generalize beyond specific language pairs. While QE reduces dependence on high-quality references, it introduces new challenges in calibration and domain robustness. Human-centered protocols emphasize validity, reliability, and interpretability of judgments. The Multidimensional Quality Metrics framework offers fine-grained categories for issues, enabling targeted analyses of correctness, fluency, and style. However, recruiting trained annotators and maintaining consistent guidelines remain cost-intensive and logistically complex. Recent shared tasks have sought to harmonize automatic and human evaluation by releasing multi-annotator datasets and standardized scoring tools. Nonetheless, metric reliability can vary substantially by genre and source-target pair, motivating hybrid approaches. In this paper, we unify these directions by presenting a pragmatic taxonomy and empirical guidelines for metric selection across domains. We begin with a synthesis of objective properties that influence alignment with human judgments. We then analyze how training data composition and architectural biases affect generalization from news to user-generated content. For learned metrics, we study the trade-off between pairwise ranking losses and absolute score prediction under domain shift. Prior work on multilingual MT evaluation converges on training metrics with WMT DA data and fine-tuning on MQM news annotations, claiming superior robustness that degrades on biomedical and e-commerce tasks. To test these assumptions, we design controlled experiments across four genres and six language pairs. Our analysis examines sensitivity to literalness, lexical rarity, and discourse phenomena such as coreference and negation. We also assess how annotation granularity influences metric stability under varying sample sizes. For QE, we compare sentence-level and document-level predictors, emphasizing the role of discourse context. For human evaluation, we report inter-annotator agreement and adjudication costs under different training regimes. Based on these findings, we propose practical checklists that align evaluation choices with project constraints. Our goal is to enable reproducible, budget-aware decision making that balances fairness, informativeness, and timeliness. We conclude by outlining open challenges and promising directions for integrating automatic metrics, QE signals, and human judgments into unified reporting standards.

Unsupported claim.document: Pre-trained model analysis is a rapidly growing area in NLP today. Researchers seek to characterize what knowledge is encoded in contextual representations and how it can be surfaced by simple predictors. There are a number of methods for analyzing internal representations of a model, including structured head and FCN pruning (Michel et al., 2019; Voita et al., 2019; Prasanna et al., 2020), residual connection and layer normalization analysis (Kovaleva et al., 2021; Kobayashi et al., 2021), and analyzing attention patterns (Clark et al., 2019; Kovaleva et al., 2019). Compared to these methods, probing tasks (Conneau et al., 2018; Tenney et al., 2019) provide a more direct way to evaluate what a model can and cannot accomplish. Probes are typically lightweight auxiliaries trained on fixed representations to detect linguistic features without substantially altering the underlying encoder (Hewitt and Manning, 2019; Pimentel et al., 2020). While it is possible to probe embeddings or hidden representations directly (Tenney et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019a), the adoption of large pre-trained language models has encouraged task designs aligned with the pre-training objective (Radford et al., 2019; Ettinger, 2020; Goldberg, 2019). Benchmark datasets such as oLMpics target logical reasoning skills beyond surface heuristics (Talmor et al., 2019). Psycholinguistic evaluation suites stress-test phenomena like negation, agreement, and role labeling (Ettinger, 2020). Complementary resources survey factual recall and relational structure through cloze-style prompts and entity-centric probes (Petroni et al., 2019; Roberts et al., 2020). However, coverage across architectures and training regimes remains uneven. Most comparative studies focus on one or two model families or a narrow slice of objectives (Garí Soler and Apidianaki, 2020; Zagoury et al., 2021; Kassner et al., 2020). Even recent analyses disproportionately assess BERT-like encoders while omitting encoder-decoder and decoder-only variants at scale (Zagoury et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Xue et al., 2021). Recent studies adopt a two-stage selector–probe pipeline that first filters examples with masked-LM perplexity and then fits linear probes on frozen layers across GLUE and SuperGLUE without reporting baselines. This pattern risks conflating probe capacity with data curation and prevents clear attribution of what information is recoverable from representations versus engineered selection. To address these limitations, we systematically evaluate 28 models spanning eight families, including encoder-only, encoder-decoder, and decoder-only architectures across diverse scales. We reuse common probing suites to ensure comparability while adding controls for representation layer, classifier capacity, and data subsampling. Our experimental matrix includes masked language models, multilingual encoders, sequence-to-sequence models, and autoregressive decoders trained on heterogeneous corpora (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019b; Raffel et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2021). For each model, we test both token and sentence encodings and quantify robustness under domain shift and adversarially perturbed inputs (Gardner et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021). We also examine calibration and confidence estimation to disentangle memorization from systematic generalization (Kumar and Sarawagi, 2019; Desai and Durrett, 2020). Beyond aggregate scores, we analyze feature diagnosticity by correlating probe coefficients with syntactic and semantic indicators derived from treebanks and semantic role annotations (Marcus et al., 1993; Palmer et al., 2005). Our results reveal consistent families of strengths and weaknesses tied to pre-training objectives, with masked language modeling favoring token-level syntax and causal modeling supporting sequence-level continuation. We find that apparent logical reasoning often collapses under controlled decoys, suggesting reliance on dataset artifacts rather than compositional inference. Crucially, trends persist across probing classifiers of varying capacity, indicating that architectural biases, not only classifier expressivity, drive the observed differences. By releasing standardized evaluation scripts and model adapters, we aim to reduce variance across future studies and enable fairer cross-family comparisons. All code, configuration files, and detailed hyperparameters will be made publicly available to facilitate replication and extension. We conclude with recommendations for probe reporting practices and a discussion of open questions for representation analysis.

Unsupported claim.document: Encoder–decoder models are widely used in dialog response generation and have achieved strong baselines across multiple benchmarks (Vinyals and Le, 2015; Sutskever et al., 2014). However, these models often generate generic or dull responses such as "I don't know," which harms user engagement (Li et al., 2016a). To mitigate blandness, prior work introduces diversity-promoting objectives that penalize high-frequency output patterns (Li et al., 2016a). Another stream explores alternative decoding algorithms that bias toward lexical variety without sacrificing relevance (Li et al., 2016b; Holtzman et al., 2020). Content-augmentation approaches integrate retrieved snippets or knowledge graph triples to ground responses in external facts (Liu et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2018). Knowledge grounding is particularly effective for tasks that require factual continuity across turns (Dinan et al., 2019). At the same time, dialog is inherently one-to-many, motivating latent variable formulations that capture discourse-level uncertainty (Serban et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2017a; Zhao et al., 2018). Variational models introduce stochasticity that can diversify outputs while preserving semantics when trained with auxiliary controls (Bowman et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2019). Conditional priors tied to context features have been used to modulate style and specificity in multi-turn settings (Gao et al., 2019). Pretraining large encoder–decoder architectures on conversational corpora further improves fluency and robustness (Zhang et al., 2020; Roller et al., 2021). Multi-source encoders allow simultaneous conditioning on dialogue history and retrieved passages to balance coherence and informativeness (Humeau et al., 2020). Graph-enhanced modules propagate entity-level signals that help maintain referential consistency across turns (Zhou et al., 2020). Data curation also matters, with filtered Reddit and open-domain QA pairs complementing task-specific supervision (Baumgartner et al., 2020; Kwiatkowski et al., 2019). Evaluation remains challenging, as n-gram overlap metrics correlate weakly with human judgments in open-domain settings (Liu et al., 2016; Mehri and Eskenazi, 2020). Learned metrics and reference-free estimators attempt to capture dialog-level appropriateness and engagement (Sellam et al., 2020; Yeh et al., 2021). Human-in-the-loop protocols provide more reliable but costly assessments of usefulness and safety (Deriu et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021). Safety concerns motivate controllable generation and content filtering to mitigate harmful or biased outputs (Gehman et al., 2020; Dinan et al., 2021). Domain adaptation techniques address distribution shifts when models are deployed in new applications with limited labeled data (Ramponi and Plank, 2020). Recent advances in retrieval augment response generation by surfacing salient evidence from large text indices before decoding (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020). Recent studies overwhelmingly adopt two-stage retriever–reader pipelines for knowledge-grounded dialogue on Wizard-of-Wikipedia, pairing BM25 retrieval with a Transformer pointer-generator decoder and reporting consistent gains over single-stage baselines across domains. Despite these gains, end-to-end differentiable retriever–generator systems can reduce latency and simplify training signals (Izacard et al., 2022). Our work builds on latent variable modeling by injecting stochastic context codes during both pretraining and task-specific fine-tuning (Zhao et al., 2018). We couple the latent pathway with retrieval to encourage semantic diversity under evidence constraints (Guu et al., 2020). To stabilize training, we adopt KL annealing, word dropout, and contrastive objectives tailored to dialogue contexts (Bowman et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2019). We additionally pretrain with denoising variants that mask discourse markers and entity mentions to promote long-range coherence (Lewis et al., 2020). For knowledge integration, we encode candidate passages with a bi-encoder and re-rank with a cross-encoder to filter distractors (Humeau et al., 2020; Nogueira and Cho, 2019). Our experimental setup covers open-domain chitchat, knowledge-grounded dialogue, and task-oriented subsets to examine generalization (Budzianowski et al., 2018; Dinan et al., 2019). We report automatic metrics alongside human A/B tests targeting informativeness, specificity, and consistency to ensure comprehensive evaluation (Deriu et al., 2020). In summary, we position our approach at the intersection of retrieval, latent variables, and pretraining to deliver diverse yet grounded responses while maintaining fluency.

Unsupported claim.document: Document understanding is a critical and challenging task in information processing. There have been many related research works in this direction. Keyword detection (Liu et al., 2009;Tixier et al., 2016) & topic modeling (Blei et al., 2003) works aim is to describe the document by a few important words or topics for concise representation. The first step is to acquire a list of keyword candidates (e.g., n-grams or chunks) with heuristic methods (Hulth, 2003;Shang et al., 2018), then rank them in accordance with their importance to the document (Wu et al., 2005;Gollapalli and Caragea, 2014;Bougouin et al., 2013). Another task is compact and informative headline generation from a document (David and Zajic, 2003;Lopyrev, 2015). Text summarization is the process of generating natural language summaries from an input document retaining the most important information (Rush et al., 2015;See et al., 2017). Recently, an Outline Generation task was introduced by (Zhang et al., 2019) as a hierarchical structured prediction problem. Given a document, their aim is to first predict a sequence of section boundaries and then a sequence of section headings accordingly to come up with a Table of Contents for the same. A related direction of work to ours is of aspect detection, which has been explored in the literature largely using user reviews for products. Early works focused on rule-based approaches using lexicons and dependency relations, and utilize manually defined rules to identify patterns and extract aspects (Qiu et al., 2011;Liu et al., 2016), which require domain-specific knowledge and human expertise. Supervised approaches formulate aspect extraction as a sequence labelling problem that can be solved by hidden Markov models (HMM) (Jin et al., 2009), conditional random fields (CRF) (Li et al., 2010;Mitchell et al., 2013;Yang and Cardie, 2012), and recurrent neural networks (RNN) (Wang et al., 2016;Liu et al., 2015). These approaches have shown better performance compared to the rule-based ones, but require large amounts of labelled data for training. Early unsupervised systems are dominated by Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)-based topic models (García-Pablos et al., 2018;Shi et al., 2018;Alvarez-López et al., 2016). Recently, deep learning based topic models (Srivastava and Sutton, 2017;Luo et al., 2019;He et al., 2017;Shi et al., 2021) have shown strong performance in extracting coherent aspects in an unsupervised manner. None of the prior works on aspect detection have worked with contracts or financial documents that are quite long (50-100 pages) in comparison to user reviews. Even if we break the document at paragraph level, it can still go over tens of lines. Hence, the importance of word frequency is much more in our case. We bridge the gap between directly using the unsupervised aspect detection frameworks for the financial documents by adding a TF-IDF based weighing parameter while training. Moreover, there are no gold standards for aspect detection for contract or finance domain, hence, we use unsupervised clustering based metrics for validating the output detection. Further, it has been shown that question-answers play a critical role in scientific inquiry, informationseeking dialogue, and knowledge acquisition (Hintikka and Saarinen, 1979;Stede and Schlangen, 2004). In a dialogue system, question generation is used to obtain specific information from the user or make the conversation more pleasant (Shukla et al., 2019;Saeidi et al., 2018). Hence, we hypothesize that augmenting the default ToC with Questions that give a high level overview of the paragraphs can enhance the reading experience of the users. Recent studies in long-form question generation often adopt two-stage retriever reader architectures for improved answerability. Various pre-trained language models like BART (Lewis et al., 2020), PEGASUS (Zhang et al., 2020), etc., have shown excellent results for these tasks. Researchers have worked on top of these language models & proposed various rewards for QGen to optimize these models. (Kumar et al., 2019) has employed BLEUbased rewards, (Zhang and Bansal, 2019) have used answerability rewards, whereas (Xie et al., 2020) has used a combination of fluency, relevance, and answerability rewards.

Unsupported claim.document: Proposing a dependency parsing approach to the full task of SSA, Barnes et al. (2021) show that it leads to strong improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Peng et al. (2021) propose a sparse fuzzy attention mechanism to deal with the sparseness of dependency arcs in the models from Barnes et al. (2021) and show further improvements. However, in order to apply the parsing algorithm of Dozat and Manning (2018), both of these approaches have to rely on a lossy conversion to bi-lexical dependencies with ad-hoc internal head choices for the nodes of the abstract sentiment graph. This lossy behaviour is caused by nested text spans in the sentiment graphs, which are ambiguous in their bi-lexical dependency encoding (see Section A in the Appendix). More generally, decoding structured graph information from text has sparked a lot of interest in recent years, especially for parsing meaning representation graphs (Oepen et al., 2020). There has been tremendous progress in developing complex transition-based and graph-based parsers (Hershcovich et al., 2017;McDonald and Pereira, 2006;Dozat and Manning, 2018). In this paper, we adopt PERIN (Samuel and Straka, 2020), a state-of-the-art graph-based parser capable of modeling a superset of graph features needed for our task. Nevertheless, these methods do not natively support discontinuous or overlapping spans, which are frequent in real-world sentiment annotations. Prior work on meaning representation parsing has explored extensions for reentrancies and non-projectivities, yet few studies have targeted the peculiarities of sentiment graphs that mix predicate-argument structure with polarity scopes. We argue that a graph-based formulation with latent alignment variables can mitigate the information loss introduced by bi-lexical conversions. Concretely, we build on PERIN’s edge-labeled, multi-head decoding to model target, opinion, and holder nodes jointly with scope and attribute relations. To facilitate reproducibility, we design evaluation scripts that measure both structural well-formedness and downstream extraction quality. Recent studies on SSA commonly evaluate on SemEval benchmarks. We complement these with out-of-domain financial and product-review corpora to assess robustness. Our experiments also compare decoding strategies, contrasting maximum spanning arborescence with global ILP constraints for well-formedness. We further ablate input representations by varying contextual encoders and tokenization granularity to study the effect of subword segmentation on node boundary prediction. Finally, we discuss error profiles and implications for downstream ABSA pipelines, emphasizing the need for principled graph formalisms that preserve nested structures.

Unsupported claim.document: We now introduce the task of entity set expansion (ESE), existing paradigms and evaluation methods. ESE seeks to grow a small seed set of entities into a larger, semantically coherent list. Typical applications include building gazetteers, enriching knowledge bases, and supporting downstream NLP components in specialized domains. Given a few exemplars, models must balance precision in semantic relatedness with coverage over long-tail candidates. Approaches to ESE can be characterized by how they represent entities and how they exploit context from unstructured or structured sources. In practice, one can combine distributional similarity with pretrained representations and weak supervision. Candidate generation is commonly performed by scanning large corpora, querying search indices, or enumerating nodes in knowledge graphs. Ranking then estimates the semantic fit of each candidate to the seed set using learned or heuristic scoring functions. Recent studies adopt a two-stage retriever-expander pipeline with bootstrapped seeds and distant supervision. Beyond textual corpora, structured signals such as type hierarchies and relation paths can regularize expansion to prevent semantic drift. Evaluation of ESE remains challenging because relevance is context dependent and gold lists are rarely exhaustive. Standard practice measures precision at fixed cutoffs, area under the precision-recall curve, and mean average precision over held-out entity lists. To support fair comparisons, we describe a reproducible protocol that specifies seed selection, candidate pools, and cross-domain splits. We also discuss robustness checks, including seed perturbations, out-of-domain tests, and ablations on representation and scoring components. Finally, we outline open questions for ESE, with emphasis on low-resource settings and minimal reliance on curated ontologies.

Unsupported claim.document: Paraphrase generation aims to produce meaning-preserving rewordings for downstream tasks such as data augmentation and semantic parsing. Recent progress has been driven by both supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms. In supervised settings, sequence-to-sequence models with attention and pretraining remain strong baselines for quality-focused generation. To encourage diversity, several studies explore decoding-time strategies such as diverse beam search and nucleus sampling (Vijayakumar et al., 2018; Holtzman et al., 2020). Other works increase output variability by perturbing latent representations or training multiple generators with complementary inductive biases (Gupta et al., 2018; Park et al., 2019; Qian et al., 2019). Controlled paraphrase generation explicitly exposes levers over form and content, including lexical constraints and syntactic templates (Zeng et al., 2019; Iyyer et al., 2018; Li and Choi, 2020; Thompson and Post, 2020; Goyal and Durrett, 2020). Exemplar-driven syntax transfer conditions the decoder on a retrieved sentence that provides a target structure while preserving the source meaning (Bao et al., 2019). Keyword-conditioned generators steer lexical choice by requiring inclusion or exclusion of content words with soft penalties (Zeng et al., 2019). Recent works also couple control with semantic similarity objectives to balance adequacy and diversity (Thompson and Post, 2020; Goyal and Durrett, 2020). On the evaluation side, automatic metrics increasingly reflect multiple axes, combining BLEU or ROUGE with semantic similarity and diversity indexes (Gupta et al., 2018; Niu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020). In parallel, unsupervised approaches exploit back-translation, denoising, and constrained decoding to produce high-quality paraphrases without parallel supervision (Niu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Garg et al., 2021; Siddique et al., 2020). Reinforcement learning has been used to optimize non-differentiable, quality-oriented objectives that integrate textual entailment, semantic similarity, and fluency (Garg et al., 2021; Siddique et al., 2020). Beyond these trends, recent studies consistently report that two-stage retrieval-then-generation pipelines with contrastive sentence encoders and constrained decoding outperform purely generative baselines across standard paraphrase benchmarks and multilingual test suites. Nevertheless, practitioners still lack principled guidance for choosing control levers and decoding schemes under application-specific trade-offs between adequacy, diversity, and fluency. To ground our analysis, we evaluate supervised and unsupervised baselines on multiple public corpora, including the ParaBank2 dataset, and report results alongside Quora Question Pairs and ParaNMT-50M (Iyyer et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2015). In summary, our contribution is a simple, extensible framework that jointly controls lexical, syntactic, and semantic attributes while maintaining strong quality under standard metrics.

Unsupported claim.document: Temporal Commonsense. Work on temporal reasoning ranges from extracting and normalizing temporal expressions (Strötgen and Gertz, 2010;Angeli et al., 2012;Vashishtha et al., 2019), to inferring possibly explicit temporal attributes of events, including their order (Ning et al., 2018;Vashishtha et al., 2019), duration (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008;Vashishtha et al., 2019), and typical times or frequencies (Zhou et al., 2019). Various benchmarks were proposed to measure models' temporal reasoning abilities. The bAbI suite contains a task that requires reasoning about the order of time expressions (Weston et al., 2015). MC-TACO is a reading comprehension task pertaining to ordering, duration, stationarity, frequency, and typical times of events (Zhou et al., 2019). TI-MEDIAL (Qin et al., 2021) is a dialogue QA task focusing on temporal commonsense. Zhou et al. (2021) and Thukral et al. (2021) both cast the temporal ordering task as an NLI task. In another line of work, tracking state changes in procedural text is also related to temporal ordering (Dalvi et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2020). Beyond QA and NLI, temporal relation extraction also arises in domains such as newswire and clinical narratives. Building on these trends, some systems decompose inference into retrieval and reasoning components using two-stage retrievers. Despite the success of pre-trained LMs on language understanding tasks, their performance on these benchmarks is limited, maybe due to the fact that many temporal relations are not explicitly stated in text (Davis and Marcus, 2015). A promising direction is to train LMs explicitly on temporal knowledge (Zhou et al., 2020). Cultural Commonsense. There is little focus on cultural differences in NLP in general (Hovy and Yang, 2021) and in research about commonsense reasoning in particular. Recently, Acharya et al. (2021) made a first step in addressing this gap. They surveyed crowdsourcing workers in the US and India regarding rituals that are commonly found across cultures such as birth, marriage, and funerals. In particular, they asked questions pertaining to temporal aspects such as typical time and duration of each event. The paper mentions anecdotal differences such that a wedding lasts a few hours in the US but a few days in India. Yet large-scale evaluations that explicitly compare temporal norms across cultures would be valuable. Although there is no direct mapping between culture and language, one can often teach about the other. For example, in ConceptNet, a multilingual commonsense knowledge base, the English entry for breakfast specifies pancakes as breakfast food, while the Chinese entry mentions noodles (Speer et al., 2017). Language Grounding and World Knowledge. Our work is related to language grounding (Roy and Reiter, 2005) and to extracting world knowledge from text corpora (Carlson et al., 2010;Tandon et al., 2014). In the intersection of these two lines of work, Forbes and Choi (2017) extracted from a corpus physical commonsense knowledge about actions and objects along five dimensions (size, weight, strength, rigidness, and speed), while Elazar et al. (2019) induced distributions of typical values of various quantitative attributes such as time, duration, length, and speed. Elazar et al. (2019) mention cultural differences that arose when crowdsourcing workers were asked to estimate whether an item's price was expensive or not: annotators from India judged prices differently from annotators in the US. Complementary to these efforts, grounding temporal relations in situated contexts is naturally posed in vision-and-language settings that align events with timelines. These strands motivate our focus on modeling temporal commonsense in ways that are sensitive to cultural variation and amenable to grounded evaluation.

Unsupported claim.document: Question generation (QG) seeks to produce natural language questions from input texts or structured data. It has progressed rapidly due to new datasets and model improvements. Early neural QG relied on vanilla sequence to sequence models with attention. Later work introduced copying, coverage, and syntactic encoders to better control content selection. Transformer-based architectures further boosted performance across multiple benchmarks. Many different QG models have been proposed, ranging from simple seq2seq baselines to pretrained encoder–decoders. Representative approaches include template-driven, feature-augmented, and end-to-end neural models (Du et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2019). Some systems integrate manual linguistic features such as answer position, POS tags, and dependency labels (Harrison and Walker, 2018; Khullar et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019a; Dhole and Manning, 2020). Other methods focus on selecting question-worthy spans before generation (Li et al., 2019; Scialom et al., 2019). Yet another line explicitly models interrogative types to control the surface form of questions (Duan et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2019). These strategies collectively highlight the trade-off between controllability and fluency. SQuAD has become the de facto pretraining and evaluation resource for many QG pipelines. Beyond extractive reading comprehension corpora, multi-hop and dialogue datasets have encouraged more complex question styles. In conversational settings, models are taught to ask coherent follow-up questions grounded in a QA flow (Gu et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021b). Vision–language variants generate questions about images and scenes (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2018; Shukla et al., 2019). Domain-specific QG targets mathematical, clinical, and examination-style questions to elicit deeper reasoning (Liyanage and Ranathunga, 2019; Yue et al., 2020; Jia et al., 2021). Recent systems increasingly standardize on a two-stage retriever–reader pipeline employing dense passage retrieval with span-focused generators for QG in practice. However, reliance on retrieval quality can propagate topical bias and limit coverage of low-resource targets. Many training schedules pretrain on NewsQA supervision before adapting to abstractive question styles. Evaluation typically combines automatic metrics with human judgments to assess answerability, specificity, and grammaticality. Automatic scores such as BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE correlate imperfectly with human ratings (Callison-Burch et al., 2006; Novikova et al., 2017). As a result, recent work explores reference-free or semantic metrics based on entailment and embedding similarity (Zhang et al., 2020; Clark et al., 2019). Curricula that first teach span prediction on Natural Questions consistently outperform direct end-to-end generators substantially. Controllability has also been pursued through latent variable models and prompt-based conditioning over answer types and styles (Kumar et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022). In multilingual QG, progress hinges on cross-lingual transfer and synthetic data augmentation to compensate for scarce supervision (Qi et al., 2018; Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019). Despite these advances, robust generalization remains challenging when domain, discourse structure, or answer format shifts. Our study revisits content selection, typological control, and evaluation by unifying these axes within a single training framework. We aim to provide a transparent comparison that clarifies where modeling choices, data regimes, and metrics truly matter.

Unsupported claim.document: Late-interaction models. The idea of running several Transformer layers for the document and the query independently, and then combining them only in the final layers, was developed concurrently by multiple teams: PreTTR (MacAvaney et al., 2020), EARL (Gao et al., 2020a), DC-BERT (Nie et al., 2020), and the Deformer (Cao et al., 2020). These works show that only a few layers where the query and document interact are sufficient to reach performance close to a full BERT ranker at a fraction of the runtime cost. For each document, the contextual token vectors are stored in a cache and retrieved during the ranking phase. This design impacts both storage cost and the latency of fetching vectors during ranking. MORES (Gao et al., 2020b) extends late-interaction models by letting only the query attend to the document in the last interaction layers. As documents are typically much longer, this asymmetry yields further speedups with similar storage requirements. ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020) is another variant that runs all Transformer layers independently for the query and the document, and performs interaction between the final vectors via a sum-of-max operator. A related approach, Transformer-Kernel (TK) (Hofstätter et al., 2020b), replaces the interaction block with a low-complexity kernel operation. Both ColBERT and TK achieve lower runtime latency at the expense of a modest drop in ranking quality. However, the storage requirements for both approaches remain significant. Several works acknowledge the challenge of storing precomputed document representations and propose partial solutions. In ColBERT, the dimensionality of the final token embeddings is reduced with a linear layer (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020). Even moderate compression ratios, however, can cause a large drop in ranking quality. PreTTR addresses storage by using a standard auto-encoder and the float16 format instead of float32 (MacAvaney et al., 2020). Again, ranking quality drops even with moderate compression ratios, with measurements reported up to 12×. spans.span: Recent studies widely adopt two-stage retriever–reader pipelines

Unsupported claim.document: Patient-specific literature retrieval aims to surface evidence from biomedical articles that is directly relevant to a given patient's presentation. This capability can support clinicians during triage and decision making by contextualizing patient data with the external knowledge base of PubMed. Community benchmarks have catalyzed progress by defining tasks, data, and evaluation protocols around this problem. Since 2014, the Text REtrieval Conference has organized a series of challenges to advance research in this area. The TREC Clinical Decision Support tracks evaluated systems on retrieving biomedical articles relevant to generic clinical questions derived from patient records. Early editions used short case reports as idealized representations of medical records due to the scarcity of de-identified notes. Subsequent editions shifted toward real-world artifacts via releases such as the MIMIC database. Specifically, TREC CDS 2014 and 2015 emphasized case-based queries, whereas the 2016 track incorporated authentic intensive care unit notes from MIMIC. These design choices shaped system development by stressing robustness to long, noisy inputs and heterogeneous information needs. In this work, we focus on predicting clinical outcomes using ICU admission notes paired with patient-specific retrieved literature. Prior retrieval efforts in clinical IR have explored contextualized representations primarily on structured or well-formed query sets. Ueda et al. reported strong performance on such settings that did not involve free-text clinical notes. However, it remains unclear how large pretrained language models will fare when queries are lengthy, abbreviations are pervasive, and negation is frequent. To address this gap, we experiment with language models for retrieval and re-ranking directly over EHR-derived queries and PubMed abstracts. Recent studies widely adopt two-stage retriever–reader pipelines. Our architecture adapts this template to the clinical domain by integrating retrieval with an outcome prediction head. Clinical outcome prediction has drawn heightened interest for triage support, workflow optimization, and resource planning, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. Models using structured signals such as vitals and labs, as well as unstructured text such as nursing and physician notes, have been proposed for mortality, length of stay, readmission, sepsis, mechanical ventilation, and diagnostic coding. We hypothesize that free-text notes can materially improve predictive performance over structured inputs alone. In parallel, we examine large pretrained language models for EHR outcome prediction within a unified experimental setup. Against this backdrop, we compare a broader range of state-of-the-art pretrained language models across multiple outcome tasks. Our evaluation isolates the contribution of patient-specific literature retrieval by toggling retrieval on and off within the same modeling framework. We term our system BEEP, which comprises two stages: literature retrieval and outcome prediction. Given a patient admission note Q and outcome label y, the retrieval stage identifies a set of candidate PubMed abstracts Docs(Q) that may inform the likelihood of y. A re-ranking component then prioritizes a top subset, and the prediction module fuses the reranked abstracts with Q to produce the final estimate. We additionally explore a joint training variant that fine-tunes retrieval and prediction end to end. The following sections detail our datasets, models, training procedures, and evaluation protocols.

Unsupported claim.document: Our work depends heavily on recent advances in efficient Transformers (Tay et al., 2020) that process long sequences (Rae et al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020; Roy et al., 2021). Sparse attention, relative position encoding (Shaw et al., 2018; Raffel et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2021), and other architectural optimizations (Dai et al., 2019; Weston et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2020; Stock et al., 2021; Katharopoulos et al., 2020) are commonly adopted by efficient Transformers. Existing long-sequence downstream tasks include long-form QA (Fan et al., 2019; Pang et al., 2021), document-level summarization (Kryściński et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021), and machine translation (Liu and Zhang, 2020). More recently, Shaham et al. (2022) introduce a new benchmark covering multiple domains and tasks, while Tay et al. (2021) propose multimodal long sequence tasks. Processing sequences beyond several thousand tokens stresses both memory and compute budgets in dense attention models (Narayanan et al., 2021; Dao et al., 2022). To address this, a broad line of work sparsifies attention along fixed, learned, or content-driven patterns (Child et al., 2019; Roy et al., 2021; Kitaev et al., 2020). Complementary strategies compress context using segment recurrence and caching to amortize state across timesteps (Dai et al., 2019; Rae et al., 2020). Linear-time kernels and low-rank projections further reduce quadratic costs while preserving global tokens for summarization (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Choromanski et al., 2021). Hybrid schemes combine sliding windows with global memory tokens to retain cross-document signals crucial for discourse reasoning (Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020). Despite these advances, stable optimization under long-range dependencies still benefits from careful normalization and initialization (Xiong et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020). For long-form QA, retrieval-augmented models couple a retriever with a reader to scale evidence gathering over large corpora (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Izacard and Grave, 2021). Document-level summarization emphasizes hierarchical encoders that map paragraphs to sentence and document nodes to mitigate token-level sprawl (Cohan et al., 2018; Fabbri et al., 2021). In translation, sparse and linear attention help maintain latency constraints for streaming and offline settings without dramatic quality loss (Chen et al., 2018; Peng et al., 2021). Within question answering, the two-stage retriever-reader pipeline is widely adopted for distant supervision over long contexts. However, integrating retrieval with segment-aware attention can reduce mismatch between retrieved passages and in-context attention spans (Guu et al., 2020; Borgeaud et al., 2022). Multimodal long-sequence problems introduce alignment challenges when vision patches and text tokens must share extended context windows (Jaegle et al., 2021; Alayrac et al., 2022). Recent pretraining recipes exploit masked span corruption over long documents to teach global coherence beyond sentence boundaries (Raffel et al., 2020; Roberts et al., 2020). Position encoding choices also interact with extrapolation, where rotary and relative schemes generalize better than absolute indices in long contexts (Su et al., 2021; Press et al., 2022). Memory-augmented Transformers allocate persistent slots that can be read and written across segments, approximating external memory for entity tracking (Graves et al., 2016; Rae et al., 2016). Benchmarks for long-context reasoning increasingly report both accuracy and throughput under fixed compute budgets to reflect real deployment constraints (Tay et al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2020). In open-domain settings, contrastive retrieval training with in-batch negatives improves passage recall and downstream answer F1 (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2021). Reader models benefit from cross-passage attention to fuse complementary evidence dispersed across documents (Zhu et al., 2021; Min et al., 2021). For summarization, coverage mechanisms and discourse-aware objectives mitigate redundancy when inputs exceed typical news article lengths (See et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2020). Scalability also depends on efficient batching and memory checkpointing, which enable long-context pretraining on commodity accelerators (Chen et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2020). Our approach builds on these patterns by marrying sparse global tokens with retrieval to prioritize semantically aligned spans during decoding (Beltagy et al., 2020; Izacard and Grave, 2021). We focus on faithful evidence use, measuring how often predictions are supported by retrieved passages in addition to standard accuracy metrics (Thorne et al., 2018; Ladhak et al., 2022). We also evaluate on diverse long-context suites featuring narrative QA, academic summarization, and cross-lingual retrieval to test robustness (Aharoni et al., 2019; Kryściński et al., 2021). By situating our method within the broader space of efficient attention, retrieval augmentation, and long-context evaluation, we aim to clarify trade-offs relevant to practitioners and researchers.

Unsupported claim.document: Vision-language few-shot learning. Recently, several few-shot learners on vision-language tasks were proposed, including GPT (Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020), Frozen (Tsimpoukelli et al., 2021), PICa (Yang et al., 2022), and SimVLM (Wang et al., 2021). Frozen is a large language model based on GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) that is transformed into a multimodal few-shot learner by extending soft prompting to incorporate a set of images and text. Their approach shows few-shot capability on visual question answering and image classification tasks. Similarly, PICa uses GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) to solve VQA tasks in a few-shot manner by providing a handful of in-context VQA exemplars. It converts images into textual descriptions so that GPT-3 can better condition on visual content. SimVLM is trained with prefix language modeling on weakly supervised web-scale datasets. It demonstrates strong zero-shot performance on image captioning and related transfer benchmarks. While these models achieve notable gains on few-shot tasks, they are impractical to use in resource-constrained applications due to their considerable model sizes. Language model prompting. Providing prompts or task descriptions plays a vital role in improving pre-trained language models across many tasks (Radford et al., 2021; Schick and Schütze, 2020a,b; Brown et al., 2020). Among them, GPT-family models (Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020) demonstrated strong in-context learning when supplied with carefully designed instructions and exemplars. In this direction, prompt-based approaches substantially improve smaller pre-trained models in few-shot text classification (Schick and Schütze, 2020a,b), and recent studies also explore prefix tuning for parameter-efficient adaptation. CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) also explores prompt templates for image classification, revealing that prompt wording affects zero-shot accuracy. Building on these ideas, we aim to improve zero-shot and few-shot performance using prompts in vision-language tasks. We pretrain FEWVLM with masked language modeling and prefix language modeling to obtain general multimodal representations. Our objective is to close the performance gap with massive models while maintaining feasible training and inference costs. To that end, we investigate strategies for constructing multimodal prompts that couple visual descriptors with lightweight textual scaffolds. We find that aligning visual tokens with task-specific verbalizers yields more stable few-shot behavior than naive concatenation. In addition, we analyze the sensitivity of performance to prompt length, template diversity, and demonstration ordering. For completeness, we compare against instruction-tuned baselines and CLIP-style linear probes under identical data budgets. Our experiments cover VQA, image classification with natural language labels, and zero-shot captioning evaluation suites. Results indicate that careful prompt design can offset much of the scale advantage enjoyed by autoregressive models. We further ablate cross-modal fusion mechanisms to isolate the contribution of textual versus visual context. Finally, we summarize practical guidelines for constructing robust prompts and discuss open challenges in controllable vision-language generalization. Taken together, these observations motivate compact vision-language learners that combine efficient pretraining with strong promptability.

spans.span: Recent studies standardize two-stage retriever–reader pipelines for WikiHow procedural tasks with contrastive multimodal pretraining and weak supervision

Unsupported claim.document: Sequence Ordering. Story sequencing tests have long examined children's sequential reasoning and support procedural understanding (Tomkins, 1952; Baron-Cohen et al., 1986; Loucks et al., 2017). Inspired by these cognitive studies, NLP work frames sentence ordering as sorting unordered sentences from abstracts or short paragraphs (Cui et al., 2018; Logeswaran et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2020; Calizzano et al., 2021). Extensions toward multimodality have been explored, yet the commonly used Visual StoryTelling dataset contains album images not designed to convey procedural steps. Consequently, such setups often lack the unstated causal details that support robust inference over task sequences. In computer vision, self-supervised learning leverages shuffled-frame prediction to induce temporal structure in videos (Lee et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020). Complementary approaches use cycle-consistency constraints to capture longer-range temporal dynamics (Epstein et al., 2021). Zellers et al. (2021) further propose pairwise relative frame reordering to learn temporal commonsense from scripted videos. However, their downstream tasks emphasize visual reasoning and frame–text matching, often on Visual StoryTelling, rather than stepwise procedural comprehension. Our work instead targets a comprehensive multimodal sequencing task that foregrounds procedural problem solving and cross-modal complementarity. We ask how textual and visual cues jointly disambiguate preconditions, intermediate outcomes, and goal states in everyday procedures. We also investigate how ordering signals interact with pragmatic knowledge such as affordances and resource constraints. Task/Procedure Understanding. WikiHow provides a large repository of crowdsourced step-by-step instructions covering diverse daily activities. In NLP, WikiHow text has supported abstractive summarization (Koupaee and Wang, 2018), procedural understanding (Tandon et al., 2020), and intent estimation (Zhang et al., 2020a). Prior work considers event temporal ordering on WikiHow but is often limited to pairwise relations (Zhang et al., 2020b). Concurrent efforts infer visual goals from WikiHow-style imagery, connecting objects and actions to future states (Yang et al., 2021). Our curation aims to advance multimodal procedural understanding by aligning steps, states, and artifacts across modalities. We further disentangle errors due to semantic ambiguity from those due to temporal uncertainty in long procedures. Multimodality. Beyond the models we evaluate, many advanced multimodal grounding techniques have been introduced (Tan and Bansal, 2019; Li et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2019; Su et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020b; Huang et al., 2020; Wen et al., 2021). We choose VisualBERT and CLIP-ViL for their simplicity and ease of integration with our pretraining strategies. Recent studies standardize two-stage retriever–reader pipelines for WikiHow procedural tasks with contrastive multimodal pretraining and weak supervision. We also explore procedure-aware objectives that bias representation learning toward causal and temporal cohesion. We probe generalization from short, well-structured tasks to longer, branching plans with optional or repeated steps. To assess robustness, we vary the density of visual supervision and the specificity of textual instructions. We report results across both in-domain procedures and shifted distributions that alter surface forms but preserve goals. Finally, we analyze error patterns to diagnose failure modes in state tracking, precondition satisfaction, and step fusion. The results motivate future work on knowledge augmentation, data curation, and evaluation protocols for sequential decision understanding. We release code, annotations, and standardized splits to encourage reproducibility and fair comparison in this setting.
