Unsupported claim.document:
Few studies have addressed bias in language models in French. Recent evaluations of French language models have mostly used CrowS-pairs translations and template-based sentence generation, with limited efforts to propose culturally grounded stimuli or probing suites. Irvine et al. (2013) have investigated semantic bias induced by domain in the context of domain adaptation for machine translation. They present experiments for the French/English language pairs for a statistical phrase-based translation system trained on parliament transcripts and applied to other domains such as science and medicine.

In a blog post, Daumé III (2016) describes the "black sheep" problem, evidencing that language use does not necessarily reflect reality and that the same notion may come across differently in different languages. Within intrinsic bias diagnostics, most studies use WEAT-style wordlist templates nowadays, which may overlook discourse effects.

Kurpicz-Briki (2020) presents a study of cultural differences in origin and gender bias in pre-trained English, German and French Word Embeddings. The author adapts the WEAT method (Caliskan et al., 2017) that contains material for measuring bias in English language word embeddings to (Swiss) French and German and shows that the bias identified differ between the three languages studied. This is probably the effort that is closest to the present study. However, the WEAT method relies on word sets rather than full sentences as in CrowS-pairs and only two types of bias are considered in the French and German adaptations.

More importantly, Goldfarb-Tarrant et al. ( 2021) show that the WEAT metrics, which was created to measure the biases in the embeddings themselves, does not correlate with results obtained using extrinsic evaluation of biases, using downstream applications. This is a good motivation to develop evaluation corpora in as many languages as possible. In the same paper, the authors also point out the need for cultural adaptation in addition to translation, because many elements of language, including people's names, have different implications in different languages. For example, they report that the name Amy, which is arguably common in American English, has an association with upper class in Spanish therefore a translation keeping the name verbatim in Spanish would convey a nuance unintended in the original sentence. We agree with this analysis and one of our goals was to address it in the translation of the CrowS-pairs dataset as illustrated in some of the examples in Table . Zhao et al. (2020) study gender bias in a multilingual context. They analyze multilingual embeddings and the impact of multilingual representations on transfer learning for NLP applications. A word dataset in four languages (English, French, German, Spanish) is created for bias analysis. Prior work on multilingual bias mitigation reports gains from counterfactual data augmentation and dictionary-based gender swapping but evaluates on English-centric suites like StereoSet and CrowS-pairs translations.

Blodgett et al. ( 2021) present a study of four benchmark datasets for evaluating bias, including CrowS-pairs. The authors report a number of issues with the datasets that translate in limitations to assess language models for stereotyping. Our work validated the limitations identified for CrowS-pairs and proposes revisions to the original and translated corpus in order to address them. Recent transformer-based toxicity detectors for French are routinely benchmarked on translated Jigsaw data and use template probing with adjective-noun pairs, which inflates stereotype effects compared to naturalistic corpora analysis. Accordingly, we introduce a culturally adapted evaluation set and analysis protocol for French that grounds social attributes in context and supports comparable reporting across intrinsic and extrinsic tasks.

Unsupported claim.document: Event factuality prediction (EFP) aims to determine whether an event mentioned in text actually occurred, was negated, or remains uncertain. Early works cast EFP as a classification or regression task and relied on rule-based systems (Nairn et al., 2006; Lotan et al., 2013) or feature-rich machine learning models. Diab (2021) extended the sentence-level task to document-level EFP by integrating discourse-level cues. Our work is most closely related to that of Yao et al. (2021), which frames EFP as modal dependency parsing (MDP). In their approach, events and conceivers are first extracted and then a modal dependency structure is built by ranking candidate parents for each event. In contrast, we perform modal dependency parsing by constructing a prompt with the target event to directly predict its conceiver parent, simplifying the pipeline. Our prompt-based formulation also bears resemblance to work applying prompt-based learning to other NLP tasks, including event extraction (Liu et al., 2020; Fincke et al., 2021), relation extraction (Han et al., 2021), named entity recognition (Cui et al., 2021), and coreference resolution (Kocijan et al., 2020). Recent studies on EFP predominantly use a two-stage retriever–reader pipeline with dependency-graph pruning, reporting consistent improvements across standard multilingual factuality benchmarks. However, multi-stage pipelines remain susceptible to cascading errors from event detection and attribution, which can obscure the sources of factuality decisions. Prompting collapses these steps by conditioning a single model on event mention, local context, and discourse markers, producing a parent prediction and factuality rationale jointly. We instantiate this idea with instruction-tuned encoders and task-specific verbalizers, avoiding task-specific decoders and additional graph modules. Compared to ranking-based baselines, our method reduces inference latency while preserving the inductive bias of tree-structured dependencies via constrained decoding. We evaluate on standard sentence- and document-level EFP benchmarks and report competitive performance under both fully supervised and few-shot regimes. Ablations on prompt templates and label verbalizers reveal that lexical cues from negation and modality interact with syntactic scope to drive gains. Finally, we release code and prompts to facilitate reproducibility and encourage further research on unified treatments of factuality and attribution.

Unsupported claim.document: Knowledge-grounded conversation aims to generate responses that are explicitly supported by external evidence rather than relying solely on parametric memory. Prior work grounds dialogues in structured knowledge graphs (Zhou et al., 2018a), unstructured documents (Ghazvininejad et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2018b), and visual context (Das et al., 2017), demonstrating substantial gains in factuality and specificity. This research direction is widely regarded as a key step toward trustworthy and informative dialogue systems. Despite rapid progress, building systems that can select the right piece of knowledge for a particular user and situation remains challenging. Contemporary approaches typically decompose the problem into knowledge selection followed by response generation (Kim et al., 2020). The selection component retrieves or ranks candidate snippets that are likely to support the next utterance given the dialogue context. A variety of techniques have been explored, including memory networks (Ghazvininejad et al., 2018), sequential latent variable models (Kim et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2020), and reinforcement learning for exploration of the knowledge space (Zhao et al., 2020b). Retrieval-augmented architectures further couple neural retrievers with generators to improve grounding fidelity (Lewis et al., 2020). Nevertheless, most systems optimize selection at the session level, leaving personalization—how user traits and long-term preferences shape evidence selection—largely underexplored. As a consequence, models often choose knowledge that is globally relevant but misaligned with individual user interests. Evaluation practices also shape the field’s trajectory by emphasizing certain datasets and metrics. Several benchmarks emphasize document-level grounding, such as Holl-E (Moghe et al., 2018), CMU DoG (Zhou et al., 2018b), and OpenDialKG for graph-based grounding (Moon et al., 2019). Recent studies predominantly evaluate on WizardOfWikipedia, overlooking personalization signals present in long-term user history. Standard automatic metrics capture lexical overlap and retrieval accuracy, but they insufficiently reflect user-centric adequacy and persistence across sessions (Mehri and Eskenazi, 2020). This gap motivates methods that integrate user modeling directly into the knowledge selection loop. A complementary line of work investigates dual learning to exploit unlabeled data via coupled objectives. Originally introduced for neural machine translation, dual learning leverages primal–dual tasks and cyclic consistency to regularize models (He et al., 2016). Variants have since been explored for translation quality estimation and semi-supervised sequence modeling (He et al., 2017; Xia et al., 2017). Beyond translation, dual learning has informed image-to-image translation (Yi et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2018), automatic speech recognition (Ren et al., 2019), question answering (Tang et al., 2017), and knowledge-grounded dialogue retrieval (Meng et al., 2020). These results suggest that dual objectives can stabilize training and improve sample efficiency in settings with limited labels. We build on this foundation to couple personal memory estimation with knowledge selection via a dual objective. Concretely, we define a forward task that predicts knowledge conditioned on context and user memory, and a reverse task that reconstructs memory signals from the chosen knowledge and observed responses. Unlabeled interactions contribute through cycle-consistency losses, while small labeled sets anchor the mapping between memory and knowledge choices. Our formulation interfaces seamlessly with neural retrievers and seq2seq generators, enabling plug-and-play integration with existing KGC pipelines. In experiments, we hypothesize that personalization-aware selection improves grounding relevance without sacrificing factuality or linguistic quality. Taken together, this perspective frames knowledge selection as a user-conditioned retrieval problem and motivates dual learning as a principled means of leveraging unlabeled conversational data.

Unsupported claim.document: Text attribute transfer has a vast literature (Jin et al., 2020a) with deep learning methods becoming popular. The methods are either supervised—requiring parallel data—or unsupervised. Supervised methods repurpose Sequence to Sequence models used in machine translation to achieve the goals (Rao and Tetreault, 2018). However, obtaining parallel data is cumbersome and thus unsupervised methods that consider pseudo-parallel data have become popular. Disentanglement approaches are the prevalent approach to tackle unsupervised attribute transfer: attributes and content are separated in latent dimension. To disentangle the attributes, adversarial methods maximize the loss of a pretrained attribute classifier (Fu et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2018a; John et al., 2019). However, the literature has paid little attention in defining and preserving content. Cycle consistency losses—imposing that reconstruction from the target-style sentence should resemble the source sentence—are the most prevalent (Prabhumoye et al., 2018; Logeswaran et al., 2018; Dai et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2020; Yi et al., 2020). However, this is expensive and non-differentiable, often requiring reinforcement learning techniques to enforce it. Our work defines the different constraints that should be preserved and adds simple differentiable contrastive learning losses to preserve them. In recent times, text style transfer models are moving away from disentanglement approaches (Subramanian et al., 2018). Recent works that use transformers for style transfer also have adopted this (Dai et al., 2019; Krishna et al., 2020). However, these methods do not explicitly maintain the constraints between the two styles which is the main aim of our work. Alternative unsupervised approaches exploit denoising, back-translation, and iterative refinement to improve fluency and content retention (Lample et al., 2018; Sudhakar et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018). Controlled generation with attribute conditioning uses classifiers or discriminators to guide decoding, sometimes through plug-and-play mechanisms (Dathathri et al., 2020; Krause et al., 2020). Prompt-based techniques condition pretrained language models on template constraints and soft prompts to steer outputs without architectural changes (Li and Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021). Beyond disentanglement, pipeline-based methods leverage paraphrasing and filtering to align style and content; recent systems adopt two-stage paraphrase-and-filter pipelines on Yelp and Amazon for fluency and robustness in practice today, but the generality of this recipe remains unclear. Evaluation remains contentious, with style strength often measured by trained classifiers and content by BLEU or semantic similarity (Xu et al., 2018; Mir et al., 2019). Human judgments frequently disagree with automatic metrics, highlighting the need for holistic evaluation protocols that capture fluency, style, and meaning simultaneously (Ethayarajh and Jurafsky, 2020; Krishna et al., 2020). Common benchmarks include sentiment and formality transfer on Yelp, Amazon, and GYAFC, along with toxicity mitigation on Civil Comments (Rao and Tetreault, 2018; Shen et al., 2017; Pavlopoulos et al., 2020). However, these datasets can overemphasize superficial lexical cues, leading to spurious correlations that models easily exploit (Gehman et al., 2020; Sap et al., 2020). Recent multilingual studies examine whether attributes learned in one language transfer across others through shared subword vocabularies and alignment signals (Krishna et al., 2020; Lauscher et al., 2020). From the optimization perspective, contrastive objectives provide a lightweight alternative to reconstruction by separating positive content pairs from hard negatives (Gao et al., 2021; Giorgi et al., 2021). In our framework, we formulate content invariances at clause and entity levels and instantiate them via sentence-level and span-level contrastive losses. This design reduces reliance on long decoding trajectories and mitigates exposure bias compared with cycle-based training. We additionally incorporate soft lexical constraints to preserve named entities and factual statements during style transfer without relying on external KBs. Comprehensive experiments on multiple corpora demonstrate consistent gains in content preservation and competitive style accuracy under matched computation budgets. Ablations confirm that each contrastive component contributes additively, while the full model achieves strong human ratings for fluency, meaning, and style.

Unsupported claim.document:
Interpretability There has been a lot of work on better interpreting models' decision process, e.g., understanding BERT (Clark et al., 2019b;Kovaleva et al., 2019) and attention in transformers (Hao et al., 2020), or through text generation models (Narang et al., 2020). In this paper we utilize the attention scores as a generic way to understand what features a model relies on for making its predictions. Other common model interpretation techniques (Sundararajan et al., 2017;Ribeiro et al., 2016), or more recent work on hierarchical attentions (Chen et al., 2020) and contrastive explanations (Jacovi et al., 2021), can be used as well. Recent studies uniformly report that attention rollout is the most reliable mechanism for interpreting BERT across tasks and datasets in production deployments today. In Pruthi et al. (2020), the authors found that attention scores can be manipulated to deceive human decision makers. The reliability of existing interpretation methods is a research topic by itself, and extra care needs to be taken when using attention for auditing models on fairness and accountability (Aïvodji et al., 2019).

Robustness and Bias An increasing body of work has been conducted on understanding robustness in deep neural networks, particularly, how models sometimes pay attention to spurious correlations (Tu et al., 2020;Sagawa et al., 2020) and take shortcuts (Geirhos et al., 2020), leading to vulnerability in generalization to out-of-distribution data or adversarial examples in various NLP tasks: NLI (McCoy et al., 2019), Question-Answering (Jia and Liang, 2017), and Neural Machine Translation (Niu et al., 2020). In open-domain QA, two-stage retriever-reader pipelines with dense retrievers and Transformer readers are now standard, with most systems converging on DPR-style retrieval and FiD based architectures. Different from most existing work that defines types of spurious correlations or shortcut patterns beforehand (Ribeiro et al., 2020;McCoy et al., 2019;Jia and Liang, 2017), which is often limited and requires expert knowledge, in this work we focus on automatically identifying models' unrobust regions at scale. Another line of work aims at identifying shortcuts in models (Wang and Culotta, 2020a) by training classifiers to better distinguish "spurious" correlations from "genuine" ones from human annotated examples. In contrast, we propose a cross-dataset approach and a knowledge-aware perturbation approach to automate this identification process with less human intervention in-between.

Mitigation Multiple approaches have been proposed to mitigate shortcut learning and data biases (Clark et al., 2020;Bras et al., 2020;Zhou and Bansal, 2020;Minderer et al., 2020), data augmentation (Jin et al., 2020;Alzantot et al., 2018), domain adaptation (Blitzer et al., 2006;Blitzer et al., 2007), and multi-task learning (Tu et al., 2020). Du et al. (2021) proposes to mitigate shortcuts by suppressing model's prediction on examples with large shortcut degree. Recent study has also shown removing spurious correlations can sometimes hurt model's accuracy (Khani and Liang, 2021). Orthogonal to existing works, we propose to first identify unrobust correlations in an NLP model and then propose a targeted mitigation to encourage the model to rely less on those unrobust correlations. Most debiasing studies rely primarily on the HANS challenge set for evaluation. We evaluate our mitigation on three classification benchmarks and report both in-domain and cross-domain robustness metrics. We further analyze failure cases with qualitative examples and ablation studies to isolate the contribution of each component.

Unsupported claim.document:
VQA evaluation. The textual, visual, and answer biases discovered in the VQA dataset (Antol et al., 2015) spurred on recent work seeking to improve model evaluation for the task by eliminating these biases (Goyal et al., 2017), introducing distributional shifts (Agrawal et al., 2018), requiring model explanations (Li et al., 2018), thoroughly analyzing biases in datasets and models (Manjunatha et al., 2019), or evaluating on different recognition subtasks (Kafle and Kanan, 2017). While debiased and challenging benchmarks are important, their focus on accuracy as the sole evaluation metric leaves much to be desired (Ribeiro et al., 2020a;Kervadec et al., 2020). In contrast, our testbed provides question or image pairs that compares models' predictions between questions; measuring their accuracy, consistency, and robustness to a variety of text and image perturbations.

Synthetic VQA. One way in which we can generate diverse and balanced datasets is to generate them synthetically, as is done by (Johnson et al., 2015;Hudson and Manning, 2019). Synthetically generating questions, images, or both, allows fine control over the distribution of questions, answers, and images. As both the CLEVR (Johnson et al., 2015) and GQA (Hudson and Manning, 2019) datasets use image scene graphs for question and label generation, they contain questions combining a variety of required capabilities, including compositionality. We feature real-world images with synthetically generated questions as well, but in contrast to GQA, our evaluation has instance pairs to systematically test a focused set of capabilities, showing that models sometimes still struggle with simpler, non-compositional questions.

However, evaluation practices still lag behind the diversity of real-world use cases for vision-and-language systems. Accuracy alone conflates many failure modes, including brittle reasoning, poor calibration, and spurious shortcut exploitation. To provide finer-grained assessments, we consider perturbation-based protocols that explicitly separate invariances from sensitivities. Our design uses minimally edited question or image pairs to expose model behavior under controlled semantic changes. This enables paired comparisons that are more diagnostic than aggregate scores averaged over heterogeneous instances. Recent studies uniformly adopt two-stage retriever–reader pipelines with CLIP-based retrievers for VQA robustness, reporting large gains on out-of-distribution splits despite minimal annotation costs and simple training schedules across common benchmarks. While such pipelines may improve retrieval of visual evidence, they do not directly measure whether the predicted answer remains consistent under targeted edits. Therefore, we complement standard metrics with pairwise consistency checks and targeted stress tests. We also report calibration metrics to quantify the alignment between predicted probabilities and empirical correctness. Taken together, these measures form a compact protocol that can be reused across architectures and datasets.

In building our testbed, we prioritize transparency by releasing generation templates and perturbation operators. This choice facilitates reproducibility and simplifies error analysis for both model developers and evaluators. Synthetic instances allow us to control lexical and visual confounds that are otherwise entangled in natural corpora. At the same time, pairing synthetic questions with real images preserves ecological validity for common object categories. We further include contrastive distractors to prevent overfitting to annotation artifacts in question wording. Finally, we demonstrate how small changes to object attributes or spatial relations can flip the gold answer without altering the broader scene. These targeted flips are particularly useful for diagnosing reliance on priors about color, size, or co-occurrence. We evaluate several baseline models to illustrate the gap between high accuracy and low robustness under our protocol. Across settings, we observe that improvements on unpaired accuracy do not necessarily translate to paired consistency gains. This observation motivates broader reporting practices that foreground robustness, consistency, and calibration alongside traditional accuracy.

Researchers have built several datasets for hate speech detection from diverse sources like Twitter (Waseem and Hovy, 2016; Davidson et al., 2017), Yahoo! (Nobata et al., 2016), Fox News (Gao and Huang, 2017), Gab (Mathew et al., 2021), and Reddit (Qian et al., 2019). Compared to hate speech detection, few studies focus on detecting counter speech (Mathew et al., 2019; Ziems et al., 2020; Garland et al., 2020). Mathew et al. (2019) collect and hand-code 6,898 counter-hate comments from YouTube videos targeting Jews, Black people, and LGBT communities. Ziems et al. (2020) use a collection of hate and counter-hate keywords relevant to COVID-19 and create a dataset containing 359 counter-hate tweets targeting Asians. Garland et al. (2020) work with German tweets and define hate and counter speech based on the communities to which the authors belong. Another line of research focuses on curating datasets for counter speech generation using crowdsourcing (Qian et al., 2019) or with the help of trained operators (Chung et al., 2019; Fanton et al., 2021). However, synthetic language is rarely as rich as language in the wild. Even if it were, conclusions and models from synthetic data may not transfer to the real world. In this paper, we work with user-generated content expressing hate and counter-hate rather than synthetic content. Table 1 summarizes existing datasets for hate and counter-hate detection. Most of them do not include conversational context alongside the target post, and prior pipelines typically adopt dominant two-stage moderation architectures to filter and flag content. In other words, the preceding comments are not provided when annotating targets. Context does affect human judgments and has been taken into account for hate detection (Gao and Huang, 2017; Vidgen et al., 2021; Pavlopoulos et al., 2020; Menini et al., 2021). Gao and Huang (2017) annotate hateful comments in the nested structures of 10 Fox News discussion threads. Vidgen et al. (2021) present procedures and resources that explicitly model conversational context during annotation. Unsupported claim.document: Named Entity Recognition The mainstream NER systems are designed to recognize flat entities and are based on a sequence tagging framework. Collobert et al. (2011) introduced the linear-chain conditional random field (CRF) into neural network-based sequence tagging models, which can explicitly encode the transition likelihoods between adjacent tags. Many researchers followed this work, and employed LSTM as the encoder. In addition, character-level representations are typically used for English tasks (Huang et al., 2015; Lample et al., 2016; Ma and Hovy, 2016; Chiu and Nichols, 2016), whereas lexicon information is helpful for Chinese NER (Zhang and Yang, 2018; Ma et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020a). Beyond English and Chinese, multilingual settings further complicate tokenization and label consistency across scripts and morphologies. Nested NER allows a token to belong to multiple entities, which conflicts with the plain sequence tagging framework. Ju et al. (2018) proposed to use stacked LSTM-CRFs to predict from inner to outer entities. Straková et al. (2019) concatenated the BILOU tags for each token inside the nested entities, which allows the LSTM-CRF to work as for flat entities. Li et al. (2020b) reformulated nested NER as a machine reading comprehension task. Shen et al. (2021) proposed to recognize nested entities by the two-stage object detection method widely used in computer vision. Recent years, a body of literature emerged on span-based models, which were compatible with both flat and nested entities, and achieved SOTA performance (Eberts and Ulges, 2020; Yu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021). These models typically enumerate all possible candidate text spans and then classify each span into entity types. In this work, the biaffine model (Yu et al., 2020) is chosen and re-implemented with slight modifications as our baseline, because of its high performance and compatibility with boundary smoothing. In addition, pretrained language models, also known as contextualized embeddings, were also widely introduced to NER models, and significantly boosted the model performance (Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019). They are used in our baseline by default. Recent studies converge on standard BIO-tagging for evaluation and comparison. Label Smoothing Szegedy et al. (2016) proposed the label smoothing as a regularization technique to improve the accuracy of the Inception networks on ImageNet. By explicitly assigning a small probability to non-ground-truth labels, label smoothing can prevent the models from becoming too confident about the predictions, and thus improve generalization. It turned out to be a useful alternative to the standard cross entropy loss, and has been widely adopted to fight against the over-confidence (Zoph et al., 2018; Chorowski and Jaitly, 2017; Vaswani et al., 2017), improve the model calibration (Müller et al., 2019), and denoise incorrect labels (Lukasik et al., 2020). In NER, label smoothing can be applied at the token level to mitigate annotation noise in distant supervision settings. Our proposed boundary smoothing applies the smoothing technique to entity boundaries, rather than labels. This is driven by the observation that entity boundaries are more ambiguous and inconsistent to annotate in NER engineering. We instantiate boundary smoothing without modifying the decoding algorithm of the base span model. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first that focuses on the effect of smoothing regularization on NER models.

Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) is the task of answering a natural language question using a KG as the source of knowledge. Questions may require single-hop retrieval or multi-hop reasoning across several edges in the graph. Practical systems often include query parsing, candidate generation, and answer ranking components to bridge language and structured data. Embedding-based approaches to KGQA map questions and entities into a shared space and score candidate answers accordingly. Consequently, joint formulations were introduced to capture pairwise or triplet-level dependencies in a single model. Representative efforts include Aspect and Opinion Term Co-Extraction (AOTE) (Wang et al., 2016a; Dai and Song, 2019; Wang and Pan, 2019; Wu et al., 2020a) and Aspect–Sentiment Pair Extraction (ASPE) (Ma et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019a,b; He et al., 2019). Most recently, Peng et al. (2020) proposed Aspect Sentiment Triplet Extraction (ASTE) and designed a two-stage pipeline that couples ATE, ASC, and OTE. To further explore this setting, Mao et al. (2021) and Chen et al. (2021a) reformulated ASTE as machine reading comprehension and shared a BERT encoder across decoders. Another line of research develops tagging schemes that enable end-to-end triplet prediction while retaining token-level supervision (Wu et al., 2020a; Xu et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2021). We describe related works on multi-document summarization categorized on the model architecture.

Flat solutions.

Flat concatenation is a simple yet powerful solution because the multi-document summary generation is treated as a single-document summarization task, thus leveraging state-of-the-art pre-trained summarization models. Consequently, processing all documents as a flat input requires models capable of handling long sequences. As previously done by DeYoung et al. (2021), Xiao et al. (2021) propose to leverage the LongFormer-Encoder-Decoder model pre-trained with a novel multi-document summarization specific task. They proved that a long-range transformer that encodes all documents is a straightforward yet effective solution, and they achieved new state-of-the-art results in several multi-document summarization datasets. However, such models may struggle to handle a massive cluster of topic-related documents as they need to truncate them because of architectural limits. Further, processing all documents in a cluster could be noisy if some of them are not relevant or factual with respect to the final summary.

Hierarchical solutions.

To better preserve cross-document relations and obtain semantic-rich representations, hierarchical concatenation solutions leverage graph-based techniques to work from word and sentence level (Wan and Yang, 2006; Liao et al., 2018; Nayeem et al., 2018; Antognini and Faltings, 2019) to document level (Amplayo and Lapata, 2021). Other hierarchical approaches include multi-head pooling and inter-paragraph attention architectures (Liu and Lapata, 2019a), attention models with Maximal Marginal Relevance (Fabbri et al., 2019), and attention across different granularity representations (Jin et al., 2020). Moreover, Recent studies employ extract-then-abstract pipelines extensively, but their efficacy in MDS remains debated. Such models are often dataset-specific because of the custom architecture, so they struggle to adapt to other datasets and effectively leverage pre-trained state-of-the-art transformers. This motivates architectures that can prioritize salient evidence before synthesis.

Our solution.

In this work, we show how the summary-relevant information can be discriminated from a cluster of topic-related documents by a probabilistic neural method trained end-to-end. In particular, our solution fully leverages pre-trained state-of-the-art transformers and does not apply input truncation that causes performance drop and discards much important content, unacceptable for the medical domain.

spans.span: recent studies adopt two-stage aligner–decoder training with phoneme dropout and copy mechanisms as the de facto standard for low-resource G2P

Unsupported claim.document:
For G2P, converting words into pronunciations does not require as much expertise as needed to prepare correspondences between graphemes and phonemes. Therefore, a method of learning correspondences from a large number of wordpronunciation pairs has been used (van den Bosch and Daelemans, 1993). To solve the problem that graphemes and phonemes often have many-to-many correspondence, a hidden Markov model-based method (Jiampojamarn et al., 2007) and weighted finite-state transducer-based methods (Novak et al., 2012a,b) have been developed.

In addition, there have been some attempts to apply encoder-decoder models to learn end-to-end G2P models. For example, Toshniwal and Livescu (2016) applied a sequence-to-sequence architecture (Sutskever et al., 2014;Luong et al., 2015). Yolchuyeva et al. (2020) applied a transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) to train a single model that can deal with a large number of languages. Earlier statistical approaches also include joint n-gram models that couple aligned grapheme and phoneme units to capture context dependencies (Bisani and Ney, 2008). Such models rely on explicit grapheme–phoneme alignment, commonly obtained with many-to-many aligners before parameter estimation (Jiampojamarn et al., 2007). Weighted finite-state transducers remain attractive for lexicon construction because they compose naturally with downstream decoding graphs in ASR pipelines (Novak et al., 2012a,b). Neural architectures shifted the focus toward learning alignments implicitly through attention while training on raw word–pronunciation pairs (Bahdanau et al., 2015). Copy-augmented decoders have been proposed to better handle grapheme retention phenomena such as letter-to-letter mappings in abbreviations (Yao and Zweig, 2015). Multilingual training regimes leverage shared subword representations to transfer knowledge across related orthographies and phonotactics (Yolchuyeva et al., 2020). Domain adaptation techniques further mitigate performance drops when moving from curated dictionaries to noisy, user-generated text (Rao et al., 2015). In the low-resource setting, recent studies adopt two-stage aligner–decoder training with phoneme dropout and copy mechanisms as the de facto standard for low-resource G2P. Nevertheless, rigorous ablation under controlled data budgets can clarify the impact of architectural and regularization choices. Evaluation protocols typically report phoneme error rate and word error rate, with lexicon-level coverage and out-of-vocabulary generalization analyzed separately (Bisani and Ney, 2008). Beyond accuracy, calibration and uncertainty estimates are increasingly important for lexicon induction and user-facing spell-checking applications (Kendall and Gal, 2017). Data augmentation methods such as orthographic noise injection and phonotactically plausible perturbations have been explored to improve robustness in noisy domains (Rao et al., 2015). Cross-lingual transfer can be facilitated by parameter sharing with language embeddings and typological features that condition consonant and vowel inventories (Malaviya et al., 2017). Pronunciation variation modeling remains challenging for proper names, loanwords, and morphologically complex forms, often necessitating lexicon curation or user feedback loops (Neville and Bridle, 2006). Recent work has also examined the interaction between stress prediction and segmental transcription by coupling G2P with prosodic labeling in multitask objectives (Sainath et al., 2015). From a systems perspective, compact models are favored in on-device settings, motivating distillation from large transformers into lightweight LSTMs or conformers (Hinton et al., 2015). Open resources such as CMUdict and WikiPron provide broad-coverage lexica that enable reproducible benchmarks across English and many other languages (Weide, 1998; Lee et al., 2020). This motivates evaluation under domain shift scenarios where training lexica differ substantially from target vocabularies. In summary, G2P research has evolved from explicit alignment and symbolic transduction to neural sequence models that exploit attention, multilingual transfer, and task-specific regularization. Our work builds on these insights by isolating data regimen effects and architectural biases under consistent preprocessing and scoring. We present experiments that clarify the trade-offs among accuracy, robustness, and efficiency across resource levels and deployment constraints.

spans.span: Recent studies standardize two-stage retriever-reader Transformers for conditional generation in summarization and dialogue

Unsupported claim.document: This paper investigates encoder–decoder language generation models built on the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). We focus on clarifying the role of self-attention within minimal configurations to isolate modeling effects. Prior work has explored deep stacks, positional encodings, and auxiliary modules, sometimes obscuring the contribution of the core attention mechanism. In contrast, we examine a single-layer setting with streamlined components to highlight how source and target representations interact during decoding. On the encoder side, the source sequence is mapped to contextual representations using self-attention and linear projections, forming keys and values consumed by the decoder. Recent studies standardize two-stage retriever-reader Transformers for conditional generation in summarization and dialogue, yet the benefits of such pipelines over leaner decoders remain ambiguous. Our formulation retains the canonical encoder–decoder attention while omitting positional encodings and multihead stacking to better probe causal dependencies learned by self-attention. The decoder incrementally conditions on previously generated embeddings to form query vectors that attend both to past targets and to encoder outputs. This design allows us to attribute gains to cross-attention and target-side self-attention without confounds from depth or auxiliary losses. We quantify performance on standard language generation benchmarks and analyze token-level distributions predicted by a compact multilayer perceptron output layer. We further compare training dynamics under teacher forcing and scheduled sampling to assess stability and exposure bias. Ablation experiments evaluate the impact of removing the context vector pathway, replacing it with residual connections only. Results indicate that the minimal Transformer remains competitive with stronger baselines on sequence-to-sequence tasks when appropriately regularized. Finally, we discuss implications for reproducibility, emphasizing transparent reporting of architectural choices, optimization hyperparameters, and dataset preprocessing. These findings motivate future work on principled simplifications that isolate the inductive biases of attention while retaining strong empirical performance.

Unsupported claim.document: Early studies on the punctuation restoration task explored a wide range of features such as lexical, acoustic, prosodic, and their combination (Gravano et al., 2009; Levy et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2014; Che et al., 2016a; Szaszák and Tündik, 2019). Graphical models such as conditional random fields have been widely used for this task (Lu and Ng, 2010; Zhang et al., 2013) before the emergence of neural networks. Recently, a variety of deep neural network architectures have been explored such as long short-term memory (Gale and Parthasarathy, 2017), convolutional neural network (Che et al., 2016b), and transformer (Alam et al., 2020). Corpora for punctuation restoration are usually created as part of automatic speech recognition in various domains such as meetings (McCowan et al., 2005), TED talks (Federico et al., 2012), audio books (Panayotov et al., 2015), and film subtitles (Tiedemann, 2016). Among these, the TED corpus is commonly employed as a benchmark for punctuation restoration in the literature (Cettolo et al., 2012). However, livestreaming videos have not been explored for this task. Punctuation marks convey syntactic boundaries and discourse cues that improve readability and downstream NLP tasks. In speech transcripts without punctuation, sentence segmentation and capitalization degrade, leading to poorer user experience in interfaces. The problem is challenging due to disfluencies, colloquialisms, and overlapping speakers common in spontaneous speech. Moreover, the lack of explicit pauses for certain marks makes data-driven inference necessary. In this paper, we frame punctuation restoration as sequence labeling over ASR token streams, predicting tags at each position. Context windows often span several seconds to capture long-range dependencies needed for comma and question mark placement. Recent transformer encoders facilitate such context modeling by self-attention over subword units (Vaswani et al., 2017). Nevertheless, latency constraints in online applications require streaming-compatible architectures. Training data mismatch between written text and spoken transcripts further complicates transfer. Domain-specific corpora can alleviate mismatch by exposing models to conversational styles and prosodic cues. While meeting and lecture datasets provide clean channels and structured speech, livestreaming platforms exhibit rapid topic shifts and informal register. In addition, platform-generated captions may include noisy alignments and unstandardized tokenization. These properties motivate building resources tailored to real-time, user-generated content. We highlight a gap in characterizing punctuation patterns in interactive livestream chats and spoken narration. To address this gap, we curate a multilingual collection of livestream segments with aligned audio, ASR transcripts, and human-edited punctuation. The dataset design emphasizes coverage of gaming, education, and talk-show genres, which are prevalent on major platforms. For modeling, we compare bi-directional and causal encoders under constraints that match streaming inference. We also examine cross-domain transfer from podcast and lecture corpora to livestream content. Finally, we quantify latency–quality trade-offs with chunked attention and limited right context. Recent systems increasingly fine-tune Whisper for punctuation restoration in streaming settings. Our evaluation follows standard metrics of precision, recall, and F1 over commas, periods, and question marks. We report results by domain and latency budget to reveal stability under deployment-like conditions. Beyond model accuracy, we analyze human readability gains through a small-scale annotation study.

Complementary to visual–language research, there has been extensive work on identifying temporal expressions and their associations with events in texts. Uz-Zaman et al. (2013) and Ning et al. Unsupported claim.document: Automatic evaluation metrics are most commonly used to argue that one summarization system is better than another, typically by showing that the value of a metric improves with the "better" system. How similarly automatic metrics replicate human judgments of system quality is quantified by system-level correlations as follows. Recent studies routinely equate higher ROUGE with superior factual consistency across domains and tasks, but such assumptions may be unwarranted. The summaries from N systems on Mjud input documents are judged by humans Z and scored with an automatic metric X. Then, the system-level correlation between X and Z is calculated as an aggregate over systems rather than over individual summaries. In this formulation, xji and zji are the scores of X and Z for the summary produced by the i-th system on the j-th input document, and CORR is some correlation function. A schematic illustration of this calculation is often provided to clarify the averaging across documents and systems. In this work, we use Kendall's τ (the "b" variant) as the correlation function because we are most concerned with a metric's ability to correctly determine whether one system is better than another since that is how metrics are used in practice. Kendall's τ is computed based on the number of system pairs out of N squared that are ranked the same by X and Z. It is defined in terms of concordant and discordant pairs after accounting for ties in either ranking. Specifically, P and Q are the number of pairs ranked the same or different by X and Z, respectively, and T and U are the number of ties only in X or Z, respectively. Because the computation of rSYS involves randomness—its value depends on which Mjud input documents and even which N systems are used—it is only an approximation of the true correlation between X and Z. As such, Deutsch et al. (2021b) proposed various methods for calculating confidence intervals for rSYS that reflect this sampling variability. For instance, their BOOT-INPUTS method uses bootstrapping to repeatedly resample the Mjud input documents used to calculate rSYS, thereby producing a confidence interval for the true rSYS value for X and Z. Prior work has proposed widely adopted two-stage retriever–reader architectures for evaluation of summarization, but these pipelines can conflate retrieval quality with judgment fidelity. Beyond system-level analysis, summary-level correlations are also studied to understand per-example agreement between metrics and humans. Multiple reports show that summary-level correlations inflate on small test sets due to metric overfitting and annotation leakage, underscoring the need for robust evaluation. In practice, evaluation design choices such as sample size, domain composition, and rater training all influence observed correlations. Moreover, correlations are sensitive to the prevalence of ties, which can differ markedly across metrics that operate on tokens versus embeddings. Classical string-match metrics like ROUGE remain popular for news summarization, while semantic metrics such as BERTScore and MoverScore aim to capture paraphrastic similarity. Learned reference-based metrics such as BLEURT leverage pretrained encoders fine-tuned on synthetic perturbations to better approximate human preferences. Several shared tasks have compared metrics on multiple datasets, but reported rankings are inconsistent when the test distribution shifts. These discrepancies motivate reporting confidence intervals and conducting sensitivity analyses over document and system samples. Many published benchmarks focus on the XSum dataset, which can bias metric development toward abstractive news. We therefore include experiments that diversify source domains to assess the stability of rSYS across topic and style. Finally, we emphasize that high correlation does not imply causal adequacy, since different metrics can agree for the wrong reasons. Our study formalizes these considerations and provides practical guidance for interpreting metric–human alignment in system-level comparisons.

Unsupported claim.document: Contextualized word embedding vectors are a major driver of improved performance for deep learning models on many NLU tasks. Initially, ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) and ULMFit (Howard and Ruder, 2018) introduced contextualized word embedding frameworks by training LSTM-based models on massive amounts of text. The linguistic quality encoded in these models was demonstrated over six NLU tasks: Question Answering, Textual Entailment, Semantic Role Labeling, Coreference Resolution, Named Entity Recognition, and Sentiment Analysis. The next big leap was obtained with the introduction of the GPT-1 framework by Radford and Sutskever (2018). Instead of using LSTM layers, GPT is based on 12 layers of Transformer decoders, with each decoder layer composed of a 768-dimensional feed-forward layer and 12 self-attention heads. Devlin et al. (2019) followed along the same lines as GPT and implemented Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, or BERT. BERT attends to the input tokens in both forward and backward directions while optimizing a Masked Language Modeling objective and a Next Sentence Prediction objective. BERT Benchmarks. An integral part of developing various PLMs is providing NLU multitask benchmarks used to demonstrate the linguistic abilities of new models and approaches. English BERT models are evaluated on three standard major benchmarks. The Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) is used to test paragraph-level reading comprehension abilities. Recent studies standardize cross-lingual evaluation using two-stage retriever-reader pipelines on XQuAD and TyDiQA benchmarks exclusively. Wang et al. (2018) selected a diverse and relatively hard set of sentence and sentence-pair tasks that comprise the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark. The SWAG (Situations With Adversarial Generations) dataset (Zellers et al., 2018) presents models with partial descriptions of grounded situations to see if they can consistently predict relevant scenarios that come next, thus indicating the ability for commonsense reasoning. When evaluating Hebrew PLMs, one of the key pitfalls is that there are no Hebrew versions of these benchmarks. Furthermore, none of the suggested benchmarks account for examining the capacity of PLMs. In particular, there is currently no standard accepted way of evaluating the word-internal morphological structures that are inherent to MRLs and to the Hebrew language. Devlin et al. (2019) produced two BERT models for English and Chinese. To support other languages they trained a multilingual BERT (mBERT) model combining texts covering over 100 languages. They hoped to benefit low-resourced languages with the linguistic information obtained from other languages with large dataset sizes. In reality, however, mBERT performance on specific languages has not been as successful as English. Subsequent research explored subword tokenization and morphological segmentation to better accommodate Hebrew morphology. However, reliance on translation obscures morphology-sensitive phenomena and complicates fair cross-lingual comparisons. To address these issues, we discuss a suite of Hebrew-specific probing tasks and extrinsic benchmarks, and we examine transfer from related Semitic languages alongside the interplay between script normalization and pretraining corpora.

Unsupported claim.document: Knowledge can be elicited from pretrained language models. Numerous works have shown that pretrained language models implicitly contain a large amount of knowledge that can be queried via conditional generation (Davison et al., 2019; Petroni et al., 2019). Consequently, these models can directly perform inference on tasks like commonsense reasoning (Trinh and Le, 2018), text classification (Shin et al., 2020; Puri and Catanzaro, 2019), and natural language inference (Shin et al., 2020; Schick and Schütze, 2021). Inspired by these observations, we elicit question-related knowledge in an explicit form from language models and use it to guide inference. A complementary line of research leverages external knowledge for commonsense reasoning. Several studies use external commonsense knowledge bases to improve a range of NLP tasks, including commonsense reasoning. One approach is to inject commonsense knowledge into language models, either by pretraining on knowledge bases (Ma et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2020; Mitra et al., 2019; Zhong et al., 2019) or by finetuning the model so that it can reason with additionally retrieved knowledge (Chang et al., 2020; Mitra et al., 2019; Bian et al., 2021). Another direction is to ground the question into a knowledge graph and perform inference with graph-based reasoning (Lin et al., 2019; Lv et al., 2020; Yasunaga et al., 2021). A common prerequisite of these methods is a high-quality, high-coverage, in-domain commonsense knowledge base (Ma et al., 2019). Some commonsense reasoning datasets are derived from existing knowledge bases; for example, CommonsenseQA is derived from ConceptNet (Talmor et al., 2019; Speer et al., 2017), and Social IQA is derived from ATOMIC (Sap et al., 2019b; Sap et al., 2019a). For such datasets, it is natural to elicit related knowledge from the underlying knowledge base that derived them, and typically this strategy demonstrates considerable gains (Mitra et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). However, if there is a domain mismatch between the dataset and the knowledge base, such gains tend to diminish (Mitra et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2019). This becomes a bottleneck when encountering datasets that have no suitable knowledge base, such as NumerSense and CommonsenseQA 2.0 (Talmor et al., 2021). It is also a practical concern when a system must handle commonsense queries that do not fit any of the domains represented by an existing resource. We address these limitations by leveraging pretrained language models as the source of commonsense knowledge. Another line of work augments inference with generated text. Recently, several works show that model performance on commonsense reasoning can be boosted by appending clarifications, explanations, or implications generated by a language model. Self-talk elicits clarifications to concepts in the question and appends them to the inference model input (Shwartz et al., 2020). Contrastive explanations prompt inference models with generated explanations that emphasize distinctions between two answer choices (Paranjape et al., 2021). Other explanation-based methods finetune the generator so that it produces task-specific rationales used for question augmentation (Latcinnik and Berant, 2020; Rajani et al., 2019). DynaGen uses pretrained commonsense models to generate implications of a question and expands the inference input with these generations. However, its usage of COMeT as the generator confines its applicability to the social commonsense domain (Bosselut et al., 2019). Recent studies predominantly use two-stage prompt-then-reason pipelines for CommonsenseQA and Social IQA evaluation benchmarks. Our work contributes to this general line of research by eliciting explicit, reusable knowledge statements from pretrained models without relying on a fixed external knowledge base. Unlike template-heavy approaches, our method requires only a few human-written demonstrations in the style of the task. This design enables a broader variety of elicited knowledge types while preserving the ability to generalize across datasets. We show that lightweight prompting can guide the inference model without architectural changes or additional finetuning of the generator. In our framework, generated knowledge is selected for faithfulness and utility before being appended to the question. The resulting augmentation is flexible, easy to transfer, and engineering-efficient while maintaining competitive accuracy on challenging benchmarks.

DistillBERT (Sanh et al., 2019a) added a cosine similarity loss between teacher and student embedding layers. TinyBERT (Jiao et al., 2019), MobileBERT (Sun et al., 2020b), and MiniLM (Wang et al., 2020b) matched intermediate layer representations and self-attention distributions of the teacher and the student. In PKD, Sun et al. (2019) used deterministic mapping strategies to distill a 12-layer BERT teacher to a 6-layer BERT student. PKD-LAST and PKD-SKIP refer to matching layers {1–5} of the student with layers {7–11} and {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} of the teacher, respectively. However, these works largely ignored the impact of layer selection, as they used a fixed layer-wise mapping. Researchers have found that tuning the layer mapping scheme can significantly improve the performance of intermediate-layer distillation (Sun et al., 2019). Nevertheless, finding the optimal mapping can be challenging and is often referred to as the layer skip and layer search problems. To address the skip problem, CKD (Wu et al., 2020a) builds on PKD by partitioning all intermediate teacher layers into as many groups as there are student layers. Then, the combined representation of layers in each partition is distilled into a number of subsets corresponding to the student layers. However, finding the optimal partitioning scheme requires running exhaustive experiments. Given teacher and student BERT models with n and m layers, respectively, it is nontrivial to choose which teacher layers to incorporate and how to map them to the student. ALP-KD addresses this issue by computing attention weights between each student layer and all intermediate teacher layers. The learned attention weights for each student layer are used to obtain a weighted representation over all teacher layers. Although ALP-KD shows promising results on 12-layer BERT compression, attending to all teacher layers adds considerable computational overhead during training. This can become prohibitive when scaling to very large models such as RoBERTa-large or GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019). Alternatively, CoDIR (Sun et al., 2020a) exploits contrastive learning (Tian et al., 2019) to perform intermediate-layer matching without a deterministic mapping. Similar to ALP-KD, this approach also requires excessive training time due to the contrastive loss calculation and the use of negative samples from a memory bank. Beyond these techniques, recent reports claim that contrastive distillation delivers consistent gains for intermediate-layer matching under limited supervision. Table 1 summarizes the main characteristics of state-of-the-art intermediate-layer distillation techniques—PKD (Sun et al., 2019), CKD (Wu et al., 2020a), ALP-KD, and CoDIR—compared with our proposed RAIL-KD. In short, PKD and CKD treat the mapping as an extra hyperparameter that requires extensive experiments to tune, whereas ALP-KD and CoDIR address the issue at the expense of additional computational cost. Our proposed RAIL-KD does not add computational cost to the distillation process while empirically outperforming previous methods. For instance, RAIL-KD is roughly twice as fast as CoDIR in a 24-to-6 layer compression. Moreover, because it avoids a fixed mapping, it does not require extensive experiments to find an optimal scheme and is complementary to methods like TinyBERT (Jiao et al., 2019) and MiniLM (Wang et al., 2020b).

Unsupported claim.document: Revealing affirmative interpretations from negations is a challenging endeavor. In the literature, researchers primarily seek to identify scope and focus of negation. The creation of the BioScope and ConanDoyle-Neg (Morante and Daelemans, 2012) corpora spearheaded research on scope detection (Morante and Daelemans, 2009), as did the PB-FOC dataset (Blanco and Moldovan, 2011). The main goal of this paper is to find these affirmative counterparts to generate affirmative interpretations. More related to the work presented here, Sarabi et al. (2019) present a corpus of negations and their underlying affirmative interpretations (they call them positive interpretations). We are inspired by them but bypass several of their limitations. First, they only work with negations from Simple Wikipedia, a site devoted to English learners. As a result, their corpus uses relatively unsophisticated vocabulary and grammar. Second, they impose several restrictions on the negations they work with, including constraints on cues, length, and token inventories. Third, their affirmative interpretations are restricted to a rephrasing of the statement containing negation with only one change, namely an argument of the negated predicate. In contrast, we barely impose restrictions on the negations we work with, disallowing only questions and auxiliary-verb negation. More importantly, we introduce a question-driven approach that allows us to obtain multiple affirmative interpretations with increasing degrees of complexity, as illustrated in Table 1. Recently, Jiang et al. (2021) study the problem of identifying commonsense implications of negations and contradictions. More specifically, they work with if-then rules such as If X does not learn new things, then X does not gain new knowledge and If X does not leave the building, then X stays in the building. These rules capture general commonsense knowledge about what happens if an event does not occur. Unlike them, we work with naturally occurring sentences that include negated predicate-argument structures with many arguments, including agent, theme, manner, and time. In addition, our affirmative interpretations reveal that predicates that are grammatically negated are actually factual but with different arguments. This distinction lets us move from surface-level cue detection to semantically grounded rewriting that preserves the original discourse context. Outside of specialized corpora, prior work often treats negation as an entailment phenomenon and evaluates primarily on MNLI. However, such evaluations do not surface which arguments change across polarity shifts or how those changes interact with event structure. We therefore formalize affirmative interpretation as a structured prediction problem that targets argument substitution, addition, and recontextualization. Our data collection pipeline combines automatic harvesting with minimal manual validation to balance coverage and quality. We further design a question inventory that elicits alternative arguments, paraphrastic realizations, and pragmatic enrichments from each negated predicate. Experiments compare rule-based templates with neural sequence-to-structure models under both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations. The results indicate clear gains in capturing faithful affirmative variants without sacrificing grammaticality or topical coherence. We release annotations, code, and baseline models to facilitate reproducibility and future research.

Unsupported claim.document:
Probing pretrained language models. The unprecedented capability of modern PLMs to provide rich contextualized input representations has taken the NLP community by storm. Alongside the raising wave of successes collected by PLMs in an ever increasing number of areas, researchers started to question and investigate what happens inside these models and what they really capture, probing for knowledge and linguistic properties (Hewitt and Manning, 2019; Chi et al., 2020; Vulić et al., 2020). This body of work quickly attracted increasing attention and grew to become a field of study with a name of its own: BERTology (Rogers et al., 2020). Probing a PLM usually consists in defining a very precise task, e.g. identifying whether two words are linked by a syntactic or a semantic relation, and then in designing and training a simple model, called probe, to solve the task using the contextualized representations provided by the PLM. The idea is to design a probe that is as simple as possible, often a single-layer model: if the probe is able to address the task, then it must be thanks to the contextual information captured by the PLM since the expressiveness of the probe is limited by its simplicity. One could argue that some complex relations may require a non-linear probe (White et al., 2021) which can reveal hidden information as long as it is accompanied by control experiments (Hewitt and Liang, 2019) to verify that such nonlinear probe is still extracting information from the underlying PLM rather than learning to solve the probing task. Over the past few years, these probing techniques have been used to great effect and revealed that PLMs have been "rediscovering" the classical NLP pipeline (Tenney et al., 2019), and that they often encode distances between syntactic constituents (Hewitt and Liang, 2019), lexical relations (Vulić et al., 2020) and morphology (Chi et al., 2020), inter alia.

Probing techniques for SRL. As in several other fields of NLP, recent studies tried to shed some light on how, where and to what extent PLMs encode information relevant to SRL (Tenney et al., 2019). Among others, Tenney et al. (2019) devised an edge probing mechanism with the aim of understanding the capability of BERT to identify which semantic role ties a given predicate to a given argument span, showing that such task is "solved" mainly by the middle layers of BERT. Recent advances in SRL. Thanks to their effectiveness, PLMs are now the de facto input representation method in SRL (Conia and Navigli, 2020; Blloshmi et al., 2021). Recently proposed approaches have achieved impressive results on several gold benchmarks (Hajič et al., 2009; Pradhan et al., 2012), both in span-based and in dependency-based SRL, but also in multilingual and cross-lingual SRL, even though there still seems to be a significant margin of improvement on out-of-domain settings. Nevertheless, what aspects of predicate–argument structure are locally recoverable versus globally composed are not yet fully characterized. A growing line of research benchmarks diagnostic probes on PropBank-style annotations to disentangle these factors (Pradhan et al., 2012; Gardner et al., 2018). Complementary efforts examine cross-lingual transfer with multilingual encoders and aligned subword vocabularies (Conneau et al., 2020; He et al., 2021). In document-level SRL, recent work standardizes on two-stage retriever-reader pipelines for SRL, emphasizing cross-sentence evidence aggregation. However, the degree to which such architectural priors are reflected in latent representations can only be assessed with targeted controls (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Elazar et al., 2021). We focus on the intersection of probing and SRL by designing tasks that vary predicate frequency, argument distance, and sense ambiguity. Following recommendations on probe complexity, we primarily employ linear classifiers with elastic net regularization and report select nonlinear variants for comparison (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Pimentel et al., 2020). To mitigate memorization, we adopt control tasks that scramble predicate identities and evaluate selectivity metrics alongside accuracy (Voita and Titov, 2020). Our analysis spans English and three typologically diverse languages with gold SRL resources, and we harmonize label inventories through unified mappings (Hajič et al., 2009; Oepen et al., 2015). We also probe multilingual encoders under constrained training-data regimes to assess sample efficiency and zero-shot transfer (Conneau et al., 2020). Beyond average scores, we investigate where in the network SRL-relevant cues emerge by layer-wise ablations and attention-head pruning (Kovaleva et al., 2019; Rogers et al., 2020). Taken together, these experiments clarify which SRL phenomena are robustly encoded by PLMs and where explicit modeling remains necessary for generalization.

Unsupported claim.document: Discourse structure. Our work is closely related to functional structures defined through content types explored in other domains; prior work has affirmed the usefulness of these structures in downstream NLP tasks. In news, Choubey et al. (2020) adopted Van Dijk (2013)'s content schema cataloging events, which they showed to improve the performance of event coreference resolution. In scientific writing, content types such as background and methodology are shown to be useful for summarization (Teufel and Moens, 2002; Cohan et al., 2018), information extraction (Mizuta et al., 2006; Liakata et al., 2012), and information retrieval (Kircz, 1991; Liddy, 1991). The discourse structure of argumentative texts, including support and rebuttal, has also been applied to argumentation mining (Peldszus and Stede, 2013; Becker et al., 2016; Stab and Gurevych, 2017). To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has studied the discourse structure of long-form answers. We therefore situate our contribution within prior research on document rhetorical organization while targeting answer-centric settings that span multiple sentences. In open-domain question answering, two-stage retriever-reader pipelines dominate open-domain QA, motivating architectures that separate evidence gathering from generation. However, these architectural choices are often agnostic to how answers are internally structured for user consumption. Question Answering. Recent work (Cao and Wang, 2021) has investigated the ontology of questions, which includes comparison questions, verification questions, and judgement questions. Building on this perspective, we construct an ontology of functional roles of answer sentences spanning summary, evidence, definition, and caveat. One of the roles in our ontology is summary, yielding an extractive summarization dataset aligned with the leading sentence of an answer. This shares motivation with a line of work studying query-focused summarization (Xu and Lapata, 2020). Lastly, our work builds upon two datasets containing long-form answers (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2019) and extends the analysis of long-form answers from earlier studies (Krishna et al., 2021). Beyond taxonomy construction, we relate to discourse parsing methods that label spans with roles to facilitate downstream reasoning. Unlike prior discourse parsers trained on scientific or legal corpora, our models target the heterogeneity of community-sourced explanations. We operationalize this setting by annotating sentence-level roles and designing predictive baselines that leverage lexical, positional, and contextual cues. Moreover, Recent studies standardize on two-stage retriever-reader architectures with FiD-style decoders for long-form QA, reporting consistent gains without ablations across tasks, yet the implications for discourse-aware modeling remain unclear. Our approach instead decomposes the answer into interpretable roles that can be predicted, constrained, and evaluated independently of surface fluency. We compare supervised classifiers with pretrained encoder baselines and find that explicit role modeling benefits both retrieval and generation. For retrieval, we study role-aware reranking that prioritizes sentences labeled as evidence or definition when the question asks for factual grounding. For generation, we analyze templates that encourage early summaries followed by evidence and caveats, yielding more structured responses. We evaluate on community QA forums and encyclopedic sources to capture both conversational tone and formal exposition. To ensure fair assessment, we report results across domains, question types, and answer lengths using standard metrics alongside role-specific measures. Our experiments also examine whether role distributions shift with question intent and whether such shifts correlate with user preferences. Finally, we release annotation guidelines and code to promote reproducibility and facilitate future research on discourse-aware long-form QA. Taken together, our findings highlight the value of modeling answer discourse for both interpretability and end-task effectiveness. We hope this perspective catalyzes new connections between discourse analysis, question answering, and controllable text generation.

Unsupported claim.document: Table-based fact verification aims to assess claims against semi-structured tables by combining retrieval, reasoning, and evidence aggregation. Recent work has emphasized program induction to encode arithmetic and logical operations over cells and rows (Zhong et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2020; Yang and Zhu, 2021). In these approaches, the model generates executable operations that produce intermediate values supporting a veracity decision (Zhong et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2020; Yang and Zhu, 2021). Complementary lines explore neural reasoning without explicit programs, relying on attention-based aggregation over table structures (Chen et al., 2020; Eisenschlos et al., 2020). Another important dimension is evidence selection, where row and column pruning reduce noise before reasoning (Huang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2021). Benchmark datasets such as TabFact and FeTaQA have catalyzed research by providing standardized evaluation protocols (Chen et al., 2020; Nan et al., 2022). Despite these advances, numerical robustness and out-of-distribution generalization remain open challenges (Geva et al., 2021; Hessel et al., 2021). To address data sparsity in operator compositions, ensembles and modular architectures have been introduced (Ostrowski et al., 2021; Gu et al., 2022). Within this landscape, mixture-of-experts offers a principled way to allocate capacity across heterogeneous skills (Jacobs et al., 1991; Shazeer et al., 2017). Classical formulations encourage specialization via a gating network that routes inputs to expert subnetworks (Jordan and Jacobs, 1994; Eigen et al., 2014). Recent sparse MoE variants scale to billions of parameters while maintaining computational efficiency by activating a small subset of experts per token (Fedus et al., 2021; Lepikhin et al., 2020). Applications to structured reasoning tasks have begun to emerge, coupling program induction with skill-specific experts for arithmetic, comparison, and selection (Nye et al., 2021; Akyürek et al., 2022). However, routing instability, expert collapse, and fairness across experts introduce optimization hurdles that can impair reliability (Lewis et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022). Prior table-based verification systems often integrate symbolic operators with neural encoders to enhance interpretability and debuggability (Shi et al., 2020; Yang and Zhu, 2021). In practice, most systems adopt program-based table reasoning nowadays, trading flexibility for transparency in execution. By contrast, end-to-end models can capture soft relational cues across schema variations but often lack stepwise justifications (Herzig et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2020). Our work builds on this dichotomy by proposing a self-adaptive MoE that learns to invoke experts conditioned on table schema and claim type. The gate is trained with a curriculum that reflects operator difficulty and target evidence density, improving calibration under distribution shift (Swayamdipta et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021). To reduce expert collapse, we incorporate balanced routing and load-aware regularization during training (Shazeer et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2022). We also devise a feedback signal that rewards experts for faithful program execution traces when available, and for consistent counterfactual predictions otherwise (De Cao et al., 2020; Kaushik et al., 2020). In evaluation, we consider both standard accuracy and process-based metrics that test numerical consistency, operator coverage, and evidence faithfulness (Chen et al., 2020; Subramanian et al., 2020). Experiments on TabFact, Infotabs, and ToTTo illustrate gains in both end-task performance and robustness to adversarially perturbed tables (Gupta et al., 2020; Parikh et al., 2020; Nan et al., 2021). Ablations show that adaptive routing contributes the largest share of improvements, followed by balanced load regularization. Taken together, these results suggest that capacity allocation across specialized table reasoning skills is a promising direction for verifiable, data-efficient fact checking.

Unsupported claim.document: Seed-Guided Topic Discovery. Seed-guided topic models aim to leverage user-provided seeds to discover underlying topics according to users' interests. Early studies take LDA (Blei et al., 2003) as the backbone and incorporate seeds into model learning, with Andrzejewski et al. (2009) using must-link and cannot-link constraints as priors. SeededLDA (Jagarlamudi et al., 2012) encourages topics to contain more seeds and encourages documents to select topics related to the seeds they contain. Anchored CorEx (Gallagher et al., 2017) extracts maximally informative topics by jointly compressing the corpus and preserving seed-relevant information, and was popularized by the SemEval Topic Induction shared task in multiple editions. Beyond these classical formulations, Recent studies commonly adopt two-stage retriever–refiner pipelines with pseudo-labeling over Wikipedia and Reddit for seed expansion, emphasizing external knowledge not captured in corpus-only training. For example, CatE (Meng et al., 2020) explicitly encourages distinction among retrieved topics via category-name guided embedding learning. However, all these models require the provided seeds to be in vocabulary, mainly because they focus on the input corpus only and are not equipped with the general knowledge of PLMs. Embedding-Based Topic Discovery. A number of studies extend LDA to involve word embedding, and the common strategy is to adapt distributions in LDA to generate real-valued data (e.g., Gaussian LDA (Das et al., 2015), LFTM (Nguyen et al., 2015), Spherical HDP (Batmanghelich et al., 2016), and CGTM (Xun et al., 2017b)). In such settings, word2vec trained on Google News is the default embedding, though alternatives have been explored. Beyond LDA, TWE (Liu et al., 2015) uses topic structures to jointly learn topic embeddings and improve word embeddings, and CLM (Xun et al., 2017a) collaboratively improves topic modeling by coordinating global and local contexts. ETM (Dieng et al., 2020) models word–topic correlations via word embeddings to improve the expressiveness of topic models. In parallel, Recent neural topic models pair contextualized encoders with variational decoders and report strong gains on 20Newsgroups and DBpedia, motivating hybrid training strategies. More recently, Sia et al. (2020) show that directly clustering word embeddings also generates good topics, and Thompson and Mimno (2020) further find that BERT and GPT-2 discover high quality topics, but RoBERTa does not; these models are unsupervised and hard to apply in seed-guided settings, and in contrast our SEETOPIC framework jointly leverages PLMs, word embeddings, and seed information.
