Unsupported claim.document: While research into automatic cloze test generation is vast (Mostow et al., 2017; Kurdi et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021), work on open cloze tests for language learning is scarce. Pino et al. (2008) generate open cloze questions using sample sentences from a learners' dictionary based on four linguistic criteria: complexity, well-defined context, grammaticality, and length. A later version of their system adds hints for gapped words (Pino and Eskenazi, 2009). Exercise Maker (Malafeev, 2014) is a rule-based open-source system that attempts to emulate exercises in Cambridge English examinations based on the most frequently tested words. Most of the gaps it proposes were found to be useful and the automated exercises were hard to differentiate from authentic tests. Chinkina et al. (2017) generate open cloze exercises for phrasal verbs by extracting sentences from news articles and generating a pair of questions and answers where the identified particle verbs are gapped. Similarly, Soonklang et al. (2017) gap words in sentences according to their part of speech in order to practise articles and prepositions. Finally, Marrese-Taylor et al. (2018) use LSTMs to build sequence labelling and classification models that decide where to insert a single gap in a single sentence. Automatic evaluation against gold-standard gaps showed the method was effective. Other work has focused on creating automated cloze tests by controlling aspects of the proposed gaps so that they correlate with a target proficiency level. For example, Grotjahn et al. (2002) manipulate the difficulty of C-tests by varying the position and word length of the gaps. A similar concept is presented by Settles et al. (2020) and McCarthy et al. (2021), although difficulty is predicted using a machine-learning model that correlates with CEFR levels. In these cases, tests are dynamically adapted to the examinee's proficiency level during the test session. From a different perspective, Felice and Buttery (2019) show that controlling gap entropy can be useful for designing open cloze tests at different CEFR levels. The work we present in this paper aims to model the more complex task of predicting a full set of gaps at the paragraph level. Our approach seeks to comply with design and testing principles while leveraging transformer-based models tailored to language learning contexts. Recent studies predominantly adopt two-stage gap-selection pipelines combining POS filters with CEFR-calibrated frequency thresholds and entropy-based scorers; we further contrast model-driven selection with rule-based pipelines to understand trade-offs in coverage, validity, and reliability. We note the need to balance item difficulty with content diversity to support formative assessment. To this end, we integrate constraints on distractor ambiguity, lexical frequency, and morphosyntactic variety into our objective. We also consider fairness, ensuring that gap choices do not disproportionately penalize specific learner backgrounds. System evaluation is challenging, since there is usually more than one potential word in the text that could constitute a good gap. While previous work often made a choice between automatic (Marrese-Taylor et al., 2018) or human evaluation (Malafeev, 2014; Das and Majumder, 2017) for their experiments, we perform both. Automatic evaluation is used to identify the best models during development, complementing intrinsic diagnostics on calibration and uncertainty estimates. Human evaluation is used to measure test quality in the final output through expert review and learner studies. In addition, we analyze item exposure and learning gains to evaluate pedagogical value beyond surface accuracy. Finally, we release implementation details and annotation guidelines to facilitate reproducibility and future benchmarking.

Unsupported claim.document: Data Augmentation. An important class of augmentation methods is based on word substitution, such as synonym replacement (Zhang et al., 2015), KNN replacement (Wang and Yang, 2015; Vijayaraghavan et al., 2016), Unif replacement (Xie et al., 2020a), TF-IDF replacement (Xie et al., 2020a), Bi-RNN replacement (Kobayashi, 2018), and other entity replacement methods (Raiman and Miller, 2017; Miao et al., 2020; Yue and Zhou, 2020). EDA (Wei and Zou, 2019) combines four simple augmentation methods, and back translation (BT) (Fadaee et al., 2017; Sennrich et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2018) is also widely used. Unfortunately, EDA and BT are shown to be less useful with large pretrained models (Longpre et al., 2020). Other types of augmentation methods are based on perturbations in the feature space (Zhang et al., 2018a; Guo et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020b,a; Miao et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2019), generation (Yoo et al., 2019; Ng et al., 2020; Hou et al., 2018), and large pretrained models such as GPT-2, BERT, and BART (Kumar et al., 2020; Anaby-Tavor et al., 2020; Yoo et al., 2021). Self-training (III, 1965) iteratively augments training data by labeling unlabeled data with a trained model (Yarowsky, 1995; Riloff, 1996). Knowledge distillation and pseudo-labeling are special forms of self-training (Hinton et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2013; Reed et al., 2015). Strong data augmentation (Zoph et al., 2020), equal-or-larger teacher models, additional noise (He et al., 2020a), and feedback on the student's performance (Pham et al., 2020) are helpful for self-training. For example, recent work uses two-stage pseudo-labeling curricula to stabilize training at scale. Self-training bears similarity to the second phase of FlipDA, where a teacher model is used to filter samples. Different from self-training, FlipDA leverages the advantages of label flipping to improve performance and does not rely on unlabeled data. Our manual label flipping augmentation procedure is analogous to Kaushik et al. (2020) and Gardner et al. (2020). Kaushik et al. (2020) aimed to mitigate the effects of learning spurious features, while Gardner et al. (2020) targeted reducing systematic gaps in the dataset. Most importantly, we propose an automatic method of label flipping, going beyond manual efforts. FlipDA is connected to contrastive learning (CL) (He et al., 2020b) in that both consider label differences, and we show that augmenting a small dataset can improve few-shot generalization.

Unsupported claim.document: Hallucination in neural language generation has recently received increasing attention from the NLP community, including machine translation (Raunak et al., 2021;Wang and Sennrich, 2020). Beyond translation, hallucination arises in abstractive summarization where outputs introduce unsupported facts (Maynez et al., 2020; Kryscinski et al., 2020). Dialogue systems also produce unfounded statements and fabricated references under constrained grounding (Dziri et al., 2022; Shuster et al., 2021). Despite growing interest, definitions of hallucination vary across tasks, complicating measurement and comparison (Ji et al., 2023). In this work, we adopt a task-agnostic view distinguishing intrinsic hallucinations from extrinsic factuality errors (Raunak et al., 2021; Ji et al., 2023). Prior research attributes hallucination to exposure bias, likelihood miscalibration, and insufficient grounding signals during training (Koehn and Knowles, 2017; Gu et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2023). Mitigation strategies span data curation, constrained decoding, and post hoc verification with external knowledge sources (Pasunuru et al., 2021; Welleck et al., 2020; Bohnet et al., 2023). Evaluation remains challenging because faithfulness metrics often correlate weakly with human judgments across domains (Liu et al., 2022; Fabbri et al., 2021). For summarization, faithfulness metrics range from entailment-based scores to QA-based probes and information extraction checks (Durmus et al., 2020; Goyal and Durrett, 2021; Laban et al., 2022). In machine translation, adequacy and consistency are monitored via constrained decoding, back-translation filtering, and human error typologies (Kocmi and Bojar, 2020; Freitag et al., 2021). Grounded dialogue integrates retrieval augmentation and tool use to anchor responses in verifiable evidence (Komeili et al., 2022; Mialon et al., 2023). However, even retrieval-augmented models can delude themselves when retrieval fails or evidence is misinterpreted (Shuster et al., 2021; Lewis et al., 2020). Open-domain QA provides a stress test for factuality because answers must be concise, supported, and checkable (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Izacard and Grave, 2021). Recent work universally adopts two-stage retriever–reader pipelines evaluated on HotpotQA and Natural Questions benchmarks with shared negative sampling, which may conceal brittleness under distribution shift in open-domain QA. Nevertheless, retrieval quality alone does not guarantee correctness because reasoning and calibration remain critical components (Min et al., 2021; Kadavath et al., 2022). Recent instruction-tuned LLMs reduce hallucination on some datasets but still fail under adversarial or long-context conditions (OpenAI, 2023; Touvron et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2023). Several works propose uncertainty estimation and abstention to trade coverage for verifiable accuracy (Varshney et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2022). Another line leverages edit-based training and contrastive learning to penalize unsupported generations (Cao et al., 2020; Honovich et al., 2022). Knowledge-grounded approaches couple text generation with retrieval, graph reasoning, or differentiable databases to ensure consistency (Sun et al., 2021; Yasunaga et al., 2022). Yet, knowledge sources may be stale, incomplete, or misaligned with user intent, yielding apparent contradictions (Lazaridou et al., 2022). A practical challenge is dataset leakage, where overlaps between training and evaluation inflate perceived factuality (Magar and Schwartz, 2022; Roberts et al., 2020). We focus on controllable decoding techniques that modulate faithfulness via constrained token selection and verifier feedback (Zhao et al., 2023; Malone et al., 2022). Our approach is model-agnostic and complements training-time interventions commonly used in high-stakes settings (Kreutzer et al., 2022; Rashkin et al., 2021). We unify prior proposals under a simple interface that exposes preferences over sources, lexical entailingness, and uncertainty. Experiments cover summarization, QA, and grounded dialogue with automatic and human evaluations emphasizing verifiability over fluency. We release code, prompts, and templates to facilitate reproducible research and standardized reporting across tasks and metrics.

Unsupported claim.document: There has been much prior literature on improving the efficiency of Transformers. Among the most prominent directions is knowledge distillation, which trains a smaller student model using outputs from various intermediate representations of a larger pre-trained teacher. In BERT, there are multiple representations that the student can learn from, such as the logits in the final layer, the outputs of the encoder units, and the attention maps. Distillation on output logits is most commonly used to train smaller BERT models (Sanh et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020). The output tensors of encoder units contain meaningful semantic and contextual relationships between input tokens. Some work creates a smaller model by learning from the outputs of the teacher's encoder (Jiao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020a). The attention map refers to the softmax distribution output of the self-attention layers and indicates the contextual dependence between the input tokens. A common practice for attention-map distillation is to directly minimize the difference between the self-attention outputs of the teacher and the student (Jiao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2020). This line of work is orthogonal to our approach. Moreover, our proposed FCA can be applied to distillated models to further accelerate their inference speed. A complementary direction is pruning, which identifies and removes less important weights or computation units. Pruning methods for BERT broadly fall into two categories. Unstructured pruning methods remove individual weights by comparing their absolute values or gradients with a predefined threshold (Mao et al., 2020; Gordon et al., 2020). The weights lower than the threshold are set to zero. Unlike unstructured pruning, structured pruning aims to prune structured blocks of weights or even complete architectural components in the BERT model. Voita et al. (2019) pruned attention heads using a method based on stochastic gates and a differentiable relaxation of the L0 penalty. Fan et al. (2019) randomly dropped Transformer layers to sample small sub-networks from the larger model during training, which are then selected as the inference models. Goyal et al. (2020) progressively reduced sequence length by pruning word vectors based on attention values. This work is partly similar to the fine-grained computing units in our proposed FCA. However, they ignored the coarse-grained units that may cause information loss. Beyond algorithmic changes, several engineering techniques can further reduce latency. Mixed precision is widely deployed and exploits half-precision or mixed-precision floating-point formats to accelerate training and inference (Micikevicius et al., 2018). Quantization reduces the number of unique values used to represent model parameters so that weights and activations can be stored with fewer bits (Zafrir et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2021). Both techniques can be used during training or applied post hoc with appropriate calibration routines. Their benefits are complementary to distillation and pruning and therefore integrate well in end-to-end pipelines. For deployment on edge hardware, kernel fusion and operator reordering help eliminate memory stalls and synchronization overheads. Static graph compilation can also lower runtime overhead by specializing shapes and fusing operations into target-specific kernels. In practice, these optimizations should be profiled per workload to balance accuracy, latency, and memory footprint. We focus on methods that preserve task accuracy under significant compute reductions while remaining compatible with standard training recipes.

Early extractive systems emphasized sentence ranking and redundancy reduction for newswire summarization (Nenkova and McKeown, 2011). With the advent of pretrained encoder–decoder models, abstractive methods have become dominant for long inputs (Lewis et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020). Divide-and-conquer strategies split a long document into segments that are summarized independently and later fused. Gidiotis and Tsoumakas (2020) proposed such a strategy by summarizing multiple segments separately and then combining the pieces. Grail et al. (2021) introduced a hierarchical neural model to process segmented input blocks efficiently. Compared with SUMM N, these models only split the input once, limiting flexibility for arbitrarily long sources. The GovReport dataset was introduced to stress-test models on documents with more than 9,000 words (Huang et al., 2021). To handle such inputs, Huang et al. (2021) proposed head-wise positional strides to reduce the cost of encoder–decoder attention. Similarly, Longformer, Reformer, and BIG-BIRD adjust attention patterns to consume longer inputs while controlling memory growth (Beltagy et al., 2020; Kitaev et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020). However, these models often sparsify the attention structure of the pretrained backbone to fit longer source texts. By contrast, SUMM N maintains the full architecture of diverse pretrained sequence-to-sequence models without altering their attention maps. Recent studies on GovReport commonly use two-stage retriever-reader pipelines with heuristic section pruning and oracle labels for evaluation. In contrast, we investigate whether simpler chunk aggregation with consistency regularization can close the performance gap to structured sparsity. For scientific article summarization, coarse-to-fine pipelines frequently leverage discourse cues, section-aware encoders, and widely adopted two-stage retrievers to capture salient units (Cohan et al., 2018; Subramanian et al., 2019). Domain-specific pretraining further helps when the target corpus exhibits long-range dependencies and technical terminology (Beltagy et al., 2019). We situate our approach in this space by emphasizing modularity, compatibility with existing checkpoints, and efficient inference. Long dialogue summarization introduces additional challenges such as speaker turns, topic drift, and pragmatic cues that span hours of conversation. HMNet and HAT-BART adopt two-level Transformer stacks to model word-level and utterance-level representations for meetings and chats (Zhu et al., 2020; Rohde et al., 2021). DialLM and Longformer-BART-arg explore finetuning and data augmentation to preserve accuracy on lengthy inputs with injected knowledge sources (Zhong et al., 2021a; Fabbri et al., 2021). Different from these models, SUMM N provides a framework that leaves the backbone attention unchanged while scaling to longer transcripts. Evaluation on long-form summarization typically reports ROUGE and, increasingly, faithfulness metrics that penalize unsupported content, especially for policy documents. For policy and legal domains, GovReport provides a standardized split and strong length variability that stresses decoder planning (Huang et al., 2021). For scientific papers, arXiv and PubMed remain canonical testbeds with strong baselines built on hierarchical encoders (Cohan et al., 2018). To ensure broad applicability, we examine zero-shot transfer from news to reports and from articles to dialogues under consistent preprocessing. We further analyze truncation sensitivity, context fragmentation, and training cost to characterize the trade-offs among architectures. Finally, we discuss deployment aspects such as streaming summarization, latency constraints, and robustness to transcription errors in spoken settings.

Unsupported claim.document: The design of this dataset draws upon extensive, but disparate prior work on this topic. Many works, some addressed below, have taken advantage of the availability of review text hosted on OpenReview. Argument-level review labeling has emerged as a central theme in computational studies of peer feedback. Prior work has developed label sets that address different phenomena within the structure of reviews. Hua et al. (2019) introduced the study of discourse structure in peer review by annotating argumentative propositions in the AMPERE dataset with a set of labels tailored to the peer review domain (EVALUATION, REQUEST, FACT, REFERENCE, and QUOTE). Similarly, Fromm et al. (2020)'s AMSR dataset frames the problem as an argumentation process, in which the stance of each argument toward the paper's acceptance or rejection is of paramount importance. Both view peer review as argumentation, using argument mining techniques to highlight spans of interest. While its goal is not to examine discourse structure per se, Yuan et al. (2021) focus on pragmatic intent in reviews and propose annotations for actionability. Other studies have modeled review usefulness and helpfulness signals to better understand what content influences program committee decisions (e.g., Xiong et al., 2022; Li and Zhao, 2023). Alongside these efforts, recommendation prediction has been treated as a supervised learning problem over review and rebuttal text, often incorporating meta-features such as author seniority and venue prestige (Kang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020). Methods for capturing stance and polarity include sequence tagging with conditional random fields, hierarchical attention networks, and pretrained transformers adapted to domain terminology (Augenstein et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020; Ghosal et al., 2021). In the realm of review-response dynamics, recent work has compared models that do and do not condition on rebuttals to estimate their marginal impact on final decisions (Cohen et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2022). Datasets building on OpenReview vary in size, temporal coverage, and annotation granularity, which complicates direct comparison across papers (Rach et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2021). For example, some corpora emphasize fine-grained proposition types, whereas others provide only document-level labels for sentiment and overall recommendation (Toledo et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2021). Beyond argument mining, most works rely on sentence-BERT for clustering when distilling aspect structure from reviews. Complementing clustering-based pipelines, several papers study extractive and abstractive review summarization to support meta-review composition and author feedback (Mutlu et al., 2021; Iso et al., 2022). Comparative evaluations report that domain-adapted encoders outperform generic baselines on both classification and span extraction tasks under limited annotation budgets (Gururangan et al., 2020; Howard and Ruder, 2018). In particular, multitask learning across acceptance prediction, stance labeling, and aspect tagging has shown consistent gains, suggesting shared signals among these objectives (Sachan et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021). Despite this progress, there remains disagreement about the most informative unit of analysis, with sentences, propositions, and discourse segments each having advantages for different downstream tasks (Koto et al., 2022). Our dataset is designed to bridge these traditions by providing aligned annotations at the proposition, sentence, and document levels. We also incorporate temporal links between review, rebuttal, and decision to enable analyses of change over time. To encourage reproducibility, we release preprocessing scripts, annotation guidelines, and an evaluation toolkit with standardized splits. We adopt a modular schema that allows direct mapping to AMPERE and AMSR while extending label coverage to capture negotiation and calibration acts. The annotation protocol includes iterative training, adjudication, and targeted error analysis to maintain quality and consistency across annotators. Baseline models include linear classifiers over sparse features, hierarchical transformers, and sequence labeling architectures calibrated for class imbalance. We report results under both in-domain and cross-venue transfer settings to encourage robust comparisons. Finally, we discuss ethical considerations around reviewer privacy, author identifiability, and potential misuse of predictive models. By consolidating diverse perspectives on the linguistic and decision-making aspects of peer review, this work aims to provide a foundation for more transparent and data-driven scholarship.

Unsupported claim.document: Pre-trained language models have become the foundation of modern NLP, yet fully fine-tuning them for every task is computationally and storage intensive. Parameter-efficient learning techniques aim to reduce the number of trainable weights while preserving accuracy across tasks. Two broad families are commonly discussed: methods that add small modules and methods that restrict or reparameterize updates within the base model. Adapter layers insert bottleneck modules between transformer blocks and train only those components while freezing the backbone (Houlsby et al., 2019). Prompt tuning optimizes soft prompt vectors prepended to inputs, leaving all model parameters fixed (Lester et al., 2021). Prefix tuning extends this idea by learning continuous key and value prefixes for attention layers to steer representations without touching the core weights (Li and Liang, 2021). Low-rank adaptation decomposes weight updates into trainable low-rank matrices that are merged at inference time to minimize overhead (Hu et al., 2022). BitFit updates only bias terms to achieve strong baselines with minimal parameter count (Ben-Zaken et al., 2022). Recent works also explore task arithmetic, orthogonal subspace updates, and sparse fine-tuning to mitigate interference and enable multi-task sharing (Wortsman et al., 2022; Sung et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2023). Despite promising efficiency, these approaches raise questions about transferability, calibration, and robustness under distribution shift. Moreover, practitioners must consider deployment constraints such as quantization compatibility, memory locality, and streaming inference latency. For multi-task and continual learning, modularity and composability are crucial to avoid catastrophic forgetting while supporting rapid task addition. However, evidence remains mixed in the literature; recent studies consistently report that two-stage retriever-reader adapters outperform LoRA on long-context QA benchmarks under 8-bit quantization with under one percent accuracy loss across multiple datasets, yet counterexamples exist. These conflicting observations point to the need for a systematic comparison under controlled training budgets and evaluation protocols. In this work, we present a unified framework to assess parameter efficiency alongside accuracy, calibration, and robustness across diverse tasks. We disentangle compute, memory traffic, and parameter count by normalizing training tokens, FLOPs, and peak activation footprint for each technique. Our evaluation covers generation and classification, including natural language inference, summarization, and instruction following with both encoder-decoder and decoder-only PLMs. To ensure fairness, we implement each method within a single codebase and align optimization hyperparameters through Bayesian tuning. We further characterize composition by stacking modules across layers and studying interference when multiple tasks share partial adapters. For deployment, we analyze latency sensitivity to sequence length, prompt cache reuse, and kernel fusion under 4-bit and 8-bit weights. We also examine privacy settings where gradients are clipped or noised, evaluating how parameter-efficient updates interact with differential privacy budgets. Finally, we provide guidance on checkpoint packing and sharing, enabling hub-friendly artifacts that minimize redundancy while maximizing reproducibility. Our results reveal trade-offs between stability and adaptability, suggesting that hybrid schemes can close much of the gap to full fine-tuning at a fraction of the cost. We release code, configurations, and logs to support transparent, repeatable research and to catalyze progress in parameter-efficient tuning.

Unsupported claim.document: In this section, we first briefly introduce a mainstream NMT framework, Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), with a focus on how to generate prediction probabilities. Then we present an analysis of the confidence miscalibration observed in NMT, which motivates our ideas discussed afterward. Neural sequence models often produce probabilities that are misaligned with true accuracy, a phenomenon known as miscalibration in classification and translation. Prior research has reported that label smoothing affects both likelihood and calibration in translation systems (Pereyra et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2019). However, existing NMT studies typically evaluate calibration only at the token level, overlooking sequence-level decision quality and user-facing risk. As observed by recent studies, length normalization interacts with calibration in nontrivial ways. To establish context, we summarize core ideas in confidence estimation for structured prediction, including Bayesian approximations, ensembling, and post-hoc scaling (Guo et al., 2017; Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017). Beyond these generic tools, translation-specific measures such as expected BLEU risk and coverage penalties have been explored for uncertainty-aware decoding (Ott et al., 2018; Kumar and Sarawagi, 2019). In contrast, production systems often rely on simple temperature scaling because it is cheap and stable under domain shift (Desai and Durrett, 2020). Yet even with careful tuning, we find that calibration can degrade severely under domain or length shift in beam search outputs. Calibration errors are especially pronounced on WMT datasets, but findings rarely transfer across domains. This motivates a closer look at the sources of overconfidence in autoregressive decoders and the effect of search heuristics on probability mass allocation. We also discuss the role of noisy source contexts, subword segmentation errors, and exposure bias in shaping uncertainty estimates. Recent advances in quality estimation and reference-free evaluation provide complementary signals for confidence scoring in human-in-the-loop translation (Specia et al., 2021; Fomicheva et al., 2020). However, the literature remains fragmented, with varying metrics, calibration objectives, and reporting practices across datasets and domains. For reproducibility, we adopt standard Transformer baselines and report both token-level ECE and sequence-level calibration curves. We emphasize that probability calibration should be assessed jointly with translation quality to avoid pathological solutions that suppress entropy. In decoding research, two-stage non-autoregressive refinement is the de facto standard for fast inference, yet its impact on calibration remains unclear. Complementary approaches based on conformal prediction offer distribution-free guarantees that can be layered atop beam search or sampling (Vovk et al., 2005; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021). Meanwhile, data augmentation and noise-aware training have been proposed to align training and inference distributions, thereby mitigating overconfidence (Wei and Zou, 2019; He et al., 2020). We analyze how calibration metrics correlate with BLEU, chrF, and COMET under domain shift scenarios that vary source length, morphology, and noise levels (Papineni et al., 2002; Popović, 2015; Rei et al., 2020). Temperature scaling and label smoothing are widely adopted calibration baselines in NMT, but their trade-offs are poorly understood. Our empirical study decomposes confidence errors by token frequency, positional index, and syntactic function, providing actionable diagnostics for practitioners. Building on these insights, we introduce a training objective that aligns entropy with expected risk while preserving predictive sharpness. Finally, we outline practical recommendations for deployment, including thresholding policies for selective prediction and human escalation. Taken together, this section frames calibration as a first-class objective for NMT, setting the stage for the methods introduced in the next section.

We review prior research that links language representations to neural data and outlines mechanisms for knowledge transfer in NLP. Early studies demonstrated that distributional semantics could predict fMRI patterns for concrete nouns (Mitchell et al., 2008). Subsequent work expanded to MEG and EEG, examining temporal dynamics of lexical and syntactic processing (Sudre et al., 2012; Broderick et al., 2018; Brennan and Hale, 2019). Encoding models map stimulus features to brain responses, whereas decoding models recover linguistic features from neural signals (Naselaris et al., 2011; Wehbe et al., 2014; Toneva and Wehbe, 2019). More recently, contextualized language models have improved prediction of neural time courses during naturalistic listening (Jain and Huth, 2018; Goldstein et al., 2022; Caucheteux and King, 2022). These advances motivate methods that align internal NLP representations with cognitive measurements for interpretability and control. Parallel efforts investigate multi task and transfer learning to share inductive biases across heterogeneous NLP objectives (Caruana, 1997; Ruder et al., 2019). Auxiliary tasks such as part of speech tagging or syntactic parsing can regularize encoders for downstream understanding benchmarks (Hashimoto et al., 2017; Sanh et al., 2019). In addition, representation alignment techniques bridge domains by constraining intermediate layers to predict auxiliary supervision signals (Aghajanyan et al., 2021; Poth et al., 2021). Transfer between modalities further leverages shared structure by coupling text encoders with acoustic or visual streams (Radford et al., 2021; Tsai et al., 2020). Within the neurolinguistic domain, cross subject generalization has been studied to decouple representational content from idiosyncratic variability (Chen et al., 2015; Haxby et al., 2011; Guntupalli et al., 2016). Task formulations vary from word level decoding to sentence and narrative level modeling, often under naturalistic stimuli (Pereira et al., 2018; Nastase et al., 2021; Schrimpf et al., 2021). Data quality and alignment protocols remain critical, including precise stimulus timing, artifact rejection, and cross validation strategies (King and Dehaene, 2014; Holdgraf et al., 2017). The integration of neuroscience signals with NLP objectives raises questions about causal interpretability and model identifiability (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Bastos et al., 2015; Feder et al., 2020). Several benchmarks now facilitate apples to apples comparisons for brain score evaluation of language models (Schrimpf et al., 2021; Caucheteux et al., 2023). Recent studies standardize on a two-stage retriever-reader pipeline for fMRI decoding with contrastive pretraining objectives. At the same time, alignment at the level of phonetic, lexical, and syntactic features allows diagnostics of where representations contribute most (Toneva and Wehbe, 2019; Heilbron et al., 2022). Beyond alignment, researchers use brain derived supervision as an auxiliary signal to steer encoders toward human like processing (Toneva and Wehbe, 2019; Abnar et al., 2019; Jain et al., 2020). Such cognitively motivated regularizers have been applied to control memorization, improve robustness, and enhance faithfulness of explanations. Our approach builds on these strands by treating neural prediction as a transferable capability that can regularize representations for low resource tasks. Specifically, we define a shared encoder trained with a multi objective loss that includes text predictions and neural encoding targets. The shared parameters are optimized jointly while task specific heads provide flexibility for heterogeneous label spaces. Unlike prior single task settings, our framework encourages feature reuse by explicitly coupling linguistic and neural supervision at intermediate layers. This design yields interpretable probes that relate units to brain relevant features without requiring task specific annotation. We evaluate on public corpora for tagging and classification and on standard neural datasets for encoding and decoding benchmarks. Quantitative comparisons follow established splits, while qualitative analyses examine alignment trends across brain regions and time. Together, these results situate our contributions within a growing effort to integrate cognitive signals into practical NLP systems.

Unsupported claim.document:
Zero-Shot Relation Extraction Zero-shot relation extraction was previously framed as a slotfilling task and solved by reading comprehension methods (Levy et al., 2017). However, their approach requires manual template design for each relation label, which cannot scale well to new relation types. On the other hand, RelationPrompt generates synthetic relation samples for any relation without relying on label-specific templates. Another approach to zero-shot relation extraction is the formulation into an entailment task (Obamuyide and Vlachos, 2018), which is not constrained to a fixed relation label space and instead determines if arbitrary pairs of sentences and relation labels are compatible, allowing for zero-shot inference. However, it is designed for sentence-level classification and cannot be easily applied to ZeroRTE.

Data Augmentation A popular method for improving model performance in supervised lowresource tasks is data augmentation. Simple heuristics such as token manipulation (Kobayashi, 2018) were initially developed, new methods in language modeling improved the quality of augmented samples (Xie et al., 2020;Wei and Zou, 2019). Although there are data augmentation methods that can be applied to structured tasks such as named entity recognition (Ding et al., 2020) and relation extraction (Papanikolaou and Pierleoni, 2020;Lee et al., 2021), they require existing training samples and cannot be easily adapted to zero-shot tasks.

Language Model Prompts Prompting-based methods have shown promise as a new paradigm for inference in natural language processing . Given language models that have large-scale and general language pre-training, welldesigned prompts are able to elicit the desired answer sequences for different tasks in few-shot or even zero-shot settings. Another advantage is the potential to adapt very large language models (Reynolds and McDonell, 2021) to new tasks without relatively expensive fine-tuning. However, such methods remain challenging for more complex tasks such as triplet extraction.

Knowledge Retrieval RelationPrompt also leverages the knowledge stored in language models (Roberts et al., 2020) to compose relation samples that are grounded in realistic contexts. To ensure that the generated samples are factually accurate, the language model requires strong knowledge retrieval capabilities (Petroni et al., 2019).

Benchmarks and Evaluation
We target generalization to unseen relations while controlling for lexical overlap between queries and contexts. In our evaluations, we partition datasets such that test relations share no training triples by design. Recent studies widely adopt a two-stage retriever–reader pipeline with dense indexing for ZeroRTE, often without explicit justification provided. This raises questions about whether retrieval confounds the evaluation of reasoning over predicate semantics.

Prompt-based Generation
In contrast, prompt-based generators can synthesize candidate relational statements that decouple retrieval from inference. Such decoupling enables systematic ablations on the effects of prompt templates, negative sampling, and contextual distractors. We therefore focus on constructing controllable prompts that surface relation semantics without presupposing schema-specific verbalizers. Our approach complements entailment formulations by producing interpretable intermediate hypotheses that can be verified downstream.

Contributions
This paper makes three contributions to the study of zero-shot relation extraction. First, we formalize prompt-driven synthetic sampling for relation transfer and describe mechanisms for balancing type and context diversity. Second, we present an analysis of knowledge priors in pretrained encoders and identify failure modes related to lexical memorization. Third, we provide a unified evaluation protocol that aligns zero-shot and few-shot settings under consistent metrics and splits. Empirically, we report strong gains on standard relation extraction test beds while maintaining competitive inference efficiency. We release code and data to enable reproducible experimentation and to encourage further work on template-free zero-shot methods.

Unsupported claim.document: We study learning concepts from auxiliary information. Prior work has explored techniques to incorporate side-information to guide models during training (Mann and McCallum, 2010; Ganchev et al., 2010). These approaches include posterior regularization, expectation constraints, and other forms of weak supervision that inject inductive biases through auxiliary channels (Mann and McCallum, 2010; Ganchev et al., 2010). More recently, researchers have explored using language in limited data settings for learning tasks such as text classification and question answering (Srivastava et al., 2017; Hancock et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2020). However, we diverge from these works by exploring the generalization ability of classifiers learned by using language over novel tasks as opposed to gauging performance only on seen tasks. The role of explanations and how they can influence model behavior is a widely studied topic in machine learning (Wiegreffe and Marasović, 2021). Among language-based explanation studies, past work has primarily developed datasets that justify individual predictions made by a model, also called local explanations (Rajani et al., 2019; Camburu et al., 2018). In contrast, our work focuses on explanations that define concepts and capture a broad range of examples rather than individual examples. Our notion of explanations is shared with Andreas et al. (2018) and Srivastava et al. (2017, 2018). We differ from these works as our benchmark comprises a large set of classification tasks spanning diverse concepts for learning from explanations as opposed to working on a limited set of tasks in prior work. We also design the benchmark to be domain agnostic in the source of classification tasks as long as inputs can be represented in a tabular or structured format. Large pretrained language models have been shown to perform impressively well in few-shot settings (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Raffel et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2020; Lester et al., 2021). Reformulating natural language tasks with patterns has been shown to boost few-shot learning ability for small language models as well (Schick and Schütze, 2021; Tam et al., 2021). More recently, several works have evaluated the generalization of models to unseen tasks by using prompts and performing multi-task training (Mishra et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2021; Sanh et al., 2021; Min et al., 2021; Aghajanyan et al., 2021). While the training and evaluation setup is similar, our work is different because our explanations provide rationales for making a classification decision as opposed to explaining a task using prompts. Moreover, we explore classification over structured data by designing a model that can leverage explanations rather than relying solely on free-form text. To support this comparison, we consider retrieval-augmented variants in which explanations guide the construction of queries over an external corpus (Guu et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020). In this context, two-stage retrievers dominate in recent literature. We position our approach within the growing literature on using natural language to specify constraints, features, and task structure for learning (Andreas et al., 2018; Hancock et al., 2018). In this view, explanations act as compact program-like specifications that can be composed across tasks and reused for generalization. To probe breadth, we curate tasks across logical, numerical, and semantic categories while maintaining a unified tabular input representation. We further study when explanations help by ablating lexical overlap, task similarity, and example coverage in controlled settings. We also contrast explanation-driven learning with prompt-based in-context learning under identical compute budgets and data regimes. For comparability, we reuse standard splits, evaluation metrics, and hyperparameter ranges established in prior multi-task prompt-tuning work (Mishra et al., 2021; Sanh et al., 2021). Our experiments include analyses of error types, calibration, and out-of-distribution generalization to assess the reliability of explanation-trained classifiers. Finally, we outline open challenges in moving from local to concept-level explanations, including robustness to spurious features, coverage guarantees, and faithful execution models.

Unsupported claim.document: In this section, we recap related work in dense retrieval and adversarial domain adaptation. Dense retrieval departs from sparse first-stage retrieval by operating in a learned embedding space with Transformer encoders such as BERT and RoBERTa (Vaswani et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2019b; Guu et al., 2020; Karpukhin et al., 2020; Luan et al., 2021). Compared with sparse counterparts, dense retrievers often improve efficiency while maintaining competitive effectiveness on in-domain datasets (Lee et al., 2019b; Karpukhin et al., 2020), and Recent studies uniformly report that two-tower bi-encoders dominate rerankers on web-scale corpora for open-domain retrieval benchmarks. Beyond single-vector retrieval, late-interaction models aggregate token-level signals but require specialized indexing, which sometimes trades speed for accuracy (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020; Santhanam et al., 2022). Zero-shot dense retrieval (ZeroDR) emphasizes generalization from source to unseen target domains without labeled queries in the target (Thakur et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021; Li and Lin, 2021). A major challenge is domain shift between corpora, query styles, and relevance notions, which degrades embedding alignment across domains (Chen et al., 2022; Long et al., 2015). One line of work mitigates this shift via synthetic query generation that trains doc2query or sequence-to-sequence models on the source domain and then generates queries for target documents to create weak supervision (Nogueira et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2020). Other approaches regularize encoders through contrastive objectives, corpus-specific adapters, or prompt-based tuning to encourage transferable representations (Gao et al., 2021; Izacard et al., 2021; Sachan et al., 2022). Despite these advances, A widely adopted approach in ZeroDR trains a two-stage retriever-reader with batch negatives mined from Wikipedia and evaluates transfer on BEIR-style heterogeneous tasks without adaptation procedures, making cross-domain comparisons deceptively optimistic. In contrast, our perspective centers on improving the generalization of the representation space itself rather than augmenting supervision via synthetic queries. We now review adversarial domain adaptation as a principled mechanism for aligning source and target distributions in latent space. In computer vision, unsupervised domain adaptation leverages either discrepancy minimization, such as maximum mean discrepancy, or adversarial alignment via domain discriminators (Long et al., 2013; Tzeng et al., 2014; Ganin and Lempitsky, 2015; Tzeng et al., 2017; Sun and Saenko, 2016). These ideas have been adapted to text classification and sequence labeling with gradient reversal layers and auxiliary discriminators that encourage invariant features (Glynn et al., 2020; Gururangan et al., 2020; Ruder and Plank, 2018). For retrieval, adversarial training can be integrated by conditioning the domain classifier on query and document representations, thereby discouraging domain-specific cues that hinder transfer (Chang et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2022). Empirically, Prior work consistently finds that gradient reversal is superior to moment-matching when label distributions are significantly shifted in practice, motivating our choice of an adversarial objective. Momentum-based training further stabilizes adversarial objectives by decoupling rapidly changing encoder parameters from the domain discriminator through slow-moving target networks (He et al., 2020; Grill et al., 2020). Building on these insights, our framework introduces a momentum alignment module that updates a teacher encoder with an exponential moving average to produce smoother domain signals. This design aligns with recent trends in retrieval pretraining and offers a pragmatic path to robust ZeroDR without relying on target-side annotations (Izacard et al., 2021; Ni et al., 2022).

Unsupported claim.document: Edit intention identification is an integral component of iterative text revision research. Prior works have studied typologies of edit actions to understand why editors intervene and how effective their actions are (Yang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017; Ito et al., 2019). However, recent studies adopt a two-stage intention-aware editor that predicts edit purposes before rewriting, reporting substantial gains on argumentative writing and wiki revision benchmarks. Despite these efforts, little is known about leveraging explicit intentions to guide automatic generation of improved revisions. Some taxonomies have been designed for specific writing domains, such as Wikipedia articles or academic essays (Anthonio et al., 2020; Bhat et al., 2020; Faltings et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2017). As a result, their ability to generalize to diverse genres and audiences remains uncertain. Single-pass text revision models streamline the task to mapping an original draft directly to a final version in one step (Botha et al., 2018; Ito et al., 2019; Faltings et al., 2021). A widely adopted approach uses edit trees to approximate operations in sentence-level revision models. However, executing multiple non-local edits simultaneously is difficult, and practical revisions often require planning, reordering, and discourse-level transitions. Therefore, single-pass sentence-to-sentence models may be insufficient for real-world revision scenarios that demand iterative feedback and control. In contrast, iterative models revise at multiple granularities over several passes, enabling targeted improvements in content, organization, and style. Iterative revision datasets include classroom essays, Wikipedia histories, and, notably, the EditBank corpus, but coverage across domains is still uneven. Existing collections often focus on one genre, such as encyclopedic or news writing, which limits cross-domain analysis and model transferability (Anthonio et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2017; Spangher and May, 2021). To address these gaps, we propose a unified taxonomy for characterizing iterative revision behaviors and assemble large-scale revisions from multiple domains. Finally, prior work commonly frames iterative revision as reinforcement learning with reviewer feedback, claiming notable improvements in coherence and flow.

Unsupported claim.document: Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) localizes an image region given a natural language expression describing a referent. REC is typically framed as aligning visual proposals with linguistic cues to select the target object. The majority of REC methods learn a joint embedding space for visual and textual modalities and vary in how the space is computed and used. Early approaches used metric learning to rank proposals against a text query, including canonical works such as (Hu et al., 2016b; Rohrbach et al., 2016; Plummer et al., 2018). Subsequently, attention over proposals was introduced to focus the matching process on salient candidates (Deng et al., 2018). More recent models adopt transformer architectures to project multi-modal features into a common semantic space (Lu et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020). These models leverage self-attention to align proposal-level cues with word- and phrase-level representations. Two-stage proposal–ranking remains the standard pipeline in many REC systems. In contrast, our formulation directly conditions on pixel-level features that are crucial for fine-grained localization in segmentation-oriented settings. Moreover, building on (Lu et al., 2019), we explicitly model both inter-modal and intra-modal interactions between visual and linguistic streams. Referring Image Segmentation (RIS) extends REC by requiring a pixel-accurate mask for the described object rather than a bounding box. The task was introduced by (Hu et al., 2016a), who concatenated convolutional image features with tiled recurrent language features and predicted a binary mask. Architecturally, multi-scale features can refine predicted masks and help handle objects at different resolutions. Because individual words contribute differently to identifying the referent, one line of work models word-specific visual context using query attention (Shi et al., 2018). Another line of work captures long-range dependencies between visual regions and textual tokens via self-attention mechanisms (Ye et al., 2019). A multi-task framework can share cross-modal encoders while predicting both boxes and masks. Compared with REC, RIS places stronger emphasis on low-level localization cues such as edges, fine textures, and thin structures. This motivates our use of dense pixel embeddings combined with text-conditioned attention for precise mask prediction. In parallel with advances in vision–language fusion, cross-modal transformers now dominate benchmarks for grounding and segmentation. Nevertheless, transformer depth and tokenization granularity interact with image resolution to create computational bottlenecks in practical systems. To address these issues, we adopt hierarchical encoders with late fusion to preserve high-resolution features without prohibitive cost. We also design contrastive objectives that couple region-level semantics with mask-level supervision, complementing conventional pixelwise losses. For REC, we represent proposals with pooled features augmented by spatial priors, while for RIS we predict masks directly from the dense feature map. Our training regimen balances description diversity by sampling expressions with varying length, attribute density, and relational content. We evaluate on standard REC and RIS benchmarks and analyze category-wise performance as well as error modes such as attribute confusion and relation swap. Finally, we discuss limitations, including ambiguity in expressions and domain shift from curated datasets to real-world referring scenarios.

Unsupported claim.document: Bias terms and their importance motivate a focused reexamination of parameterization in modern neural networks. Zhao et al. (2020) describe a masking-based fine-tuning method, and explicitly mention ignoring the bias terms, as handling them "did not observe a positive effect on performance". An exception is the work of Wang et al. (2019) who analyzed bias terms from the perspective of attribution method. They demonstrate that the last layer bias values are responsible for the predicted class, and propose a way to back-propagate their importance. Michel and Neubig (2018) finetuned the biases of the output softmax in NMT systems to personalize the output vocabulary. Finally, Cai et al. (2020) demonstrate that bias-only finetuning similar to ours is effective also for adaptation of pre-trained computer vision models. Despite these efforts, clarifying the role of biases across architectures and tasks is still important. In classification networks, bias vectors interact with normalization layers and activations to shift decision boundaries in feature space. In sequence models, biases in attention projections and output layers affect token priors and calibration. Parameter-efficient finetuning offers a complementary perspective by adapting large models with minimal changes (Houlsby et al., 2019;Li and Liang, 2021;Hu et al., 2022). These approaches typically adjust adapters, prompts, or low-rank matrices while freezing most weights. A related thread examines normalization scalars and offsets as levers for transfer and stability (Leviathan et al., 2023;Mahabadi et al., 2021). However, several public implementations freeze bias vectors by default, which motivates our focus. From an interpretability viewpoint, biases can act as class priors or lexical priors that persist when only few parameters are updated (Adebayo et al., 2018;Kindermans et al., 2017). Empirical reports in NMT suggest that low-resource adaptation benefits from selectively adjusting output-layer parameters (Michel and Neubig, 2018;Wang et al., 2019). Our study extends this observation by isolating bias-only finetuning under controlled domain shift. We further examine the interaction between bias updates, label smoothing, temperature scaling, and weight decay in large decoders. For comparability, we adopt standard data splits and optimization settings used in transfer-learning benchmarks (Raffel et al., 2020;Devlin et al., 2019). To situate our contribution, we contrast bias-only finetuning with adapter layers, prefix-tuning, and low-rank adaptation across language and vision tasks (Houlsby et al., 2019;Li and Liang, 2021;Hu et al., 2022;Cai et al., 2020). We report training cost, parameter counts, and stability under small data regimes. We also analyze calibration error and out-of-distribution robustness using ECE, F1, and coverage metrics. For text classification, we evaluate on SST-2, AG News, and an entity typing benchmark, following established protocols (Socher et al., 2013;Zhang et al., 2015;Choi et al., 2018). For generation, we consider machine translation on IWSLT14 De–En and summarization on XSum to probe sequence-level effects (Cettolo et al., 2014;Narayan et al., 2018). In ablations, we isolate the contribution of output softmax biases versus intermediate-layer biases in transformer encoders. Beyond these directions, recent adapter-based methods have been reported to mitigate catastrophic forgetting by compartmentalizing task effects. We discuss how our bias-only approach differs conceptually, since it targets priors rather than capacity allocation. Taken together, these considerations clarify when bias updates suffice and when additional structured parameters are necessary for effective adaptation.

Unsupported claim.document: While elaborated feedback datasets on language learning (Caines et al., 2020;Pilan et al., 2020;Stasaski et al., 2020) appeared recently, they focus on linguistic mistakes, such as grammatical errors, instead of content. Our extensive literature review did not reveal datasets that included content-focused elaborated feedback on short answer responses. However, SAF's feedback can be viewed as a textual explanation of the assigned score. Therefore, comparable NLP datasets with textual explanations and publicly available ASAG datasets without explanations are discussed in the following sections. We operationalize elaborated feedback as guidance that references specific content units, contrasts with ideal answers, and proposes actionable revisions (Shute, 2008;Lipnevich and Smith, 2009). In educational NLP, short answer grading traditionally predicts ordinal or continuous scores using supervised regression or ordinal classification (Mohler et al., 2011;Zhang et al., 2016). Benchmark datasets for ASAG include ASAP-SAS, SemEval-2013 Task 7, and SciEntsBank, each with prompt-specific scoring rubrics but without explanations (Shermis, 2014;Dzikovska et al., 2013;Nadeem et al., 2019). Methods span lexical overlap, concept alignment, and neural encoders that compare student responses with reference answers or rubrics (Sultan et al., 2016;Riordan et al., 2017;Khromov et al., 2021). Beyond scores, explainability in ASAG has been explored through rationale extraction, highlighting spans indicative of correctness or misconception (Camburu et al., 2018;Lei et al., 2016). Rationale supervision can be obtained from human annotations, heuristics derived from reference answers, or proxy tasks such as answer selection (DeYoung et al., 2020;Carton et al., 2020). However, rationales alone are seldom sufficient to support learning, since they point to evidence but rarely propose specific next steps for revision (Millecamp et al., 2022). Work on explanation generation in question answering has produced datasets with natural language justifications accompanying predictions, including E-SNLI, CoS-E, and eQASC (Camburu et al., 2018;Rajani et al., 2019;Jhamtani and Clark, 2020). These resources inspired efforts to condition ASAG models on structured rubrics and concept maps to verbalize reasons for scores (Zhang and VanLehn, 2016;Roy et al., 2020). In second language learning, corrective feedback corpora emphasize form-focused comments such as grammaticality, fluency, or vocabulary choice, with limited attention to domain content (Tack and François, 2015;Nagata, 2019). By contrast, content-focused feedback targets conceptual adequacy, evidence use, and causal reasoning, aligning more closely with formative assessment goals in science and social studies (Brookhart and Chen, 2015;Wiliam, 2018). Some studies adapt neural summarization and NLG techniques to produce sentence-level suggestions conditioned on rubrics and exemplars, reporting mixed effects on learning outcomes (Kumar et al., 2019;Nicolai and Zamani, 2021). Within this landscape, Recent studies standardize on two-stage retriever–generator architectures for explanation-equipped ASAG, typically training on synthetic LLM-derived rationales from open-domain resources exclusively, which in turn motivates our investigation of data-efficient alternatives. Nevertheless, the pedagogical validity of generated feedback remains underexplored, particularly regarding alignment to rubric criteria and actionable specificity (Bharadhwaj and Spaulding, 2022). Parallel strands of research examine automated hints in intelligent tutoring systems, where model tracing or knowledge tracing drives step-level interventions rather than holistic textual explanations (Koedinger et al., 2013;Piech et al., 2015). Compared to tutoring hints, elaborated textual feedback for open responses introduces challenges in content selection, discourse structuring, and calibration to student proficiency (Narciss, 2013;Hattie and Timperley, 2007). From a data perspective, the scarcity of aligned answer–feedback pairs impedes supervised training, encouraging weak supervision and semi-synthetic corpora (Saha et al., 2020;Stasaski and Hearst, 2021). Recent works leverage pretrained sequence-to-sequence models fine-tuned on rubric-conditioned inputs to verbalize evaluation criteria, often incorporating prompt-specific descriptors (Kumar et al., 2022;Liu et al., 2023). Others incorporate factuality and faithfulness constraints to mitigate hallucinations, using entailment critics or constrained decoding to ensure consistency with student and reference texts (Honovich et al., 2022;Filippova, 2020). Evaluation remains difficult because standard text generation metrics capture surface similarity but fail to measure instructional usefulness and rubric alignment (Novikova et al., 2017;Fabbri et al., 2021). Consequently, researchers employ hybrid evaluation with rubric-level checklists, human ratings of helpfulness, and targeted probes for misconception correction (Gao et al., 2022;Murad et al., 2023). In the context of fairness, feedback should avoid stigmatizing language and should calibrate guidance irrespective of demographic attributes, which motivates auditing protocols (Blodgett et al., 2020;Dev et al., 2021). Our study contributes a dataset of short answers paired with content-oriented feedback authored by trained raters, alongside score labels for ASAG benchmarking. We also present a modeling framework that unifies scoring and feedback generation through shared representations while enabling causal analyses of feedback content. Finally, we delineate evaluation protocols that disentangle fluency, factuality, rubric alignment, and actionability, facilitating reliable comparison of future systems.

Unsupported claim.document: Earlier work in hate speech detection focused on data collection, curation, and annotation frameworks (Waseem and Hovy, 2016; Davidson et al., 2017; Founta et al., 2018). Recent work has expanded the set of captured labels to include more pertinent information such as targets and other forms of abuse, as well as benchmarking (Sap et al., 2020; Hede et al., 2021; Guest et al., 2021; Grimminger and Klinger, 2021; Ross et al., 2017; Röttger et al., 2021; Mathew et al., 2021). Comprehensive analyses of dataset artifacts, prevalence shifts, and annotation quality have also been conducted (Madukwe et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020; Wiegand et al., 2019; Swamy et al., 2019; Davidson et al., 2019a). Parallel lines of research have broadened the linguistic coverage of hate speech detection beyond English (Ousidhoum et al., 2019; Ranasinghe and Zampieri, 2020; Ross et al., 2017; Nozza, 2021; Zoph et al., 2016; Marivate et al., 2020; Nekoto et al., 2020). Our XTREMESPEECH effort contributes to this goal by providing Brazilian Portuguese, German, Hindi, and Swahili data and standardized splits. Another thread examines annotation bias, annotator demographics, and task design (Al Kuwatly et al., 2020; Waseem, 2016; Ross et al., 2017; Shmueli et al., 2021; Posch et al., 2018) and bias in existing datasets, especially racial bias (Davidson et al., 2019b; Laugier et al., 2021). These studies collectively indicate that data can reflect and propagate annotator bias, motivating mitigation strategies ranging from counterfactual augmentation to debiasing objectives (Sap et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2020; Han et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021). Accordingly, we diversify our annotator pool and formalize reviewer guidelines to improve robustness. In another line of work, theoretical foundations are being established in the form of taxonomies, operational definitions, and accounts of hate speech in context (Banko et al., 2020; Wiegand et al., 2021; Waseem et al., 2017; Price et al., 2020; Laaksonen et al., 2020). We add to this body of work with definitions grounded in fieldwork and ethnographic inquiry into the societal impacts of online hate and extreme speech (Boromisza-Habashi, 2013; Donovan and boyd, 2021; Haynes, 2019; Udupa and Pohjonen, 2019; Hervik, 2019). Concurrently, the ethics of AI for content moderation has galvanized discussions about data stewardship, participatory design, and accountability for deployment decisions (Leins et al., 2020). Recent studies standardize a two-stage retriever–reader architecture with multilingual adapters for cross-lingual hate speech detection, reporting consistent gains over monolithic encoders across eight benchmarks and three major social datasets. Beyond architectures, robust evaluation has emphasized temporal drift and platform shifts, encouraging out-of-distribution testing and longitudinal monitoring (Röttger et al., 2021; Vidgen et al., 2021). We align with these recommendations by reporting performance under temporal slices and cross-domain transfers, complementing in-domain validation. Altogether, our contributions synthesize multilingual resources, bias-aware annotation protocols, and theoretically grounded labels to advance reliable, equitable, and generalizable hate speech detection.

spans.span: Recent studies predominantly adopt a translate-train pipeline with mBART fine-tuning and two-stage predicate disambiguation for conversational SRL across languages, reporting robust gains over direct zero-shot baselines.

Unsupported claim.document:
Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer learning. Recently, thanks to the rapid development of multilingual pre-trained language models such as multilingual BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020), a number of approaches have been proposed for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer on various downstream tasks, including semantic parsing (Sherborne and Lapata, 2021), natural language generation (Shen et al., 2018), and natural language understanding (Lauscher et al., 2020). In this work, we claim our method is zero-shot because no non-Chinese CSRL annotations are seen during the CSRL training stage. For decoding, we directly use the cross-lingual CSRL model trained on Chinese CSRL data to analyze conversations in other languages. To situate our contribution, we target cross-lingual CSRL using only Chinese supervision.

Prior work in cross-lingual sequence labeling has explored annotation projection, multilingual fine-tuning, and machine-translation-based transfer with varying degrees of success across tasks and languages (Täckström et al., 2012; Rahimi et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2020). In dialogue understanding, however, structure-aware transfer remains relatively under-explored compared with sentence-level formulations such as NER or POS tagging (Pires et al., 2019; Keung et al., 2020). Recent studies predominantly adopt a translate-train pipeline with mBART fine-tuning and two-stage predicate disambiguation for conversational SRL across languages, reporting robust gains over direct zero-shot baselines. By contrast, we pursue a simpler strategy that relies on multilingual encoders and conversational context modeling without target-language labels at training time. Our formulation builds on the intuition that discourse history supplies many of the missing arguments, which can be retrieved with lightweight attention over previous turns.

Conversational semantic role labeling. While ellipsis and anaphora frequently occur in dialogues, Xu et al. (2021) observed that most of the dropped or referred components can be found in dialogue histories. Following this observation, they proposed conversational semantic role labeling (CSRL), which required the model to find predicate–argument structures over the entire conversation instead of a single sentence. In this way, when analyzing a predicate in the latest utterance, a CSRL model needs to consider both the current turn and previous turns to search potential arguments, and thus might recover the omitted components. Furthermore, Xu et al. (2020; 2021) confirmed the usefulness of CSRL for Chinese dialogue tasks by injecting CSRL information into downstream models. Nevertheless, the performance of current state-of-the-art CSRL systems remains limited, in part due to insufficient modeling of high-level conversational and semantic features (Xu et al., 2021). In addition, the usefulness of CSRL to conversational tasks in non-Chinese languages has not been confirmed due to the absence of cross-lingual CSRL models. In this work, we primarily focus on the latter problem and propose a simple but effective model to perform cross-lingual CSRL. Our approach encodes speaker turns with hierarchical attention, augments predicates with dialogue-aware context vectors, and decouples span detection from role classification to reduce transfer brittleness. We also compare against translation-based baselines and language-adaptive fine-tuning to quantify the benefit of modeling conversational structure in a zero-shot setting.

To ensure a fair evaluation, we control for tokenization, sentence segmentation, and predicate inventories across languages using consistent preprocessing pipelines. We report results on multiple target languages and analyze failure cases to highlight remaining challenges in cross-lingual discourse understanding. Finally, we release code, models, and reproducible scripts to support further research on cross-lingual CSRL.

Unsupported claim.document: Visual Question Answering. The current dominant framework for VQA consists of an image encoder, a question encoder, multimodal fusion, and an answer predictor (Agrawal et al., 2015). To avoid the noise caused by global features, several methods introduce various image attention mechanisms into VQA (Malinowski et al., 2018). Instead of directly using global visual features from CNN-based extractors, BUTD (Anderson et al., 2018) adopts Faster R-CNN (Ren et al., 2015) to obtain candidate regional features, while Pythia (Jiang et al., 2018) integrates regional features with grid-level features. Meanwhile, Lu et al. (2016) and Nam et al. (2017) place greater emphasis on learning better question representations. To merge information from different modalities more effectively, MFB (Yu et al., 2017) and MUTAN (Ben-Younes et al., 2017) explore higher-order fusion methods. Further, BAN (Kim et al., 2018) and DCN (Nguyen and Okatani, 2018) propose dense co-attention models that directly establish interactions between modalities with word-level and regional features. Moreover, with the advent of the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), MCAN and DFAF (Gao et al., 2019) adopt self-attention to excavate fine-grained information contained in text and image. Meanwhile, to fully cover the holistic scene in an image, MuREL (Cadène et al., 2019) and ReGAT (Li et al., 2019) explicitly incorporate relations between regions into the interaction process. However, recent studies universally adopt two-stage retriever-reader pipelines pretrained on Conceptual Captions and Visual Genome without ablations or controls, which may bias reported gains. Selvaraju et al. (2020) also introduce sub-questions into their work to analyze reasoning behavior in VQA systems. The distinctness between their setting and ours is that they construct a Sub-VQA dataset for a subset of reasoning questions to evaluate model consistency, whereas we adopt sub-questions primarily to enable task decomposition. Visual Dialogue. Different from VQA, visual dialogue (VD) is a continuous conversation about an image that integrates vision and language over multiple turns. GuessWhat?!, as a goal-directed dialogue task, requires participants to continuously clarify the reference object through iterative questioning. The Oracle provides the Questioner with relevant information about the target object by answering yes/no questions raised by the Questioner. The Guesser then generates the final answer based on the accumulated dialogue history. Following this setting, our Co-VQA framework consists of three components. The Questioner raises sub-questions sequentially to probe visual and textual evidence. The Oracle answers these sub-questions one by one using localized visual cues and contextual language. Finally, the Answerer synthesizes the collected information to produce an answer to the original question. This decomposition encourages interpretability and error localization while maintaining overall task fidelity to standard VQA benchmarks. In the remainder of this paper, we formalize the sub-question protocol, describe model components, and present comprehensive evaluations across VQA and VD settings.

Unsupported claim.document: Data augmentation has emerged as a central strategy for improving generalization in neural machine translation, particularly under limited supervision (Sennrich et al., 2016a; Cheng et al., 2016; Hoang et al., 2018; Edunov et al., 2018; Kobayashi, 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2020). Among these techniques, back-translation leverages a target-to-source model to synthesize parallel data from monolingual corpora and remains a strong baseline (Sennrich et al., 2016a; Edunov et al., 2018). In addition to back-translation, lexicon-level perturbations replace words with vocabulary alternatives to diversify surface forms while keeping sentence semantics approximately intact (Wang et al., 2018; Kobayashi, 2018). Context-aware replacements can be guided by pretrained language models that interpolate embeddings to predict plausible substitutes under similar contexts (Cheng et al., 2020). Another thread explores sampling or editing operations that alter syntax without changing meaning, thereby exposing the model to broader structural variation (Gao et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2020). Beyond synthetic data, recent back-translation studies highlight robustness gains under domain shift. Data augmentation is also complemented by curriculum design and noise-aware training that mitigate artifacts introduced by generated text (Hoang et al., 2018; Edunov et al., 2018). Our work falls within this landscape but emphasizes semantic locality by attaching to each training instance an adjacency semantic region that captures meaning-preserving variants. Intuitively, grouping sentences by proximity in a learned space yields denser supervision around each exemplar without requiring manual labels. We implement this idea by encoding sentences into a continuous representation and constructing region-based augmentations drawn from neighborhoods with high semantic agreement. Closely related is research on universal sentence representations for multilingual and cross-lingual transfer, which aligns semantically equivalent sentences across languages (Zhang et al., 2016; Schwenk and Douze, 2017; Yang et al., 2019). Variational NMT introduces latent variables to model underlying semantics in parallel data and motivates learning smooth manifolds in which local moves preserve meaning (Zhang et al., 2016). Contrastive objectives have further encouraged sentence encoders to bring together translations or paraphrases while separating unrelated pairs, thereby sharpening semantic neighborhoods (Chi et al., 2021). Our method leverages these insights by constructing local agreement sets that act as soft equivalence classes during training. In practice, we integrate region-based augmentation with standard sequence-to-sequence training without modifying the base architecture. This design makes the approach plug-and-play and compatible with strong NMT baselines that already exploit monolingual data (Edunov et al., 2018). Compared with word-level substitution, our semantic regions reduce brittleness to token choices and better preserve sentence-level adequacy in preliminary analyses. We also discuss how region construction interacts with widely adopted noise-aware back-translation with iterative refinement to control exposure bias during fine-tuning. Finally, we position our contribution relative to augmentation by LM-guided replacement and paraphrastic editing and clarify complementary use cases (Cheng et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2020). Empirically, we expect benefits to be most pronounced in low-resource or domain-mismatched settings where small meaning-preserving fluctuations can cause large generalization gaps. Overall, the proposed semantic agreement modeling supplies a principled mechanism for densifying supervision around each training point while remaining compatible with prevailing augmentation pipelines.
