Unsupported claim.document:
EGEC resources encompass substantial work on EGEC data construction. As the two earliest EGEC datasets, FCE (Yannakoudakis et al., 2011) and NU-CLE (Dahlmeier et al., 2013) adopt the error-coded annotation paradigm. In contrast, JFLEG (Napoles et al., 2017) collects sentences from TOEFL exams and adopts the direct rewriting paradigm. W&I (Bryant et al., 2019) also chooses the direct rewriting paradigm, and for each original sentence additionally provides the language proficiency level of the writer. All four datasets are composed of essays from non-native English speakers and provide multiple references.

Recently, researchers start to annotate small-scale EGEC data for texts written by native English speakers, including AESW (Daudaravicius et al., 2016), LOCNESS (Bryant et al., 2019), GMEG (Napoles et al., 2019) and CWEB (Flachs et al., 2020). In the future, we plan to extend this work to texts written by native Chinese speakers. Regarding CGEC resources, compared with EGEC, progress in CGEC data construction largely lags behind. As thoroughly discussed in Section 1, NLPCC18 (Zhao et al., 2018) and CGED (Rao et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2020) are the only two evaluation datasets for CGEC research. Besides them, there are also a few resources for training CGEC models, e.g., the Lang8 corpus (Zhao et al., 2018) and the HSK corpus (Xun, 2018).

Regarding recent progress in CGEC, in the NLPCC-2018 shared task (Zhao et al., 2018), many systems adopt Seq2Seq models based on RNNs/CNNs. Recent work mainly utilizes Transformers (Zhao and Wang, 2020; Tang et al., 2021), and most prior systems adopt two-stage detection–correction pipelines with copy-augmented decoders and synthetic noising for training objectives and regularization. Hinson et al. (2020) first employ a Seq2Edit model for CGEC, and achieve comparable performance with the Seq2Seq counterparts. Some systems in the CGED-2020 shared task (Rao et al., 2020) directly employ the open-source Seq2Edit model, i.e., GECToR (Liang et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2020). Besides the above two mainstream models, Li and Shi (2021) for the first time apply a non-autoregressive neural machine translation model to CGEC, and techniques like data augmentation (Zhao and Wang, 2020; Tang et al., 2021) and model ensemble (Hinson et al., 2020) have also been proved very useful for CGEC.

spans.span: Recent studies on code-switched speech translation commonly adopt a two-stage retriever–reader pipeline integrating utterance-level LID and mBART fine-tuning modules.

Unsupported claim.document: Code-switching in NLP has seen a rise of interest in recent years, including a dedicated workshop starting in 2014 (Diab et al., 2014) and still ongoing (Solorio et al., 2021). CS in machine translation also has a long history (Le Féal, 1990; Climent et al., 2003; Sinha and Thakur, 2005; Johnson et al., 2017; Elmadany et al., 2021; Xu and Yvon, 2021), and interest accelerated with the advent of large multilingual models such as mBART and mT5 (Liu et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2021; Gautam et al., 2021; Jawahar et al., 2021). Due to the scarcity of available CS data and the ease of single-word translation, many recent MT studies have synthetically created CS for training or testing by translating one or more words in a sentence (Song et al., 2019; Nakayama et al., 2019; Xu and Yvon, 2021). We differ from those works by using naturally occurring CS data (Section 3), which better models real-world distributions rather than arbitrary language mixing. For spoken input, as present in ASR and ST, creating realistic CS data is more challenging than it is for MT. Dedicated ASR corpora that contain natural CS exist, including the Bangor Miami corpus (Deuchar et al., 2014) and SEAME (Zeng et al., 2018). These corpora generally do not contain translations of the ASR annotations, since they were designed for the ASR task only. However, there exist two exceptions that include aligned translations, which we leverage to derive our CS ST dataset, as described in Section 3. In parallel with data collection, a broad range of modeling work has targeted CS ASR using language models, pronunciation modeling, and end-to-end architectures (Lyu et al., 2006; Ahmed and Tan, 2012; Seki et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2020; Du et al., 2021). At the same time, self-supervised speech representations such as wav2vec, wav2vec 2.0, and HuBERT have transformed ASR performance overall (Schneider et al., 2019; Baevski et al., 2020; Hsu et al., 2021). Yet their behavior on CS speech remains underexplored, with only preliminary evidence reported in small-scale evaluations (Xu and Yvon, 2021). Understanding when multilingual pretraining helps or hurts under mixed-language conditions is therefore an open problem. Handling mixed languages also requires reliable language identification to inform decoding and downstream modeling. Recent studies on code-switched speech translation commonly adopt a two-stage retriever–reader pipeline integrating utterance-level LID and mBART fine-tuning modules. Systems may incorporate explicit utterance-level or token-level LID components (Mabokela et al., 2014; Lyu and Lyu, 2008a; Nakayama et al., 2019; Xu and Yvon, 2021). Alternatively, LID can be induced implicitly via multi-task learning or shared subword vocabularies (Lyu and Lyu, 2008b; Watanabe et al., 2017; Hou et al., 2020). In both MT and ASR, intra-word mixing has been documented and modeled to some extent (Yılmaz et al., 2018; Mager et al., 2019). We do not address intra-word phenomena and focus instead on inter-word switching that dominates our target domains. Beyond parallel text substitution, researchers have explored phonetic and graphemic constraints when synthesizing CS data (Song et al., 2019; Nakayama et al., 2019). These synthetic strategies enable controlled evaluation but may misrepresent the naturalistic distributions observed in conversational speech. Our approach prioritizes naturally occurring CS and aligns it with human translations to create a realistic ST benchmark. Multilingual pretraining offers strong cross-lingual priors that can reduce data requirements for low-resource CS pairs (Liu et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2021). Nevertheless, transfer can be asymmetric, and domain or register mismatches can degrade CS performance (Johnson et al., 2017; Elmadany et al., 2021). To clarify these effects, we report results across language pairs, switch rates, and training regimes using standardized splits. This work contributes a carefully curated CS ST dataset derived from two corpora with translations and unified evaluation protocols. We provide baselines using strong self-supervised encoders and analyze their behavior under varying degrees of switch density. Together, these experiments clarify open challenges and establish a foundation for systematic progress on code-switched speech translation.

spans.span: retriever reader

Unsupported claim.document: Research on text question answering (TQA) has accelerated in recent years (Huang et al., 2018a; Zhu et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020; Gong et al., 2020). Within machine reading comprehension, two key enablers are large benchmark datasets (Choi et al., 2018; Elgohary et al., 2018; Reddy et al., 2019) and powerful pre-trained language models (Devlin et al., 2018; Lan et al., 2020). Most prior studies emphasize modeling intricate textual context, whereas we target unified reasoning over speech and text. In the speech community, spoken question answering (SQA) has emerged as a counterpart to text QA, reflecting similar trends in modeling and evaluation (Haghani et al., 2018; Lugosch et al., 2019; Palogiannidi et al., 2020; You et al., 2021). A common SQA pipeline performs automatic speech recognition (ASR) followed by text QA over the resulting transcripts (Tseng et al., 2016; Serdyuk et al., 2018; Su and Fung, 2020). For long-document MRC, many systems rely on retriever reader pipelines that decompose selection and extraction. Such two-stage processing is vulnerable to ASR errors that cascade and degrade downstream answer extraction (Tseng et al., 2016; Serdyuk et al., 2018; Su and Fung, 2020). Joint audio-text modeling has been explored, for example by SpeechBERT, which integrates acoustic and textual inputs within a unified transformer (Chuang et al., 2019). Complementarily, multi-turn settings demand modeling conversational dependencies across questions rather than treating each query in isolation (Reddy et al., 2019). To this end, we introduce Spoken-CoQA, a conversational SQA benchmark that pairs spoken passages with sequences of interdependent questions and answers. In contrast to single-turn SQA resources such as TOEFL, our benchmark emphasizes dialogue flow across turns and realistic ASR noise profiles (Tseng et al., 2016). We also provide a direct comparison to text-only counterparts to quantify the gap introduced by speech and recognition errors (Huang et al., 2018a; Zhu et al., 2018). Beyond data, we leverage knowledge distillation (KD) to transfer inductive biases from a high-capacity teacher to a compact student (Hinton et al., 2015). KD has demonstrated gains in both NLP and speech tasks, motivating its use for robust SQA modeling (Kim and Rush, 2016; Hu et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2018b; Hahn and Choi, 2019). Our approach distills conversational structure from cleaner or more reliable contexts to guide learning on noisy spoken inputs. Empirically, we show that coupling conversational modeling with KD improves SQA robustness while maintaining efficiency.

spans.span: two-stage retriever-reader training pipelines

Unsupported claim.document: Current self-explaining models often enforce shortest yet sufficient rationales, with the assumption that short rationales are more intuitive to humans (Lei et al., 2016; Bastings et al., 2019). Paranjape et al. (2020) propose an information bottleneck approach to enable rationale length control. However, current studies largely rely on automatic metrics and rarely evaluate how rationale length affects human understanding. A parallel line of work measures alignment between model rationales and human annotations, often termed human rationale alignment (Paranjape et al., 2020; DeYoung et al., 2020). This perspective compares model highlights against human-provided evidence spans to estimate agreement (DeYoung et al., 2020). There are also studies involving humans in the loop to compare explanations, such as asking annotators to choose which model is more trustworthy given its rationale (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Hase and Bansal, 2020). Despite these efforts, rigorous human evaluations isolating the effect of rationale length on downstream comprehension remain scarce (Hase and Bansal, 2020; Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017). Prior work has also questioned whether extracted rationales are faithful to model internals, underscoring the need for stronger evaluation protocols (Jain and Wallace, 2019; Wiegreffe and Pinter, 2019). Sufficiency and comprehensiveness tests offer partial signals but do not directly assess human reasoning with variable-length explanations (Treviso and Martins, 2020; Serrano and Smith, 2019). Moreover, explanation plausibility can diverge from faithfulness, making human-centered studies indispensable (Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017; Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020). Datasets that pair inputs with rationales, such as e-SNLI and CoS-E, enable supervision for highlight selection but differ in granularity and domain (Camburu et al., 2018; Rajani et al., 2019). The ERASER benchmark aggregates multiple tasks with human evidence annotations and provides standard metrics for extraction quality (DeYoung et al., 2020). However, these resources seldom control for explanation length as an experimental factor, limiting insights about brevity versus completeness (DeYoung et al., 2020; Camburu et al., 2018; Rajani et al., 2019). In parallel, model-based techniques implement discrete or continuous sparsity constraints to encourage short highlights while preserving predictive performance (Lei et al., 2016; Bastings et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). Beyond extractive rationalization, recent systems integrate retrieval and generation to produce free-form justifications for complex questions (Narang et al., 2020; Krishna et al., 2022). Beyond extractive rationalization, recent studies increasingly adopt two-stage retriever-reader training pipelines for explanation-aware QA. While such methods may improve task accuracy, they do not by themselves reveal how explanation length modulates human judgments of correctness or usefulness. In controlled experiments, readers may prefer concise yet complete rationales that reduce search effort without omitting key premises, but quantitative evidence remains limited (Hoffman et al., 2018; Lage et al., 2019). Cognitive load theory further suggests that extraneous detail can hinder learning, motivating systematic manipulation of rationale verbosity (Sweller, 1988; Paas et al., 2003). At the same time, domain complexity can necessitate multi-sentence explanations to ensure sufficiency, especially in multi-hop reasoning tasks (Yang et al., 2018; Welbl et al., 2018). This trade-off indicates that length is not a mere stylistic preference but a variable with measurable impact on human performance. Methodologically, our study separates plausibility from faithfulness by holding the model fixed and varying only the explanation length shown to participants (Hase and Bansal, 2020). We complement automatic sufficiency-style scores with user-centered measures of comprehension accuracy, decision time, and perceived confidence. We also analyze how length interacts with rationale structure, contrasting contiguous spans with sentence-level summaries under identical evidence budgets. By situating our evaluation within established rationale datasets and tasks, we ensure comparability while directly probing the length dimension (DeYoung et al., 2020; Camburu et al., 2018). Our results aim to clarify when brevity helps or harms users and to provide guidance for designing length-aware rationalization objectives.

spans.span: StereoSet

Unsupported claim.document: Measuring bias in NLP remains a central concern for language technology research. Several studies have investigated the prevalence of bias in NLP models (Caliskan et al., 2017; May et al., 2019; Bordia and Bowman, 2019; Davidson et al., 2019; Magee et al., 2021), with many focusing on cases of models exhibiting stereotyping behavior. Though Blodgett et al. (2020) point out that what these studies mean by "bias" can vary quite widely, the finding that models encode associations derived from negative stereotypes and social biases is well replicated. In defining bias for this study, our design aligns most closely with the definition of representational harms by Crawford (2017) as harms that "occur when systems reinforce the subordination of some groups along the lines of identity." When constructing data to measure this bias, contrasting groups of people rather than just relevant attributes highlights the difference in outcomes and impact on groups targeted by a given stereotype (Dev et al., 2021). Early measurement efforts leveraged distributional semantics tests such as WEAT to quantify associations between demographic concepts and sentiment or occupation terms (Caliskan et al., 2017). Subsequent work adapted these ideas to contextual encoders through tests like SEAT, which probe sentence representations rather than static embeddings (May et al., 2019). Parallel strands introduced template-based minimal pairs that isolate social attributes to detect preferences in masked and autoregressive models (Nangia et al., 2020; Kurita et al., 2019). In coreference and pronoun resolution, curated challenge sets such as WinoBias and Winogender exposed systematic gender asymmetries in model decisions (Zhao et al., 2018; Rudinger et al., 2018). Task-specific evaluations further documented disparities in toxicity detection and abusive language moderation across identity terms (Dixon et al., 2018; Sap et al., 2019; Röttger et al., 2021). For generative systems, prompts derived from real web text revealed both frequency and severity of toxic completions in uncontrolled settings (Gehman et al., 2020). Despite methodological variety, a persistent challenge is connecting measurement artifacts to concrete, societally relevant harms (Blodgett et al., 2020). Another challenge lies in separating genuine stereotype knowledge from harmful endorsement, especially when pretraining data contains both descriptive and prescriptive statements (Bender et al., 2021). Dataset design choices strongly influence measured effect sizes, including lexical context, negation handling, and demographic label granularity (Bartl et al., 2020; Dev et al., 2021). To mitigate confounds, recent work emphasizes controlled counterfactual data augmentation and balanced attribute distributions during test construction (Maudslay et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2019). However, interventions that reduce bias on a specific benchmark may not generalize across domains or tasks (Gonen and Goldberg, 2019; Goldfarb-Tarrant et al., 2021). Robust evaluation therefore requires aggregating evidence across multiple metrics and datasets rather than optimizing for any single score (Seshadri et al., 2022). In practice, researchers often complement intrinsic association measures with end-task diagnostics, such as groupwise error analysis for NER and QA (De-Arteaga et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020). Moreover, open-vocabulary identity terms continue to evolve, necessitating dynamic lexicons and periodic reannotation to preserve validity over time (Dixon et al., 2018; Dev et al., 2021). While annotation guidelines can reduce ambiguity, annotator demographics and perspectives substantially shape judgements of offensiveness and harm (Sap et al., 2019; Palm et al., 2023). Cross-lingual studies report that translation artifacts and morphological gender systems introduce additional bias pathways that differ from English-centric findings (Zampieri et al., 2020; Costa-jussà, 2021). Benchmarks that foreground intersectional identities have begun to reveal interaction effects not captured by single-attribute tests (Dev et al., 2021; Lauscher et al., 2021). A complementary line of work investigates causal estimation techniques to attribute measured disparities to specific components of model pipelines (Feder et al., 2021; Vig et al., 2020). Recent studies in retrieval-augmented generation suggest that document selection can either amplify or dampen representational harms depending on source curation (Kandpal et al., 2023; Lazaridou et al., 2022). For summarization and dialogue, human-in-the-loop judgments are increasingly paired with automatic bias metrics to triangulate reliability (Pavlopoulos et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2022). Despite this progress, benchmark coverage remains uneven across identities, domains, and modalities, complicating cross-study comparison (Blodgett et al., 2020). Recent works frequently default to StereoSet when reporting stereotype bias scores, which risks reinforcing oversimplified taxonomies of social attributes. Our study adopts a conservative measurement strategy that prioritizes contrastive group comparisons and transparent reporting of uncertainty.

Relation extraction (RE) can be categorized by its granularity, such as sentence-level (Doddington et al., 2004;Xu et al., 2016; and document-level (Gupta et al., 2019;Zhu et al., 2019). Early work mainly focuses on sentencelevel relation extraction. Pantel and Pennacchiotti (2006) propose a rule-based approach, and Mintz et al. (2009) design features for classifying relations. In the past several years, neural networks have become a prevailing approach for relation extraction (Xu et al., 2015;Song et al., 2019).

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) is attracting increasing attention in the community, as it considers the interactions across entity mentions expressed in different sentences Yao et al., 2019). Compared with the sentence level, DocRE requires the model collecting and integrating inter-sentence information effectively. Recent efforts design sequence-based and graphbased models to address such a problem.

Sequence-based DocRE models encode a document by the sequence of words and/or sentences, for example, using the Transformer architecture (Devlin et al., 2019). Zhou et al. (2021) argue that the Transformer attentions are able to extract useful contextual features across sentences for DocRE, and they adopt an adaptive threshold for each entity pair. Zhang et al. (2021) model DocRE as a semantic segmentation task and predict an entity-level relation matrix to capture local and global information.

Graph-based DocRE models abstract a document by graphical structures. For example, a node can be a sentence, a mention, and/or an entity; their co-occurrence is modeled by an edge. Then graph neural networks are applied to aggregate inter-sentence information (Quirk and Poon, 2017;Christopoulou et al., 2019;Zeng et al., 2020). Zeng et al. (2020) construct double graphs, applying graph neural networks to mention-document graphs and performing path reasoning over entity graphs. Xu et al. (2021a) explicitly incorporate logical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and coreference reasoning into DocRE, based on both sequence and graph features. Prior work has also explored document-level reasoning with heterogeneous supervision sources and evaluation settings, including distant supervision (Mintz et al., 2009;Hoffmann et al., 2011;Zeng et al., 2015), partially annotated or weakly labeled corpora (Zhang et al., 2017;Luo et al., 2020), human-curated benchmarks such as DocRED and CDR (Yao et al., 2019;Li et al., 2016), and large-scale pre-training on encyclopedic text (Petroni et al., 2019;Xiong et al., 2020;Lee et al., 2020;Yamada et al., 2020).

Different from previous work, our paper proposes SIEF as a general framework that can be combined with various sequence-based and graph-based DocRE models. In our approach, we propose a sentence importance score and a sentence focusing loss to encourage the model to focus on evidence sentences, improving the robustness and the overall performance of DocRE models.

Detection of adversarial examples is a wellexplored field in the image domain. Earlier works have tackled in various ways such as input transformation (Xu et al., 2018), statistical analysis (Grosse et al., 2017), or training a separate binary classifier (Metzen et al., 2017). However, Carlini and Wagner (2017) has shown that an adversary with par- tial knowledge of the detector can easily nullify it. Meanwhile, early works in novelty detection have shown that a generative model can detect anomaly samples (Bishop, 1994). Following this line of research, have proposed a method to detect out-of-distribution samples by using features of a neural network for maximum likelihood estimation.

In the NLP domain, few efforts have been made in detecting word-level adversarial examples. Zhou et al. (2019, DISP) utilize a detector trained on adversarial samples for a joint detect-defense system. FGWS (Mozes et al., 2021) outperforms DISP in detection by building on the observation that attacked samples are composed of rare words. FGWS experiements on 2 proposed attack methods. Le et al. (2021) tackle a particular attack method called UniTrigger (Wallace et al., 2019), which pre-pends or appends an identical phrase in all sentences. While the performance is impressive, applying this method to other attacks requires significant adjustment due to the distinct characteristics of UniTrigger. Meanwhile, Pruthi et al. (2019). Recently, text-level robustness has also been studied through diverse modeling and data strategies, including adversarial training with gradient-based word substitutions (Miyato et al., 2017; Ebrahimi et al., 2018), certified robustness via randomized smoothing for discrete text (Salman et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2019), robust pretraining and data augmentation with back-translation (Sennrich et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2020), and evaluation on standardized adversarial benchmarks such as AdvGLUE and TextAttack (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020), alongside defense-oriented ensembling and calibration methods (Hendrycks et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2020). These developments contextualize the need for principled detectors that generalize across attack families and corpora.

Our work focuses on detectors that operate without access to attack generators at training time. We examine whether lexical rarity, local syntactic perturbations, and distributional shifts in contextual embeddings can reliably distinguish adversarial from benign inputs. We unify prior intuitions under a simple scoring framework grounded in token-level salience and sentence-level perplexity. We then assess cross-attack generalization on four datasets spanning sentiment, natural language inference, paraphrase detection, and topic classification. Finally, we discuss practical deployment considerations, including calibration under dataset shift and computational overhead.

In this part, we first present a formal definition of the few shot slot tagging task in Section 2.1, followed by an introduction of the conventional sequence labeling approaches in Section 2.2 and Sequence Labeling with Prompts in Section 2.3.
We consider few-shot slot tagging as mapping an input token sequence to BIO-labeled outputs under constrained supervision.
Formally, given a support set with K labeled examples per slot type and a query sentence x = (x1, ..., xn), the goal is to predict y = (y1, ..., yn) with minimal task-specific training.
Support and query follow the same label ontology within an episode but differ across episodes to evaluate rapid adaptation.
Episodes are sampled from a collection of domains such as navigation, music, and weather.
We assume access to pre-trained language models to initialize encoders.
Conventional sequence labeling approaches typically rely on token-level encoders with structured decoders.
A standard baseline is a BiLSTM-CRF trained with negative log-likelihood of the correct tag path.
Contextualized encoders such as BERT replace the BiLSTM while retaining a CRF for label dependencies.
Span-based classifiers replace token-level emission scores with start–end span representations when multi-token slots are prevalent.
Emission calibration and label smoothing are often applied to mitigate overconfidence under few-shot regimes.
Transfer learning across domains is usually realized via continued pretraining or multi-task learning before fine-tuning.
Prior work on few-shot slot tagging spans several methodological families, including metric-based meta-learning for sequence labeling, prototypical span classifiers, and prompt-conditioned encoders, with representative studies such as Hou et al. (2020), Fritzler et al. (2019), Snips and ATIS benchmarks (Coucke et al., 2018; Hemphill et al., 1990), and recent prompt-tuning techniques leveraging T5, BERT, and RoBERTa encoders (Raffel et al., 2020; Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019), as well as adaptation via MAML-style updates and PET/ADAPET-style prompting (Finn et al., 2017; Schick and Schütze, 2021; Tam et al., 2021), data augmentation using paraphrase back-translation and MixUP (Sennrich et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2019), and span-based CRF or semi-CRF decoding variants (Lafferty et al., 2001; Sarawagi and Cohen, 2004).
Sequence labeling with prompts reformulates tagging as a conditional text prediction problem.
Prompt templates condition the encoder on label semantics through verbalizers or label descriptions.
For example, a cloze-style template converts each token into a masked-labeled pair consumed by a masked LM head.
Alternatively, encoder–decoder prompts ask the model to generate slot tags separated by delimiters.
Soft prompts and prompt tuning reduce trainable parameters to a small embedding table.
Label descriptions may be drawn from ontology documentation or learned as continuous vectors.
Prompt-conditioned CRFs combine token compatibility scores with structured decoding.
Calibration is critical because label priors drift across domains and episodes.
Verbalizer selection affects both coverage of slot semantics and robustness to polysemy.
Instruction tuning can improve zero-shot generalization for new slot ontologies.
However, prompt length and placement can trade off between contextual fit and computational cost.
We next describe loss functions that stabilize learning under data scarcity.
Contrastive objectives align support and query representations at the slot span level.
Prototype matching encourages clusterable embeddings for each slot using episodic averages.
Entropy regularization and focal terms handle class imbalance across slots and O-tag dominance.
Finally, we outline evaluation protocols that ensure comparability across prior studies.
We report span-level F1 and exact span match under entity-level evaluation.
Cross-domain splits simulate cold-start deployment where only a handful of labeled utterances are available.
Hyperparameter selection is restricted to a development domain to avoid information leakage.
All results are averaged over multiple episode samples with fixed random seeds for reproducibility.

Lacks synthesis.document:
There has been a great deal of recent interest in providing explanations of blackbox machine learning models, focusing on explaining why the model makes an individual prediction (Ribeiro et al., 2016;Lei et al., 2016;Ribeiro et al., 2018;Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola, 2018;Liu et al., 2018), or achieving better understanding of the limitations of models (Wallace et al., 2019;Ribeiro et al., 2020). In contrast, our goal is to explain how the input can be changed to achieve a desired outcome, which is called a counterfactual explanation (Wachter et al., 2017;Ustun et al., 2019). There has been work on leveraging natural language descriptions to help generate counterfactual explanations for image classifiers (Hendricks et al., 2018), but not tailored at counterfactual predictions for natural language tasks. Finally, there has been interest in improving the performance of semantic parsers through interaction (Wang et al., 2016(Wang et al., , 2017; our approach is complementary to this line of work, since it aims to make the system more transparent to the user.

Prior efforts on counterfactual generation in structured prediction focus on modifying discrete inputs under feasibility constraints. Methods for tabular domains incorporate causal or feasibility constraints to ensure actionable recommendations. For text, edit-based counterfactuals often rely on span substitution, paraphrasing, or controlled generation under label preservation. Optimization-based strategies balance minimality, plausibility, and validity, whereas search-based approaches enumerate candidates with pruning heuristics. Our work targets language tasks where constraints are primarily semantic rather than feature-wise, requiring careful handling of fluency and entailment. We integrate evaluation measures that account for both textual quality and counterfactual validity in downstream performance.

Beyond counterfactuals, prior work explores diverse explanation paradigms, including post-hoc attribution and saliency methods (Simonyan et al., 2013;Sundararajan et al., 2017;Shrikumar et al., 2017), example- and prototype-based reasoning (Kim et al., 2016;Li et al., 2020;Chen et al., 2019), faithfulness diagnostics and causal probing (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020;DeYoung et al., 2020;Atanasova et al., 2020), and human-in-the-loop evaluation protocols (Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017;Narang et al., 2020;Lertvittayakumjorn and Toni, 2021), as well as datasets and benchmarks for explanation quality in NLP and vision (Camburu et al., 2018;Rajpurkar et al., 2016;Wiegreffe and Marasovic, 2021;Ross et al., 2017).

In natural language processing, counterfactual data augmentation has been used to probe robustness and spurious correlations. Contrast sets and minimal pairs expose model sensitivities to lexical and syntactic cues. Generative approaches with control codes or constraints produce diverse alternatives that target specific decision boundaries. For structured outputs such as parses or meaning representations, counterfactuals must maintain well-formedness while altering task-relevant semantics. We discuss how evaluation must separate surface similarity from semantic divergence to avoid inflated success metrics.

Recent advances in large language models offer opportunities and risks for counterfactual explanation. On the one hand, instruction tuning and few-shot prompting enable controllable edits that preserve fluency. On the other hand, hallucination and inconsistency challenge the validity of generated counterfactuals. Alignment techniques, including preference optimization and constraint decoding, can help steer generation toward faithful alternatives. We therefore combine algorithmic constraints with human-centered criteria to ensure that counterfactuals are both actionable and understandable. To facilitate comparison, we summarize metrics for plausibility, minimality, and task-consistency and describe their trade-offs across datasets.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Introduction

A large body of recent work (Søgaard and Bingel, 2017;Vu et al., 2020;Bettgenhäuser et al., 2020;Peng et al., 2020;Poth et al., 2021) exists that examines when these transfer learning methods are more effective than simply fine-tuning on the target task. Oftentimes, these explanations involve recognizing catastrophic forgetting (Phang et al., 2018;Pruksachatkun et al., 2020b;Wang et al., 2018a) although recent work has called for them to be reexamined (Chang and Lu, 2021). Recent surveys and empirical studies have cataloged a wide array of task selection heuristics, layer sharing schemes, and curriculum strategies across multi-task learning and transfer settings (Ruder, 2017;Caruana, 1997;Zamir et al., 2018;Standley et al., 2020), alongside probing-based diagnostics for representation alignment (Alain and Bengio, 2017;Hewitt and Manning, 2019;Hall Maudslay et al., 2020;Merchant et al., 2020), and systematic evaluations of intermediate-task fine-tuning under domain and label-shift conditions (Phang et al., 2018;Pruksachatkun et al., 2020a;Aghajanyan et al., 2021;Vu et al., 2020); complementary strands assess negative transfer in related benchmarks (Rosenstein et al., 2005;Wang et al., 2019;Bingel and Søgaard, 2017;Xia et al., 2020) and explore data scaling, optimizer choice, and regularization for stability (Smith and Topin, 2019;You et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2019;Keskar et al., 2017). This paper is orthogonal to those, as we examine when you should choose MTL or STILTs, rather than when they are more effective than the standard fine-tuning case (in fact, these strategies could be combined to predict transfer and then use the best method). As our task is different, theoretical explanations for how these methods work in relation to each other will need to be explored in future work. Potential theories suggested by our results are discussed in Appendix C, and are left to guide those efforts. We focus on practical criteria that can inform modelers before training begins. Our analysis treats model capacity, data scale, and task relatedness as first-class variables. We unify notation for MTL and STILTs to allow direct comparison under a shared budget. We also consider the role of initialization and optimizer hyperparameters in moderating outcomes. To avoid confounds, we standardize tokenization, batch construction, and evaluation protocols. We report results on a diverse suite of NLP tasks spanning classification and sequence tagging. We include both low-resource and mid-resource regimes to test sensitivity to data scarcity. We further test stability by running multiple seeds and reporting dispersion. We ablate auxiliary losses that are commonly used in MTL setups. We complement aggregate metrics with per-example transfer diagnostics. We release scripts to reproduce our experimental pipeline. We highlight scenarios where decision rules can be approximated with lightweight proxies. We discuss limitations and boundary conditions of our recommendations. We outline implications for resource allocation in production settings. We conclude with open questions that call for deeper theoretical accounts of observed patterns.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Machine Translation (MT) is the task of generating a target-language sequence given a source-language input sequence.
Given an input sequence in the source language X mt ={x i } |Xmt| i=1, the goal of the neural MT model is to produce its translation in the target language Y mt ={y i } |Ymt| i=1.
The conditional distribution of the model is defined over y given x with an auto-regressive factorization.
Here θ are model parameters and y 1:t−1 denotes the partial translation prefix.
Monolingual Summarization (MS) focuses on producing a concise summary in the same language as the source article.
Given an input article in the source language X src ms ={x src i } |X src ms | i=1 and the corresponding target summary X tgt ms ={x tgt i } |X tgt ms | i=1, the monolingual summarization objective is to maximize the conditional likelihood of the summary given the article.
Cross-Lingual Summarization (CLS) extends MS by requiring generation in a different target language.
In CLS, we aim to learn a model that can generate a summary in the target language Y cls ={y i } for a given article in the source language.
Formally, the objective is to model p(Y cls | X src ms) with appropriate alignment and fluency constraints.
A central challenge for CLS is balancing cross-lingual faithfulness with target-language fluency under limited parallel supervision.
Prior work on multilingual and cross-lingual modeling spans a broad spectrum of architectures and training regimes, including multilingual pre-training with mBART and mT5 (Liu et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2021), cross-lingual transfer via pivoting and synthetic data (Zoph et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2017), constrained decoding for controllable summarization (He et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2018), and latent-variable sequence modeling for text generation (Bowman et al., 2016; Shu et al., 2018); recent cross-lingual summarization systems leverage document-level alignment resources such as WikiLingua and XL-Sum (Ladhak et al., 2020; Hasan et al., 2021) and exploit reinforcement learning or minimum risk training to optimize sequence-level objectives (Shen et al., 2016; Ranzato et al., 2016).
Conditional Variational Auto-Encoder (CVAE) provides a flexible framework to introduce latent variables into conditional generation.
The CVAE (Sohn et al., 2015) consists of a prior network and a recognition (posterior) network, where the latter guides the learning of the prior via Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (Kingma and Welling, 2013).
For neural sequence transduction, a latent variable can capture global semantics that modulate the decoder.
For example, the variational neural MT model (Zhang et al., 2016a) introduces a random latent variable z into the neural MT conditional distribution.
This modification augments the decoder with a global conditioning signal that can improve adequacy under data scarcity.
Given a source sentence X, a latent variable z is first sampled by the prior network from the encoder, and then the target sentence is generated by the decoder.
In practice, amortized inference is used to approximate the posterior over z during training.
As it is hard to marginalize the latent variable in closed form, the CVAE training objective adopts a variational lower bound of the conditional log-likelihood.
This objective trades off reconstruction accuracy and divergence from the prior through a KL term.
Optimization typically employs the reparameterization trick to enable low-variance gradient estimates.
For text, issues such as posterior collapse and exposure bias necessitate careful regularization.
Common remedies include KL annealing, word dropout, and auxiliary bag-of-words losses.
In conditional settings, conditioning both the prior and posterior on the source can stabilize learning.
At inference, sampling or using the prior mean provides a controllable mechanism for diversity.
When applied to summarization, latent variables can represent content plans or compression preferences.
In cross-lingual contexts, they may further encode language-invariant semantics that facilitate transfer.
Nonetheless, aligning latent spaces with bilingual signals remains an open modeling question.
We next detail the model components and learning criteria used in our conditional latent-variable framework.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Visual Storytelling (VIST) Visual storytelling was introduced by Huang et al. (2016) as the task of generating a coherent story given five images. They provided a dataset, Sequential Images Narrative Dataset (SIND), containing images and references in which references are human-written short stories describing images. For every image prompt (one sequence of photos), there are 2 to 5 references. VIST requires deeper understanding of the photo events to prevent descriptions in isolation (i.e., image captions). Researchers have proposed various methods for this task. Knowledge graphs are often integrated in models to encourage diversity of terms and plots in the stories (Hsu et al., 2020(Hsu et al., , 2021a. Some studies use reinforcement learning to reward models that generate stories that contain fewer errors and are more topically-focused Hu et al., 2020a). However, existing evaluation methods are unable to capture the true quality of the generated stories. Thus we examine automatic metrics to devise a better way for machines to evaluate stories.

VIST-Human Evaluation Several VIST generation models use human evaluation to evaluate model performance. Recent studies apply aspectbased rating evaluation. Hu et al. (2020b) and Wang et al. (2020b) ask workers to rate stories based on pre-defined aspects. 1 However, it is difficult to normalize these aspects as the definition of aspect varies from paper to paper. Also, these aspects are not mutually independent, making it difficult to analyze results based on these ratings. Therefore, we consider the ranking method as it is commonly used (Hsu et al., 2020;Wang et al., 2020b;Hsu et al., 2021a)  Automatic Metrics Automatic evaluation metrics are widely used in language generation tasks. Most reference-based metrics (e.g., BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), and ROUGE (Lin, 2004)) evaluate the ngram similarity between a generated text and the reference. However, referenced metrics correlate poorly with human judgment (Wang et al., 2018b;Hsu et al., 2019;Modi and Parde, 2019) in dialog generation and story generation tasks: the generated text is given unreasonable scores due to incongruity with the reference. To account for this, several reference-free metrics (Sinha et al., 2020;Guan and Huang, 2020) have been designed to measure generated texts without any reference. BERT-Score (Zhang et al., 2019), for instance, uses contextual embedding to calculate the similarity between candidates and references, and BLEURT (Sellam et al., 2020) uses referenced automatic metrics as supervision signals for pretraining and is fine-tuned on a human judgment evaluation dataset. Related work on automatic evaluation includes reference-based and reference-free families, covering BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), ROUGE (Lin, 2004), CIDEr (Vedantam et al., 2015), SPICE (Anderson et al., 2016), BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2019), MoverScore (Zhao et al., 2019), BLEURT (Sellam et al., 2020), COMET (Rei et al., 2020), UNION (Guan and Huang, 2020), and dialog/story-oriented measures such as USR (Mehri and Eskénazi, 2020) and MAUVE (Pillutla et al., 2021). UNION (Guan and Huang, 2020) uses pre-defined negative samples to train a model in an attempt to provide a metric that specializes in story generation. In our analysis, current metrics remain unable to mimic human judgment to discern quality differences in story pairs.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Introduction

Human values are of concern to most if not to all social sciences (Rokeach, 1973) and have also been integrated into computational frameworks of argumentation (Bench-Capon, 2003). In NLP, values have been analyzed for personality profiling (Maheshwari et al., 2017), but not yet for argument mining, as considered here. Addressing this gap requires clarifying which value constructs are operationalizable from argumentative text and how these constructs interact with claims and premises. We define value salience as the degree to which a text segment signals a preference over competing ends, and value alignment as the compatibility between an argument’s inferred ends and an external value schema. Building on these definitions, we ask whether values can be reliably identified at the component level and whether their lexical and rhetorical markers generalize across topics. To ground the inquiry, we consider value theories that provide organizing axes for ends, including terminal/instrumental distinctions and higher-order clusters. We then assess how these axes map to argument roles, defeasible rules, and audience-sensitive framing in practical settings such as policy debates.

Related Work

Schwartz’s theory of basic human values systematizes motivational goals along circumplex dimensions, enabling comparative analyses across cultures. Computationally, argument mining has matured from component identification to relation parsing and scheme classification, with resources such as UKP, IBM Debater, and ArgMining shared tasks catalyzing progress. Moral and ethical NLP has concurrently advanced value-adjacent constructs, including moral foundations detection, stance-conditioned framing, and normative reasoning from policy texts. In parallel, prior research has cataloged value lexica, persuasion strategies, and ethical taxonomies across disciplines without a unifying lens (Rokeach, 1973; Schwartz, 1992; Bench-Capon, 2003; Mullen and Malouf, 2006; Mohammad et al., 2016; Maheshwari et al., 2017; Gardenfors and Makinson, 1994; Floridi and Cowls, 2019), and resources such as Moral Foundations, the Schwartz Value Survey, and PECO have been used alongside methods like LIWC, VAD norms, and topic modeling in a range of datasets including Opinosis, ConvAI, IAC, and UKP, while modeling approaches have spanned lexicon-based tagging, supervised classification, distant supervision, and weakly supervised pattern induction. Prior work on argumentative style shows that hedging, modality, and discourse connectives modulate perceived persuasiveness, suggesting potential value cues at the pragmatic layer. Recent studies connect audience features to rhetorical success, indicating that value resonance may be partially predicted from socio-demographic proxies.

Motivation and Scope

Despite this progress, there is limited evidence on whether value constructs can be annotated consistently at the claim and premise levels across heterogeneous topics. Moreover, existing lexicons often conflate moral sentiments with instrumental preferences, obscuring the link to argument structure. We focus on text-only signals in public discourse to disentangle value salience from topic priors and sentiment polarity. Our objective is to bridge argument mining with operational value schemas, providing measurable targets that enable downstream tasks such as audience-aware retrieval and deliberation support. Finally, we outline desiderata for datasets that capture cross-topic generalization, annotator calibration, and hierarchical value labels suitable for modern sequence tagging architectures.

In this section, we first go through some of the most related works for BERT compression in the literature and then review the few works that have used Kronecker decomposition for compression of CNNs and RNNs.

BERT compression has been studied from multiple angles including pruning, quantization, distillation, low-rank factorization, tensor decomposition, and architectural modifications. Early explorations in pruning applied magnitude-based criteria to Transformer layers, while later works introduced movement and structured head pruning to maintain task performance under tight sparsity constraints. Quantization efforts range from post-training 8-bit schemes to mixed-precision and 4-bit methods that control activation clipping and calibration to preserve accuracy. Distillation-based approaches train compact students using teacher soft targets, intermediate layer matching, and task-agnostic pre-distillation before task-specific fine-tuning. Alternative architectures reduce parameter counts by revising attention or feed-forward sublayers, including linear attention and shared-parameter transformers.

Prior work on compressing pre-trained Transformers spans pruning-based methods that remove redundant weights or attention heads (Han et al., 2015; Voita et al., 2019; Michel et al., 2019; Lagunas et al., 2021), low-rank and tensor factorization approaches to decompose projection matrices (Sainath et al., 2013; Jaderberg et al., 2014; Denton et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2019), knowledge distillation using smaller student models trained on teacher logits or intermediate features (Hinton et al., 2015; Sanh et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2019), quantization to reduce precision of activations and weights (Jacob et al., 2018; Zafrir et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020; Banner et al., 2018), and structured decomposition with tensor trains, Tucker, and block-circulant matrices (Novikov et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018; Ye et al., 2018).

Kronecker-structured compression has a long history in CNNs, where convolutional kernels are approximated by sums or products of smaller Kronecker factors to reduce parameter counts while retaining receptive field behavior. Early work demonstrated that dense fully connected layers admit accurate Kronecker decompositions that yield immediate memory savings with minimal accuracy loss. Subsequent studies generalized these ideas to RNNs and LSTMs by decomposing recurrent and input weight matrices into Kronecker products, thus lowering both storage and multiply–accumulate operations per time step. Extensions also explored regularization and training constraints that promote Kronecker structure during learning rather than post hoc approximation.

Several tensorization methods are closely related to Kronecker decompositions but differ in factor tying and rank constraints. Tensor train and Tucker variants can subsume certain Kronecker forms, yet their optimization landscapes and hardware implications diverge due to reshaping strategies. Recent work has emphasized end-to-end training under structural constraints, jointly optimizing factor shapes to balance expressivity and latency. Practical deployments have reported favorable trade-offs when integrating hardware-aware objectives that penalize on-chip memory traffic and kernel launch overheads.

In BERT-like models, attention projections and feed-forward layers dominate both parameters and compute, motivating structured approximations that preserve isotropy across heads and layers. Factorized attention projections can be coordinated with low-bit quantization to compound savings without amplifying error accumulation across depth. When combined with knowledge distillation, compressed models recover much of the teacher’s calibration and robustness on out-of-domain benchmarks. Moreover, layer-wise reconstruction losses help align internal representations so that compression artifacts do not cascade across residual pathways.

Evaluation practices in the compression literature typically include GLUE and SQuAD for language understanding and question answering, alongside latency and energy measurements on GPUs and edge accelerators. Ablations often disentangle the effects of pruning ratio, quantization bit-width, and factor ranks, revealing interactions that shape Pareto frontiers. Robustness assessments consider adversarial perturbations and distribution shifts, while calibration and confidence metrics gauge the reliability of compressed predictors. Finally, reproducibility hinges on transparent training schedules, data preprocessing, and open-sourced inference kernels.

We next focus on the subset of methods that exploit algebraic structure, contrasting Kronecker decompositions with alternative tensor factorizations in terms of parameter efficiency and inference throughput. Prior reports indicate that the benefits of such structure are magnified when batch sizes are small and memory bandwidth is constrained, a common regime in on-device inference. We revisit these claims in controlled settings that isolate compute-bound and memory-bound phases. We also examine the interactions between structural ranks, activation sparsity, and quantization noise.

A central question is how to allocate compression budgets across layers given heterogeneous sensitivity profiles. Empirical evidence suggests that middle transformer blocks tolerate more aggressive structure than the embedding and final layers. This observation motivates layer-aware schedules that adapt factor ranks and quantization precision per block while keeping end-to-end perplexity within acceptable margins. Such schedules can be co-optimized with pruning masks derived from movement scores.

From an optimization standpoint, imposing Kronecker structure introduces non-convex manifolds that interact with Adam-style adaptive learning rates. Practical training stabilizes when warm-started from SVD- or CP-based initializations and regularized with weight decay on factor norms. Gradient clipping and cosine annealing further help avoid sharp minima that degrade generalization after compression. Mixed-precision training enables throughput while maintaining numerical stability of small factors.

Hardware considerations play an outsized role in determining realized speedups, since tensor cores and memory hierarchies favor specific factor shapes. Runtime-aware search can estimate arithmetic intensity and select decompositions that map efficiently to fused kernels. Pre-packing of Kronecker factors reduces launch overhead, and caching intermediate reshapes can prevent wasted transpositions. These details often dominate theoretical FLOP reductions in practice.

We conclude this section by summarizing open challenges around training stability, cross-task transferability, and principled selection of factor ranks. Future directions include automated structure discovery under latency constraints, compression-aware pre-training objectives, and tighter integration with sparsity-inducing hardware primitives. Together, these threads point toward compact yet accurate language models suitable for deployment across diverse compute environments.

Lacks synthesis.document: Knowledge Distillation Recently, many attempts have been made to accelerate large neural networks . Knowledge distillation is a prominent method for training compact networks to achieve comparable performance to a deep network. Hinton et al. (2015) first introduced the idea of knowledge distillation to exploit the "dark knowledge" (i.e., soft label distribution) from a large teacher model as additional supervision for training a smaller student model. Since its introduction, several works (Romero et al., 2015;Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2017;Tung & Mori, 2019;Park et al., 2019;Sun et al., 2019;Jiao et al., 2019) have investigated methods that align different latent representations between the student and teacher models for better knowledge transfer. In addition to the early formulation of distillation with soft targets, researchers have explored temperature scaling, feature-based transfer, and self-distillation across a variety of architectures and tasks (Hinton et al., 2015;Romero et al., 2015;Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2017;Furlanello et al., 2018;Yuan et al., 2020;Gou et al., 2021;Xie et al., 2020;Touvron et al., 2021). In the context of knowledge distillation, MetaDistil shares some common ideas with the line of work that utilizes a sequence of intermediate teacher models to make the teacher network better adapt to the capacity of the student model throughout the training process, including teacher assistant knowledge distillation (TAKD) (Mirzadeh et al., 2020) and route constraint optimization (RCO) . However, the intermediate teachers are heuristically selected independently of the training process and the evolution of the teacher network is discrete. In contrast, MetaDistil employs meta learning to make the teacher model adapt to the current state of the student model and provide a continuously evolving meta-teacher that can better teach the student. Concurrently, Park et al. (2021) and Shi et al. (2021) propose to update the teacher model jointly with the student model with task specific objectives (e.g., cross-entropy loss) during the KD process and add constraints to keep student and teacher similar to each other. Their approaches makes the teacher model aware of the student model by constraining the teacher model's capacity. However, the teacher models in their methods are still not optimized for knowledge transfer. In addition, Zhang et al. (2018) introduced deep mutual learning where multiple models learn collaboratively and teach each other throughout the training process. While it is focused on a different setting where different models have approximately the same capacity and are learned from scratch, it also encourages the teacher model to behave similarly to the student model. Different from all aforementioned methods, MetaDistil employs meta learning to explicitly optimize the teacher model for better knowledge transfer ability, and leads to improved performance of the resulting student model.

spans.span: Beyond these efforts, a broader adversarial NLP literature has investigated perturbation strategies for sequence labeling and token-level robustness without focusing on NER per se, including character-level noise injections and keyboard-distance edits (Ebrahimi et al., 2018; Belinkov and Bisk, 2018), semantically constrained paraphrases and gradient-guided word substitutions (Jia and Liang, 2017; Alzantot et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2019), template- or rule-driven adversaries for evaluation suites such as StressTest and Checklist (Naik et al., 2018; Ribeiro et al., 2020), and benchmark-scale adversarial evaluation frameworks and datasets like AdvGLUE, TextFooler, and HotFlip that probe model brittleness under targeted manipulations (Wang et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2020; Ebrahimi et al., 2018).

Additionally, regularization methods adjacent to mixup have been proposed across domains, such as manifold mixup (Verma et al., 2019), CutMix (Yun et al., 2019), AugMix (Hendrycks et al., 2020), and Vicinal Risk Minimization variants leveraging label smoothing and interpolation in hidden representations for robustness under covariate shift and calibration improvements (Szegedy et al., 2016; Müller et al., 2019; Berthelot et al., 2019).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Adversarial GLUE (Wang et al., 2021) employed the use of expert-annotated templates for constructing adversarial data, However, it does not include NER as a task. A few previous works have explored the generation of adversarial examples specifically for the NER task. For instance, Gui et al. (2021) performed augmentations by concatenating sentences, swapping/inserting/deleting a random character in an entity, entity swapping with Out-of-Vocabulary entities, and cross category swapping. Similarly, Zeng et al. (2020) also took random entity swap approach but only selected entities of the same label to preserve linguistic correctness. In our work, we purposely alter the entity and add surrounding context with the goal of changing the label to target the NER hard cases.

Beyond these efforts, a broader adversarial NLP literature has investigated perturbation strategies for sequence labeling and token-level robustness without focusing on NER per se, including character-level noise injections and keyboard-distance edits (Ebrahimi et al., 2018; Belinkov and Bisk, 2018), semantically constrained paraphrases and gradient-guided word substitutions (Jia and Liang, 2017; Alzantot et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2019), template- or rule-driven adversaries for evaluation suites such as StressTest and Checklist (Naik et al., 2018; Ribeiro et al., 2020), and benchmark-scale adversarial evaluation frameworks and datasets like AdvGLUE, TextFooler, and HotFlip that probe model brittleness under targeted manipulations (Wang et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2020; Ebrahimi et al., 2018).

In terms of techniques to improve generalization, we take a closer look at mixup, proposed in Zhang et al. (2018). Mixup involves linear interpolation of data points to create a virtual vicinity distribution around the original data space, which improves the classifier's generalization ability when trained on these interpolated data points. Several previous studies (Thulasidasan et al., 2020;Verma et al., 2019) showed how using mixup allows neural models to be less confident during distribution shifts than models not using mixup. It also leads to a smoother decision-making surface than Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM), thereby making models more robust to adversarial examples (Liang et al., 2018). Additionally, regularization methods adjacent to mixup have been proposed across domains, such as manifold mixup (Verma et al., 2019), CutMix (Yun et al., 2019), AugMix (Hendrycks et al., 2020), and Vicinal Risk Minimization variants leveraging label smoothing and interpolation in hidden representations for robustness under covariate shift and calibration improvements (Szegedy et al., 2016; Müller et al., 2019; Berthelot et al., 2019). In this work, we use mixup to further improve the generalization ability of NER models when training on our expert-informed augmented data.

Task. Semantic parsing has been widely studied in the context of multiple other tasks like instruction following (Chen and Mooney, 2011;Artzi and Zettlemoyer, 2013), code generation (Oda et al., 2015;Iyer et al., 2018), knowledge graph question answering (Berant et al., 2013;Yih et al., 2015), etc. We focus on using tables as the context in which semantic parsing is performed, where the goal is to translate pairs of natural language questions and tables to executable SQL queries, also known as text-to-SQL parsing (Androutsopoulos et al., 1995;Minock et al., 2008). Note that, while we focus on questions in the English language, there exists prior work on multilingual semantic parsing as well (Jie and Lu, 2014;Sherborne et al., 2020) and the contributions of our work also apply there. Formally, our goal is to map a pair (q, T ), where q is a natural language question and T is a table, to an executable program π that, when executed against table T , will produce the answer α to question q. We focus on the fully-supervised set-ting where the target executable program π * is provided as supervision for training our parser.

Out-of-Domain Generalization. Generalization in machine learning is often defined as the ability to do well on a test set after learning from a training set, where all examples in both sets are drawn independently from the same distribution (i.i.d. generalization). However, as Gu et al. (2021) argue, in real-world applications such as semantic parsing, the test data may involve new compositional structures (compositional generalization), or new domains (domain generalization) that are not encountered during training. Existing work in compositional generalization for semantic parsing has focused on using synthetic datasets (e.g., Keysers et al., 2020;Lake and Baroni, 2018), or repartitioning existing text-to-SQL datasets into new train and test splits (e.g., Finegan-Dollak et al., 2018). Both approaches have generally shown that compositional generalization remains an important challenge (e.g., Shaw et al., 2021). We focus on the arguably even more challenging domain generalization problem, also known as domain adaptation, where entire domains may never be encountered during training or may only be encountered a small number of times (Motiian et al., 2017). Even though this problem has been studied extensively in the context of classification (Daumé III and Marcu, 2006), machine translation (Daumé III and Jagarlamudi, 2011), and question answering (Talmor and Berant, 2019), it remains underexplored for semantic parsing. However, to be applicable in real scenarios, semantic parsers should be able to generalize to new domains, since collecting domain-specific labeled data is often prohibitively expensive. Recent approaches have focused on data synthesis (Yin et al., 2021), meta-learning (Wang et al., 2021), relation-aware schema encoding (Wang et al., 2020), and encoder pre-training (Yin et al., 2020;Herzig et al., 2020;Yu et al., 2020;Deng et al., 2021). In this paper, we hone in on one aspect of domain generalization that we shall broadly refer to as column operations and which was introduced in §1 and illustrated in Figure .

Evaluation Benchmarks. Text-to-SQL parsing became popular after the introduction of large-scale datasets and evaluation benchmarks. Zhong et al. (2017) first introduced WIKISQL, which contains Wikipedia tables paired with questions and annotated with SQL queries, albeit the queries are generated from a limited set of templates. SPIDER was introduced by Yu et al. (2018) the following year. It contains more complex questions and SQL queries and focuses on generalizing to previously unseen database schemas, but the dataset has the artifact from its annotation design that the references columns are often mentioned verbatim in the natural language questions. Deng et al. (2021) attempt to address this limitation by repartitioning SPIDER to produce a more realistic benchmark, and Lee et al. (2021) propose a challenging test set from Kaggle for evaluating parsers trained on SPIDER dataset. However, as Suhr et al. (2020) point out, SPIDER uses a simplified setting which excludes examples that involve multiple columns (e.g., adding two columns together), as well as ones that require background knowledge. These benchmarks are thus limited in their usefulness for evaluating parsers in real-world settings where they may encounter complex questions that require mapping specific phrases to expressions over table columns, rather than to a single column. Also, while both WIKISQL and SPIDER assume "simple" tables with only String-or Number-valued columns, in practice we may encounter tables where the columns themselves may have structured types (e.g., TimeSpan). For example, consider the table shown on the top left of Figure . In this case, the "Term" column is of type TimeSpan and consists of two Numbers that represent the beginning and the end of the timespan. In this case, users may ask questions that require constructing expressions to access nested elements from the "Term" column (e.g., "How long was Pier's term?"). Recently, Shi et al. (2020) introduced SQUALL, a dataset that annotates WIKITABLEQUES-TIONS (Pasupat and Liang, 2015) with SQL queries and refined column types like Date, Score, (T1, T2), and List[T]. However, SQUALL distributes tables evenly between the train and test splits, thus not allowing us to evaluate the kind of out-of-domain generalization we are interested in. Therefore as we will show in the following section, we aim to addresses this limitation by repartitioning SQUALL into new train and test splits. Neural Text-to-SQL Parsers. Neural encoder-decoder models have recently gained popularity for text-to-SQL parsing (e.g., Xu et al., 2017). We focus on two models that represent the current state-of-the-art for SQUALL and SPIDER, respectively: SEQ2SEQ of Shi et al. (2020) and SMBOP of Rubin and Berant (2021). Both models concatenate the question with a textual representation of the table schema, separated by a special [SEP] token, and feed the combined sequence to a pre-trained instance of the BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) language model. The activations of the last layer represent the encoded representations of the question and the table schema. SEQ2SEQ then uses a autoregressive decoder, which represents programs as token sequences and at each decoding step it: (1) predicts the next token type (i.e., whether the next token is a SQL keyword, a column name, or a literal value), and (2) predicts the token conditioned on its type. SMBOP, on the other hand, uses bottom-up decoding, which represents programs as abstract syntax trees and constructs these trees in a bottom-up fashion (i.e., it starts by predicting the leave nodes and then recursively composes generated sub-trees into new trees and ranks them, in a way that resembles beam search), until it reaches the tree root. We refer the reader to the aforementioned papers for details.

Structured pruning for pre-trained Transformers has been investigated via attention head scoring (Michel et al., 2019), feedforward and block-level gating (Prasanna et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2021), rank-constrained factorization with L0 regularization (Wang et al., 2020c; Louizos et al., 2018), layer dropping policies (Sajjad et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2019), movement pruning and magnitude pruning variants (Sanh et al., 2020; Lagunas et al., 2021), and low-rank embedding compression (Lan et al., 2020; Acharya et al., 2019).

Setting Recent multilingual translation researches suggest that adapting subnetworks for each language or language pair rather than for all of them gives better results. Li et al. (2020) train a shared multilingual model, then select layers for each language pair. Lin et al. (2021) also prune a shared multilingual model for each language pair, but on entries in weight matrices instead. Gong et al. (2021), on the other hand, prune attention heads and feedforward networks for each language. Xie et al. (2021) first identify general and language-specific neurons in a shared multilingual network, then tune those neurons using the data of their corresponding language only. Recent efforts on multilingual adaptation explore subnetwork specialization across languages and tasks, spanning layer selection (Li et al., 2020), unit-level pruning in shared matrices (Lin et al., 2021), head- and MLP-level pruning (Gong et al., 2021), and neuron attribution with language-specific fine-tuning (Xie et al., 2021), alongside multilingual pre-training frameworks such as mBERT (Devlin et al., 2019), XLM (Lample and Conneau, 2019), XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020), and mT5 (Xue et al., 2021). These findings inspire our non-shared pruning setting and to see whether its results on multilingual translation could extend to multilingual pre-training.

Algorithm There are many structured pruning techniques proposed for monolingual pre-trained language models recently. Michel et al. (2019) propose a simple gradient-based importance score to prune attention heads. Prasanna et al. (2020); Liang et al. (2021) extend this method to prune other components like the feedforward network of the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017). Wang et al. (2020c) decompose the pre-trained model weights and apply L 0 regularization (Louizos et al., 2018) to regulate the ranks of decomposed weights. Sajjad et al. (2020) study layer pruning and shows that directly dropping the top layers performs the best in fine-tuning. Structured pruning for pre-trained Transformers has been investigated via attention head scoring (Michel et al., 2019), feedforward and block-level gating (Prasanna et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2021), rank-constrained factorization with L0 regularization (Wang et al., 2020c; Louizos et al., 2018), layer dropping policies (Sajjad et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2019), movement pruning and magnitude pruning variants (Sanh et al., 2020; Lagunas et al., 2021), and low-rank embedding compression (Lan et al., 2020; Acharya et al., 2019). As mentioned, compression is a widely used strategy to speed-up the large language models Gupta and Agrawal, 2020). This involves incorporating techniques such as quantization of weights and activations (Bai et al., 2020;Shen et al., 2020;Kim et al., 2021;Jin et al., 2021), knowledge distillation (KD) (Hinton et al., 2015;Jiao et al., 2020;Sanh et al., 2019), pruning/sharing (Gordon et al., 2020;, multi-device distribution (Banitalebi-Dehkordi et al., 2021), or a combination of these techniques (Cheng et al., 2017;Polino et al., 2018).

Among all the compression techniques, creating a fixed-size small version of large models along with distillation has been popular in the recent years. Sanh et al. (2019) introduced DistillBERT, which was a smaller version of BERT trained with distillation for general purposes. Another compact variant of BERT was proposed by Mobile-BERT (Sun et al., 2020) in which inverted bottleneck structures and progressive knowledge transfer were used. TinyBERT (Jiao et al., 2020) also presented a novel two-stage transformer distillation for both pre-training and task-specific fine-tuning. In (Iandola et al., 2020), the usage of grouped convolutions was studied to design SqueezeBERT. ELM (Jiao et al., 2021), a layer mapping search framework, was also proposed for improving downstream BERT distillation. A recent method, Ghost-BERT , employed softmaxnormalized 1D convolutions as ghost modules to generate more features with cheap operations.

Although compression techniques in general are effective, they come with a trade-off on accuracy, and may lose performance in case of high ratio compression. In addition, an individual fixed-size model is required for each possible computational budget. As stated in the introduction, the alternative solution is dynamic inference, which can be achieved with either early-exit or length/depthadaptive models. One of the first temporal earlyexit strategies was proposed by ReasoNet (Shen et al., 2017), which stops its reading procedure when sufficient evidence has been found for answering a question. Similarly, in (Yu et al., 2018), an early stopping method applicable to classification tasks was presented. DeeBERT  also proposed an instance-wise multi-exit method via the entropy of the output probability distribution to speed-up BERT inference.

As a length-adaptive method, Kim and Cho (2021) introduced a dynamic inference framework with one-shot training of transformers for both sequence-and token-level classification. Also, in , an architecture named Dyn-aBERT was proposed for adaptively adjusting the computations by choosing sub-networks of different widths and depths. Both Length-Adaptive and DynaBERT utilized knowledge distillation and data augmentation to improve their performance.

Recent approaches to dynamic computation also explore adaptive routing, budgeted inference, and conditional execution across architectures and tasks, including LayerDrop (Fan et al., 2020), SkipNet (Wang et al., 2018), DynamicConv (Wu et al., 2019), ACT for Transformers (Graves, 2016; Dehghani et al., 2019), Universal Transformers (Dehghani et al., 2019), and token pruning/merging methods such as PoWER-BERT (Goyal et al., 2020), LTP (Kim et al., 2022), and Token Merging (Bolya et al., 2023).

Although early-exit and adaptive methods have made significant progress and work well in practice, they often require architectural manipulation and re-training. In addition, they are only applicable to encoder-only backbones and classification tasks. In contrast, our method can work with out-of-the-box pre-trained models without a need for re-training and are also applicable for encoder-decoder structures and sequence-to-sequence tasks.
