Lacks synthesis.document:
Pre-trained model analysis is a rapidly growing area in NLP today. There are a number of methods for analyzing internal representations of a model, including structured head and FCN pruning (Michel et al., 2019;Voita et al., 2019;Prasanna et al., 2020), residual connection and layer normalization analysis (Kovaleva et al., 2021;Kobayashi et al., 2021), and analyzing attention patterns (Clark et al., 2019;Kovaleva et al., 2019).

Compared to these methods, probing tasks (Conneau et al., 2018;Tenney et al., 2019) provide a more direct way to evaluate what a model can and cannot accomplish. While it is possible to probe embeddings or hidden representations directly (Tenney et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2019a), with the adoption of pre-trained language models has made it possible to evaluate such models by framing probing tasks close to the original model objective (Radford et al., 2019;Talmor et al., 2019;Ettinger, 2020;Goldberg, 2019).

However, when a research area moves this quickly, it can be hard to keep up with many new models. Most of the existing research (Garí Soler and Apidianaki, 2020;Zagoury et al., 2021;Kassner et al., 2020) papers compare only one or two model families. Even some of the most recent works only probe BERT or very similar models (Zagoury et al., 2021;Liu et al., 2021). Only a small number of analysis papers have probed multiple (three or more) model families (Zhou et al., 2021;Ilharco et al., 2021).

Recent overviews have cataloged numerous probing and analysis angles without consolidating them into a single comparative lens, including attention attribution and faithfulness studies (Jain and Wallace, 2019; Serrano and Smith, 2019; Wiegreffe and Pinter, 2019), causal mediation and intervention analyses (Vig et al., 2020; Feder et al., 2021; Elazar et al., 2021), linear probes and information separation (Alain and Bengio, 2017; Hewitt and Manning, 2019; Voita and Titov, 2020), model editing and knowledge localization (Meng et al., 2022; De Cao et al., 2021; Sinitsin et al., 2020), and dataset-driven stress tests for linguistic capabilities (Warstadt et al., 2019; Naik et al., 2018; Ribeiro et al., 2020; Gardner et al., 2020).

In contrast to existing work, we perform a largescale probing of 28 models across 8 different model families. We apply the existing probing benchmarks, namely, oLMpics (Talmor et al., 2019) and psycholinguistic datasets (Ettinger, 2020), to models that differ in the pre-training objective, datasets, size, architecture, and directionality. We further control for tokenization differences and sequence length limits to ensure that performance discrepancies are not attributable to preprocessing artifacts. Our evaluation isolates architectural and objective-driven factors by grouping models into consistent families and reporting variance within and across families. We also include both masked and autoregressive models to assess whether directionality mediates the depth of linguistic generalization. To facilitate reproducibility, we standardize hyperparameters, calibration procedures, and early stopping criteria across all runs. Beyond aggregate scores, we analyze item-level error patterns that reveal contrasts between syntactic sensitivity and world knowledge reliance. Finally, we release a unified probing suite and standardized model adapters to make cross-family analyses easier for future work.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Introduction

Encoder–decoder models are widely used in dialog response generation, yet they often produce generic, non-committal replies (e.g., I don't know), reflecting exposure bias and weak modeling of conversational intent. To mitigate this, researchers have explored diversity-promoting objectives (Li et al., 2016a), alternative decoding algorithms (Li et al., 2016b), auxiliary content infusion such as topical or persona cues (Xu et al., 2019), and the integration of large-scale knowledge graphs for grounding (Liu et al., 2018). While these strategies improve surface-level variety and informativeness, they may not fully capture discourse-level variability needed for multi-intent turns.

Another class of methods tackles the one-to-many nature of dialog with latent-variable models that aim to represent high-level discourse factors. Variational approaches and hierarchical latent structures have been shown to increase response diversity and reduce blandness (Serban et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2017a; Zhao et al., 2018). However, instability during training and posterior collapse can limit their effectiveness without careful architectural and objective choices.

A parallel strand surveys retrieval-augmented generation and controllable decoding in open-domain dialog, including knowledge-grounded systems that index external corpora or APIs for factuality (Dinan et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2021; Shuster et al., 2021; Komeili et al., 2022), plug-and-play control via attribute models or gradient-based steering (Dathathri et al., 2020; Krause et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2022; Yang and Klein, 2021), prompt- and instruction-tuned conversational LMs (Ouyang et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2022; Sanh et al., 2022), and evaluation datasets targeting humanness, engagement, and factual consistency (Dinan et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2020; Mehri and Eskenazi, 2020; Honovich et al., 2022).

Despite progress, aligning diverse generation with conversational goals remains challenging when supervision is sparse and context spans are long. Prior work indicates that modeling discourse acts and latent intents can bridge surface diversity with goal-directed behavior, but consistent conditioning across multi-turn histories is still underexplored. Moreover, pre-training objectives often emphasize next-token likelihood rather than hierarchical discourse signals, leaving a gap between language modeling and dialog-level control.

In this work, we revisit latent-variable modeling with a focus on injecting discourse-aware structure early in training. We couple pre-training of latent variables with utterance- and session-level signals to stabilize inference and preserve variability through fine-tuning. Our approach seeks to retain the benefits of latent representations while improving controllability and grounding in realistic multi-turn settings.

We evaluate across knowledge-grounded and chit-chat scenarios to test both informativeness and stylistic breadth. Experimental results demonstrate substantial gains in distinctness, entailment-checked factuality, and user-rated engagement without sacrificing coherence. Ablations highlight the role of pre-trained latent priors and hierarchical conditioning in preventing degeneration and maintaining response specificity. Finally, we discuss limitations regarding domain transfer and safety constraints, pointing to future work on adaptive priors and risk-sensitive decoding.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Document understanding is a critical and challenging task in information processing. There have been many related research works in this direction. Keyword detection (Liu et al., 2009;Tixier et al., 2016) & topic modeling (Blei et al., 2003) works aim is to describe the document by a few important words or topics for concise representation. The first step is to acquire a list of keyword candidates (e.g., n-grams or chunks) with heuristic methods (Hulth, 2003;Shang et al., 2018), then rank them in accordance with their importance to the document (Wu et al., 2005;Gollapalli and Caragea, 2014;Bougouin et al., 2013). Another task is compact and informative headline generation from a document (David and Zajic, 2003;Lopyrev, 2015). Text summarization is the process of generating natural language summaries from an input document retaining the most important information (Rush et al., 2015;See et al., 2017). Recently, an Outline Generation task was introduced by (Zhang et al., 2019) as a hierarchical structured prediction problem. Given a document, their aim is to first predict a sequence of section boundaries and then a sequence of section headings accordingly to come up with a Table of Contents for the same.

A related direction of work to ours is of aspect detection, which has been explored in the literature largely using user reviews for products. Early works focused on rule-based approaches using lexicons and dependency relations, and utilize manually defined rules to identify patterns and extract aspects (Qiu et al., 2011;Liu et al., 2016), which require domain-specific knowledge and human expertise. Supervised approaches formulate aspect extraction as a sequence labelling problem that can be solved by hidden Markov models (HMM) (Jin et al., 2009), conditional random fields (CRF) (Li et al., 2010;Mitchell et al., 2013;Yang and Cardie, 2012), and recurrent neural networks (RNN) (Wang et al., 2016;Liu et al., 2015). These approaches have shown better performance compared to the rule-based ones, but require large amounts of labelled data for training. Early unsupervised systems are dominated by Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)-based topic models (García-Pablos et al., 2018;Shi et al., 2018;Alvarez-López et al., 2016). Recently, deep learning based topic models (Srivastava and Sutton, 2017;Luo et al., 2019;He et al., 2017;Shi et al., 2021) have shown strong performance in extracting coherent aspects in an unsupervised manner. None of the prior works on aspect detection have worked with contracts or financial documents that are quite long (50-100 pages) in comparison to user reviews. Even if we break the document at paragraph level, it can still go over tens of lines. Hence, the importance of word frequency is much more in our case. We bridge the gap between directly using the unsupervised aspect detection frameworks for the financial documents by adding a TF-IDF based weighing parameter while training. Moreover, there are no gold standards for aspect detection for contract or finance domain, hence, we use unsupervised clustering based metrics for validating the output detection.

Further, it has been shown that question-answers play a critical role in scientific inquiry, informationseeking dialogue, and knowledge acquisition (Hintikka and Saarinen, 1979;Stede and Schlangen, 2004). In a dialogue system, question generation is used to obtain specific information from the user or make the conversation more pleasant (Shukla et al., 2019;Saeidi et al., 2018). Hence, we hypothesize that augmenting the default ToC with Questions that give a high level overview of the paragraphs can enhance the reading experience of the users. Question generation can also be seen as a summarization or seq2seq task. Various pre-trained language models like BART (Lewis et al., 2020), PEGASUS (Zhang et al., 2020), etc., have shown excellent results for these tasks. Researchers have worked on top of these language models & proposed various rewards for QGen to optimize these models. (Kumar et al., 2019) has employed BLEUbased rewards, (Zhang and Bansal, 2019) have used answerability rewards, whereas (Xie et al., 2020) has used a combination of fluency, relevance, and answerability rewards.

Previous question generation literature has focused on generating questions based on an entity, phrase, or sentence. In this work, we explore longform question generation, i.e., question-based long text. We explore deep reinforcement learning techniques for the same. as they have shown competitive results in various natural language generation tasks such as summarization (Pasunuru and Bansal, 2018), style transfer (Liu et al., 2021;Goyal et al., 2021), question generation (Hosking and Riedel, 2019;Xie et al., 2020) etc. Motivated by this we use BART as our base model. As there is a lack of labeled question datasets in financial domain, to overcome the domain shift problem, we train the model with additional rewards in a reinforcement learning setup to make more suitable for a general domain.

There are several commercial products for reading documents across devices, but all of them have a fixed document navigation, based on chapters and headings. To the best of our knowledge, there is no prior art looking into providing an end-to-end persona-based navigation. The mentioned technologies address only part of the required solutions. Following are the key contributions of our work:

1. We propose a novel DYNAMICTOC technology to enable persona-based non-linear navigation for efficient consumption of long documents.

2. We extend the unsupervised aspect detection to long domain-specific documents by combining TF-IDF with aspect detection process to make it more robust and show the improvements experimentally.

3. We propose a method to generate questions based on the content of the paragraph maximizing the information coverage, entity correctness & answerability of the question.

4. We showcase the viability of our pipeline and evaluate it using metric-based and a human survey-based evaluation.

3 Datasets SEC Filing: The SEC filing is a financial statement document submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Public companies, certain insiders, and broker-dealers are required to make regular SEC filings. There are many types of documents available on the EDGAR website (Eg. 10-K, 10-Q, Form 4, etc.). For our work, we focused on the SEC 10-K documents available on the EDGAR website 1 . For a given company, the 10-k documents are available in HTML, XBRL and XML format. The complete submission text file for a 10-k document (XML) was used for parsing. We split the document content into different items ranging from item 1 to item 16. These 10-K documents range from 50 to 120 pages and contain multiple tables along with text paragraphs. ELI5: We use the ELI5 dataset (Fan et al., 2019) to train the question generation model. ELI5 or Explain Like I'm 5, is a question-answer dataset scraped from the subreddit r/explainlikeimfive/. The subreddit rules encourage people to ask a question about any topic and get an answer for it. To maintain the dataset's quality, we only select those question-answer pairs with more than two upvotes. Note that no dataset for such question generation task exists for contractual and financial documents. Hence, we resort to use the ELI5 dataset for supervised training and use that model for inferencing on documents from a different domain. To test the model's performance on the domainspecific dataset, we also scrape question-answer pairs from two different subreddits -r/AskLegal and r/AskEconomics. As the name suggests, they contain questions (and answers) from the legal and economics domain respectively. Table  includes the statistics of the three datasets.

Lacks synthesis.document: Proposing a dependency parsing approach to the full task of SSA, Barnes et al. (2021) show that it leads to strong improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Peng et al. (2021) propose a sparse fuzzy attention mechanism to deal with the sparseness of dependency arcs in the models from Barnes et al. (2021) and show further improvements. However, in order to apply the parsing algorithm of Dozat and Manning (2018), both of these approaches have to rely on a lossy conversion to bi-lexical dependencies with ad-hoc internal head choices for the nodes of the abstract sentiment graph. This lossy behaviour is caused by nested text spans in the sentiment graphs, as illustrated by Figure , which are ambiguous in their bi-lexical dependency encoding (see Section A in the Appendix). More generally, decoding structured graph information from text has sparked a lot of interest in recent years, especially for parsing meaning representation graphs (Oepen et al., 2020). There has been tremendous progress in developing complex transition-based and graph-based parsers (Hershcovich et al., 2017;McDonald and Pereira, 2006;Dozat and Manning, 2018). Recent work on general graph parsing and structured prediction spans a spectrum of models and resources without a unifying perspective, including transition-based AMR parsers that leverage stack-pointer networks (Zhang et al., 2019), biaffine graph parsers for semantic dependencies (Dozat and Manning, 2018; Dozat and Manning, 2017), neural encoders for UCCA and MRP with cross-framework evaluation (Hershcovich et al., 2017; Oepen et al., 2020), and pretrained language model adaptations such as BERT-based semantic parsers for AMR 2.0 and AMR 3.0 (Cai and Lam, 2020; Bevilacqua et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2020). In this paper, we adopt PERIN (Samuel and Straka, 2020), a state-of-theart graph-based parser capable of modeling a superset of graph features needed for our task. We focus on sentiment structure analysis (SSA) where graph nodes may correspond to nested spans, operators, and roles that exceed bi-lexical formalisms. Prior work has often reduced these structures to trees or bilexical arcs, sacrificing expressivity when dealing with discontinuities and reentrancies. Our formulation treats SSA as a typed, labeled graph prediction problem over spans and anchors with constraints inspired by meaning representation parsing. PERIN provides a natural foundation as it supports multi-head edges, latent anchors, and edge reentrancies. We extend PERIN with span-level representations derived from contextual encoders to better handle nested sentiment constituents. Additionally, we introduce a graph decoding constraint set that preserves well-formedness while allowing multiple overlapping spans. To evaluate these modeling choices, we compare against dependency-based baselines and conversion pipelines on established SSA benchmarks. We report results across standard precision, recall, and F1 for nodes, edges, and role labels under exact and partial span matching. Our experiments further analyze error types related to nested spans, discontinuities, and operator-role confusion. Finally, we discuss implications for downstream sentiment summarization and controllable opinion generation.

Lacks synthesis.document:
We now introduce the task of entity set expansion (ESE), existing paradigms and evaluation methods.
ESE aims to grow a small set of seed entities that exemplify a semantic category into a more complete set drawn from a large corpus or knowledge source.
Given seeds such as {France, Germany, Italy}, the system should return additional countries while avoiding near-misses like cities or regions.
Applications include schema completion, query suggestion, knowledge base augmentation, and support for downstream NLP tasks that require lexicons.
Classical methods rely on distributional similarity, pattern harvesting, and bootstrapping to generalize from the seeds to candidate entities.
Recent approaches span distributional similarity with static embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014), context-sensitive encoders and prompt-based retrieval (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2021), bootstrapping and graph-based propagation (Thelen and Riloff, 2002; Kozareva et al., 2008; Velikovich et al., 2010), query log mining (Sarmento et al., 2007; Wang and Cohen, 2007), pattern-based extraction (Hearst, 1992; Pasca, 2004), and weakly supervised or distant supervision strategies (Mintz et al., 2009; Ren et al., 2015), along with benchmarks such as SEAL, WiCE, and ESE-Graph that report precision@k and AUC metrics.
A central challenge in ESE is balancing recall with precision, especially under seed sparsity and domain shift.
Ambiguity further complicates ranking because surface forms like "Apple" or "Amazon" may refer to multiple entity types.
Moreover, lexical patterns and distributional contexts vary across domains, making fixed similarity thresholds brittle.
To compare methods fairly, evaluations typically fix a seed budget, control candidate vocabulary, and standardize scoring metrics such as precision@k, mean average precision, and normalized discounted cumulative gain.
Open-world settings introduce long-tail candidates that require calibrated uncertainty estimates and robust negative sampling strategies.
In addition, bias can be introduced by seed selection, corpus domain, and knowledge base coverage, necessitating transparent experimental protocols.
Recent work explores interactive and iterative ESE where user feedback reshapes the exploration frontier, trading off exploration and exploitation over successive rounds.
Cross-lingual ESE leverages multilingual representations and alignment signals to transfer category structure across languages with minimal supervision.
In what follows, we formalize the problem setting, define the evaluation protocol, and outline the components of our approach to entity set expansion.
We also delineate the assumptions under which our analysis holds and specify the datasets, metrics, and ablations used to assess performance.

spans.span: The broader landscape of controllable text generation has also included style transfer (Shen et al., 2017;Fu et al., 2018;Lample et al., 2019), controllable summarization (Fan et al., 2018;He et al., 2020;Schumann et al., 2020), attribute-conditioned generation (Hu et al., 2017;Keskar et al., 2019;Dathathri et al., 2020;Krause et al., 2020), and syntactic control via parse templates or structured encoders (Iyyer et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2020;Sun et al., 2021;Yang and Klein, 2021), along with benchmarking efforts on paraphrase corpora such as Quora Question Pairs, MRPC, and ParaNMT (Dolan and Brockett, 2005;Iyer et al., 2017;Wieting and Gimpel, 2018).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Many recent works on paraphrase generation have been focused on attempting to achieve high-quality paraphrases. These works can be divided into supervised and unsupervised approaches.

Supervised Approaches To achieve diversity, some works focused on diverse decoding using heuristics such as Hamming distance or distinct n-grams to preserve diverse options during beam search (Vijayakumar et al., 2018). Other works MSCOCO WikiAns ParaBank2 q sem ↑ q syn ↑ q lex ↑ i-BLEU↓ q sem ↑ q syn ↑ q lex ↑ i-BLEU↓ q sem ↑ q syn ↑ q lex ↑ i-BLEU↓ Gold 29.9 34. generate multiple outputs by perturbing latent representations (Gupta et al., 2018;Park et al., 2019). or by using distinct generators (Qian et al., 2019). These methods achieve some diversity, but do not control generation in an interpretable manner.

The works that are most similar to ours strive to gain diversity using controlled-paraphrase generation, by exposing control mechanisms that are manipulated to produce either lexically (Zeng et al., 2019;Thompson and Post, 2020) or syntactically Goyal and Durrett, 2020) diverse paraphrases. One approach is to use an exemplar sentence for guiding the syntax of the generated paraphrase Bao et al., 2019). An alternative is to directly employ constituency tree as the syntax guidance (Iyyer et al., 2018;Li and Choi, 2020). Goyal and Durrett (2020) promote syntactic diversity by conditioning over possible syntactic rearrangements of the input. Zeng et al. (2019) use keywords as lexical guidance for the generation process. The broader landscape of controllable text generation has also included style transfer (Shen et al., 2017;Fu et al., 2018;Lample et al., 2019), controllable summarization (Fan et al., 2018;He et al., 2020;Schumann et al., 2020), attribute-conditioned generation (Hu et al., 2017;Keskar et al., 2019;Dathathri et al., 2020;Krause et al., 2020), and syntactic control via parse templates or structured encoders (Iyyer et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2020;Sun et al., 2021;Yang and Klein, 2021), along with benchmarking efforts on paraphrase corpora such as Quora Question Pairs, MRPC, and ParaNMT (Dolan and Brockett, 2005;Iyer et al., 2017;Wieting and Gimpel, 2018). Here we introduce a simple model for jointly controlling the lexical, syntactic and semantic aspects of the generated paraphrases.

Unsupervised Approaches Niu et al. (2020) rely on neural models to generate high quality paraphrases, using a decoding method that enforces diversity by preventing repetitive copying of the input tokens. Liu et al. (2020) optimize a quality oriented objective by casting paraphrase generation as an optimization problem, and searching the sentence space to find the optimal point. Garg et al. (2021) and Siddique et al. (2020) use reinforcement learning with quality-oriented reward combining textual entailment, semantic similarity, expression diversity and fluency. In this work, we employ similar metrics for guiding the generation of paraphrases within the supervised framework.

spans.span: Recent advances in temporal commonsense also include methods and resources that emphasize structured temporal knowledge and probing of pre-trained models without explicitly relating these strands to a unifying objective, such as CaTeRS for event relations (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016), TimeQA for temporally-aware question answering (Chen et al., 2021), TEA-GNN architectures for temporal event graphs (Ning et al., 2019), temporal probing suites for LMs (Zhou et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2020), and hybrid neural-symbolic temporal reasoning frameworks (Lee et al., 2020), alongside evaluations on TimeBank-Dense and MATRES (Cassidy et al., 2014;Ning et al., 2018).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Temporal Commonsense. Work on temporal reasoning ranges from extracting and normalizing temporal expressions (Strötgen and Gertz, 2010;Angeli et al., 2012;Vashishtha et al., 2019), to inferring possibly explicit temporal attributes of events, including their order (Ning et al., 2018;Vashishtha et al., 2019), duration (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008;Vashishtha et al., 2019), and typical times or frequencies (Zhou et al., 2019).

Various benchmarks were proposed to measure models' temporal reasoning abilities. The bAbI suite contains a task that requires reasoning about the order of time expressions (Weston et al., 2015). MC-TACO is a reading comprehension task pertaining to ordering, duration, stationarity, frequency, and typical times of events (Zhou et al., 2019). TI-MEDIAL (Qin et al., 2021) is a dialogue QA task focusing on temporal commonsense. Zhou et al. (2021) and Thukral et al. (2021) both cast the temporal ordering task as an NLI task. In another line of work, tracking state changes in procedural text is also related to temporal ordering (Dalvi et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2020). Despite the success of pre-trained LMs on language understanding tasks, their performance on these benchmarks is limited, maybe due to the fact that many temporal relations are not explicitly stated in text (Davis and Marcus, 2015). A promising direction is to train LMs explicitly on temporal knowledge (Zhou et al., 2020). Recent advances in temporal commonsense also include methods and resources that emphasize structured temporal knowledge and probing of pre-trained models without explicitly relating these strands to a unifying objective, such as CaTeRS for event relations (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016), TimeQA for temporally-aware question answering (Chen et al., 2021), TEA-GNN architectures for temporal event graphs (Ning et al., 2019), temporal probing suites for LMs (Zhou et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2020), and hybrid neural-symbolic temporal reasoning frameworks (Lee et al., 2020), alongside evaluations on TimeBank-Dense and MATRES (Cassidy et al., 2014;Ning et al., 2018).

Cultural Commonsense. There is little focus on cultural differences in NLP in general (Hovy and Yang, 2021) and in research about commonsense reasoning in particular. Recently, Acharya et al. (2021) made a first step in addressing this gap. They surveyed crowdsourcing workers in the US and India regarding rituals that are commonly found across cultures such as birth, marriage, and funerals. In particular, they asked questions pertaining to temporal aspects such as typical time and duration of each event. The paper mentions anecdotal differences such that a wedding lasts a few hours in the US but a few days in India.

Although there is no direct mapping between culture and language, one can often teach about the other. For example, in ConceptNet, a multilingual commonsense knowledge base, the English entry for breakfast specifies pancakes as breakfast food, while the Chinese entry mentions noodles (Speer et al., 2017).

Language Grounding and World Knowledge. Our work is related to language grounding (Roy and Reiter, 2005) and to extracting world knowledge from text corpora (Carlson et al., 2010;Tandon et al., 2014). In the intersection of these two lines of work, Forbes and Choi (2017) extracted from a corpus physical commonsense knowledge about actions and objects along five dimensions (size, weight, strength, rigidness, and speed), while Elazar et al. (2019) induced distributions of typical values of various quantitative attributes such as time, duration, length, and speed. Elazar et al. (2019) mention cultural differences that arose when crowdsourcing workers were asked to estimate whether an item's price was expensive or not: annotators from India judged prices differently from annotators in the US.

spans.span: Recently, several lines of work in neural ranking and retrieval have explored architectural simplifications, efficiency-oriented interaction designs, and dense retrieval objectives without cross-attention, including ANCE (Xiong et al., 2021), DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020), COIL (Gao et al., 2021), ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al., 2022), SPLADE (Formal et al., 2021), and RocketQA (Qu et al., 2021), as well as approximate nearest neighbor toolkits such as FAISS (Johnson et al., 2017) and ScaNN (Guo et al., 2020), and compression-oriented methods like product quantization (Jegou et al., 2011) and scalar quantization baselines (Gong et al., 2014).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Late-interaction models. The idea of running several transformer layers for the document and the query independently, and then combining them in the last transformer layers, was developed concurrently by multiple teams: PreTTR (MacAvaney et al., 2020), EARL (Gao et al., 2020a), DC-BERT (Nie et al., 2020), DiPair , and the Deformer (Cao et al., 2020). These works show that only a few layers where the query and document interact are sufficient to achieve results close to the performance of a full BERT ranker at a fraction of the runtime cost. For each document, the contextual token vectors are stored in a cache and retrieved during the document ranking phase. This impacts both storage cost as well as latency cost of fetching these vectors during the ranking phase. MORES (Gao et al., 2020b), extends lateinteraction models, where in the last interaction layers only the query attends to the document (and not vice-versa). As document are typically much longer, this results in additional performance improvements with similar storage requirements. Col-BERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020) is another variant that runs all transformer layers independently for the query and the document, and the interaction between the final vectors is done through a sumof-max operator. A similar work, the Transformer-Kernel (TK) (Hofstätter et al., 2020b), has an interaction block based on a low-complexity kernel operation. Both ColBERT and TK result in models with lower runtime latency at the expense of a drop in ranking quality. However, the storage requirements for both approaches are still significant. Some of the works above acknowledge the issue of storing the precomputed document representations and proposed partial solutions. In Col-BERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020), the authors proposed to reduce the dimension of the final token embedding using a linear layer. However, even moderate compression ratios caused a large drop in ranking quality. In the PreTTR model (MacAvaney et al., 2020), it was proposed to address the storage cost by using a standard auto-encoder architecture and the float16 format instead of float32. Again, the ranking quality drops even with moderate compression ratios (they measured up to 12x).

Several other works (Guu et al., 2020;Karpukhin et al., 2020;Xiong et al., 2021;Qu et al., 2020;Lu et al., 2020) proposed representing the queries and documents as vectors (as opposed to a vector per token), and using dot product as the interaction block. While this ranker architecture approach is simple (and can also be used for the retrieval step via an approximate nearest neighbor search such as FAISS (Johnson et al., 2017) or ScaNN (Guo et al., 2020)), the overall ranking quality is generally lower compared to methods that employ a query-document cross-attention interaction. Recently, several lines of work in neural ranking and retrieval have explored architectural simplifications, efficiency-oriented interaction designs, and dense retrieval objectives without cross-attention, including ANCE (Xiong et al., 2021), DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020), COIL (Gao et al., 2021), ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al., 2022), SPLADE (Formal et al., 2021), and RocketQA (Qu et al., 2021), as well as approximate nearest neighbor toolkits such as FAISS (Johnson et al., 2017) and ScaNN (Guo et al., 2020), and compression-oriented methods like product quantization (Jegou et al., 2011) and scalar quantization baselines (Gong et al., 2014).

Compressed embeddings. Our work reduces storage requirements by reducing the number of bits per floating-point value. Quantization gained attention and success in reducing the size of neural network parameters (Gupta et al., 2015;Essam et al., 2017;Wang et al., 2018;Wu et al., 2018) and distributed learning communication costs (Suresh et al., 2017;Alistarh et al., 2017;Konečnỳ and Richtárik, 2018;Vargaftik et al., 2021b). Specifically, compressing word embeddings has been studied as an independent goal. May et al. (2019) studied the effect of quantized word embeddings on downstream applications and proposed a metric for quantifying this effect with simple linear models that operate on the word embeddings directly. As our work is concerned with compressing contextual embeddings, these methods do not apply since the set of possible embeddings values is not bounded by the vocabulary size. Nevertheless, as in (May et al., 2019), we also observe that simple quantization schemes are quite effective. Our work uses recent advances in this area to further reduce storage requirements for document representation, which, to the best of our knowledge, were not previously attempted in this context.

spans.span: Recent retrieval-oriented modeling for clinical text has also drawn from general-domain neural IR and biomedical QA, including dense retrievers and late-interaction models (Karpukhin et al., 2020;Xiong et al., 2021;Khattab and Zaharia, 2020), biomedical sentence selection for evidence gathering (Wiese et al., 2017;Beltagy et al., 2019), clinical concept linking with UMLS-aware encoders (Mullenbach et al., 2018;Peng et al., 2020), and large biomedical language models for document ranking and re-ranking (Lee et al., 2020;Gururangan et al., 2020;Gu et al., 2021;Singhal et al., 2023).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Patient-Specific Literature Retrieval. Since 2014, the Text REtrieval Conference (TREC) has organized a series of challenges to advance research in this area. The TREC Clinical Decision Support (CDS) tracks focused on evaluating systems on the task of retrieving biomedical articles relevant for answering generic clinical questions about patient medical records (e.g., identifying potential diagnoses, treatments, and tests) (Simpson et al., 2014;Roberts et al., 2015Roberts et al., , 2016). TREC CDS 2014 and 2015 used short case reports as idealized representations of medical records due to the lack of available de-identified records. TREC 2016 shifted to using real-world medical records from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC) database (Johnson et al., 2016). In our work, our focus is on predicting clinical outcomes using ICU admission notes and patient-specific retrieved literature. Ueda et al. (2021) use contextualized representations on more structured retrieval tasks not involving clinical notes (Voorhees et al., 2021), leaving open the question of how large pretrained language models would fare on long, noisy EHR text. We explore this by experimenting with language models for retrieval based on EHR text. Recent retrieval-oriented modeling for clinical text has also drawn from general-domain neural IR and biomedical QA, including dense retrievers and late-interaction models (Karpukhin et al., 2020;Xiong et al., 2021;Khattab and Zaharia, 2020), biomedical sentence selection for evidence gathering (Wiese et al., 2017;Beltagy et al., 2019), clinical concept linking with UMLS-aware encoders (Mullenbach et al., 2018;Peng et al., 2020), and large biomedical language models for document ranking and re-ranking (Lee et al., 2020;Gururangan et al., 2020;Gu et al., 2021;Singhal et al., 2023). Clinical Outcome Prediction. The idea of using automated outcome prediction for assisting clinical triage, workflow optimization, and hospital resource management has received much interest recently, especially given the conditions of the COVID-19 pandemic. Predictive models based on structured and unstructured information have been built for key clinical outcomes including mortality (Jain et al., 2019;Feng et al., 2020), length of hospital stay (van Aken et al., 2021), readmission (Jain et al., 2019), sepsis (Feng et al., 2020), prolonged mechanical ventilation, and diagnostic coding (Jain et al., 2019;van Aken et al., 2021). Increasingly, models have leveraged unstructured text from notes since they can contain key information for outcome prediction (Boag et al., 2018;Jin et al., 2018). Most recently, van Aken et al. (2021) attempted this using large pretrained language models. Our work compares the performance of a broader range of state-of-the-art pretrained language models on outcome prediction tasks.

Figure: Complete system pipeline, unpacking the high-level overview seen in Figure. For a given patient ICU admission note, the literature retrieval module first retrieves relevant biomedical abstracts from a clinical outcome-specific index, then reranks a top-ranked subset of abstracts. The outcome prediction module aggregates information from these reranked abstracts and fuses it with the admission note to make the final prediction from EHR notes by augmenting them with relevant biomedical literature. BEEP consists of two main stages: (i) literature retrieval, and (ii) outcome prediction. We also briefly experiment with a formulation that trains both jointly. Given a patient EHR note Q and a clinical outcome of interest y, the first stage is to identify a set of biomedical abstracts Docs(Q) = {D1, ..., Dn} from PubMed that may be helpful in assessing the likelihood of the patient having that outcome. The next stage is to augment the input to an EHR-based outcome prediction model with these retrieved abstracts (Q ∪ Docs(Q)) and predict the final outcome. Figure provides a high-level illustration of BEEP, and Figure unpacks it with more detail. Next, we describe our system's main components.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Our work depends heavily on recent advances in efficient Transformers (Tay et al., 2020) that process long sequences (Rae et al., 2020;Beltagy et al., 2020;Zaheer et al., 2020;Roy et al., 2021). Sparse attention , relative position encoding (Shaw et al., 2018;Raffel et al., 2020;Guo et al., 2021) and other tricks (Dai et al., 2019;Weston et al., 2015;Shen et al., 2020;Stock et al., 2021;Katharopoulos et al., 2020) are commonly adopted by efficient Transformers. Existing long-sequence downstream tasks include long-form QA (Fan et al., 2019;Pang et al., 2021), document-level summarization (Kryściński et al., 2021;Huang et al., 2021), and machine translation (Liu and Zhang, 2020). More recently, Shaham et al. (2022) introduce a new benchmark covering multiple domains and tasks, while Tay et al. (2021) propose multimodal long sequence tasks.

We focus on modeling dependencies that span thousands of tokens in practical settings such as legal and scientific corpora. Prior work shows that architectural inductive biases significantly affect the ability to capture long-range structure under fixed memory budgets. Recent surveys catalog numerous memory-augmented and sparse-attention variants, including Reformer (Kitaev et al., 2020), BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020), Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020), Linformer (Wang et al., 2020), Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021), Routing Transformer (Roy et al., 2021), ETC (Ainslie et al., 2020), and Memorizing Transformers (Wu et al., 2022), alongside benchmarks such as NarrativeQA (Kočiský et al., 2018), GovReport (Huang et al., 2021), Qasper (Dasigi et al., 2021), and Long Range Arena (Tay et al., 2020), as well as training methods like gradient checkpointing (Chen et al., 2016), mixed-precision (Micikevicius et al., 2018), and sequence packing (Kundu et al., 2021). However, the interaction between positional encodings and block-sparse routing remains underexplored in domain-specific settings.

In addition to architecture, data curriculum and pretraining objectives shape long-context competence. Span corruption and permutation-based denoising have been found to improve extrapolation to longer sequences without architectural change. Yet, these results vary across tasks, suggesting that evaluation protocols for long-context models require careful control of confounds such as retrieval difficulty and discourse structure. To probe these factors, we consider evaluation suites that vary context length, redundancy, and adversarial distractors.

Finally, we situate our contributions within efforts to unify retrieval-augmented modeling and long-context Transformers. While retrieval augments effective context via external memory, long-context models amortize access by expanding the attention window. Our approach bridges these lines by integrating retrieval-aware positional priors with sparsity patterns designed for document-scale reasoning, and we validate the design on heterogeneous corpora with strict compute budgets.

Prompting strategies span manual templates (Schick and Schütze, 2020a,b;Petroni et al., 2019), automatic template search (Gao et al., 2021;Shin et al., 2020), soft or continuous prompts (Lester et al., 2021;Li and Liang, 2021;Hambardzumyan et al., 2021), instruction tuning and in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020;Sanh et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022;Ouyang et al., 2022), and multimodal prompt tuning for CLIP-like models (Radford et al., 2021;Zhou et al., 2022;Yao et al., 2021;Lu et al., 2022), alongside calibration and selection methods for few-shot settings (Zhao et al., 2021;Rubin et al., 2022;Holtzman et al., 2021;Min et al., 2022).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Vision-language few-shot learning. Recently, several few-shot learners on vision-language tasks were proposed including GPT (Radford et al., 2019;Brown et al., 2020), Frozen (Tsimpoukelli et al., 2021), PICa (Yang et al., 2022), SimVLM (Wang et al., 2021), OFA (Wang et al., 2022), BLIP (Li et al., 2022), and Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022), with related advances in multimodal prompting and retrieval-augmented modeling (Jia et al., 2021;Khandelwal et al., 2021;Li et al., 2023;Yu et al., 2022). Frozen (Tsimpoukelli et al., 2021) is a large language model based on GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019), and is transformed into a multimodal few-shot learner by extending the soft prompting to incorporate a set of images and text. Their approach shows the fewshot capability on visual question answering and image classification tasks. Similarly, PICa uses GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) to solve VQA tasks in a few-shot manner by providing a few in-context VQA examples. It converts images into textual descriptions so that GPT-3 can understand the images. SimVLM is trained with prefix language modeling on weakly-supervised datasets. It demonstrates its effectiveness on a zero-shot captioning task. While these models achieve improvement on few-shot tasks, they are impractical to use in real-world applications due to their model sizes.

Language model prompting. Providing prompts or task descriptions play an vital role in improving pre-trained language models in many tasks (Radford et al., 2021;Schick and Schütze, 2020a,b;Brown et al., 2020). Among them, GPT models (Radford et al., 2019;Brown et al., 2020) achieved great success in prompting or task demonstrations in NLP tasks. In light of this direction, prompt-based approaches improve small pre-trained models in few-shot text classification tasks (Schick and Schütze, 2020a,b). CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) also explores prompt templates for image classification which affect zero-shot performance. Prompting strategies span manual templates (Schick and Schütze, 2020a,b;Petroni et al., 2019), automatic template search (Gao et al., 2021;Shin et al., 2020), soft or continuous prompts (Lester et al., 2021;Li and Liang, 2021;Hambardzumyan et al., 2021), instruction tuning and in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020;Sanh et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022;Ouyang et al., 2022), and multimodal prompt tuning for CLIP-like models (Radford et al., 2021;Zhou et al., 2022;Yao et al., 2021;Lu et al., 2022), alongside calibration and selection methods for few-shot settings (Zhao et al., 2021;Rubin et al., 2022;Holtzman et al., 2021;Min et al., 2022). We follow these core ideas so we aim to improve zero-shot and few-shot performance using prompts in visionlanguage tasks. We pretrain FEWVLM with masked language modeling (MaskedLM) and prefix language modeling (Pre-fixLM).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Sequence Ordering. Story sequencing test is a popular way of examining children's abilities on sequential reasoning which is shown evident for procedural understanding (Tomkins, 1952;Baron-Cohen et al., 1986;Loucks et al., 2017). In NLP, existing works attempt the sequencing task as sorting a series of unordered sentences Cui et al., 2018;Logeswaran et al., 2018;Oh et al., 2019;Lee et al., 2020;Calizzano et al., 2021) from paper abstracts or short paragraphs, and related efforts on commonsense and narrative ordering draw on ROCStories (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016), BookCorpus (Zhu et al., 2015), Story Cloze Test (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016), and narrative coherence modeling (Barzilay and Lapata, 2008; Li and Hovy, 2014; Chen et al., 2019) alongside discourse-based methods (Pitler et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2011; Ji and Eisenstein, 2014) and pretraining with sentence order prediction (Lan et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019; Conneau and Lample, 2019). While certain prior work also attempts to extend it to incorporate multimodality , the dataset used, Visual StoryTelling , features album images that were not intended to be procedural nor supply unstated details to complement the texts. In computer vision, existing work leverages shuffle frame prediction for learning video representations (Lee et al., 2017;Xu et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2020;Li et al., 2020) as well as cycle consistency constraints for learning temporal dynamics (Epstein et al., 2021). (Zellers et al., 2021) also features a pairwise relative frame reordering objective to learn temporal common sense from scripted videos, however, as their downstream   We again only list the categories with total instance count >10.

tasks mainly concern visual reasoning and ordering by frame-text-matching (also on Visual Story-Telling), the re-ordering objective is more focused on the visual modality. Our work takes a different perspective to tackle a comprehensive multimodal sequencing task with a focus on the procedural tasksolving knowledge and gauging the helpfulness of complementary information in different modalities.

Task/Procedure Understanding. Other works have utilized WikiHow for learning task knowledge.

In NLP, textual descriptions of WikiHow have been used for abstractive summarization (Koupaee and Wang, 2018), procedural understanding Tandon et al., 2020), and intent estimation (Zhang et al., 2020a). Prior work (Zhang et al., 2020b) considers WikiHow for learning event temporal ordering, but limited to only pairwise relations. A concurrent work uses WikiHow to infer visual goals (Yang et al., 2021). We hope our curation can help advancing the goal of comprehensive multimodal procedural understanding.

Multimodality. Beside models used in this work, there are several recent advanced multimodal grounding techniques (Tan and Bansal, 2019;Li et al., 2019;Lu et al., 2019;Su et al., 2020;Chen et al., 2020b;Huang et al., 2020;Wen et al., 2021).

We utilize VisualBERT and CLIP-ViL for their simplicity to be adapted to our task and easier integration to our proposed pretraining techniques, however, our framework is able to incorporate any of the aforementioned multimodal models.

spans.span: Recent work on temporal robustness in NLP and vision has cataloged a range of dataset shifts and evaluation protocols across time without converging on consistent mitigation strategies, including approaches for domain adaptation under time-stamped distributions (Rabanser et al., 2019;Zhang et al., 2021), retrospective calibration and reweighting (Ovadia et al., 2019;Ashukha et al., 2020), continual and lifelong learning to address non-stationarity (Parisi et al., 2019;Delange et al., 2021), evaluation frameworks for robustness under distribution shift (Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019;Taori et al., 2020), and language drift analyses measuring token- and discourse-level changes over decades (Hamilton et al., 2016;Rosenfeld and Erk, 2018;Shoemark et al., 2019;Gururangan et al., 2020).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Temporal Drift Temporal drift has been studied in several NLP tasks, including document classification Paul, 2018, 2019), sentiment analysis (Lukes and Søgaard, 2018), Named Entity Recognition (NER) (Rijhwani and Preotiuc-Pietro, 2020), Neural Machine Translation (NMT) (Levenberg et al., 2010) and Language Modelling (Lazaridou et al., 2021). None of these papers focus on class imbalance and temporal concept drift. These papers have mainly been diagnostic, not providing technical solutions that are applicable in our case.

Recent work on temporal robustness in NLP and vision has cataloged a range of dataset shifts and evaluation protocols across time without converging on consistent mitigation strategies, including approaches for domain adaptation under time-stamped distributions (Rabanser et al., 2019;Zhang et al., 2021), retrospective calibration and reweighting (Ovadia et al., 2019;Ashukha et al., 2020), continual and lifelong learning to address non-stationarity (Parisi et al., 2019;Delange et al., 2021), evaluation frameworks for robustness under distribution shift (Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019;Taori et al., 2020), and language drift analyses measuring token- and discourse-level changes over decades (Hamilton et al., 2016;Rosenfeld and Erk, 2018;Shoemark et al., 2019;Gururangan et al., 2020). This line of research underscores the breadth of temporal phenomena encountered by modern models. However, its implications for multi-label classification under skew remain underexplored in practice.

Multi-label Class Imbalance Class imbalance in multi-label classification has so far been studied through the lens of network architectures, searching for the best neural architecture for handling few-and zero-shot labels in the multi-label setting. To improve the performance for underrepresented (few-shot) classes, (Snell et al., 2017) introduced Prototypical Networks that average all instances in each class to form prototype label vectors (encodings), a form of inductive bias, which improved few-shot learning. In a similar direction, Mullenbach et al. (2018) developed the Label-Wise Attention Network (LWAN) architecture, in which label-wise document representations are learned by attending to the most informative words for each label, using trainable label encodings (representations). Rios and Kavuluru (2018) extended LWAN and the idea of prototype label encodings. They combined label descriptors with information from a graph convolutional network (Kipf and Welling, 2017) that considered the relations of the label hierarchy to improve the results in few-shot and zeroshot settings. Alternatives to LWAN were considered by Chalkidis et al. (2020a), presenting minor improvements in the few-shot setting, but harming the overall performance.

Sampling and calibration strategies have complemented architectural advances for label skew. Class-balanced losses adjust the effective number of samples per label to reduce dominance of frequent tags. Focal variants reweight hard examples to curb overconfidence on head classes. Deferred reweighting schedules modulate label importance across epochs. Cost-sensitive margin tuning has been explored to separate tails in extreme multi-label regimes. Post-hoc calibration has been applied to realign probabilities under heavy-tailed distributions. Nevertheless, their performance under temporal shift is not well-documented.

Fairness The literature on inducing approximately fair models from biased data is rapidly growing. See Mehrabi et al. (2021) for a recent survey. We rely on this literature in how we define fairness, and for the algorithms that we compare in our experiments below. The fairness-promoting learning algorithms we evaluate are discussed in detail in Section 4. Recent studies targeting fairness show that class imbalance has connections to bias (Blakeney et al., 2021;Subramanian et al., 2021), i.e., mitigating class-wise disparities has a chain effect on lowering group-wise disparities.

Robust optimization has been adapted to classification settings with imbalance across demographic groups. Distributionally robust objectives constrain the worst-group loss during training. Group DRO estimates group-wise risks and updates on the hardest group per batch. Reweighting methods adjust gradients to match target risk profiles. Minimax formulations and uncertainty sets provide theoretical guarantees under bounded shift. Extensions to multi-label problems have been proposed but evaluated primarily on static snapshots.

We focus on (large-scale) multi-label document classification and study a fundamental component of the learning process leading to performance disparities across labels, i.e., the underlying optimization algorithm used for training. We consider group-robust optimization algorithms initially proposed to mitigate group disparities given specific protected attributes (e.g., gender, race), but re-frame these algorithms to optimize for good performance across labels rather than across groups. We further examine the interaction between temporal drift and label skew when training with reweighted or robust objectives. Our study isolates optimization effects from representation and data augmentation factors. We use a temporally ordered corpus with held-out eras to assess generalization under shift.

Our contributions are three-fold. First, we provide a comprehensive evaluation of robust objectives for multi-label imbalance under temporal drift. Second, we design a protocol that decouples drift-aware validation from standard random splits. Third, we analyze calibration and coverage across the label frequency spectrum. We release code and processing scripts for reproducibility. We also report ablations on class-balanced losses and focal variants.

Dataset and protocol overview. We construct chronologically partitioned splits with non-overlapping time windows for training, validation, and testing. We ensure label vocabularies are consistent across splits while allowing label frequencies to evolve over time. We report macro-averaged metrics to reflect tail performance alongside micro-averaged scores. We measure risk under temporal extrapolation using forward-only evaluation. We include per-era error analyses to surface drift-sensitive labels.

Implementation details. All models share the same encoder to control for representational differences. We optimize with identical schedules and early stopping based on time-aware validation. Hyperparameters for robust objectives are tuned via grid search on the validation era. We apply temperature scaling per era for calibrated comparisons. Confidence intervals are computed with paired bootstrap across documents.

Limitations. Our analysis does not exhaust all forms of temporal shift, such as abrupt regime changes. We focus on text-only signals and do not address multimodal covariates. The label ontology is assumed fixed, which may not hold in dynamic taxonomies. Future work should consider online adaptation with principled drift detection.

Ethical considerations. Evaluating fairness under time-aware imbalance highlights risks of entrenching historical patterns. We avoid using protected attributes at inference time. We discuss the implications of worst-label optimization for downstream decision-making. Transparency artifacts accompany our release to aid responsible use.

We consider three chronological splits: training (20k, 1975-2002), development (8.5k, 2002-2008), and test (8.5k, 2008-2018). The splits are constructed to prevent leakage from future to past. We standardize preprocessing and vocabulary across eras. We provide detailed label frequency histograms per split in the appendix. We now proceed to describe baselines and robust optimization objectives.

Lacks synthesis.document:
OTD in Text Classification

Early approaches to OTD relied primarily upon dictionaries like hatebase 3 to lookup offensive words and phrases. The creation of OTD datasets enabled the development of ML-based approaches utilizing simple features, such as bag-of-word representations. With the advent of social media platforms, many resources have been developed for identifying toxic comments in web text (Waseem and Hovy, 2016;, including a number of deep learning-based methods (Pitsilis et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2018b;Casula et al., 2020;Yasaswini et al., 2021;Djandji et al., 2020;Badjatiya et al., 2017;Park and Fung, 2017;Founta et al., 2018;Davidson et al., 2017). Notably, all of these methods can be described as building a contextual representation of a sentence (whether trained end-to-end or on top of existing pre-trained language models), and making a classification based on this representation. However, the generalization challenges posed by domain shift across platforms and time have motivated research into robustness and calibration for toxicity classifiers. Prior work has explored subword modeling and character-level cues to mitigate spelling variation and adversarial obfuscation while preserving recall on colloquial forms. Complementary efforts have examined metadata and conversational context, showing that user- and thread-level signals can reduce false positives arising from reappropriated slurs and quoted speech. Beyond architecture, dataset construction practices—such as annotator guidelines, multi-label taxonomies, and adversarially curated negatives—have been shown to influence measurement of both fairness and utility. Cross-lingual and code-switching scenarios further complicate the landscape, as direct translation of lexicons or labels often fails to capture pragmatic force and sociolinguistic nuance. Recent studies have therefore combined translation with culture-specific reannotation, yielding improved agreement but at higher curation cost. In parallel, pre-training on large-scale web corpora has enabled transfer to rare toxicity categories, yet raises questions about spurious correlations inherited from upstream data. Evaluations increasingly adopt stress tests and counterfactual augmentations to separate performance on identity terms from true detection of abusive intent. Despite these advances, a consistent gap remains in systematically disentangling toxicity from legitimate expressions of identity, irony, and reclaimed language. Addressing this gap requires methods that couple representation learning with semantically grounded constraints and auditable decision rationales. Our work contributes to this direction by formalizing a framework that partitions lexical, pragmatic, and contextual evidence and by introducing diagnostics that quantify overreliance on identity markers. We further present a modular training regimen that integrates counterfactual supervision with distributionally robust objectives to stabilize performance under domain shift. Finally, we release evaluation suites aligned with these objectives to promote reproducible assessment of robustness, fairness, and interpretability in OTD models.

spans.span: Foundational approaches to algorithmic fairness span pre-processing adjustments that rebalance datasets (Kamiran and Calders, 2012; Feldman et al., 2015; Calmon et al., 2017), in-processing constraints that regularize or constrain models during training (Zafar et al., 2017; Agarwal et al., 2018; Cotter et al., 2019; Celis et al., 2019), and post-processing techniques that modify decision thresholds to equalize error rates or acceptance rates across groups (Hardt et al., 2016; Pleiss et al., 2017; Kleinberg et al., 2017; Corbett-Davies and Goel, 2018).

Recent work in robustness and distribution shift connects to fairness through worst-group risk and spurious correlation mitigation, including techniques such as domain-adversarial training (Ganin et al., 2016), group-DRO and its variants (Sagawa et al., 2020; Hashimoto et al., 2018), invariant predictors from causal perspectives (Peters et al., 2016; Arjovsky et al., 2020; Rosenfeld et al., 2021), and calibration-aware or conformal methods for reliable uncertainty under shift (Guo et al., 2017; Kuleshov et al., 2018; Romano et al., 2020; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021).

Lacks synthesis.document: Fair machine learning The literature on inducing approximately fair models from biased data is rapidly growing. See Mehrabi et al. (2021) for a recent survey. We rely on this literature in how we define fairness, and for the algorithms that we compare in our experiments below. As already discussed, we adopt a capability-centered approach to fairness and define fairness in terms of performance parity (Hashimoto et al., 2018) or equal risk (Donini et al., 2018). The fairness-promoting learning algorithms we evaluate are discussed in detail in §4. Some of these -Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (Sagawa et al., 2020) and Invariant Risk Minimization (Arjovsky et al., 2020) -have previously been evaluated for fairness in the context of hate speech (Koh et al., 2021). Foundational approaches to algorithmic fairness span pre-processing adjustments that rebalance datasets (Kamiran and Calders, 2012; Feldman et al., 2015; Calmon et al., 2017), in-processing constraints that regularize or constrain models during training (Zafar et al., 2017; Agarwal et al., 2018; Cotter et al., 2019; Celis et al., 2019), and post-processing techniques that modify decision thresholds to equalize error rates or acceptance rates across groups (Hardt et al., 2016; Pleiss et al., 2017; Kleinberg et al., 2017; Corbett-Davies and Goel, 2018). We focus on supervised classification and structured prediction where sensitive attributes may be observed or only weakly inferred. Our scope includes group fairness criteria that trade off utility with parity constraints and individual fairness notions grounded in similarity metrics. We also consider the practicalities of limited labels and resource constraints in high-stakes domains. A substantial body of work debates the compatibility of fairness metrics, emphasizing impossibility theorems and calibration trade-offs. These discussions motivate careful selection of evaluation criteria aligned with deployment goals. We build on these insights to construct robust benchmarks and ablations. We detail our datasets, metrics, and model classes in the following section. In particular, we highlight settings with pronounced subgroup heterogeneity and label imbalance. We further examine the stability of fairness metrics under resampling and perturbation. Our analysis emphasizes reproducibility and transparent reporting of group-specific outcomes. We also report cost-sensitive metrics relevant to clinical and judicial use cases. We now turn to historical precedents that illustrate societal risks from predictive systems. This background informs our emphasis on distribution shift and equity. has a limited history. In a classic study, Angwin et al. (2016) analyzed the performance of the Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions (COMPAS) system, which was used for parole risk assessment (recidivism prediction) in the US. The system relied on 137 features from questionnaires and criminal records. Angwin et al. (2016) found that blacks were almost twice as likely as whites to be mislabeled as high risk (of re-offending), revealing a severe racial bias in the system. The system was later compared to crowdworkers in Dressel and Farid (2018). Subsequent critiques expanded the discussion to measurement error and construct validity in recidivism labels. These examples underscore challenges in defining harm and accountability. Beyond criminal justice, similar concerns arise in credit scoring and hiring. We include tasks from these domains to stress-test fairness claims. We finally connect to robustness and generalization under distribution shift. Our experiments probe worst-case risk across predefined groups and latent clusters. We complement aggregate metrics with subgroup-conditioned calibration analysis. This design reflects practical deployment constraints. Recent work in robustness and distribution shift connects to fairness through worst-group risk and spurious correlation mitigation, including techniques such as domain-adversarial training (Ganin et al., 2016), group-DRO and its variants (Sagawa et al., 2020; Hashimoto et al., 2018), invariant predictors from causal perspectives (Peters et al., 2016; Arjovsky et al., 2020; Rosenfeld et al., 2021), and calibration-aware or conformal methods for reliable uncertainty under shift (Guo et al., 2017; Kuleshov et al., 2018; Romano et al., 2020; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021). We implement strong baselines and identify failure modes under reweighting and data augmentation. We conclude by outlining the criteria used to interpret fairness-utility trade-offs.

spans.span: Recent efforts on knowledge-grounded dialogue and document-grounded response generation have surveyed and advanced a broad set of techniques spanning retrieval-augmented generation, graph-enhanced reasoning, and memory-augmented architectures, including retrieval-then-read pipelines for conversational grounding (Dinan et al., 2019;Lewis et al., 2020;Komeili et al., 2022), graph neural models that encode structured commonsense for response planning (Zhou et al., 2018b;Liu et al., 2021;Xie et al., 2022), memory networks and differentiable knowledge access for task-oriented settings (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015;Madotto et al., 2018;Eric et al., 2017), and pre-training strategies tailored to knowledge selection with topic or entity supervision (Lian et al., 2019;Zhao et al., 2020a;Kim et al., 2020).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Sequence-to-sequence models (Vinyals and Le, 2015;Sutskever et al., 2014) have long been used for natural language generation (NLG) tasks. Stemming off the vanilla encoder-decoder architecture -introduced initially for neural machine translation (Shang et al., 2015), a variety of models have been developed for enhancing the quality of the responses generated (Li et al., 2016a;Zhao et al., 2017;Tao et al., 2018) to effectively select the conversational context in multi-turn dialogues (Serban et al., , 2017Xing et al., 2017;Zhang et al., 2019); and to model persona while conversing (Li et al., 2016b;Zhang et al., 2018). Recent advances aim at enhancing dialogue generation by making it more humanized by means of incorporating knowledge based on the dialogue context or from external sources, such as the unstructured documents or the structured knowledge graphs.

Pre-trained language models (Devlin et al., 2019;Radford et al., 2019) have been utilized for dialogue generation (Edunov et al., 2019;Zhang et al., 2020). They have been extended to leverage the knowledge from the unstructured documents and other auxiliary sources via knowledge selection and various attention fusion techniques (Zhao et al., 2020c;Cao et al., 2020). The task was explored in low-resource setting (Zhao et al., 2020b) using a disentangled response decoder, and the usability of language models itself as a knowledge base has also been investigated (Zhao et al., 2020d). An issue with language models is the extra noise which they introduce. To limit the noise by generative models, knowledge selection (Zheng et al., 2021) by estimation of the weights for every term in the knowledge and using the most important terms in the response were studied. (Zhao et al., 2020a) proposed a pre-training based multiple knowledge syncretic transformer that uses a single framework to integrate knowledge from multiple sources. Knowledge based end-to-end memory networks have been developed for task-oriented dialogue generation Reddy et al., 2019;Chen et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2020) using multi-level, working, and dynamic types of memory. In DDMN (Wang et al., 2020), the flow of history information during conversations is dynamically tracked to retain the important parts from both dialogue and KB, using a memory manager for each.

Prior studies (Young et al., 2018;Zhou et al., 2018a; have demonstrated the feasibility of including commonsense knowledge into the dialogue systems. Further, in ConKADI (Wu et al., 2020a), felicitous facts highly relevant to the context were selected and effectively integrated in the generated response by means of fusion mechanisms. Recently, co-reference resolution has been utilized for obtaining coref-informed pre-trained models (Ye et al., 2020), task-oriented dialogue generation (Jun Quan and Hu, 2019), and dialogue understanding . Further, (Huang et al., 2021) demonstrated the improvement upon explicitly incorporating co-reference information to enhance the attention mechanism for the reading comprehension task.

Recent efforts on knowledge-grounded dialogue and document-grounded response generation have surveyed and advanced a broad set of techniques spanning retrieval-augmented generation, graph-enhanced reasoning, and memory-augmented architectures, including retrieval-then-read pipelines for conversational grounding (Dinan et al., 2019;Lewis et al., 2020;Komeili et al., 2022), graph neural models that encode structured commonsense for response planning (Zhou et al., 2018b;Liu et al., 2021;Xie et al., 2022), memory networks and differentiable knowledge access for task-oriented settings (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015;Madotto et al., 2018;Eric et al., 2017), and pre-training strategies tailored to knowledge selection with topic or entity supervision (Lian et al., 2019;Zhao et al., 2020a;Kim et al., 2020).

In this paper, we show how structured and unstructured knowledge can be used to improve the task of document-grounded dialogue generation. We propose an effective knowledge-grounded dialogue model named CNTF, which is built with multi-source heterogeneous knowledge. Experiments on knowledge-based dialogue generation benchmark datasets, viz. Wizard of Wikipedia and CMU_DoG, show the efficacy of our proposed approach. Our method employs a large-scale named entity enhanced commonsense knowledge network as well as a domain-specific factual knowledge base to aid in the comprehension of an utterance as well as the generation of a response using a novel mutli-hop attention based model.

Introduction

Generalized quantifiers (GQs) are developed upon first-order predicate logic, denoting relations between sets (Mostowski, 1957). Given a universe E, a quantifier Q would be treated as a mapping Q E from the Cartesian product of powersets P(E) × P(E) to the set {false,true} or, as a binary relation on subsets of E (Dvořák and Holčapek, 2015). GQs are generalizations of the ∀,∃ quantifiers from first-order predicate logic (Mostowski, 1957;Lindström, 1966;Montague, 1973;Bach et al., 1995;Keenan and Paperno, 2012). A generalized quantifier is, abstractly, a relation between sets. Generalized quantifier theory, while developed by logicians, is used by formal linguists to analyze the meaning of quantifier words in combination with referential expressions (Barwise and Cooper, 1981;Higginbotham and May, 1981).

Most human languages contain ways of expressing generalized quantifiers, and their semantics exhibit striking similarities across languages (Matthewson, 2004;Fintel and Matthewson, 2008;Steinert-Threlkeld, 2019). At the same time, generalized quantifiers can be instantiated very differently across languages due to pragmatic considerations (Grice, 1989) or cognitive economy and cost-benefit optimisation in the exchange of information (Sperber and Wilson, 1986;Levinson et al., 2000). Quantifier words also exhibit syntactic differences, e.g., with some languages having specialized words to express quantity, while others rely on metaphorical usage of common nouns (Katsos et al., 2012). In English, most is a determiner, but Spanish and French express the same concept through common nouns, la mayoría and la majorité. The relative stability of the core semantics of quantifiers makes a cross-linguistic comparison possible, but the syntactic and pragmatic variation associated with the expression of generalized quantifiers poses a challenge for multilingual NLU. We consult quantifier taxonomy studies (Keenan and Westerståhl, 1997;Peters and Westerståhl, 2006;Szymanik and Thorne, 2015;Szymanik, 2016) and derive a categorization set for quantifier analysis in NLU benchmarks. In Table , we list the 11way quantifier categorization set and their logical denotation based on set theory.

Related Work

While other foci of formal linguistics have attracted the attention of NLP researchers—including coreference (Ogrodniczuk et al., 2019;Ogrodniczuk et al., 2020), negation (Hossain et al., 2020;Hartmann et al., 2021), and consistency (Li et al., 2019;Ribeiro et al., 2019;Asai and Hajishirzi, 2020)—there has been little work on generalized quantifiers as a source of error in NLU, let alone in multilingual NLU. Researchers have explored compositional semantics in neural models (Lake and Baroni, 2018;Li et al., 2019;Keysers et al., 2020;Hupkes et al., 2020;Goodwin et al., 2020), evaluated monotonicity reasoning (Icard and Moss, 2014;Hu and Liang, 2018;Yanaka et al., 2019;Geiger et al., 2020), and examined cross-lingual entailment and QA benchmarks (Conneau et al., 2018;Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019;Xue et al., 2021;Lewis et al., 2020), alongside resources targeting scalar implicature and pragmatics (Potts, 2015;Talmor et al., 2020;Jeretic et al., 2020;Ruis et al., 2020). It remains an open problem whether LMs represent the semantics of quantifiers words adequately, or if they provide a basis for resolving scopal ambiguities.
