spans.span: Beyond SRL, probing has also been applied to a wide range of linguistic phenomena, including syntax and semantics (Hewitt and Manning, 2019; Tenney et al., 2019), lexical relations and morphology (Vulić et al., 2020; Chi et al., 2020), compositionality and hierarchical structure (Jawahar et al., 2019; Goldberg, 2019), coreference and discourse (Clark et al., 2019; Prasad et al., 2019), and multilingual transfer (Pires et al., 2019; Conneau et al., 2020), with concurrent lines of work examining calibration and selectivity of probes (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Voita and Titov, 2020) and alternative interpretability methods such as attention analyses and causal interventions (Jain and Wallace, 2019; Elazar et al., 2021).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Probing pretrained language models. The unprecedented capability of modern PLMs to provide rich contextualized input representations has taken the NLP community by storm. Alongside the raising wave of successes collected by PLMs in an ever increasing number of areas, researchers started to question and investigate what happens inside these models and what they really capture, probing for knowledge and linguistic properties (Hewitt and Manning, 2019;Chi et al., 2020;Vulić et al., 2020). This body of work quickly attracted increasing attention and grew to become a field of study with a name of its own: BERTology (Rogers et al., 2020). Probing a PLM usually consists in defining a very precise task, e.g. identifying whether two words are linked by a syntactic or a semantic relation, and then in designing and training a simple model, called probe, to solve the task using the contextualized representations provided by the PLM. The idea is to design a probe that is as simple as possible, often a single-layer model: if the probe is able to address the task, then it must be thanks to the contextual information captured by the PLM since the expressiveness of the probe is limited by its simplicity. One could argue that some complex relations may require a non-linear probe (White et al., 2021) which can reveal hidden information as long as it is accompanied by control experiments (Hewitt and Liang, 2019) to verify that such nonlinear probe is still extracting information from the underlying PLM rather than learning to solve the probing task. Over the past few years, these probing techniques have been used to great effect and revealed that PLMs have been "rediscovering" the classical NLP pipeline (Tenney et al., 2019), and that they often encode distances between syntactic constituents (Hewitt and Liang, 2019), lexical relations (Vulić et al., 2020) and morphology (Chi et al., 2020), inter alia.

Probing techniques for SRL. As in several other fields of NLP, recent studies tried to shed some light on how, where and to what extent PLMs encode information relevant to SRL. Among others, Tenney et al. (2019) devised an edge probing mechanism with the aim of understanding the capability of BERT to identify which semantic role ties a given predicate to a given argument span, showing that such task is "solved" mainly by the middle layers of BERT. Recent advances in SRL. Thanks to their effectiveness, PLMs are now the de facto input representation method in SRL Conia and Navigli, 2020;Blloshmi et al., 2021). Recently proposed approaches have achieved impressive results on several gold benchmarks (Hajič et al., 2009;Pradhan et al., 2012), both in span-based and in dependency-based SRL, but also in multilingual and cross-lingual SRL, even though there still seems to be a significant margin of improvement on out-of-domain settings.

spans.span: Early studies take LDA (Blei et al., 2003) as the backbone and incorporate seeds into model learning. For example, Andrzejewski et al. (2009) consider must-link and cannot-link constraints among seeds as priors. SeededLDA (Jagarlamudi et al., 2012) encourages topics to contain more seeds and encourages documents to select topics related to the seeds they contain. Anchored CorEx (Gallagher et al., 2017) extracts maximally informative topics by jointly compressing the corpus and preserving seed relevant information. Subsequent work also explores user interaction, posterior regularization, and semi-supervision in related formulations (Ramage et al., 2009; Mei et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2014; Zhai et al., 2013).

The common strategy is to adapt distributions in LDA to generate real-valued data (e.g., Gaussian LDA (Das et al., 2015), LFTM (Nguyen et al., 2015), Spherical HDP (Batmanghelich et al., 2016), and CGTM (Xun et al., 2017b)). Some other studies think out of the LDA backbone. For example, TWE (Liu et al., 2015) uses topic structures to jointly learn topic embeddings and improve word embeddings. CLM (Xun et al., 2017a) collaboratively improves topic modeling and word embedding by coordinating global and local contexts. ETM (Dieng et al., 2020) models word-topic correlations via word embeddings to improve the expressiveness of topic models. More recently, Sia et al. (2020) show that directly clustering word embeddings (e.g., word2vec or BERT) also generates good topics; Thompson and Mimno (2020) further find that BERT and GPT-2 discover high quality topics, but RoBERTa does not.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Seed-Guided Topic Discovery. Seed-guided topic models aim to leverage user-provided seeds to discover underlying topics according to users' interests. Early studies take LDA (Blei et al., 2003) as the backbone and incorporate seeds into model learning. For example, Andrzejewski et al. (2009) consider must-link and cannot-link constraints among seeds as priors. SeededLDA (Jagarlamudi et al., 2012) encourages topics to contain more seeds and encourages documents to select topics related to the seeds they contain. Anchored CorEx (Gallagher et al., 2017) extracts maximally informative topics by jointly compressing the corpus and preserving seed relevant information. Subsequent work also explores user interaction, posterior regularization, and semi-supervision in related formulations (Ramage et al., 2009; Mei et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2014; Zhai et al., 2013). Recent studies start to utilize embedding techniques to learn better word semantics. For example, CatE (Meng et al., 2020) explicitly encourages distinction among retrieved topics via categoryname guided embedding learning. However, all these models require the provided seeds to be invocabulary, mainly because they focus on the input corpus only and are not equipped with general knowledge of PLMs.

Embedding-Based Topic Discovery. A number of studies extend LDA to involve word embedding. The common strategy is to adapt distributions in LDA to generate real-valued data (e.g., Gaussian LDA (Das et al., 2015), LFTM (Nguyen et al., 2015), Spherical HDP (Batmanghelich et al., 2016), and CGTM (Xun et al., 2017b)). Some other studies think out of the LDA backbone. For example, TWE (Liu et al., 2015) uses topic structures to jointly learn topic embeddings and improve word embeddings. CLM (Xun et al., 2017a) collaboratively improves topic modeling and word embedding by coordinating global and local contexts. ETM (Dieng et al., 2020) models word-topic correlations via word embeddings to improve the expressiveness of topic models. More recently, Sia et al. (2020) show that directly clustering word embeddings (e.g., word2vec or BERT) also generates good topics; Thompson and Mimno (2020) further find that BERT and GPT-2 discover high quality topics, but RoBERTa does not. These models are unsupervised and hard to be applied to seed-guided settings. In contrast, our SEETOPIC framework joint leverages PLMs, word embeddings, and seed information.

Lacks synthesis.document:
While research into automatic cloze test generation is vast (Mostow et al., 2017;Kurdi et al., 2020;Yang et al., 2021), work on open cloze tests for language learning is scarce. Pino et al. (2008) generate open cloze questions using sample sentences from a learners' dictionary based on four linguistic criteria: (grammatical) complexity, welldefined context (collocations), grammaticality and length. A later version of their system adds hints for gapped words (Pino and Eskenazi, 2009). Exercise Maker (Malafeev, 2014) is a rule-based open source system that attempts to emulate exercises in Cambridge English examinations based on the most frequently tested words. Most of the gaps it proposes were found to be useful and the automated exercises were hard to differentiate from authentic tests. Chinkina et al. (2017) generate open cloze exercises for phrasal verbs by extracting sentences from news articles and generating a pair of questions and answers where the identified particle verbs are gapped. Similarly, Soonklang et al. (2017) gap words in sentences according to their part of speech in order to practise articles, prepositions, etc. Finally, Marrese-Taylor et al. (2018) use LSTMs to build sequence labelling and classification models that decide where to insert a single gap in a single sentence. Automatic evaluation against goldstandard gaps showed the method was effective.

Other work has focused on creating automated cloze tests by controlling aspects of the proposed gaps so that they correlate with a target proficiency level. , for example, manipulate the difficulty of C-tests (open cloze tests with hints, Grotjahn et al. (2002)) by varying the position and word length of the gaps. A similar concept is presented by Settles et al. (2020) and McCarthy et al. (2021), although difficulty is predicted using a machine-learning model that correlates with CEFR levels. In these cases, tests are dynamically adapted to the examinee's proficiency level during the test session. From a different perspective, Felice and Buttery (2019) show that controlling gap entropy can be useful for designing open cloze tests at different CEFR levels. The work we present in this paper, however, aims to model the more complex task of predicting a full set of gaps at the paragraph level that comply with design and testing principles and is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to employ and adapt transformer-based models for this task.

System evaluation is also challenging, since there is usually more than one potential word in the text that could constitute a good gap. While previous work often made a choice between automatic (Marrese-Taylor et al., 2018) or human evaluation (Malafeev, 2014;Das and Majumder, 2017) for their experiments, we perform both: automatic evaluation to identify the best models during development and human evaluation to measure test quality in the final output.

Data Augmentation. An important type of augmentation methods are based on word substitution, such as synonym replacement (Zhang et al., 2015), KNN replacement (Wang and Yang, 2015;Vijayaraghavan et al., 2016), Unif replacement (Xie et al., 2020a), TF-IDF replacement (Xie et al., 2020a), Bi-RNN replacement (Kobayashi, 2018), and other entity replacement methods (Raiman and Miller, 2017;Miao et al., 2020;Yue and Zhou, 2020) etc. EDA (Wei and Zou, 2019) combines four simple augmentation methods, and back translation (BT) (Fadaee et al., 2017;Sennrich et al., 2016;Yu et al., 2018) is also widely used. Unfortunately, EDA and BT are shown to be less useful with large pretrained models (Longpre et al., 2020).

Other types of augmentation methods are based on the perturbation in the feature space (Zhang et al., 2018a;Guo et al., 2020;Chen et al., 2020b,a;Miao et al., 2020;Kumar et al., 2019), generation Yoo et al., 2019;Ng et al., 2020;Hou et al., 2018), and large pretrained models (such as GPT-2, BERT, and BART) (Kumar et al., 2020;Anaby-Tavor et al., 2020;Yoo et al., 2021), etc. Self-training. Self-training (III, 1965) iteratively augments training data by labeling unlabeled data with a trained model (Yarowsky, 1995;Riloff, 1996). Knowledge distillation and pseudo-labeling are special forms of self-training (Hinton et al., 2015;Lee et al., 2013;Reed et al., 2015). Strong data augmentation (Zoph et al., 2020), equal-orlarger model , additional noise He et al., 2020a), and feedback of the student's performance (Pham et al., 2020) are helpful for self-training.

Self-training bears similarity to the second phase of FlipDA where a teacher model is used to filter samples. Different from self-training, FlipDA leverages the advantages of label flipping to improve performance and does not rely on unlabeled data. Label Flipping. Our manual label flipping augmentation procedure is analogous to (Kaushik et al., 2020) and (Gardner et al., 2020). Kaushik et al. (2020) aimed to mitigate the effects of learning spurious features. Gardner et al. (2020) targeted reducing systematic gaps in the dataset. In contrast, we target improving few-shot generalization. Moreover, we measure the performance on an existing i.i.d. test set while Kaushik et al. (2020) and Gardner et al. (2020) created more challenging test sets. Most importantly, we propose an automatic method of label flipping, going beyond manual efforts. Contrastive Learning. FlipDA is connected to contrastive learning (CL) (He et al., 2020b; in that they both improve generalization by considering label differences. CL uses data augmentation to generate positive instances and uses samples existing in the dataset as negative samples, while FlipDA shows that negative samples can be automatically generated. While previous work on CL focuses on training with large datasets, our experiments show that augmenting a small dataset can improve few-shot generalization.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Introduction

Hallucination in neural language generation has recently received increasing attention from the NLP community, including machine translation (Raunak et al., 2021;Wang and Sennrich, 2020). While early work highlighted semantic drift and unsupported content in summarization (Maynez et al., 2020) and dialogue (Nie et al., 2021), subsequent analyses have emphasized the spectrum of phenomena from minor factual slips to fully fabricated entities (Ji et al., 2023). Definitions of hallucination vary across tasks, with some focusing on faithfulness to input (Kryściński et al., 2020) and others on external factual consistency (Manakul et al., 2023), which complicates both evaluation and mitigation.

Related Work

Measurement frameworks now include automatic factuality metrics, human evaluation protocols, and hybrid checkers. Automatic metrics such as QAGS (Wang et al., 2020), FactCC (Kryściński et al., 2020), and SummaC (Laban et al., 2022) aim to quantify input groundedness in summarization. For dialogue and open-ended generation, methods leverage question answering probes and entailment-based tests to assess consistency with provided context or retrieved evidence (Honovich et al., 2022;Rashkin et al., 2021). Human protocols standardize annotation of error types and severities, though inter-annotator agreement remains a challenge (Pagnoni et al., 2021).

Recent studies catalog a variety of mitigation strategies spanning constrained decoding and calibration (Kumar and Talukdar, 2021;Nie et al., 2021), post-hoc factuality ranking (Kryściński et al., 2020;Goyal and Durrett, 2021), retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020;Izacard and Grave, 2021), instruction tuning and preference optimization (Ouyang et al., 2022;Rafailov et al., 2023), and automatic verification with external knowledge bases or tool use (Thorne et al., 2018;Schick et al., 2023;Creswell et al., 2022). However, the interaction between these interventions and domain shift, prompt sensitivity, and input noise is not yet fully characterized by standardized stress-testing.

In machine translation, hallucinations often manifest as fluent yet semantically unrelated outputs or as overconfident insertions of non-source content (Raunak et al., 2021). Regularization with source-conditioned confidence and coverage penalties has been found to reduce such errors, though trade-offs with adequacy and fluency persist (Wang and Sennrich, 2020). Domain adaptation and terminology constraints offer complementary levers but may amplify brittleness when constraints are mis-specified (Song et al., 2021;Chen et al., 2020).

For knowledge-intensive tasks, retrieval augmentation lowers the rate of fabrications by grounding generation in evidence, yet susceptibility to retrieval drift and spurious matches can reintroduce inconsistencies (Lewis et al., 2020;Izacard and Grave, 2021). Adaptive retrieval policies and reranking improve evidence quality, but latency and memory constraints limit applicability in interactive settings. Recent tool-use approaches integrate verifiers or calculators, which help in narrow domains but struggle to generalize verification schemas across heterogeneous data sources (Schick et al., 2023;Creswell et al., 2022).

Our work situates within this landscape by targeting robustness to perturbations that commonly degrade grounding. We focus on evaluating factual consistency under controlled input corruptions that emulate realistic user and data pipeline noise. We further analyze failure modes that evade current factuality metrics and propose diagnostics that connect model calibration, retrieval quality, and generation dynamics under perturbation.

Lacks synthesis.document:
There has been much prior literature on improving the efficiency of Transformers.
The most common technologies include: Knowledge distillation refers to training a smaller student model using outputs from various intermediate representations of larger pre-trained teacher models.
In the BERT model, there are multiple representations that the student can learn from, such as the logits in the final layer, the outputs of the encoder units, and the attention maps.
The distillation on output logits is most commonly used to train smaller BERT models (Sanh et al., 2020;Sun et al., 2019;Jiao et al., 2020;Sun et al., 2020).
The output tensors of encoder units contain meaningful semantic and contextual relationships between input tokens.
Some work creates a smaller model by learning from the outputs of teacher's encoder (Jiao et al., 2020;Sun et al., 2020;Li et al., 2020a).
Attention map refers to the softmax distribution output of the self-attention layers and indicates the contextual dependence between the input tokens.
A common practice of distillation on attention maps is to directly minimize the difference between the self-attention outputs of the teacher and the student (Jiao et al., 2020;Sun et al., 2020;Mao et al., 2020).
This line of work is orthogonal to our approach and our proposed FCA can be applied to the distillate models to further accelerate their inference speed.
Recent studies present a range of compression and acceleration strategies for pre-trained Transformers across tasks and modalities, including layer dropping and head pruning in encoder-only models (Voita et al., 2019; Michel et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2019), width/depth scaling for efficient pre-training and fine-tuning (Turc et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2022), structured sparsity and block-wise pruning for deployment efficiency (Lagunas et al., 2021; Frantar and Alistarh, 2023; Mao et al., 2020), low-bit quantization with post-training and quantization-aware variants (Zafrir et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020; Dettmers et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2021), and retrieval-augmented or mixture-of-experts architectures that trade parameter count for conditional computation (Lewis et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2021; Du et al., 2022; Artetxe et al., 2021).
Pruning refers to identifying and removing less important weights or computation units.
Pruning methods for BERT broadly fall into two categories.
Unstructured pruning methods prune individual weights by comparing their absolute values or gradients with a pre-defined threshold (Mao et al., 2020;Gordon et al., 2020;.
The weights lower than the threshold are set to zero.
Unlike unstructured pruning, structured pruning aims to prune structured blocks of weights or even complete architectural components in the BERT model.
Voita et al. (2019) pruned attention heads using a method based on stochastic gates and a differentiable relaxation of the L0 penalty.
Fan et al. (2019) randomly dropped Transformer layers to sample small sub-networks from the larger model during training which are selected as the inference models.
Goyal et al. (2020) progressively reduced sequence length by pruning word-vectors based on the attention values.
This work is partly similar to the fine-grained computing units in our proposed FCA.
However they ignored the coarse-grained units that may cause information loss.
In addition, there are some engineering techniques to speed up the inference speed, such as Mixed Precision (Micikevicius et al., 2018) and Quantization (Zafrir et al., 2019;Fan et al., 2021).
Using half-precision or mixed-precision representations of floating points is popular in deep learning to accelerate training and inference speed.
Quantization refers to reducing the number of unique values required to represent the model weights, which in turn allows to represent them using fewer bits.
Quantization-aware training further reduces the accuracy gap by modeling quantization effects during learning.
Mixed-precision training typically relies on loss scaling to maintain numerical stability under reduced precision.
Careful calibration of activation ranges and per-channel scaling are common practices to preserve accuracy at low bitwidths.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Long Document Summarization Long document summarization has been studied in multiple domains, such as news (Nallapati et al., 2016), patterns (Trappey et al., 2009, books , scientific publications (Qazvinian and Radev, 2008), and med-ical records (Cohan et al., 2018). Gidiotis and Tsoumakas (2020) proposed a divide-and-conquer method by splitting the input into multiple segments, summarizing them separately, and combining the summary pieces. Grail et al. (2021) proposed a hierarchical neural model to process segmented input blocks. Compared with SUMM N , these models only split the input once, implying the lack of flexibility when handling longer input.

The GovReport dataset was recently introduced containing documents with more than 9000 words, thus greatly challenging the capabilities of current models such as PEGASUS , TLM (Subramanian et al., 2019), and BIG-BIRD (Zaheer et al., 2020). To handle this dataset, Huang et al. (2021) proposed head-wise positional strides to reduce the cost of the encoderdecoder attention. Similarly, models such as Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020) and Reformer (Kitaev et al., 2020) adjust attention mechanisms in Transformers to consume longer inputs. However, these models sparsify the attention structure of the pretrained model to fit the longer source text. By contrast, SUMM N is able to maintain the full structure of various pretrained models.

Long Dialogue Summarization Various models have also been proposed to handle long dialogue summarization. HMNet (Zhu et al., 2020) and HAT-BART (Rohde et al., 2021) leverage a twolevel transformer-based model to obtain word level and sentence level representations. DialLM (Zhong et al., 2021a), Longformer-BART-arg (Fabbri et al., 2021) use finetuning or data augmentation to incorporate the external knowledge to maintain the accuracy of lengthy input. Different from these models, SUMM N is a framework without modifying the structure of the backbone attention model.

Lacks synthesis.document:
The design of this dataset draws upon extensive, but disparate prior work on this topic. Many works, some addressed below, have taken advantage of the availability of review text hosted on OpenReview.

Argument-level review labeling Prior work has developed label sets that address different phenomena. Hua et al. (2019) introduced the study of discourse structure in peer review by annotating argumentative propositions in the AMPERE dataset with a set of labels tailored to the peer review domain (EVALUATION, REQUEST, FACT, REFERENCE, and QUOTE). Similarly, Fromm et al. (2020)'s AMSR dataset frames the problem as an argumentation process, in which the stance of each argument towards the paper's acceptance or rejection is of paramount importance. Both view peer review as argumentation, using argument mining techniques to highlight spans of interest.

While its goal is not to examine discourse structure per se, Yuan et al. (2021)

The scope of peer-review text analysis has broadened to include aspects such as rating prediction, calibration, and meta-review synthesis. Several studies investigate score rationales by linking textual evidence to score justifications, while others examine disagreement patterns across reviewers and the effect of rebuttals on final decisions. Recent efforts also leverage large-scale datasets and modeling resources that explore review helpfulness, score calibration, and rebuttal dynamics without a unified perspective on how these strands relate to one another or converge on design principles (Kang et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2022; Ghosal et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2022; Li et al., 2020; Miguel et al., 2021). In parallel, domain adaptation and cross-venue analyses have revealed differences in reviewing norms that complicate direct model transfer.

Task formulations related to argumentative structure emphasize span-level identification over document-level summarization. This distinction has motivated the use of multi-task architectures in which proposition detection, relation extraction, and stance classification can share representations. Despite this progress, label ontologies have remained heterogeneous across datasets, making cross-corpus evaluation challenging. A small number of works report mapping strategies among label sets to enable partial comparability, but these mappings often collapse fine-grained distinctions.

Our dataset design focuses on unifying argumentative and evaluative signals with explicit alignment to decision-oriented outcomes. We operationalize this by defining a compact label schema that preserves argumentative granularity while enabling consistent aggregation to review-level judgments. To mitigate annotation drift, we employ a calibration protocol with periodic adjudication rounds, and we release detailed guidelines and counter-examples to reduce ambiguity. We further incorporate meta-information about paper sections and reviewer roles to contextualize propositions without conflating them with stance cues.

In constructing the corpus, we sample across venues, years, and subfields to capture variation in reviewing norms and writing styles. We balance positive and negative decisions and include borderline cases to stress-test models on nuanced rationales. Our annotation interface supports evidence linking between propositions and cited passages, encouraging annotators to ground stance and evaluation in text. Inter-annotator agreement is monitored continuously with targeted re-annotation of low-consensus items.

To support robust benchmarking, we partition the data by venue and year, enabling both in-domain and cross-domain evaluation protocols. Baseline models include span classification with contextual encoders, graph-based relation predictors, and joint sequence tagging architectures. We report metrics at the proposition, relation, and document levels, and we provide error taxonomies to facilitate diagnostic analysis. Finally, we release train, validation, and test splits with standardized preprocessing to ensure reproducibility.

Beyond labeling, we provide auxiliary resources for calibration and disagreement modeling. These include per-proposition uncertainty annotations, reviewer confidence scores, and rebuttal linkage metadata. Together, these artifacts enable research on how argumentative content translates into panel decisions under uncertainty. We anticipate that this dataset will serve both as a unifying benchmark and as a resource for studying the micro-structure of peer review.

Ethical considerations guide our release, with de-identification, venue policies, and consent practices carefully documented. We also include a data card detailing collection procedures, limitations, and appropriate use cases. Known risks include potential overfitting to specific venues and the temptation to automate high-stakes decisions; we recommend human-in-the-loop deployment and transparent reporting. All code, guidelines, and annotation artifacts will be released to encourage rigorous and responsible research.

Lacks synthesis.document: Parameter-Efficient Tuning of PLMs. As it is increasingly infeasible to train and store full copies of large PLMs for various downstream tasks, how to efficiently tune the PLMs with few trainable parameters becomes critical. Existing PELT methods can be largely divided into two categories based on whether new trainable parameters are introduced. Specifically, one may either train a subset of the model parameters such as the prediction head or inject small modules that modulate frozen backbones. Classic full fine-tuning offers strong task performance but scales poorly in memory and deployment cost. Adapters insert small bottlenecks per layer to reduce the number of updated weights while preserving frozen parameters. Low-rank updates such as LoRA reduce memory and compute by constraining update matrices to be low rank. Prompt-based techniques optimize task-specific continuous prompts or prefixes that steer the model without updating core weights. BitFit constrains updates to biases, and mask-based schemes select a sparse set of parameters to train. Quantization-aware parameter-efficient tuning further reduces memory by combining low-bit storage with lightweight adaptation. Recent literature has explored adapters that insert lightweight bottleneck layers between transformer blocks (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2021; He et al., 2022), low-rank adaptation that decomposes weight updates into rank-constrained matrices (Hu et al., 2022; Dettmers et al., 2023), prompt- and prefix-tuning that condition the model via learned continuous vectors (Li and Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Qin and Eisner, 2021; Liu et al., 2023), as well as reparameterization strategies including BitFit and bias-only tuning (Ben-Zaken et al., 2022) and sparse masking approaches (Sung et al., 2021; Ansell et al., 2022), along with quantization-aware PEFT that adapts low-bit backbones (Frantar et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023). Despite numerous advances, open questions remain regarding trade-offs among capacity, stability, and transfer across tasks. Empirically, parameter-efficient methods can approach full fine-tuning on many classification and generation tasks, yet systematic regressions appear under distribution shift. The interplay between adaptation placement, optimizer choice, and initialization often dictates convergence speed and final accuracy. From a systems perspective, PEFT facilitates multi-tenant serving by sharing a frozen backbone across many lightweight adapters. Storage and I/O costs are dominated by the base model, while swapping small deltas amortizes deployment overhead. In multilingual and multi-domain settings, PEFT variants can selectively capture domain idiosyncrasies without catastrophic interference. However, the design space is large, and best practices vary with model size and task complexity. Robust evaluation therefore needs to cover diverse tasks, metrics, and data regimes. For sequence-to-sequence and instruction-following tasks, careful prompt formatting and stabilization tricks mitigate optimization brittleness. When data are scarce, strong regularization and calibration of prompt length or rank improve reliability. Finally, reproducibility demands transparent reporting of hyperparameters, data preprocessing, and model variants. We now present our framework that unifies adapter placement with rank-constrained updates and stable prompt initialization. Our experiments target both low-resource and cross-domain generalization benchmarks. We quantify memory-accuracy Pareto frontiers under realistic serving constraints. We also ablate architectural and optimization choices to isolate their effects. Results indicate consistent gains in stability without sacrificing parameter efficiency. We release code and configuration files to facilitate community adoption.

spans.span: Recent advances in calibration and uncertainty for sequence models report diverse strategies across architectures and tasks without a unified perspective (Guo et al., 2017;Kumar et al., 2019;Minderer et al., 2021;Mejia et al., 2022;Wang et al., 2021;Desai and Durrett, 2020;Kong et al., 2020;Ott et al., 2018), spanning temperature scaling, label smoothing, focal losses, Bayesian approximations, and post-hoc mapping functions.

Lacks synthesis.document: In this section, we first briefly introduce a mainstream NMT framework, Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), with a focus on how to generate prediction probabilities. We describe how token-level probabilities are produced by the decoder through attention-mediated context fusion and softmax normalization over the vocabulary. We then review standard training objectives, including cross-entropy with teacher forcing, and discuss how label smoothing alters the target distribution. Next, we summarize how beam search converts local token probabilities into sequence-level hypotheses under length and coverage normalizations. We also outline how exposure bias and search heuristics interact with probability estimates at inference time. Building on these preliminaries, we turn to the problem of confidence estimation and calibration in neural machine translation. Recent advances in calibration and uncertainty for sequence models report diverse strategies across architectures and tasks without a unified perspective (Guo et al., 2017;Kumar et al., 2019;Minderer et al., 2021;Mejia et al., 2022;Wang et al., 2021;Desai and Durrett, 2020;Kong et al., 2020;Ott et al., 2018), spanning temperature scaling, label smoothing, focal losses, Bayesian approximations, and post-hoc mapping functions. We next quantify miscalibration by measuring Expected Calibration Error at both token- and sequence-level granularities. Specifically, we compute reliability diagrams for predicted probabilities, examining overconfidence in high-frequency tokens and underconfidence in rare constructions. We additionally assess segment-level confidence using minimum Bayes risk decoding with utility-weighted calibration metrics. Our analysis reveals systematic deviations between predicted confidence and empirical accuracy across domains and language pairs. We find that domain shift exacerbates miscalibration, particularly when training data underrepresents morphology-rich targets. Furthermore, we observe that length normalization can mask severe token-level overconfidence in long outputs. These findings motivate approaches that adjust probabilities with structure-aware post-hoc transforms. We therefore investigate calibration mechanisms that couple token contexts with sequence constraints. Finally, we discuss practical implications for risk-sensitive applications such as interactive translation and quality estimation. We conclude by outlining evaluation protocols to ensure fair comparisons across calibration methods.

Our work is related to cognitively inspired NLP and a variety of learning formalisms that involve knowledge transfer across different tasks. We briefly review these topics within the scope of NLP and the constraint of space.

2.1 Cognitively Inspired NLP Using NLP Representations for Brain Activity Prediction Since the pioneering work (Mitchell et al., 2008), connecting statistical NLP representations with cognition has attracted widespread attention. A substantial body of research has explored how distributed word and sentence representations correlate with neural signals measured via fMRI, EEG, MEG, and ECoG across a range of stimuli and tasks. Recent efforts span representational similarity analysis linking embeddings to fMRI (Huth et al., 2016; Caucheteux and King, 2022), MEG decoding with transformer layers (Toneva and Wehbe, 2019; Jain and Huth, 2018), EEG alignment to surprisal and entropy (Frank et al., 2015; Heilbron et al., 2022), probing semantic vectors with intracranial recordings (Pereira et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020), cross-modal alignment with CLIP-style pretraining (Radford et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022), and task-driven analyses of language areas using fine-tuned LMs (Schrimpf et al., 2021; Caucheteux et al., 2023), alongside benchmark datasets such as Pereira2018, Narratives, and BOLD5000. Collectively, this literature underscores shared structure between linguistic computation and brain activity while raising open questions about temporal dynamics and causal mechanistic explanations. Parallel strands in cognitive modeling evaluate how inductive biases and training curricula shape the emergence of linguistic abstractions under capacity limitations. Work on multi-task and transfer learning indicates that auxiliary supervision can bias representations toward features beneficial for generalization across tasks and domains. In representation learning, contrastive objectives and masked language modeling have been examined as implicit curricula that align with human-like predictive processing constraints. The intersection of these threads suggests a framework in which neural language models provide testable hypotheses about representational geometry and processing costs in the brain. Within NLP, task transfer methods exploit shared substructures to improve sample efficiency and robustness under distribution shift. Modular approaches further decompose learning into reusable components that can be recombined across tasks with minimal adaptation. Recent benchmarks have emphasized low-resource and cross-domain generalization to stress-test the reliability of transfer methods. Methodologically, progress relies on precise evaluation protocols that disentangle gains from data scale, architecture, and supervision types. Finally, we highlight the need for standards that bridge cognitive plausibility with engineering desiderata, enabling cumulative progress on both scientific and applied fronts.

Prompting for information extraction has likewise diversified across cloze-style prompts (Petroni et al., 2019;Jiang et al., 2020;Shin et al., 2020), instruction-tuned models (Sanh et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022;Ouyang et al., 2022;Mishra et al., 2022), automatic prompt search and calibration (Gao et al., 2021;Zhao et al., 2021;Lester et al., 2021;Liu et al., 2023), and constrained decoding for structured outputs (Lu et al., 2022;Creswell et al., 2022;Zhong et al., 2021;Creswell and Shanahan, 2022). Lacks synthesis.document:
Zero-Shot Relation Extraction Zero-shot relation extraction was previously framed as a slotfilling task and solved by reading comprehension methods (Levy et al., 2017). However, their approach requires manual template design for each relation label, which cannot scale well to new relation types. On the other hand, RelationPrompt generates synthetic relation samples for any relation without relying on label-specific templates. Another approach to zero-shot relation extraction is the formulation into an entailment task (Obamuyide and Vlachos, 2018), which is not constrained to a fixed relation label space and instead determines if arbitrary pairs of sentences and relation labels are compatible, allowing for zero-shot inference. However, it is designed for sentence-level classification and cannot be easily applied to ZeroRTE.

Zero-shot methods for relation extraction have explored a wide array of formulations and resources, including slot filling with reading comprehension templates (Levy et al., 2017), natural language inference casts of relation labels (Obamuyide and Vlachos, 2018;Yin et al., 2019;Soares et al., 2019), semantic matching with description encoders (Broscheit, 2019;Chen and Li, 2021;Han et al., 2018), and concept-level generalization with knowledge-graph text corpora (Xiong et al., 2018;Baldini Soares et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2020). Parallel advances combine meta-learning with episodic training over relation descriptions (Geng et al., 2021;Bansal et al., 2020) and use large pretrained encoders to align entity mentions and label semantics (Wu et al., 2020;Gao et al., 2021;Ye et al., 2022). Recent benchmarks and resources provide open-domain settings for evaluating unseen relations (Levy et al., 2017;TACRED-ZS;FewRel;Wiki-ZSL).

Data Augmentation A popular method for improving model performance in supervised lowresource tasks is data augmentation. Simple heuristics such as token manipulation (Kobayashi, 2018) were initially developed, new methods in language modeling improved the quality of augmented samples (Xie et al., 2020;Wei and Zou, 2019). Although there are data augmentation methods that can be applied to structured tasks such as named entity recognition (Ding et al., 2020) and relation extraction (Papanikolaou and Pierleoni, 2020;Lee et al., 2021), they require existing training samples and cannot be easily adapted to zero-shot tasks.

Language Model Prompts Prompting-based methods have shown promise as a new paradigm for inference in natural language processing . Given language models that have large-scale and general language pre-training, welldesigned prompts are able to elicit the desired answer sequences for different tasks in few-shot or even zero-shot settings. Another advantage is the potential to adapt very large language models (Reynolds and McDonell, 2021) to new tasks without relatively expensive fine-tuning. However, such methods have not yet proven effective for more complex tasks such as triplet extraction.

Prompting for information extraction has likewise diversified across cloze-style prompts (Petroni et al., 2019;Jiang et al., 2020;Shin et al., 2020), instruction-tuned models (Sanh et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022;Ouyang et al., 2022;Mishra et al., 2022), automatic prompt search and calibration (Gao et al., 2021;Zhao et al., 2021;Lester et al., 2021;Liu et al., 2023), and constrained decoding for structured outputs (Lu et al., 2022;Creswell et al., 2022;Zhong et al., 2021;Creswell and Shanahan, 2022). Complementary strands include pretrained relation matching heads (Baldini Soares et al., 2019), entity-centric prompting (Cui et al., 2021;Zhong and Chen, 2021), and retrieval-augmented prompting pipelines that integrate external evidence into generation (Lewis et al., 2020;Izacard and Grave, 2021;Shi et al., 2023;Borgeaud et al., 2022).

Knowledge Retrieval RelationPrompt also leverages the knowledge stored in language models (Roberts et al., 2020) to compose relation samples that are grounded in realistic contexts. To ensure that the generated samples are factually accurate, the language model requires strong knowledge retrieval capabilities (Petroni et al., 2019).

In this section, we recap related work in dense retrieval and adversarial domain adaptation.

Dense Retrieval Different from sparse first stage retrieval models, dense retrieval with Transformerbased models (Vaswani et al., 2017) such as BERT  conducts retrieval in the dense embedding space (Lee et al., 2019b;Guu et al., 2020;Karpukhin et al., 2020;Luan et al., 2021).
Compared with its sparse counterparts, DR improves retrieval efficiency and also provides comparable or even superior effectiveness for in-domain datasets.
Recent advances highlight the role of pretraining objectives, indexing strategies, and supervision regimes in shaping dense representations across tasks.
Benchmarks like MS MARCO, Natural Questions, and BEIR have standardized evaluations and exposed fragility under domain shift.
Training signals range from supervised clicks to synthetic pairs, while indexing spans flat, IVF, and product quantization backends.
Prior work on cross-domain retrieval and adaptation reports improvements from diverse techniques without a unifying perspective, including dual-encoder pretraining on MS MARCO and Natural Questions (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2019b), lexical-dense hybrids such as ColBERT and SPLADE (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020; Formal et al., 2021), contrastive distillation from cross-encoders (Hofstätter et al., 2021; Gao and Callan, 2021), domain-adaptive pretraining on target corpora (Gururangan et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2021), pseudo-labeling with BM25 and DPR teachers (Izacard and Grave, 2021; Oğuz et al., 2022), query reformulation and prompt-based expansion (Nogueira et al., 2019; Mao et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2022), and test-time retrieval-time adaptation mechanisms (Zhan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022).
These findings collectively underscore the importance of transferable matching functions under limited supervision.

Recently, challenges of ZeroDR have attracted much attention (Thakur et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2021;Li and Lin, 2021).
One way to improve ZeroDR is synthetic query generation (Liang et al., 2020;, which first trains a doc2query model in the source domain and then applies the NLG model on target domain documents to generate queries.
The target domain documents and generated queries form weak supervision labels for DR model training.
Another strand explores distributionally robust objectives that emphasize hard negatives drawn from shifted corpora.
A complementary line tunes retrieval with contrastive signals derived from weakly aligned parallel resources.
Resource-constrained settings motivate lightweight retrievers that preserve performance while limiting memory footprint.
Zero-shot evaluation protocols in BEIR and MIRACL further reveal systematic failure modes tied to lexical drift and entity shift.
Effective calibration remains challenging when score distributions differ substantially across domains.

Our method differs from them and focuses on directly improving the generalization ability of the learned representation space.
We adopt a modular design that decouples representation learning from index adaptation to isolate sources of shift sensitivity.
We also consider robustness to annotation artifacts and synthetic query biases that may propagate spurious correlations.
The approach prioritizes stable training dynamics under heterogeneous negative sampling mixtures.
Ablations assess the contribution of each component under identical compute budgets and index configurations.

Adversarial Domain Adaptation Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has been studied extensively for computer vision applications.
For example, maximum mean discrepancy (Long et al., 2013;Tzeng et al., 2014;Sun and Saenko, 2016) measures domain difference with a pre-defined metric and explicitly minimizes the difference; adversarial domain adaptation tries to adversarially trained the main model to confuse the domain classifier (Ganin and Lempitsky, 2015;Bousmalis et al., 2016;Tzeng et al., 2017;Luo et al., 2017).
Self-training with confidence thresholds and entropy minimization provide alternative routes to align feature distributions.
In NLP, gradient reversal and virtual adversarial training have been adapted to sequence encoders with mixed success.
Hardness-aware discriminators that focus on boundary examples can mitigate mode collapse in representation spaces.
Multi-source UDA introduces additional challenges of conditional shift and conflicting label priors across datasets.
MoDIR builds upon the success of these UDA methods and introduces a new momentum learning technique that is necessary to address the unique challenges in ZeroDR.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Edit Intention Identification. Identification of edit intentions is an integral part of the iterative text revision task. Prior works have studied the categorization of different types of edit actions to help understand why editors do what they do and how effective their actions are (Yang et al., 2017;Zhang et al., 2017;Ito et al., 2019). However, these works do not further explore how to leverage edit intentions to generate better-revised documents. Moreover, some of their proposed edit intention taxonomies are constructed with a focus  on specific domains of writing, such as Wikipedia articles (Anthonio et al., 2020;Bhat et al., 2020;Faltings et al., 2021) or academic essays (Zhang et al., 2017). As a result, their ability to generalize to other domains remains an open question.

Single-Pass Text Revision Models. Some prior works Botha et al., 2018;Ito et al., 2019;Faltings et al., 2021) simplify the text revision task to a single-pass "original-to-final" sentence-to-sentence generation task. However, it is very challenging to conduct multiple perfect edits at once. For example, adding transition words or reordering the sentences are required to further improve the document quality. Therefore, singlepass sentence-to-sentence text revision models are not sufficient to deal with real-world challenges of text revision tasks. In this work, we explore the performance of text revision models in multiple iterations and multiple granularities.

Iterative Text Revision Datasets. While some prior works have constructed iterative text revision datasets, they are limited to singular writing domains, such as Wikipedia-style articles (Anthonio et al., 2020), academic essays (Zhang et al., 2017 or news articles (Spangher and May, 2021). In this work, we develop a unified taxonomy to analyze the characteristics of iterative text revision behaviors across different domains and collect large scale text revisions of human writings from multiple domains. Beyond revision-specific research, related strands include document-level rewriting and controllable editing in general, where approaches range from sequence-to-sequence editing with learned operation tags to plan-based or constraint-driven revision pipelines (Dong et al., 2019; Malmi et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Reid and Neubig, 2022; Kumar et al., 2022; Panthaplackel et al., 2021; Krishna et al., 2023). Lacks synthesis.document:
Referring Expression Comprehension: Localizing a bounding box/proposals based on an NLE is a task commonly referred to as Referring Expression Comprehension (REC). The majority of methods for REC learn a joint embedding space for visual and linguistic modalities and differ in how joint space is computed and how it is used. Earlier methods, (Hu et al., 2016b;Rohrbach et al., 2016;Plummer et al., 2018) used joint embedding space as a metric space to rank proposal features with linguistic features. Later methods like Deng et al., 2018; utilized attention over the proposals to select the appropriate one. More Recent Methods like (Lu et al., 2019;Chen et al., 2020) utilize transformer-based architecture to project multi-modal features to common semantic space. Specifically, they utilize a self-attention mechanism to align proposal-level features with linguistic features. In our work, we utilize pixel-level image features which are crucial for the task of RIS. Additionally, compared to (Lu et al., 2019), we explicitly capture inter-modal and intra-modal interactions between visual and linguistic modalities.

Referring Image Segmentation: Bounding Boxbased methods in REC are limited in their capabilities to capture the inherent shape of the referred object, which led to the proposal of the RIS task.

It was first introduced in (Hu et al., 2016a), where they generate the referent's segmentation mask by directly concatenating visual features from CNN with tiled language features from LSTM.  generates refined segmentation masks by incorporating multi-scale semantic information from the image. Since each word in expression makes a different contribution in identifying the desired object, (Shi et al., 2018) model visual context for each word separately using query attention. (Ye et al., 2019) uses a self-attention mechanism to capture long-range correlations between visual and textual modalities while improving feature aggregation. Recent extensions consider compositional reasoning and cross-modal alignment with graph structures, transformers, and multi-stage fusion, reporting gains on standard benchmarks and datasets without detailing implications for downstream RIS or REC design (Liu et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Kamath et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2022; Krishna et al., 2017; Kazemzadeh et al., 2014; Mao et al., 2016; Plummer et al., 2015; Pont-Tuset et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2019; Deng et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2016b; Rohrbach et al., 2016; Plummer et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2018; Ye et al., 2019). Despite these advances, challenges remain in segmenting small or heavily occluded referents and in resolving ambiguous expressions that require fine-grained relational cues. In this work, we build upon dense pixel-level multi-modal alignment to better capture fine structures while maintaining robustness to distractors. We adopt a modular design that disentangles language grounding, visual refinement, and cross-scale fusion, allowing the model to adapt to expressions of varying granularity. Our approach leverages proposal-free backbones to avoid biases induced by detection anchors and to preserve spatial precision. We further incorporate soft linguistic priors that modulate feature propagation across scales to favor regions consistent with the expression semantics. Finally, we evaluate on multiple benchmarks to assess generalization across domains and expression styles, and we analyze the contributions of each component through targeted ablations.

spans.span: Related directions span a broad space including bias mitigation in NLP (Zhao et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020; Barocas et al., 2019), parameter-efficient transfer methods such as adapters and LoRA (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2022; Lester et al., 2021), calibration and logit adjustment for imbalanced learning (Menon et al., 2020; Cui et al., 2019; Gong et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2017), and output-layer modeling in sequence tasks (Press and Wolf, 2017; Yang et al., 2018; Shazeer, 2019; He et al., 2021).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Bias terms and their importance are rarely discussed in the literature 4 . Zhao et al. (2020) describe a masking-based fine-tuning method, and explicitly mention ignoring the bias terms, as handling them "did not observe a positive effect on performance". An exception is the work of Wang et al. ( 2019) who analyzed bias terms from the perspective of attribution method. They demonstrate that the last layer bias values are responsible for the predicted class, and propose a way to back-propagate their importance. Michel and Neubig (2018) finetuned the biases of the output softmax in an NMT systems, to personalize the output vocabulary. Finally, Cai et al. (2020) demonstrate that bias-only finetuning similar to ours is effective also for adaptation of pre-trained computer vision models.

Despite this scattered attention, the conceptual role of biases in modern deep architectures remains under-specified. In classification heads, biases shift logits and thus directly affect decision thresholds. In sequence models, biases accumulate over timesteps and can encode token-level priors. Empirically, biases can capture domain frequency effects that are difficult to learn through weights alone. The practical implication is that biases can be leveraged for adaptation when feature subspaces are brittle. However, most training pipelines tie biases to weight updates without explicit control. This makes it hard to isolate their contribution during optimization. Consequently, the field lacks principled protocols to evaluate bias-only interventions. Addressing this gap requires careful disentanglement of representational and scalar effects.

Related directions span a broad space including bias mitigation in NLP (Zhao et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020; Barocas et al., 2019), parameter-efficient transfer methods such as adapters and LoRA (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2022; Lester et al., 2021), calibration and logit adjustment for imbalanced learning (Menon et al., 2020; Cui et al., 2019; Gong et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2017), and output-layer modeling in sequence tasks (Press and Wolf, 2017; Yang et al., 2018; Shazeer, 2019; He et al., 2021). These strands highlight tooling that touches either the output distribution or the efficiency of adaptation. Yet the specific mechanics of bias vectors remain comparatively opaque. Prior reports often treat biases as incidental offsets rather than controllable levers. Moreover, evaluation typically emphasizes accuracy without decomposing calibration or margin sensitivity. This obscures when and why bias-only updates help. A clearer taxonomy would separate initialization, constraint, and regularization schemes for bias parameters. It would also align measurement with hypothesized causal pathways.

We focus on linear readouts atop frozen encoders to isolate the contribution of biases. This setting removes confounds from representation drift during fine-tuning. Within this controlled regime, biases can be probed for domain shift robustness. We consider both closed-set classification and multi-label tagging. For each, we measure effects on calibration, margin distributions, and error consistency. The analysis operationalizes bias importance through targeted perturbations. It further examines sensitivity under class imbalance and limited-data scenarios. Ultimately, this framework seeks to clarify when bias-centric updates are preferable to weight-centric ones. The following sections formalize the setup, metrics, and empirical findings.

While elaborated feedback datasets on language learning (Caines et al., 2020;Pilan et al., 2020;Stasaski et al., 2020) appeared recently, they focus on linguistic mistakes, such as grammatical errors, instead of content. Our extensive literature review did not reveal datasets that included content-focused elaborated feedback on short answer responses. However, SAF's feedback can be viewed as a textual explanation of the assigned score. Therefore, comparable NLP datasets with textual explanations and publicly available ASAG datasets without explanations are discussed in the following sections.

Comparable resources span explanation-augmented datasets such as E-SNLI (Camburu et al., 2018), CoS-E (Rajani et al., 2019), e-SNLI-VE (Kayser et al., 2021), and ECQA (Aggarwal et al., 2021), alongside rationale-centric corpora like ERASER (DeYoung et al., 2020), MultiRC rationales (Khashabi et al., 2018), HotpotQA supporting facts (Yang et al., 2018), and FEVER evidence (Thorne et al., 2018), as well as program-of-thought and chain-of-thought style collections derived from GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), StrategyQA (Geva et al., 2021), AQuA-RAT (Ling et al., 2017), and OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018). In parallel, automatic short-answer grading (ASAG) research has built benchmarks including ASAP-SAS (Kaggle/ASAP, 2012), Mohler et al. (2011), SemEval-2013 STS student response corpora (Agirre et al., 2013), Beetle/Beetle2 (Dzikovska et al., 2012; Dzikovska et al., 2013), SciEntsBank (Dzikovska et al., 2013), and CREG (Ott et al., 2012), while related evaluation-oriented datasets cover BEA grammatical error corpora (Bryant et al., 2019), MACE/H-Swag style annotation aggregation resources (Hovy et al., 2013; Zellers et al., 2019), and rubric-aligned assessment sets such as ASAP-Reader variants, RACE (Lai et al., 2017), and SQuAD rationales (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), together with explanation-trained models like BART-Large (Lewis et al., 2020), T5-11B (Raffel et al., 2020), DeBERTaV3 (He et al., 2021), and Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020), and classic similarity methods including BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009), SBERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), TF–IDF, and Word Mover’s Distance (Kusner et al., 2015), as well as counterfactual and perturbation datasets such as CheckList (Ribeiro et al., 2020), ANLI (Nie et al., 2020), and AdvGLUE (Wang et al., 2021). These corpora and methods collectively delineate a diverse landscape of explanation-bearing resources and assessment tools. Yet the relationship between these assets and content-focused elaborated feedback for short answers remains to be clarified in terms of task-specific requirements, alignment with rubrics, and the granularity of feedback. Consequently, we next outline the operational characteristics of SAF and its annotation protocol to situate it within the broader ecosystem of explanatory and assessment datasets. We emphasize aspects of content validity, evidence localization, and pedagogical actionability that differentiate feedback-oriented annotation from mere justification text. We also discuss licensing, data splits, and quality control procedures relevant to reproducible evaluation. Finally, we sketch anticipated usage scenarios for formative assessment, model critique, and teacher-in-the-loop workflows.

We define elaborated content feedback as diagnosis-and-rationale text that targets conceptual correctness, coverage, and misconceptions in student answers rather than grammatical form. In this framing, the unit of analysis is a claim-aligned span that links a cited evidence snippet to a rubric criterion and a remediation suggestion. We distinguish feedback granularity from explanation length, because actionable guidance may be concise yet structurally rich. Our annotation guidelines therefore prioritize error type taxonomy, evidence anchoring, and rubric traceability over stylistic consistency. We also include calibration tasks to monitor annotator agreement on content validity and evidence sufficiency. To facilitate downstream modeling, we release both raw annotations and normalized JSON with canonicalized rubric tags. We report descriptive statistics on span counts, evidence density, and inter-annotator agreement to characterize data variability. For transparency, we document annotator training, adjudication processes, and sampling strategies to mitigate topical bias. We further describe baselines for automatic feedback generation using retrieval-augmented sequence models and similarity-based selectors. We conclude by outlining evaluation protocols that separate scoring accuracy, evidence faithfulness, and feedback utility for instruction.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer learning. Recently, thanks to the rapid development of multilingual pre-trained language models such as multilingual BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020), a number of approaches have been proposed for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer learning on various downstream tasks, including semantic parsing (Sherborne and Lapata, 2021), natural language generation (Shen et al., 2018) and understanding Lauscher et al., 2020). In this work, we claim our method is zeroshot because no non-Chinese CSRL annotations are seen during the CSRL training stage. For decoding, we directly use the cross-lingual CSRL model trained on Chinese CSRL data to analyze conversations in other languages. To our best knowledge, our work is the first step to cross-lingual CSRL. Recent work on cross-lingual generalization also surveys multilingual adapters (Pfeiffer et al., 2020;Ansell et al., 2021), translation-based transfer with knowledge distillation (Kim et al., 2020;Tang et al., 2020), task-adaptive pretraining across languages (Gururangan et al., 2020;Eisenschlos et al., 2019), multilingual prompts and prefix-tuning (Lester et al., 2021;Zhong et al., 2021;Minixhofer et al., 2022), evaluation suites such as XTREME and XGLUE (Hu et al., 2020;Liang et al., 2020), and parameter-efficient fine-tuning frameworks like BitFit and LoRA (Zaken et al., 2022;Hu et al., 2022).

Conversational semantic role labeling. While ellipsis and anaphora frequently occur in dialogues, Xu et al. (2021) observed that most of the dropped or referred components can be found in dialogue histories. Following this observation, they proposed conversational semantic role labeling (CSRL) which required the model to find predicateargument structures over the entire conversation instead of a single sentence. In this way, when analyzing a predicate in the latest utterance, a CSRL model needs to consider both the current turn and previous turns to search potential arguments, and thus might recover the omitted components. Furthermore, Xu et al. (2020Xu et al. ( , 2021) also confirmed the usefulness of CSRL to Chinese dialogue tasks by applying CSRL information into downstream dialogue tasks. However, there are still two main problems to be solved for CSRL task: (1) the performance of current state-of-the-art CSRL model (Xu et al., 2021) is still far from satisfactory due to the lack of high-level conversational and semantic features modeling; (2) the usefulness of CSRL to conversational tasks in non-Chinese languages has not been confirmed yet due to the lack of cross-lingual CSRL models. In this work, we primarily focus on the latter problem and propose a simple but effective model to perform cross-lingual CSRL. We would like to distinguish our work from the concurrent work (Wu et al., 2021b) which purely focuses on improving the monolingual CSRL performance where they try to model predicate-aware representations. This solution could benefit to monolingual CSRL task, but hurt the cross-lingual performance, because the relative positions of the predicates may differ from language to language.

Lacks synthesis.document: Visual Question Answering. The current dominant framework for VQA consists of an image encoder, a question encoder, multimodal fusion, and an answer predictor (Agrawal et al., 2015). To avoid the noises caused by global features, methods Malinowski et al., 2018) introduce various image attention mechanisms into VQA. Instead of directly using visual features from CNN-based feature extractors, to improve the performance of model, BUTD (Anderson et al., 2018) adopts Faster R-CNN (Ren et al., 2015) to obtain candidate regional features while Pythia (Jiang et al., 2018) integrates the regional feature with grid-level features. Meanwhile, Lu et al. (2016); Nam et al. (2017) put more attention on learning better question representations. To merge information from different modalities sufficiently, MFB (Yu et al., 2017), MUTAN (Ben-younes et al., 2017), MLB (Kim et al., 2016), BLOCK (Ben-Younes et al., 2019), and MFH (Yu et al., 2018) explored higher-order fusion methods, while SAN (Yang et al., 2016), HAN (Lu et al., 2016), UpDn (Anderson et al., 2018), and ViLBERT (Lu et al., 2019) represent notable alternatives that rely on distinct attention or co-attention formulations without a unifying perspective on their comparative trade-offs. Further, BAN (Kim et al., 2018) and DCN(Nguyen and Okatani, 2018) propose dense co-attention model which directly establish interaction between different modalities with word-level and regional features. Moreover, with the proposal of Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), MCAN and DFAF (Gao et al., 2019) adopt self-attention mechanism to fully excavate the fine-grained information contained in text and image. Meanwhile, to fully cover the holistic scene in an image, MuREL (Cadène et al., 2019) and ReGAT (Li et al., 2019) explicitly incorporate relations between regions into the interaction process. Selvaraju et al. ( 2020) also introduces sub questions into their work, the distinctness between us is that it constructs a Sub-VQA dataset for the subset of reasoning questions in VQA dataset to evaluate consistency of VQA models while we adopt sub questions to achieve task-dividing. Visual Dialogue. Different from VQA, Visual dialogue(VD) is a continuous conversation for images. Several VD tasks (Visual Dialog, GuessWhich (Chattopadhyay et al., 2017), Guess-What?! (de Vries et al., 2017), MMD (Saha et al., 2018)) have been proposed. GuessWhat?!, as a goal-directed dialogue task, requires both players to continuously clarify the reference object through dialogue. The Oracle provides the Questioner with relevant information about the target object by constantly answering yes/no questions raised by the Questioner, and the Guesser generates the final answer based on the historical dialogue. Following the setting, our Co-VQA framework consists of three components, in which Questioner raises SQs, and Oracle answers them one-by-one, finally, Answerer obtains the answer to the original question.

We describe related studies on Chinese BERT model and probing of BERT, respectively.

The authors of BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) provided the first Chinese BERT model which was trained on Chinese Wikipedia data. On top of that, Cui et al. (2019) trained RoBERTa-wwm-ext with WWM on extended data. Cui et al. (2020) further trained a Chinese ELECTRA model and MacBERT, both of which did not have [MASK] tokens. ELEC-TRA was trained with a token-level binary classification task, which determined whether a token was the original one or artificially replaced. In MacBERT, [MASK] tokens were replaced with synonyms and the model was trained with WWM and ngram masking. ERNIE (Sun et al., 2019) was trained with entity masking, similar to WWM yet tokens corresponding to an entity were masked at once. Language features are considered in more recent works. For example, AMBERT and Lattice-BERT (Lai et al., 2021) both take word information into consideration, Chinese-BERT (Sun et al., 2021) utilizes pinyin and glyph of characters, ERNIE (Sun et al., 2019) performs entity-level masking, RoBERTa-wwm-ext (Cui et al., 2019) adopts whole-word masking, and MacBERT (Cui et al., 2020) replaces [MASK] with near-synonyms. Chinese-BERT (Sun et al., 2021) utilizes pinyin and glyph of characters to enrich sub-character features. These developments highlight the variety of pretraining objectives and input representations explored for Chinese.

Probing aims to examine the language understanding ability of pretrained models like BERT when model parameters are clamped, i.e., without being fine-tuned on downstream tasks. Petroni et al. (2019) study how well pretrained models learn factual knowledge. The idea is to design a natural language template with a [MASK] token, such as "the wife of Barack Obama is [MASK].". If the model predicts the correct answer "Micheal Obama", it shows that pretrained models learn factual knowledge to some extent. Similarly, Davison et al. (2019) study how pretrained models learn commonsense knowledge and Talmor et al. (2020) examine on tasks that require symbolic understanding. Recent work expands probing beyond English to assess typologically diverse languages. Benchmarks for Chinese include character-level cloze, word segmentation diagnostics, and knowledge completion tasks designed to minimize spurious cues. Probes vary from linear classifiers on frozen representations to causal and intervention-based tests that control for confounds. Evaluations often consider calibration and prompting sensitivity to separate memorization from generalization. In addition, multilingual settings complicate probe design due to script differences and tokenization granularity. Careful control experiments are needed to rule out artifacts from vocabulary construction and subword frequency. Finally, reproducibility hinges on standardized templates, label spaces, and scoring protocols across datasets and probes. We follow established practices in reporting template variance and calibration sensitivity while emphasizing Chinese-specific considerations. To facilitate comparison, we outline probe categories, dataset coverage, and evaluation metrics used in prior studies. These considerations inform our experimental choices and interpretation of probing outcomes.

We now turn to open challenges that motivate our study. First, differences in tokenization and lexicon resources create uneven access to word-level cues across models. Second, entity-rich probes for Chinese remain limited in coverage and lack disambiguation controls for homographs. Third, the interaction between sub-character signals and whole-word masking in knowledge-centric probes is poorly characterized. Addressing these gaps requires controlled datasets and analyses that disentangle pretraining objectives from linguistic priors.

Data Augmentation. Data augmentation (Sennrich et al., 2016a;Cheng et al., 2016;Hoang et al., 2018;Edunov et al., 2018;Kobayashi, 2018;Wang et al., 2018;Cheng et al., 2018;Gao et al., 2019;Wei et al., 2020) has been widely used in neural machine translation to deal with the generalization problem of models trained on limited labeled data.

The most popular one is back-translation (Sennrich et al., 2016a), which utilizes a target-to-source model to translate monolingual target sentences back into the source language. Wang et al. (2018) proposed to augment each training instance with multiple literal forms by replacing random words with other words in the vocabulary. Cheng et al. (2020) proposed to replace words with other words that are predicted using language model under the same context by interpolating their embeddings.

Recent advances span diverse strategies including back-translation variants that leverage iterative dual learning (He et al., 2016; Hoang et al., 2018; Edunov et al., 2018; Niu et al., 2018), token- and phrase-level substitution guided by contextualized embeddings (Kobayashi, 2018; Wei and Zou, 2019; Wu et al., 2019; Karimi et al., 2021), noise-injection and word-order perturbations for robustness (Xie et al., 2017; Lample et al., 2018; Clark et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021), and mixup or manifold interpolation techniques for representation smoothing (Guo et al., 2019; Verma et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020).

Our approach also belongs to the family of data augmentation, but we augment each training instance with an adjacency semantic region that covers adequate variants under the same meaning. Semantic Agreement Modeling. Learning the universal representation (Zhang et al., 2016;Schwenk and Douze, 2017;Yang et al., 2019) for multiple semantically-equivalent sentences is also related to our approach. In their early work, variational NMT (Zhang et al., 2016) introduced a continuous vector to model underlying semantics of the parallel sentences in the machine translation task. and Chi et al. (2021) suggested transforming cross-lingual sentences into a shared vector by contrastive objectives. In this context, our method mainly focused on using the well-learned continuous space to overcome the substantial challenge of making more unseen instances under with limited training data.

Parallel lines of work investigate multilingual and cross-lingual alignment using sentence-level encoders and contrastive losses (Schwenk and Douze, 2017; Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019; Conneau and Lample, 2019; Feng et al., 2020), multilingual pre-trained Transformers for universal semantics (Devlin et al., 2019; Conneau et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2021; Chi et al., 2021), supervised and unsupervised bitext mining methods (Artetxe and Schwenk, 2018; Schwenk et al., 2019; Keung et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2021), and sentence embedding benchmarks that evaluate transferability across tasks and languages (Cer et al., 2018; Conneau and Kiela, 2018; Reimers and Gurevych, 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
