The rapid growth of the legal text processing field is demonstrated by numerous papers presented in top-tier conferences in NLP and artificial intelligence (Luo et al., 2017;Zhong et al., 2018;Chalkidis et al., 2019a;Valvoda et al., 2021) as well as surveys (Chalkidis and Kampas, 2018;Zhong et al., 2020b). Moreover, specialized workshops on NLP for legal text (Aletras et al., 2019;Di Fatta et al., 2020;Aletras et al., 2020) are regularly organized.

A core task in this area has been legal judgment prediction (forecasting), where the goal is to predict the outcome (verdict) of a court case. In this direction, there have been at least three lines of work. The first one (Aletras et al., 2016;Chalkidis et al., 2019a;Medvedeva et al., 2020Medvedeva et al., , 2021) predicts violations of human rights in cases of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). The second line of work (Luo et al., 2017;Zhong et al., 2018;Yang et al., 2019) considers Chinese criminal cases where the goal is to predict relevant law articles, criminal charges, and the term of the penalty. The third line of work (Ruger et al., 2004;Katz et al., 2017;Kaufman et al., 2019) includes methods for predicting the outcomes of cases of the Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS).

The same or similar tasks have also been studied with court cases in many other jurisdictions including France (S ¸ulea et al., 2017), Philippines (Virtucio et al., 2018), Turkey (Mumcuoglu et al., 2021), Thailand (Kowsrihawat et al., 2018), United Kingdom (Strickson and De La Iglesia, 2020), Germany (Urchs et al., 2021), and Switzerland (Niklaus et al., 2021). Apart from predicting court decisions, there is also work aiming to interpret (explain) the decisions of particular courts (Ye et al., 2018;Chalkidis et al., 2021c;Branting et al., 2021).

Another popular task is legal topic classification. Nallapati and Manning (2008) highlighted the challenges of legal document classification compared to more generic text classification by using a dataset including docket entries of US court cases. Chalkidis et al. (2020a) classify EU laws into Eu-roVoc concepts, a task earlier introduced by Mencia and Fürnkranzand (2007), with a special interest in few-and zero-shot learning. Luz de Araujo et al. (2020) also studied topic classification using a dataset of Brazilian Supreme Court cases. There are similar interesting applications in contract law (Lippi et al., 2019;Tuggener et al., 2020).

Several studies (Chalkidis et al., , 2019cHendrycks et al., 2021) explored information extraction from contracts, to extract important information such as the contracting parties, agreed payment amount, start and end dates, applicable law, etc. Other studies focus on extracting information from legislation (Cardellino et al., 2017;Angelidis et al., 2018) or court cases (Leitner et al., 2019).

Legal Question Answering (QA) is another task of interest in legal NLP, where the goal is to train models for answering legal questions (Kim et al., 2015;Ravichander et al., 2019;Kien et al., 2020;Zhong et al., 2020a,c). Not only is this task interesting for researchers but it could support efforts to help laypeople better understand their legal rights. In the general task setting, this requires identifying relevant legislation, case law, or other legal documents, and extracting elements of those documents that answer a particular question. A notable venue for legal QA has been the Competition on Legal Information Extraction and Entailment (COLIEE) (Kim et al., 2016;Kano et al., 2017Kano et al., , 2018). Recent studies explore retrieval-augmented readers, entailment-oriented ranking, and domain-specific adaptations of pre-trained encoders (Rabelo et al., 2020;Shinoda and Aoki, 2019;Kornilova and Eidelman, 2019;Zheng et al., 2021;Xiao et al., 2021), alongside datasets such as LEDGAR, LexGLUE, and JEC-QA that support varied formulations of the task.

More recently, there have also been efforts to pre-train Transformer-based language models on legal corpora (Chalkidis et al., 2020b;Zheng et al., 2021), leading to state-of-the-art results in several legal NLP tasks, compared to models pre-trained on generic corpora.

Overall, the legal NLP literature is overwhelming, and the resources are scattered. Documentation is often not available, and evaluation measures vary across articles studying the same task. Our goal is to create the first unified benchmark to access the performance of NLP models on legal NLU. As a first step, we selected a representative group of tasks, using datasets in English that are also publicly available, adequately documented and have an appropriate size for developing modern NLP methods. We also introduce several simplifications to make the new benchmark more standardized and easily accessible, as already noted.

Lacks synthesis.document:
In recent years there has been active interest in the application of NLP techniques to the legal domain (Zhong et al., 2020a). A number of tasks and models have been proposed, inter alia, Legal Judgment Prediction (Chalkidis et al., 2019), Legal Summarization (Bhattacharya et al., 2019;Tran et al., 2019), Prior Case Retrieval (Jackson et al., 2003;Shao et al., 2020), Legal Question Answering , Catchphrase Extraction (Galgani et al., 2012). Legal Judgement Prediction (LJP) involves predicting the final decision from the facts and arguments of the case. Majority of corpora for Legal-NLP tasks have been in English; recently, there have been efforts to address other languages as well, for example, Xiao et al. (2018), have created a large-scale Chinese criminal judgment prediction dataset with over 2.68 million legal documents. Work on Legal-NLP in languages other than English is still in its incipient stages. Our paper contributes towards these efforts by releasing corpus in Hindi.

Majority of the work in the legal domain has focused on the higher court (Malik et al., 2021;Strickson and De La Iglesia, 2020;Zhong et al., 2020b); however, the lower courts handle the maximum number of cases. We try to address this gap by releasing a large corpus of district court level legal documents. The literature on multilingual legal-NLP includes benchmarks and shared tasks that enumerate resources without a unifying outlook, including the Competition on Legal Information Extraction/Entailment (COLIEE) corpora and tasks (Rabelo et al., 2019;Rabelo et al., 2020), the LeSicIL shared tasks for Italian legal text processing (Cecchini et al., 2020), the CUAD contract understanding dataset for clause extraction (Hendrycks et al., 2021), the MultiLegalPile corpus for multilingual pretraining (Alemany et al., 2023), the CaseHOLD dataset for legal multiple-choice question answering (Zheng et al., 2021), and the EUR-Lex and ECHR datasets used for European legislation and case-law analysis (Mencia and Fürnkranz, 2007;Chalkidis et al., 2019).  et al., 2019, 2017) have published legal data in Japanese, along with their English translation. The competition had two sub-tasks, a legal information retrieval task and an entailment identification task between law articles and queries. Multiple datasets in Chinese have been released for different tasks, namely Reading Comprehension (Duan et al., 2019), Similar Case Matching (Xiao et al., 2019), Question Answering (Zhong et al., 2020b). Duan et al. (2019) proposed Chinese judicial reading comprehension (CJRC) dataset with about 10K documents and almost 50K questions with answers. Zhong et al. (2020b) presented JEC-QA, a legal question answering dataset collected from the National Judicial Examination of China with about 26K multiple-choice questions. They augment the dataset with a database containing the legal knowledge required to answer the questions and also assign meta information to each of the questions for in-depth analysis. Xiao et al. (2019) proposed CAIL2019-SCM, a dataset containing 8,964 triplets of the case document, with the objective to identify which two cases are more similar in the triplets. Similar case matching has a crucial application as it helps to identify comparable historical cases. A historical case with similar facts often serves as a legal precedent and influences the judgement. Such historical information can be used to make the legal judgement prediction models more robust. Kleinberg et al. (2017) proposed bail decision prediction as a good proxy to gauge if machine learning can improve human decision making. A large number of bail documents along with the binary decision (granted or denied) makes it an ideal task for automation. In this paper, we also propose the bail prediction task using the HLDC corpus.

These lines of work further include controlled generation with style and politeness transfer (Rao and Tetreault, 2018; Niu and Bansal, 2018), persona-grounded persuasion (Zhang et al., 2018; Mazaré et al., 2018), and interactive tutoring systems emphasizing scaffolding over direct recommendation (Graesser et al., 2004; Nye et al., 2014).

Beyond recommendation and persuasion, dialogue data creation has drawn from task-oriented benchmarks such as MultiWOZ (Budzianowski et al., 2018), Schema-Guided Dialogue (Rastogi et al., 2020), Taskmaster (Byrne et al., 2019), and MetalWOZ (Lee et al., 2019), as well as open-domain corpora like DailyDialog (Li et al., 2017), BlendedSkillTalk (Smith et al., 2020), ConvAI2 (Zhang et al., 2019), and Topical-Chat (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2019). Methods include self-play simulation (Shah et al., 2018; Takanobu et al., 2020), knowledge-grounded prompting (Dinan et al., 2019; Komeili et al., 2022), and instruction-tuned data mixtures (Sanh et al., 2022; Longpre et al., 2023), alongside alignment techniques using human preference data (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Our work is related to dataset construction for building persuasive dialogue systems that try to persuade the participant to take a specific action. Hiraoka et al. (2014) annotated 34 dialogues, in which an experienced salesperson tries to convince a customer to buy a camera. Yoshino et al. (2018) requested crowdsourcing workers to generate 200 persuasive dialogues. In each dialogue, one participant persuaded another one to adopt his suggestion such as cleaning a room.  collected 1017 dialogues, in which one of the participants was convinced to donate to a specific charity. We can see that the covered conversation scenarios in these datasets were strictly limited to specific tasks, while our scenarios are more general and can be easily extended to different cases. Also, our constructed dataset is about three times larger than the prior work, indicating the usefulness of the recent pre-trained paradigm.

Recent work on persuasion and social influence in dialogue also documents varied settings and supervision signals without connecting them, including persuasion-as-debate with stance shifts (Wang et al., 2019), argument quality estimation for convincingness (Habernal and Gurevych, 2016; Gretz et al., 2020), goal-directed motivational interviewing corpora (Rollnick and Miller, 1995; Tanana et al., 2016), large-scale Reddit negotiations and bargaining (He et al., 2018; Lewis et al., 2017), and scripted campaign persuasion datasets (Durmus and Cardie, 2018; Yang et al., 2019). These lines of work further include controlled generation with style and politeness transfer (Rao and Tetreault, 2018; Niu and Bansal, 2018), persona-grounded persuasion (Zhang et al., 2018; Mazaré et al., 2018), and interactive tutoring systems emphasizing scaffolding over direct recommendation (Graesser et al., 2004; Nye et al., 2014).

The topic of conversational recommendation systems is also related to our work. A number of attempts have been made to collect training data for conversational recommendation systems. These studies (Wu et al., 2019;Zhou et al., 2020;Xu et al., 2020) first extracted a path consisting of an entity or attribute nodes from a knowledge base. Then they asked annotators to write conversational recommendation dialogues. The flow of mentioned topics in a dialogue should follow the extracted path. Similarly,  also built a dataset by asking human workers to create dialogues based on a topic path. It should be noted that, in these datasets, the goal of such systems is to only make entity recommendations instead of tasks, while our work goes beyond them in naturally transferring from chit-chat to task-oriented dialogues and completing a task the user may want.

Another related work is generating a transition between two given open-domain utterances. Tang et al. (2019) proposed to generate the transition conditional on a specific word, because they want the generated transition can drive the conversation topic to the specified word. Sevegnani et al. (2021) collected a new dataset of human-created one-turn topic transitions. Each dialogue contains 2 utterances with different topics and 1 transition in the middle of them.

There are some recent studies trying to merge chit-chat and task-oriented dialogues, but the purposes of merged dialogues differ from ours. Sun et al. (2021) enhanced the utterances in taskoriented dialogues by appending chit-chat sen-tences. They hope that the agent gains more social, personalized, and engaging communication skills. Ennen et al. (2021) proposed a dialogue system that can transfer the style of generated response from chit-chat to task-oriented styles. However, the system is a prototype model, there is still a large gap to properly bridge chitchat and task-oriented dialogues. The motivation of our work is closely similar to that of the study by Yu et al. (2017). They manually created several task-oriented response generation strategies specifically designed for the movie promotion scenario. In addition, the expert knowledge was utilized to design reinforcement learning rewards that help their dialogue system to decide which action to take (i.e., continuing chitchat or selecting a task-oriented strategy to reply).

However, we can observe that the prior work in these studies heavily relied on human efforts (data collection, expert-created strategies, etc.). Therefore, it can be expensive and hard to extend their data or method the practical cases due to the requirement of larger-scale training data. Our proposed framework benefits from the pre-trained models and shows its outstanding conversational capability. The flexibility of extending to diverse cases is also validated, considering that all components inside the framework can be easily substituted by the updated models, and the generated data can be used by semi-supervised or unsupervised methods for cold-start scenarios.

Beyond recommendation and persuasion, dialogue data creation has drawn from task-oriented benchmarks such as MultiWOZ (Budzianowski et al., 2018), Schema-Guided Dialogue (Rastogi et al., 2020), Taskmaster (Byrne et al., 2019), and MetalWOZ (Lee et al., 2019), as well as open-domain corpora like DailyDialog (Li et al., 2017), BlendedSkillTalk (Smith et al., 2020), ConvAI2 (Zhang et al., 2019), and Topical-Chat (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2019). Methods include self-play simulation (Shah et al., 2018; Takanobu et al., 2020), knowledge-grounded prompting (Dinan et al., 2019; Komeili et al., 2022), and instruction-tuned data mixtures (Sanh et al., 2022; Longpre et al., 2023), alongside alignment techniques using human preference data (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022).

spans.span: Recent multilingual transfer work in NLP provides several avenues that appear relevant to readability assessment across languages, including multilingual masked language models and sentence encoders as general-purpose backbones and evaluation targets, with studies on cross-lingual zero-shot classification and regression, cross-lingual sentence retrieval and similarity, and language-agnostic sentence embeddings learned via translation ranking or contrastive alignment (Devlin et al., 2019;Conneau et al., 2020;Reimers and Gurevych, 2020;Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019;Feng et al., 2020).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Readability Assessment has been an active area in educational research for almost a century. Early research on this topic focused on the creation of readability "formulae", which relied on easy to calculate measures such as word and sentence length, and presence of words from some standard word list (Lively and Pressey, 1923;Flesch, 1948;Stenner, 1996). More than 200 such formulae were proposed in the past few decades. DuBay (2007) provides a detailed summary of such formulae. The advent of NLP and machine learning resulted in more data driven research on ARA over the past two decades. Starting from statistical language models (Si and Callan, 2001), a range of lexical and syntactic features (Heilman et al., 2007;Petersen and Ostendorf, 2009;Ambati et al., 2016) as well as inter-sentential features (Pitler and Nenkova, 2008;Todirascu et al., 2013;Xia et al., 2016) were explored in machine learning based ARA research in the past. Features motivated by related disciplines such as psycholinguistics (Howcroft and Demberg, 2017), and cognitive science (Feng et al., 2009) were also explored.

In the past few years, ARA research has been primarily focused on textual embeddings and deep learning based architectures. Word embeddings in combination with other attributes such as domain knowledge or language modeling (Cha et al., 2017;Jiang et al., 2018) were used for ARA. A range of neural architectures, from multi attentive RNN (Azpiazu and Pera, 2019) to deep reinforcement learning (Mohammadi and Khasteh, 2019) were proposed. Recent research explored combining transformers with linguistic features (Deutsch et al., 2020;Meng et al., 2020;Lee et al., 2021;Imperial, 2021). While Deutsch et al. (2020) did not report any improvements with linguistic features, the others reported that combining linguistic features with deep learning approaches result in better ARA models.

Although a lot of this research evolved on English, the past decade saw ARA research in other languages such as German (Hancke et al., 2012), French (François and Fairon, 2012), Italian (Dell'Orletta et al., 2011), Bangla (Sinha et al., 2012) etc., which employed language specific feature sets. While most ARA research modeled one language at a time, some research created language agnostic feature sets and architectures and experimented with 2 to 7 languages (Shen et al., 2013;Azpiazu and Pera, 2019;Madrazo Azpiazu and Pera, 2020a,b;Martinc et al., 2021;Weiss et al., 2021). Although only one language is considered per model in all this research, there are two important exceptions. Madrazo Azpiazu and Pera (2020b) explored whether combining texts from related languages during training improves ARA performance for low resource languages. Weiss et al. (2021) used a model trained on English texts on German, based on a common, broad set of handcrafted linguistic features. However, to our knowledge, zero-shot cross lingual transfer of text embeddings, without any handcrafted features, was not explored for this task in the past.

ARA is traditionally treated as a classification problem in NLP research, although there are some exceptions. Heilman et al. (2008) compared linear, ordinal, and logistic regression and concluded that ordinal with a combination of lexical and grammatical features worked the best for ARA, although subsequent research was still dominated by classification approaches. There is some past work that considered ARA as a pairwise ranking problem, using SVM/SVM rank and hand crafted linguistic features (Pitler and Nenkova, 2008;Tanaka-Ishii et al., 2010;Ma et al., 2012;Mesgar and Strube, 2015;Ambati et al., 2016;Howcroft and Demberg, 2017). While Tanaka-Ishii et al. (2010) and Ma et al. (2012) showed that ranking performs better than traditional features and classification/regression respectively, Xia et al. (2016) did not find ranking to be consistently better across the board. In this background, we take a fresh look at the application of ranking for ARA, by proposing a new neural pairwise ranking model. Recent multilingual transfer work in NLP provides several avenues that appear relevant to readability assessment across languages, including multilingual masked language models and sentence encoders as general-purpose backbones and evaluation targets, with studies on cross-lingual zero-shot classification and regression, cross-lingual sentence retrieval and similarity, and language-agnostic sentence embeddings learned via translation ranking or contrastive alignment (Devlin et al., 2019;Conneau et al., 2020;Reimers and Gurevych, 2020;Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019;Feng et al., 2020).

spans.span: Prior analyses of contextual representations have examined anisotropy reduction techniques (Mu and Viswanath, 2018), geometry of embedding spaces (Ethayarajh, 2019; Gao et al., 2019), probing-based diagnostics (Hewitt and Manning, 2019; Tenney et al., 2019), and sense-specific clustering behavior across layers and models (Peters et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Reif et al., 2019), as well as cross-lingual alignment and multilingual transfer in contextual encoders (Conneau et al., 2020; Pires et al., 2019), contextual subspace methods (Kovaleva et al., 2019; Voita et al., 2019), and layer-wise information flow measured via mutual information or CKA (Kornblith et al., 2019; Raghu et al., 2017).

Lacks synthesis.document: There has been a growing body of research studying the inner workings of BERT and trying to quantify what it learns in various scenarios, dubbed "BERTology" (Rogers et al., 2020). Of particular interest to this paper is work that analyzes BERT's output embeddings. Prior analyses of contextual representations have examined anisotropy reduction techniques (Mu and Viswanath, 2018), geometry of embedding spaces (Ethayarajh, 2019; Gao et al., 2019), probing-based diagnostics (Hewitt and Manning, 2019; Tenney et al., 2019), and sense-specific clustering behavior across layers and models (Peters et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Reif et al., 2019), as well as cross-lingual alignment and multilingual transfer in contextual encoders (Conneau et al., 2020; Pires et al., 2019), contextual subspace methods (Kovaleva et al., 2019; Voita et al., 2019), and layer-wise information flow measured via mutual information or CKA (Kornblith et al., 2019; Raghu et al., 2017). Recent studies have found that embeddings created from the final layer of BERT tend to cluster according to word senses (Wiedemann et al., 2019), though this varies somewhat based on the position of a word in a sentence (Mickus et al., 2020). The final BERT layers also produce more contextualized word embeddings than the earlier layers (Ethayarajh, 2019), a finding we revisit using paraphrases in Section 3.3. To situate our analysis, we next delineate the operational definition of sense separation adopted in this study. We define sense separation as the degree to which examples of a polysemous lemma partition into distinct regions of the embedding space. We operationalize regions using density-based clustering applied to contextual tokens sampled from balanced corpora. We complement clustering with a nearest-neighbor sense attribution protocol based on lexicographic sense inventories. We then evaluate stability across paraphrase-preserving rewrites and across syntactic alternations. We also compare layer-wise trends between BERT base and large configurations. We assess the role of subword segmentation by conditioning on wordpiece length. We distinguish positional effects by stratifying contexts according to sentence-internal orderings. We compute layer similarity profiles using CKA to relate sense separation to representational drift. We measure anisotropy and apply common normalization techniques before clustering. We estimate uncertainty via bootstrap resampling to quantify variability in cluster counts. We further examine cross-domain robustness using newswire, Wikipedia, and conversational corpora. We finally report statistical significance using permutation tests with multiple-comparison control. Collectively, these components form a comprehensive framework for analyzing embedding behavior under controlled paraphrase variation. The ensuing sections detail datasets, preprocessing, and evaluation metrics. Section 3 presents empirical findings with ablations and sensitivity analyses. Section 4 discusses implications for contextual meaning representation and outlines limitations. Section 5 concludes with directions for scalable diagnostics and downstream integration.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Prior approaches focused on framing DST as question answering (Ruan et al., 2020;Ma et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2021). Many MultiWoZ cross-domain models leverage slot names/descriptions (Wu et al., 2019;Lin et al., 2021a).

Pretrained generative LLMs (Raffel et al., 2020;Brown et al., 2020) have enable framing NLP tasks as seq2seq problems. Some DST papers (Zhao et al., 2021a;Feng et al., 2021) look at settings with no train-test discrepancy. Many studies explore the efficacy of task-specific prompts (Jiang et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2021). Madotto et al. (2020) prime LMs with examples for dialogue tasks, but without finetuning. Wei et al. (2021) fine-tune language models to understand prompts for a different task. A broader line of work examines prompt-based and instruction-tuned approaches across diverse NLP tasks without restricting to dialogue state tracking, including pattern-exploiting training and automatic prompt search (Schick and Schütze, 2021; Gao et al., 2021), calibration and template engineering for zero-shot classification (Zhao et al., 2021b; Holtzman et al., 2021), chain-of-thought prompting and rationale-augmented decoding (Wei et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023), in-context learning with retrieval or demonstration selection (Rubin et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022), and instruction tuning with mixtures of datasets such as FLAN, T0, and Super-NaturalInstructions (Sanh et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022).

Despite these advances, DST in noisy, multi-domain settings remains challenging due to annotation inconsistencies and slot ontology drift. The literature has also examined leveraging semi-structured knowledge and schema linking to reduce manual engineering. Recent benchmarks highlight brittleness to paraphrase and domain shift, motivating approaches that better separate representation from ontology-specific constraints. We focus on settings with limited supervised data and heterogeneous slot formulations. Our study targets cross-domain generalization under realistic distribution shift and weak supervision. We compare generative and discriminative formulations while controlling for prompt design and calibration. We further analyze failure modes related to long-context dialogues and compositional slot dependencies. Finally, we discuss implications for robust deployment and evaluation protocols in evolving task ontologies.

spans.span: Recent work on multimodal pretraining and grounding spans a broad spectrum of objectives and data regimes, including contrastive image–text alignment (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2021), region-level grounding with phrase localization (Plummer et al., 2015; Akbari et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020), compositional reasoning benchmarks (Hudson and Manning, 2019; Johnson et al., 2017; Bahdanau et al., 2019), and emergent communication for symbol use in referential games (Lazaridou et al., 2017; Havrylov and Titov, 2017; Mordatch and Abbeel, 2018; Chaabouni et al., 2020).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Symbol Grounding. Contemporary grounders extensively utilize batch learning (e.g. Shridhar and Hsu (2018)). Yet, ITL requires incremental learning because without it the teacher guidance cannot influence the learner's inferences about plans as and when the advice is given. Further, many grounders assume that the learner starts out with a complete and accurate conceptualisation of the domain using pre-defined visual features and a known vocabulary (Kennington et al., 2015;Kennington and Schlangen, 2017;Wang et al., 2017). In ITL, both of these assumptions are unrealistic; therefore in this paper we explore models for which these assumptions don't apply. Finally, in contrast to all prior grounders, we support incremental learning when the training exemplars feature REs that are linguistically complex: e.g., "two red circles that aren't to the right of both green squares".

Representation Learning. Models for jointly learning a representation for vision and language utilize either explicit alignment via bounding boxes or instance segmentation (Lu et al., 2019;Chen et al., 2020;Tan and Bansal, 2019;Kamath et al., 2021;Yu et al., 2021), or a large-volume of weakly labeled data in the form of image-caption pairs (Radford et al., 2021). These models rely on offline learning with large datasets. This work, on the other hand, explores how to incrementally extract knowledge in a few-shot manner, using sequentially observed evidence that consists of weakly-labelled annotations, including neologisms.

Grounded Language Acquisition. This task is commonly realized as grounded grammar induction from image-caption pairs (Shi et al., 2019;Zhao and Titov, 2020), or as (neural) semantic parsers learning from a reward signal (Williams, 1992) in visual question answering Yi et al., 2018) or in planning (Azaria et al., 2016;Wang et al., 2016Wang et al., , 2017Karamcheti et al., 2020). In these scenarios, the primary objective is to learn mappings from linguistic expressions to logical forms, which in turn get associated with certain visual percepts during the learning process. This paper does not tackle learning logical forms. Instead, we obtain them from an existing broad-coverage grammar and focus on exploiting the logical consequences of those logical forms during symbol grounding-i.e., our focus is to utilise the interpretation of logical forms, and in particular the truth functional meanings of close-class words like quantifiers and negation, to inform the learning of mappings from (open-class) symbols like red to their denotations, given the visual percepts.

Visual Questions Answering (VQA) is a task of answering free-form questions about an image (Antol et al., 2015). VQA has reached impressive performance in recent years (Fukui et al., 2016;, yet VQA models struggle with out-of distribution generalization for new types of questions, requiring multi-step reasoning, with analysis revealing that they often rely on shortcuts (Jiang and Bansal, 2019;Subramanian et al., , 2020. Grounded VQA models like (Yi et al., 2018) and Bogin et al. (2021) tackle these shortcomings by learning to ground parts of the question and then learning to compose those parts via the question's syntax to compute the answer. They thus estimate denotations of linguistic parts that are not denoted by the answer to the question. By doing so, these models achieve out-of-distribution generalization for novel questions. However, these models lack the ITL's requirement for incremental learning: model training relies on batch learning. Furthermore, while their performance is impressive, error analysis shows that it tends to make mistakes on sentences containing logical concepts like quantifiers and negation (e.g. Bogin et al. (2021) Figure  shows that the determiner most incorrectly denotes an arbitrary subset of entities). Our view is that there is little benefit in trying to learn to ground these concepts as they are domain independent and can be interpreted using formal semantics. In our experiments, we are testing the extent to which knowing and reasoning with the logical meanings of these symbols helps incremental grounding, and in particular estimating denotations of symbols within an RE that aren't designated by that RE.

Visual Reference Resolution. In previous experimental setups, it is often assumed that there is a unique referent in the visual scene for the given RE in the test phase (e.g., Kazemzadeh et al. (2014); Whitney et al. (2016)). We aim to cope with situations where the RE has multiple referents: identifying all the referents that satisfy an RE enables efficient planning, because it affords free choice when executing certain commands-e.g., "move a circle to the left." when there is more than one circle affords choosing a control policy so that resources are optimized.

Lacks synthesis.document:
A Brief History of NLU Datasets. As a core module of ToD systems, NLU has been researched since the early 1990s, when the Airline Travel Information System (ATIS) project was started (Hemphill et al., 1990), consisting of spoken queries on flightrelated information. Over the next two decades, very few NLU resources were released. The lack of ToD NLU resources ended in 2013, with the beginning of the 'dialogue state tracking (DST) era' (Williams et al., 2013;Henderson et al., 2014;Kim et al., 2016). Instead of just classifying each turn of the user, DST deals with keeping track of the user's goal over the entire dialogue history, i.e., all the previous user and system turns. Several datasets were released during the DST challenges, all of them comprising simple intent sets (usually tagged as dialogue acts).

To adapt to the increasing data requirements of deep learning models, increasingly larger dialogue datasets have been released in recent years (Budzianowski et al., 2018;Wei et al., 2018;Rastogi et al., 2019;Peskov et al., 2019). However, the design of ToD datasets comes with some profound differences to datasets for e.g. machine translation or speech recognition, which affect current ToD datasets. First, the domain-specific nature of ToD datasets made the data tied to its ontologies, not allowing data reusability across different domains. Second, the domain-specific ontologies required a lot of expertise for annotation, therefore many annotation mistakes were made (Eric et al., 2019). Third, coverage mismatches between the ontology and real user needs induce cascading errors in state tracking and policy learning. Fourth, the lack of standardized evaluation for multi-domain compositionality complicates comparisons across releases and baselines. Fifth, data collection protocols often privilege scripted interactions, which underrepresent repair, ambiguity, or goal shifts.

Recent efforts to mitigate these issues have emphasized scalable schema definitions, crowd-driven corrections, and programmatic consistency checks. Benchmarks now increasingly include out-of-distribution slots, unseen goal compositions, and cross-domain goal transfers to probe generalization. Recent efforts also expanded beyond English and single-domain settings, including cross-lingual and multi-domain corpora and benchmarks that emphasize schema diversity and compositional generalization (Bapna et al., 2017;Schuster et al., 2019;Zhou et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2020;Ponti et al., 2020;Lai et al., 2021;FitzGerald et al., 2022;Hudeček and Dušek, 2023). At the same time, dataset creators have incorporated richer dialog phenomena such as corrections, hesitations, and ellipses to better approximate real user behavior. The introduction of standardized slot ontologies and interface layers has further facilitated adapter-based reuse across domains.

Despite this progress, open problems remain regarding long-horizon goal tracking, fine-grained correction semantics, and privacy-preserving annotation pipelines. A notable challenge is aligning evolving business taxonomies with stable public benchmarks without invalidating historical baselines. Another tension lies in balancing breadth of domains with depth of annotations to support both end-to-end training and targeted error analysis. Complementary synthetic data generation has shown promise for rare slot values and edge-case dialog flows. Weak supervision and distant labeling techniques can help scale annotation while preserving quality guarantees. Looking forward, we anticipate hybrid curation pipelines that blend targeted expert review with automatic consistency estimation and continual schema evolution. Establishing principled evaluation slices for robustness, fairness, and transfer will be crucial for the next generation of ToD NLU datasets.

Lacks synthesis.document:
In this section, we discuss related studies with repect to the contrastive learning framework and sentence embedding.
Contrastive learning has emerged as a unifying paradigm for representation learning across vision and language, grounded in instance discrimination and mutual information estimation.
Early formulations emphasize noise-contrastive objectives and negative sampling to separate semantically distinct instances while aligning augmented views of the same input.
In sentence embedding, contrastive objectives have been adapted to textual augmentations, dropout-induced views, and in-batch negatives to produce semantically meaningful vector spaces.
Recent work spans a diverse set of architectures and training regimes, including SimCLR (Chen et al., 2020), MoCo v2 (Chen et al., 2020b), BYOL (Grill et al., 2020), SimSiam (Chen and He, 2021), CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), ALIGN (Jia et al., 2021), CoCLR (Han et al., 2020), TSDAE (Wang et al., 2021), SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021), DeCLUTR (Giorgi et al., 2021), Sentence-BERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), InfoNCE and its temperature variants (Oord et al., 2018; Wang and Isola, 2020), hard-negative mining strategies (Xiong et al., 2020; Karpukhin et al., 2020), and large-scale weakly supervised datasets such as YFCC100M (Thomee et al., 2016) and LAION-400M/5B (Schuhmann et al., 2021; 2022), as well as evaluation benchmarks like STS tasks (Cer et al., 2017; Marelli et al., 2014) and BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021).
A central challenge is balancing the strength of positive augmentations against the diversity of negatives, which influences both isotropy and semantic clustering in the learned space.
Temperature scaling, queue memory, and large-batch training each alter gradient magnitudes and the effective hardness of negatives.
For text encoders, dropout-as-augmentation, adversarial perturbations, and back-translation offer complementary routes to generate positive pairs without requiring paraphrase corpora.
Hard-negative mining, whether mined offline from retrieval indices or online via cross-encoder re-ranking, has been shown to reduce representation collapse and improve retrieval robustness.
Cross-modal extensions, particularly image–text contrast, reveal benefits of aligning complementary modalities, which can regularize language representations through grounded supervision.
At the same time, purely unsupervised sentence encoders benefit from domain-adaptive pretraining that narrows the distribution shift between generic corpora and target evaluation tasks.
Evaluation practices typically rely on semantic textual similarity, transfer to downstream classification, and zero-shot retrieval, but increasingly include robustness and calibration metrics.
Several studies note that margin-based variants and angular losses can encourage wider separation among negatives while preserving local semantic neighborhoods.
Regularization strategies, such as whitening, uniformity losses, and debiased contrastive terms, further shape the geometry of sentence spaces.
Finally, scaling laws observed for contrastive objectives suggest predictable gains with model and data size, though diminishing returns appear without improved negative curation and augmentation design.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Label Smoothing The original label smoothing can be formalized as:

K denotes the number of classes, α is the label smoothing parameter, α/K is the soft label, ŷ is a vector where the correct label equals to 1 and others equal to zero and ŷLS is the modified targets.

Label smoothing is first introduced to image classification (Szegedy et al., 2016) and was later adopted across language modeling and machine translation as a simple yet effective regularizer. It modulates one-hot targets toward a uniform prior to reduce overconfidence while preserving task-specific signal in the majority mass on the gold class. Empirically, it improves calibration and sometimes top-1 accuracy, though excessive smoothing can harm rare-class discrimination.

Prior work spans a broad range of techniques and settings, including regularization for calibration and overconfidence reduction in vision models (Szegedy et al., 2016; Müller et al., 2019; Pereyra et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017), sequence-to-sequence training under label uncertainty (Pereyra et al., 2017; Chorowski and Jaitly, 2017; Kannan et al., 2018; Müller et al., 2020), token-level smoothing for translation quality and robustness (Pereyra et al., 2017; Vaswani et al., 2017; Edunov et al., 2018; Ott et al., 2018), distributional targets and knowledge distillation variants (Hinton et al., 2015; Yuan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2021), and multi-task or multilingual transfer regimes in which shared label spaces interact with smoothing (Johnson et al., 2017; Conneau et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020).

Despite its simplicity, the choice of smoothing prior, schedule, and interaction with data imbalance remains unsettled. Recent analyses highlight that uniform priors can be suboptimal when class frequencies are highly skewed or label noise is structured. This motivates examining priors tied to observed confusion patterns or semantic similarity among classes.

Vocabulary Sharing Vocabulary sharing is widely applied in most neural machine translation studies (Vaswani et al., 2017;Song et al., 2019;Lin et al., 2020;Pan et al., 2021). Shared subword vocabularies facilitate parameter tying across source and target embeddings and can reduce the model footprint while improving transfer in morphologically related languages. In multilingual settings, vocabulary sharing also affects cross-lingual generalization by aligning token statistics and enabling consistent segmentation across languages.

However, vocabulary sharing introduces trade-offs between compression and expressivity, especially for distant language pairs with divergent morphologies and scripts. Overly aggressive sharing can increase token collision, degrade rare-word representation, and alter gradient allocation during training. Prior work explores segmentation granularity, script-aware tokenization, and adaptive vocabularies to mitigate these issues.

Connections between label smoothing and vocabulary sharing have begun to emerge in multilingual translation. Both mechanisms influence the distribution of probabilities over tokens and can indirectly regulate the entropy of the output distribution. When combined, their effects on calibration, robustness to noise, and low-resource transfer may be non-additive, suggesting the need for principled joint tuning.

In this paper, we study how smoothing priors interact with shared vocabularies under data imbalance and domain shift. We analyze calibration, BLEU, and robustness to synthetic noise across language pairs with varying script overlap. We further consider schedules that adapt smoothing strength to token frequency and evaluate their impact on rare-word recall and calibration under distributional shift.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we present a taxonomy of smoothing priors that incorporates frequency-aware, class-similarity, and temperature-scaled variants relevant to token-level models. Second, we provide an experimental protocol that disentangles effects from segmentation and vocabulary size by controlling for tokenizer-induced changes to sequence length. Third, we release code and pre-tokenized corpora to facilitate reproducible ablations.

We aim to clarify when uniform smoothing suffices and when structure-aware priors are warranted in the presence of shared subword inventories. The results underline the importance of jointly selecting vocabulary size, segmentation policy, and smoothing schedule to meet calibration and accuracy targets. Finally, we discuss deployment considerations, including computational overhead, hyperparameter stability across domains, and compatibility with distillation-based training.

We conclude by highlighting open questions on learning priors from data and integrating uncertainty estimates into decoding. Future work may explore curriculum-based schedules, multilingual adapters that modulate smoothing per language, and semi-supervised objectives that reconcile pseudo-label confidence with calibrated targets.

spans.span: Prior work on procedural text processing spans sequence labeling for step identification (Paris et al., 2002; Delpech and Saint-Dizier, 2008; Zhang et al., 2012), temporal and causal reasoning over instructional narratives (Takechi et al., 2003; Regneri et al., 2010; Tandon et al., 2020; Rajagopal et al., 2020), script and schema induction from large corpora (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008; Balasubramanian et al., 2013; Weber et al., 2018; Rudinger et al., 2015), and the construction of task-oriented knowledge bases using wikiHow or similar resources (Jung et al., 2010; Chu et al., 2017; Park and Motahari Nezhad, 2018; Koupaee and Wang, 2018).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Introduction

Linking procedural events across heterogeneous instructional corpora enables knowledge consolidation, reuse, and high-coverage downstream reasoning.
Lagos et al. (2017) share the same task formulation as ours.
Both works try to link steps (or spans within steps) to other wikiHow articles.
We make several important contributions over their work: (1) a search-then-rerank method significantly increases the linking recall; (2) more comprehensive experiments with human and downstream evaluation that showcase the quality and the usefulness of the linked data; and (3) a more beneficial data structure with broader coverage over all of wikiHow, not just the Computer domain.
Our framing also emphasizes cross-article compositionality, allowing links to serve as latent connectors for implicit prerequisites and shared subgoals.

Related Work

Procedural knowledge is commonly formalized through scripts and schemata, which capture stereotyped event sequences and role bindings.
Early cognitive theories introduced scripts (Abelson and Schank, 1977) and schemata (Rumelhart, 1975) as abstractions for routine activities, later instantiated in NLP as event chains, frames, and procedural graphs.
Prior work on procedural text processing spans sequence labeling for step identification (Paris et al., 2002; Delpech and Saint-Dizier, 2008; Zhang et al., 2012), temporal and causal reasoning over instructional narratives (Takechi et al., 2003; Regneri et al., 2010; Tandon et al., 2020; Rajagopal et al., 2020), script and schema induction from large corpora (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008; Balasubramanian et al., 2013; Weber et al., 2018; Rudinger et al., 2015), and the construction of task-oriented knowledge bases using wikiHow or similar resources (Jung et al., 2010; Chu et al., 2017; Park and Motahari Nezhad, 2018; Koupaee and Wang, 2018).
Recent datasets target fine-grained procedural reasoning, but trade off scale for annotation depth, limiting generalization in open-domain settings.
Crowdsourced collections have been influential yet typically small after adjudication (Singh et al., 2002; Regneri et al., 2010; Li et al., 2012; Wanzare et al., 2016; Rashkin et al., 2018).
Large-scale acquisition from community instruction portals promises coverage but raises challenges in normalization, step alignment, and link reliability.
Efforts to leverage wikiHow for knowledge-base construction demonstrate feasibility at scale (Jung et al., 2010; Chu et al., 2017; Park and Motahari Nezhad, 2018), while leaving open questions about intrinsic link quality and downstream task impact.
Our study addresses these gaps by coupling retrieval-augmented linking with human validation and task-based evaluation.
We further quantify how search-then-rerank improves recall without sacrificing precision, and we analyze link utility for intent reasoning and subtask transfer.
Finally, we release a normalized, cross-article graph with broader topical coverage, enabling reproducible experimentation and future extensions.

spans.span: Recent efforts further broaden this landscape with block-sparse Transformers (Child et al., 2019), routing-based sparsity in Switch Transformers (Fedus et al., 2021), linearized attention kernels such as Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021), kernelized low-rank projections in Linformer (Wang et al., 2020), and long-context pretraining strategies exemplified by LED (Beltagy et al., 2020) and UL2 (Tay et al., 2023).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Sparse attention mechanism The full attention mechanism has a quadratic memory cost. Prior research works have proposed different sparse attention mechanisms to reduce the memory cost. Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020) uses a dilated sliding window of blocks and global attention patterns. BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) employs sliding window and random blocks. Reformer (Kitaev et al., 2020) uses the locality-sensitive hashing. In addition to optimizing the encoder self-attention, Huang et al. (2021) proposes head-wise positional strides to reduce the cost of the encoder-decoder attention. Recent efforts further broaden this landscape with block-sparse Transformers (Child et al., 2019), routing-based sparsity in Switch Transformers (Fedus et al., 2021), linearized attention kernels such as Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021), kernelized low-rank projections in Linformer (Wang et al., 2020), and long-context pretraining strategies exemplified by LED (Beltagy et al., 2020) and UL2 (Tay et al., 2023). However, sparse attention diminishes the benefits of pretraining and sacrifices parts of the receptive field.

Extract-then-generate method The model first extracts salient text snippets from the input, followed by generating a concise overall summary. Most two-stage summarization approaches (Zhang et al., 2019;Lebanoff et al., 2019;Xu and Durrett, 2019;Bajaj et al., 2021) are trained separately, which suffer from information loss due to the cascaded errors. Some approaches attempt to reduce that loss by bridging the two stages. Chen and Bansal (2018) adopts reinforcement learning with a sentence-level policy gradient method. Bae et al. (2019) proposes summary-level policy gradient. In addition to the drawbacks explained in Section 2.3, our model is different as we jointly train an extractthen-generate model for summarization using latent variables.

Divide-and-conquer approach A common approach in long input summarization is divide-andconquer (Gidiotis and Tsoumakas, 2020;Grail et al., 2021). This approach breaks a long input into multiple parts, which are summarized separately and combined to produce a final complete summary. However, these models do not capture the contextual dependencies across parts and assumes a certain structure of the input (such as paper sections).

Hierarchical models Various hierarchical models have been proposed to handle the longer inputs. Cohan et al. (2018) models the document discourse structure with a hierarchical encoder and a discourse-aware decoder to generate the summary. HAT-Bart (Rohde et al., 2021) proposes a new Hierarchical Attention Transformer-based architecture that attempts to capture sentence and paragraphlevel information. HMNet (Zhu et al., 2020) builds a hierarchical structure that includes discourselevel information and speaker roles. However, these models focus mainly on model performance and not on reducing the memory and computational cost.

spans.span: Sentence rewriting IUR can be considered to be similar to the sentence rewriting task (Xu and Veeramachaneni, 2021;Lin et al., 2021;Chen and Bansal, 2018;Cao et al., 2018), and related advances also include controllable paraphrasing (Iyyer et al., 2018;Krishna et al., 2020), style transfer for text (Shen et al., 2017;Li et al., 2018), edit-based revision (Guu et al., 2018;Dong et al., 2019), and constrained decoding with lexical control (Hu et al., 2019;Post and Vilar, 2018).

Lacks synthesis.document: Sentence rewriting IUR can be considered to be similar to the sentence rewriting task (Xu and Veeramachaneni, 2021;Lin et al., 2021;Chen and Bansal, 2018;Cao et al., 2018), and related advances also include controllable paraphrasing (Iyyer et al., 2018;Krishna et al., 2020), style transfer for text (Shen et al., 2017;Li et al., 2018), edit-based revision (Guu et al., 2018;Dong et al., 2019), and constrained decoding with lexical control (Hu et al., 2019;Post and Vilar, 2018). Recent studies have been addressed the IUR task with various sophisticated methods. Text generation IUR can be formulated as text generation by using the seq2seq model (Pan et al., 2019;Huang et al., 2021). For the generation, several well-known pre-trained models have been applied (Lewis et al., 2020;Brown et al., 2020;Raffel et al., 2020) with promising results. We employ the T5 model (Raffel et al., 2020) as the main component to rewrite utterances. To address the problem of missing important tokens in model's rewriting, we enhance T5 by introducing a Picker and two labeling methods (Section 3.2). The learning of Θ is composed by only using utterance generation (the generator) or the combination of two tasks: important token identification (the picker) and utterance generation (the generator). To situate IUR within broader dialog modeling, prior work has explored context-aware rewriting for ASR repair and disfluency removal (Rao et al., 2020;Cho et al., 2021), user-intent preserving paraphrase generation (Zhang et al., 2020), and slot-focused reformulation in task-oriented systems (Elgohary et al., 2019). Compared to classification-style IUR approaches that detect and tag utterance issues (Kim et al., 2021), our focus remains on direct generation with explicit token guidance. We assume access to dialogue context and system schema, and we condition the generator on these signals to improve factual retention. The picker identifies salient tokens that must be preserved or emphasized during rewriting, thereby reducing omissions of entity names, slot values, and negations. We further introduce two supervision strategies for the picker, one derived from alignment heuristics and one from gradient-based salience, to balance precision and coverage. The generator is a T5-based encoder–decoder with constrained copy bias, while the picker is a lightweight token scorer that outputs hard and soft masks. Training proceeds in two stages, starting with generator pretraining on synthetic rewrites and followed by joint finetuning with picker guidance. Inference uses a constrained beam search that respects hard masks and prioritizes soft-mask tokens through a modified length-normalized score. We evaluate on multi-domain dialog benchmarks with entity-rich utterances and report improvements in content preservation and factuality over strong pretrained baselines. Ablations demonstrate that both picker supervision strategies are complementary and that the constrained decoding contributes most to recall of critical tokens.

spans.span: Recent neural and probabilistic approaches to unsupervised word and morpheme segmentation span Bayesian models with hierarchical priors (Goldwater et al., 2009;Mochihashi et al., 2009;Teh, 2006b), heuristic or constraint-based algorithms evaluated on morph-rich languages (Creutz and Lagus, 2005;Virpioja et al., 2013), subword modeling for ASR and MT using BPE and unigram LM segmentation (Sennrich et al., 2016;Kudo, 2018), and evaluation on benchmark corpora such as Brent and CHILDES for English as well as Mboshi and Japhug for low-resource settings (Brent, 1999;MacWhinney, 2000;Boito et al., 2018;Jacques, 2016).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Going from audio recordings to fully annotated transcripts implies two successive segmentation steps: the first segments words and happens during the production of phonemic or orthographic transcripts; the second further splits words into morphs, which are then annotated with syntactic information and glosses. We mostly focus on the former task, assuming a two-step process: first, the computation of a phonemic transcript, that we assume are given; then the segmentation into words for which we consider two settings: batch and online learning. The word and morpheme segmentation tasks are closely related and rely on similar tools: using the Japhug corpus, which contains both levels of segmentations, we also study the implications of using lists of words vs. morphemes as weak supervision.

In its baseline form, the word segmentation process is fully unsupervised, and the only training material is a set of transcribed sentences (see Fig.). Prior work has emphasized that purely unsupervised models benefit from simple priors when data are scarce. Recent neural and probabilistic approaches to unsupervised word and morpheme segmentation span Bayesian models with hierarchical priors (Goldwater et al., 2009;Mochihashi et al., 2009;Teh, 2006b), heuristic or constraint-based algorithms evaluated on morph-rich languages (Creutz and Lagus, 2005;Virpioja et al., 2013), subword modeling for ASR and MT using BPE and unigram LM segmentation (Sennrich et al., 2016;Kudo, 2018), and evaluation on benchmark corpora such as Brent and CHILDES for English as well as Mboshi and Japhug for low-resource settings (Brent, 1999;MacWhinney, 2000;Boito et al., 2018;Jacques, 2016). This landscape motivates a closer examination of probabilistic assumptions under limited supervision.

We rely on Bayesian non-parametric approaches to word segmentation (see (Cohen, 2016) for a thorough exposition), and our baselines are the unigram version of the dpseg model (Goldwater et al., 2009) and a variant where the underlying Dirichlet Process is replaced by a Pitman-Yor Process as in (Neubig, 2014). We selected unigram models for their simplicity, which (a) makes them amenable to the processing of very small sets of sentences; (b) makes the online learning setting tractable. While using higher order models or more sophisticated models of the same family (Teh, 2006b;Mochihashi et al., 2009) may improve the performance (see for an experimental comparison), we believe that in our low-resource conditions these variations would be small, and would not change our main conclusions.

Word segmentation models fundamentally rely on probabilistic models for word sequences defining P(w = w1 . . . wT); word sequences can also be viewed as segmented sequences of characters y = y1 . . . yL, so that the same model can be used for the joint probability of (y, b), with b = b1 . . . bL representing the vector of boundary locations where value bt = 1 (resp. bt = 0) denotes a boundary (resp. no boundary) after symbol yt. In an unsupervised setting, these boundaries are hidden and are latent variables in the model. Such models lend themselves well to Gibbs sampling, which repeatedly produces samples of each boundary given all the other boundaries in the corpus.

In dpseg, the underlying sequence model is a unigram model: P(w1 . . . wT) = ΠT t=1 P(wt). The probability of individual words corresponds to a Dirichlet Process with parameters α, the concentration parameter, and P0, the base distribution, and yields the following formulation for the conditional probability of wt given the past words w<t:

where nw(w<t) counts the number of times w has occurred in the past. With lower values of α, the most frequent words tend to be generated more (hence, concentration), while with higher values, the words are more smoothly distributed. P0, the base distribution, assigns scores to arbitrary character strings; Goldwater et al. (2009) use a length model and a uniform character model. For word w made of characters y1, ..., ym, P0 is computed as:

where p# is the probability to end the word. For this model, Gibbs sampling compares at each position t two sequences of words wt=0 (no boundary at position t) and wt=1 (a boundary is inserted). As these sequences only differ minimally, terms such as P(bt = 0|y, b−t) are readily derived (see eg. (Goldwater et al., 2009)). Gibbs sampling is performed for a number of iterations that are sufficient to reach convergence, and we use the last iteration to uncover the resulting segmentation. To speed up mixing, Goldwater et al. (2009) also use annealing, so that a larger search space is explored.

An extension of dpseg, denoted pypseg, uses a Pitman-Yor Process (PYP) instead of the DP and generalises equation (1) with an additional discount parameter, which enables better control of the generation of new words. PYPs are introduced in (Teh, 2006b;Mochihashi et al., 2009); a fast implementation is in (Neubig, 2014). For our experiments, both models have been re-implemented in Python. This implementation will be publicly released. We also adopt a consistent tokenization pipeline across corpora to ensure comparability of results.

We consider both batch and online learning regimes to highlight trade-offs between convergence stability and adaptation speed. In batch mode, we process shuffled sentence sets and tune α and p# on a held-out split. In online mode, we process sentence streams with periodic hyperparameter updates using marginal likelihood estimates. For weak supervision, we experiment with lexicon priors derived from either word lists or morpheme inventories. These priors are injected into P0 via a mixture with a lexicon-backed distribution controlling the mass on attested units. We further analyze how lexicon noise impacts boundary decisions under different concentration settings. Finally, we report segmentation quality using boundary F1 and lexicon precision and recall on the Japhug and Mboshi corpora.

spans.span: Several works have since shifted focus toward the more challenging phoneme discovery problem by formulating it as a self-supervised learning problem where the semantics of the speech are known, such as from translation, phonemelevel language models or other sensory modalities such as vision. (Jansen, 2013) has studied the use of pairwise word identity labels for training phoneme discovery models based on Gaussian mixture models (GMM); (Harwath and Glass, 2019) analyzes the hidden layers of a two-branch neural network trained to retrieve spoken captions with semantically related images and finds strong correlation between segment representation and phoneme boundaries. (Harwath et al., 2020) adds hierarchical vector quantization (VQ) layers in the same retrieval network and is able to find a much smaller codebook than the unsupervised neural approach (Baevski et al., 2020), and achieve high correlation with the phoneme inventory. (Godard et al., 2018;Boito et al., 2019) has studied the possibility of learning semantic units using an attention-based speech-to-text translation system, though the units appear to correlate more with words.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Due to the challenge of learning phonemes, early works on unsupervised speech representation learning (Park and Glass, 2005;Lee and Glass, 2012;Ondel et al., 2016) focus on learning speech segments sharing similar acoustic properties, or phones, without taking into account the meaning of the speech they are part of. There are two main approaches in this direction. One approach is to learn discrete phone-like units without any textual labels by modeling phone labels of the speech segments as latent variables. In particular, (Park and Glass, 2005;Jansen et al., 2010) first detect segments with recurring patterns in the speech corpus followed by graph clustering using the similarity graph formed by the segments. (Lee and Glass, 2012;Ondel et al., 2016;Kamper et al., 2016) develop probabilistic graphical models to jointly segment and cluster speech into phone-like segments. An extension to the latent variable approach is to introduce additional latent variables such as speaker identity (Ondel et al., 2019) or language identity (Yusuf et al., 2020) and develop mechanisms to disentangle these variables.

With the advance of deep learning, neural network models have also been proposed to learn unsupervised phone-level representation either by first learning a continuous representation (Chung et al., 2019;Feng et al., 2019;Nguyen et al., 2020) followed by off-line clustering, or by learning a discrete representation end-to-end with Gumbel softmax (Eloff et al., 2019b;Baevski et al., 2020) or vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) (van den Oord et al., 2017;Chorowski et al., 2019;. However, codebooks learned by the neural approaches tend to be much larger than the number of phonemes (Baevski et al., 2020), leading to low scores in standard phoneme discovery metrics. The second approach utilizes weak supervision such as noisy phone labels predicted by a supervised, multilingual ASR system trained on other languages. Along this direction, ( Żelasko et al., 2020;Feng et al., 2021a) systematically study the performance of zero-shot crosslingual ASR on 13 languages trained with international phonetic alphabet (IPA) tokens and found that the system tends to perform poorly on unseen languages. Instead, (Feng et al., 2021b) is able to discover phone-like units by clustering bottleneck features (BNF) from a factorized time-delay neural network (TDNN-f) trained with phone labels predicted by a crosslingual ASR (Feng et al., 2021a).

Several works have since shifted focus toward the more challenging phoneme discovery problem by formulating it as a self-supervised learning problem where the semantics of the speech are known, such as from translation, phonemelevel language models or other sensory modalities such as vision. (Jansen, 2013) has studied the use of pairwise word identity labels for training phoneme discovery models based on Gaussian mixture models (GMM); (Harwath and Glass, 2019) analyzes the hidden layers of a two-branch neural network trained to retrieve spoken captions with semantically related images and finds strong correlation between segment representation and phoneme boundaries. (Harwath et al., 2020) adds hierarchical vector quantization (VQ) layers in the same retrieval network and is able to find a much smaller codebook than the unsupervised neural approach (Baevski et al., 2020), and achieve high correlation with the phoneme inventory. (Godard et al., 2018;Boito et al., 2019) has studied the possibility of learning semantic units using an attention-based speech-to-text translation system, though the units appear to correlate more with words. Works on unsupervised speech recognition  attempt to learn to recognize phonemes by leveraging the semantic information from a phoneme language model unpaired with the speech, typically by matching the empirical prior and posterior distributions of phonemes either using cross entropy (Yeh et al., 2019) or adversarial loss Baevski et al., 2021). Throughout the paper, we use P{•} to denote probability. We use capital letters to denote random variables and lower-case letters to represent samples of random variables. We use P X := P{X = x} to denote both probability mass and density functions of random variable X, depending on whether it is continuous or discrete. Further, denote P Y |X (y|x) := P{Y = y|X = x} as the true conditional probability distribution of random variable Y = y given random variable X = x. The probability simplex in R d is denoted as ∆ d .

spans.span: Prior work on political text classification spans lexicon-based approaches (e.g., LIWC; Pennebaker et al., 2015), neural encoders pre-trained on general corpora (Mikolov et al., 2013; Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019), election-specific stance and ideology datasets (SemEval-2016 Task 6; Iyyer et al., 2014; Johnson and Goldwasser, 2016; Conover et al., 2011), and domain adaptation methods including adversarial invariance (Ganin et al., 2016), parameter-efficient adapters (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020), and prompt tuning (Lester et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023).

Lacks synthesis.document:
This section provides background and motivation for task and domain adaptability applied to concern detection in the 2017 French Election domain ( §2.1, §2.2), including concern values induced from Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) ( §2.3).
We focus on the challenge of detecting moral concern categories in short, noisy political texts under distribution shift across topics and sources.
Task adaptability refers to transferring a concern detector trained on one label schema or annotation guideline to another without extensive relabeling.
Domain adaptability addresses generalization from one electoral context, medium, or time period to another where lexical and pragmatic cues differ.
We ground our study in MFT, which posits a set of moral dimensions (e.g., Care/Harm, Fairness/Cheating, Loyalty/Betrayal, Authority/Subversion, Sanctity/Degradation) that can be operationalized as concern values at the utterance level.
Prior work on political text classification spans lexicon-based approaches (e.g., LIWC; Pennebaker et al., 2015), neural encoders pre-trained on general corpora (Mikolov et al., 2013; Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019), election-specific stance and ideology datasets (SemEval-2016 Task 6; Iyyer et al., 2014; Johnson and Goldwasser, 2016; Conover et al., 2011), and domain adaptation methods including adversarial invariance (Ganin et al., 2016), parameter-efficient adapters (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020), and prompt tuning (Lester et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023).
Concern detection has been explored in the context of moral rhetoric and persuasion, with early studies employing hand-crafted features and later work leveraging contextual representations.
However, most existing resources are centered on English-language debates or social media, limiting direct transfer to French political discourse.
The 2017 French Election provides a natural stress test for adaptability due to rapid agenda shifts, multilingual media ecosystems, and evolving party coalitions.
We curate a corpus that interleaves campaign speeches, televised debates, and Twitter posts, annotated with MFT-derived concern values.
To examine task adaptability, we consider mappings between fine-grained moral cues and coarser concern categories used by different annotator groups.
To examine domain adaptability, we analyze shifts across platforms and time segments within the campaign timeline.
Our methodology compares label-space alignment techniques with representation-level adaptation under controlled data budgets.
We report performance under zero-shot, few-shot, and continual adaptation regimes to assess robustness and data efficiency.
Finally, we discuss implications for building portable concern detectors that remain stable under policy salience changes and linguistic variability.
We release data splits, annotation guidelines, and code to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

spans.span: Recent works (Petroni et al., 2019;Davison et al., 2019;Jiang et al., 2020) design prompts to probe the factual and commonsense knowledge encoded within a PLM. Recent works (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b;Gao et al., 2021) demonstrate that even smaller PLMs have similar few-shot learning capacity. Le Scao and Rush (2021) analyzes the effect of prompting and concludes that a single prompt may be worth 100 training examples in fine-tuning. In parallel, studies on cloze-style prompting and calibration report sensitivity to template wording and verbalizers (Zhao et al., 2021;Holtzman et al., 2021;Min et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022). Additional lines of work examine prompt transfer across tasks and domains (Vu et al., 2021;Logan IV et al., 2022;Lester et al., 2021;Liu et al., 2023). Efforts on prompt ensembling and selection explore stability and robustness (Shin et al., 2020;Ben-David et al., 2023;Zhong et al., 2021;Rubin et al., 2022).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Discrete Prompts The release of GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) has led to interest in prompting, a new way to leverage pretrained language models (PLM). Brown et al. (2020) proposes an intuitive in-context learning paradigm by concatenating a few input and output examples and feeding them to the language model and let the model autoregressively generate answers for new examples. Recent works (Petroni et al., 2019;Davison et al., 2019;Jiang et al., 2020) design prompts to probe the factual and commonsense knowledge encoded within a PLM. Recent works (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b;Gao et al., 2021) demonstrate that even smaller PLMs have similar few-shot learning capacity. Le Scao and Rush (2021) analyzes the effect of prompting and concludes that a single prompt may be worth 100 training examples in fine-tuning. In parallel, studies on cloze-style prompting and calibration report sensitivity to template wording and verbalizers (Zhao et al., 2021;Holtzman et al., 2021;Min et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022). Additional lines of work examine prompt transfer across tasks and domains (Vu et al., 2021;Logan IV et al., 2022;Lester et al., 2021;Liu et al., 2023). Efforts on prompt ensembling and selection explore stability and robustness (Shin et al., 2020;Ben-David et al., 2023;Zhong et al., 2021;Rubin et al., 2022).

Instead of manually designing prompts (i.e., prompt engineering), some recent studies also explore automatic prompt generation. PETAL (Schick et al., 2020) augments Pattern Exploiting Training (PET, Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b) with automatically identified label words; Gao et al. (2021) uses re-ranking to find the best label words by fine-tuning a RoBERTa model on the candidates searched by RoBERTa, and using an external generation model for data augmentation of prompt templates; AutoPrompt (Shin et al., 2020) uses a gradient-based search to determine both prompts and label words. However, these methods require parameter updates with gradient descent, which is infeasible without access to the model weights (e.g., GPT-3). PET and its variants also require a large unlabeled set and need to be fine-tuned multiple times. AutoPrompt uses discretization techniques to approximately map a continuous vector back to tokens in the vocabulary (i.e., "vocablization"). These searched prompts and labels are often uninterpretable by humans. Different from these prior studies, our proposed AMuLaP is a simple and interpretable method for few-shot prompting that can work well with and without access to model weights. Concurrently to our work,  propose a method that exploits an external knowledge base to find label mapping. Other contemporaneous efforts include calibration strategies for verbalizer selection (Zhao et al., 2021;Holtzman et al., 2021), soft-prompt tuning and prefix methods for parameter-efficient adaptation (Lester et al., 2021;Li and Liang, 2021;Prefix-Tuning), retrieval-augmented prompting that conditions on external corpora (Lewis et al., 2020;Izacard and Grave, 2021;Borgeaud et al., 2022), and evaluation frameworks for prompt sensitivity across datasets (Perez et al., 2021;Liu et al., 2023;Sanh et al., 2022;Mishra et al., 2022).

spans.span: Recent neural methods for idiom and multiword expression processing span contextualized representation learning and task-specific architectures, including sequence tagging with BiLSTMs and CRFs (Ma and Hovy, 2016;Gharbieh et al., 2016), transformer-based encoders fine-tuned for idiom token identification (Devlin et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2019;Reddy et al., 2021), probing studies of idiomaticity in BERT-like models (Nivre et al., 2020;Ettinger, 2020;Liu et al., 2022), and contrastive learning frameworks for compositionality (Wu et al., 2020;Chiang et al., 2022;Zeng and Bansal, 2023); complementary resources include PARSEME MWE corpora (Ramisch et al., 2018;Baldwin and Kim, 2010), the VNC-Tokens dataset (Cook et al., 2008), and idiom lexica such as IDIX and SemEval-2013 Task 5 (Korkontzelos et al., 2013).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Many idiom detection models build on insights about unconventional meaning in metaphor. A number of approaches use distributional models, such as Kintsch (2000), Utsumi (2011), Sa-Pereira (2016), and Shutova et al. (2012, the latter of which was one of the first to implement a fully unsupervised approach for encoding relationships between words, their contexts, and their dependencies. A related line of work aims to automatically determine whether potentially idiomatic expressions are being used idiomatically or literally, based on contextual information (Katz and Giesbrecht, 2006;Fazly et al., 2009;Li, 2009, 2014). Our measure of conventionality is inspired by the insights of these models; as described in Section 3.2, our measure uses differences in embeddings across contexts. Meanwhile, approaches to collocation detection have taken a probabilistic or informationtheoretic approach that seeks to identify collocations using word combination probabilities. PMI is a frequently-used quantity for measuring cooccurrence probabilities (Fano, 1961;Church and Hanks, 1990). Other implementations include selectional association (Resnik, 1996), symmetric conditional probability (Ferreira and Pereira Lopes, 1999), and log-likelihood (Dunning, 1993;Daille, 1996).

While much of the literature in NLP recognizes that idioms share a cluster of properties, including semantic idiosyncrasy, syntactic inflexibility, and institutionalization (e.g., Sag et al., 2002;Fazly and Stevenson, 2006;Fazly et al., 2009), our approach is novel in attempting to characterize idioms along two orthogonal dimensions that correspond to specific proposals from the cognitive science literature. To situate these choices, we first review recent work that operationalizes idiomaticity within neural language models. Recent neural methods for idiom and multiword expression processing span contextualized representation learning and task-specific architectures, including sequence tagging with BiLSTMs and CRFs (Ma and Hovy, 2016;Gharbieh et al., 2016), transformer-based encoders fine-tuned for idiom token identification (Devlin et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2019;Reddy et al., 2021), probing studies of idiomaticity in BERT-like models (Nivre et al., 2020;Ettinger, 2020;Liu et al., 2022), and contrastive learning frameworks for compositionality (Wu et al., 2020;Chiang et al., 2022;Zeng and Bansal, 2023); complementary resources include PARSEME MWE corpora (Ramisch et al., 2018;Baldwin and Kim, 2010), the VNC-Tokens dataset (Cook et al., 2008), and idiom lexica such as IDIX and SemEval-2013 Task 5 (Korkontzelos et al., 2013). In Section 4 we describe how we instantiate our dimensions in a model-agnostic scoring pipeline. We also clarify how our dataset selection controls for lexical frequency and topical confounds. Our measures may offer a new avenue for tackling the problem of automatic idiom detection. We report empirical results on three benchmarks to quantify the contribution of each dimension. Finally, we outline limitations and opportunities for broader generalization beyond English idioms. We conclude by discussing implications for cognitively informed representations in NLP.
