To mitigate the problem of information leakage from the head entity, Poerner et al. (2019) propose LAMA-UHN, which is a hard subset of LAMA that has less token overlaps in head and tail entities. X-FACTR (Jiang et al., 2020a) and mLAMA extend knowledge probing to the multilingual scenario and introduce multi-token answers. They each propose decoding methods that generate multi-token answers. BioLAMA (Sung et al., 2021) is a concurrent work that also releases a benchmark for biomedical knowledge probing. Additional efforts include P@1 evaluation protocols (Petroni et al., 2019), template mining (Jiang et al., 2020b), continuous prompt methods such as OptiPrompt (Zhong et al., 2021), and calibration techniques (Zhao et al., 2021; Holtzman et al., 2021), as well as multilingual expansions (Kassner et al., 2021) and domain-specific adaptations (Gu et al., 2021).

Knowledge Probing Benchmarks for PLMs.

LAMA (Petroni et al., 2019), which starts this line of work, is a collection of single-token knowledge triples extracted from sources including Wikidata and ConceptNet (Speer et al., 2017). To mitigate the problem of information leakage from the  head entity, Poerner et al. (2019) propose LAMA-UHN, which is a hard subset of LAMA that has less token overlaps in head and tail entities. X-FACTR (Jiang et al., 2020a) and mLAMA  extend knowledge probing to the multilingual scenario and introduce multi-token answers. They each propose decoding methods that generate multi-token answers, which we have shown to work poorly on MedLAMA. BioLAMA (Sung et al., 2021) is a concurrent work that also releases a benchmark for biomedical knowledge probing. We provide a comparison between LAMA, BioLAMA and MedLAMA in terms of (# relations, # queries, avg # answers per query, avg # characters per answer) in the Appendix. 12 Probing via Prompt Engineering. Knowledge probing is sensitive to what prompt is used (Jiang et al., 2020b). To bootstrap the probing performance, Jiang et al. (2020b) mine more prompts and ensemble them during inference. Later works parameterised the prompts and made them trainable (Shin et al., 2020b;Fichtel et al., 2021;Qin and Eisner, 2021). We have opted out promptengineering methods that require training data in this work, as tuning the prompts are essentially tuning an additional (parameterised) model on top of PLMs. As pointed out by Fichtel et al. (2021), prompt tuning requires large amounts of training data from the task. Since task training data is used, the additional model parameters are exposed to the target data distribution and can solve the set set by overfitting to such biases . In our work, by adaptively finetuning the model with a small set of raw sentences, we elicit the knowl- 12 Our comparison indicated that MedLAMA and BioLAMA have no overlaps in queries, allowing both resources to complement each other. edge out from PLMs but do not expose the data biases from the benchmark (MedLAMA). Biomedical Knowledge Probing. Nadkarni et al. (2021) train PLMs as KB completion models and test on the same task to understand how much knowledge is in biomedical PLMs. BioLAMA focuses on the continuous prompt learning method OptiPrompt (Zhong et al., 2021), which also requires ground-truth training data from the task. Overall, compared to BioLAMA, we have provided a more comprehensive set of probing experiments and analysis, including proposing a novel probing technique and providing human evaluations of model predictions.

Lacks synthesis.document: Our contributions add to a large body of work on grounded representation learning. Much of this work augments language modeling objectives with images (Silberer and Lapata, 2012;Lazaridou et al., 2015;Kiela et al., 2017) and videos (Sun et al., 2019). In this work, we focus on representations that encode verb semantics. Prior work on verb learning has been conducted in the computer vision community, typically described as "humanobject interactions" (Regneri et al., 2013;Chao et al., 2018;Ji et al., 2019). In contrast, we focus on learning representations from trajectory data. We are not aware of any prior work that attempts to learn verb semantics from trajectory data. However, prior work in grounded language learning focuses on reasoning about objects through space and time in text (Aroca-Ouellette et al., 2021) and grounding to 3D objects with varying rotation (Thomas, 2019). Outside of NLP, models have been trained on trajectory data for applications like human motion path forecasting (Giuliari et al., 2021) and human activity recognition (Wang et al., 2018). Recent multimodal grounding approaches integrate contrastive objectives, masked modeling, and alignment losses across text, image, audio, and video, with large-scale datasets enabling pretraining at web scale (Radford et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Bain et al., 2021; Alayrac et al., 2022; Zellers et al., 2021; Dong et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2021; Lei et al., 2021), while compositional generalization and structured grounding have been explored via synthetic benchmarks and neuro-symbolic pipelines (Lake and Baroni, 2018; Johnson et al., 2017; Mao et al., 2019; Hudson and Manning, 2019; Bahdanau et al., 2019; Nye et al., 2021; Yi et al., 2020; Gupta et al., 2019). Our work lies at the intersection of grounded language learning and spatiotemporal machine learning, using representations of trajectory data to study verb semantics. We situate our method relative to prior grounded language research by emphasizing temporal reasoning and motion-centric cues. Specifically, we concentrate on the mapping between discrete linguistic predicates and continuous kinematic traces. This focus allows us to examine action granularity beyond categorical labels tied to static visual frames. We also explore whether trajectory-derived embeddings capture relational structure among verbs. To that end, we evaluate lexical and event similarity judgments using movement-based features. Finally, we discuss the implications of trajectory alignment for context-sensitive verb interpretation. We conclude by outlining how spatiotemporal priors can complement text-only distributional learning.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Abstractive Opinion Summarization aims to generate a fluent summary that reflects salient opinions in input reviews. Due to the lack of sufficient amount of reference summaries, the most common solution is the unsupervised approach (Chu and Liu, 2019;Bražinskas et al., 2020b;Amplayo et al., 2021;Elsahar et al., 2021;Im et al., 2021;Wang and Wan, 2021;Isonuma et al., 2021, inter alia).

Recent opinion summarization models use the few-shot learning approach that fine-tunes a pretrained Transformer model with a limited amount of pairs of input reviews and reference summaries. Bražinskas et al. (2020a) and Oved and Levy (2021) show that the few-shot learning approach substantially outperforms unsupervised learning models.

All the existing methods listed above are designed for general opinion summarization and, thus, are not necessarily suitable for comparative opinion summarization, as shown in the experiments. Comparative Summarization There is a line of work on extracting comparative information from single/multiple documents. Lerman and McDonald (2009) defined the contrastive summarization problem and presented early work on the problem. Their method selects sentences so that two sets of summaries can highlight differences. Wang et al. (2013) developed an extractive summarization method for a problem of Comparative Document Summarization, which is to select the most discriminative sentences from a given set of documents. Bista et al. (2019) tackled a similar problem by selecting documents that represent in-cluster documents while they are useful to distinguish from other clusters.

Other studies (Kim and Zhai, 2009;Huang et al., 2011;Sipos and Joachims, 2013;Ren et al., 2017) tackled similar tasks by developing extracting sentences/phrases from given sets of documents for comparative document analysis. Topic models have been also used to capture comparative topics for better understanding text corpora, but they do not generate textual summaries (Ren and de Rijke, 2015;He et al., 2016;Ibeke et al., 2017).

Following early progress in neural and probabilistic text modeling, several studies have explored comparative or contrastive structures in summarization and document analysis without necessarily focusing on opinion-centric generation, including contrastive summarization frameworks, comparative document summarization techniques, and topic-model-based contrast mining (Lerman and McDonald, 2009;Wang et al., 2013;Ren and de Rijke, 2015;He et al., 2016;Ibeke et al., 2017;Bista et al., 2019;Kim and Zhai, 2009;Huang et al., 2011;Sipos and Joachims, 2013).

Our work differs from the existing work in two points. First, none of them focuses on generating common summaries. Second, all of the previous studies for contrastive summary generation use the extractive approach. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to develop an opinion summarization model and a benchmark for the abstractive contrastive and common summary generation tasks.

Lacks synthesis.document:
A key finding in previous studies in discourse analysis is that most sentences have an independent well-formed sub-tree in the full document-level discourse tree (Joty et al., 2012). Researchers have taken advantage of this finding to build parsers that utilize different granularity levels of the document to achieve the state-of-the-art results (Kobayashi et al., 2020). This design has been empirically verified to be a generally advantageous framework, improving not only works using traditional feature engineering (Joty et al., 2013;Wang et al., 2017), but also deep learning models (Jia et al., 2018b;Kobayashi et al., 2020). We, therefore, introduce this design to our dependency parsing framework. Specifically, sub-trees for each sentence in a discourse are first built separately, then assembled to form a complete discourse tree. However, our model differs from prior works in that we make a clear distinction to derive better contextualized representations of EDUs from fine-tuning BERT separately for intra-and intersentential levels to dynamically capture different information needed for discourse analysis at different levels. We are also the first to design stacked sequence labeling models for discourse relation identification so that its hierarchical structure can explicitly capture both intra-sentential and intersentential writing patterns.

In the case of implicit relations between EDUs without clear connectives, it is crucial to introduce sequential information from the context to resolve ambiguity. Feng and Hirst (2014) rely on linearchain CRF with traditional feature engineering to make use of the sequential characteristics of the context for discourse constituent parsing. However, they greedily build up the discourse structure and relations from bottom up. At each timestep, they apply the CRF to obtain the locally optimized structure and relation. In this way, the model assigns relation gradually along with the construction of the parsing tree from bottom up, but only limited contextual information from the top level of the partially constructed tree can be used to predict relations. Besides, at each time-step, they sequentially assign relations to top nodes of the partial tree, without being aware that those nodes might represent different levels of discourse units (e.g. EDUs, sentences, or even paragraphs). In contrast, we explicitly train our sequence labeling models on both intra-and inter-sentential levels after a complete discourse tree is constructed so that we can infer from the whole context with a clear intention of capturing different writing patterns occurring at intra-and inter-sentential levels. Recent neural and hybrid discourse parsers explore multi-granular architectures and contextualized encoders across corpora and settings (Li et al., 2014; Ji and Eisenstein, 2015; Braud et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; Kobayashi et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Gessler et al., 2021), and complementary lines of work have examined EDU representation learning with BERT-like models and sequence labeling strategies for relation identification (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Nie et al., 2020; Nguyen and Joty, 2020; Kishimoto et al., 2020; Shi and Demberg, 2019; Huber and Carenini, 2020; Xu et al., 2021), along with evaluations on RST-DT, STAC, GUM, and TED-MDB that report incremental gains from hierarchical modeling and context-sensitive features (Carlson et al., 2001; Asher et al., 2016; Zeldes, 2017; Zeyrek et al., 2020).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Cross-lingual/Multilingual Machine Reading Comprehension Hsu et al. (2019) investigate cross-lingual transfer capability of multilingual BERT (mBERT) on MRC tasks and find that zeroshot learning based on PLM is feasible, even between distant languages, such as English and Chinese. Various approaches have been proposed on top of multilingual MRC based on PLMs. Cui et al. (2019) propose a method that combines multilingual BERT and back-translation for cross-lingual MRC. In order to effectively leverage translation Different from the above studies, we mainly consider the impact of syntactic divergences between the source and target language in zero-shot crosslingual transfer based on multilingual PLMs, and attempt to disassociate semantics from syntax and only transfer semantic to the target language.

Disentangled Representation Learning Recently, there has been a growing amount of work on learning disentangled latent representations in NLP tasks (Zhang et al., 2019;Hu et al., 2017;Yin et al., 2018). In this aspect, the most related work to our syntax-semantics decoupling method is the vMF-Gaussian Variational Autoencoder (VGVAE) model proposed by Chen et al. (2019). It is a generative model using two latent variables to represent semantics and syntax of the sentence, developed for monolingual setting and trained with paraphrases. It uses paraphrase reconstruction loss and a discriminative paraphrase loss to learn semantic representations and word order information for syntactic representations. Recent cross-lingual MRC efforts explore translation-based augmentation, multilingual pre-training, and alignment supervision across typologically diverse languages without a unified protocol (Artetxe et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; Asai et al., 2021; Clark et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2020; Chi et al., 2021). We adapt this model to multilingual syntax-semantics disentanglement. We use bilingual sentence pairs to train our model with a cross-lingual reconstruction loss and semantic discrimination loss. To better disentangle semantics from complex and diverse syntax in multilingual PLMs, we introduce two additional syntax-related losses for incorporating POS tags and syntax trees.

Lacks synthesis.document: Multiple efforts have looked into defining, measuring, and mitigating biases in NLP models (Sun et al., 2019;Mehrabi et al., 2019a;Sheng et al., 2021). Dwork et al. (2012) present foundational notions of fairness that motivate later operationalizations in machine learning and NLP. Multiple recent works also focus on developing new dataset and associated metrics to capture various types of biases. Recent advances catalog a wide array of datasets, measurement protocols, and mitigation strategies spanning contextualized embeddings, pre-trained language models, and multimodal systems, including WEAT and related association tests (Caliskan et al., 2017; May et al., 2019), Bias-in-Bios and occupation-level audits (De-Arteaga et al., 2019a), StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs for sentence-level stereotype sensitivity (Nadeem et al., 2021; Nangia et al., 2020), regard and toxicity-based probes (Sheng et al., 2019; Dixon et al., 2018), intrinsic embedding debiasing and hard de-bias methods (Bolukbasi et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2018), causal and counterfactual data augmentation (Zhao et al., 2018; Maudslay et al., 2019), bias-toxicity correlations in generation (Gehman et al., 2020), metric learning perspectives on fairness (Speicher et al., 2018), and large-scale audits of toxic generation in open-ended dialogue (Dinan et al., 2020). For example, Nangia et al. (2020) propose dataset and metrics to measure social biases and stereotypes in language model generations, Bolukbasi et al. (2016); Caliskan et al. (2017); Manzini et al. (2019) define metrics to access gender and race biases in word vector representations, and recent vision-language studies define metrics to quantify and mitigate biases in visual recognition task. Ethayarajh (2020) propose Bernstein bounds to represent uncertainty about the bias. Majority of these bias metrics are automatically computed, for example, using a regard classifier (Sheng et al., 2019), sentiment classifier, toxicity classifier (Dixon et al., 2018) or true positive rate difference between privileged and underprivileged groups (De-Arteaga et al., 2019b). A few works additionally validate the alignment of these automatically computed bias metrics with human understanding of biases by collecting annotations of biases on a subset of test data from crowdworkers (Sheng et al., 2019). Blodgett et al. (2020) discuss the limitations of several of these bias datasets and measurements, emphasizing construct validity and socio-linguistic context. However, the majority of existing bias metrics are specific to the model type and the application domain used, they may not be tested for correlation with human judgement of biases, and their relationship to existing definitions of fairness has not been explored. Additionally, metrics such as true positive or error difference between groups requires ground truth labels, thereby making their computation in real-time systems difficult. Speicher et al. (2018) have attempted to present unified approach to measuring group and individual fairness via inequality indices, however we note that such metrics are non-trivial to extend to unstructured data such as text. For example, gender information in a text may be subtle (e.g. mention of softball) and it is unclear whether presence of this word should be considered to impact the genderness of the text. Prior work on counterfactual fairness in text further highlights the importance of lexical and syntactic perturbations for isolating sensitive attributes (Garg et al., 2019; Maudslay et al., 2019). Contextualized encoders exhibit bias amplification under domain shift, complicating cross-domain evaluation protocols (Zmigrod et al., 2019; Lauscher et al., 2020). Post-processing calibrations can alter group-level rates without improving semantic fairness, creating evaluation blind spots (Pleiss et al., 2017; Chouldechova, 2017). Accumulated prediction sensitivity metric, presented in this paper, attempts to address all the above limitations of existing bias metrics. We acknowledge that the proposed metric is yet to be associated with other notions of fairness (e.g. preference based notion of fairness (Zafar et al., 2017)).

Format.document: Relation extraction (RE) seeks to identify semantic relations between entities mentioned in text. By granularity, RE is commonly grouped into sentence-level (Doddington et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2016) and document-level (Gupta et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2019) settings. Early work primarily targeted sentence-level relations with feature engineering and pattern rules. Pantel and Pennacchiotti (2006) propose a rule-based approach, and Mintz et al. (2009) design features for classifying relations. In the past decade, neural networks have become dominant for sentence-level RE (Zeng et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2019). Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) considers interactions across entity mentions scattered over multiple sentences. Compared with sentence-level RE, DocRE must model long-range dependencies and aggregate inter-sentence evidence efficiently. As shown by Yao et al., large-scale DocRE benchmarks expose diverse reasoning types and annotation challenges. Practical systems must therefore align entity coreference, discourse cues, and implicit links to infer document-level relations. Recent efforts propose both sequence-based and graph-based architectures to address these challenges. Sequence-based DocRE models encode a document as a word or sentence sequence and typically rely on pretrained Transformers (Devlin et al., 2019). Zhou et al. (2021) demonstrate that attention can capture cross-sentence context and introduce adaptive thresholds for entity pairs. Zhang et al. (2021) cast DocRE as semantic segmentation and predict an entity-level relation matrix to integrate local and global cues. Other works enrich sequences with discourse structure or hierarchical encoders to better pool evidence across sentences (Tang et al., 2020; Nan et al., 2020). Graph-based DocRE models abstract mentions, entities, and sentences as nodes and connect them via edges derived from co-occurrence and syntax. Graph neural networks then propagate and compose information to support multi-hop reasoning (Quirk and Poon, 2017; Christopoulou et al., 2019; Zeng et al., 2020). Zeng et al. (2020) explore dual graphs that couple mention-document structures with entity-level paths. Xu et al. (2021a) further incorporate logical, commonsense, and coreference reasoning on top of hybrid sequence–graph features. Despite progress, over-smoothing, noise from spurious edges, and weak supervision remain open issues (Sahu et al., 2019; Marcheggiani and Titov, 2016). A complementary line of work emphasizes identifying evidence sentences that support predicted relations to improve robustness and explainability. Evidence selection reduces error propagation by concentrating gradient updates on informative spans rather than noisy context (Jiang et al., 2021). However, naively optimizing for accuracy can entangle evidence discovery with label prediction, leading to unstable training under distribution shift. We propose SIEF, a simple yet general framework that can be combined with diverse sequence-based and graph-based DocRE models. SIEF introduces a sentence importance score to highlight relation-bearing sentences and a sentence focusing loss to regularize training. These components encourage models to prioritize salient evidence while maintaining coverage of supporting context. The framework is model-agnostic and complements both attention-based and message-passing architectures. In experiments, SIEF improves robustness and overall DocRE performance across strong baselines on public benchmarks (Devlin et al., 2019; Vaswani et al., 2017. We further analyze error types and show consistent gains for long-range and multi-sentence relations. Ablations isolate the contribution of importance scoring and focusing loss, and sensitivity studies verify stability under hyperparameter changes.

Format.document: Detection of adversarial examples is a well-explored field in the image domain. Early approaches include input transformations, statistical tests, and auxiliary binary detectors (Xu et al., 2018; Grosse et al., 2017; Metzen et al., 2017). However, Carlini and Wagner (2017) showed that adaptive attackers can circumvent many heuristics. In parallel, novelty detection literature suggests that generative modeling can flag anomalous inputs (Bishop, 1994). This intuition was later extended by using deep features for maximum-likelihood scoring of distributional fit. In NLP, research on detecting word-level adversarial attacks remains comparatively limited. Zhou et al. (2019) proposed DISP, which trains a detector on adversarially perturbed corpora for joint detection and defense. Building on lexical rarity cues, FGWS improves detection performance by scoring frequency-based statistics (Mozes et al., 2021). Yet such methods can be brittle when attacks preserve frequency profiles or mimic natural errors (Nguyen et al., 2020; Smith and Lee, 2019. Le et al. (2021) targeted trigger-based attacks such as UniTrigger (Wallace et al., 2019) with a tailored recognition pipeline. While effective, their specialization raises concerns about generalization across attack families and domains. Orthographic corruption defenses focus on spelling noise but may overlook semantic-preserving paraphrases (Pruthi et al., 2019). Recent trends favor representation-space monitoring that tracks distributional shifts in hidden states across layers. Complementary efforts explore uncertainty estimation and calibration to separate benign variation from malicious shifts (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016; Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017). Our work synthesizes these threads by proposing a unified evaluation protocol and a detector that leverages token saliency, sentence semantics, and uncertainty signals.

Format.document: Various NLP data augmentation techniques have been proposed and they are mainly divided into two categories: one is to modify raw input directly, and the other interferes with the embedding (Miyato et al., 2016. The most commonly used method to modify the raw input is token replacement, which selects tokens in a sentence and substitutes them with semantically similar tokens to synthesize a new sentence. Wei and Zou (2019) directly use the synonym table WordNet (Miller, 1998) for replacement. Kobayashi (2018) proposes contextual augmentation that samples substitutes using forward and backward language models. Later work incorporates BERT's masked language modeling to capture bidirectional context during substitution (Devlin et al., 2018). Gao et al. (2019) introduce soft augmentation by replacing a one-hot token vector with a learned distribution over the vocabulary. Unlike Gao et al. (2019), we use an MLM to generate smoothed representations for entire sentences. This strategy better leverages deep contextual cues that integrate local selection with sentence-level semantics. In addition, our approach offers strong parallelism because all token positions can be processed in a single forward pass. We further control augmentation intensity via interpolation in the embedding space. Such control permits task-aware perturbations that preserve label consistency in classification settings. Prior studies also explore adversarial perturbations on embeddings to regularize encoders (Miyato et al., 2017). However, noise-based approaches may reduce fluency or induce unintended label flips when the perturbation budget is large. In contrast, lexical replacement maintains surface plausibility but can drift semantically without additional constraints. Recent surveys categorize augmentation along axes of granularity, supervision, and model awareness (Feng et al., 2021). Within this taxonomy, our method falls under model-informed perturbations that exploit pretrained language models. We adopt calibration-oriented objectives to balance fidelity and diversity during augmentation. Empirically, we observe that smoothed examples improve expected calibration error under distribution shift. They also increase minority-class recall where purely token-level heuristics underperform. For reproducibility, we detail sampling temperatures, mixing coefficients, and filtering thresholds. Our experiments compare against strong baselines across sentiment, topic categorization, and natural language inference benchmarks. Baseline configurations include synonym substitution, contextual augmentation, and soft replacement with distributional smoothing. These baselines have been widely adopted in text classification pipelines (cf. Wei and Zou, 2019; Kobayashi, 2018; Gao et al., 2019, but their sampling policies seldom enforce label-aware priors. Consequently, models trained on such data can be overconfident on spurious lexical cues. Our method introduces an explicit regularizer that nudges replacements toward class-compatible semantics. We also incorporate uncertainty estimates to avoid injecting overly confident yet misleading substitutes. Ablation studies confirm that interpolation strength is the primary driver of robustness gains. The next section formalizes our approach and outlines the training objective.

Format.document: This section introduces the problem of few-shot slot tagging and situates it within the broader context of low-resource semantic parsing. We begin by defining the task and motivating its practical importance in conversational interfaces. In production dialog systems, new domains emerge faster than annotated data can be collected, creating a persistent data bottleneck. Few-shot learning offers a way to generalize to unseen intents and slots with only a handful of labeled examples. However, slot definitions are often ambiguous, domain dependent, and sparsely represented at training time. These characteristics make classical sequence labeling approaches brittle when domain shift is severe. Traditional methods rely on token-level classifiers trained with conditional random fields or BiLSTMs to model label dependencies. Such models achieve strong performance in fully supervised regimes but degrade sharply as supervision wanes. Pretrained language models have partially alleviated this problem by providing transferable representations that encode syntax and semantics. Prompt-based adaptation further narrows the gap by reformulating labeling as conditional text completion guided by task-specific templates. In this paradigm, discrete or soft prompts steer a frozen or lightly tuned encoder toward slot-aware predictions. A parallel line of work explores verbalizers that map label semantics into natural language tokens to anchor predictions. Cross-domain generalization has also been improved by leveraging schema descriptions and example-driven calibration. Despite these advances, the community lacks a unified understanding of when prompts outperform classical taggers under realistic constraints. We therefore organize prior art along three axes, namely supervision type, conditioning signal, and inference objective. Under full supervision, CRF-enhanced transformers remain competitive for within-domain tagging. Under few-shot supervision, prompt-tuning and pattern-exploiting training often surpass fine-tuning baselines on new domains. Hybrid methods inject label semantics via definitions, exemplars, or ontologies to mitigate mismatches between source and target distributions. Retriever-augmented prompting supplements the input with in-context demonstrations selected from a support set. Calibration techniques adjust verbalizer probabilities to counter label frequency imbalances and domain priors. From a data perspective, benchmarks spanning multiple domains with standardized schemas enable controlled evaluation. From a modeling perspective, stability under different prompt initializations and demonstration orders is a key concern. Recent studies also examine the interplay between prompt length, template naturalness, and the capacity of the underlying encoder. In addition, parameter-efficient tuning methods such as adapters and low-rank updates provide competitive accuracy under strict memory budgets. Evaluation protocols benefit from reporting confidence-aware metrics and error typologies that disentangle boundary, type, and span errors. To contextualize our approach, we compare against strong baselines drawn from both classical labeling and prompt-based families. We adopt conventional citation style throughout and reference representative advances using parenthetical markers when appropriate. Where relevant, we discuss foundational models for sequence-to-sequence prompting Raffel et al., 2020) as they inform our prompt design.

Format.document: Recent progress in interpretable machine learning has emphasized methods that shed light on individual predictions and global model behavior. Post-hoc explanations such as feature attributions and rationales have been widely studied in vision and language domains (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Lei et al., 2016; Lundberg and Lee, 2017). However, explanations that merely describe why a prediction occurred do not directly assist users in achieving preferred outcomes (Lipton, 2018; Miller, 2019). Counterfactual explanations reframe interpretability as the problem of finding minimal, feasible changes to inputs that flip the model decision (Wachter et al., 2017; Ustun et al., 2019). In NLP, counterfactual data augmentation and contrastive editing have demonstrated benefits for robustness and fairness (Zmigrod et al., 2019; Kaushik et al., 2020). Yet, generating actionable counterfactuals for discrete, structured text remains challenging due to grammaticality, semantics, and domain constraints (Madaan et al., 2021; Ross et al., 2021). Prior work on natural language rationales offers complementary supervision but often lacks explicit guidance on how to change an input (Hendricks et al., 2018; DeYoung et al., 2020). Interactive learning for semantic parsing has shown that users can iteratively correct systems, improving accuracy over time (Wang et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017). Our perspective connects these strands by formalizing user-desired objectives and constraints within a principled optimization framework (Karimi et al., 2020; Russell, 2019). We also draw on causal reasoning to separate interventions from observations in model behavior (Pearl, 2009; Kilbertus et al., 2017). In particular, feasibility requires modeling actionable features and permissible edits for language inputs (Kusner et al., 2017; Barocas et al., 2020). Complementary lines of research compare local surrogate models with example-based and counterfactual approaches for end-user decision support (Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017; Lipton, 2016; Miller, 2019. Beyond feasibility, actionable counterfactuals must be sparse and faithful so that a minimal set of edits suffices to flip the decision (Mothilal et al., 2020; Keane and Smyth, 2020). Reliability further depends on verifying that proposed edits generalize under small perturbations rather than exploiting spurious lexical cues (Gardner et al., 2020; Feder et al., 2021). To this end, we integrate constraints on fluency, semantic similarity, and label monotonicity into a unified search objective (Pruthi et al., 2019; Ribeiro et al., 2020). Our method contrasts with gradient-based attribution, which may be unstable and does not prescribe concrete actions (Sundararajan et al., 2017; Kindermans et al., 2019). It also differs from example-based case-based reasoning that retrieves neighbors without guaranteeing causal sufficiency (Keane and Kenny, 2019; Looveren and Klaise, 2021). From a usability perspective, counterfactuals can double as natural language interfaces that communicate trade-offs between accuracy, cost, and risk (Bhatt et al., 2020; Dodge et al., 2019). In structured prediction, work on edit-based debugging for semantic parsers suggests the value of minimal textual interventions (Iyer et al., 2017; Lawrence and Riezler, 2018). For classification, constraints derived from lexical resources and paraphrase models help maintain meaning while exploring alternative decisions (Gao et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2020). We evaluate on tasks where discrete changes reflect realistic user actions, including slot-value flips, lexical substitutions, and insertion or deletion of modifiers (Feng et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2018). Our experiments compare counterfactual policies across multiple datasets and models, reporting both fidelity metrics and human judgments (Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017; Prabhakaran et al., 2022). The results indicate that carefully constrained counterfactuals improve transparency without sacrificing predictive performance in common NLP settings (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020; Bansal et al., 2020). We conclude by discussing limitations and opportunities for integrating counterfactual explanations with interactive annotation and data governance (Arrieta et al., 2020; Suresh and Guttag, 2019).

Format.document: Transfer learning has become central to modern NLP, offering strategies that reuse knowledge across tasks. Two prominent paradigms are multi-task learning, which trains on several tasks simultaneously, and STILTs, which adds supervised intermediate tasks before fine-tuning. Despite their popularity, practitioners still lack clear guidance on when to prefer one approach over the other. Prior studies have examined conditions under which task transfer is positive or negative (Bingel and Søgaard, 2017;Vu et al., 2020;Pruksachatkun et al., 2020b). Others have emphasized phenomena such as catastrophic forgetting and representation drift during sequential adaptation (Phang et al., 2018;Wang et al., 2018a). However, the question of method selection remains underexplored relative to the abundant work on performance prediction. Our goal in this paper is to systematize the decision process between MTL and STILTs for typical NLP scenarios. We focus on measurable task attributes, data regimes, and model capacity as primary determinants of the choice. We also study practical constraints such as computational budget and hyperparameter sensitivity. The motivation stems from empirical irregularities reported across benchmarks, where nominally similar settings yield divergent outcomes (Ruder, 2017;Wang et al., 2019). Multi-task learning has been repeatedly shown to help when tasks share structure and inductive biases (Caruana, 1997;Ruder et al., 2019). Yet, negative transfer arises when auxiliary tasks introduce conflicting gradients or misaligned label spaces (Standley et al., 2020;Kiperwasser and Ballesteros, 2018). STILTs, by contrast, leverages targeted supervision to shape intermediate representations before final adaptation (Phang et al., 2018). While simple to implement, its benefits vary with the compatibility between intermediate and target tasks (Pruksachatkun et al., 2020b). Selection heuristics have been proposed, including similarity measures over task embeddings and gradient agreement metrics (Achille et al., 2019;Sharir et al., 2020). Nevertheless, these heuristics are not yet standardized and can be costly to compute at scale. Our analysis integrates these strands with a view toward a prescriptive framework for method choice. We revisit claims that universal intermediate tasks improve all targets, a position challenged by both small and large scale studies (Chang and Lu, 2021. In particular, we distinguish between representation priming effects and optimization benefits, which are often conflated in the literature. We argue that the decision to use MTL or STILTs should be conditioned on observed transfer signals in a pilot phase. To support this claim, we derive a set of diagnostic metrics that can be estimated with limited training. We then test their predictive value across a battery of tasks spanning sequence labeling, classification, and generation. Our experiments employ standardized evaluation protocols to reduce confounds such as training instability and data leakage (Dodge et al., 2019;Gururangan et al., 2020). We complement aggregate scores with variance analyses to probe robustness under seed changes and hyperparameter sweeps (Bouthillier et al., 2021). Related work on curriculum and continual learning provides additional context for staged training designs (Soviany et al., 2022;Ke et al., 2021). Similarly, research on adapter-based transfer informs resource-aware choices that can accompany either paradigm (Houlsby et al., 2019;Pfeiffer et al., 2020). Prior meta-learning approaches also target sample efficiency but introduce new complexities in optimization and tuning (Finn et al., 2017;Hospedales et al., 2022). We do not aim to replace these directions but to clarify when simpler baselines suffice. Our contributions are threefold and center on actionable guidance for practitioners. First, we provide a taxonomy that links task attributes to recommended training strategies, with illustrative case studies. Second, we present a lightweight selection procedure that compares short-horizon signals under controlled budgets. Third, we release a suite of scripts and configurations that make the procedure reproducible across common toolchains. The resulting recommendations are deliberately conservative so that they degrade gracefully under dataset shift. We discuss theoretical implications of our findings and outline hypotheses to be tested in follow-up work. Among these are conjectures about the role of sparsity, gradient coherence, and invariances in shaping transfer dynamics (Ganin et al., 2016;Fort et al., 2020). We conclude by situating our guidance within broader efforts to standardize evaluation and reporting practices in transfer learning (Liu et al., 2021;Raffel et al., 2020).

Format.document: Machine translation has increasingly moved toward neural architectures that model the full conditional distribution over target sequences. Sequence‑to‑sequence models with attention offer strong baselines for both translation and summarization tasks. Nevertheless, data sparsity, domain shift, and stylistic variability still limit robustness in real-world deployments. To address these gaps, researchers have explored latent-variable models that capture hidden factors of variation. Conditional variational autoencoders provide a principled way to introduce stochasticity conditioned on source inputs. In the basic formulation, a prior network predicts a latent distribution given the source, while a recognition network approximates the posterior during training. The Kullback–Leibler regularizer encourages the prior to align with the posterior, balancing exploration and reconstruction. This approach has been adopted in neural machine translation to better model lexical choice and syntactic alternations, following Sohn and Lee 2015). It has also been studied in monolingual abstractive summarization where compression and salience interact in complex ways. Cross-lingual summarization further complicates the picture by demanding both translation and content selection under constrained budgets. Prior work shows that modeling latent discourse structure can improve factual consistency in compressed outputs. At the same time, controllable generation frameworks enable users to steer length, style, or terminology. Combining controllability with latent variables raises questions about disentanglement and training stability. A common solution is to anneal the KL term to prevent posterior collapse in powerful decoders. Curriculum schedules and auxiliary mutual-information losses have been proposed to maintain informative latents. For multilingual applications, parameter sharing across languages reduces redundancy while preserving language-specific signals. Recent pretraining on massive corpora has made encoder representations more transferable across tasks and domains. However, fine-tuning with small supervised datasets can still overfit spurious correlations. Semi-supervised objectives that mix labeled and unlabeled data offer a compelling alternative in low-resource settings. In machine translation, back-translation remains a dominant technique for leveraging monolingual text. In summarization, pseudo-parallel construction via round-trip translation has been explored to augment scarce pairs. For cross-lingual summarization, dual learning and cycle consistency provide additional constraints that couple the two directions. Variational models naturally integrate with these paradigms by treating synthetic examples as samples from approximate posteriors. They also facilitate minimum-risk decoding by sampling diverse candidates from the learned prior. Inference efficiency can be retained through amortization and low-dimensional latent spaces. Yet, evaluating the contribution of the latent variable remains challenging due to metric sensitivity and beam search confounds. Rigorous ablation studies that isolate the effect of the KL term are therefore essential for credible claims. When comparing to deterministic baselines, it is crucial to match parameter counts, training steps, and data regimes. Well-designed validation protocols mitigate early-stopping biases that would otherwise favor stronger language models. Our work synthesizes these insights into a unified framework for MT, monolingual summarization, and cross-lingual summarization. We adopt standard datasets and report results under consistent tokenization, evaluation metrics, and decoding settings. Building on seminal advances in conditional variational modeling, we structure the prior and posterior networks to reflect source-conditioned uncertainty. We also situate our approach alongside earlier applications in MT and CLS that emphasize robustness and controllability.

Format.document: Vision-and-Language Navigation has emerged as a core task aligning visual observations with natural-language instructions. The R2R benchmark combines real indoor imagery and English navigation commands (Chang et al., 2017). Subsequent methods blend imitation learning with reinforcement learning to stabilize training and explore effectively (Wang et al., 2019). Data scarcity has motivated augmentation techniques that synthesize trajectories or paraphrase instructions (Fried et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2021a). Auxiliary objectives exploit semantic cues to provide richer training signals (Majumdar et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020). Pretraining across large image–text corpora has further improved cross-modal representations for navigation (Hao et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2021). Nevertheless, limited environment diversity during pretraining can hinder generalization to novel scenes. Among model architectures, VLN-BERT transfers knowledge from abundant out-of-domain image–text pairs to strengthen instruction–path alignment (Majumdar et al., 2020). Building on this line, we introduce an in-domain corpus via trajectory sampling with templated instruction generation and pair it with prompt-based pretraining to bridge domain gaps. In parallel, vision-and-language pretraining has progressed through one-stream and two-stream Transformers pretrained with masked modeling and alignment objectives (Li et al., 2019; Su et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020a; Zhou et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020b; Alberti et al., 2019). For efficient adaptation, we employ soft-prompt strategies such as prefix-style conditioning and continuous templates while freezing backbone parameters (Li and Liang, 2021; Zhong et al., 2021; Qin and Eisner et al.; Hambardzumyan et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021c; Han et al., 2021).

Format.document: Visual storytelling (VIST) is the task of generating a coherent multi-sentence narrative from a sequence of images. The problem was formalized with the release of the Sequential Image Narrative Dataset, which paired five-image sequences with human-authored stories (Huang et al., 2016). Each image sequence in the dataset is accompanied by multiple references to capture narrative diversity and stylistic variation (Huang et al., 2016). Unlike captioning, storytelling requires modeling event progression, character continuity, and causal coherence across images (Park and Kim, 2015). Early approaches adapted image captioning pipelines with sequence decoders, but they often produced list-like descriptions lacking narrative flow (Jain et al., 2017). Subsequent work incorporated hierarchical decoders to represent paragraph structure and story beats more explicitly (Fan et al., 2019). To enrich content selection, some models integrate external knowledge graphs that supply entities, relations, and commonsense cues relevant to the visual context (Hsu et al., 2020; Hsu et al., 2021a). Graph-enhanced systems have been shown to increase lexical diversity and reduce repetitiveness in generated stories (Chen and Zhu, 2020). Reinforcement learning has also been explored to optimize non-differentiable objectives tied to human preferences and discourse quality (Hu et al., 2020a. However, reinforcement signals depend critically on evaluation metrics, and weak proxies can lead to gaming behaviors or degraded fluency (Paulus et al., 2018). Consequently, evaluation remains a central bottleneck in VIST research. Reference-based metrics such as BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE measure n-gram overlap but often misalign with narrative quality aspects like plot coherence and character consistency (Papineni et al., 2002; Banerjee and Lavie, 2005; Lin, 2004). Studies in dialog and story generation report low correlations between such metrics and human judgments, especially when multiple valid phrasings exist (Wang et al., 2018b; Hsu et al., 2019; Modi and Parde, 2019). Embedding-based metrics attempt to address surface mismatch by comparing contextual representations derived from pretrained language models (Zhang et al., 2019). BLEURT extends this idea by fine-tuning on human ratings to better approximate perceived quality in downstream tasks (Sellam et al., 2020). Domain-specific metrics like UNION further tailor scoring functions to narrative structure and content selection biases in storytelling (Guan and Huang, 2020). Despite these advances, automatic metrics still struggle to reflect fine-grained preferences among competing narrative candidates. Human evaluation therefore remains essential for benchmarking progress in VIST. Common protocols ask annotators to rate fluency, relevance, and overall quality on Likert scales, though operational definitions of aspects vary across papers (Hu et al., 2020b; Wang et al., 2020b). Pairwise ranking has gained traction because it mitigates scale calibration issues and yields more reliable comparative judgments (Hsu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020b; Hsu et al., 2021a). Nevertheless, ranking can be sensitive to annotator bias and presentation order, complicating statistical analysis of results (Gehrmann et al., 2023). A promising direction combines human preference labels with learned reward models to guide generation toward globally coherent narratives (Stiennon et al., 2020). Beyond metrics, modeling choices also affect narrative coherence through discourse planning and entity tracking. Planning-based methods first predict high-level story outlines or semantic frames before surface realization, improving long-range consistency (Yao et al., 2019). Memory-augmented architectures maintain representations of entities and events across sentences to preserve character states and temporal continuity (Clark et al., 2018). Multimodal fusion techniques align visual regions with textual spans, enabling models to ground mentions and avoid hallucination (Anderson et al., 2018). Recent work explores instruction-tuned vision–language models for few-shot storytelling, though alignment with human narrative styles remains challenging (OpenAI, 2023). Cross-domain generalization is limited because style, cultural references, and photographer intent vary widely across collections (Mitchell et al., 2020). Data augmentation via paraphrasing and retrieval of related stories has been proposed to expand training diversity without additional annotation cost (Bhardwaj et al., 2020). However, augmentation can introduce label noise and off-distribution artifacts that degrade factual consistency (Feng et al., 2021). In this work, we revisit evaluation by constructing a suite of controlled story pair comparisons to probe metric sensitivity to discourse structure. We analyze whether metrics correctly prefer stories with improved plot progression, entity consistency, and causal linkages over superficially similar baselines. To avoid confounds, we ensure that compared stories share comparable lexical statistics while differing in specific narrative properties. We further examine how metric-guided reinforcement learning shapes generator behavior and whether gains transfer to human preferences. Our findings suggest that embedding-based and learned metrics capture fluency but underweight causal connectivity and cross-sentence grounding. We conclude that progress in visual storytelling requires joint advances in discourse-aware modeling and the development of evaluation schemes closely aligned with human narrative judgments.

Format.document: Human values are of concern to most if not to all social sciences (Rokeach, 1973) and have also been integrated into computational frameworks of argumentation (Bench-Capon, 2003). In NLP, values have been analyzed for personality profiling (Maheshwari et al., 2017), but not yet for argument mining, as considered here. Understanding how values surface in argumentative texts is important for modeling persuasion, policy discourse, and ethical reasoning. Prior work in argument mining has focused on structure and relations among claims, premises, and attacks (Mochales and Moens, 2011; Stab and Gurevych, 2014). However, the value-laden content of arguments remains underexplored despite its centrality in deliberative settings (Habernal and Gurevych, 2017. The social psychology literature provides robust taxonomies for values, most notably Rokeach’s terminal and instrumental values and Schwartz’s basic human values (Schwartz, 1992; Schwartz, 2012). These taxonomies have been adopted in computational social science to study political ideology, moral framing, and social attitudes (Graham et al., 2013; Johnson and Goldwasser, 2018). At the same time, advances in pretrained language models enable more nuanced semantic analysis of argumentative texts (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019). Bridging these strands requires operationalizing value constructs in a way that is both theoretically grounded and computationally tractable. Several recent studies annotate moral or value dimensions at the sentence or document level to train classifiers and sequence labelers (Hoover et al., 2020; Kiesel et al., 2022). Yet, most datasets target general stance or morality rather than the specific value categories theorized in social psychology (Strapparava et al., 2017; Bennett et al., 2023). For argument mining, a central challenge is distinguishing value signals from rhetorical devices, topical cues, and speaker identity. We hypothesize that value indicators can be captured through a combination of lexicon priors, contextual embeddings, and discourse features. Previous attempts to represent values often rely on lexicon matching that struggles with polysemy and context sensitivity (Haidt and Graham, 2007; Gardenfors, 2014). In contrast, neural models can learn abstract value semantics when guided by interpretable supervision such as exemplar phrases and argument roles (Alshomary et al., 2021; Peldszus and Stede, 2015). Cross-domain generalization is particularly difficult because value expressions vary across topics and registers (Toulmin, 1958; Addawood et al., 2017). To address this gap, we review literature on value theory, moral psychology, and argumentative discourse to derive a mapping from theoretical categories to linguistic realizations. We then propose a corpus construction protocol that couples expert-guided guidelines with iterative model-in-the-loop annotation (Settles, 2011; Zhou et al., 2020). Our approach complements prior work on moral foundations by emphasizing instrumental and terminal goals that motivate argumentative moves (Frimer et al., 2017; Roy et al., 2021). We also situate value detection within the pipeline of argument mining, connecting value cues to claim types and inference schemes (Walton et al., 2008; Stede and Schneider, 2018). From a methodological standpoint, we compare feature-based baselines, transformer encoders, and prompt-based models under low-resource constraints (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019; Lester et al., 2021). We further evaluate cross-topic transfer to test whether value representations are more stable than topic indicators (Guerra et al., 2014; Bamman et al., 2015). For interpretability, we adapt post-hoc concept activation techniques to quantify the contribution of value prototypes to model predictions (Kim et al., 2018; Koh and Liang, 2017). We position our work relative to broader ethical NLP discussions that advocate modeling social constructs with transparent assumptions (Bender and Friedman, 2018; Hovy and Spruit, 2016). Unlike stance detection, value identification requires disentangling reasons from goals, which may co-occur within the same argumentative unit (Sobhani et al., 2015; Bar-Haim et al., 2017). Our review reveals consistent gaps in multilingual resources for value-centric argument mining despite growing interest in cross-lingual argument analysis (Cabrio and Villata, 2018; Eger et al., 2018). Accordingly, we outline an agenda for multilingual value annotation and knowledge transfer using aligned taxonomies and shared semantic spaces (Conneau et al., 2020; Pires et al., 2019). Altogether, this introduction clarifies the conceptual landscape and motivates a principled approach to modeling values in argumentative text.

Format.document: Several data augmentation methods have been introduced for compositional semantic parsing. Early work on recombination explored grammar-guided transformations over utterance–logical form pairs. Jia and Liang (2016) recombined data by SCFG to produce adversarial yet meaning-preserving examples. Andreas (2019) used simple rules to exchange tokens with shared contexts and to inject lexical diversity. However, these approaches relied on superficial grammars or rules with limited capacity to capture deep structure. Akyürek et al. (2020) learned to recombine and resample data with a prototype-based generative model in lieu of hand-written rules. Substructure substitution has also been studied for augmentation in other NLP tasks (Shi et al., 2021). Dependency tree cropping and rotation were used for low-resource POS tagging (Şahin and Steedman, 2019) and for dependency parsing (Vania et al., 2019). Tree swapping and controlled perturbations have been explored for low-resource dependency parsing (Dehouck and Gómez-Rodríguez, 2020). Despite this progress, subtree substitution with fine-grained meaning functions remains understudied in semantic parsing. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to explore tree manipulation tailored to compositional meaning. Beyond augmentation, advances in neural architectures have reshaped semantic parsing methodologies. Sequence-to-sequence models with attention established strong baselines for mapping language to programs (Dong and Lapata, 2016). Subsequent work investigated copying and pointer mechanisms to better align tokens with symbols (Gu et al., 2016; See et al., 2017). Pretrained language models substantially improved data efficiency across semantic parsing benchmarks (Devlin et al., 2019; Lewis et al., 2020). Encoder–decoder pretraining further enabled low-shot generalization to novel compositional combinations (Xia et al., 2021). In parallel, constrained decoding and grammar-aware networks were introduced to ensure well-typed outputs (Yin and Neubig, 2017; Krishnamurthy et al., 2017). Program synthesis with neural-guided search offered complementary benefits under weak supervision (Akkalyoncu Yilmaz et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020). Data augmentation remains crucial because labeled logical forms are expensive to obtain at scale. Paraphrase generation using back-translation produced lexical variety without altering denotations (Sennrich et al., 2016; Iyer et al., 2018). Graph-based rewrites attempted to manipulate compositional templates while preserving executability (Herzig and Berant, 2021). Contrastive learning over meaning-preserving pairs improved encoder invariance to surface form (He et al., 2020; Giorgi et al., 2021). Nevertheless, uncontrolled perturbations can drift semantics and silently corrupt program executability. This motivates augmentation schemes that explicitly track and preserve meaning functions at the subtree level. We build on structured operations that respect type signatures and argument orderings common in executable formalisms. Our approach is compatible with modern pretrained encoders and decoders widely used in semantic parsing. Recent encoder–decoder models such as T5 Raffel et al., 2020) and BART (Lewis et al., 2020) have demonstrated robust transfer to compositional tasks. We therefore study how principled tree manipulations interact with pretrained initialization and decoding constraints. In particular, we control the locus of change to isolate operator, argument, and scope alterations. This control allows us to generate examples that probe both systematicity and generalization beyond seen compositions. We evaluate on standard semantic parsing datasets that require compositional generalization (Lake and Baroni, 2018; Finegan-Dollak et al., 2018). Our experiments compare rule-based, learned, and hybrid augmentation strategies under identical training budgets. We report accuracy, denotation correctness, and calibration across grids of data sizes and perturbation strengths. Ablation studies examine the contribution of type-aware selection, rewrite depth, and structural diversity. Error analyses reveal common failure modes, including scope misattachment and spurious lexical cues. Finally, we discuss broader implications for augmentation in structured prediction and outline directions for scalable curation.

Format.document: Large-scale pre-training models such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), T5 (Raffel et al., 2019), wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski et al., 2020), and HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021) have drawn substantial attention for their generalization capacity over massive corpora. These frameworks unify representation learning across tasks and enable efficient adaptation with lightweight fine-tuning (Devlin et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019; Lewis et al., 2020). Nevertheless, most advances still emphasize single-modal objectives that either read text or process speech, but rarely both within a single training recipe. As a result, cross-modal generation and understanding remain fragmented across model families and evaluation suites. Early attempts in speech-language pre-training improved spoken language understanding via encoders augmented with task-specific heads (Chung et al., 2021b; Kim et al., 2021). However, these pipelines seldom pre-train decoders for generative targets such as speech synthesis or abstractive summarization. The proposed SpeechT5 method is closely related to T5 as a sequence-to-sequence architecture that casts tasks into a text-to-text format (Raffel et al., 2019). SpeechT5 extends this idea by generalizing the interface to accept and emit both speech and text through modality-specific pre and post nets. Unlike single-purpose encoders, the approach seeks a shared encoder-decoder backbone that can be fine-tuned on diverse spoken language tasks with minimal architectural changes. Related lines of work include Speech Chain, which forms a closed learning loop between ASR and TTS for leveraging unlabeled data (Tjandra et al., 2020). Another example is SpeechNet, which designs a modular system for multi-task speech processing under a unified training objective (Chen et al., 2021b). In contrast, SpeechT5 pursues a unified multimodal backbone that is jointly pre-trained on large-scale speech and text to facilitate transfer across generation and recognition settings. Benchmarking initiatives such as SUPERB standardize evaluation for frozen encoders with small task heads, revealing broad capabilities and gaps (Yang et al., 2021). While SUPERB highlights the value of shared representations, it deliberately constrains decoders to lightweight predictors, limiting generative assessment. For research on universal encoder-decoder frameworks, richer pretraining signals and task mixtures are therefore essential. SpeechT5 addresses this need by aligning acoustic and textual tokens within a single modeling space to encourage transfer. The strategy benefits downstream tasks like ASR, TTS, and spoken translation, where cross-modal supervision is abundant in semi-parallel corpora. It also improves data efficiency in low-resource scenarios by reusing abstractions learned from complementary modalities. Prior multimodal learning explored audio-text contrastive objectives to connect speech segments with textual captions (Radford et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021). However, contrastive schemes often learn shallow correspondences and may underperform on sequence-level generation compared to encoder-decoder pretraining. Multi-task transducers and hybrid CTC-attention models have also been used to share encoders across ASR and auxiliary tasks (Graves et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2017). Despite these successes, pretraining that unifies both modalities within a generative backbone remains comparatively underexplored. Survey articles have noted increasing interest in joint speech-text modeling but point to open questions on data curation and scaling laws (Zhang et al., 2022). For a comprehensive discussion, see (see Wang et al., 2021 on cross-modal transfer. Compared to these directions, our perspective is to integrate speech and text under a shared vocabulary and training objective. Concretely, we hypothesize that aligning discrete speech units with subword tokens can simplify multi-task supervision across modalities. We also posit that the decoder should be pre-trained to autoregress over both acoustic and textual tokenizations to unify generation interfaces. This design allows reusing infrastructure for datasets, schedulers, and evaluation across ASR, TTS, and spoken dialogue systems. It further enables parameter-efficient adapters that selectively route computation for robustness under domain shift (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020). Nevertheless, careful accounting is required to avoid label leakage between tasks when constructing mixed-modality batches. We evaluate in settings that mirror SUPERB but add generative tracks for TTS and summarization to stress-test the decoder. The results indicate consistent gains over strong baselines across languages, speaker conditions, and noise regimes. Error analyses show that improvements correlate with tasks that benefit from cross-modal priors rather than pure scaling of acoustic data (Park et al. 1). Ablations also suggest that curriculum over input modalities stabilizes optimization and prevents collapse in early training. We additionally compare against targeted data augmentation methods and find complementary effects when mixing pseudo-parallel pairs. Finally, we highlight ethical considerations in collecting speech-text corpora, including consent, demographic balance, and potential misuse.

Format.document: In this section, we first go through some of the most related works for BERT compression in the literature and then review the few works that have used Kronecker decomposition for compression of CNNs and RNNs. Model compression for transformers has progressed along four main axes: pruning, distillation, quantization, and low-rank factorization. Pruning methods remove redundant parameters or attention heads while preserving downstream accuracy (Michel et al., 2019; Voita et al., 2019). Unstructured magnitude pruning and movement pruning have also demonstrated competitive sparsity–accuracy trade-offs for BERT-like encoders (Gordon et al., 2020; Sanh et al., 2020). Knowledge distillation compresses large teachers into smaller students via soft targets or intermediate-layer matching (Hinton et al., 2015; Jiao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2019). Quantization further reduces memory and latency by lowering precision with minimal calibration (Jacob et al., 2018; Zafrir et al., 2019). Low-rank and tensor factorizations approximate weight matrices to cut compute, building on classical SVD approaches and modern tensor decompositions (Denton et al., 2014; Novikov et al., 2015; Tai et al., 2016). Within this family, Kronecker-structured approximations have emerged as particularly effective for convolutional kernels and recurrent transitions (Li et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019 showing promising speedups. Early CNN work factorized 4D convolutional tensors into sums of Kronecker products to reduce both parameters and FLOPs (Luo et al., 2017; Wang and Zhang, 2018). For RNNs, Kronecker-factored recurrent matrices have been used to accelerate training while maintaining expressive power (Martens and Grosse, 2015; Thomas et al., 2018). These structural constraints complement channel pruning and group sparsity techniques that operate at higher architectural granularity (He et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017). In transformer settings, low-rank or block-structured parameterizations of attention and feed-forward layers have yielded notable gains without retraining from scratch (Lan et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2021). However, transferring Kronecker ideas to transformers is less straightforward because parameter tying and multi-head patterns break simple separability assumptions (Kovaleva et al., 2019). Recent studies therefore combine Kronecker factors with layer-wise distillation and quantization-aware fine-tuning to mitigate loss spikes after factor replacement (Zhang et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2020). Beyond raw compression ratios, evaluation increasingly emphasizes on-device latency, energy, and fairness impacts in multilingual and specialized domains (Ganesh et al., 2020; Hooker, 2021). Our review synthesizes these strands to motivate a unified view of Kronecker-structured compression for sequence models and to identify open questions in scaling, robustness, and task transfer.

Format.document: Knowledge Distillation Recently, many attempts have been made to accelerate large neural networks. Knowledge distillation is a prominent method for training compact networks to achieve comparable performance to a deep network. Hinton et al. (2015) first introduced the idea of knowledge distillation to exploit the "dark knowledge" (i.e., soft label distribution) from a large teacher model as additional supervision for training a smaller student model. Since its introduction, several works (Romero et al., 2015; Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2017; Tung & Mori, 2019; Park et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2019) have investigated methods that align different latent representations between the student and teacher models for better knowledge transfer. In the context of knowledge distillation, MetaDistil shares some common ideas with the line of work that utilizes a sequence of intermediate teacher models to make the teacher network better adapt to the capacity of the student model throughout the training process, including teacher assistant knowledge distillation (TAKD) (Mirzadeh et al., 2020) and route constraint optimization (RCO). However, the intermediate teachers are heuristically selected independently of the training process and the evolution of the teacher network is discrete. In contrast, MetaDistil employs meta learning to make the teacher model adapt to the current state of the student model and provide a continuously evolving meta-teacher that can better teach the student. Concurrently, Park et al. (2021) and Shi et al. (2021) propose to update the teacher model jointly with the student model with task specific objectives (e.g., cross-entropy loss) during the KD process and add constraints to keep student and teacher similar to each other. Their approaches make the teacher model aware of the student model by constraining the teacher model's capacity. However, the teacher models in their methods are still not optimized for knowledge transfer. In addition, Zhang et al. (2018) introduced deep mutual learning where multiple models learn collaboratively and teach each other throughout the training process. While it is focused on a different setting where different models have approximately the same capacity and are learned from scratch, it also encourages the teacher model to behave similarly to the student model. Different from all aforementioned methods, MetaDistil employs meta learning to explicitly optimize the teacher model for better knowledge transfer ability, and leads to improved performance of the resulting student model. Beyond feature alignment, several studies explore logit matching, temperature scaling, and data augmentation to stabilize teacher signals in low-capacity regimes (Gou et al., 2021 and report consistent improvements across benchmarks (Yuan et al., 2020). Prior work on online knowledge distillation further suggests co-training strategies where a dynamic teacher is formed as an ensemble of students to mitigate confirmation bias (Zhang et al., 2018; Anil et al., 2018). Recent efforts also address domain shift by transferring from a teacher trained in a source domain to a student deployed in a target domain using curriculum schedules and regularization (Mensi et al., 2022; Pham et al., 2021). To this end, meta learning has been proposed as a way to adapt teacher behavior to the evolving student, but existing implementations still rely on fixed schedules or manually chosen checkpoints (Rusu et al., 2019). A related line models the teacher update as a bilevel optimization problem and derives gradients through the student update to directly improve transfer efficiency in the next step (Liu et al., 2018). Practical applications in vision and NLP report gains when the teacher is made aware of the student’s architecture and capacity constraints via auxiliary losses and architecture-conditioned distillation (Touvron et al., 2021; Sanh et al., 2019). Nevertheless, many pipelines keep the teacher static and emphasize student-side regularization such as label smoothing, confidence calibration, and mixup training (Müller et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021), following Hinton et al. In our formulation, the meta-teacher is optimized to anticipate the student’s next improvement, thereby turning the outer loop into an explicit objective for transferability rather than task accuracy alone (Finn et al., 2017). For fair comparison, we also consider strong baselines that jointly update teacher and student under task losses with similarity constraints, as advocated by prior concurrent work (Park et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2021). We note that early expositions of the distillation principle continue to influence modern practice, including the role of temperature, softened targets, and the balance between hard and soft losses, as originally discussed by Hinton et al. (2015). Finally, we position MetaDistil as a general framework that unifies assistant teachers, online ensembling, and bilevel updates while preserving simplicity for large-scale training in real systems.

Format.document: Adversarial evaluation has become essential for stress-testing NLP models beyond standard benchmarks. Adversarial GLUE (Wang et al., 2021) introduced expert-designed templates to synthesize challenging inputs for multiple tasks. Despite its breadth, the suite does not include named entity recognition (NER), leaving open questions about token-level robustness. Prior work on adversarial NER has explored perturbing entity spans and contexts to elicit label flips. For example, Gui et al. (2021) concatenate sentences, inject character-level noise, and swap entities across categories to study failure modes. Zeng et al. (2020) propose constrained swaps that preserve the original entity type to maintain grammaticality. In contrast, our approach targets hard cases by altering mentions while expanding supportive context to induce controlled relabeling. Similar template-driven resources have informed adversarial test design in (Wang et al., 2021, but their protocols emphasize sentence-level phenomena over token-level supervision. Beyond adversarial inputs, augmentation strategies that modify the training distribution can improve generalization for sequence labeling. Mixup, introduced by Zhang et al. (2018), interpolates examples and labels to construct a vicinal distribution around the data manifold. In classification, mixup reduces overconfidence under shift and smooths decision boundaries (Thulasidasan et al., 2020; Verma et al., 2019). Recent studies adapt mixup for token classification by applying interpolation at representation, logit, or span levels (Liang et al., 2018; Chen and Yu, 2021). However, the interaction between adversarially augmented corpora and mixup has been underexplored for NER. We hypothesize that mixing adversarial and natural instances can regularize boundary decisions around ambiguous contexts. To situate our study, we compare augmentation families spanning character noise, paraphrasing, entity replacement, and context-controlled relabeling. Comparative surveys highlight these themes in (Smith et al., 2019; Jones and Lee, 2020; Kim, 2021) while noting gaps for token-level robustness benchmarks. Building on these observations, we design perturbations that preserve syntactic plausibility yet challenge entity typing decisions. We then couple these perturbations with mixup during training to calibrate confidence under distribution shift. Our contributions include a taxonomy of NER-specific adversarial manipulations, an evaluation protocol, and evidence that mixup amplifies robustness without degrading in-domain accuracy.
