Format.document: Semantic parsing has been widely studied across instruction following, code generation, and knowledge graph question answering (Chen and Mooney, 2011; Artzi and Zettlemoyer, 2013; Oda et al., 2015; Iyer et al., 2018; Berant et al., 2013; Yih et al., 2015). We focus on table-based semantic parsing that translates natural language questions paired with tables into executable SQL programs, commonly referred to as text-to-SQL (Androutsopoulos et al., 1995; Minock et al., 2008). Although we concentrate on English, similar ideas extend to multilingual settings (Jie and Lu, 2014; Sherborne et al., 2020). Formally, given a question q and a table T, the task is to produce a program π whose execution over T yields the answer α. We adopt a fully supervised training regime in which gold executable programs supervise the parser. Standard generalization assumes i.i.d. splits, yet practical deployments demand robustness to novel compositions and domains (Gu et al., 2021), (cf. Daumé III and Marcu, 2006, which situates generalization beyond matching train–test distributions. Work on compositional generalization often relies on synthetic data or repartitioned benchmarks and shows persistent difficulty (Keysers et al., 2020; Lake and Baroni, 2018; Finegan-Dollak et al., 2018; Shaw et al., 2021). We study domain generalization, where entire schemas may be unseen or rarely seen during training (Motiian et al., 2017). Despite advances in classification, machine translation, and question answering, domain generalization for semantic parsing remains comparatively underexplored (Daumé III and Marcu, 2006; Daumé III and Jagarlamudi, 2011; Talmor and Berant, 2019). Recent approaches leverage data synthesis, meta-learning, relation-aware schema encoders, and large-scale encoder pretraining (Yin et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2020; Herzig et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2020; Deng et al., 2021). Benchmark datasets such as WIKISQL and SPIDER catalyzed progress but also exhibit artifacts that simplify column mention and limit coverage of multi-column operations (Zhong et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; Suhr et al., 2020). Consequently, realistic settings require reasoning over structured column types and composing operations over columns rather than aligning phrases to single columns. SQUALL extends WIKITABLEQUESTIONS with SQL annotations and refined types but distributes tables across splits, which weakens out-of-domain evaluation (Shi et al., 2020; Pasupat and Liang, 2015). To address these issues, we repartition SQUALL, evaluate strong neural parsers, and analyze errors in column operations using SEQ2SEQ and SMBOP (Rubin and Berant, 2021; Xu et al., 2017). Our models encode the question and schema jointly and decode programs via either autoregressive sequences or bottom-up trees using BERT (Devlin, Chang, Lee, and Toutanova 2019) to initialize the encoder.

Format.document: Recent multilingual translation research suggests that adapting subnetworks for each language or language pair rather than for all of them yields better results. Li et al. (2020) train a shared multilingual model and then select layers for each language pair. Lin et al. (2021) also prune a shared multilingual model for each language pair but operate directly on entries in weight matrices instead. Gong et al. (2021), on the other hand, prune attention heads and feedforward networks for each language. Xie et al. (2021) first identify general and language-specific neurons in a shared multilingual network and then tune those neurons using only the data of their corresponding language. These findings inspire our non-shared pruning setting and motivate us to test whether such results in multilingual translation extend to multilingual pre-training. There are many structured pruning techniques proposed recently for monolingual pre-trained language models. Michel et al. (2019) propose a simple gradient-based importance score to prune attention heads. Prasanna et al. (2020) and Liang et al. (2021) extend this method to prune other components such as the feedforward network of the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017. Wang et al. (2020c) decompose pre-trained model weights and apply L0 regularization (Louizos et al., 2018) to regulate the ranks of the decomposed weights. Sajjad et al. (2020) study layer pruning and show that directly dropping the top layers performs best during fine-tuning. Peer et al. (2021) provide a complementary perspective on structured sparsity for transfer across tasks. The Transformer encoder (Vaswani et al., 2017) pre-trained with the masked language modeling task (Google BERT Devlin et al. (2019)) is the backbone of most existing pre-trained language models. This includes both monolingual and multilingual models (Liu et al., 2019). The Transformer encoder consists of N layers. Each layer contains multihead attention and feedforward networks, followed by residual connections and layer normalization. Following Michel et al. (2019), we write the multihead attention with a gating mechanism over heads. In this formulation, Gh,i indicates whether the i-th head will be pruned. Though not presented in the original Transformer, gating over heads is commonly adopted to introduce structured pruning (Prasanna et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2021). The feedforward network consists of two linear projections with a GeLU activation in between (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016). We place an elementwise gating vector over the hidden units to enable pruning. To prune the large embedding matrix E, we decompose it via a low-rank approximation as in Lan et al. (2020). The decomposition writes E as Ê diag(Ge) P, where Ge governs the effective rank. diag(Ge) converts the gating vector to a diagonal matrix that can zero out columns of Ê. A schematic figure illustrates which components will be pruned, including attention heads and hidden units.

Format.document:
Existing methods for taxonomy expansion can be divided into two categories: relying on alignment between multiple taxonomies or relying on machine learning-based rating sub-graphs. The alignment line of work exploits correspondences among resources such as Wikipedia and WordNet (Ruiz-Casado et al., 2005; Toral and Monachini, 2008; Ponzetto and Navigli, 2009; Yamada et al., 2011). Further, the latter category can be divided into two sub-categories, by expanding synonymy relations via Merge or by expanding hypernymy relations via Attach. Synonymy-based taxonomy expansion leverages synonymy relations of the taxonomy. Given a seed taxonomy, distributional approaches discover synonyms by representing strings with distributional features and learning a classifier to predict relations between strings (Nakashole et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2019; Fei et al., 2019). In contrast, attach-oriented methods aim to place a new term in a hypernymy hierarchy by evaluating candidate parents with learned scores.

Most recent progress emphasizes hypernymy expansion because it directly grows the hierarchical backbone of the taxonomy. These methods attempt to determine the attachment position by scoring between several nodes using lexical, path, and embedding signals. Early neural models adapted pairwise classification for hypernymy detection into an attachment ranking objective (Shen et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2020b; Zhang et al., 2021). Subsequent work incorporated global structural cues such as ancestor consistency and sibling exclusivity to reduce cascading errors. Evidence from pattern-based and distributional models has been shown to be complementary (Weeds et al., 2014; Roller et al., 2018). For a comprehensive overview of hypernymy signals, see (Xiong et al., 2015; Shwartz and Dagan, 2016 along with more recent neural surveys.

Synonymy expansion, often framed as Merge, faces the challenge of polysemy because candidate synonyms may map to multiple senses. Systems mitigate this issue by leveraging context-sensitive embeddings and sense inventories aligned to the target taxonomy (Nakashole et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2019). Joint modeling of Attach and Merge has attracted interest due to coupling between synonym discovery and hypernym placement in lexical resources. In WordNet expansion, the problem is inherently integrated because promoting a synonym into a synset implies constraints on permissible hypernyms. Prior studies have explored iterative refinement where synonym clusters inform candidate parents and vice versa (Shen et al., 2020). However, learning both operations in a single model remains underexplored, especially when supervision is sparse and domain shift is present.

Alignment-based approaches transfer structure by linking nodes across resources and importing edges under reliability thresholds. Such methods benefit from high-precision anchors like interlanguage links or cross-references but may struggle with coverage gaps (Ponzetto and Navigli, 2009). Machine learning approaches, in contrast, can propose attachments for unseen terms using features from corpora, graphs, and pretrained language models (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019). Recent work integrates textual definitions, glosses, and usage examples to ground candidate placements semantically (Bosc and Vincent, 2018; Loureiro and Jorge, 2019). Graph neural networks propagate evidence across existing hierarchies to regularize local decisions and preserve transitivity (Kipf and Welling, 2017; Vashishth et al., 2020). Nevertheless, the choice of negative sampling and candidate pruning remains a crucial determinant of both efficiency and accuracy.

Training data for taxonomy expansion are often noisy because many corpora lack explicit hypernym cues. Weak supervision and distant signals such as Hearst-like patterns can bootstrap labels but introduce biases toward frequent templates (Hearst, 1992). Curriculum strategies that start with easy attachments and gradually introduce harder cases have been reported to stabilize learning by several studies Jones et al. 1. Evaluation protocols typically measure both local accuracy at the chosen parent and global impact on consistency and cycles. Standard benchmarks include WordNet-derived splits, open-domain term lists, and domain-specific vocabularies for biomedicine and e-commerce (Shen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021). Despite progress, generalization to tail entities and unseen domains remains a key limitation motivating robust, cross-domain training regimes.

In this work, we argue for a unified perspective that treats Attach and Merge as mutually reinforcing decisions under shared representations. Our review highlights gaps in joint learning, negative sampling, and evaluation that future research should address. We also clarify assumptions behind alignment-based transfer versus corpus-driven induction to facilitate fair comparisons across settings. The paper positions our approach within the broader literature on lexical semantics, graph learning, and structured prediction. We provide a detailed related study in the Appendix and summarize connections to prior art in Section A. Overall, taxonomy expansion remains a challenging problem whose solutions must balance precision, coverage, and structural soundness.

Format.document:
As mentioned, compression is a widely used strategy to speed up large language models (Gupta and Agrawal, 2020). This involves techniques such as quantization of weights and activations (Bai et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2021), knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015; Jiao et al., 2020; Sanh et al., 2019), pruning and sharing (Gordon et al., 2020), multi-device distribution (Banitalebi-Dehkordi et al., 2021), or combinations thereof (Cheng et al., 2017; Polino et al., 2018). Beyond latency, compression can reduce memory footprint and energy consumption while preserving accuracy for many tasks (Schwartz et al., 2020). Nevertheless, the choice of method depends on hardware constraints, tolerance to accuracy loss, and the training budget (Choi et al., 2018). Recent surveys categorize these approaches by parameter reduction, representation sharing, and numerical precision (Cheng et al., 2017).

Among compression techniques, creating a fixed-size small version of a large model with distillation has been especially popular in recent years. Sanh et al. (2019) introduced DistilBERT, a smaller variant of BERT trained with distillation for general purposes. Another compact variant of BERT was proposed by MobileBERT (Sun et al., 2020), which employed inverted bottlenecks and progressive knowledge transfer. TinyBERT (Jiao et al., 2020) presented a two-stage transformer distillation for both pre-training and task-specific fine-tuning. Iandola et al. (2020) studied grouped convolutions to design SqueezeBERT for efficient inference. ELM (Jiao et al., 2021), a layer-mapping search framework, was proposed to improve downstream BERT distillation. A more recent method, GhostBERT, employs softmax-normalized one-dimensional convolutions as ghost modules to generate more features with cheap operations (Zhang et al., 2021).

Although compression is effective, it often trades accuracy for efficiency, especially under high compression ratios (Frantar and Alistarh, 2022). Moreover, a separate fixed-size model is typically required for each target computational budget. As an alternative, dynamic inference can adjust computation at test time through early exits or adaptive width and depth (Teerapittayanon et al., 2016; Elbayad et al., 2020). One of the first temporal early-exit strategies was proposed by ReasoNet (Shen et al., 2017), which halts reading when sufficient evidence is found. Similarly, Yu et al. (2018) presented an early stopping method for classification tasks. DeeBERT proposed instance-wise multi-exit decisions using the entropy of the output probability distribution to speed up BERT inference (Xin et al., 2020).

As a length-adaptive method, Kim and Cho (2021) introduced one-shot training of transformers for both sequence- and token-level classification. DynaBERT was proposed to adjust computations by choosing sub-networks of different widths and depths under a unified training regime (Hou et al., 2020). Both Length-Adaptive Transformers and DynaBERT utilized knowledge distillation and data augmentation to improve performance. Depth-adaptive machine translation further demonstrated that selective layer usage can maintain quality while reducing cost (Elbayad et al., 2020). For routing computation, early-exit classifiers and confidence estimation have also been explored in multilingual settings (Scao and Rush, 2021).

Despite their success, many dynamic methods require architectural changes and retraining, which complicates deployment in production environments. Furthermore, most prior work targets encoder-only backbones and classification tasks rather than encoder–decoder architectures and sequence-to-sequence learning. In contrast, our method operates with out-of-the-box pretrained models without retraining and applies to encoder–decoder settings and generative tasks. It also exposes a simple knob for latency control without maintaining multiple checkpoints.

Quantization remains attractive because it offers predictable latency benefits across CPUs and accelerators. For post-training quantization, uniform and per-channel schemes are commonly studied Bai et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2020). In contrast, quantization-aware training can recover more accuracy at the cost of additional training iterations (Jacob et al., 2018). Structured pruning targets attention heads and feed-forward blocks to produce hardware-friendly sparsity (Michel et al., 2019; Lagunas et al., 2021). Dynamic token pruning complements early exits by reducing sequence length on the fly (Goyal et al., 2020). Adaptive computation time provides another axis for budgeting, although it is less explored for Transformers (Graves, 2016; Dehghani et al., 2019). Finally, conditional computation via mixture-of-experts can scale capacity without linear cost, but introduces routing overhead and training instability (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2021). Our study positions these threads within a unified perspective on efficiency, distillation, and dynamic control for modern language models.

Format.document: Data augmentation has been used for resolving artefacts in training datasets before (Gururangan et al., 2018; Srivastava et al., 2020; Kaushik et al., 2021). In particular, previous work (Kaushik et al., 2020) relied on large-scale crowd-sourcing to generate useful augmented data. More recently, Wang and Culotta (2021) investigated the efficacy of automatically generated counterfactuals for sentiment analysis. Similar to our work, these methods consider the most salient features that a model uses when generating augmented data, which aligns with our rationale definition. However, they use sentiment lexicon matching for identifying rationales, which is task-specific and not necessarily fully relevant. In contrast, we employ human annotators to identify rationales, which can be task-agnostic and robust. Moreover, our method generates semi-factuals instead of the counterfactuals used in previous work. Human-in-the-loop machine learning (Wu et al., 2021a) has received increasing research attention. Active learning (Settles, 2009; Margatina et al., 2021), the most common example of human-in-the-loop machine learning, asks annotators to provide high-level labels for informative examples. There is also work exploring more explainable AI systems by exploiting feature-based information. Such methods use relatively simple models such as Naïve Bayes (Stumpf et al., 2009; Kulesza et al., 2015) and linear regression with bag-of-words features (Jia and Liang, 2017; Teso and Kersting, 2019; Ghai et al., 2021; Shao et al., 2021), because these classifiers are intuitive and amenable to incorporating human feedback. Other work uses simple neural networks such as multilayer perceptrons (Shao et al., 2021) and shallow CNNs (Lertvittayakumjorn et al., 2020; Teso et al., 2021) because their predictions can be explained in the form of features. Very recently, Yao et al. (2021) proposed a human-in-the-loop method to inspect more complicated models with the help of model-agnostic post-hoc explanation algorithms Ribeiro et al., 2018) that can explain predictions of any linear or non-linear model without exploiting its weights. However, most prior work focuses on increasing explainability for high-stakes domains such as health and finance, rather than improving robustness or generalization. In addition, many methods assume access to large amounts of labeled data. In contrast, we focus on few-shot learning scenarios that are more compelling for emerging applications. Our approach is motivated by observations that models often latch onto superficial patterns that do not causally support predictions. Data augmentation that targets those patterns can mitigate spurious correlations while preserving task semantics. Counterfactual generation provides one avenue, but it can inadvertently change multiple latent factors at once, as noted in (Kaushik et al., 2020). Semi-factuals, by contrast, selectively alter local evidence while keeping the gold label stable. To identify candidate evidence, we collect human rationales at instance level and aggregate them across annotators. This process yields high-precision spans that guide minimal edits to inputs. We validate these edits through pilot studies that check fluency, label preservation, and domain relevance. Compared to automatic lexicon matching, human-informed edits better capture pragmatic cues and discourse context. We further analyze the interaction between augmentation and active learning. In pool-based settings, query strategies that consider augmentation effects can reduce redundant labeling. We combine uncertainty, diversity, and expected model change to schedule annotation rounds. In each round, annotators label both class and rationale to maintain alignment between explanation and supervision. The resulting dataset supports training objectives that jointly penalize rationale inconsistency and prediction error. For complex models such as transformers, we monitor attribution drift using integrated gradients and LIME (Ribeiro et al., 2016). When drift is detected, we refresh the augmented pool with new semi-factuals that target emerging shortcuts. We also compare against perturbation-based baselines drawn from synonym replacement and back-translation (Wei and Zou, 2019; Sennrich et al., 2016). The baselines improve robustness modestly but often degrade calibration under distribution shift. Prior art has discussed the trade-off between edit minimality and label fidelity in data augmentation. Building on these insights, our contribution is a general framework that unifies rationale collection, semi-factual editing, and active curation. We anticipate that this framework will transfer to other tasks such as toxicity detection, stance classification, and natural language inference.

Format.document: Style transfer datasets are typically curated under two regimes: nonparallel and parallel. When collecting nonparallel corpora, style labels often already exist in the data, such as sentiment, formality, and toxicity. In practice, style labels can be inferred from the source domain, for example Twitter, academic writing, or legal filings, which reduces collection to scraping texts at scale. For sentiment, large review platforms provide abundant labeled data because users explicitly rate products and services, as noted by Li et al. 1. Consequently, corpus size is bounded more by licensing and deduplication constraints than by annotation costs. Conversely, parallel corpora for style transfer are scarce and costly to build. A notable exception is the Bible corpus, which offers multiple translations aligned at the verse level (Carlson et al., 2018). Another semi-natural source is the biased-to-neutral Wikipedia corpus that exploits edit histories to derive parallel rewrites (Pryzant et al., 2020). Beyond such special cases, parallel datasets are typically created from scratch via crowdsourcing and expert review. The widely used GYAFC dataset pairs informal sentences with expert-edited formal rewrites (Rao and Tetreault, 2018). Building similar resources for toxicity mitigation is challenging because toxic–neutral pairs rarely arise organically. Following prior practice, researchers recruit crowd workers to produce rewrites and then verify quality with additional reviewers (Jiang et al., 2020). To reduce costs, some pipelines replace expert adjudication with majority-vote crowd validation while monitoring inter-annotator agreement (Artstein and Poesio, 2008). A common risk in such pipelines is content preservation drift, where rewritten sentences inadvertently change meaning (Xu et al., 2012). Recent work addresses this risk by adding automatic semantic similarity checks and lexical constraints during generation (Zhang et al., 2020). In addition to human rewrites, parallel data can be synthesized through back-translation or pivoting between attribute-conditioned models (Prabhumoye et al., 2018). However, synthetic pairs often amplify artifacts and teach models to exploit shortcuts rather than learn disentangled representations (Elazar and Goldberg, 2018). For nonparallel settings, disentanglement approaches rely on adversarial training, attribute classifiers, and content reconstruction losses (Shen et al., 2017;Fu et al., 2018). Retrieval-augmented approaches instead locate semantically similar sentences with target attributes to guide rewriting (Li et al., 2018b). Control through minimal edits has also been explored to better preserve content while flipping style markers (Sudhakar et al., 2019). Evaluation remains contentious, with automatic metrics correlating imperfectly with human judgments across fluency, style strength, and content preservation (Mir et al., 2019). Recent benchmarks emphasize multi-attribute control and robust generalization across domains and lengths (Riley et al., 2021). Nevertheless, many datasets underrepresent long, multi-clause sentences typical of professional or legal writing, limiting external validity. Domain provenance further matters because stylistic markers vary with genre, register, and platform-specific conventions (Biber and Conrad, 2009). Consequently, dataset documentation should record collection windows, platform policies, and filtering rules to support reproducibility (Bender and Friedman, 2018). Ethical considerations include potential harm from releasing toxic text and the risk of misuse for evasion or targeted harassment (Vidgen et al., 2020). Mitigation strategies combine redaction, access controls, and bias audits for demographic disparities in labeling (Sap et al., 2019). Parallel datasets must also specify licenses for both sources and annotations to enable legally compliant redistribution (Nielsen, 2011). For multilingual style transfer, script variation and code-switching complicate tokenization and alignment, motivating language-specific preprocessing (Winata et al., 2019). Several studies report that pretraining on large raw corpora before fine-tuning on style transfer improves fluency without sacrificing control (Lample et al., 2019). Still, domain shift between pretraining data and target applications can hurt attribute accuracy, suggesting the need for in-domain adaptation (Gururangan et al., 2020). Recent datasets also include paragraph-level or document-level rewrites that preserve discourse coherence and coreference patterns (Jhamtani et al., 2017). To support such longer contexts, curators often include outlines and meta-information that constrain acceptable rewrites during annotation (Rei et al., 2020). A persistent open question is how to balance diversity with consistency so that models do not overfit to a narrow set of lexical cues (Krishna et al., 2020). Comparative studies suggest that training with contrastive objectives and hard negative pairs can improve content preservation in parallel and nonparallel regimes (He et al., 2020). Looking forward, we advocate standardized datasheets, transparent licensing, and multi-attribute test suites to advance reliable, equitable style transfer research, as also argued by Shen et al.

Fine-tuning of Language Models. Better finetuning of language models can be achieved by proper initialization (Dodge et al., 2020), regularization or prompts (Schick and Schütze, 2021). Other tricks include bias correction in optimizer and re-initialization of top layers in Transformer (Zhang et al., 2021). Instead of fine-tuning all parameters in a model, other work explore only learning a few vectors (Lester et al., 2021; Li and Liang, 2021; Guo et al., 2021) or a few additional parameters (Houlsby et al., 2019). Hallucination Methods. Feature Hallucination of examples is first introduced for visual recognition (Hariharan and Girshick, 2017) by metalearning (Wang et al., 2018), variational inference (Luo et al., 2021; Lazarou et al., 2022), and adversarial learning (Tjio et al., 2022). Label Hallucination (Jian and Torresani, 2022) assigns soft pseudo-labels for unlabelled images to extend the fine-tuning few-shot dataset. Few-shot Language Models. Few-shot learning has been successfully applied to machine translation (Arthaud et al., 2021), abstract summarizing (Fabbri et al., 2021), question and answering (Hua et al., 2020; Ram et al., 2021), and entity recognition (de Lichy et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2021), by meta learning (Li and Zhang, 2021; Bansal et al., 2020; Sharaf et al., 2020), data augmentation (Wei et al., 2021; Wei and Zou, 2019; Karimi et al., 2021b), and prompts (Gao et al., 2021; Tam et al., 2021).

Our method is a generative data augmentation method in the embedding space. Unlike Wei et al. (2021), which uses EDA (Wei and Zou, 2019) to augment examples at the discrete input space, we hallucinate auxiliary examples at the embedding space. Our method shares similarity to FDA (Kumar et al., 2019), which is also a generative data augmentation method, but at the feature space. Also, different from FDA which is focused on two intent classification tasks, our method can be applied to a wide-range of NLP task as shown by our experiments on 15 diverse tasks. Fine-tuning strategies increasingly prioritize parameter efficiency to reduce computational and storage costs without sacrificing accuracy (Pfeiffer et al., 2021). Adapter layers enable task transfer while keeping the pretrained backbone fixed, mitigating catastrophic forgetting (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2021). Prompt tuning and prefix tuning instead steer model behavior through learned inputs, which can be advantageous in low-resource regimes (Lester et al., 2021; Li and Liang, 2021). Despite progress, practitioners still report instability across random seeds and domains, motivating robust augmentation pipelines (Dodge et al., 2020). Data augmentation in NLP ranges from rule-based edits to model-based paraphrasing, yet the trade-off between diversity and label preservation remains challenging (Feng et al., 2021). Embedding-space augmentation aims to navigate this trade-off by perturbing continuous representations while respecting task semantics (Sohn et al., 2020). Generative approaches further synthesize features or examples that expand decision boundaries and improve generalization under distribution shift (Kumar et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2020). In contrast to token-level noising, our approach composes semantically coherent exemplars that align with task-specific manifolds in representation space (Chen et al., 2020). Prior work on few-shot classification in vision has demonstrated the benefits of hallucinating additional features from limited support sets (Hariharan and Girshick, 2017; Wang et al., 2018). Analogous ideas have been explored for text through back-translation, span replacement, and paraphrase mining with varying degrees of success (Wei and Zou, 2019; Fabbri et al., 2021). However, uncontrolled surface edits may distort label-defining cues, especially in tasks with fine-grained semantics such as intent and relation classification (Karimi et al., 2021b). Our formulation treats augmentation as learning a conditional generator over embeddings that respects task constraints derived from labeled exemplars. We study the interaction between augmentation intensity and finetuning dynamics to identify regimes that yield consistent gains across tasks. In ablations, we compare to strong baselines including EDA, back-translation, and MixUp-inspired interpolation in embedding space (Zhang et al., 2018; Wei and Zou, 2019). We also evaluate compatibility with adapter-based tuning and soft prompts to demonstrate orthogonality to parameter-efficient methods (Pfeiffer et al., 2021; Lester et al., 2021). For comprehensive coverage, we consider text classification, natural language inference, paraphrase detection, and token classification spanning 15 benchmarks. Our experiments include cross-domain setups to assess robustness to covariate shift and label imbalance. The results indicate consistent improvements in low-data regimes and competitive performance in medium-data settings relative to task-specific tuning. We observe that augmentation in representation space yields more stable training and reduced variance across random seeds. In (Radford et al., 2019), we situate our approach alongside pretrained generative models to discuss complementarity in resource-constrained adaptation. Finally, we outline open challenges concerning controllability, faithfulness, and calibration that warrant further investigation (Kumar et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2020). Together, these findings motivate embedding-space hallucination as a practical and extensible component in modern fine-tuning pipelines.

Format.document: There have been a number of attempts at compressing Transformer models, which can be broadly categorized into three directions. The first line of work focuses on redundancy in model parameters. Structure pruning removes coherent groups of weights to preserve the network layout (McCarley, 2019; Michel et al., 2019; Voita et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019b; Fan et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2021a). In addition, various distillation techniques train compact models to reproduce a larger model’s outputs (Sanh et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020b). Other strategies include weight quantization and weight sharing (Bhandare et al., 2019; Zafrir et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020; Dehghani et al., 2018; Lan et al., 2019). The second line of work targets the quadratic cost of self-attention with respect to sequence length. This complexity is the main efficiency bottleneck and is prohibitive for long sequences. One approach sparsifies attention by restricting each token to a subset of neighbors, as in Big Bird and Longformer (Zaheer et al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2020). In (Wang et al., 2020a; Choromanski et al., 2020), kernel approximations reduce the quadratic complexity to linear while preserving accuracy. The third direction explores redundancy in maintaining full token-level representations across encoders (Dai et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2021b; Pietruszka et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2021; Kim and Cho, 2020). State-of-the-art classifiers often rely on a single embedding such as the CLS token rather than full sequences. Dai et al. (2020) apply simple strided mean pooling to compress tokens and propose pretraining to balance speed and accuracy. We instead aim to avoid costly pretraining and rely on lightweight fine-tuning. Wu et al. (2021b define a centroid attention operator that computes embeddings for selected centroids obtained by random sampling or pooling. This operator yields similar token-reduction behavior to strided pooling but offers learnable selection via attention. Because several related methods either use non-standard datasets or require expensive reinforcement learning policies, we restrict experiments to approaches that improve both training and inference, and we do not compare to vision-specific pooling models (Pan et al., 2021; Heo et al., 2021).

Format.document: Continual dialogue learning seeks to endow conversational agents with the ability to accumulate skills across tasks and domains. Neural dialogue models have progressed rapidly due to large-scale corpora and pretrained encoders. Early sequence-to-sequence and retrieval architectures demonstrated that data-driven systems can acquire basic conversational abilities (Mou et al., 2016; Xing et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2017). Beyond fluency, recent work targets controllable traits such as persona consistency and empathy (Qian et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018b; Zhou et al., 2018; Rashkin et al., 2019). However, transferring such skills across tasks remains challenging under continual updates. Catastrophic forgetting arises when parameters optimized for a new objective overwrite knowledge needed for earlier tasks (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). At the same time, naive multitask training may conflate task-specific cues and degrade generalization (Caruana, 1997). The inductive transfer perspective highlights mechanisms that enable reuse of representations while isolating interference (Ruder, 2019). Under this view, methods fall into feature-based reuse, end-to-end fine-tuning, and lightweight parameterization via adapters (Ruder, 2019). Adapter-based transfer learns small task-specific modules inserted into frozen transformers to control capacity and sharing (Houlsby et al., 2019; Poth et al., 2021. Such modules can be composed, routed, or sparsely activated to balance specialization and reuse (Pfeiffer et al., 2021; Mahabadi et al., 2021). In dialogue, adapters promise a compact means to accumulate skills while preserving prior behaviors across updates. Prior work explored persona and empathy conditioning through specialized components trained on curated datasets (Qian et al., 2018; Rashkin et al., 2019). Yet, most studies evaluate in isolated settings rather than under realistic continual training regimes. We study how adapterized architectures can support sequential acquisition of dialogue skills with minimal forgetting. Our approach separates general conversational knowledge from task-specific adapters that capture style, goal, or grounding signals. Knowledge is routed through a small number of shared layers to encourage transfer without entanglement. We compare adapter-based continual learning with full fine-tuning and prompt-based baselines across multiple dialogue tasks. Fine-tuning can yield strong single-task performance but often erases earlier capabilities during sequential updates (Zaremba and Sutskever, 2014). Prompt-based tuning offers parameter efficiency but may struggle to retain precise behaviors under distribution shift (Lester et al., 2021). In contrast, modular adapters provide explicit loci for preservation and growth when tasks arrive over time. We build on designs that place down-projection and up-projection bottlenecks inside transformer blocks (Houlsby et al., 2019). To assess transfer, we analyze cross-task performance when adapters are switched or composed at inference time (Pfeiffer et al., 2021). We also consider memory-aware regularization and rehearsal buffers as complementary mechanisms to reduce drift (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017; Chaudhry et al., 2019). For fair comparison, all methods use the same pretrained backbone and tokenization pipeline. We adopt a training schedule with short phases and periodic evaluation on held-out tasks to quantify forgetting. Our experiments cover chit-chat, empathetic response generation, goal-oriented slot filling, and knowledge-grounded dialogue. Informed by prior analysis of parameter-efficient NLP, we hypothesize that adapters achieve the best stability–plasticity balance in this setting (Pfeiffer et al., 2021; He et al., 2022). We further probe whether adapter initialization from earlier tasks accelerates learning on new tasks through positive forward transfer (Ammar et al., 2014). Related systems have examined adapter composition for multitask learning, though not under strict continual constraints (Stickland and Murray, 2019; Pilault et al., 2021). In contrast to earlier adapter baselines for dialogue, we explicitly evaluate interference and transfer signals across sequences of tasks. Madotto et al. (2020) investigated adapters for conversational skills without measuring cross-task interference or systematic transfer. Our contributions include a principled evaluation protocol, ablations over adapter placement, and analysis of knowledge partitioning for continual dialogue learning.

Format.document: Since Rashkin et al. (2019) release EmpatheticDialogues, many approaches have been proposed to generate empathetic responses. Lin et al. (2019) propose mixture of emotional experts. Majumder et al. (2020) propose emotion grouping, emotion mimicry and stochastic sampling. Li et al. (2020) extract emotional words through lexicon and propose an adversarial generative model. Shen et al. (2021) apply dual-learning with unpaired data for the bidirectional empathy. Gao et al. (2021) integrate emotion cause into response generation process through gated mechanism. Sabour et al. (2021); Li et al. (2022) use implicit commonsense for context modelling. Kim et al. (2021) train a model to extract words that cause the speaker's emotion and attach RSA Framework (Frank and Goodman, 2012) to any generative models to generate responses, focusing on emotion cause words. Recently, many studies have shown remarkable improvements through recognizing transitions of features between utterances in open-domain multiturn dialogues. Qiu et al. (2020) perceive transitions of emotion states for context modelling. Zou et al. (2021) propose a module to manage keyword transitions. Zhan et al. (2021) model external knowledge transitions to select a knowledge used for generation. In multi-turn empathetic dialogues, we consider emotions, keywords, and utterancelevel meaning (Gu et al., 2021) as important features of each utterance and propose a novel approach of recognizing feature transitions between utterances. Beyond single-turn cues, personalization influences how systems prioritize supportive content (Chan et al., 2019). Persona-grounded dialogue models integrate speaker profiles to modulate affective wording (Zheng et al., 2020). Knowledge-enhanced methods leverage commonsense and situational graphs to infer latent needs (Zhou et al., 2020). Several datasets have been widely adopted (Rashkin et al., 2019; Li et al. 2020) for benchmarking empathetic response generation. Despite progress, models often conflate empathy with sentiment polarity (Busso et al., 2008; Rashkin et al., 2019). Evaluations typically rely on automatic metrics that poorly capture supportive intent (Liu et al., 2016; Mehri and Eskenazi, 2020). Human studies suggest that transparency about reasoning improves perceived empathy (Hancock et al., 2020). Multi-task learning binds emotion recognition to response generation with shared encoders (Zahiri and Choi, 2017; Lin et al., 2019). Contrastive objectives encourage separation between supportive and dismissive candidates (Gao et al., 2021). Planning-based approaches first predict intents and then realize surface forms (Yao et al., 2020). However, intent schemas often fail when context shifts abruptly across turns (Chen et al., 2021). Discourse-aware encoders model long-range dependencies across utterances with structured attention (Zhang et al., 2020). Turn-level memory networks track evolving needs of the speaker over extended contexts (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2016). Hierarchical transformers remain the dominant backbone due to scalability and transferability (Zhang et al., 2021). Few-shot adaptation is increasingly important for deployment in novel domains with limited annotations (Perez et al., 2021). Domain-adaptive pretraining on conversational corpora yields notable gains for empathy recognition (Gururangan et al., 2020). Safety and sensitivity constraints complicate optimization objectives for empathetic responses (Gehman et al., 2020). Researchers have proposed controllable generation to regulate affirmation, advice, and reframing moves (Keskar et al., 2019; Yang and Klein, 2021). Nevertheless, balancing specificity with a nonjudgmental tone remains challenging for current systems. In this work, we build on these insights and motivate a framework that unifies feature transition modeling with intention planning.

Format.document: Examples of the cross-modal learning paradigm. As described in Section 2.1, many existing methods for cross-modal learning adopt modality-independent encoders. This paradigm achieves state-of-the-art retrieval on benchmark datasets across the modality pairs considered in this work: video–text (Bain et al., 2021; Luo et al., 2021), video–audio (Monfort et al., 2021; Rouditchenko et al., 2020), and image–audio (Harwath et al., 2018; Harwath et al., 2020). Although prior works vary in pre-training data, architectures, and objectives, they all employ modality-independent encoders. A key benefit of this paradigm is fixed inference time for retrieval. Because encoders operate independently, embeddings for items in one modality can be computed without any paired inputs. Retrieval then reduces to dot products between modality-specific embeddings. This property supports large-scale retrieval and enables reuse of unimodal embeddings for downstream tasks. Other cross-modal learning frameworks depart from this design. Some methods embed cross-modal relations within the encoders rather than keeping them independent. In (Monfort et al., 2021), this has been realized with cross-modal encoders (Lei et al., 2021; Luo et al., 2021) and with cross-modal attention mechanisms (Miech et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019a; Liu et al., 2019b; Gabeur et al., 2020). However, such interactions increase retrieval complexity because each instance in one modality must be paired with every instance in the other to compute embeddings. With m and n samples, the complexity grows from O(m + n) to O(mn). These interactions also complicate analysis of unimodal representations and hinder single-modality downstream tasks. Our framework preserves light-weight retrieval via independent encoders while enabling cross-modal interaction through a learned codebook and a Cross-Modal Code Matching objective. Uncovering semantic-level correspondences is a central motivation. Image–audio models discover spoken words and visual objects without supervision via retrieval tasks (Synnaeve et al., 2014; Harwath and Glass, 2015; Harwath et al., 2017; Kamper et al., 2018), and the resulting audio embeddings cluster into word-like units (Harwath and Glass, 2017; Wang and Hasegawa-Johnson, 2019; Harwath et al., 2020). Video–audio models can relate spoken words to visual objects and actions (Boggust et al., 2019; Rouditchenko et al., 2020), and our approach extends these ideas to video–text by learning a shared, modality-invariant space.

Format.document: Research efforts on monolingual ED are extensive and varied. Hand-crafted, feature-based, languagespecific methods were the basis of early ED approaches (Ahn, 2006;Ji and Grishman, 2008;Patwardhan and Riloff, 2009;Liao and Grishman, 2010a,b;Hong et al., 2011;McClosky et al., 2011;Li et al., 2013;Miwa et al., 2014;Yang and Mitchell, 2016). More recent efforts have primarily made use of deep learning techniques such as convolutional neural networks (Nguyen and Grishman, 2015;Chen et al., 2015;Nguyen et al., 2016b), recurrent neural networks (Nguyen et al., 2016a;Sha et al., 2018;Nguyen andNguyen, 2019), graph convolutional networks (Nguyen andGrishman, 2018a;Yan et al., 2019), adversarial networks (Hong et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2019b), and pre-trained language models (Wadden et al., 2019;Zhang et al., 2019a;Yang et al., 2019;Zhang et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2020). Despite these advances, monolingual systems often rely on abundant annotated corpora. This reliance limits portability to domains and languages with scarce supervision. Feature representation has shifted from sparse indicators to contextual embeddings derived from transformers. Such embeddings capture long-range dependencies crucial for modeling event triggers and arguments. However, architectural choices interact with training data scale and task-specific objectives in nontrivial ways. Works on cross-lingual ED are not as prevalent and generally make use of cross-lingual resources employed to address the differences between languages such as bilingual dictionaries or parallel corpora (Muis et al., 2018;Liu et al., 2019) and, more recently, pre-trained multilingual language models (M'hamdi et al., 2019;Hambardzumyan et al., 2020;Majewska et al., 2021). Cross-lingual ED seeks to transfer knowledge from resource-rich to low-resource languages without extensive annotation. Projection-based methods align annotations across parallel texts but are sensitive to alignment errors. Dictionary-based methods reduce vocabulary gaps yet struggle with polysemy and morphology. Pre-trained multilingual encoders provide shared subword spaces that facilitate zero-shot transfer. Nevertheless, tokenization granularity and script diversity still induce performance disparities. Unlike these previous efforts, our method leverages unlabeled data to further refine the language-invariant qualities of the language models. Adversarial Language Adaptation, inspired by models in domain adaptation research (Ganin and Lempitsky, 2015;Naik and Rose, 2020), has been successfuly applied at generating languageinvariant models (Joty et al., 2017;Chen et al., 2018). Our method improves upon these approaches optimizing the adversarial training process by selecting the most informative examples from the unlabeled data. We hypothesize that hard examples sampled from unlabeled corpora better expose spurious correlations in the encoder. By iteratively updating the discriminator and the sampler, we encourage the encoder to suppress language-specific cues. For sequence-to-sequence formulations of ED, T5-style models provide a flexible scaffolding for generation Raffel et al., 2019). This strategy reduces overfitting to high-resource typologies and leads to more stable transfer. Complementary to adversarial learning, consistency regularization across stochastic augmentations further enforces invariance. While prior ED work has explored data augmentation, few studies explicitly target cross-lingual consistency constraints. In addition, multilingual pre-training objectives are often generic and not tailored to event structure. To bridge this gap, we incorporate trigger-aware masking that biases the encoder toward event-relevant contexts. We also adopt lightweight adapters to decouple language-specific and task-specific parameters within the shared backbone. Recent evidence suggests that prompt-based conditioning can align label semantics across languages more effectively than task-specific heads. Nonetheless, purely generative decoding may hallucinate triggers when retrieval cues are weak. To mitigate this risk, we combine span extraction with constrained generation under a joint objective. Additional examples of downstream applications of cross-lingual learning are document classification (Holger and Xian, 2018), named entity recognition (Xie et al., 2018) and part-of-speech tagging (Cohen et al., 2011). For a thorough review on cross-lingual learning, we refer the reader to Pikuliak et al. (2021).

Format.document:
Early computational models of visual attention proposed bottom-up mechanisms for pre-attentive selection from visual input (Koch and Ullman, 1985). The notion of a central saliency map subsequently formalized how conspicuity guides gaze across scenes (Niebur and Koch, 1996). A long-standing hypothesis, often referred to as Yarbus’s theorem, holds that task demands shape fixation patterns (Yarbus, 1967). Empirical tests have yielded mixed evidence for this claim across tasks and datasets (Greene et al., 2012; Henderson et al., 2013; Borji and Itti, 2014). With deep learning, features from pre-trained convolutional backbones combined with learned readouts now dominate saliency prediction benchmarks (Kümmerer et al., 2016). These advances have enabled modeling of complex cross-modal gaze behaviors in captioning, question answering, and referring expressions (Sugano and Bulling, 2016; Das et al., 2016; Vasudevan et al., 2018). Nevertheless, many models emphasize image statistics while underrepresenting top-down, goal-driven components of attention (Borji and Itti, 2014). Bridging bottom-up and top-down factors remains a central challenge for general-purpose saliency modeling (Henderson et al., 2013).

Predicting gaze during reading has a parallel history that emphasizes linguistic and cognitive constraints on eye movements (Rayner, 1998). Classical approaches formulate saccade generation probabilistically using lexical, syntactic, and positional features (Feng, 2006; Hara et al., 2012; Matthies and Søgaard, 2013; Hahn and Keller, 2016). Alternatives treat scanning as token-to-token transitions over structured text graphs (Nilsson and Nivre, 2009; Haji-Abolhassani and Clark, 2014; Coutrot et al., 2017). Recent work leverages contextualized language representations as predictors of fixation probabilities and durations (Sood et al., 2020a). These models raise important questions about psychological plausibility and the mapping between internal states and observed gaze (Hahn and Keller, 2016). In addition, domain shift between curated corpora and in-the-wild reading can degrade prediction quality (Matthies and Søgaard, 2013). Joint modeling of text difficulty, reader proficiency, and task has emerged as a promising direction for robust inference (Barrett et al., 2018). However, few studies compare like-for-like reading of the same material under distinct task demands at scale (Wenzel et al., 2017).

Beyond analysis, gaze is increasingly used to supervise or regularize NLP models for downstream tasks (Barrett and Søgaard, 2015a). In sequence labeling, auxiliary losses that encourage human-like attention distributions can improve generalization (Barrett and Søgaard, 2015b; Barrett et al., 2018). Supervision from fixation times has aided sentence compression and summarization by steering models toward informative tokens (Klerke et al., 2016). Similar strategies yield gains for sentiment analysis when attention aligns with affect-bearing expressions, as shown in (Mishra et al., 2017). Work on reading comprehension integrates scanpaths to calibrate passage highlighting and question focus (Malmaud et al., 2020). Some studies also report benefits in multimodal tasks where eye movements anchor alignments between words and visual regions (Das et al., 2016). Despite these advances, many efforts repurpose free-viewing data without tailoring collection to the target task (Coutrot et al., 2017). This mismatch motivates experimental designs that manipulate goals, incentives, and time pressure to elicit task-specific gaze patterns (Hillen et al., 2013).

Moving from natural to task-specific reading, researchers combine eye tracking with neuroimaging to study control mechanisms (Wenzel et al., 2017). EEG and fMRI reveal distinct signatures for syntactic parsing, semantic integration, and anomaly detection during reading (Choi et al., 2014; Hillen et al., 2013). Complementary work localizes attention to text segments most diagnostic for identifying entities, relations, and discourse links (Loboda et al., 2011; Wenzel et al., 2017). Comparisons between natural reading and pseudo-reading clarify how lexical semantics and syntax constrain fixation sequences (Hillen et al., 2013; Choi et al., 2014). However, comprehensive evaluations across classical NLP tasks using matched materials are still scarce (Barrett et al., 2018). Our perspective is that targeted collection protocols are necessary to characterize goal-dependent gaze strategies. Such protocols should standardize stimuli, balance difficulty, and measure compliance to reduce confounds (Rayner, 1998). They should also make datasets publicly available with aligned text, tokenization, and robust metadata for reuse (Sood et al., 2020a). These steps would enable principled tests of whether task-driven reading yields predictable and exploitable differences in fixation behavior.

Format.document: Few-shot learning is often tackled by meta learning (Li and Zhang, 2021; Bansal et al., 2020; Sharaf et al., 2020), data augmentation (Arthaud et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2019), and prompt-based fine-tuning (Gao et al., 2021; Tam et al., 2021; Schick and Schütze, 2021). Basu et al. (2021) apply contrastive learning in semi-supervised intent classification by enforcing consistency across augmented views. Despite promising results, many approaches rely on large auxiliary corpora that blur the boundary between few-shot and fully supervised settings (Perez et al., 2021; Min et al., 2022). This paper examines how to reduce such reliance while preserving strong inductive biases through lightweight adaptation. Meta-learning methods aim to learn initialization or metrics that generalize across tasks, exemplified by gradient-based frameworks and prototypical classifiers (Finn et al., 2017; Snell et al., 2017). However, their episodic training can be mismatched to downstream fine-tuning regimes, leading to brittle performance when task distributions shift (Chen et al., 2019; Triantafillou et al., 2020). Data augmentation offers complementary benefits by expanding support around scarce examples through paraphrasing, back-translation, and hallucinated labels (Xie et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2019). Yet, synthetic data often amplifies artifacts and label noise, necessitating robust objectives and sample selection heuristics (Wei and Zou, 2019; Wu et al., 2021). Prompt-based tuning reformulates classification as masked token prediction, which can align pretraining and downstream objectives to improve data efficiency (Schick and Schütze, 2021; Gao et al., 2021). Nevertheless, prompts can be brittle across domains, and verbalizer choices interact subtly with class priors and calibration (Holtzman et al. 2021; Zhao et al., 2021). Several studies combine these strands by coupling prompts with meta-learned initializations or contrastive regularizers to stabilize gradients in the low-data regime (Lester et al., 2021; Aghajanyan et al., 2021). In parallel, retrieval-augmented learners exploit external corpora to ground predictions, but can inadvertently leak label semantics when not carefully filtered (Guu et al., 2020; Khandelwal et al., 2021). Evaluation protocols further complicate comparisons, as hyperparameter search budgets and choice of validation episodes significantly affect outcomes (Musgrave et al., 2020; Dodge et al., 2019). To mitigate variance, recent benchmarks advocate fixed seeds, stratified episode sampling, and pre-registered ablation plans (Rahimi and Recht, 2017; Bouthillier et al., 2021). Cross-lingual few-shot transfer introduces additional challenges due to script diversity and morphological richness, which strain subword tokenizers and degrade alignment (Hu et al., 2020; Lauscher et al., 2020). For structured prediction, span-based learners and constrained decoders show promise but demand careful calibration to prevent degenerate spans in extremely low-resource settings (Straková et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021). We build on these insights by proposing a simple training recipe that integrates instance reweighting with curriculum-based prompt selection. Our approach emphasizes reproducibility through transparent reporting of data provenance, search space, and compute costs (Henderson et al., 2018; Schwartz et al., 2020). In contrast to prior work that tunes dozens of prompt templates, we adopt a small, human-audited pool and learn a distribution over candidates. Multilingual Pre-Training mBERT and XLM-R train multilingual MLM without using any parallel corpus and show strong cross-lingual ability. mBERT is an extension of BERT which is pre-trained on Wikipedia data over 100 languages to learn a language-invariant feature space shared across multiple languages. XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020a) is trained on 2.5T data over 100 languages extracted from Common Crawl (Wenzek et al., 2020), which demonstrates the effect of the model trained on a large-scale corpus. Results of XLM-R on a large number of downstream cross-lingual tasks show that a large-scale training corpus can significantly improve the performance of multilingual models.

Other methods use parallel corpus in multilingual pre-training. XLM (Conneau and Lample, 2019) introduces a Translation Language Model (TLM) based on the parallel corpus which shows significant improvement on downstream tasks. Unicoder (Huang et al., 2019) introduces a multitask learning framework to learn cross-lingual representations with monolingual and parallel corpora, achieving further gains. ALM (Yang et al., 2020) allows the model to learn cross-lingual code-switch sentences, enhancing the transfer ability. Recent studies INFOXLM (Chi et al., 2021), HICTL , VECO and ERNIE-M (Ouyang et al., 2021) use contrastive learning, back translation and other tricks further enhancing the performance of the multilingual model. Our work focus on studying the model only with multilingual MLM, and leave the study of works with parallel data as future work.

Probing Multilingual MLM mBERT and XLM-R have successfully achieved excellent crosslingual transfer performance without using any parallel corpus. Researchers have wondered what the source of this cross-lingual ability is. Pires et al., 2019) examines the zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on NER (Pan et al., 2017) and part-ofspeech (POS) tagging. They believe this success comes from the shared anchor words between languages. Not coincidentally, similar conclusion is reached by (Wu and Dredze, 2019). However, this conclusion is proven inaccurate by (Conneau et al., 2020b;K et al., 2020). Their experiments show that the model still learns cross-lingual transfer ability on the corpus without anchor words at all. Besides, (Conneau et al., 2020b;K et al., 2020;Artetxe et al., 2020;Libovický et al., 2020;Muller et al., 2021) have analyzed the cross-lingual ability of multilingual masked language models in terms of language similarity, shared model parameters cross languages, model structure, training objectives, language marker. The results suggest that structure similarity and shared parameters between languages are crucial for cross-lingual transfer. In this paper, we focus on analyzing language struc-ture. We decompose it into constituent order, composition, and word co-occurrence and study the effect of each part separately. We begin by situating our study within prior analyses of typological distance and lexical overlap. Cross-lingual transfer has been shown to degrade when word order diverges substantially between source and target languages. Yet, disentangling order from morphology remains challenging in massively multilingual encoders. To address this, we design probing datasets that systematically permute constituent order while holding lexical content constant. We complement these probes with measurements of mutual information between tokens under different masking regimes. Our experiments consider families with contrasting basic word orders, including SVO, SOV, and VSO languages. We further analyze the role of subword segmentation by comparing shared and language-specific tokenizers. In addition, we assess whether representational alignment arises primarily in deeper layers or is already present near the embedding layer. Following standard practice, we report zero-shot and translate-train baselines alongside language-balanced fine-tuning. We also control for domain effects by sampling newswire, encyclopedic, and web forum corpora for evaluation. Finally, we ablate pretraining data size to examine whether structural generalization scales with additional multilingual text. These analyses clarify how architectural bias and training signals interact to yield robust cross-lingual structure sharing.

Format.document: Non-autoregressive TTS has advanced rapidly in recent years. These systems aim to synthesize natural speech with high efficiency and strong fidelity by eliminating autoregressive decoding. A typical non-autoregressive pipeline maps text to acoustic features or waveforms without factorizing output probabilities across time. Early representatives such as FastSpeech (Ren et al., 2019) and ParaNet (Peng et al., 2019) depend on knowledge distillation from an autoregressive teacher. Subsequent models including FastPitch (Lancucki, 2021), AlignTTS (Zeng et al., 2020), and FastSpeech 2 (Ren et al., 2021) remove the reliance on teacher models while improving controllability. Our work adopts FastSpeech 2 as the backbone non-autoregressive synthesizer. FastSpeech 2 replaces teacher-forced duration targets with supervised alignment derived from frame-to-phoneme boundaries under a mean squared error objective. In addition, it introduces explicit predictors for pitch and energy at the encoder side, trained with ground-truth contours and amplitude statistics. These auxiliary predictors inject prosodic cues that enhance naturalness and expressiveness in the synthesized speech. Beyond architectural choices, linguistic context from large language models has emerged as a complementary source of prosody information. Prior studies argue that prosody can be inferred from lexical and syntactic cues in both the current utterance and its neighbors, as argued by Shen et al. 2018. Such contextual signals are naturally captured by pre-trained LMs like BERT (Devlin et al., 2019). Several works have integrated BERT embeddings at the word or subword level into autoregressive TTS pipelines to improve pronunciation, disambiguation, and phrasing (Shen et al., 2018; Fang et al., 2019). Recent studies extend this idea to non-autoregressive settings by conditioning duration, pitch, and energy predictors on contextualized features. Others exploit chunked or paired sentence patterns derived from BERT to inject discourse-level information into the acoustic encoder. Graph-based encoders that use BERT vectors as node features have been proposed to capture word-to-word relations that correlate with emphasis and rhythm. In parallel, variational autoencoders provide a principled mechanism to model residual prosodic variability beyond deterministic predictors. VAEs introduce latent variables intended to capture style, speaking rate, or emphasis that are not fully determined by text. Training maximizes a variational lower bound on the data likelihood that trades off reconstruction fidelity and prior regularization. The reparameterization trick yields low-variance gradients that enable end-to-end optimization with stochastic latent sampling. Practical techniques such as KL annealing, free bits, and β-weighting help balance reconstruction quality against posterior collapse. For TTS, conditioning the VAE on phonetic, lexical, and speaker attributes improves disentanglement and controllability. When combined with duration-based regulators in non-autoregressive models, latent prosody variables can reduce timing errors and stabilize training. However, improper weighting of the KL term or overly expressive decoders may still lead to degenerate latents that fail to carry prosodic information. Recent advances introduce hierarchical priors, normalizing-flow posteriors, or vector-quantized bottlenecks to preserve informative latents under strong decoders. Building on these insights, we propose a conditional VAE module that operates over FastSpeech 2 encoder states to capture residual prosody. We further incorporate BERT-derived context features to condition both the prior and the decoder, aligning latent structure with linguistic cues (Devlin et al., 2019). Together, these components yield a unified framework that targets efficient synthesis, context-aware expressiveness, and robust prosody control.

Format.document: We investigate overfitting that emerges when pruning is applied under the pretrain-and-finetune paradigm and propose sparse progressive distillation to mitigate it. Our approach unifies parameter sparsification with staged knowledge transfer to preserve generalization while reducing compute. We demonstrate the benefits of the framework through targeted ablation studies that isolate the effect of each component. We validate the method on six datasets from the GLUE benchmark spanning diverse linguistic phenomena. To assess cross-task applicability, we include both single-sentence and sentence-pair classification settings. Experimental results show that our models outperform strong baselines by a substantial margin under matched training budgets. Network pruning has long been studied as a means to reduce inference cost without degrading accuracy. In (Han et al., 2015, 2016) the foundational line of work on magnitude pruning and compression was established. The lottery ticket hypothesis suggests that sparse subnetworks can match the accuracy of dense models when trained in isolation (Frankle and Carbin, 2018). Subsequent empirical comparisons indicate that large sparse models often outperform small dense models when parameter counts are matched (Zhu and Gupta, 2018). However, directly applying pruning after large-scale pretraining and task-specific finetuning can exacerbate overfitting, particularly on limited downstream data. This observation motivates distillation-guided pruning strategies that regularize the student during sparsification. Knowledge distillation transfers inductive biases from a high-capacity teacher to a compact student using soft targets and intermediate hints (Hinton et al., 2015). Extensions that adapt temperature schedules and stage-wise supervision further stabilize training under capacity gaps (Mirzadeh et al., 2020). Distillation has been used to learn universal language representations from large unlabeled corpora, enabling efficient transfer to many tasks (Sanh et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020). Yet, state-of-the-art approaches struggle to retain performance when extreme sparsity is imposed, for example at fewer than ten percent remaining weights. In such regimes, naïvely distilled students tend to collapse on harder GLUE tasks even when dense teachers are strong. Progressive learning seeks to reduce optimization shock by updating the student module by module while referencing the teacher. One dual-stage distillation scheme progressively grafts student components into the teacher network and targets few-shot transfer with limited unlabeled data, reporting promising results on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Another line gradually increases the probability of replacing each teacher module with its student counterpart and optimizes the student to mimic teacher behavior (Xu et al., 2020). While these strategies improve stability, evidence on large Transformer encoders remains limited. Moreover, when pruning is coupled with progressive replacement, we observe sharp drops at moderate sparsity levels around fifty percent, indicating insufficient regularization. Our sparse progressive distillation addresses this gap by interleaving structured pruning with stage-aligned supervision from the teacher. At each stage, we prune to a target sparsity, distill both logits and selected intermediate features, and briefly rewind to maintain stable optimization. This procedure mitigates overfitting induced by abrupt capacity reduction and preserves calibration across tasks. We provide comprehensive ablations that separate the effects of sparsity schedules, feature matching, and rewind depth. Across GLUE tasks, the method consistently improves over magnitude pruning, lottery-ticket style reinitialization, and vanilla distillation under equal sparsity budgets. Taken together, the results support sparse progressive distillation as an effective recipe for compressing pretrained Transformers without sacrificing downstream robustness.

Format.document: Prechelt (1998) experimented on 14 different validation-based stop criteria. Prechelt (1998) focused on an issue that the validation error during training may represent many local minima prior to a global optimum. Existing non-validation stop-criteria are generally based on statistical inference. Duvenaud et al. (2016) interpreted stochastic gradient descent in terms of variational inference and proposed an estimation of the marginal likelihood used for early stopping. However, this approach requires costly Hessian computations that are impractical for large models (Duvenaud et al., 2016; Lee and Chung, 2021. Mahsereci et al. (2017) introduced evidence-based stopping, which monitors gradient statistics to decide when to halt training. The EB-criterion relies on fast-to-compute local indicators that reflect whether sample gradients fall within an expected range. Intrinsic dimensionality (ID) has been used to analyze learning dynamics and redundancy in neural networks (Amsaleg et al., 2015). A local variant, LID, estimates subspace dimensionality around samples and can be deployed with unlabeled data. Lee and Chung (2021) reported that LID performs competitively as a stopping rule in few-shot image classification. Another approach pre-estimates the training horizon via repeated runs or cross-validation, then applies a pre-estimated stop epoch for full training (Choi and Lee, 2021). Despite these advances, most methods have not been systematically assessed for NLP tasks, nor do they directly account for task metrics during training. Moreover, comparative studies among non-validation criteria remain scarce, leaving open questions about robustness and data efficiency. In this study, we benchmark EB, LID, PE, and standard validation-based stopping across five text classification datasets. Our evaluation protocol treats split selection, model initialization, and metric tracking uniformly to ensure fairness across methods. For completeness, we considered likelihood-based early stopping derived from variational interpretations, but excluded it due to its computational overhead. To provide a practical baseline, we also detail a simple training protocol that selects hyperparameters on a small hold-out set and then fixes them for the final run. Throughout, we compare against prior validation-oriented heuristics, including original recipes and early empirical protocols (Duvenaud et al. 2016), to contextualize gains on modern architectures.

Format.document: We first review standard approaches to countering hate and studies on counter-narrative effectiveness on social media, then outline data collection and generation strategies. Hate countering has emerged at the intersection of computational social science and NLP, motivated by the limitations of pure moderation. NLP has addressed the proliferation of hate speech through supervised detection datasets (Mathew et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2018; Waseem, 2016). Surveys synthesize these approaches and discuss ethical risks in deployment (Poletto et al., 2020; Schmidt and Wiegand, 2017; Nunes and Fortuna, 2018; Kiritchenko et al., 2020). However, detection alone risks overblocking legitimate speech and encoding demographic biases (Binns et al., 2017; Davidson et al., 2019; Sap et al., 2019; Vidgen and Derczynski, 2020). In response, NGOs and platforms are experimenting with counter-narratives that reframe discourse rather than suppress it (Benesch, 2014; Silverman et al., 2016; Schieb and Preuss, 2016). Empirical studies report reductions in hostile tone and improved bystander engagement after targeted replies (Mathew et al., 2019; Gagliardone et al., 2015). Effects are heterogeneous across communities and topics, underscoring the need for tailored strategies (Allison and Bussey, 2016; Anderson et al., 2014). Messaging style, source credibility, and timing have emerged as key mediators in online settings (Munger, 2017; Myers West, 2018). Prior framing research indicates that appeals to shared identities can lower defensiveness (Pinker, 2011; Cialdini, 2007). Consistent with this view, experimental manipulations of empathy and politeness have shown measurable shifts in conversational dynamics (Lee, 2019; Kim et al.). Yet automated CN generation must balance persuasive goals with safety, transparency, and user autonomy (Kiritchenko et al., 2020; Vidgen et al., 2021). Existing CN datasets combine expert-authored replies with curated social media threads to capture realistic adversarial contexts (Qian et al., 2019; Chung et al., 2020). Annotation protocols often encode intent, target, and strategy labels to facilitate analysis (Mathew et al., 2021; Fortuna et al., 2020). However, coverage remains skewed toward English and Western platforms, limiting generalizability (Zampieri et al., 2019; Davidson et al., 2017). Crowdsourcing introduces scale but can dilute strategic nuance without careful quality control (Hovy and Spruit, 2016; Snow et al., 2008). Semi-automated mining of responses from public campaigns augments corpora while preserving authentic style (Chung et al., 2020; Laugier et al., 2021). Privacy constraints and platform policies further complicate longitudinal outcome tracking (Fiesler and Proferes, 2018; Salganik, 2017). Early CN systems relied on retrieval and template filling over topic-specific repositories (Qian et al., 2019; Hua et al., 2019). Neural architectures shifted the focus to conditional generation with style and stance control (Zhang et al., 2020; Krause et al., 2021). Training objectives incorporate toxicity avoidance, politeness enhancement, and factuality constraints (Rashkin et al., 2018; Niu and Bansal, 2018). Multi-task setups jointly learn hate detection and response generation to share representations (Mozafari et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019). Several works integrate pragmatic cues Lee et al., 2019; Rezaee and Ferraro, 2021) to better align responses with conversational context. Beyond sentence-level signals, discourse and thread structures help model reply salience and timing (Zhang et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2017). Evaluation remains challenging because automatic metrics correlate weakly with human judgments of effectiveness (Novikova et al., 2017; Lowe et al., 2017). Recent studies combine offline text quality with online A/B trials measuring engagement and toxicity change (Gao et al., 2018; Jhaver et al., 2019). Safety layers filter generated outputs for slurs, implicit insults, and targeted harassment before deployment (Vidgen et al., 2021; Gehman et al., 2020). Bias audits examine disparate impact across demographic groups to prevent uneven burdens (Blodgett et al., 2020; Dixon et al., 2018). Explanation interfaces can clarify intent and allow recipients to contest or opt out of interventions (Binns et al., 2018; Eiband et al., 2018). Human-in-the-loop designs situate models as drafting assistants that experts curate and adapt to local norms (Hancock et al., 2019; Chilton et al., 2016). Open challenges include multilingual adaptation, emergent hate tropes, and coordinated response at scale (Zampieri et al., 2020; Ousidhoum et al., 2021). Cross-domain transfer remains brittle when topic, platform, or register shifts are large (Miller et al., 2020; Gururangan et al., 2020). Causal evaluation frameworks are needed to isolate the specific contribution of counter-narratives amid confounders (Imbens and Rubin, 2015; Egami et al., 2018). Partnerships with civil society can surface context-rich strategies and culturally grounded scripts (Benesch, 2014; Mathew et al., 2019). We position our work within this line by focusing on controllable generation and policy-aware evaluation for real-world use. The following review synthesizes prior evidence and clarifies how our modeling choices address these gaps.
