Format.document:
Quality Estimation Current SOTA models in sentence-level QE, which is typically framed as a regression task, mainly use multilingual representations from pre-trained transformers (Devlin et al., 2018), notably XLM-R Conneau et al., 2019). The input to a sentence-level QE model is a concatenation of the source and translated sentences, separated by the [SEP] token. The sequence is encoded by the pre-trained Transformer model, and the [CLS] token is passed through a multilayer perceptron (MLP) layer to obtain a sentence-level score. During fine-tuning both the parameters of the pre-trained model and the parameters corresponding to the MLP layer are updated.

Word-level QE is typically addressed as a binary classification task, where the QE model needs to predict a binary label indicating whether a word is correct or wrong for each word in the MT output (Lee, 2020). As illustrated in Figure (left), some supervised approaches use both sentence-level and word-level objectives in a multi-task setting, which results in superior performance (Kim et al., 2017;Lee, 2020). Methods that do not require word-level training data either need access to the MT model (Rikters and Fishel, 2017;Fomicheva et al., 2020b), or still treat the problem as a supervised task but use synthetically generated data for supervision (Tuan et al., 2021).

Rationale Extraction for NLP SOTA NLP models based on deep neural networks achieve high performance in a variety of tasks, often at the cost of interpretability (Lipton, 2016). Recent work aims to address this issue by focusing on two different goals. On the one hand, the aim is to produce justifications for model predictions that are plausible to the users, in order to increase users' trust (Ribeiro et al., 2016). On the other hand, the aim is to reveal the inner workings of the model and faithfully explain its predictions, so the explanation can be useful to model developers (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020).

Typically, explainability methods operate by selecting a portion of the input that justifies model prediction for a single data point. This can be done either by modifying the model architecture, or by trying to explain the predictions of a given model. The first type of approaches (a.k.a. rationalization by construction) involves imposing restrictions on the generated rationales to satisfy certain constraints, e.g. compactness (Yu et al., 2019; Chalkidis et al., 2021. Note that such restrictions often result in lower performance and indeed are not guaranteed to explain the behaviour of an unconstrained model (Jain et al., 2020). The second type of approaches (the so called post hoc) usually rely on feature attribution methods, which assign an importance value to each input feature of a network (Sundararajan et al., 2017;Schulz et al., 2020). These methods do not allow for introducing useful biases during training, but focus on faithfully explaining model behaviour.

Feature attribution has a long tradition in image recognition tasks (Simonyan et al., 2013) and only recently have been applied to some NLP tasks, most commonly text classification (DeYoung et al., 2019). QE is fundamentally different from text classification where clues are typically separate words or phrases (Zaidan et al., 2007) which often can be considered independently of the rest of the text. This independence assumption does not hold for the task of evaluating translation quality where a word cannot be identified as a clue (e.g. translation error) without considering the surrounding context. Furthermore, SOTA NLP models based on contextualized representations for input words make rationale extraction especially challenging, as the representation for a given word can encode not only the word identity but also its interactions with other words in the text. Recent work has revealed various interesting properties that characterize the information flow through hidden layers in deep transformer models (Voita et al., 2019;De Cao et al., 2020;Yun et al., 2021). We provide additional insights on this topic in Section 5.2. We summarize implications for downstream evaluation in Section 6.

Format.document: Synthetic translations have become a central tool for improving neural machine translation (NMT) by leveraging abundant monolingual data. Prior work distinguishes forward translation, which translates source monolingual text into the target to create pseudo-parallel pairs, from back-translation, which translates target monolingual text back into the source to augment training data (Zhang and Zong, 2016;Sennrich et al., 2016a). These strategies have repeatedly improved generalization in low-resource and domain-mismatched scenarios (Edunov et al., 2018;Caswell et al., 2019). Beyond simple augmentation, several studies repurpose synthetic translations to reshape the training distribution and stabilize learning. For example, researchers generate multiple candidate translations for each side of a sentence and combine them with authentic bitext to train robust ensembles (Nguyen et al., 2020;Jiao et al., 2020). Another influential line frames synthetic data as a vehicle for sequence-level knowledge distillation, where a strong teacher produces translations that a smaller student model can imitate (Kim and Rush, 2016). Such distillation has proven particularly helpful for non-autoregressive and semi-autoregressive architectures that benefit from smoother targets (Gu et al., 2017;Ghazvininejad et al., 2019). A commonly hypothesized explanation is that distilled outputs reduce sequence-level entropy and prune spurious modes, making optimization easier (Zhou et al., 2019a;Xu et al., 2021). Nevertheless, synthetic data are not a panacea, and their efficacy depends on data selection, model capacity, and noise control. Quality filtering of mined or generated sentences remains crucial to prevent domain drift and exposure bias amplification (Koehn et al., 2018;Wenzek et al., 2020). In domain adaptation, synthetic translations offer a practical bridge between scarce in-domain bitext and plentiful in-domain monolingual corpora (Chu and Wang, 2018). Beyond supervised settings, synthetic supervision also underpins unsupervised and weakly supervised MT by creating cross-lingual signals through iterative self-training (Lample et al., 2018b;Artetxe et al., 2018). The interplay between synthetic data and pretraining has further reshaped the NMT landscape, as large pretrained encoders and decoders can be fine-tuned more effectively when guided by curated pseudo-parallel examples (Conneau and Lample, 2019;Liu et al., 2020). At the same time, over-reliance on synthetic pairs may entrench translationese artifacts that harm downstream performance if not carefully mitigated (Edunov et al., 2020). Recent research thus emphasizes data diversification, curriculum design, and dynamic sampling to balance authenticity and syntheticity throughout training (Wang et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2019). In parallel, advances in tokenization, denoising objectives, and multilingual transfer have interacted synergistically with synthetic pipelines. For instance, subword regularization and noising during decoding can broaden coverage while maintaining fluency in pseudo-targets (Kudo, 2018;He et al., 2020). Moreover, multilingual pretraining helps propagate improvements from high-resource directions to low-resource ones when combined with targeted back-translation (Aharoni et al., 2019;Tang et al., 2020). Despite these successes, open questions persist regarding how much synthetic data to generate, how to schedule its introduction, and how to evaluate its marginal utility across domains. Empirical studies suggest diminishing returns beyond certain ratios of synthetic to authentic pairs, yet the break-even point varies with task difficulty and architecture (Ott et al., 2018;Nguyen et al., 2020). There is also debate about whether iterative back-translation saturates too quickly or continues to yield steady improvements under stronger teachers (Hoang et al., 2018;Popel et al., 2020). On the evaluation side, reliance on BLEU alone may obscure gains in adequacy or terminology that synthetic methods can deliver, motivating broader metrics and human studies (Post, 2018;Mathur et al., 2020). From a systems perspective, generating, filtering, and retraining on synthetic data introduces additional compute and engineering complexity that must be justified by consistent gains. Practical pipelines therefore integrate lightweight data selection, caching, and asynchronous generation to amortize costs over multiple training runs (Junczys-Dowmunt, 2018;Schwenk et al., 2021). In our study, we revisit synthetic translation strategies through the lens of model capacity, data source heterogeneity, and feedback-enabled generation. We compare conventional single-pass back-translation with iterative, quality-aware loops that exploit uncertainty estimates and constrained decoding (Edunov et al., 2018;Kumar and Sarawagi, 2019). We also examine how the presence of pretrained sequence encoders changes the optimal balance between authentic and synthetic supervision. To that end, we assess teacher choice and student receptivity when initializing with large-scale contextual representations like BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) and mBART (Liu et al., 2020b). Crucially, we interrogate whether distilled targets overly simplify long-range reordering phenomena, and whether selective reintroduction of original bitext can remedy this effect (Zhou et al., 2019a;Sun et al., 2020). Our experiments span high-resource and mid-resource directions with varied morphology and typology to test generality. We report automatic and human evaluations and analyze error typologies relevant to synthetic data, including literalness, omission, and hallucination (Raunak et al., 2021;Lee et al., 2019). Finally, we situate our findings within the broader shift toward data-centric NMT development and articulate open challenges for scalable, trustworthy augmentation. Together, these results refine practical guidance for using synthetic translations across architectures, data regimes, and domains.

Format.document:
Conversational question answering. In recent years, several conversational question answering datasets have emerged, such as QuAC (Choi et al., 2018), CoQA (Reddy et al., 2019), andDoQA (Campos et al., 2020). Different from singleturn QA datasets (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), CQA requires the model to understand the question in the context of conversational history. There have been many methods proposed to improve CQA performance (Ohsugi et al., 2019;Chen et al., 2020;Qu et al., 2019;Kim et al., 2021) and significant improvement has been made on CQA benchmarks.

Besides text-based CQA tasks, there also exist CQA benchmarks that require other forms of modeling ability, such as combining textual evidence with background knowledge (Saeidi et al., 2018), utilizing structured knowledge base (Saha et al., 2018;Guo et al., 2018), as well as CQA in other modalities (Das et al., 2017).

Evaluation with predicted history. Only recently has it been noticed that the current method of evaluating CQA models is flawed. Mandya et al. (2020); Siblini et al. (2021) point out that using gold answers in history is not consistent with the realworld scenario and propose to use predicted history for evaluation. Different from prior work, in this paper, we conduct a large scale human evaluation to support our claims, identify the issues with predicted history, and propose rewriting questions to further mitigate the gap to human evaluation. Our analysis begins by examining how error propagation from earlier turns degrades reasoning in later turns. We show that even minor lexical changes in the history can trigger large shifts in retrieval, span selection, and unanswerability detection. These effects are amplified in settings with limited context windows, where truncation disproportionately removes early disambiguating cues. To quantify such effects, we compare performance under gold, beam, and sampled histories across multiple model sizes and decoding strategies (Mandya et al., 2020; Siblini et al., 2021. We further ablate the contributions of answer calibration, turn-level confidence, and context weighting to isolate failure modes. The results indicate that robustness varies markedly by dataset, suggesting differences in topic distribution and paraphrase density. We therefore revisit dataset construction practices and recommend balancing dialog depth, entity reoccurrence, and coreference chains. Beyond input noise, we evaluate whether instruction-tuned models internalize dialog conventions that regularize follow-up questions. We find that models trained with iterative rewriting generate questions that are both more specific and more self-contained. This observation motivates a pipeline in which a question rewriter precedes a standard extractive or generative QA model. Crucially, rewriting must preserve answer equivalence while reducing reliance on brittle cross-turn dependencies. We operationalize this requirement through constrained decoding and automatic consistency checks against retrieved passages. Human raters confirm that rewritten questions reduce ambiguity and improve transparency of failure cases. Finally, we discuss practical implications for evaluation leaders, including dataset refresh cycles and standardized predicted-history protocols. We release guidelines and scripts to facilitate adoption of these practices in future CQA benchmarks.

Camburu et al. 2018

Format.document: Natural language inference has become a central testbed for evaluating reasoning in neural models. Alongside accuracy improvements, researchers increasingly seek explanations that justify predictions to human readers. Early work formalized desiderata for faithful and plausible explanations and built benchmark protocols. Pioneering model-agnostic explanation techniques demonstrated the value of local rationales for classification decisions (Ribeiro et al., 2016). Subsequent efforts adapted these ideas to neural architectures for text classification and NLI (Chen et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Thorne et al., 2019). In parallel, domain-specific criteria for interpretability were explored in fact verification and question answering (Kumar and Talukdar, 2020). Feature-based explanations quantify the contribution of inputs or representations through gradients, perturbations, or attention (Li et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2015; Samek et al., 2017). Attention as explanation remains controversial, but its structure can still provide useful diagnostic signals when carefully analyzed (Jiang et al., 2021). Rationale extraction methods aim to highlight minimal subsets of tokens that preserve label predictions under a compactness constraint (Feng et al., 2018; Gururangan et al., 2018). Sentence-level justifications are attractive because they are concise and easy to evaluate with human judgment (Camburu et al., 2018; Talmor et al., 2018). However, most explanation techniques were originally developed as post hoc addons without training-time integration into the predictor. This separation can weaken faithfulness, since the predictor may exploit features that the explainer cannot capture. Joint learning frameworks address this gap by optimizing predictive performance and rationale quality simultaneously. Policy-gradient and continuous relaxation approaches have been proposed for end-to-end rationale selection in NLI (Lei et al., 2016; Bastings et al., 2019). Prior comparisons reported mixed results — Chen et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018 — depending on dataset shifts and training regimes. Building on multi-task training, some works couple label prediction with auxiliary objectives that reward consistency between predicted labels and extracted evidence (Thorne et al., 2019). Contrastive learning has further encouraged explanations that distinguish entailment from contradiction by maximizing margins between counterfactual rationales (Pruthi et al., 2020). From a modeling standpoint, sentence-level evidence can be selected via retrieval over the premise or an external corpus (DeYoung et al., 2020). Retrieval-driven explanations benefit from dense encoders but require calibration to avoid cherry-picked support (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Izacard and Grave, 2021). Evaluation practices for explanations remain unsettled, with tradeoffs between automatic overlap metrics and human studies (Narang and Klein, 2021). To assess faithfulness, causal sufficiency and necessity tests intervene on highlighted tokens and measure output stability (Atanasova et al., 2020). Robustness analyses show that spurious correlations can masquerade as explanations unless models are stress-tested under distribution shifts (Gardner et al., 2021). Recent work emphasizes explanation use as a learning signal rather than a byproduct of prediction (Hase and Bansal, 2020). In NLI, this perspective motivates architectures that exchange information between an inference head and an explanation head during training. Our approach operationalizes this idea via a mutual promotion mechanism that iteratively refines predictions and evidence. Concretely, the evidence selector proposes candidate sentences, the predictor conditions on them, and feedback from prediction updates the selector. This co-training loop resembles expectation–maximization, but it is implemented with differentiable modules for efficiency. We instantiate the selector with a lightweight retriever and the predictor with a pretrained encoder fine-tuned for NLI (Devlin et al., 2019). To mitigate confirmation bias, we regularize against agreement with high-entropy predictions and encourage diversity in selected sentences (Jain et al., 2020). We also integrate calibration objectives so that explanation confidence aligns with predictive uncertainty (Guo et al., 2017). For comparability with prior work, we evaluate on e-SNLI and FEVER and include ablations on training dynamics (Camburu et al., 2018; Thorne et al., 2019). Qualitative analysis illustrates when the mechanism helps, especially on long premises with multiple plausible supports Camburu et al. 2018. Overall, the results support the claim that tightly coupling inference and explanation can improve accuracy while producing more faithful justifications.

Format.document:
2.1 Security and Privacy Concern of Pre-trained Models

Pre-trained models like BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) and GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) rely on vast plain-text corpora to achieve human-like performance. While these models excel across benchmarks, their deployment raises acute concerns about the handling of sensitive information embedded in training or inference data. Sensitive domains such as clinical notes (Christoph et al., 2015), search logs (Shen et al., 2007), and other personally identifiable information must be protected to meet ethical and regulatory expectations. Beyond obvious leakage through inputs and outputs, trained parameters themselves can memorize rare or unique strings from the underlying data (Carlini et al., 2021). This phenomenon motivates rigorous analysis of privacy risks specific to modern language models and their training pipelines. In parallel, organizations must navigate legal frameworks like GDPR and HIPAA that impose strict requirements on data minimization and accountability (Voigt and Bussche, 2017; McGraw and Pratt, 2014). As a result, there is growing interest in techniques that enable learning from sensitive data without exposing raw content to centralized servers (Konečný et al., 2016; Bonawitz et al., 2019). Threat models studied in the literature include membership inference, where an adversary predicts whether a record was part of the training set (Shokri et al., 2017; Yeom et al., 2018). Property inference attacks attempt to recover aggregate attributes not intended by the task designer (Ganju et al., 2018). Model inversion and reconstruction attacks aim to reveal textual snippets or attributes of individual examples by querying outputs or gradients (Fredrikson et al., 2015; Song and Shmatikov, 2019). Recent work has further shown verbatim extraction of memorized sequences from large generative models using carefully crafted prompts (Carlini et al., 2023). These risks persist even when models are accessed only through APIs, because adversaries can adaptively probe outputs under black-box constraints. One research direction focuses on training-time defenses based on differential privacy, notably DP-SGD, which bounds worst-case disclosure from any single example (Abadi et al., 2016; Dwork et al., 2014). Complementary approaches leverage federated learning with secure aggregation to keep raw data on device while still enabling global optimization (Konečný et al., 2016; Bonawitz et al., 2017). Knowledge transfer via teacher ensembles provides an alternative route through the PATE framework that privatizes labels before training students (Papernot et al., 2017). For text applications, TextHide proposes mixing hidden representations to obscure instance-level details while retaining task signal (Huang et al., 2020). However, TextHide remains better suited to sentence-level classification and struggles with token-level objectives such as named entity recognition (Huang et al., 2020). Due to its mixup mechanism, the method degrades alignment needed for span extraction and semantic role labeling. Another line of work studies differentially private fine-tuning of large language models, but reports substantial utility loss at practical privacy budgets, as shown by Kerrigan et al., 2020 and Yu et al. (2021). In particular, perplexity and downstream task accuracy can deteriorate sharply as noise multipliers increase and clipping thresholds tighten. Hardware-assisted approaches like trusted execution environments and secure enclaves reduce exposure yet still face side-channel and scalability concerns (Hunt et al., 2018; Costan and Devadas, 2016). Cryptographic solutions using homomorphic encryption or secure multiparty computation offer strong guarantees but are costly in latency and energy for long sequences (Acar et al., 2018; Mohassel and Zhang, 2017). Beyond defenses, pre-publication data curation that removes PII and redacts highly unique strings is essential for responsible dataset construction (Dodge et al., 2021). Post-hoc auditing methods aim to detect and quantify memorization, including extraction probes and influence-function based attribution (Feldman, 2020; Koh and Liang, 2017). Recent auditing frameworks also estimate per-example privacy risk under realistic attack models to inform policy decisions (Song et al., 2021). In industry settings, federated evaluation and on-device personalization are combined with guardrails to reduce the chance of emitting sensitive content at inference time (Bonawitz et al., 2019; Apple, 2022). Nevertheless, open questions remain about balancing utility, cost, interpretability, and verifiable privacy in large-scale NLP systems. Our work situates these concerns within the context of pre-trained transformers used for sensitive domains like healthcare and finance. We survey attack surfaces, evaluate representative defenses, and distill practical recommendations for data stewards and model builders. Specifically, we analyze trade-offs among DP-SGD, federated optimization, representation mixing, and selective redaction using standardized tasks and threat models. We also discuss governance mechanisms, including documentation practices and privacy audits, that complement technical safeguards (Mitchell et al., 2019; Raji et al., 2020). Finally, we outline open research directions in scaling privacy techniques to frontier models while preserving competitiveness on real-world workloads. By grounding privacy evaluation in realistic deployments, we aim to inform principled choices for training and serving pre-trained models responsibly.

Format.document: Pretrained language models have transformed multilingual NLP by enabling transfer across languages with limited supervision (Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019). Contextual encoders such as ELMo and BERT learn shared subword statistics that generalize beyond monolingual boundaries (Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019). Multilingual BERT, XLM, and XLM-R demonstrate strong cross-lingual transfer compared to static cross-lingual word embeddings (Pires et al., 2019; Wu and Dredze, 2019). Despite these advances, practitioners still face open questions about scalability, typological coverage, and fairness across scripts (Ruder et al., 2019; Lauscher et al., 2020). Early evidence of zero-shot capabilities came from part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, and NLI benchmarks (Pires et al., 2019. Follow-up studies analyzed when subword overlap, shared alphabets, and domain effects drive transfer rather than deeper semantic alignment (Karthikeyan et al., 2020; Wu and Dredze, 2020). However, the benefits of adding more pretraining languages do not increase monotonically, a phenomenon dubbed the curse of multilinguality (Conneau et al., 2020). This effect suggests that capacity dilution and negative interference can offset gains from broader coverage (Aharoni et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020). In practice, model scaling and data curation strategies can mitigate interference but rarely eliminate it entirely (Xue et al., 2021; Conneau et al., 2020). Our work revisits these dynamics by disentangling seen and unseen languages during pretraining and evaluation. We ask whether zero-shot performance on held-out languages follows the same saturation pattern observed for languages included in the pretraining mix. To this end, we design controlled partitions over language families and scripts while holding constant the pretraining budget. We also examine whether auxiliary objectives such as translation language modeling or contrastive alignment improve transfer without heavy supervision (Lample and Conneau, 2019; Fang et al., 2020). A key challenge is separating lexical memorization from true structural generalization across typologically distant languages (Ponti et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2019). We therefore incorporate diagnostic tasks that stress morphology, word order, and agreement in addition to sentence-level semantics (Liu et al., 2020; Warstadt et al., 2020). Prior work has reported that language identity conditioning and adaptive vocabulary selection can reduce interference for low-resource targets (Bapna and Firat, 2019; Zhao et al., 2020). Complementary evidence shows that continued pretraining on target-language unlabeled data yields sizable gains over pure zero-shot baselines (Gururangan et al., 2020; Chronopoulou et al., 2020). Yet such adaptations may obscure whether a model possesses inherent cross-lingual abstractions or simply benefits from domain proximity (Ke et al., 2020; Artetxe et al., 2020). Our experimental design emphasizes frozen encoders and standardized evaluation to foreground representational quality over fine-tuning tricks. We validate our splits using language relatedness metrics and corpus similarity measures to rule out spurious advantages. We further probe subword overlap to estimate how much lexical sharing explains transfer under different tokenization regimes (Kudo and Richardson, 2018; Bostrom and Durrett, 2020). Notably, we replicate the headline results on multilingual saturation reported in prior work (Conneau et al., 2020). At the same time, we highlight domains where adding training languages degrades performance on typologically distant held-out languages. For background on early cross-lingual evaluations in contextual models, see Pires et al. (2019). Our findings align with the hypothesis that capacity, data balance, and objective choice interact in nontrivial ways to shape transfer (Rust et al., 2021; Pfeiffer et al., 2020). We also contrast our setup with resource-intensive alignment approaches that rely on parallel data or dictionaries (Ruder et al., 2019; Artetxe et al., 2018). Finally, we situate our contributions relative to the original curse of multilinguality study by Conneau et al. 1 and outline open problems in scaling to truly universal models. Taken together, this paper frames a principled agenda for multilingual representation learning that is sensitive to typology, capacity, and evaluation design.

Format.document: We review prior work on visual semantic AI, on the geometry and semantic properties of representations formed by language models, and on semantic intrinsic evaluation tasks. Visual semantic AI investigates how perceptual inputs align with linguistic structure to support reasoning and communication. Early systems focused on supervised image captioning with attention mechanisms that grounded tokens in regions (Xu et al., 2015). Subsequent advances introduced modular reasoning for visual question answering to encourage compositionality (Andreas et al., 2016). Transformer-based multimodal models such as ViLBERT and LXMERT improved cross-modal fusion via co-attention (Lu et al., 2019; Tan and Bansal, 2019). Contrastive pretraining further scaled alignment by pairing images and text from the web (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021). Despite progress, grounding at the level of fine-grained semantics remains brittle in out-of-distribution settings (Hendricks et al., 2018). A complementary literature examines the geometry of language representations that many multimodal systems inherit from text encoders. Foundational work on distributional semantics established vector spaces where analogy structure can be linearly recovered (Mikolov et al., 2013). Later analyses documented anisotropy and frequency effects that distort similarity judgments (Mu and Viswanath, 2018; Ethayarajh, 2019). Sentence-level encoders have been optimized for isotropy and clustering quality using contrastive objectives (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). Probing studies relate representational geometry to syntactic and semantic control tasks (Conneau et al., 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019). Within vision-language research, similar probes test whether learned alignments capture attributes, relations, and compositional templates (Goyal et al., 2017; Cirik et al., 2018). Evaluation practices differ, however, between end-to-end task metrics and intrinsic assessments that isolate properties of the embedding space. Classic intrinsic tasks include word similarity, lexical analogy, and clustering, all of which provide fast feedback about semantic organization (Schnabel et al., 2015; Faruqui et al., 2016). More recent benchmarks target sentence retrieval, paraphrase mining, and structure-aware neighborhood tests for hierarchical concepts; see (cf. Vatswani et al., 2019 for discussion. These approaches illuminate how training objectives shape geometry, but they also reveal tensions between alignment and discrimination. For example, aggressive contrastive learning can compress local neighborhoods and harm fine-grained category boundaries (Wang and Isola, 2020). A strand of work argues for inductive biases that preserve manifold structure during multimodal fusion (Kiros et al., 2014; Ganea et al., 2021). Similarly, research on prompt-based adaptation shows that steering textual encoders can modulate cross-modal transfer without retraining backbones (Lester et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021). Survey papers emphasize the need for evaluation protocols that unify extrinsic and intrinsic views for robust model development (Du et al., 2022). In this study we focus on the intersection of visual grounding and semantic geometry to articulate practical criteria for representation quality. In particular, we synthesize findings on anisotropy mitigation, calibration under shift, and compositional generalization as converging objectives (Gao et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2021). We finally outline open challenges in scalable curation, multilingual grounding, and transparent reporting to guide future benchmarks and methods.

Format.document: Neural machine translation has benefited substantially from pretraining and large-scale parallel corpora. Nevertheless, model predictions can remain brittle when test inputs diverge from the training distribution. Retrieval-augmented translation addresses this gap by consulting example-based memories at inference time. Among these approaches, kNN-MT retrieves nearest neighbors from a datastore built over encoder-decoder states to refine the output distribution. While effective, vanilla kNN-MT relies on a fixed neighborhood size, which can be suboptimal across tokens and contexts. Adaptive kNN-MT introduces a lightweight meta-k network that fuses predictions from multiple k values, aiming to balance precision and robustness. This idea connects to classic instance-based learning while retaining the fluency of neural decoders. In practice, an adaptive scheme must decide how to weigh heterogeneous signals when local retrievals are noisy or sparse. It also contends with the construction of the target-side datastore, whose coverage and density crucially influence performance. Prior analyses show that the optimal k varies with token frequency, domain mismatch, and alignment uncertainty. Moreover, the computational overhead of multiple retrievals per step raises concerns for real-time systems. Recent work proposes compact indexes, approximate search, and selective activation to reduce latency without sacrificing accuracy. Another line of research integrates lexical constraints and translation memories within the same retrieval framework. These developments complement efforts to enhance calibration of the fused distribution with temperature scaling and margin-based reweighting. Despite these advances, there remains limited understanding of how to generalize across domains with heterogeneous retrieval quality. Our review highlights architectural choices that determine robustness, including query representations, neighbor filtering, and value aggregation. In adaptive designs, the meta-k network typically observes features derived from distances, vote counts, and contextual embeddings. It then outputs normalized weights over a candidate set of k values, which are used to interpolate probability distributions, as proposed in Zheng et al., 2021a; Khandelwal et al., 2021). When the validation set is small, regularization and monotonicity priors can stabilize the learned weighting. An orthogonal question concerns how to update or prune the datastore as domains evolve over time. Streaming maintenance strategies prevent catastrophic drift while keeping memory usage bounded. In comparison with alternative external memory methods, adaptive kNN-MT preserves token-level transparency that aids error analysis. For example, analysts can inspect retrieved neighbors to attribute specific lexical choices to concrete exemplars. Nevertheless, naive fusion can overemphasize frequent patterns and underrepresent rare but correct alternatives. Curriculum retrieval and diversity-aware sampling have been explored to mitigate this bias. Empirical studies report consistent gains on benchmarks when adaptively combining neighborhoods across granularities. A representative approach leverages a two-layer feed-forward selector with nonlinear activation to compute fusion coefficients. The selector is trained to minimize translation loss while attending to distance profiles and neighbor counts. Under this paradigm, performance hinges on careful validation of the weighting scheme to avoid degeneracy toward a single k. Related work on cache-based language models and memory-augmented decoders offers complementary insights into temporal locality. Furthermore, efficient approximate nearest neighbor search broadens practical adoption by lowering retrieval costs at scale. Open challenges include principled uncertainty estimation for retrieval contributions and domain-adaptive datastore curation. We also note inconsistencies in reported evaluation protocols that complicate fair comparison across systems. To situate our discussion, we reference both the original kNN-MT formulation and its adaptive extensions described in prior work. Overall, adaptive kNN-MT exemplifies how hybridization of parametric and nonparametric evidence can yield resilient translation.

Format.document:
Early work on simplification relied on rules, e.g., to split or shorten long sentences (Chandrasekar and Srinivas, 1997;Carroll et al., 1998;Vickrey and Koller, 2008). Later work treated simplification as a monolingual phrase-based machine translation (MT) task (Coster and Kauchak, 2011;Wubben et al., 2012), with syntactic information added, such as constituency trees (Zhu et al., 2010). Recent work, reviewed below, leverages neural models in a generative and revision-based manner.

Supervised Generative Methods employ Seq2Seq (Sutskever et al., 2014) models to implicitly learn simplification operations from aligned complex-simple sentence pairs. Inspired by the success of Seq2Seq neural MT models, Nisioi et al. (2017) applied a Seq2Seq model for text simplification. Zhang and Lapata (2017) used reinforcement learning to optimize a reward based on simplicity, fluency and relevance, building on a Seq2Seq model. Recent methods build on transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) models, by integrating external databases containing simplification rules (Zhao et al., 2018), using an additional loss function to generate diverse outputs (Kriz et al., 2019), combining syntactic rules (Maddela et al., 2021), and conditioning on length and syntactic and lexical complexity features (Martin et al., 2020a).

Unsupervised Generative Methods rely on non-aligned complex and simple corpora instead of aligned complex-simple sentence pairs. Zhao et al. (2020) adopted a back-translation framework, whereas Surya et al. (2019) used an unsupervised style transfer paradigm. Martin et al. (2020b) used a pre-trained BART model fine-tuned on a paraphrased sentence pairs.

Controllable Generative Methods produce outputs at specified grade levels (Scarton and Specia, 2018;Nishihara et al., 2019), or apply syntactic or lexical constraints on the generated sentences (Martin et al., 2020a,b). However, these models do not provide any insights into how the simplification process is done and thus lack interpretability.

Supervised Revision-Based Methods use complex-simple sentence pairs to learn where to apply edit operations iteratively. Alva-Manchego et al. (2017) proposed a model using keep, replace, and delete operations. Some recent work used iterative non-autoregressive models to edit sentences by either predicting token-level editoperations (Omelianchuk et al., 2021) or using a fixed pipeline of edit operations (Agrawal et al., 2021). Dong et al. (2019) proposed a hybrid method with explicit edit operations in an endto-end generative model. Though these methods are more interpretable and controllable than generative methods, they still require complex-simple sentence pairs for training.

Unsupervised Revision-Based Methods such as Narayan and Gardent (2016) may apply a pipeline of edit operations in a fixed order. Kumar et al. (2020) then presented a general unsupervised revision-based approach by modelling text simplification as an unsupervised search problem. While GRS also relies on a revision-based framework and an unsupervised search strategy, we integrate a generative paraphrasing model into the framework to leverage the strengths of both text generation and text revision approaches.

Evaluation of simplification commonly relies on automatic metrics that correlate with human judgments. SARI has become the de facto measure for lexical simplification quality, complementing BLEU and FKGL. Subsequent studies examined content preservation versus simplicity trade-offs in supervised and unsupervised settings (Xu et al., 2016;Alva-Manchego et al., 2020). In (Sulem et al., 2018), human evaluation protocols for grammaticality and meaning retention were consolidated across datasets. Datasets for sentence simplification include aligned corpora derived from Wikipedia and news sources, with high variance in alignment quality (Zhu et al., 2010;Hwang et al., 2015). The Newsela corpus provides professionally simplified articles at multiple grade levels and supports controllable generation research (Xu et al., 2015;Scarton and Specia, 2018). However, licensing restrictions have limited its widespread use in benchmarking. Format.document: The pretraining-finetuning paradigm (Howard and Ruder, 2018) shows tremendous success in fewshot NLU tasks. Various methods have been developed such as [CLS] classification Devlin et al., 2018), prompting-based methods with discrete prompts (Schick and Schütze, 2021b;Gao et al., 2020) or continuous prompts (Liu et al., 2021b;Shin et al., 2020;Li and Liang, 2021;Lester et al., 2021), and methods that calibrate the output distribution (Yang et al., 2021;Zhao et al., 2021). The fact that few-shot learning is sensitive to many factors and thus is extremely unstable (Liu et al., 2021a;Lu et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2020;Dodge et al., 2020) increases the difficulty of fewshot evaluation. Several works address evaluation protocols to mitigate the effects of instability: Gao et al. (2020) and Liu et al. (2021b) adopt a held-out set to select models. Perez et al. (2021) proposed K-fold cross-validation and minimum description length evaluation strategies. Our work differs from these works on few-shot evaluation in several aspects: (1) we propose three metrics to evaluate data split strategies; (2) while most prior work proposed evaluation protocols without justification, we conduct comprehensive experiments to support our key design choice; (3) we formulate a general evaluation framework; (4) our re-evaluation under the proposed framework leads to several key findings. Bragg et al. (2021) andYe et al. (2021) proposed few-shot NLP benchmarks FLEX and Cross-Fit respectively. Both FLEX and CrossFit study principles of designing tasks, datasets, and metrics, while we focus on addressing inherent problems of the evaluation procedure. We position our framework as complementary to benchmark design, emphasizing the statistical properties of evaluation rather than leaderboard optimization. We analyze how prompt initialization and verbalizer choice interact with sample selection to influence variance and bias. Building on standard risk decomposition, we quantify how different split strategies trade off approximation error and estimation error. We further compare stratified, adversarial, and chronological splits in terms of distributional divergence and training stability. Our analysis highlights when calibration should be applied at inference time versus during training to ensure comparability across models, aligning with observations by Liu et al., 2022). The proposed framework also clarifies how hyperparameter search should be bounded to prevent leakage across splits. Finally, we release code and standardized templates to facilitate reproducible few-shot evaluation in future work.

Format.document: Neural encoder–decoder architectures have underpinned many open-domain dialogue systems. Early end-to-end conversational agents were built on vanilla sequence-to-sequence models (Shang et al., 2015; Vinyals and Le, 2015). Subsequent work introduced hierarchical encoders and context trackers to better model multi-turn structure (Serban et al., 2016; Serban et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019a). Beyond structure, researchers addressed blandness and repetition with diversity-promoting objectives and sampling strategies (Li et al., 2015; Xing et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2018). Control mechanisms were later explored to steer style, sentiment, and specificity in generated responses (Xu et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018; See et al., 2019). Persona-based modeling further grounded responses in speaker traits to improve consistency (Li et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018). More recently, knowledge-grounded dialogue has emerged as a promising direction to increase informativeness and factuality. Knowledge can be sourced from structured graphs such as commonsense and encyclopedic resources (Zhou et al., 2018b; Moon et al., 2019; Tuan et al., 2019). Alternatively, systems may retrieve spans from unstructured documents and condition generation on evidence passages (Dinan et al., 2019; Lian et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020a; Kim et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020). Visual context, including images and situated cues, has also been integrated to enrich dialogue grounding (Mostafazadeh et al., 2017; Shuster et al., 2018; Huber et al., 2018). While retrieval and fusion have improved content selection, expressing knowledge faithfully and coherently remains challenging. In this work, we focus on document-grounded dialogue generation with explicit mechanisms for representing and realizing evidence. We argue that modeling the structure of how evidence is verbalized is as important as selecting the right evidence. The idea of sequence modeling via segmentation offers a principled way to capture latent template structure in text. In the text segmentation literature, researchers proposed probabilistic segmental models and the Sleep-WAke Network to model sequences as compositions of segments. In machine translation, neural phrase-based decoders have been explored to capture target-side phrasal structure using segmental generation. For data-to-text generation, a neural HSMM decoder enables template-like realizations with tractable learning via dynamic programming (Wiseman et al., 2018). To relax the weak Markov assumption in segment transitions, later work explicitly segments targets, aligns fragments to records, and jointly learns segmentation and correspondence (Shen et al., 2020). These advances suggest that segmental abstractions can facilitate controllable and faithful surface realization in knowledge-grounded dialogue. Compared with standard token-level decoders, segment-aware models can plan content units before lexicalization. They can also better aggregate redundant evidence by operating at the level of phrases and propositions. In document-grounded settings, planning segments that correspond to salient claims, entities, and relations can improve factual precision. Moreover, separating planning from realization allows the system to paraphrase evidence without drifting semantically. We therefore study a framework that first induces a latent segment plan and then conditions a generator on that plan and retrieved passages. Our approach complements dense retrieval and reranking modules commonly used in prior work (Dinan et al., 2019. It also interfaces naturally with persona and style controls developed in controllable text generation (Xu et al., 2019). For evaluation, we emphasize both automatic metrics and human judgments that capture faithfulness, specificity, and discourse quality. We situate our study among strongly related persona-grounded and document-grounded dialogue systems and analyze when segmental planning yields gains. Finally, we discuss limitations and future directions, including improved segment induction and tighter coupling with retrieval.

Format.document: Toxicity detection systems are typically trained on datasets annotated at the post level, where each comment is labeled as toxic or non-toxic (Schmidt and Wiegand, 2017; Pavlopoulos et al., 2017c; Zampieri et al., 2019). Such post-level annotations enable robust benchmarking but conflate the presence of toxicity with its exact location in text (Wulczyn et al., 2017; Borkan et al., 2019). In contrast, toxic span detection targets the specific substrings that express abusive or harmful content rather than whole-document labels. Framing the problem as span extraction aligns it with attribution and rationale paradigms in explainable NLP (Li et al., 2016; Ribeiro et al., 2016). Despite this alignment, prior work has largely emphasized document-level moderation pipelines and coarse-grained interventions. Finer-grained annotations can support user education, content redaction, and context-preserving moderation actions in community platforms. However, collecting reliable span-level labels introduces challenges in annotation guidelines, inter-annotator agreement, and privacy preservation. We therefore propose a new corpus and evaluation setup that emphasize high-quality span supervision under realistic social media conditions. Our dataset includes posts from multiple domains, accompanied by character-offset spans and rationales linking spans to taxonomy categories. To mitigate privacy risks, we enforce anonymization protocols during curation and release the final resources under a permissive CC0 licence. At the modeling level, span extraction invites comparisons with sequence labeling and span proposal architectures common in information extraction. Recent advances in pretrained encoders and token classification offer strong starting points for this task (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019). Nevertheless, vanilla token-level cross-entropy can reward overly diffuse predictions that fail to capture compact abusive expressions. We address this by incorporating loss functions that balance precision and recall over contiguous spans and by evaluating with boundary-aware metrics. As related work in content moderation has shown, contextual cues and pragmatics are crucial for disambiguating sarcasm, slurs, and profanities (Fortuna and Nunes, 2018; Vidgen and Derczynski, 2020). Building on earlier efforts in span-level supervision, Pavlopoulos et al. demonstrated the feasibility of annotating toxic substrings in community data. Multi-task and multi-label strategies can further exploit hierarchical relations between toxicity categories and linguistic phenomena (Waseem and Hovy, 2016; Founta et al., 2018). Positive-unlabeled learning and debiasing approaches are also relevant given pervasive label noise and representation disparities across demographic groups (Davidson et al., 2017; Sap et al., 2019). A key difference from document-level toxicity detection is the need for evaluation protocols that penalize spurious highlights while tolerating minor boundary deviations. Accordingly, we design span-level F1, overlap-aware IoU, and character-level precision metrics to complement token-based scoring. We benchmark a suite of sequence taggers, span proposal models, and post-hoc explanation methods adapted for extraction rather than classification. For baseline comparability, we reproduce established dataset splits and hyperparameter settings reported in recent shared tasks (Zampieri et al., 2020; Pitenis et al., 2020). Complementing automated measures, we collect human judgments on highlight usefulness and harm-minimization effects in redaction scenarios. Our contributions include a new public dataset, a rigorous evaluation suite, and extensive analyses that reveal strengths and failure modes of current approaches.

Format.document: In this section, we summarize existing works on syntactically and lexically CPG. Syntactic CPG generates a paraphrase constrained by a prespecified sentence of a certain syntactic structure, namely an exemplar. However, the exemplar is only available during inference, resulting in a key challenge: obtaining manual exemplars for existing paraphrasing training datasets is prohibitively expensive. To address this, some previous works construct syntactic features from target sentences during training, such as POS tags, constituent trees, and masked templates, as illustrated in Table X. For instance, SCPN (Iyyer et al., 2018) makes the first attempt to introduce a linearized constituent tree (LCT) of the target sentence into paraphrasing, where the LCT is predicted based on predefined parse templates. Similarly, GuiG (Li et al., 2020) proposes two models to expand a partial template LCT and to generate paraphrases, respectively. Different from using LCT, SGCP (Kumar et al., 2020) introduces a graph encoder to encode the constituent tree of the exemplar as the condition. Besides, masked templates replace several words of the exemplar with a special token to form a controllable template. For example, BCPG (Liu et al., 2020b) follows BERT (Devlin et al., 2019 to randomly mask exemplar words, and ParafraGPT (Bui, 2019) makes the first attempt to integrate keywords with a copy mechanism. Despite these advances, existing works typically focus on a single conditioning signal under either lexical or syntactic CPG. In comparison, GCPG jointly includes lexical and syntactic CPG, flexibly combining conditions in a unified framework. Lexically controlled paraphrase generation usually specifies desired keywords, synonyms, or constraints such as inclusion or exclusion lists (Mao et al., 2020). Keyword-guided seq2seq models enforce coverage via copy mechanisms or constrained decoding (Hokamp and Liu, 2017; Post and Vilar, 2018). Exemplar-based paradigms condition on a retrieved prototype sentence to steer structure while preserving meaning (Guu et al., 2018; Weston et al., 2018). In paraphrase tasks, structural control aims to disentangle syntax from semantics so that models can reuse target-side structural priors (Zhang and Bowman, 2019). Recent transformer backbones have further reduced the cost of control via prompting and soft constraints (Lewis et al., 2020; Raffel et al., 2020). Nevertheless, aligning heterogeneous controls remains challenging because lexically feasible tokens may conflict with syntactic realizations when fluency is enforced by beam search (Stahlberg and Byrne, 2019). To mitigate this, several studies formulate control as a multi-source problem with learned fusion between exemplar encoders and lexical planners (Bawden et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020). Other work applies constrained decoding using finite-state controllers or differentiable relaxations to satisfy hard lexical constraints while respecting parse templates (Anderson et al., 2017; Miao et al., 2019). Beyond architecture, training data scarcity for paired exemplars has prompted weak supervision, back-translation, and retrieval-augmented pretraining (Edunov et al., 2018; Lewis et al., 2020). Evaluation remains difficult because BLEU and ROUGE under-reward structural control, leading to the adoption of parse-accuracy, tree-edit distance, and targeted acceptability judgments (Sulem et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). For fairness, researchers also examine paraphrase faithfulness with entailment and semantic similarity metrics to detect meaning drift under strong control (Wieting et al., 2019; Maynez et al., 2020). In practical deployments, controllable paraphrasing supports data augmentation, privacy-preserving text transformation, and controllable simplification (Kumar et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2022). Our study situates GCPG within this line by unifying structural templates, lexical keys, and exemplar graphs under a single training objective that preserves semantic equivalence. We next detail the problem formulation, modeling choices, and evaluation protocols used to assess controllability and faithfulness across diverse benchmarks.

Format.document: Lifelong Learning for PLMs. Lifelong learning aims at incrementally acquiring new knowledge, and in the meantime, mitigating the catastrophic forgetting issue. Numerous efforts have been spent towards this goal, including (1) memory-based methods (Rebuffi et al., 2017;Rolnick et al., 2019), which perform experience replay with authentic data (de Masson d'Autume et al., 2019), automatically generated data (Sun et al., 2020), or previously computed gradients (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017) conserved in the memory, (2) consolidationbased methods (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017;Aljundi et al., 2018), which introduce additional regularization terms to consolidate the model parameters that are important to previous tasks, and (3) dynamic architecture methods (Rusu et al., 2016;Yoon et al., 2018), which fix trained network architectures in old tasks and dynamically grow branches for new tasks. Lifelong learning is also a hot topic for PLMs. Some target at domain adaptation through continual pre-training (Gururangan et al., 2020), parameter-efficient adapters (He et al., 2021) and sparse expert models (Gururangan et al., 2021). Others focus on the incremental acquisition of factual knowledge that changes over time (Dhingra et al., 2021;Jang et al., 2021). However, the existing works seldom consider our lifelong learning setting where streaming data from multiple sources is sequentially gathered. A concurrent work conducts empirical studies on conventional continual learning algorithms for PLM adaptation. However, they do not focus on PLM's training efficiency, which is different from our setting. More detailed comparisons are left in appendix F. Efficient Pre-training in NLP. Many attempts have been made towards improving the efficiency of pre-training, such as designing novel pretraining tasks (Clark et al., 2020), model architectures (Zhang and He, 2020), optimization algorithms (You et al., 2020) and parallel architectures (Shoeybi et al., 2019;Shazeer et al., 2018). Until recently, researchers propose to "back distill" the knowledge from existing PLMs to accelerate large PLMs' pre-training (Qin et al., 2021). Related advances in curriculum pre-training emphasize staged corpora selection as a lever for efficiency, see Gururangan et al. 2021 1 for a broader survey. Another line of work proposes progressive training to dynamically expand an existing PLM's size through parameter recycling (Gong et al., 2019;Chen et al., 2021). However, these methods typically focus on training PLMs on one static corpus, and thus cannot be directly applied to our lifelong pre-training setting.

Format.document: Semantic parsing via paraphrasing began with Berant and Liang (2014), who proposed completing the mapping through an intermediate natural-language reformulation. Subsequent work generated canonical paraphrase candidates from grammars and scored partial derivations against target formal languages (Wang et al., 2015; Marzoev et al., 2020). However, these methods largely predated and therefore did not exploit pretrained sequence models for generating paraphrases. Compositional generalization remains central because formal languages are inherently compositional. Approaches inject inductive bias via modular architectures (Dong and Lapata, 2018), symbolic-neural hybrids, and latent-variable or intermediate representations (Zheng and Lapata, 2020) alongside program-like learning signals (Lake, 2019). A complementary line performs data augmentation to expand combinatorial coverage before training (Andreas, 2019; Zhong et al., 2020; Akyürek et al., 2020). Pretrained encoders and decoders have also improved compositional parsing performance (Oren et al., 2020; Furrer et al., 2020). Prompt-based methods span tuning-free cloze prompting (Petroni et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2020) and few-shot in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020; Shin et al., 2021). Parameter-efficient prompt tuning reduces adaptation cost while preserving strong performance (Li and Liang, 2021; Schucher et al., 2021; Qin and Eisner, 2021; Liu et al., 2021b), and fixed-prompt LM tuning aligns with our setting. Related work also explores prompt decomposition during tuning-free prompting by Mishra et al., 21, with corroborating results on other NLP tasks. In parallel, zero-shot pretrained models show stronger out-of-distribution robustness than fine-tuned counterparts, motivating weight ensembling and model editing for robustness transfer (Wortsman et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2021).

Format.document: Textual entailment asks whether a premise entails, contradicts, or is neutral with respect to a hypothesis (Dagan et al., 2006). The task is widely known as Natural Language Inference. Recent advances rely on large pre-trained language models that achieve strong performance on standardized benchmarks (Lan et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019; Conneau et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; He et al., 2021). These models are typically fine-tuned on manually annotated datasets such as SNLI, MNLI, FEVER, and ANLI (Bowman et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2018; Thorne et al., 2018; Nie et al., 2020). Despite these gains, generalization and robustness remain open challenges for NLI systems. Prompt-based and pivot-task learning have been proposed to address data scarcity in downstream classification tasks (Le Scao and Rush, 2021; Min et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021a). Both discrete prompts and continuous prompts have produced sizable improvements across tasks (Schick and Schütze, 2021a; Schick and Schütze, 2021b; Schick and Schütze, 2021c; Liu et al., 2021b). Related lines of work leverage high-resource supervised tasks such as question answering or entailment as pivots to bootstrap low-resource tasks (Yin et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Sainz and Rigau, 2021; McCann et al., 2018). Early studies even converted question answering examples into entailment pairs, both manually and automatically (Dagan et al., 2006; Demszky et al., 2018). Other semantic tasks including named entity recognition, relation extraction, and semantic role labeling have been reformulated as entailment through automatic conversion of labels and instances (White et al., 2017; Poliak et al., 2018a; Levy et al., 2017). Multi-task learning with a unified prompting interface aggregates heterogeneous datasets to improve target performance (Subramanian et al., 2018; Raffel et al., 2020; Aribandi et al., 2021). Zero-shot and few-shot settings particularly benefit from task-unified training when prompts are well designed (Sanh et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2021a). Nevertheless, effectiveness can depend strongly on model size and pretraining scale. For instance, contradictory results across similar setups have been reported for instruction tuning and prompting (Wei et al., 2021a; Mishra et al., 2021). Using question answering itself as a pivot has shown mixed outcomes in multi-task scenarios (McCann et al., 2018). In this work we explore multi-source learning, where datasets drawn from related tasks inform a model for the target entailment task. Event Argument Extraction is a subtask of event extraction concerned with identifying argument fillers for predefined roles in event templates. Historically, the task was explored in the Message Understanding Conferences and later in the ACE Program (Grishman and Sundheim, 1996; Doddington et al., 2004). Earlier evaluations emphasized sentence-level extraction due to annotation and modeling challenges. More recent benchmarks such as RAMS and WikiEvents emphasize document-level context for argument identification (Ebner et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021b). Despite this shift, much research continues to focus on sentence-level modeling. End-to-end event extraction models have integrated argument identification within unified architectures (Wadden et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021a), (Li et al., 2020a; Zhang et al., 2019. Other approaches treat EAE as an independent module or as a step in a pipeline to reduce error propagation (Du and Cardie, 2020a; Lyu et al., 2021). Prompt-based methods have reframed EAE as question answering or constrained generation with task-specific templates and verbalizations (Feng et al., 2020; Du and Cardie, 2020b; Wei et al., 2021b; Lyu et al., 2021; Du et al., 2021). In contrast, we cast EAE as textual entailment to exploit a uniform decision interface across roles and event types. Casting diverse information extraction problems as entailment can simplify annotation schemas and consolidate training losses. Moreover, shared entailment representations can encourage cross-task transfer when label spaces overlap partially. However, hypothesis-only and lexical overlap artifacts can inflate performance if not carefully controlled (Poliak et al., 2018b; Gururangan et al., 2018). Calibration choices, verbalizer design, and soft-prompt initializations all influence downstream gains (Gao et al., 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021). Data augmentation, counterfactual rewriting, and adversarial training further improve robustness in entailment-style reformulations (Kaushik et al., 2020; Gardner et al., 2021). When aggregating multiple sources, domain shift and dataset imbalance introduce optimization instabilities (Ben-David et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019). Mixture-weighting schedules and curriculum strategies can mitigate negative interference during joint training (Wu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020). We hypothesize that entailment-pivoted EAE particularly benefits from leveraging document-level evidence and cross-sentence coreference. To test this hypothesis, we design role-conditioned hypotheses that verbalize argument expectations for each event type. We evaluate the approach on RAMS, WikiEvents, and ACE subsets under both in-domain and cross-domain splits. Our analysis highlights consistent gains in low-resource regimes and clarifies failure modes for future research.

Format.document: There have been a series of attempts to utilize phonetic representations of language to improve or extend automatic speech recognition (ASR) models. Some of these jointly model text and audio data using sequences of phonemes combined with sequences of text characters. Sundararaman et al. (2021), for example, uses a joint transformer architecture that encodes sequences of phonemes and sequences of text simultaneously. However, this joint model is utilized to learn representations that are more robust to transcription errors. The architecture still requires text inputs from ASR transcriptions and generates outputs in both text and phoneme representations. In contrast, our approach allows for text input, audio input, or text plus audio input to language models. Baevski et al. (2021) transforms unlabeled text, not aligned with corresponding audio files, into phonemes in a scheme to train speech recognition models without any labeled data. This scheme involves a generator model trained jointly with a discriminator model. The generator converts audio, segmented into phonetic units, into predicted phonemes, and the discriminator attempts to separate these from phonemes transliterated from unlabeled text. Although both text and audio are utilized in this work, they are not input to the same model and the primary output is a model that creates good phonetic speech representations from audio. Outside of speech recognition focused work, Shen et al. (2020) attempt to fuse audio and text at the word level for emotion recognition. They introduce another architecture that internally represents both modalities, but the WISE framework relies on speech recognition to generate the text corresponding to audio frames in real time. The current work explicitly avoids reliance on speech recognition and targets flexible conditioning on phonetic content (cf. Shen et al., 2020. The 2021 Multimodal Sentiment Analysis challenge continues this vein of research integrating audio, video, text, and physiology data in an emotion recognition task (Stappen et al., 2021). Contributions to this challenge, such as Vlasenko et al. (2021), explore a variety of ways to fuse audio and text inputs but remain focused on sentiment analysis. Complementary efforts on “textless” NLP train language models directly on audio units without any text, advancing self-supervised speech methods but not providing the flexibility we pursue (Lakhotia et al., 2021).

Format.document: Prior work leveraging Knowledge Graphs for knowledge-intensive NLP can be grouped into retrieval-augmented and parameterized-knowledge approaches. Retrieval-augmented systems consult external structured or textual memory during inference to ground predictions. Representative methods include the retrieval-augmented REALM and the fact-indexed FILM (Guu et al., 2020; Verga et al., 2021. FILM extends BERT with an auxiliary memory module for storing and attending to facts. REALM pre-trains a retriever and reader jointly to surface evidence on the fly for downstream tasks. In contrast, parameterized-knowledge approaches aim to internalize KG information into model weights. ERNIE learns with masked entities and relations over aligned text–triple corpora to infuse structured semantics. KnowBert incorporates Wikipedia and WordNet via entity embeddings and knowledge attention within a BERT backbone. BERT-MK adapts graph contextual features from a medical KG to demonstrate the value of graph-level knowledge. COMET trains a commonsense generator that predicts textual assertions conditioned on KG edges and node types. KELM converts triples into natural sentences to augment pretraining data for language models. Beyond architecture, recent work examines how retrieval and parameterization trade off efficiency, controllability, and robustness. Retrieval modules can improve factuality but may incur latency and sensitivity to index drift. Conversely, fully internalized models offer fast inference yet risk hallucinating or overgeneralizing when data are sparse. Hybrid methods therefore explore lightweight retrieval hints that guide parametric decoders without heavy external memory. T5-style encoder–decoders have been widely adopted for KG-to-text and text-to-KG tasks Raffel et al., 2019). For example, template-conditioned generation can verbalize relations while preserving entity surface forms for downstream linking. Our work follows this line by probing how compact adapters can absorb schema-level knowledge without retrievers.

Format.document:
Our proposed semantic perturbation functions generalize the existing textual adversarial attacks.

For typo-based perturbation function F T , ex-isting work (Li et al., 2018;Ebrahimi et al., 2017) applies character-level perturbation to carefully crafted typo words (e.g., from "foolish" to "fo0lish"), thus making the model ignore or misunderstand the original statistical cues. Knowledge-based perturbation function F K uses knowledge base to constrain the search space. For example, Zang et al. (2020) uses sememe-based knowledge base from HowNet (Dong et al., 2010) to construct a search space for word substitution.

Different from our contextualized semantic perturbation function F C , other work (Jin et al., 2020;Li et al., 2018) uses a non-contextualized word embedding from GLoVe (Pennington et al., 2014) or Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) to build synonym candidates, by querying the cosine similarity or euclidean distance between the original and candidate word and selecting the closet ones as the replacements. However, some antonyms also have high cosine similarity in the Word2Vec space. Thus, additional hand-crafted filtering rules are needed to ensure that the meaning is not changed.

Other work (Garg and Ramakrishnan, 2020; Li et al., 2020) also leverages BERT to generate contextualized perturbations by masked language modeling, which is a parallel work to SemAttack, where we explore the BERT embedding clusters to generate high-quality adversarial examples.

In terms of optimization, unlike the heuristicbased previous work that uses greedy (Jin et al., 2020) or genetic algorithms (Zang et al., 2020) to search for the optimal perturbations or other gradient-based methods (Wang et al., 2020) searching for perturbation on a tree-autoencoder with only syntactic constraints, we use an optimizationbased method to efficiently and effectively search for the optimal adversarial perturbation in the semantic preserving spaces to ensure the validity and naturalness of perturbed sentences.

Early adversarial methods targeted sentiment analysis and machine translation, demonstrating transferability across models and domains (Ebrahimi et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2018). Subsequent research emphasized semantic preservation by constraining edits with lexical resources, paraphrase databases, or embedding neighborhoods (Alzantot et al., 2018; Ribeiro et al., 2020). Despite progress, evaluation protocols remain inconsistent, with varying constraints on fluency, label invariance, and human judgment (Pruthi et al., 2019; Michel et al., 2019). Contextualized encoders enable perturbations that align with sentence-level meaning rather than surface form alone (Kassner and Schütze, 2020). Works also examine robustness to paraphrases and counterfactuals by leveraging task-specific data augmentation (Kaushik et al., 2020; Gardner et al., 2020). However, alignment between candidate generation and selection criteria is often weak, yielding adversaries that exploit annotation artifacts instead of model brittleness (Gururangan et al., 2018). Our framework unifies these lines by explicitly modeling semantic neighborhoods under task-aware constraints while preserving fluency via masked language modeling. Format.document:
PLMs are at the core of many success stories in natural language processing (NLP). However, it remains unclear to what extent PLMs understand the syntactic and semantic properties of the human language. A series of probing tasks have been conducted on PLMs and have found them lacking or falling short on some language properties. Among the many findings of these probing tasks, PLMs have been found to be insensitive to the order of sentences when generating representations (Pham et al., 2020;Gupta et al., 2021;Sinha et al., 2021a), struggle to comprehend number-related representations (Wallace et al., 2019;Lin et al., 2020;Nogueira et al., 2021), and display a lack of semantic content understanding (Ravichander et al., 2020;Elazar et al., 2021).

In addition to the above faulty behaviours, Ettinger et al. and Kassner and Schütze 2020 show that PLMs fail to comprehend negation, which is an important property of language in many natural language understanding (NLU) tasks. Ettinger (2020) checks the ability of PLMs to understand the meaning of negation in given contexts. In their work, they check whether models are sensitive in their completions of sentences that either include negation or not. Under normal circumstances, the completions are expected to vary in truth depending on the presence or absence of negation in given sentences. Their results show that PLMs are insensitive to the impacts of negations when completing sentences. Kassner and Schütze (2020) construct the negated LAMA dataset by inserting negation elements (e.g., "not") in the LAMA cloze questions (Petroni et al., 2019). They use negated and original question pairs to query PLMs and establish that models are equally prone to make the same predictions for both the original and negated questions. In a well-informed setting, it is expected that PLMs should make different predictions for the original and negated questions. This shows that PLMs struggle to comprehend negation.

In light of the highlighted faulty behaviours of PLMs, especially their struggle to comprehend negation, Hosseini et al. (2021) propose a remedy to alleviate the problem. In their remedy, they augment the language modelling objective with an unlikelihood objective (Welleck et al., 2019) based on negated sentences from the training corpus. They use a syntactic augmentation method to generate negated sentences. In this method, the dependency parse of the sentences, POS tags and morphological information of each word are taken as input and the negation of sentences is done using sets of dependency tree regular expression patterns, such as Semgrex (Chambers et al., 2007). During training, they replace objects in negated sentences with [MASK] tokens and use unlikelihood training to make the masked-out tokens unlikely under the PLM distribution. To ensure that negated sentences are factually false, they use the corresponding positive sentences as context for the unlikelihood prediction task.

Previous studies, e.g., Kassner and Schütze (2020), have mostly limited the scope of the logical negation property only to the negation expressions (e.g., "no" and "not"). However, the core spirit of the property is opposite-meaning, which is not only limited to negation. Welleck et al. (2019) consider negating sentences using dependency tree regular expression patterns. This widens the scope of negation, as it is not only limited to negation expressions "no" and "not". However, their approach relies on other components, such as Semgrex, and dependency and POS parsers which could impact the quality of the data, hence impact the models' performance; in this work, we consider other perturbation methods to generate the opposite-meaning sentences to investigate whether PLMs satisfy the logical negation property, and we propose a remedy called intermediate-training on meaning-matching (IM 2 ) that hardly employs additional linguistic components.
