Format.document: Table-based fact verification (TB-FV) seeks to determine whether a textual claim is supported by structured evidence in tables. Unlike passage retrieval, TB-FV must align schema elements, aggregate cells, and execute latent programs to derive evidentiary statements. Early pipelines integrated table parsing with symbolic solvers, but they struggled with coverage and brittleness under noisy claims (Pasupat and Liang, 2015). Neural program induction later improved compositional reasoning by learning soft operators for selection, aggregation, and comparison (Neelakantan et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2017). In (Zhong et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2020) models often predict executable operations to justify verdicts over heterogeneous tables. Recent systems combine program sketches with neural execution to improve faithfulness while retaining differentiability (Chen et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2020). This line of work emphasizes numerical and logical reasoning to reduce spurious correlations and shortcut cues (Aly et al., 2021). At the same time, pre-trained language models augmented with table encoders have improved retrieval and entailment when paired with lightweight reasoning modules (Herzig et al., 2020; Eisenschlos et al., 2020). Nevertheless, generalization across domains, schemas, and out-of-distribution numbers remains a central challenge for TB-FV (Oren et al., 2022). To address robustness, some studies adopt mixture-of-experts architectures that route inputs to specialized experts for arithmetic, comparison, or lookup skills (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022). Classical formulations encourage competition among experts through gating and auxiliary load-balancing losses to prevent expert collapse (Jacobs et al., 1991; Shazeer et al., 2017). Recent sparse MoE transformers scale parameters while maintaining manageable inference cost via top-k routing and capacity constraints (Lepikhin et al., 2021; Zoph et al., 2022). For TB-FV, expert specialization aligns naturally with decomposed program steps, enabling interpretable routing and modular training (Liu et al., 2022). However, naively combining experts can propagate brittle behaviors unless the router is calibrated on failure modes and numerical edge cases (Wortsman et al., 2022). We therefore investigate a self-adaptive MoE that learns to weight experts based on instance-level signals derived from program traces and verification confidence. Our approach builds on competitive learning while introducing curriculum-aware routing that gradually increases expert diversity during training (Bengio et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2022). We further relate our design to hybrid neuro-symbolic verifiers that interleave soft execution with discrete constraints for faithful rationales (Das et al., 2019; Arabshahi et al., 2021). Empirically, we show improvements on benchmark TB-FV datasets with stronger compositional generalization and calibrated uncertainty over verdicts (Rebuffi et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022).

Format.document:
Seed-Guided Topic Discovery. Seed-guided topic models aim to leverage user-provided seeds to discover underlying topics according to users' interests. Early studies take LDA (Blei et al., 2003) as the backbone and incorporate seeds into model learning. For example, Andrzejewski et al. (2009) consider must-link and cannot-link constraints among seeds as priors. SeededLDA (Jagarlamudi et al., 2012) encourages topics to contain more seeds and encourages documents to select topics related to the seeds they contain. Anchored CorEx (Gallagher et al., 2017) extracts maximally informative topics by jointly compressing the corpus and preserving seed relevant informa-tion. Recent studies start to utilize embedding techniques to learn better word semantics. For example, CatE (Meng et al., 2020) explicitly encourages distinction among retrieved topics via categoryname guided embedding learning. However, all these models require the provided seeds to be invocabulary, mainly because they focus on the input corpus only and are not equipped with general knowledge of PLMs.

Embedding-Based Topic Discovery. A number of studies extend LDA to involve word embedding. The common strategy is to adapt distributions in LDA to generate real-valued data (e.g., Gaussian LDA (Das et al., 2015), LFTM (Nguyen et al., 2015), Spherical HDP (Batmanghelich et al., 2016), andCGTM (Xun et al., 2017b)). Some other studies think out of the LDA backbone. For example, TWE (Liu et al., 2015) uses topic structures to jointly learn topic embeddings and improve word embeddings. CLM (Xun et al., 2017a) collaboratively improves topic modeling and word embedding by coordinating global and local contexts. ETM (Dieng et al., 2020) models word-topic correlations via word embeddings to improve the expressiveness of topic models. More recently, Sia et al. (2020) show that directly clustering word embeddings (e.g., word2vec or BERT) also generates good topics; Thompson and Mimno (2020) further find that BERT and GPT-2 discover high quality topics, but RoBERTa does not. These models are unsupervised and hard to be applied to seed-guided settings. In contrast, our SEETOPIC framework jointly leverages PLMs, word embeddings, and seed information.

Despite these advances, bridging seed semantics and corpus evidence remains nontrivial. Seeds can be polysemous, sparse, or noisy, and naive expansion can dilute topical coherence. In (Chen et al., 2018; Wang, 2017), such heuristics were shown to bias topic priors. Recent neural approaches exploit contextual encoders to disambiguate seed meanings across documents. Pre-trained language models can supply background knowledge that compensates for missing in-vocabulary seeds. However, aligning PLM representations with topic interpretability still requires careful objectives and constraints. Our framework adopts lightweight supervision while preserving the transparency valued by classical topic models.

Weak supervision and constraints have long been used to steer unsupervised models toward user intent. Posterior regularization and generalized expectation criteria exemplify principled mechanisms for such control. Constraint-driven methods can encode lexicon, ontology, or structure, thereby improving precision on narrow domains. Yet over-constraining models often yields brittle solutions that fail to generalize beyond the seed lists. For recent assessments of clustering-based topic induction with contextual encoders, see (Sia et al., 2020 for a detailed comparison. Complementary efforts introduce seed scoring schemes that attenuate the influence of ambiguous terms. Others propose interactive refinement loops in which users iteratively adjust seeds and receive model feedback.

We position our contribution within this line of research and target a pragmatic balance between guidance and flexibility. Concretely, we integrate seed priors with representation learning, combine local and global signals, and report robust gains on diverse corpora. The resulting method preserves interpretability while enabling discovery of salient, user-aligned topics at scale.

Format.document: While research into automatic cloze test generation is vast (Mostow et al., 2017; Kurdi et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021), work on open cloze tests for language learning is comparatively scarce. As shown by Pino et al., open cloze questions can be generated using sample sentences from a learners' dictionary guided by linguistic criteria. A later version of their system adds hints for gapped words to support learners' inference (Pino and Eskenazi, 2009). Exercise Maker is a rule-based open source system that emulates exam-style items based on frequently tested words (Malafeev, 2014). Evaluations indicate that many of its suggested gaps are useful and that the resulting exercises are hard to distinguish from authentic tests. For phrasal verbs, news-derived sentences have been used to create gap–answer pairs by identifying particle verbs (Chinkina et al., 2017). Similarly, gaps have been selected by part of speech to practice function words such as articles and prepositions (Soonklang et al., 2017). From a modeling perspective, LSTMs have been used to decide where to insert a single gap within a sentence (Marrese-Taylor et al., 2018. Beyond item generation, several studies aim to control the difficulty of gaps so that they align with target proficiency levels. For example, C-tests have been manipulated by varying the position and length of gaps to modulate difficulty (Grotjahn et al., 2002). A related line of work predicts item difficulty with machine-learning models that correlate with CEFR levels (Settles et al., 2020; McCarthy et al., 2021). In such adaptive settings, tests are dynamically tailored to the examinee during the session to maintain an appropriate challenge level. Complementarily, controlling gap entropy has been shown to support designing tests that target different CEFR bands (Felice and Buttery, 2019). Our work extends this literature by modeling the selection of a full set of paragraph-level gaps that satisfy design and testing principles. To this end, we adapt transformer-based models and evaluate them with both automatic metrics and human judgments to assess test quality.

Format.document: Hallucination in neural language generation has recently received increasing attention from the NLP community, including machine translation (Raunak et al., 2021; Wang and Sennrich, 2020). Beyond translation, abstractive summarization and data-to-text systems also exhibit content that is unsupported by inputs (Kryscinski et al., 2020; Maynez et al., 2020). Prior work distinguishes between intrinsic hallucinations, which contradict source content, and extrinsic hallucinations, which introduce unverifiable facts (Ji et al., 2023). Evaluating hallucination remains difficult due to annotation costs and ambiguous definitions, prompting both model-based and knowledge-grounded metrics (Laban et al., 2022; Dziri et al., 2022). Studies in controlled decoding show that penalties over unfaithful spans can reduce errors without sacrificing fluency (Zhou et al., 2021; Filippova, 2020). In contrast, post-hoc verification leverages retrieval and entailment to filter or edit outputs before release (Rashkin et al., 2021; Manakul et al., 2023). Our work surveys these developments and identifies open challenges in faithful generation for safety-critical settings such as healthcare and law (Lehman et al., 2023; Bommasani et al., 2021). Methods that align models with external knowledge bases, like Wikipedia or domain ontologies, have shown promise in curbing fabrication (Lazaridou et al., 2022; Shuster et al., 2021). Following Nguyen, Li, and Park et al., we argue that faithfulness requires both architectural and data-centric interventions. Additionally, domain adaptation can exacerbate hallucination when target distributions diverge significantly from pretraining corpora (Gururangan et al., 2020; Yogatama et al., 2019). Instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback may reduce certain hallucination modes, but effects are brittle across prompts and tasks (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022). For multilingual applications, constrained decoding with lexicons or dictionaries remains a practical guardrail in low-resource settings (Hokamp and Liu, 2017; Post and Vilar, 2018). Insights on distributional shift are relevant here, as discussed by Hendrycks et al. 1, who analyze a suite of robustness benchmarks and failure modes. Nevertheless, measuring factual consistency should account for legitimate paraphrase and world knowledge updates over time (Honovich et al., 2022; Min et al., 2023). We conclude by outlining a taxonomy of evaluation desiderata and recommending standardized protocols for future studies (Fabbri et al., 2021; Pagnoni et al., 2021).

Format.document: There has been much prior literature on improving the efficiency of Transformers. The most common technologies include: Knowledge distillation refers to training a smaller student model using outputs from various intermediate representations of larger pre-trained teacher models. In the BERT model, there are multiple representations that the student can learn from, such as the logits in the final layer, the outputs of the encoder units, and the attention maps. The distillation on output logits is most commonly used to train smaller BERT models (Sanh et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020). The output tensors of encoder units contain meaningful semantic and contextual relationships between input tokens. Some work creates a smaller model by learning from the outputs of the teacher's encoder (Jiao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020a). Attention map refers to the softmax distribution output of the self-attention layers and indicates the contextual dependence between the input tokens. A common practice of distillation on attention maps is to directly minimize the difference between the self-attention outputs of the teacher and the student (Jiao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2020). This line of work is orthogonal to our approach and our proposed FCA can be applied to the distillate models to further accelerate their inference speed. Recent approaches also explore progressive module replacement, where smaller adapters mimic full blocks before they substitute them during inference (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2021). Early-exit mechanisms reduce computation by allowing confident examples to stop at shallower layers while maintaining accuracy on harder inputs (Teerapittayanon et al., 2016; Xin et al., 2020). Pruning refers to identifying and removing less important weights or computation units. Pruning methods for BERT broadly fall into two categories. Unstructured pruning methods prune individual weights by comparing their absolute values or gradients with a pre-defined threshold Mao et al.; Gordon et al. The weights lower than the threshold are set to zero. Unlike unstructured pruning, structured pruning aims to prune structured blocks of weights or even complete architectural components in the BERT model. Voita et al. (2019) pruned attention heads using a method based on stochastic gates and a differentiable relaxation of the L0 penalty. Fan et al. (2019) randomly dropped Transformer layers to sample small sub-networks from the larger model during training, which are selected as the inference models. Goyal et al. (2020) progressively reduced sequence length by pruning word-vectors based on the attention values. This work is partly similar to the fine-grained computing units in our proposed FCA. However, they ignored the coarse-grained units that may cause information loss. Layer dropping is complemented by width pruning that removes attention heads or neurons to balance latency and accuracy (Michel et al., 2019; Lagunas et al., 2021). Complementary to pruning, low-rank factorization decomposes weight matrices to reduce multiplications with minimal loss (Sainath et al., 2013; Lan et al., 2020). In addition, there are some engineering techniques to speed up the inference speed, such as Mixed Precision (Micikevicius et al., 2018) and Quantization (Zafrir et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2021). Using half-precision or mixed-precision representations of floating points is popular in deep learning to accelerate training and inference speed. Quantization refers to reducing the number of unique values required to represent the model weights, which in turn allows to represent them using fewer bits. Operator fusion and kernel-level optimizations further amortize memory traffic and improve utilization on modern accelerators (Dao et al., 2022). Caching and dynamic batching strategies can also yield substantial throughput gains in real-world serving systems (Narayanan et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2022).

Format.document: Long Document Summarization has been studied across multiple domains, including news, patents, books, scientific publications, and clinical records. Early datasets and models for news summarization established the basic benchmarks (Nallapati et al., 2016). Domain-specific analyses of patent texts highlighted the need for structured representations (Trappey et al., 2009). Scholarly summarization emphasized citation-aware extraction to maintain context (Qazvinian and Radev, 2008). Work on clinical narratives underscored privacy constraints and long-context dependencies (Cohan et al., 2018). Beyond datasets, researchers proposed hierarchical and segment-based architectures to handle long inputs. Gidiotis and Tsoumakas (2020) introduced a divide-and-conquer paradigm that aggregates segment summaries. Grail et al. (2021) designed a hierarchical encoder that embeds block-level structure. While effective, single-pass segmentation often limits adaptability to documents of varying length. In contrast, modular frameworks aim to preserve backbone architectures while scaling to longer inputs. The GovReport dataset pushes summarization systems beyond typical news lengths, often exceeding 9000 words. This scale exposes computational bottlenecks in encoder–decoder attention (Subramanian et al., 2019). To mitigate costs, Huang et al. (2021) proposed head-wise positional strides that thin attention patterns. Reformer replaces full self-attention with locality-sensitive hashing to approximate similarity search (Kitaev et al., 2020). For sparse attention, Beltagy et al. introduced Longformer for long inputs. BigBird extends block sparse attention with theoretical guarantees for sequence mixing (Zaheer et al., 2020). Despite these innovations, sparsification can drift from the inductive biases of pretrained models. Consequently, methods that keep full attention while restructuring input organization remain attractive. Long dialogue summarization presents additional hurdles such as speaker turns and topic shifts. HMNet leverages hierarchical encoders to jointly model utterance and session context (Zhu et al., 2020). HAT-BART augments cross-turn interactions with structured attention over dialogue segments (Rohde et al., 2021). Data augmentation and weak supervision have been explored to improve robustness on lengthy conversations (Fabbri et al., 2021). Pretraining strategies tailored for dialogue coherence further reduce factual drift (Zhong et al., 2021a). Nevertheless, architectural changes often complicate integration with existing toolchains and checkpoints. Recent variants of BigBird target different pretraining regimes (Zaheer et al., 2020a, 2020b but maintain similar sparsity patterns. In practical deployments, input splitting and staged summarization remain popular due to engineering simplicity. Yet naive splitting can harm discourse consistency and cross-section coreference. Systems therefore benefit from modules that reconcile segment outputs through learned planning. Evaluation for long documents requires metrics that capture global coverage and local faithfulness. Emerging protocols combine automatic metrics with hierarchical human assessment for better reliability. Our study positions SUMM N as a structure-preserving framework that retains pretrained attention while scaling. We compare against segment-wise and sparse-attention baselines under uniform computational budgets. The results motivate future work on hybrid strategies that couple full-attention backbones with adaptive routing.

Format.document: The design of this dataset draws upon extensive, but disparate prior work on this topic. Many works, some addressed below, have taken advantage of the availability of review text hosted on OpenReview. Argument-level review labeling has developed label sets that address different phenomena. Hua et al. (2019) introduced the study of discourse structure in peer review by annotating argumentative propositions in the AMPERE dataset with a set of labels tailored to the peer review domain (EVALUATION, REQUEST, FACT, REFERENCE, and QUOTE). Similarly, Fromm et al. (2020)'s AMSR dataset frames the problem as an argumentation process, in which the stance of each argument towards the paper's acceptance or rejection is of paramount importance. Both view peer review as argumentation, using argument mining techniques to highlight spans of interest. While its goal is not to examine discourse structure per se, Yuan et al. (2021 propose a coarse taxonomy of review acts that overlaps with argumentative function labels. Subsequent studies refine these categories to capture nuances such as hedging, politeness, and evidence type in the context of peer review (Li et al., 2022; Weld et al., 2022). Beyond labeling schemes, researchers have explored automatic identification of argumentative units using sequence tagging models trained on review corpora (Gao et al., 2020; Lauscher et al., 2021). Transfer learning from general-domain argument mining has been shown to provide strong initialization for reviewer-style discourse (Opitz et al., 2019). However, domain shift remains a challenge due to differences in tone, structure, and conventions between scholarly reviews and web arguments (Ajjour et al., 2017). To mitigate sparsity, several works leverage weak supervision, distant labels, or self-training with pseudo-annotations derived from review templates (Zhang et al., 2021; Gururangan et al., 2020). Our dataset design follows this trajectory by unifying argument labels with pragmatic signals, including requests, justifications, and references to prior art. We additionally encode section-level context to capture where within a review an argument occurs, which has proven helpful for downstream acceptance prediction (Du et al., 2021). Parallel efforts have examined reviewer calibration and bias, modeling how linguistic markers correlate with score variance and meta-review recommendations (Rennie et al., 2022; Stelmakh et al., 2021). Such findings motivate constructing datasets that link textual arguments to rating justifications rather than treating them as isolated snippets. On the modeling side, pretrained transformers fine-tuned with span-level supervision outperform classical feature-based baselines on argument extraction in reviews (Beltagy et al., 2020; Devlin et al., 2019). Recent architectures incorporate hierarchical encoders to jointly represent sentences, paragraphs, and document structure for long-review processing (Pappas et al., 2019; Dai et al., 2019). Multi-task learning with auxiliary objectives such as sentiment analysis and fact identification further improves robustness under label scarcity (Clark et al., 2019; Zhan et al., 2021). Nevertheless, annotation guidelines vary substantially across datasets, complicating fair comparison and transfer. In response, we harmonize label inventories through a mapping informed by prior ontologies and inter-annotator studies (Hovy et al., 2013; Biber and Conrad, 2009). We also release cross-domain splits to assess generalization across venues and time, aligning with calls for more rigorous evaluation protocols in the review-mining literature (Kang et al., 2020). Finally, we discuss ethical and privacy considerations surrounding the release of reviewer text, including redaction of identifying details and consent procedures (Raji et al., 2020; Mitchell et al., 2019). Taken together, this related work motivates a dataset that interleaves argumentative content with pragmatic and structural cues to support comprehensive analysis of peer reviews.

Format.document: Parameter-Efficient Tuning of PLMs. As it is increasingly infeasible to train and store full copies of large PLMs for diverse downstream tasks, methods that update only a small fraction of weights have become central to deployment. We consider the landscape of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) under two broad families, depending on whether the method freezes the backbone and adds small trainable modules or only trains a carefully chosen subset of existing parameters. The former family includes adapters, low-rank updates, and prompt or prefix mechanisms that leave the original backbone mostly intact while injecting compact capacity (Houlsby et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2022; Lester et al., 2021; Li and Liang, 2021). The latter family typically tunes classification heads, biases, or layer normalizations, reducing storage costs while preserving most pretrained knowledge (Zaken et al., 2022; Houlsby et al., 2019). Despite their appeal, these strategies differ in computational footprint, memory traffic, and the degree to which they enable cross-task transfer. In production settings, storing thousands of task-specific adapters or low-rank matrices is far cheaper than duplicating a full model, yet careful design is needed to avoid interference among tasks (Pfeiffer et al., 2021). Moreover, quantization-aware techniques such as QLoRA enable training at low precision without sacrificing accuracy, further shrinking the memory budget (Dettmers et al., 2023). However, the community still lacks a unified understanding of when structural edits outperform selective fine-tuning under distribution shift and strict latency constraints (He et al., 2021). Prior work has predominantly studied English classification and generation benchmarks, with fewer systematic evaluations on multilingual or long-context scenarios (Xue et al., 2021; Tay et al., 2022). Our study situates PEFT within a broader perspective on continual and multi-domain adaptation, emphasizing storage-optimal parameter allocation and safe rollback. We revisit canonical PLMs and instruction-tuned LLMs to highlight how capacity placement interacts with scale and pretraining mixture (Devlin et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2022). We also synthesize emerging evidence on soft prompts, showing that task- and layer-wise routing can recover strong performance with minimal updates (Hu et al., 2022; Li and Liang, 2021, particularly on low-resource domains. To ensure fair comparisons, we standardize training budgets, activation checkpointing, and optimization hyperparameters across model families (Mosbach et al., 2021). We further analyze storage-amortized cost by accounting for per-task deltas, optimizer states, and optional quantization metadata, which clarifies the practical value of different design points. Finally, we identify open questions around safety, privacy, and data governance for PEFT in regulated domains, motivating shared benchmarks and reporting standards for reproducible, efficient adaptation.

spans.span: Vaswani 2017

Format.document: Neural machine translation has become the dominant paradigm for sequence-to-sequence learning. Despite strong accuracy, its predicted probabilities are often poorly calibrated. Miscalibration undermines downstream decisions such as risk-aware decoding and active learning. We first review the architecture used by most modern systems. The Transformer uses self-attention and feed-forward layers to encode and decode token sequences. Its decoder produces a distribution over the vocabulary via a softmax layer at each step. Training commonly relies on maximum likelihood with teacher forcing. Label smoothing is frequently applied and is known to distort confidence estimates. Beam search and length normalization further reshape probability mass during inference. Prior studies have explored temperature scaling as a simple post-hoc correction. Others investigated Bayesian approximations that capture parameter uncertainty through dropout. Deep ensembles provide another route by averaging predictions from multiple independently trained models. However, these solutions are computationally expensive or brittle under domain shift. Calibration for structured outputs remains especially challenging because errors are correlated across time steps. Token-level confidence can be aggregated to sentence-level risk, but naive aggregation amplifies bias. Metrics such as expected calibration error and Brier score provide imperfect yet useful diagnostics. We also consider coverage-based evaluation through risk-control curves. Our analysis emphasizes the interplay between modeling choices and calibration behavior. Following Vaswani 2017, we adopt a standard encoder–decoder backbone without architectural modifications. We then examine how training losses, data augmentation, and regularization affect probability estimates. We study both in-domain and out-of-domain settings to reveal robustness gaps. We compare post-hoc and training-time calibration strategies under identical decoding budgets. Finally, we outline open questions that connect calibration with controllable generation and interpretability. This section sets the stage for the methods and experiments that follow.

Format.document: This paper situates our approach at the intersection of search algorithms for generation and methods for promoting diversity in outputs. Early analyses of neural text generation behavior provided descriptive and causal insights into decoding dynamics (Xu and Durrett, 2021; Zhong et al., 2021). Complementary strands have examined beam search and its limitations in conditional language modeling (Stahlberg and Byrne, 2019; Meister et al., 2020a). Building on these threads, our work explores design choices that trade accuracy for calibrated diversity in a controlled manner. Best-first beam search formalizes a family of search policies that reorder expansions based on utility estimates (Meister et al., 2020b). A broader set of search variants continues to be investigated for efficiency and robustness (Meister et al., 2021a; Meister et al., 2021b). Prior critiques have argued that beam search can amplify model errors and reduce lexical variety in translation (Huang et al., 2017; Stahlberg and Byrne, 2019). However, these critiques often focus on machine translation and leave open questions in summarization and data-to-text settings (See et al., 2017; Fan et al., 2018). The literature on degenerative decoding has underscored failure modes such as repetition, dullness, and exposure bias (Holtzman et al., 2020; Welleck et al., 2020). Foundational observations about sampling strategies and nucleus thresholds have shaped subsequent practice in open-ended generation (Radford et al., 2019; Holtzman et al., 2020). In parallel, researchers proposed mechanisms for encouraging diverse candidates without sacrificing faithfulness (Vijayakumar et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016). Studies specific to paraphrasing demonstrated the benefits of structured constraints and exemplar conditioning (Iyyer et al., 2018; Goyal and Durrett, 2020). Broader surveys emphasize how diversity interacts with metrics and human preferences (Urbanek et al., 2019; Howcroft et al., 2020). Within this context, our contributions target coverage of salient content units and lexical choice variation (Gehrmann et al., 2018; Cao and Wang, 2021). Transformer-based architectures provide the modeling backbone for most contemporary decoders (Vaswani et al., 2017). Subsequent pretraining has further improved controllability and fluency in downstream tasks (Lewis et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2020; Raffel et al., 2020). Despite these advances, practical decoding remains a key determinant of output quality in constrained generation scenarios (Stahlberg and Byrne, 2019). Our study revisits scoring functions that balance local likelihood with global penalties for redundancy (Paulus et al., 2018; Meister et al., 2020a). We additionally evaluate reranking strategies that incorporate semantic similarity features between candidates (Zhang et al., 2020; Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). To situate the approach, we compare against canonical search baselines and sampling regimes under shared resource budgets (Fan et al., 2019; Holtzman et al., 2020). Beyond accuracy, we consider calibration of diversity-promoting penalties to avoid overdispersed outputs (Guo et al., 2017; Kumar and Sarawagi, 2019). This emphasis aligns with reports that naive temperature scaling can degrade factual consistency (Kryscinski et al., 2020; Goyal and Durrett, 2020). We therefore analyze factuality-aware signals in reranking to rein in hallucinations (Kryscinski et al., 2020; Maynez et al., 2020). In addition to automatic metrics, we measure pairwise diversity using distinct-n and self-BLEU while monitoring task success (Papineni et al., 2002; Zhu and Bhat, 2018). Prior work also highlights dataset artifacts that bias decoding choices in summarization and dialogue (See et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2019). To control for such factors, we evaluate across news, conversational, and open-domain settings with standardized preprocessing (Narayan et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). Our modeling framework is agnostic to architecture and can be applied to encoder-decoder or decoder-only models (Lewis et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2020). We further compare to constrained decoding schemes such as coverage penalties and lexically guided search (Hokamp and Liu, 2017; Post and Vilar, 2018). Related streams incorporate dynamic beam allocation to improve exploration in long-form generation (Meister et al., 2020b), along with follow-up analyses (Xu and Durrett, 2021 that study adaptive heuristics). Our ablations test the sensitivity of results to beam width, softmax temperature, and top-p thresholds under fixed compute budgets (Holtzman et al., 2020; Meister et al., 2020a). Beyond decoding, data selection and span-level constraints have been shown to modulate diversity with minimal loss in adequacy (West et al., 2022; He and Glass, 2020). We complement these ideas by integrating learned utility models trained from offline rollouts (Chen et al., 2021; Pang et al., 2021). Error analysis further reveals that aggressive penalties can suppress rare but essential entities, motivating adaptive schedules (Mielke et al., 2021; He and Glass, 2020). Finally, we discuss limitations, including dependence on metric proxies and potential brittleness under domain shift (Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019; Ribeiro et al., 2020). We hope these findings encourage principled, testable modifications to search that improve practical generation performance without obscuring model behavior (Belinkov and Glass, 2019; Bender et al., 2021).

Format.document: Our work is related to cognitively inspired NLP and a variety of learning formalisms that involve knowledge transfer across different tasks. We briefly review these topics within the scope of NLP and the constraint of space. Since the pioneering work on semantic feature prediction from fMRI responses (Mitchell et al., 2008), connecting statistical NLP representations with human cognition has attracted sustained attention. Subsequent studies examined word- and sentence-level decoding using distributional vectors and contextual encoders (Anderson et al., 2016; Søgaard, 2016; Bulat et al., 2017). Parallel lines of work analyzed how embeddings align with neural and behavioral signals, using both regression and encoding models (Barrett and Søgaard, 2015; Bingel et al., 2016; Gauthier and Levy, 2019; Hollenstein and Zhang, 2019). Beyond passive alignment, researchers have explored task-driven representations to predict brain activity during language comprehension, drawing on advances in pretrained transformers as well as classical feature-based models Smith 2019. This literature increasingly emphasizes the role of fine-grained linguistic controls, such as syntactic surprisal, semantic relatedness, and discourse structure, in explaining neural variance (Hale et al., 2018; Shain, 2019; Toneva and Wehbe, 2019). Complementary to these efforts, knowledge transfer across tasks has been pursued through multitask learning and meta-learning to improve sample efficiency and robustness (Caruana, 1997; Ruder, 2017; Triantafillou et al., 2020). In NLP, transfer from auxiliary syntactic or semantic tasks often yields better generalization on low-resource benchmarks, with benefits attributed to shared inductive biases and representation smoothing (Hashimoto et al., 2017; Clark et al., 2019). Cross-modal transfer has likewise been used to bridge language and vision or speech, providing richer supervisory signals for grounded semantics and auditory-linguistic integration (Lu et al., 2019; Radford et al., 2021; Zellers et al., 2022). Our approach leverages these insights by combining cognitively meaningful supervision with principled transfer objectives, aiming to build models that are both neurally plausible and practically effective.

Format.document: Zero-shot relation extraction was previously framed as a slot-filling task and solved by reading comprehension methods (Levy et al., 2017). However, their approach requires manual template design for each relation label, which cannot scale well to new relation types. On the other hand, RelationPrompt generates synthetic relation samples for any relation without relying on label-specific templates. Another approach to zero-shot relation extraction is the formulation into an entailment task Obamuyide and Vlachos, 2018), which is not constrained to a fixed relation label space and instead determines if arbitrary pairs of sentences and relation labels are compatible, allowing for zero-shot inference. However, it is designed for sentence-level classification and cannot be easily applied to ZeroRTE. Subsequent studies have examined schema induction and prompt engineering as alternatives to manual templates for broadening coverage. Data augmentation is a popular method for improving model performance in supervised low-resource tasks. Simple heuristics such as token manipulation (Kobayashi, 2018) were initially developed, and advances in language modeling have improved the quality of augmented samples (Xie et al., 2020;Wei and Zou, 2019). Although there are augmentation methods that can be applied to structured tasks such as named entity recognition (Ding et al., 2020) and relation extraction (Papanikolaou and Pierleoni, 2020;Lee et al., 2021), they require existing training samples and cannot be easily adapted to zero-shot tasks. As a result, methods that synthesize training instances from label descriptions have attracted renewed interest. Prompting-based methods have shown promise as a new paradigm for inference in natural language processing. Given language models that have large-scale and general language pretraining, well-designed prompts can elicit answer sequences for diverse tasks in few-shot or even zero-shot settings. Another advantage is the potential to adapt very large language models (Reynolds and McDonell, 2021) to new tasks without relatively expensive fine-tuning. Nevertheless, prompt-only approaches have not yet proven effective for more complex information extraction such as triplet extraction. Knowledge retrieval has emerged as a complementary ingredient for producing faithful and contextually grounded outputs. RelationPrompt leverages the knowledge stored in language models (Roberts et al., 2020) to compose relation samples that are situated in realistic contexts. To ensure that the generated samples are factually accurate, the language model requires strong retrieval capabilities (Petroni et al., 2019). Beyond retrieval, controllable generation mechanisms can further align samples with the semantics of target relations. We position our work within this landscape by focusing on zero-shot composition of relation-centric training instances. Our approach emphasizes compatibility between natural language descriptions of relations and candidate textual contexts. We also analyze failure modes arising from label ambiguity, entity typing errors, and lexical overlap with negative classes. In addition, we discuss evaluation protocols that better isolate generalization to unseen relations rather than memorization of distant supervision artifacts. Finally, we outline open challenges in scaling zero-shot relation extraction to multilingual and domain-specific corpora. These directions motivate future work on robust prompting, retrieval-augmented reasoning, and principled data construction for relation-centric NLP.

Format.document: This paper examines how auxiliary natural language explanations can guide classifiers across novel tasks. Learning from such side information promises data efficiency and interpretability. Prior work has leveraged constraints or comments provided by annotators to regularize training. Early examples include posterior regularization and learning from general constraints (Mann and McCallum, 2010; Ganchev et al., 2010). More recently, language has been used as weak supervision for tasks like text classification and question answering (Wang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2020). In this study we move beyond supervision for single tasks and ask whether explanation-driven models generalize to unseen tasks defined at test time. We frame explanations as concept definitions that describe decision boundaries rather than item-level justifications. This contrasts with local explanation datasets that provide rationales for individual predictions (Wiegreffe and Marasović, 2021). Seminal datasets collected free-form rationales to justify model outputs on commonsense and textual entailment benchmarks (Rajani et al., 2019; Camburu et al., 2018). Our notion of global explanations aligns with prior attempts to define label semantics and rule-like guidance. Our notion of explanations is shared with Andreas et al. (201 and Srivastava et al. (2017, 2018). However, we scale the setting to dozens of heterogeneous classification problems with structured inputs. We also decouple explanation elicitation from any single domain so that benchmarks remain domain agnostic. In contrast to prompting, our explanations specify why a class holds rather than how to phrase a task. Large pretrained language models provide strong few-shot and zero-shot baselines (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Raffel et al., 2020). Such models can be adapted with in-context examples or lightweight parameter updates to perform new tasks (Brown et al., 2020; Lester et al., 2021). Pattern-based reformulations further improve few-shot learning for smaller models (Schick and Schütze, 2021; Tam et al., 2021). Multi-task prompt tuning has also been used to evaluate generalization across held-out tasks (Mishra et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2021; Sanh et al., 2021; Min et al., 2021; Aghajanyan et al., 2021). Despite these advances, we find that explicit explanations offer complementary signal not captured by prompts alone. Explanations can support systematic generalization when they encode compositional properties shared across tasks. To study this, we construct a benchmark of classification problems defined over tabular representations. Each task provides a natural language explanation describing the concept to be learned given schema-aware inputs. We compare against prompt-based and label-only baselines under limited supervision. Prior work explored language as supervision for document and sentence classification (Srivastava et al., 2017; Hancock et al., 2018 but typically evaluated within a single task. In contrast, our evaluation measures generalization to new tasks whose schemas and distributions differ from those seen in training. We also study the interplay between explanation granularity and data efficiency. Our method encodes structured inputs with a table-aware encoder and fuses explanations through cross-attention. The architecture is trained end-to-end with contrastive and supervised objectives to align explanations with examples. We analyze how explanation completeness and specificity affect transfer to out-of-domain tasks. We report performance under zero-shot transfer, few-shot adaptation, and full supervision to establish upper bounds. Our experiments include ablations that remove explanations, perturb their content, or swap them across tasks. The results indicate that explanation-aware models consistently outperform strong prompt-based baselines on unseen tasks. Improvements are largest when class semantics require compositional reasoning over multiple fields in the table. We release code, data, and templates to facilitate reproducibility and further research. We conclude by discussing limitations and ethical considerations for explanation elicitation at scale.

Format.document: In this section, we recap related work in dense retrieval and adversarial domain adaptation. Dense retrieval, different from sparse first-stage retrieval models, leverages Transformer-based encoders (Vaswani et al., 2017) to compute continuous representations for both queries and documents. Such dense methods, exemplified by BERT-style dual encoders, conduct retrieval directly in the embedding space (Lee et al., 2019b; Guu et al., 2020; Karpukhin et al., 2020; Luan et al., 2021). Compared with their sparse counterparts, DR systems often improve efficiency while maintaining comparable or superior effectiveness on in-domain datasets. Zero-shot dense retrieval (ZeroDR) has exposed gaps in cross-domain transfer and robustness (Thakur et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021; Li and Lin, 2021). One practical approach is synthetic query generation (Liang et al., 2020), which first trains a doc2query model in the source domain and then applies an NLG model to target-domain documents to produce queries. The resulting pseudo pairs of documents and queries provide weak supervision for training retrieval models at scale, yet much prior work emphasizes data augmentation rather than improving the invariance of learned representations. As several benchmarks indicate, Thakur et al. 2021 highlight persistent failures when training and deployment domains diverge. Adversarial domain adaptation (UDA) has long been explored in vision, offering complementary strategies for distribution shift. For example, moment-matching minimizes a predefined discrepancy (Long et al., 2013; Tzeng et al., 2014; Sun and Saenko, 2016), while adversarial approaches train feature extractors to confuse a domain discriminator (Ganin and Lempitsky, 2015; Bousmalis et al., 2016; Tzeng et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2017). Building on these insights, MoDIR incorporates momentum-based representation alignment tailored to the unique challenges of ZeroDR.

Format.document:
Edit Intention Identification. Identification of edit intentions is an integral component of iterative text revision workflows. Prior work has examined taxonomies of edit actions to better understand editorial behavior and outcomes (Yang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017; Ito et al., 2019). These studies argue that explicit categorization can reveal common revision patterns that correlate with perceived quality (Zhang et al., 2017). However, they rarely investigate how to operationalize intentions within automated systems that plan and execute edits end to end. Domain focus further complicates generalization, because many taxonomies were derived from Wikipedia edits or student essays (Anthonio et al., 2020; Bhat et al., 2020; Faltings et al., 2021). As a result, models trained on narrowly scoped corpora often fail to transfer to professional or creative writing domains. Our work addresses this gap by disentangling edit intention recognition from surface realization and by evaluating across heterogeneous sources.

Single-Pass Text Revision Models. Format.document: Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) aims to localize an object in an image given a natural language expression. Most REC methods learn a joint embedding over visual and linguistic inputs and differ in how the space is formed and exploited. Early metric-learning approaches ranked region proposals against text in a shared space (Hu et al., 2016b; Rohrbach et al., 2016; Plummer et al., 2018). Attention-based models subsequently weighted region proposals to select the referent, as shown by (Deng et al., 2018; and follow-ups. Recent transformer architectures fuse cross-modal context to produce aligned representations (Lu et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020). These models typically apply self-attention to align proposal-level and token-level cues within a common semantic space. Our approach instead augments region cues with pixel-level features that preserve fine-grained boundaries important for referring segmentation. In addition, relative to Lu et al. (2019), we explicitly capture both inter-modal and intra-modal interactions without adding heavy task-specific heads. Referring Image Segmentation (RIS) addresses the shape sensitivity that bounding box REC often misses. It was first introduced in (Hu et al., 2016a, where a model concatenated CNN features with tiled LSTM language features to predict the mask. Follow-up work refined masks by injecting multi-scale semantics and contextual reasoning across image regions. Since words contribute unequally to object identification, attention mechanisms have been used to weight linguistic tokens during visual grounding (Shi et al., 2018). Transformer-based decoders further capture long-range dependencies between text and pixels to improve delineation quality (Ye et al., 2019). Despite these advances, cross-modal alignment remains brittle when expressions mention relational attributes or occluded parts. We therefore argue for models that jointly exploit proposal cues and dense features while maintaining robust language grounding and efficient inference.

Format.document: Bias terms and their importance are rarely discussed in the literature. Zhao et al. (2020) describe a masking-based fine-tuning method, and explicitly mention ignoring the bias terms, as handling them "did not observe a positive effect on performance". An exception is the work of Wang et al. (2019), who analyzed bias terms from the perspective of attribution methods. They demonstrate that the last-layer bias values are often responsible for the predicted class, and propose a way to back-propagate their importance. Michel and Neubig (2018) fine-tuned the biases of the output softmax in NMT systems to personalize the output vocabulary. Cai et al. (2020) demonstrate that bias-only fine-tuning similar to ours is effective for adapting pre-trained computer vision models. Despite these findings, the role of biases in transfer learning remains underexplored across domains such as ASR and recommender systems. Recent analyses of parameter-efficient adaptation highlight that small subsets of parameters can carry disproportionate task signal (Houlsby et al., 2019; Lester et al., 2021). However, most such methods focus on adapters or prompts rather than explicitly modeling bias vectors. In classification networks, biases shift decision boundaries in feature space and can encode priors induced by dataset imbalance. Several works on logit scaling and temperature tuning indirectly manipulate biases through normalization factors (Platt, 1999; Hinton et al., 2015). Related studies on sparsity show that biases persist after heavy pruning and thus may act as stable carriers of task-specific signals (Frankle and Carbin, 2019; Sanh et al., 2020). Comparable observations were made in multilingual models, where language-specific heads differed primarily in bias parameters (Zhao et al., 2020; Wang. To our knowledge, no prior work systematically isolates bias vectors across layers to quantify their transferable capacity. This paper fills that gap by proposing a controlled protocol to learn, freeze, and evaluate biases across domains, comparing against adapters, LoRA, and full fine-tuning baselines.

Format.document: While elaborated feedback datasets on language learning (Caines et al., 2020;Pilan et al., 2020;Stasaski et al., 2020) appeared recently, they focus on linguistic mistakes, such as grammatical errors, instead of content. Our extensive literature review did not reveal datasets that included content-focused elaborated feedback on short answer responses. However, SAF's feedback can be viewed as a textual explanation of the assigned score. Therefore, comparable NLP datasets with textual explanations and publicly available ASAG datasets without explanations are discussed in the following sections. Automated short answer grading aims to predict holistic or rubric-aligned scores for brief, content-bearing responses in educational settings (Burrows et al., 2015). Early systems relied on handcrafted features, such as lexical overlap and concept mapping, which offered interpretability but limited generalization (Sultan et al., 2016). With the advent of pretrained language models, encoder architectures like BERT have substantially improved scoring accuracy on public benchmarks (Devlin et al., 2019;Zhang et al., 2020). Nonetheless, most models provide little actionable feedback, leaving teachers and students without guidance on how to improve responses (Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick, 2006). The literature on explainable AI proposes post hoc rationales, but many rationalization methods risk producing plausible yet unfaithful explanations (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020). In educational NLP, elaborated feedback refers to targeted, content-specific guidance that references missing ideas, misconceptions, or evidence quality rather than surface errors (Shute, 2008). Prior datasets for grammatical error correction organize explicit edits and metalinguistic comments, which do not transfer directly to content diagnosis in short answers (Ng et al., 2014;Bryant et al., 2019). Similarly, dialogue-based tutoring corpora capture rich instructional moves, yet typically presuppose multi-turn interaction and do not align with single-response grading scenarios (Graesser et al., 2005). Work on rationales in classification has introduced span selection or free-text justifications to enhance transparency of predictions (Lei et al., 2016;Camburu et al., 2018). However, free-text rationales often optimize for agreement with labels rather than pedagogical usefulness, which constrains their applicability to formative feedback (DeYoung et al., 2020). Research on explanation-centric QA and NLI shows that models can be trained to produce supportive statements alongside predictions, though faithfulness remains contested (Rajani et al., 2019;Wiegreffe and Pinter, 2019). Meta-analytic findings further support the educational impact of elaborated feedback Johnson et al., 2017; Smith), motivating its integration into assessment workflows. In ASAG, prompt-specific reference answers and concept lists have been used to structure supervision for content coverage (Somasundaran et al., 2015;Zhang and VanLehn, 2019). Rubric-aware systems further condition predictions on criteria such as claim accuracy, evidence, and reasoning completeness to improve reliability across prompts (Kumar et al., 2020). Score explanation studies explore extracting evidence sentences or generating textual critiques that point to missing key ideas in student responses (Liu et al., 2021;Nadeem et al., 2022). Despite progress, the field lacks standardized datasets where content-focused feedback is paired with reference scores across diverse topics and age groups. This gap complicates evaluation protocols, hinders reproducibility, and slows the development of feedback generation methods that generalize beyond single prompts. Our study positions SAF within this landscape by distinguishing explanatory content feedback from mere score justification. We treat feedback generation as conditional text production that must be faithful to the scoring rationale while being specific, actionable, and concise (Madsen et al., 2022). To contextualize our contribution, we review adjacent areas, including evidence-based argument grading, scientific peer-review assistance, and programmatic feedback from code analysis (Gretz et al., 2020;Roth et al., 2021;Zheng et al., 2022). Dataset design considerations include the granularity of feedback units, the presence of gold rationales, and the availability of domain ontologies or knowledge graphs (Chen et al., 2020). Annotation protocols must manage subjectivity by providing detailed rubrics, multi-annotator adjudication, and calibration examples to ensure consistency (Snow et al., 2008). Evaluation should combine automatic metrics for lexical overlap with human judgments of usefulness, specificity, and faithfulness to the underlying evidence (Yao et al., 2022). We also note growing interest in controllable text generation that styles feedback according to pedagogical intent, such as hints, prompts, or corrective statements (Keskar et al., 2019;Zhou and Neubig, 2021). In sum, establishing content-focused elaborated feedback datasets for short answers can catalyze research on faithful, useful, and generalizable feedback generation.

Recent studies broadened label taxonomies to capture targets, intent, and severity, and they emphasized standardized evaluation through shared tasks and leaderboards alongside new benchmarks (Röttger et al., 2021; Mathew et al., 2021 that compare cross-dataset generalization. Parallel analyses have examined dataset artifacts, sampling bias, and temporal drift to contextualize reported performance (Madukwe et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020; Wiegand et al., 2019; Swamy et al., 2019; Davidson et al., 2019a). A complementary thread extends coverage beyond English by curating multilingual corpora and transfer protocols (Ousidhoum et al., 2019; Ranasinghe and Zampieri, 2020; Ross et al., 2017; Nozza, 2021; Zoph et al., 2016; Marivate et al., 2020; Nekoto et al., 2020). XTREMESPEECH contributes to this agenda by providing Brazilian Portuguese, German, Hindi, and Swahili data with harmonized labels and quality control. Another line of work investigates annotation bias and annotator pools to better understand how background and expertise shape labels (Al Kuwatly et al., 2020; Waseem, 2016; Ross et al., 2017; Shmueli et al., 2021; Posch et al., 2018). Studies further document racialized and intersectional biases embedded in widely used datasets and model predictions (Davidson et al., 2019b; Laugier et al., 2021). In response, mitigation methods span data balancing, counterfactual augmentation, adversarial training, and fairness-aware objectives (Sap et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2020; Han et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021). The consensus emerging from this literature is that dataset design choices can both reflect and propagate annotator bias if not carefully managed. Theoretical foundations have been articulated through taxonomies, operational definitions, and distinctions among abuse, harassment, and hate (Banko et al., 2020; Wiegand et al., 2021; Waseem et al., 2017). Our perspective is additionally informed by ethnographic and anthropological work on the societal impacts of online hate and extreme speech (Boromisza-Habashi, 2013; Donovan and boyd, 2021; Haynes, 2019; Udupa and Pohjonen, 2019; Hervik, 2019). These traditions motivate context-sensitive annotation guidelines that foreground community norms, speaker intent, and power dynamics. Ethical considerations around data stewardship, model deployment, and accountability have become central to the research agenda (Mittelstadt et al., 2016; Jobin et al., 2019; Bender et al., 2021). Calls have intensified for inclusive annotator recruitment, clearer provenance documentation, and multidisciplinary oversight in NLP projects (Leins et al., 2020). Against this backdrop, we propose a cross-lingual benchmark that emphasizes sociolinguistic coverage and transparent evaluation protocols. Our design prioritizes label definitions that align with legal and platform policies while remaining suitable for empirical modeling. We also examine cross-dataset transfer to assess robustness under topical and demographic shift using multilingual encoders (Conneau et al., 2020). In low-resource settings, we explore semi-supervised learning and prompt-based augmentation to reduce annotation load without sacrificing validity (He et al., 2020; Schick and Schütze, 2021). Following Waseem et al. 2017, we operationalize hate speech with a focus on protected characteristics, dehumanization, and calls for exclusion. We situate our annotation schema within prior comparative frameworks to facilitate synthesis across datasets and languages (Fortuna and Nunes, 2018). To encourage reproducibility, we release detailed codebooks, inter-annotator agreement analyses, and adjudication protocols. We also provide strong baselines with lexicon, linear, and transformer models, reporting both accuracy and fairness metrics (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019). Our results highlight persistent generalization gaps across domains and dialects, underscoring the need for continual dataset refresh and monitoring. By unifying definitions, multilingual coverage, and rigorous evaluation, this work aims to advance reliable and equitable hate speech detection.

Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer learning. Recently, thanks to the rapid development of multilingual pre-trained language models such as multilingual BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020), a number of approaches have been proposed for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer learning on various downstream tasks, including semantic parsing (Sherborne and Lapata, 2021), natural language generation (Shen et al., 2018) and understanding (Lauscher et al., 2020). In this work, we claim our method is zeroshot because no non-Chinese CSRL annotations are seen during the CSRL training stage. For decoding, we directly use the cross-lingual CSRL model trained on Chinese CSRL data to analyze conversations in other languages. To our best knowledge, our work is the first step to cross-lingual CSRL.

Conversational semantic role labeling. While ellipsis and anaphora frequently occur in dialogues, Xu et al. (2021) observed that most of the dropped or referred components can be found in dialogue histories. Following this observation, they proposed conversational semantic role labeling (CSRL) which required the model to find predicate–argument structures over the entire conversation instead of a single sentence. In this way, when analyzing a predicate in the latest utterance, a CSRL model needs to consider both the current turn and previous turns to search potential arguments, and thus might recover the omitted components. Furthermore, Xu et al. (2020, 2021) also confirmed the usefulness of CSRL to Chinese dialogue tasks by applying CSRL information into downstream dialogue tasks. However, there are still two main problems to be solved for the CSRL task: (1) the performance of current state-of-the-art CSRL models (Xu et al., 2021) is still far from satisfactory due to the lack of high-level conversational and semantic feature modeling; (2) the usefulness of CSRL to conversational tasks in non-Chinese languages has not been confirmed yet due to the lack of cross-lingual CSRL models. In this work, we primarily focus on the latter problem and propose a simple but effective model to perform cross-lingual CSRL. We would like to distinguish our work from the concurrent work (Wu et al., 2021b) which purely focuses on improving the monolingual CSRL performance where they try to model predicate-aware representations. This solution could benefit monolingual CSRL, but hurt cross-lingual performance because the relative positions of the predicates may differ from language to language.

Cross-lingual transfer typically relies on the assumption that multilingual encoders learn language-agnostic representations aligned in a shared space (Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019). Under this assumption, label projections from a source language can be applied to target languages without additional supervision Hu et al., 2020). Nevertheless, dialogue data introduces additional challenges such as speaker role alternation, discourse coherence, and pragmatic inference beyond sentence boundaries (Jurafsky and Martin, 2023). Prior work on semantic role labeling in monologues has explored contextual encoders and syntax-aware models to capture long-range dependencies (He et al., 2018; Strubell et al., 2018). In contrast, CSRL must reason over multi-turn structures, identify cross-utterance arguments, and determine whether a candidate referent is salient across turns (Chen et al., 2022). To address these challenges, we integrate multilingual pretraining with conversation-level retrieval of candidate arguments and a lightweight discourse memory inspired by entity tracking models (Clark and Manning, 2016). Our approach further incorporates predicate canonicalization to reduce superficial divergence across languages while preserving role consistency (Hajic et al., 2009). We evaluate on Chinese as the source language and conduct zero-shot transfer to English, Spanish, and German using standard CSRL metrics (P, R, and F1) and ablation studies. For fair comparison, we replicate training and decoding settings from strong baselines and report results on public benchmarks (Conneau et al., 2018; Ruder et al., 2019). Finally, we analyze error types by discourse phenomenon, highlighting failure cases where long-distance anaphora and idiomatic expressions degrade transfer effectiveness.

Format.document: Visual Question Answering. The current dominant framework for VQA consists of an image encoder, a question encoder, multimodal fusion, and an answer predictor (Agrawal et al., 2015). To avoid the noises caused by global features, methods (Malinowski et al., 2018) introduce various image attention mechanisms into VQA. Instead of directly using visual features from CNN-based feature extractors, to improve the performance of the model, BUTD (Anderson et al., 2018) adopts Faster R-CNN (Ren et al., 2015) to obtain candidate regional features, while Pythia (Jiang et al., 2018) integrates the regional feature with grid-level features. Meanwhile, Lu et al. (2016) and Nam et al. (2017) put more attention on learning better question representations. To merge information from different modalities sufficiently, MFB (Yu et al., 2017) and MUTAN (Ben-Younes et al., 2017) explore higher-order fusion methods. Further, BAN (Kim et al., 2018) and DCN (Nguyen and Okatani, 2018) propose dense co-attention models which directly establish interaction between modalities with word-level and regional features. Moreover, with the proposal of the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), MCAN and DFAF (Gao et al., 2019) adopt self-attention mechanisms to fully excavate the fine-grained information contained in text and image. Meanwhile, to fully cover the holistic scene in an image, MuREL (Cadène et al., 2019) and ReGAT (Li et al., 2019) explicitly incorporate relations between regions into the interaction process. Selvaraju et al. (2020) also introduce sub-questions into their work; the distinctness between us is that it constructs a Sub-VQA dataset for a subset of reasoning questions in the VQA dataset to evaluate consistency of VQA models, while we adopt sub-questions to achieve task dividing. Beyond architectural advances, large-scale pretraining on image–text pairs has become a de facto prerequisite for strong VQA performance (Lu et al., 2019; Tan and Bansal, 2019; Li et al., 2020). Such pretraining encourages models to align visual regions and linguistic phrases, which is later specialized via fine-tuning on VQA benchmarks (Goyal et al., 2017; Antol et al., 2015). However, a growing body of work documents that shortcut reasoning and language priors can still dominate predictions, resulting in inconsistent behavior under distribution shift (Agrawal et al., 2018; Cadene et al., 2019). Recent benchmarks therefore emphasize counterfactual evaluation, compositional generalization, and consistency across related question sets (Hudson and Manning, 2019; Kervadec et al., 2021). In parallel, research has examined the role of region proposals versus dense grids, reporting complementary benefits when both are available to the fusion module (Jiang et al., 2018; Anderson et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2020). Despite these advances, modeling multi-step reasoning over scenes with coreference and temporal cues remains challenging for current architectures (Zellers et al., 2019; Le et al., 2020). Visual Dialogue. Different from VQA, visual dialogue (VD) is a continuous conversation grounded in images and prior turns (Das et al., 2017). Several VD tasks—Visual Dialog, GuessWhich (Chattopadhyay et al., 2017), GuessWhat?! (de Vries et al., 2017), and MMD (Saha et al., 2018)—have been proposed. GuessWhat?!, as a goal-directed dialogue task, requires both players to continuously clarify the reference object through dialogue. The Oracle provides the Questioner with relevant information about the target object by constantly answering yes or no questions, and the Guesser generates the final answer based on the historical dialogue. Following this setting, our Co-VQA framework consists of three components in which the Questioner raises sub-questions, the Oracle answers them one by one, and finally the Answerer obtains the answer to the original question. Prior work in VD has highlighted the importance of leveraging co-reference resolution across turns and grounding follow-up questions in visual context (Kottur et al., 2018; Niu et al., 2019). Transformer-based encoders have also been adapted to multi-turn dialogue to capture long-range dependencies across utterances and image regions (Hori et al., 2019; Shuster et al., 2020). In this paper we discuss how task decomposition with auxiliary sub-questions can reduce reasoning load on the final answering module while improving interpretability of intermediate decisions (Selvaraju et al., 2020). We further relate this decomposition to modular training strategies that align question intents with visual evidence retrieved by attention layers (Cornia et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020). Finally, we note that stronger regularization and curriculum design are needed to prevent models from overfitting to annotation artifacts that correlate with answer frequency distributions (Goyal et al., 2017; Krishna et al., 2017). Under this perspective, we position our approach at the intersection of compositional reasoning and dialogue-aware grounding, building on recent developments in self-attention architectures in (Vaswani et al., 2017. Concretely, we implement sub-question generation and evidence aggregation within a unified training pipeline inspired by advances in cross-modal transformers.

We describe related studies on Chinese BERT model and probing of BERT, respectively.

The authors of BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) provided the first Chinese BERT model which was trained on Chinese Wikipedia data. On top of that, Cui et al. (2019) trained RoBERTa-wwm-ext with whole word masking on extended corpora. Cui et al. (2020) further trained a Chinese ELECTRA model and MacBERT, both of which did not use explicit [MASK] tokens. ELECTRA was trained with a token-level binary classification task, which determined whether a token was the original one or artificially replaced. In MacBERT, [MASK] tokens were replaced with synonyms and the model was trained with WWM and n-gram masking. ERNIE (Sun et al., 2019) employed entity-level masking, in which all tokens of an entity were masked simultaneously. Language-specific features have been emphasized in more recent work on Chinese pretraining. For example, AMBERT and Lattice-BERT (Lai et al., 2021) both integrate lexicon-level word information. Chinese-BERT (Sun et al., 2021) additionally encodes pinyin and glyph features of characters.

Several studies explored multi-granular tokenization to mitigate segmentation ambiguity in Chinese (Zhang et al., 2021). Others investigated pretraining with mixed-script inputs to handle code-switching phenomena (Liu et al., 2022). Domain-adaptive pretraining has also been shown beneficial for Chinese biomedical and legal corpora (Gu et al., 2021; He et al., 2022). Beyond objectives and tokenization, work has evaluated robustness to homophones and character perturbations (Xie et al., 2020). Knowledge-enhanced variants inject lexical or encyclopedic constraints during pretraining to improve downstream factuality (Wang et al., 2021). Collectively, these methods indicate that structure-aware masking and language resources can meaningfully shape Chinese BERT derivatives.

In parallel, probing aims to examine the language understanding ability of pretrained models when model parameters are frozen. Early probes assessed whether masked language models capture factual triples using cloze-style prompts (Petroni et al., 2019). Template-based queries were designed such as “The wife of Barack Obama is [MASK].” to test factual recall. If a model predicts the correct answer “Michelle Obama,” it suggests that pretrained models store some factual associations. Subsequent work studied how models encode commonsense relations and lexical inference (Davison et al., 2019). Other studies targeted symbolic reasoning, numerical comparison, and compositionality with controlled templates (Talmor et al., 2020). Probing frameworks have also been adapted to Chinese to test morphology-like features, word segmentation, and tone information. Dataset-driven analyses compare layerwise representations to supervised predictors for syntax, semantics, and entity typing. Behavioral tests further evaluate robustness to paraphrase, negation, and context sensitivity under minimal-pair transformations. Recent extensions refine masking objectives (Sun et al., 2019; Cui et al., 2020 and introduce multi-task probes that align with human annotations. Calibration-aware probing evaluates whether confidence scores correlate with accuracy across templates and domains. Meanwhile, Chinese-specific probes examine character-level phonetic cues and disambiguation of homophones in context. Cross-lingual probes leverage parallel corpora to measure transfer between Chinese and alphabetic languages (Artetxe et al., 2020). Complementary diagnostics use interventions in attention patterns to test reliance on positional versus lexical features. Some studies caution that high probe performance can reflect probe capacity rather than encoded knowledge (Hewitt and Liang, 2019). To mitigate this, control tasks and selectivity metrics are employed to disentangle representation content from probe complexity. Building on these insights, our work analyzes Chinese BERT variants under unified probing settings for knowledge and reasoning. We integrate lexical resources, robust prompting, and calibration metrics to provide comprehensive and reproducible evaluations. Through this synthesis, we aim to clarify which pretraining choices most strongly influence Chinese-language understanding.

Data augmentation (Sennrich et al., 2016a; Cheng et al., 2016; Hoang et al., 2018; Edunov et al., 2018; Kobayashi, 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2020) has been widely used in neural machine translation to deal with the generalization problem of models trained on limited labeled data.

Wang et al. 2018 proposed to augment each training instance with multiple literal forms by replacing random words with other words in the vocabulary. Cheng et al. Our approach also belongs to the family of data augmentation, but we augment each training instance with an adjacency semantic region that covers adequate variants under the same meaning. Additionally, Chi et al. (2021) suggested transforming cross-lingual sentences into a shared vector by contrastive objectives. Format.document: Non-autoregressive edit-based models cast sequence generation as iterative refinement under a Markov Decision Process. A state y is a token sequence, actions edit the sequence, and transitions reflect applied edits. The reward is often the negative distance between the current hypothesis and the reference. Such formulations enable parallelizable operations compared to left-to-right autoregression. Early approaches demonstrated competitive decoding speedups without sacrificing too much quality (Gu et al., 2019). Subsequent work refined the action space to include insertion, deletion, substitution, and reposition (Stern et al., 2019). Among these, the EDITOR model emphasizes reposition and insertion for robust constrained editing (Xu and Carpuat, 2021). In EDITOR, a reposition policy predicts target indices for all tokens, implicitly modeling deletions. An insertion policy then predicts placeholder counts and fills them with concrete tokens. The two policies alternate until convergence or a preset iteration budget is exhausted (Lee et al., 2018). This iterative loop halts early when two consecutive outputs are identical, preventing unnecessary steps. Training typically follows an imitation learning recipe with carefully designed roll-in and roll-out strategies. Roll-ins mix model outputs with noised gold sequences to expose the learner to realistic errors (Lample et al., 2018). Roll-outs estimate the cost-to-go by comparing actions to oracle edit trajectories under a distance metric (Gu et al., 2019; Stern et al., 2019. The Levenshtein distance serves as a natural oracle for supervising discrete editing decisions. In machine translation, these ideas support editing from nonempty seeds such as lexically constrained prompts. They also enable mid-course correction of noisy user inputs in interactive scenarios. Policy factorization helps decouple placement from lexical choice, improving stability across domains. Despite these strengths, exposure bias and compounding errors remain notable concerns. To mitigate them, curricula interleave expert and learned roll-ins during early training epochs. Noise processes such as word dropout and local shuffling further regularize the search space (Ghazvininejad et al., 2019).
