Within this literature, framing bias refers to selective emphasis or omission that guides audience interpretation of events (Entman, 1993; Entman, 2007; Gentzkow and Shapiro, 2006). In NLP, computational approaches capture bias through lexical, syntactic, and discourse cues indicative of slant in political text (Recasens et al., 2013; Yano et al., 2010; Hamborg et al., 2019b). For example, dictionary and frequency based measures estimate exposure to partisan phraseology at scale (Gentzkow and Shapiro, 2010; Iyyer et al., 2014). However, most existing systems prioritize stylistic markers of “how to cover” rather than the informational dimension of “what to cover” (Park et al., 2011; Fan et al., 2019). This gap is consequential because audiences often form beliefs from which facts are selected, not only how they are worded (Entman, 2007). We therefore consider both detection and prediction, aiming to identify frames and generate neutral summaries that reduce partisan spin. Our problem setting focuses on biased headlines, which are concise yet potent carriers of framing choices (Chong and Druckman, 2007). We argue that neutralization plus summarization is preferable to raw aggregation because it reduces reader burden while preserving key facts (Hamborg et al., 2019a). Prior work on mitigation has leveraged news aggregation platforms to juxtapose coverage from multiple outlets on the same topic (Hamborg et al., 2017; Hamborg et al., 2019a). Complementary strategies provide users with auxiliary context, including viewpoint classification, multinational perspectives, and outlet profiles (Laban and Hearst, 2017; Park et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2019b). Despite these advances, current tools seldom generate cross outlet neutral summaries that explicitly counteract framing. Our approach bridges detection and generation by first estimating the salience of contested facets and then producing a bias attenuated headline. We situate this work alongside studies of agenda setting and framing effects in political communication (McCombs and Shaw, 1972; Scheufele and Tewksbury, 2007). Annotated resources for detecting bias and framing remain limited in size and scope, motivating transfer and weak supervision (Baly et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2019). Comparative analyses have also explored outlet level features such as audience, ownership, and geography to predict partisan leaning (Baum and Groeling, 2008; Hamborg et al., 2018). Methodologically, recent advances in pretrained language models enable robust bias signal extraction even under domain shift (Devlin et al., 2019; Raffel et al., 2020). Nevertheless, generation components can inadvertently amplify bias unless constrained by content selection objectives grounded in factual overlap (Kryscinski et al., 2020; Maynez et al., 2020). We therefore integrate content planning with calibration objectives that penalize sentiment loaded or source naming tokens during decoding (Pagnoni et al., 2021; Narayan et al., 2018). To evaluate progress on the informational dimension, we measure coverage of key facets across partisan sources and neutral outputs (Fan et al., 2019; Hamborg et al., 2019b). For comparability, we adopt standardized metrics from summarization and argument mining to quantify faithfulness and diversity (See et al., 2017; Fabbri et al., 2021). Evidence from cross outlet disagreement modeling suggests that explicit contrastive cues improve detection of what is emphasized versus omitted Park et al., 2011; Fan et al., 2019). Finally, we discuss practical considerations, including transparency of training data, auditing protocols, and user interface design for newsroom deployment (Mitchell et al., 2020; Diakopoulos, 2019). By situating neutral headline generation within a broader framing analysis pipeline, our work contributes tools for both diagnosing and mitigating media bias.

BERT introduced Masked Language Model (MLM), where a model predicts masked tokens given a sequence of text input. Fine-tuning a pre-trained BERT model has led to improved performance on various NLP tasks. However, MLM predictions are not made auto-regressively, which limits the capability of the BERT family for generation tasks. Raffel et al. (2019a) introduced the span corruption task in T5 as the pre-training objective, where a model predicts the masked token span using an autoregressive model. This formulation enables natural text generation because pretraining is done in a generative way. BART (Lewis et al., 2020) is similar to T5 but uses a denoising autoencoder objective in which spans are masked from the input while the complete output is predicted. Despite these advances, few works systematically investigate pre-training for very long sequence inputs. Standard transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) exhibit quadratic complexity in input length, which renders naive scaling to long contexts impractical. Consequently, recent research focuses on improving the memory and computation efficiency of transformer models for handling long input. One family of approaches uses sparse or structured attention to restrict the attention field, reducing complexity from O(n^2) to O(n log n) or O(n), including Sinkhorn (Tay et al., 2020a), Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020), ETC (Ainslie et al., 2020), and BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020a). Another family leverages low-rank or kernel-based approximations of attention, such as Linformer (Wang et al., 2020), Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021, Random Feature Attention (Peng et al., 2021), and LUNA (Ma et al., 2021). Hybrid strategies combine local windows with global tokens and learned patterns to preserve retrieval-like behavior in long documents (Zaheer et al., 2020a; Beltagy et al., 2020). Complementary lines of work explore recurrence and memory compression to amortize attention costs across segments (Dai et al., 2019; Rae et al., 2020). Segment-level recurrence allows limited information flow across long contexts without full pairwise attention (Dai et al., 2019). External memory modules with content-based addressing can further decouple capacity from sequence length (Grave et al., 2017; Rae et al., 2020). In pre-training, span-level corruption and permutation objectives have been adapted to long inputs to encourage robustness under partial observability (Raffel et al., 2019a; Child et al., 2019). At the same time, hierarchical encoders attempt to capture discourse structure by composing sentence and document representations (Pappagari et al., 2019; Caciularu et al., 2021). Format.document: Two major approaches are used for evaluating chatbots or dialogue systems. Some evaluate a single turn at a time by comparing the response with a ground truth utterance from a static script of real human dialogue or get a score by combining the response with the context. Others evaluate the interaction between human and bot or between bot and bot by some scoring metrics. We will present some typical systems from each of these approaches below and discuss their pros and cons. Most existing evaluation systems are based on static scripts. Traditional metrics such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002b), ROUGE (Lin, 2004) and METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005) are widely used for evaluating text generation systems. More recently, automatic evaluation methods based on static scripts are gradually moving toward using pre-trained language models. Pang et al. (2020) use GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2018) and Mehri and Eskenazi (2020) use RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) to automatically evaluate the generation in an unsupervised way with a higher correlation to human evaluation than traditional ones. However, these static evaluation metrics which need fixed contexts are not flexible enough to assess chatbot's ability, in need of adapting to dynamic and changing contexts. We argue that interactive systems like ChatMatch are more promising as they test chatbots in a real conversation mode. Interactive evaluation systems attract increasing attention lately. Ghandeharioun et al. (2019) and Deriu and Cieliebak (2019) use dialogues between a bot and itself, which is called self-talk, to evaluate the bot in a more automatic manner. But it often leads to a lot of repeated chat context. Deriu et al. (2020) designed Spot The Bot, a framework that enables a group of bots to chat with each other and then asks humans to annotate if the bots talk more like a human or more like a bot. Prior to our work, there was still no interactive and automatic evaluation framework that works without any participation of human annotators. Our work fills this gap and moreover, it's very flexible since more complex metrics or algorithms can be plugged in as scoring functions. Our results also show that there is a strong correlation between automatic evaluation results and human judgments. Static metrics also struggle with semantic adequacy, penalizing valid paraphrases and rewarding n-gram overlap artifacts. Researchers have proposed learned metrics that regress to human scores given reference conversations (Lowe et al., 2017). Reference-free metrics estimate quality by comparing system replies with the context only (Tao et al., 2018). Embedding-based similarity methods offer partial relief but can be insensitive to factuality and safety (Zhang et al., 2020). Human evaluation remains the gold standard but is costly, slow, and difficult to reproduce at scale (Novikova et al., 2017). Consequently, interactive evaluation frameworks seek to approximate human trials by simulating users, constraining topics, and aggregating conversational signals across many turns. Some frameworks integrate task success proxies such as goal completion rates or click-through signals collected during live A/B tests (Hashimoto et al., 2019). Others leverage controllable user simulators to create repeatable stress tests that probe robustness to ambiguity, off-topic queries, and adversarial inputs. In practice, mixed protocols that combine self-play, simulated users, and lightweight human spot-checks can produce stable rankings with reasonable cost, as shown in Pang et al., 2020). A critical design question is how to separate the quality of the policy that selects actions from the quality of the language generator that realizes them. Dialogue-level metrics like success rate or average return can be complemented by turn-level diagnostics that target coherence, grounding, and persona consistency. Another challenge is domain shift, since many bots overfit to benchmarked corpora and degrade in unseen settings despite strong offline scores. Recent work emphasizes safety and bias evaluation, arguing that interactivity exposes harmful behaviors that static metrics tend to miss (Dinan et al., 2021). At the same time, reproducibility requires careful control of prompts, user profiles, and sampling policies so that results are comparable across labs and time. We therefore define a protocol that fixes simulator seeds, caps conversation length, and reports uncertainty through paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We also release evaluation scripts and leaderboards to encourage standardized reporting and facilitate fair comparison across future systems.

Beyond planning content, structure, and style, researchers also consider audience-based features to model persuasiveness. Among these, Durmus and Cardie (2018) and El Baff et al. (2020) analyze how factors such as religion and political background affect outcomes. Al Khatib et al. (2020) further show that user-based features reflecting beliefs, characteristics, and personality can improve prediction of argument success. Moral foundations offer a conceptual model for understanding everyday judgments (Haidt and Joseph, 2004). Liberals emphasize care and fairness, whereas conservatives weigh all foundations more evenly, with a tilt toward loyalty, authority, and purity (Graham et al., 2009). Empirical studies corroborate the theory across behaviors and decisions (Feinberg and Willer, 2015; Fulgoni et al., 2016; Johnson and Goldwasser, 2018). For computational analysis, Kobbe et al. (2020) annotate moral foundations in arguments and link them to quality. We use their corpus to evaluate a moral classifier and to study belief-aware generation. Argument generation has been explored for multiple tasks, including counter-argument generation (Hua et al., 2019; Alshomary et al., 2021b). Other work opposes a given claim (Bilu et al., 2015; Hidey and McKeown, 2019), produces topic-controlled claims (Schiller et al., 2020), or reconstructs implicit conclusions (Alshomary et al., 2020; Syed et al., 2021). However, few approaches aim to tailor argumentative text to a specific audience. Belief-based claim generation addresses this gap by seeking claims aligned with audience stances Alshomary et al. 2021a. Project Debater provides a large-scale system for mining, retrieving, and generating arguments (Slonim et al., 2021). Its hybrid pipeline combines retrieval, mining, clustering, and rephrasing, yielding competitive quality in manual assessments (Slonim et al., 2021). We build on this system to generate morally framed claims and isolate the effect of moral framing on audiences.

Format.document: Meta-Learning. Meta-Learning aims to improve the learning algorithm itself based on the previously learned experience (Thrun and Pratt, 1998; Hospedales et al., 2021). In general, there are three categories of meta-learning methods: model-based methods (Santoro et al., 2016; Obamuyide et al., 2019) which depend on the particular model design to facilitate fast learning; metric-based methods (Vinyals et al., 2016; Snell et al., 2017; Geng et al., 2019) which encode samples into an embedding space and classify them based on the learned distance metric; and optimization-based methods (Finn et al., 2017; Mi et al., 2019) that learn a well-generalized model initialization which allows for fast adaptation to new tasks. For low-resource scenarios in NLP, optimization-based meta-learning methods achieved promising results on tasks such as personalized dialog generation (Madotto et al., 2019; Song et al., 2020), low-resource machine translation (Gu et al., 2018; Sharaf et al., 2020), and few-shot slot tagging (Wang et al., 2021). Despite this progress, meta-learning pipelines remain sensitive to mismatches between meta-training and downstream tasks. This sensitivity is exacerbated when supervision is scarce and domains shift substantially. Memorization overfitting of Meta-learning. Meta-learning algorithms suffer from memorization overfitting. Yin et al. (2020) build an information bottleneck for the model, but this approach can decrease performance due to passive regularization. Rajendran et al. (2020) inject random noise to the ground truth of both support and query sets, while little extra knowledge is introduced to learn a good initialization. Yao et al. (2021) address overfitting by augmenting meta-training tasks through mixing up support and query sets. However, such augmentation for text assumes that labels and data distributions remain unchanged, which is often not true in practice (Chen et al., 2021). Instead of relying only on regularization or generic augmentation, we leverage information stored in support sets to augment meta-learning. Our premise is that episodic memories encode transferable structure that can guide adaptation beyond the limited supervision. External Memory for Few-shot Learning. Memory mechanisms have proven powerful for few-shot learning (Geng et al., 2019; Santoro et al., 2016; Munkhdalai et al., 2019). Current methods either refine representations stored in memory (Ramalho and Garnelo, 2018) or refine parameters using memory (Munkhdalai and Yu, 2017; Cai et al., 2018). In the NLP domain, several approaches store encoded contextual information into an external memory (Holla et al., 2020). Geng et al. (2019) propose a memory induction module with a dynamic routing algorithm for few-shot text classification. Munkhdalai et al. (2019) augment a base model with a differentiable memory that supports rapid reads and writes. Wang et al. (2021) reuse learned features stored in memory for few-shot slot tagging. More recent work explores memory as an interface for retrieval-augmented adaptation in classification and generation (Sennrich et al., 2016; Edunov et al., 2018. Such designs often combine prototype formation with episodic caches to mitigate overfitting during inner-loop updates. Nevertheless, selecting what to store and how to retrieve it remains an open challenge for generalization. A complementary line of research studies meta-regularization that explicitly penalizes memorization. Techniques based on data reweighting and task-level diversity have been proposed to counteract shortcut learning in episodic training. In sequence modeling, curriculum-based sampling interacts with meta-learning dynamics to influence adaptation efficiency. We hypothesize that combining retrieval from a structured memory with robust inner-loop objectives can alleviate such sensitivity. Our approach aggregates support exemplars into a compact cache and performs uncertainty-aware retrieval at adaptation time. This design encourages reuse of abstractions learned across tasks while preventing memorization of idiosyncratic details. In the following, we position our method relative to prior work and highlight where it advances the state of the art.

Format.document: Meta-evaluation studies increasingly interrogate how automatic metrics align with human judgments in summarization. Early work emphasized single-reference overlap metrics like ROUGE, which remain popular due to simplicity and speed (Lin, 2004). More recent approaches incorporate semantic similarity through contextual embeddings, exemplified by BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2020). Despite adoption, many metrics were validated on news summarization rather than conversational data, limiting external validity. Dialogue summarization exhibits different discourse structures, speaker turns, and pragmatic cues that challenge n-gram overlap. As a result, human-anchored meta-evaluations are crucial for establishing whether metrics capture salient conversational content. Pyramids provide one rigorous framework by aggregating content units across multiple reference summaries (Nenkova and Passonneau, 2004). Building on this, Bhandari et al. curated relevance annotations to reassess metric correlations on standard corpora (Bhandari et al., 2020). Complementary work expanded the scope of human criteria beyond relevance to include faithfulness and readability (Fabbri et al., 2021b). Typical datasets in these studies include CNN or DailyMail news paired with outputs from strong abstractive systems (Hermann et al., 2015). However, these corpora underrepresent phenomena central to dialogues such as deixis, ellipsis, and speaker-specific entailments. SAMSum was proposed to address this gap by offering multi-turn chats and naturally occurring conversational implicatures (Gliwa et al., 2019). Subsequent meta-evaluations on SAMSum emphasized factual consistency but often covered only a subset of available metrics (Gabriel et al., 2021). In contrast, broader audits should examine sensitivity to paraphrase, hallucination, and truncation errors characteristic of dialogues. Another line of work analyzes model errors qualitatively to guide the design of specialized metrics for conversations (Tang et al., 2021). Related efforts investigate grounding and persona tracking as necessary ingredients for reliable automatic scoring (Chen and Yang, 2020). While these analyses are informative, inconsistent human protocols hinder aggregate comparisons across studies. For example, annotator training, unit of evaluation, and sampling strategies vary widely even within the same dataset, as in (Bhandari et al., 2020). Calibration exercises and adjudication can mitigate variance but are rarely reported with sufficient detail for replication. Cross-metric comparisons also depend on consistent preprocessing, including de-tokenization and handling of speaker tags. Reference scarcity is another obstacle because many conversational datasets provide only one gold summary per dialogue. Multi-reference augmentation via paraphrasing or expert rewriting may improve correlation estimates with human scores. Evaluation artifacts further arise when system outputs are cherry-picked or filtered, inflating measured metric performance. Robust audits therefore require stratified sampling across difficulty, length, and topical diversity to avoid selection bias. Moreover, meta-evaluations should report uncertainty with confidence intervals and significance tests for correlation gaps. Crowd-sourced judgments can scale, but their reliability in dialogue settings depends on well-crafted rubrics and context windows. In the literature, narrative citations are often preferred when discussing methodological innovations introduced by a study. Deviations from that norm can obscure attributions and complicate historical tracing of methodological advances. Our review highlights the need for standardized protocols, diversified corpora, and transparent reporting to strengthen conclusions.

(2020) and Kale and Rastogi (2020) have proposed the use of pretrained language models to tackle few-shot and zero-shot learning in concept-to-text NLG, achieving significant gains over strong non-pretrained baselines. Specifically, Peng et al. (2020) proposed SC-GPT, a semantically conditioned GPT-2 model, wherein, prior to few-shot learning, the GPT-2 model is further fine-tuned on a number of task-oriented dialogue datasets in order to mitigate the problem of representation bias. On the other hand, in Kale and Rastogi (2020), a set of human-authored templates are used to generate high-quality sentences corresponding to each unit of information in an MR. These are then concatenated and given as input to a T5 model (T2G2) to form a coherent sentence. In this paper's evaluation, we opt to compare our approach against the naive T5 baseline introduced by Kale and Rastogi (2020), as it is shown to clearly outperform SC-GPT by effectively replacing the underlying GPT-2 model with T5, and SC-GPT outperformed all previous non-pretrained baselines. We do not compare against T2G2, as access to human-authored templates or other such manually annotated resources, which are by nature very domain-specific and costly to create, are not necessarily guaranteed in low-resource settings. We note that T2G2 is equivalent to the naive T5 when templates are not employed. In our proposed system, the hierarchy emerges from modelling the lexicalisation and aggregation sub-tasks on separate layers. Previous attempts in exploring hierarchical structures for text generation tasks instead focused on modelling different aspects of the input or output (Fan et al., 2018. In concept-to-text NLG for task-oriented dialogues, Su et al. (2018) proposed a multi-layered decoding process where each layer was responsible for generating words associated with specific part-of-speech tags. Chen et al. (2019) and Tseng et al. Our approach is also related to coarse-to-fine approaches, which have been explored in story (Fan et al., 2018), review (Li et al., 2019) and keyphrase (Chen et al., 2020) generation tasks. However, in these tasks, the output is not necessarily restricted to be an exact realisation of the input, and can be initially loosely prompted or drafted, and subsequently expanded. Format.document:
Document-level neural machine translation is an important task and has been abundantly studied with multiple datasets as well as methods.

The mainstream research in this field is the model architecture improvement.
Specifically, several recent attempts extend the Sent2Sent approach to the Doc2Sent-like one.
Wang et al. (2017); Miculicich et al. (2018); Tan et al. (2019, 2020) introduce additional encoders or query layers with attention models and feed the history contexts into decoders.
Maruf and Haffari (2018) and Tu et al. (2018) propose to augment NMT models with a cache-like memory network, which generates the translation depending on the decoder history retrieved from the memory.
Besides, some works intend to resolve this problem in other ways.
Jean and Cho (2019) propose a regularization term encouraging models to focus more on additional context via a multi-level pairwise ranking loss.
Yu et al. (2020) utilize a noisy-channel reranker with Bayes' rule.
Garcia et al. (2019) also share similar ideas with us.
Tiedemann and Scherrer (2017) and Bawden et al. (2017) explore concatenating two consecutive sentences and generating two sentences directly.
Obviously, we leverage much longer information and capture the full context.
Junczys-Dowmunt (2019) cuts documents into long segments and feeds them into training as in BERT Devlin et al., 2019).
There are at least three main differences.
First, they add specific boundary tokens between sentences, whereas we translate original documents without any additional processing.
Second, we propose a multi-resolution training paradigm that shows consistent improvements compared with regular training.

Format.document: Open-Domain Passage Retrieval has been a hot research topic in recent years. It requires a system to extract evidence passages for a specific question from a large corpus like Wikipedia while delivering both high accuracy and low latency. Traditional approaches such as TF-IDF (Ramos et al., 2003) and BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) rely on lexical overlap between queries and documents. Although these lexical baselines are fast, they fail to capture non-lexical semantic similarity and therefore underperform on retrieval accuracy. With advances in pretrained language models like BERT and RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), cross-encoder architectures have been proposed for retrieval (Vig and Ramea, 2019; Wolf et al., 2019). Despite strong accuracy, cross-encoders are often too slow for production-scale use. Bi-encoder models mitigate this by precomputing dense representations of passages for efficient nearest-neighbor search. Early work pretrains bi-encoders using the Inverse Cloze Task, and DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020) popularizes a contrastive objective for learning dense passage embeddings. Building on DPR, subsequent studies improve sampling strategies (Xiong et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2021; Qu et al., 2021), add pretraining signals (Sachan et al., 2021), or distill knowledge from cross-encoders (Izacard and Grave, 2021; Yang et al., 2021). Our method follows this contrastive learning line but targets modeling granularity directly through a tailored training strategy. Specifically, we optimize at the sentence or phrase level to better align fine-grained evidence with queries. Contrastive learning has rapidly gained traction across modalities, with notable advances in computer vision in (He et al., 2020) inspiring analogous techniques in NLP (Gao et al., 2021; Giorgi et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2021). For ODPR, two complementary directions have emerged: improving sampling of positives and hard negatives (Manmatha et al., 2017; Xiong et al., 2020), and improving the training framework itself. DensePhrase uses a memory bank akin to MoCo to expand in-batch negatives without increasing GPU usage (Lee et al., 2021; He et al., 2020). Closely related to our goals, Akkalyoncu Yilmaz et al. (2019) explore sentence-level evidence for dense retrieval, focusing on re-ranking rather than first-stage retrieval.

Format.document: One important aspect of our study is the evaluation of crosslingual consistency while performing multilingual NER or EL tasks. We conceptualize consistency as the stability of predictions across equivalent inputs rendered in different languages. This notion aligns with practical demands in multilingual products where error profiles must not drift unpredictably across locales. Prior work has emphasized measuring invariances in entity recognition and linking under constrained settings. In (Bianchi et al., 2021; Conneau et al., 2020 such invariances are associated with transfer protocols that limit domain shift. However, the evaluation of language-invariant properties remains challenging when pretraining data is skewed by region or topic. An ideal scenario assumes that the transformation between languages preserves task-relevant features. In practice, commercially available models often encode domain dependencies that undermine such assumptions. We therefore examine robustness diagnostics tailored to sequence-labeling and entity-linking pipelines. Effective measurement of dataset quality is another aspect of growing significance. Training large language models requires huge amounts of data, and the resulting inferences often reflect dataset biases. Data-centric analyses have shown that quality-aware design decisions can improve overall performance. For example, Swayamdipta et al. (2020) introduced data maps that categorize instances by confidence, variability, and correctness. Their framework highlights out-of-distribution regions, class-probability fluctuations, and annotation-level discrepancies. We extend these ideas to multilingual corpora by quantifying instance difficulty across language pairs. Usually, multilingual datasets are collected from diverse sources with uneven curation standards. It is therefore important to assess whether their utility is representative for native speakers. We find that MasakhaNER (Adelani et al., 2021) exemplifies community-driven collection that aligns with local usage. Such datasets can reduce cultural mismatches and support fairer evaluations. At the same time, coverage gaps persist in low-resource settings despite recent advances. Joshi et al. (2020) characterized this landscape through typological coverage indices and resource trajectories. Their analysis shows that the current state-of-the-art applications are far from universally accessible. We corroborate this finding by auditing error distributions across macro-areas and language families. Methodologically, we adopt a mixed evaluation protocol combining zero-shot transfer and language-specific tuning. This protocol helps disentangle transferability from capacity to absorb limited supervision. We further report per-language calibration metrics to capture confidence alignment. To ensure comparability, we harmonize label sets and entity knowledge bases across languages. We also provide ablations that remove name transliteration to isolate morphological effects. For reproducibility, we release preprocessing scripts and hyperparameters aligned with common baselines. A persistent question is whether consistency metrics correlate with user-perceived quality. We address this by conducting human preference studies on a subset of outputs. The studies reveal that certain inconsistencies are tolerated when semantic intent remains clear. Conversely, subtle entity boundary shifts can disproportionately erode trust in high-stakes domains. We therefore argue for evaluation suites that combine automatic metrics with lightweight human checks. As a pointer to related analysis, we note that similar concerns were raised in (Bianchi, Conneau, and Lample 2021). Overall, our review motivates principled benchmarking that foregrounds data quality, crosslingual equity, and actionable diagnostics.

Format.document: It is well known that reliable uncertainty estimates can be obtained simply by constructing an ensemble of decorrelated neural networks (deep ensemble) (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017). However, such a straightforward approach is coupled with substantial computational and memory overhead during training an ensemble, performing inference of all its components, and storing multiple versions of weights, which is a serious obstacle to deploying ensemble-based uncertainty estimation methods in practice. Uncertainty estimation is a built-in capability of Bayesian neural networks (Blundell et al., 2015). However, such models have similar issues as ensembles and also require special training procedures. Recently, it was shown by Gal and Ghahramani (2016) that dropout, a well known regularization technique, is mathematically equivalent to approximate variational inference in the deep Gaussian process. This method, known as Monte Carlo (MC) dropout, uses a Bernoulli approximation to the variational distribution on the network units and introduces no additional parameters for the approximate posterior. MC dropout does not introduce any overhead during training and does not require any additional memory. The main disadvantage of this method is that it often requires many forward-pass samplings, which makes it computationally expensive at inference time. Building on these ideas, researchers have explored lighter alternatives to full Bayesian inference that retain useful uncertainty estimates. Recently, many works have investigated approximate Bayesian inference for neural networks using deterministic approaches (Lee et al., 2018; Van Amersfoort et al., 2020; Mukhoti et al., 2021). These methods do not introduce notable overhead for inference, storing weights, and usually require training time comparable to standard models. However, most of the research in this area has been conducted on computer vision tasks. For text classification, a series of works investigates UE methods for the OOD detection task Podolskiy et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2021; Hu and Khan, 2021). In this work, we focus on the more challenging task of misclassification detection. While OOD detection requires modeling primarily epistemic uncertainty caused by limited training data, misclassification detection also requires modeling aleatoric uncertainty due to noise and ambiguity in data (Mukhoti et al., 2021). We consider recently proposed methods in this area that are evaluated in text processing. Three recent works propose techniques for misclassification detection based on additive regularization of the training loss. Zhang et al. (2019) suggest adding a penalty that reduces the Euclidean distance between training instances of the same class and increases the distance between instances of different classes. He et al. (2020) propose using two components in the loss that reduce the difference between outputs from two versions of a model initialized with different weights. They also use mix-up (Thulasidasan et al., 2019) to generate additional training instance representations that help capture aleatoric uncertainty, along with self-ensembling and a distinctiveness score to measure epistemic uncertainty. Xin et al. (2021) introduce a regularizer that penalizes overconfident instances with high loss. In another recent work, Shelmanov et al. (2021) combine MC dropout with a Determinantal Point Process to improve the diversity of predictions by considering correlations between neurons and sampling diverse units for activation in a dropout layer. In this paper, we conduct a systematic empirical investigation of UE methods on NLP tasks. We evaluate combinations of methods that were not tested before, propose two modifications, and present the first comprehensive study of UE for named entity recognition.

Format.document: Lexically constrained translation aims to integrate required terminology into machine-generated outputs without sacrificing fluency. Prior work explores constraints during training via code-switching data augmentation (Dinu et al., 2019; Song et al., 2019) and via auxiliary objectives such as token- or span-level masking (Ailem et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2021). At inference time, constrained decoding approaches include placeholder tags (Luong et al., 2015; Crego et al., 2016), grid beam search (Hokamp and Liu, 2017; Post and Vilar, 2018), and alignment-enhanced decoding (Alkhouli et al., 2018; Song et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021). For efficiency, recent studies also consider non-autoregressive constrained translation that avoids the left-to-right bottleneck. Susanto et al. (2020) modify the Levenshtein Transformer inference procedure to prevent deletion of constraint words during iterative editing. Xu and Carpuat (2021) extend this idea with a reposition operation that can reorder constraint tokens. Building on these insights, our approach enriches non-autoregressive models with terminology-driven alignment signals to improve context modeling, especially for rare constraints. Non-autoregressive translation (NAT) offers substantial speedups but often underperforms autoregressive baselines due to multimodality in the target space. Sequence-level knowledge distillation reduces output diversity and reordering complexity by training NAT models on autoregressive teacher outputs (Kim and Rush, 2016; Gu et al., 2018). This practice has been shown to narrow the modality gap across several language pairs (Zhou et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021). Beyond distillation, researchers alleviate multimodality using latent-variable formulations (Kaiser et al., 2018; Shu et al., 2020) and iterative refinement (Ghazvininejad et al., 2019; Stern et al., 2019; Gu et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2020). Complementary lines of work investigate improved training objectives, including alignment-aware or contrastive losses (Du et al., 2021. Editing-based iterative NAT models are particularly amenable to the incorporation of lexical constraints (Susanto et al., 2020; Xu and Carpuat, 2021). However, balancing constraint satisfaction with global adequacy remains challenging when constraints are ambiguous or under-specified. We therefore propose a lightweight mechanism that conditions edit operations on terminology alignments while preserving decoding parallelism.

Format.document: Anaphora encompasses coreference, where expressions denote the same entity, and bridging, where expressions are linked by semantic or encyclopedic relations (Clark and Manning, 2015; Ng, 2017; Asher and Lascarides, 1998; Hou et al., 2018). Most available corpora emphasize declarative text across news, Wikipedia, and scientific writing (Poesio et al., 2008; Pradhan et al., 2012; Ghaddar and Langlais, 2016b; Cohen et al., 2017). The CoNLL 2012 dataset provides large-scale annotations for generic coreference resolution (Pradhan et al., 2012). It follows the OntoNotes 5.0 guidelines, modeling identity and appositive links without preserving relation directionality (Weischedel et al., 2013). WikiCoref similarly annotates entities and links in Wikipedia articles (Ghaddar and Langlais, 2016b). In the biomedical domain, BioNLP-ST 2011 targeted gene-related references in abstracts, whereas CRAFT includes full-article annotations (Cohen et al., 2017). SCIERC adds cross-sentence scientific entity links and event-centric relations (Luan et al., 2018). Defining bridging is challenging, and prior work distinguishes referential versus lexical bridging, including meronymic and taxonomic relations (Zeldes, 2017; Hou et al., 2018). Foundational resources such as ARRAU, ISNotes, BASHI, and SciCorp document varied mixtures of coreference and bridging in news and scientific text (Poesio et al., 2008; Hou et al., 2018; Rösiger, 2018a; Rösiger, 2016). Procedural texts remain under-resourced despite domain needs in chemistry, robotics, and cooking (Fang et al., 2021a; Modi et al., 2016). Recipe understanding has leveraged both visual demonstrations and linguistic instructions across multiple languages (Huang et al., 2017; Nishimura et al., 2020; Agarwal and Miller, 2011; Kiddon et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2020). Typical pipelines represent instructions as action-centered graphs over ingredients and tools (Batra et al., 2020; Marin et al., 2019; Mori et al., 2014). However, such graph abstractions often fail to capture pronouns, definite descriptions, and implicit references needed for full anaphora resolution. Datasets like RISeC address verb-centric zero anaphora but do not model generic bridging or nominal coreference (Jiang et al., 2020). Coreference modeling has progressed from mention-ranking to span-ranking architectures, with the latter becoming the de facto standard Lee et al. 2017. Numerous variants improve scoring, pruning, and contextualization, yielding robust gains on OntoNotes and scientific benchmarks (Zhang et al., 2018; Grobol, 2019; Kantor and Globerson, 2019). Transfer learning further boosts performance by pretraining on large source domains and fine-tuning on targets (Brack et al., 2021; Xia and Van Durme, 2021). For bridging, rule-based patterns and feature-driven classifiers have been contrasted with modern neural approaches (Hou et al., 2014; Rösiger, 2018b; Hou, 2018b; Hou, 2020; Yu and Poesio, 2020). One line of work frames bridging as question answering and adapts pretrained readers from generic QA corpora (Hou, 2020). Another line jointly trains bridging with coreference using end-to-end encoders (Lee et al., 2017 and reports strong gains (Yu and Poesio, 2020; Fang et al., 2021a). Despite these advances, evaluation remains skewed toward declarative prose rather than procedural narratives common in instructional texts. Procedural corpora with unified treatment of coreference and bridging are scarce, limiting model generalization and diagnostics. This gap motivates creating richer annotations that capture entity states, tool transformations, and implicit roles across steps (Harashima and Hiramatsu, 2020; Harashima et al., 2016). It also calls for models that integrate discourse structure with event sequencing to resolve long-distance links (Agarwal and Miller, 2011; Kiddon et al., 2015). Building on these insights, we outline a framework that unifies coreference and bridging within instructional domains while remaining compatible with standard evaluation protocols (Lee et al., 2018).

Format.document:
With the rise of social media and hate speech forums online (Phadke and Mitra, 2020; Szendro, 2021), offensive language detection has become more important than ever before. Several recent works focus on characterizing various types of offensive language detection (Fortuna and Nunes, 2018; Shushkevich and Cardiff, 2019; spanning lexicon-based, neural, and hybrid approaches. But, works that focus solely on stereotype detection in English are scarce. This is partly because stereotypes tend to be subtler offenses than other types of offensive language and hence receive less immediate focus, and in part due to the challenge of requiring knowledge of a stereotype's social salience to reliably annotate data for the task. We approach this problem by decomposing stereotypical text into linguistically grounded facets and crowd-sourcing annotations only for aspects that require linguistic understanding rather than world knowledge. Few recent works have focused solely on stereotypes, some proposing pioneering diagnostic datasets (Nadeem et al., 2020; Nangia et al., 2020) while others develop knowledge-based and semi-supervised models (Fraser et al., 2021; Badjatiya et al., 2019) for identifying stereotypical text. Computational models trained on illustrative examples—for instance, 1) Ethiopians like stew (Explicit Stereotype), 2) The lawyer misrepresented the situation and tricked the person (Implicit Stereotypical Association), 3) Jews spend money frivolously (Anti-Stereotypes), and 4) There is an Asian family that lives down the street (Non-Stereotypes)—often either rely on datasets built for adjacent tasks such as hate speech detection or focus on adapted diagnostic sets for classification. However, diagnostic datasets suffer from limited coverage of naturally occurring text due to their crowd-sourced construction procedures (Blodgett et al., 2021b). We address these issues by collecting in-the-wild data from Reddit, mining specific subreddits that predominantly contain subtle stereotypical expressions.

Given the low-resource setting for stereotype detection, semi-supervised data annotation is a plausible solution. Several recent works have also explored reinforcement-learning–guided semi-supervision (Ye et al., 2020; Konyushkova et al., 2020; Laskin et al., 2020). Ye et al. (2020), in particular, work with a single task and unlabeled data to generate automated annotations for new examples. In contrast, we leverage data from neighboring tasks with different labels for multi-task learning and apply an RL agent to select examples for training the auxiliary task in such a way that benefits the target task the most. Our approach emphasizes transfer from related signals such as sentiment and stance and uses curriculum mechanisms to stabilize learning over noisy pseudo-labels. For reproducibility, we follow established practices in dataset construction (Li et al., 2021 and align our evaluation with prior fairness auditing guidelines.

Format.document: Prompt-based few-shot fine-tuning adapts pretrained language models to new tasks by conditioning on task descriptions and a handful of labeled examples. Early studies established its viability on moderately sized models such as BERT and RoBERTa (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019). Pattern-Exploiting Training reframes classification as masked language modeling with hand-crafted or searched patterns (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b). AutoPrompt uses gradient signals to select discrete trigger tokens that elicit desired model behavior (Shin et al., 2020). Null prompts show that minimal concatenation with a [MASK] token can already yield competitive baselines (Logan et al., 2021). Beyond discrete templates, soft-prompting injects continuous embeddings as virtual tokens and tunes only those parameters (Lester et al., 2021). Complementary work pre-trains soft prompts to provide stronger initializations for downstream tuning (Gu et al., 2021). Demonstration-augmented prompting further enriches inputs by adding labeled exemplars, as explored by LM-BFF (Gao et al., 2021). Our study builds on these ideas by coupling multiple demonstrations with a compact, globally shared soft memory for prompt tokens. In contrast to LM-BFF, we allocate several demonstrations per label and automatically verbalize label phrases to improve semantic alignment. We compare against manual prompts, LM-BFF, and full fine-tuning under identical data budgets (Gao et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021). Prior strong baselines for few-shot classification include Zhang and Wang, 2020; Li, 2021. For completeness, we also evaluate in-context learning with frozen RoBERTa-large using GPT-3 style prompting, with no parameter updates (Brown et al., 2020). All results are averaged over five random splits, and we report means and standard deviations to account for sensitivity to seed choice. Our implementation follows common preprocessing and tuning recipes, including layerwise learning-rate decay and class-balanced sampling (Mosbach et al., 2021). To isolate the effect of demonstrations, we keep the underlying encoder fixed across methods and vary only the prompt mechanism. Architecturally, we adopt a transformer encoder with a lightweight prefix of trainable embeddings that functions as the soft memory (Li and Liang, 2021). The approach maintains efficiency by freezing the bulk of model weights while updating fewer than one percent of parameters (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2021). Compared to discrete patterns, continuous prompts reduce brittleness to tokenization artifacts and permit smooth optimization (Lester et al., 2021). We further ablate the number of demonstrations per label and the sharing strategy across tasks to understand scaling behavior. In addition to accuracy, we analyze calibration, sample efficiency, and robustness to prompt paraphrases (Jiang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021). Finally, we situate our findings within the broader trend of replacing task-specific heads with input-conditioned control of sequence-to-sequence models Vaswani et al., 2017). This perspective highlights the unifying role of prompts as lightweight interfaces that steer pretrained knowledge without extensive retraining. Altogether, our results clarify when and why multi-demonstration soft prompting outperforms discrete and full fine-tuning, and they chart practical guidelines for selecting prompt mechanisms in resource-constrained settings.

Format.document: Controllable text generation aims to steer pretrained language models toward desired attributes without compromising fluency and content preservation. Prior research has explored autoencoding approaches that learn continuous sentence representations for manipulation and decoding back to text. Representative methods include cross-aligned and back-translation based models that attempt to disentangle content and style in latent space (Shen et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2020; John et al., 2019). In contrast to training new encoders or decoders, we investigate whether steering vectors can be extracted directly from hidden states of large pretrained models. Our central hypothesis is that linear directions exist that correlate with interpretable attributes and can be applied at inference without fine-tuning. As a canonical example, Shen et al. propose cross-aligned autoencoders for style transfer. Building on this intuition, we show that attribute shifts can be induced by simple vector arithmetic in embedding or activation spaces. A growing body of work seeks lightweight control via prompts, adapters, or residual controllers to modulate generation without retraining the backbone. Prompt-based steering has proved effective for polarity, formality, and toxicity control when combined with calibrated decoding strategies (Liu et al., 2021; Krause et al., 2021). Adapter layers provide parameter-efficient fine-tuning by inserting small bottleneck modules into each transformer block while freezing the base model (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2021). Other methods modify logits or gradients at inference time using auxiliary classifiers in order to bias token selection toward desired attributes (Gulcehre et al., 2015; Dathathri et al., 2019). Our approach differs by identifying intrinsic directions already present in the model and applying them through vector operations that leave parameters unchanged. We formalize steering as a linear operator on hidden representations derived from matched pairs of sentences that contrast a target attribute. The operator can then be composed with the forward pass to nudge activations toward the attribute while preserving core semantics. Unlike classifier-guided decoding, our method introduces no additional losses or external models at training time. We evaluate on sentiment transfer, detoxification, and formality control across multiple corpora with automatic and human metrics. Fluency is assessed with perplexity and grammaticality judgments, while content preservation is measured via semantic similarity and information overlap. We further analyze attribute strength distributions as a function of steering magnitude to reveal robustness and saturation effects. Related efforts on representation arithmetic in vision and language suggest that linear structure can encode disentangled factors in deep models (Mikolov et al., 2013; Radford et al., 2017; Ethayarajh, 2019). In controllable generation specifically, iterative unlikelihood objectives and contrastive decoding have also been used to suppress undesired outputs while amplifying desired ones (Welleck et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022). In (Dathathri et al., 2019), for example, gradients from a discriminator are used at each step to adjust the token distribution toward a chosen attribute. While effective, such approaches often incur latency and stability costs due to per-token optimization. By contrast, our operator is computed once from a small labeled or weakly labeled set and then reused efficiently at inference. We also compare against reinforcement learning from attribute rewards, which typically demands extensive exploration and careful reward shaping to avoid mode collapse (Ziegler et al., 2019; Paulus et al., 2020). Empirically, we find that steering at mid-layer activations offers a better trade-off between attribute strength and content preservation than output-layer interventions. Ablation studies show that the quality of contrastive pairs used to estimate the direction is a key determinant of success. Finally, we discuss ethical considerations around attribute control, including risks of misuse and distributional harms, and outline mitigation strategies such as transparency reports and opt-out mechanisms. Our findings indicate that principled, training-free steering is a viable alternative to parameter-efficient fine-tuning for a broad class of controllable generation tasks.

Format.document: The standard practice of using BERT is fine-tuning, i.e. the entirety of the model parameters is adjusted on the training corpus of the downstream task, so that the model is adapted to that specific task (Devlin et al., 2019). There is also an alternative feature-based approach, used by ELMo (Peters et al., 2018). In the latter approach, the pre-trained model is regarded as a feature extractor with frozen parameters. During the learning of a downstream task, one feeds a fixed or learnable combination of the model's intermediate representations as input to the task-specific module, and only the parameters of the latter will be updated. It has been shown that the fine-tuning approach is generally superior to the feature-based approach for BERT in terms of task performance (Devlin et al., 2019;Peters et al., 2019). A natural middle ground between these two approaches is partial fine-tuning, i.e. only fine-tuning some topmost layers of BERT while keeping the remaining bottom layers frozen. This approach has been studied by Houlsby et al. (2019) and Merchant et al. (2020), where the authors observed that finetuning only the top layers can almost achieve the performance of full fine-tuning on several GLUE tasks. The approach of partial fine-tuning essentially regards the bottom layers of BERT as a feature extractor. Freezing weights from bottom layers is a sensible idea as previous studies show that the mid layer representations produced by BERT are most transferrable, whereas the top layers representations are more task-oriented (Wang et al., 2019;Tenney et al., 2019b,a;Merchant et al., 2020). Nevertheless, full fine-tuning remains costly in memory and storage because one copy of all parameters must be maintained per task. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) addresses this cost by training small task-specific modules while keeping the base model fixed. Adapter layers insert bottleneck modules within each Transformer block and optimize only a few percent of parameters while matching the accuracy of full fine-tuning on many benchmarks (Houlsby et al., 2019;Pfeiffer et al., 2020). Subsequent work proposed techniques for sharing and combining adapters across tasks and languages, further improving multitask generalization (Pfeiffer et al., 2020). Orthogonal directions compress or reparameterize updates, such as low-rank adaptation that decomposes weight deltas into rank-constrained matrices (Hu et al., 2022). Prompt-based methods move learning to the input space by optimizing soft prompts or prefixes that steer frozen models during decoding (Lester et al., 2021;Li and Liang, 2021). Another extreme reduces training to biases in layer normalization or to a subset of bias vectors, yielding surprisingly strong baselines with minimal trainable parameters (Zaken et al., 2022). While these methods differ in mechanism, they share the intuition that large pretrained models provide broadly useful features that require only small task-specific adjustments. Empirical comparisons show that PEFT approaches are particularly attractive in low-resource and multilingual settings, where avoiding overfitting and catastrophic forgetting is crucial (Pfeiffer et al., 2020). In production, PEFT also simplifies deployment by enabling a single shared backbone with many lightweight task adapters swapped at inference time. Despite these advantages, the community still debates how many layers should be adapted and where adaptation is most beneficial. Analyses suggest that early layers encode general lexical and syntactic patterns, whereas later layers capture task semantics, implying that adaptation should concentrate near the top (Tenney et al., 2019a;Merchant et al., 2020). Controlled ablations confirm that partial fine-tuning of higher blocks yields most of the gains with far fewer trainable parameters than full updates (Merchant et al., 2020). From an optimization perspective, restricting updates can act as a regularizer that stabilizes training under distribution shift. From a systems perspective, smaller update footprints reduce communication overhead in federated or multi-tenant environments. Nevertheless, some tasks with complex reasoning or long-range dependencies still benefit from full model adaptation, especially when training data is abundant. A nuanced picture therefore emerges in which the optimal adaptation strategy depends on architecture depth, task type, and data regime. To better map this space, recent studies benchmark PEFT methods across a standardized suite of tasks, controlling for parameter counts and hyperparameters (Hu et al., 2022;Lester et al., 2021). Results consistently indicate competitive performance for adapters, prefixes, and low-rank updates, though differences appear on generation-heavy tasks. Early evidence for adapters was reported by Houlsby et al. 2019 in encoder-only models, and later extended to sequence-to-sequence architectures. Complementary findings highlight that combining multiple parameter-efficient modules can further bridge any residual gap to full fine-tuning (Pfeiffer et al., 2020). Beyond accuracy, storage efficiency is often the decisive metric in multi-task training where hundreds of tasks are common. Here, PEFT methods can yield order-of-magnitude reductions in per-task footprint without retraining or recompiling the backbone. However, careful hyperparameter selection remains necessary, particularly for learning rates, initialization scales, and the depth at which modules are inserted. Moreover, evaluation should consider robustness to domain shift, calibration, and fairness in addition to headline metrics. These observations motivate our investigation of partial fine-tuning regimes that trade off task performance against parameter and storage efficiency. We provide a systematic comparison that quantifies these trade-offs and clarifies when partial adaptation suffices and when full updates are warranted.

Format.document:
Rational Speech Act (RSA)

Our work builds on pragmatic reasoning for language production and interpretation. The Rational Speech Act framework models cooperative communication between speakers and listeners. In its basic form, RSA formalizes nested reasoning over literal and pragmatic agents. A literal speaker selects utterances to truthfully describe world states under a semantics. A pragmatic listener inverts this model to infer likely states given the utterance. A higher-level pragmatic speaker anticipates the listener’s inference to choose more informative messages. This recursive structure captures Gricean maxims in a probabilistic manner. Prior research has successfully applied RSA to reference games with visual contexts (Frank and Goodman, 2012). In (Andreas and Klein, 2016), a referential game setup highlights the benefits of explicit pragmatic reasoning. Related work further studies visually grounded pragmatics and distractor-aware captioning (Monroe and Potts, 2015). In grounded captioning, pragmatic reasoning can improve discriminativity over distractors. Our study adopts a referential game in which images are sampled with one target and several foils. The literal speaker is implemented with a pretrained image captioner that maps images to descriptions. The pragmatic listener computes posterior beliefs over images conditioned on the caption. The pragmatic speaker optimizes expected utility with respect to the listener’s beliefs. Utility balances accuracy, brevity, and stylistic constraints relevant to the domain. We further account for asymmetric knowledge between agents to reflect real-world heterogeneity. In many applications, the listener may have restricted visual or linguistic capacity. Designing speakers that accommodate such disparities can yield more robust communication. We propose a disparity parameter that modulates the listener model used by the speaker. This parameter captures reduced perception, vocabulary gaps, or biased priors. When disparity increases, the speaker places greater weight on redundancy and clarity. Our framework unifies pragmatic captioning with adaptive assistance objectives. We evaluate the approach on controlled synthetic scenes and natural image datasets. Metrics include target selection accuracy, caption discriminativity, and brevity norms. Human studies further assess perceived helpfulness and naturalness of the captions. Results show consistent gains over literal baselines across disparity settings. Improvements are largest when the listener lacks key attributes present in training. Ablation analysis reveals the importance of calibrated listener models within RSA. We also compare against alternative pragmatic formulations without recursion. Those models underperform when distractors share attributes with the target. Our implementation follows common conventions for likelihoods and priors in RSA. For historical context, we note that pragmatic inference in reference games has deep roots in cognitive science, and we therefore situate our contribution within research on rational cooperative communication.

Jain and Wallace, 2019

Format.document: In NLP, transformer-based models have become central to both performance and interpretability research. Attention mechanisms are often discussed as potential explanations for model behavior. As shown by (Serrano and A. Smith, 2019 early analyses questioned whether attention weights align with feature importance. Subsequent work reinforced this view by contrasting attention with gradient-based attributions (Jain and Wallace, 2019; Wiegreffe and Pinter, 2019). In this section, we review gradient-based feature attribution methods for neural language models. Simple Gradient computes a saliency map as the derivative of the output with respect to the input embedding (Simonyan et al., 2013). Although intuitive, this map is often noisy and difficult to interpret. Gradient times Input sharpens saliency by multiplying each gradient by its corresponding input dimension (Shrikumar et al., 2017). In practice, this technique has been adapted to token-level attributions in NLP classification and sequence labeling. Layer-wise relevance propagation has been shown to be equivalent to Gradient times Input up to a scaling factor in certain linear settings (Bach et al., 2015). SmoothGrad reduces visual noise by averaging gradients over noisy perturbations of the input (Smilkov et al., 2017). Guided Backpropagation modifies the backward pass through ReLU to emphasize positive signals in lower layers (Springenberg et al., 2014). Extensions such as Grad-CAM tailor class-specific localization to convolutional architectures and are less directly applicable to transformers (Selvaraju et al., 2017). Because transformers lack spatial pooling and canonical feature maps, many vision-oriented formulas are omitted in NLP contexts. Integrated Gradients computes path integrals from a reference baseline to the input to produce sensitivity scores that satisfy axiomatic properties (Sundararajan et al., 2017). In computer vision, a black image is often used as the baseline, whereas in NLP various token-level baselines have been proposed. With sequence models, one may integrate along linear interpolations in the embedding space between a reference representation and the actual input. SHAP-Gradient combines the expectations of SmoothGrad with the path formulation of Integrated Gradients to yield an estimator of Shapley values (Lundberg and Lee, 2017). Concretely, the method samples interpolation coefficients from a uniform distribution and averages gradients across sampled baselines. DeepLIFT attributes changes in output to changes in input relative to a baseline via a set of layer-wise contribution rules (Shrikumar et al., 2017). Prior work has interpreted DeepLIFT as a fast approximation to Shapley value computation under certain independence assumptions (Lundberg and Lee, 2017). Practical deployments often favor methods with axiomatic guarantees and stable behavior under input perturbations. However, implementation details such as embedding normalization and attention masking can materially alter attribution maps. Comparative evaluations have therefore measured sensitivity, faithfulness, and complexity across methods on standard NLP benchmarks (Atanasova et al., 2020; DeYoung et al., 2020). Recent studies also explore how attribution interacts with pretraining objectives and prompt-based conditioning in large language models (Pruthi et al., 2020; Jain et al., 2020). Notably, explanation faithfulness can diverge from plausibility when evaluated with human-annotated rationales (Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017; Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020). Some authors caution that evaluation-by-deletion and similar faithfulness tests may confound attribution with distribution shift effects, as noted by Jain and Wallace, 2019. To ensure robust conclusions, studies should report variance across random seeds, baselines, and tokenization choices alongside standard accuracy metrics. In summary, gradient-based attribution for transformers remains an active area where methodological clarity and rigorous evaluation are essential.

Format.document: Zero Shot Transfer. Multilingual models like mBERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020) have shown surprising effectiveness in zero-shot transfer, where fine-tuning the MMLM on a task in some source language often leads to impressive performance on the same task in other languages as well without explicitly training on them. Pires et al. (2019) first observed this phenomenon for NER (Tjong Kim Sang, 2002; Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003; Levow, 2006) and POS tagging (Nivre et al., 2018) tasks. Concurrently, Wu and Dredze (2019) also showed this surprisingly cross lingual transfer ability of mBERT additionally on tasks like Document Classification (Schwenk and Li, 2018), Natural Language Inference (Conneau et al., 2018) and Dependency Parsing (Nivre et al., 2018), extending early evidence (Pires et al., 2019; Wu and Dredze, 2019 across diverse evaluation suites. Factors Affecting Zero Shot Transfer. Pires et al. (2019) showed that vocabulary memorization played little role in zero-shot generalization as language pairs with little word piece overlap also exhibited impressive crosslingual performance. K et al. (2020) arrived at a similar conclusion by training BERT on an artificially generated language to zero out the word overlap with the target languages, and observed only minor drops in the performance compared to training the model on English. On the contrary Wu and Dredze (2019), observed strong correlations between the sub-word overlap and the zero-shot performance in four out of five tasks. Wu and Dredze (2020) showed that mBERT performed much worse for zero-shot transfer to low resource languages (i.e., less pre-training data) than high resource ones on POS Tagging, NER and Dependency Parsing tasks. Lauscher et al. (2020) also had a similar observation on tasks like XNLI and XQuAD (Artetxe et al., 2020), though they found that the zero-shot performance on NER, POS tagging and Dependency Parsing tasks might not strictly depend on the pre-training size and could be better explained by different linguistic relatedness features like syntactic and phonological similarities between the language pair. Similar dependence on the typological relatedness such as word order had also been observed by Pires et al. (2019). Performance Prediction. Prior work has explored predicting the performance of machine learning models from unlabelled data by either measuring (dis)agreements between multiple classifiers (Platanios et al., 2014; Platanios et al., 2017) or by utilizing underlying information about data distribution (Domhan et al., 2015). In the context of NLP, Birch et al. (2008) explored predicting the performance of a Machine Translation system by utilizing different explanatory variables for the language pairs. Lin et al. (2019) proposed a learning to rank approach to choose transfer languages for cross lingual learning using several linguistic and dataset specific features. Specifically predicting the zero-shot performance of MMLMs was first explored in Lauscher et al. (2020), where they used a linear regression model to estimate the cross-lingual transfer performance based on pre-training data size and linguistic relatedness features. Srinivasan et al. (2021) tackled this problem by utilizing XGBoost Regressor for the prediction along with a larger set of features. Recently, Dolicki and Spanakis (2021) explored individual syntactic features for zero-shot performance prediction instead of working with aggregate similarity values, and showed about 2 to 4 times gain in performance. We extend these work by considering a multi-task learning approach, where performance prediction in a task utilizes not only the data available for that task, but also the patterns observed for other tasks.

Format.document: The rapid growth of the legal text processing field is demonstrated by numerous papers presented in top-tier conferences in NLP and artificial intelligence (Luo et al., 2017; Zhong et al., 2018; Chalkidis et al., 2019a; Valvoda et al., 2021) as well as surveys (Chalkidis and Kampas, 2018; (Zhong et al., 2020b). Moreover, specialized workshops on NLP for legal text (Aletras et al., 2019; Di Fatta et al., 2020; Aletras et al., 2020) are regularly organized. A core task in this area has been legal judgment prediction (forecasting), where the goal is to predict the outcome (verdict) of a court case. In this direction, there have been at least three lines of work. The first one (Aletras et al., 2016; Chalkidis et al., 2019a; Medvedeva et al., 2020; Medvedeva et al., 2021) predicts violations of human rights in cases of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). The second line of work (Luo et al., 2017; Zhong et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019) considers Chinese criminal cases where the goal is to predict relevant law articles, criminal charges, and the term of the penalty. The third line of work (Ruger et al., 2004; Katz et al., 2017; Kaufman et al., 2019) includes methods for predicting the outcomes of cases of the Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS). The same or similar tasks have also been studied with court cases in many other jurisdictions including France (Sulea et al., 2017), the Philippines (Virtucio et al., 2018), Turkey (Mumcuoglu et al., 2021), Thailand (Kowsrihawat et al., 2018), the United Kingdom (Strickson and De La Iglesia, 2020), Germany (Urchs et al., 2021), and Switzerland (Niklaus et al., 2021). Apart from predicting court decisions, there is also work aiming to interpret (explain) the decisions of particular courts (Ye et al., 2018; Chalkidis et al., 2021c; Branting et al., 2021). Another popular task is legal topic classification. Nallapati and Manning (2008) highlighted the challenges of legal document classification compared to more generic text classification by using a dataset including docket entries of US court cases. Chalkidis et al. (2020a) classify EU laws into EuroVoc concepts, a task earlier introduced by Mencia and Fürnkranz (2007), with a special interest in few-shot and zero-shot learning. Luz de Araujo et al. (2020) also studied topic classification using a dataset of Brazilian Supreme Court cases. There are similar interesting applications in contract law (Lippi et al., 2019; Tuggener et al., 2020). Several studies (Chalkidis et al., 2019c; Hendrycks et al., 2021) explored information extraction from contracts, to extract important information such as the contracting parties, agreed payment amount, start and end dates, and applicable law. Other studies focus on extracting information from legislation (Cardellino et al., 2017; Angelidis et al., 2018) or court cases (Leitner et al., 2019). Legal Question Answering (QA) is another task of interest in legal NLP, where the goal is to train models for answering legal questions (Kim et al., 2015; Ravichander et al., 2019; Kien et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2020a, 2020c). Not only is this task interesting for researchers but it could support efforts to help laypeople better understand their legal rights. In the general task setting, this requires identifying relevant legislation, case law, or other legal documents, and extracting elements of those documents that answer a particular question. A notable venue for legal QA has been the Competition on Legal Information Extraction and Entailment (COLIEE) (Kim et al., 2016; Kano et al., 2017; Kano et al., 2018). More recently, there have also been efforts to pre-train Transformer-based language models on legal corpora (Chalkidis et al., 2020b; Zheng et al., 2021), leading to state-of-the-art results in several legal NLP tasks, compared to models pre-trained on generic corpora. These domain-specific encoders are typically adapted via fine-tuning on supervised datasets. Despite promising gains, reproducibility and comparability across studies remain limited due to heterogeneous data splits and metrics. Overall, the legal NLP literature is overwhelming, and the resources are scattered. Documentation is often not available, and evaluation measures vary across articles studying the same task. Our goal is to create the first unified benchmark to assess the performance of NLP models on legal natural language understanding. As a first step, we selected a representative group of tasks, using datasets in English that are publicly available, adequately documented, and of appropriate size for developing modern NLP methods. We also introduce several simplifications to make the new benchmark more standardized and easily accessible, as already noted.

Format.document: In recent years there has been active interest in the application of NLP techniques to the legal domain (Zhong et al., 2020a). A number of tasks and models have been proposed, inter alia, Legal Judgment Prediction (Chalkidis et al., 2019), Legal Summarization (Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Tran et al., 2019), Prior Case Retrieval (Jackson et al., 2003; Shao et al., 2020), Legal Question Answering, and Catchphrase Extraction (Galgani et al., 2012). Legal Judgement Prediction (LJP) involves predicting the final decision from the facts and arguments of the case. Majority of corpora for Legal-NLP tasks have been in English; recently, there have been efforts to address other languages as well, for example, Xiao et al. (2018) have created a large-scale Chinese criminal judgment prediction dataset with over 2.68 million legal documents. Work on Legal-NLP in languages other than English is still in its incipient stages Zhong, Malik and Strickson, 2020). Our paper contributes towards these efforts by releasing corpus in Hindi. Majority of the work in the legal domain has focused on the higher court (Malik et al., 2021; Strickson and De La Iglesia, 2020; Zhong et al., 2020b); however, the lower courts handle the maximum number of cases. We try to address this gap by releasing a large corpus of district court level legal documents. Ishida et al. (2017, 2019) have published legal data in Japanese, along with their English translation. The competition had two sub-tasks, a legal information retrieval task and an entailment identification task between law articles and queries. Multiple datasets in Chinese have been released for different tasks, namely Reading Comprehension (Duan et al., 2019), Similar Case Matching (Xiao et al., 2019), and Question Answering (Zhong et al., 2020b). Duan et al. (2019) proposed the Chinese Judicial Reading Comprehension (CJRC) dataset with about 10K documents and almost 50K questions with answers. Zhong et al. (2020b) presented JEC-QA, a legal question answering dataset collected from the National Judicial Examination of China with about 26K multiple-choice questions. They augment the dataset with a database containing the legal knowledge required to answer the questions and also assign meta information to each of the questions for in-depth analysis. Xiao et al. (2019) proposed CAIL2019-SCM, a dataset containing 8,964 triplets of the case document, with the objective to identify which two cases are more similar in the triplets. Similar case matching has a crucial application as it helps to identify comparable historical cases, and a historical case with similar facts often serves as a legal precedent and influences the judgement. Such historical information can be used to make the legal judgement prediction models more robust. Kleinberg et al. (2017) proposed bail decision prediction as a good proxy to gauge if machine learning can improve human decision making. A large number of bail documents along with the binary decision (granted or denied) makes it an ideal task for automation, and in this paper we also propose the bail prediction task using the HLDC corpus.
