Format.document: Our work is related to dataset construction for building persuasive dialogue systems that try to persuade the participant to take a specific action. Hiraoka et al. (2014) annotated 34 dialogues, in which an experienced salesperson tries to convince a customer to buy a camera. Yoshino et al. (2018) requested crowdsourcing workers to generate 200 persuasive dialogues. In each dialogue, one participant persuaded another one to adopt a suggestion such as cleaning a room. Wang et al. (2019) collected 1017 dialogues, in which one of the participants was convinced to donate to a specific charity. We can see that the covered conversation scenarios in these datasets were strictly limited to specific tasks, while our scenarios are more general and can be easily extended to different cases. According to (Hiraoka et al., 2014; Yoshino 2018), such narrow settings may constrain model transfer to broader contexts. Also, our constructed dataset is about three times larger than the prior work, indicating the usefulness of the recent pre-trained paradigm. The topic of conversational recommendation systems is also related to our work. A number of attempts have been made to collect training data for conversational recommendation systems. These studies (Wu et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020) first extracted a path consisting of entity or attribute nodes from a knowledge base. Then they asked annotators to write conversational recommendation dialogues. The flow of mentioned topics in a dialogue should follow the extracted path. Li et al. (2021) also built a dataset by asking human workers to create dialogues based on a topic path. It should be noted that, in these datasets, the goal of such systems is to only make entity recommendations instead of tasks, while our work goes beyond them in naturally transferring from chit-chat to task-oriented dialogues and completing a task the user may want. In contrast, our collected conversations explicitly track intentions that evolve from casual talk to concrete commitments. Another related work is generating a transition between two given open-domain utterances. Tang et al. (2019) proposed to generate the transition conditional on a specific word, because they wanted the generated transition to drive the conversation topic to the specified word. Sevegnani et al. (2021) collected a new dataset of human-created one-turn topic transitions. Each dialogue contains two utterances with different topics and one transition in the middle of them. These efforts emphasize local coherence but do not account for long-horizon task fulfillment. Our approach integrates topic transition modeling with downstream action planning in a unified framework. There are some recent studies trying to merge chit-chat and task-oriented dialogues, but the purposes of merged dialogues differ from ours. Sun et al. (2021) enhanced the utterances in task-oriented dialogues by appending chit-chat sentences. They hoped that the agent would gain more social, personalized, and engaging communication skills. Ennen et al. (2021) proposed a dialogue system that can transfer the style of generated responses from chit-chat to task-oriented styles. However, the system is a prototype model, and there is still a large gap to properly bridge chit-chat and task-oriented dialogues. The motivation of our work is closely similar to that of the study by Yu et al. (2017). They manually created several task-oriented response generation strategies specifically designed for the movie promotion scenario. In addition, expert knowledge was utilized to design reinforcement learning rewards that help their dialogue system decide which action to take (i.e., continuing chit-chat or selecting a task-oriented strategy to reply). Unlike rule-heavy pipelines, our system can adapt its strategy based on data rather than hand-crafted templates. However, we can observe that the prior work in these studies heavily relied on human efforts (data collection, expert-created strategies, etc.). Therefore, it can be expensive and hard to extend their data or methods to practical cases due to the requirement of larger-scale training data. Our proposed framework benefits from pre-trained models and shows outstanding conversational capability. The flexibility of extending to diverse cases is also validated, considering that all components inside the framework can be easily substituted by updated models, and the generated data can be used by semi-supervised or unsupervised methods for cold-start scenarios.

Format.document:
As more powerful SSL models are proposed with promising performance on various tasks, researchers continually try to find extensive evaluation methods to assess model performance, and wish to holistically understand the capability of the learned representations in these models.

SUPERB (Yang et al., 2021) is a framework to benchmark the SSL models on 10 speech tasks by learning task-specific prediction heads on top of the frozen shared SSL models. Although the tasks in SUPERB span across different domains, most of them are simple classification problems, or only require utilization of shallow semantics. In contrast, we focus on harder semantic and generative tasks.

Another recently proposed benchmark is the LeBenchmark Evain et al. (2021), investigating the performance of SSL models trained on French data with three semantic tasks. However, they only consider wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski et al., 2020) with different architectures as their upstream models (i.e., networks pre-trained with SSL). Here, we evaluate a diverse set of SSL models, and offer a more comprehensive analysis.

The Zero Resource Speech Benchmark 2021 (Nguyen et al., 2020) introduces unsupervised speech processing tasks, particularly the spoken language modeling problem. They evaluate the SSL models via zero-shot probings at four linguistic levels. While their benchmark task is specific for certain domain, we use various tasks to evaluate different aspects of SSL models.

The HEAR 2021 Challenge aims to develop general-purpose audio representation by focusing on audio tasks beyond speech that include sound event detection, speech commands and pitch chroma classification. We specifically focus on various aspects of speech processing, thus providing a wide variety of spoken language tasks. Beyond benchmarking, our analysis examines transfer across languages and domains, connecting to work on universal self-supervised objectives (Hsu et al., 2021). To contextualize our contributions within broader auditory representation learning, we reference the community challenge reports (Turian et al., 2022 while adopting evaluation protocols suited to speech rather than general audio. Overall, our work complements existing resources by emphasizing semantically rich tasks, comprehensive metrics, and transparent, reproducible evaluation practices.

Format.document:
Readability Assessment has been an active area in educational research for almost a century. Early research on this topic focused on the creation of readability "formulae", which relied on easy to calculate measures such as word and sentence length, and presence of words from some standard word list (Lively and Pressey, 1923;Flesch, 1948;Stenner, 1996). More than 200 such formulae were proposed in the past few decades, and DuBay (2007) provides a detailed summary of such formulae. The advent of NLP and machine learning resulted in more data driven research on ARA over the past two decades. Starting from statistical language models (Si and Callan, 2001), a range of lexical and syntactic features (Heilman et al., 2007;Petersen and Ostendorf, 2009;Ambati et al., 2016) as well as inter-sentential features (Pitler and Nenkova, 2008;Todirascu et al., 2013;Xia et al., 2016) were explored in machine learning based ARA research in the past. Features motivated by related disciplines such as psycholinguistics (Howcroft and Demberg, 2017), and cognitive science (Feng et al., 2009) were also explored.

In the past few years, ARA research has been primarily focused on textual embeddings and deep learning based architectures. Word embeddings in combination with other attributes such as domain knowledge or language modeling (Cha et al., 2017;Jiang et al., 2018) were used for ARA. A range of neural architectures, from multi attentive RNN (Azpiazu and Pera, 2019) to deep reinforcement learning (Mohammadi and Khasteh, 2019) were proposed, and recent research explored combining transformers with linguistic features Deutsch et al. (2020;Meng et al., 2020;Lee et al., 2021;Imperial, 2021). While Deutsch et al. (2020) did not report any improvements with linguistic features, the others reported that combining linguistic features with deep learning approaches result in better ARA models.

Although a lot of this research evolved on English, the past decade saw ARA research in other languages such as German (Hancke et al., 2012), French (François and Fairon, 2012), Italian (Dell'Orletta et al., 2011), Bangla (Sinha et al., 2012) etc., which employed language specific feature sets. While most ARA research modeled one language at a time, some research created language agnostic feature sets and architectures and experimented with 2 to 7 languages (Shen et al., 2013;Azpiazu and Pera, 2019;Madrazo Azpiazu and Pera, 2020a,b;Martinc et al., 2021;Weiss et al., 2021). Although only one language is considered per model in all this research, there are two important exceptions. Madrazo Azpiazu and Pera (2020b) explored whether combining texts from related languages during training improves ARA performance for low resource languages, and Weiss et al. (2021) used a model trained on English texts on German, based on a common, broad set of handcrafted linguistic features. However, to our knowledge, zero-shot cross lingual transfer of text embeddings, without any handcrafted features, was not explored for this task in the past.

ARA is traditionally treated as a classification problem in NLP research, although there are some exceptions. Heilman et al. (2008) compared linear, ordinal, and logistic regression and concluded that ordinal with a combination of lexical and grammatical features worked the best for ARA, although subsequent research was still dominated by classification approaches. There is some past work that considered ARA as a pairwise ranking problem, using SVM/SVM rank and hand crafted linguistic features (Pitler and Nenkova, 2008;Tanaka-Ishii et al., 2010;Ma et al., 2012;Mesgar and Strube, 2015;Ambati et al., 2016;Howcroft and Demberg, 2017), and while Tanaka-Ishii et al. (2010) and Ma et al. (2012) showed that ranking performs better than traditional features and classification/regression respectively, Xia et al. (2016) did not find ranking to be consistently better across the board. In this background, we take a fresh look at the application of ranking for ARA, by proposing a new neural pairwise ranking model.

Format.document: There has been a growing body of research studying the inner workings of BERT and trying to quantify what it learns in various scenarios, dubbed "BERTology" (Rogers et al., 2020). Of particular interest to this paper is work that analyzes BERT's output embeddings. Recent studies have found that embeddings created from the final layer of BERT tend to cluster according to word senses (Wiedemann et al., 2019), though this varies somewhat based on the position of a word in a sentence (Mickus et al., 2020). The final BERT layers also produce more contextualized word embeddings than the earlier layers (Ethayarajh, 2019), a finding we revisit using paraphrases in Section 3.3. Foundational analyses show that representations evolve from lexical to syntactic to semantic across depth (Tenney et al., 2019). Other work probes linear structure in embedding spaces, such as syntax trees captured by distances (Hewitt and Manning, 2019). Attention heads have been linked to interpretable functions, albeit imperfectly, including coreference and dependency relations (Clark et al., 2019). However, attention may not be explanation by itself, and sparsity can often be increased without hurting performance (Jain and Wallace, 2019). Studies of layer selectivity indicate redundancy and overparameterization in Transformers (Kovaleva et al., 2019). At the same time, pruning experiments suggest that many attention heads are dispensable (Michel et al., 2019). Probing with control tasks has raised concerns about probe expressivity overshadowing the encoded information (Hewitt and Liang, 2019). Subsequent information-theoretic analyses quantify mutual information between representations and tasks to ameliorate this issue (Pimentel et al., 2020). Beyond task probes, geometric characterizations such as local linearity and anisotropy reveal systematic biases in embedding distributions (Ethayarajh, 2019). Contextual similarity has been tied to paraphrase behavior and lexical substitution performance (Reif et al., 2019). Cross-lingual transfer evidence suggests partially shared abstraction layers in multilingual BERT (Pires et al., 2019). While BERT remains a central model, developments in pretraining objectives and architectures complicate direct comparisons (Liu et al., 2019). Training regimes based on masked language modeling interact with corpus composition to shape representational geometry (Gururangan et al., 2020). For reference, the canonical Transformer encoder defines the backbone used by BERT Vaswani et al., 2017. Our focus is not on architecture variants per se but on the empirical properties of output embeddings across contexts. Sense-specific clustering has been shown to improve with additional context windows in sentence-level models (Amrami and Goldberg, 2019). Dynamic subspace methods further disentangle polysemy by projecting tokens into sense-aware manifolds (Coenen et al., 2019). Despite these advances, distinguishing contextualization from memorization remains challenging (Zhang et al., 2021). Recent work emphasizes dataset artifacts that inflate apparent linguistic competence (McCoy et al., 2019). To avoid confounds, we employ paraphrase-driven evaluation that varies surface forms while holding semantics constant (Wieting and Gimpel, 2018). Complementary diagnostics measure how neighborhood structures shift under synonym substitutions (Wang et al., 2020). Robustness analyses also consider domain shift, showing degradation when topical priors change (Hendrycks et al., 2020). In the context of lexical semantics, attraction and repulsion forces across layers suggest distinct roles for shallow and deep features (Voita et al., 2019). Furthermore, token type and position embeddings interact to modulate attention patterns in subtle ways (Press et al., 2021). We build on these findings to articulate hypotheses about when final-layer embeddings capture sense distinctions faithfully. Specifically, we test whether paraphrase consistency increases with deeper layers relative to middle layers. We also analyze whether contextual isotropy correlates with stability under word order perturbations (Gao et al., 2019). Our contributions complement survey narratives by providing targeted, reproducible measurements on widely used checkpoints (Rogers et al., 2020). Together, this related work motivates a systematic study of contextualized output embeddings and their dependence on syntax, semantics, and domain.

Format.document: Prior approaches focused on framing DST as question answering (Ruan et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021). Many MultiWoZ cross-domain models leverage slot names or descriptions (Wu et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2021a). Pretrained generative LLMs (Raffel et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2020) have enabled framing NLP tasks as seq2seq problems. Some DST papers (Zhao et al., 2021a; Feng et al., 2021) look at settings with no train–test discrepancy. Many studies explore the efficacy of task-specific prompts (Jiang et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021). Madotto et al. (2020) prime language models with examples for dialogue tasks without finetuning. Wei et al. (2021) fine-tune language models to understand prompts for a different task. Recent work on instruction following suggests that generalization can emerge from diverse task mixtures during pretraining (Sanh et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2022). Nevertheless, dialogue state tracking remains sensitive to domain shift and ontology drift across datasets (Zhang et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2021b). Early slot-filling pipelines relied on span extraction and rule-based normalization (Henderson et al., 2014; Mrkšić et al., 2017). Neural architectures gradually replaced hand-crafted pipelines with attention mechanisms and contextual encoders (Xie et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020). Schema-guided approaches extended these models to unseen services by conditioning on natural language descriptions (Rastogi et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021). In multi-domain settings, sharing parameters across slots reduces data requirements but complicates calibration (Zhao et al., 2021b; Feng et al., 2022). Prompt-based DST reframes state tracking as conditional generation under textual constraints (Hou et al., 2022; Ding et al., 2023). Empirical comparisons indicate that generative decoders are competitive with span extractors when constrained by ontological priors (Peng et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2022). However, brittle alignment between templates and ontology labels often limits portability to new domains (Kim et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023a). Semi-supervised methods exploit unlabeled dialogue corpora with consistency regularization and pseudo-labeling (Chen et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020). Active learning further reduces annotation cost by querying informative turns under uncertainty (Settles, 2009; Lowell et al., 2019). A parallel strand studies retrieval-augmented dialogue tracking that grounds slot values in external tables or documents (Gao et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2023). Cross-lingual transfer has been explored by aligning slot semantics via multilingual encoders (Xu et al., 2020; Lai et al., 2022). Despite these advances, assumptions about clean ontology alignment in evaluation benchmarks can inflate reported gains (Eric et al., 2020; Budzianowski et al., 2018). In contrast, real-world deployments face noisy user inputs, implicit preferences, and evolving taxonomies (Zhou et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023). To bridge this gap, some studies advocate abstraction over slot names using free-form descriptions, but they often disregard disambiguation costs (Lin et al., 2021a; Lee et al., 2022). Zero-shot generalization is further complicated by spurious correlations between domain keywords and slot values (Xie et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022). Evaluation protocols increasingly emphasize calibration, coverage, and abstention under ontological uncertainty (Desai and Durrett, 2020; Kumar and Sarawagi, 2019). Another line of work treats DST as iterative constrained decoding guided by a structured prior over admissible states (Zhang et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2023). Few-shot prompting with in-context examples reduces the need for task-specific finetuning in DST variants (Brown et al., 2020; Min et al., 2022). However, empirical results remain sensitive to prompt order, demonstrations, and verbalizers (Lu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2021c). Recent analyses argue that instruction-tuned LLMs can internalize schema knowledge yet still benefit from task-specific adapters (Wang et al., 2023b; Hu et al., 2021). Conversely, compact encoder-decoders with targeted finetuning offer stronger latency–accuracy trade-offs for production systems (Tay et al., 2022; Lester et al., 2021). Prior QA-style formulations inspired copy-based decoders that extract slot spans from the dialogue context (Ruan et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2020), and follow-ups refined negative span handling in ambiguous turns (Zhang et al., 2021). Nevertheless, the mapping from questions to slots can entangle surface patterns with domain heuristics in ways documented by (Ruan 2020) and later ablations. Building on schema descriptions, contrastive pretraining increases robustness to paraphrases of slot definitions (Chen et al., 2022; Su et al., 2022). Our perspective synthesizes these threads by decoupling ontology access, grounding, and state summarization under a uniform prompting framework (Raffel et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2022). In the remainder, we motivate design choices, review alternatives, and outline evaluation protocols that stress robustness and transfer (Budzianowski et al., 2018; Rastogi et al., 2020).

Format.document:
Symbol Grounding. Contemporary grounders extensively utilize batch learning (e.g., Shridhar and Hsu, 2018). Yet, ITL requires incremental learning because without it the teacher guidance cannot influence the learner's inferences about plans as and when the advice is given. Further, many grounders assume that the learner starts out with a complete and accurate conceptualisation of the domain using pre-defined visual features and a known vocabulary (Kennington et al., 2015; Kennington and Schlangen, 2017; Wang et al., 2017). In ITL, both of these assumptions are unrealistic; therefore in this paper we explore models for which these assumptions don't apply. Finally, in contrast to all prior grounders, we support incremental learning when the training exemplars feature REs that are linguistically complex: e.g., "two red circles that aren't to the right of both green squares".

Representation Learning. Models for jointly learning a representation for vision and language utilize either explicit alignment via bounding boxes or instance segmentation (Lu et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Tan and Bansal, 2019; Kamath et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021), or a large-volume of weakly labeled data in the form of image-caption pairs (Radford et al., 2021). These models rely on offline learning with large datasets. This work, on the other hand, explores how to incrementally extract knowledge in a few-shot manner, using sequentially observed evidence that consists of weakly-labelled annotations, including neologisms.

Grounded Language Acquisition. This task is commonly realized as grounded grammar induction from image-caption pairs (Shi et al., 2019; Zhao and Titov, 2020), or as (neural) semantic parsers learning from a reward signal (Williams, 1992) in visual question answering (Yi et al., 2018) or in planning (Azaria et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017; Karamcheti et al., 2020). In these scenarios, the primary objective is to learn mappings from linguistic expressions to logical forms, which in turn get associated with certain visual percepts during the learning process. This paper does not tackle learning logical forms. Instead, we obtain them from an existing broad-coverage grammar and focus on exploiting the logical consequences of those logical forms during symbol grounding—i.e., our focus is to utilise the interpretation of logical forms, and in particular the truth functional meanings of close-class words like quantifiers and negation, to inform the learning of mappings from (open-class) symbols like red to their denotations, given the visual percepts.

Visual Question Answering (VQA) is a task of answering free-form questions about an image (Antol et al., 2015). VQA has reached impressive performance in recent years (Fukui et al., 2016), yet VQA models struggle with out-of-distribution generalization for new types of questions requiring multi-step reasoning, with analysis revealing that they often rely on shortcuts (Jiang and Bansal, 2019; Subramanian et al., 2020). Grounded VQA models like (Yi et al. 2018) and Bogin et al. (2021) tackle these shortcomings by learning to ground parts of the question and then learning to compose those parts via the question's syntax to compute the answer. They thus estimate denotations of linguistic parts that are not denoted by the answer to the question. By doing so, these models achieve out-of-distribution generalization for novel questions. However, these models lack the ITL's requirement for incremental learning: model training relies on batch learning. Furthermore, while their performance is impressive, error analysis shows that it tends to make mistakes on sentences containing logical concepts like quantifiers and negation (e.g., Bogin et al., 2021, Figure shows that the determiner most incorrectly denotes an arbitrary subset of entities). Our view is that there is little benefit in trying to learn to ground these concepts as they are domain independent and can be interpreted using formal semantics. In our experiments, we are testing the extent to which knowing and reasoning with the logical meanings of these symbols helps incremental grounding, and in particular estimating denotations of symbols within an RE that aren't designated by that RE.

Visual Reference Resolution. In previous experimental setups, it is often assumed that there is a unique referent in the visual scene for the given RE in the test phase (e.g., Kazemzadeh et al., 2014; Whitney et al., 2016). We aim to cope with situations where the RE has multiple referents: identifying all the referents that satisfy an RE enables efficient planning, because it affords free choice when executing certain commands—e.g., "move a circle to the left." When there is more than one circle, this affords choosing a control policy so that resources are optimized.

Format.document: A Brief History of NLU Datasets. As a core module of task-oriented dialogue systems, natural language understanding has been studied since the early 1990s with the Airline Travel Information System initiative (Hemphill et al., 1990). ATIS consisted of spoken queries about flight-related information and spurred early research in semantic parsing for slot filling. Over the next two decades, only a few reusable NLU resources were released for dialog applications. The scarcity began to change in 2013 with the advent of the dialogue state tracking paradigm that emphasized tracking user goals across turns (Williams et al., 2013; Henderson et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2016). Rather than classifying each turn independently, state tracking emphasizes maintaining a compact representation of user goals throughout the conversation. Several datasets were introduced during the DST challenges, generally covering narrow domains and simple intent or act inventories. In parallel, the deep learning era brought demand for larger and more diverse corpora to train data-hungry models (Budzianowski et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2018; Rastogi et al., 2019; Peskov et al., 2019). However, task-oriented datasets differ from machine translation or speech recognition corpora in that schemas and ontologies are domain specific and hard to reuse across tasks (Williams et al., 2013; Henderson et al., 2014. This tight coupling often impedes cross-domain transfer and complicates benchmarking under unified evaluation protocols. Annotation quality also varies widely because domain experts are required and guidelines evolve over time (Eric et al., 2019). Consequently, many corpora exhibit label sparsity, ontology drift, and inconsistent slot value normalization. Recent work has sought to mitigate these issues by proposing schema-guided annotation, improved ontology design, and synthetic augmentation using simulators (Rastogi et al., 2020; Shah et al., 2018; Campagna et al., 2020). Other efforts target multilingual and cross-lingual NLU, where the lack of aligned ontologies and parallel annotations remains a key obstacle (Schuster et al., 2019; Castellucci et al., 2019). To support end-to-end modeling, several benchmarks now integrate NLU with dialogue management and generation while exposing explicit state labels for analysis (Hosseini-Asl et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020). Despite this progress, reproducibility still depends critically on how datasets define intents, slots, and context windows, as subtle choices can change reported performance. We argue that future resources should emphasize compositional generalization, realistic user behavior, and robust evaluation under distribution shift. Accordingly, we review dataset design patterns, synthesize best practices, and identify open challenges to guide future NLU dataset construction.

Format.document: In this section, we discuss related studies with respect to the contrastive learning framework and sentence embedding. Early work on distributed sentence representations emphasized supervised objectives aligned with downstream tasks. Methods such as InferSent leveraged natural language inference labels to capture transferable features (Conneau et al., 2017). Subsequent research explored unsupervised heuristics, including next sentence prediction and masked language modeling as pretext signals (Devlin et al., 2019). However, these approaches often underperform on semantic textual similarity without fine-tuning. Contrastive learning reframed representation learning by pulling semantically related pairs together while pushing unrelated samples apart (Hadsell et al., 2006). In natural language processing, contrastive objectives were adapted by constructing positive pairs from data augmentations, paraphrases, or contextual neighbors (Gao et al., 2021;Yan et al., 2021). SimCSE highlighted the efficacy of minimal augmentation via dropout to produce strong baselines for sentence embeddings (Gao et al., 2021). Other studies incorporated syntactic or semantic constraints to enrich positive pairs and mitigate representation collapse (Kim et al., 2021;Zhang and Wu, 2022). Beyond instance discrimination, alignment with external knowledge graphs has been examined to refine relational structure (Wang et al., 2021). Hard negative mining remains a central concern, as naive sampling can lead to spurious gradients and diminished margins (Robinson et al., 2021). Curriculum strategies and dynamic queues have been proposed to regulate negative hardness over training Conneau et al., 2017). Data augmentation for sentences poses unique challenges compared to images, where perturbations such as cropping and color jitter preserve labels. Textual augmentations risk altering meaning, prompting methods that generate paraphrases via back-translation or neural editing (Feng et al., 2021;Iyyer et al., 2018). Recent work also leverages multi-view contexts from retrieval corpora to create positive pairs grounded in shared evidence (Izacard et al., 2021). From an architectural perspective, most systems adopt transformer encoders with pooled token representations (Vaswani et al., 2017;Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). Pooling strategies such as CLS, mean pooling, and attention pooling affect isotropy and downstream calibration (Gao et al., 2019;Li et al., 2020). Regularization with whitening, temperature scaling, and adaptive margins has been shown to stabilize training and improve calibration (Su and Kuo, 2022). Cross-lingual sentence embeddings extend these ideas by aligning parallel or comparable corpora to share a joint semantic space (Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019;Feng et al., 2022). In multilingual settings, the balance between language-specific nuances and language-agnostic structure is especially delicate (Lauscher et al., 2020). Evaluation protocols typically rely on semantic textual similarity, clustering, and retrieval benchmarks to assess generalization (Cer et al., 2017;Wang et al., 2022). Nevertheless, inconsistencies across datasets and metrics complicate comparisons, motivating standardized suites and fair training budgets (Musgrave et al., 2020). Recent analyses further decompose gains into augmentation effects, objective design, and data scale, revealing complementary contributions (Chuang et al., 2020;Khosla et al., 2020). Building on these insights, our work investigates robust negative sampling and multi-view supervision to advance sentence-level representation learning.

Format.document: Label smoothing has become a standard regularization technique in classification tasks. Originally proposed for image classification by Szegedy et al. (2016), it relaxes hard targets into a distribution. Formally, K denotes the number of classes, α is the smoothing parameter, and α/K redistributes probability mass from the gold label. The modified targets mitigate overconfidence and improve calibration (Müller et al., 2019; Pereyra et al., 2017). Subsequent work studied its interaction with data augmentation and temperature scaling (Xie et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2017). In neural machine translation, label smoothing is often combined with subword tokenization to stabilize training (Vaswani et al., 2017). Vocabulary sharing further reduces parameters by tying input and output embeddings across languages or tasks (Press and Wolf, 2017; Inan et al., 2017). It has become standard in encoder–decoder architectures with joint BPE vocabularies (Sennrich et al., 2016. Empirical studies report gains in both perplexity and BLEU when embeddings are tied and labels are smoothed (Edunov et al., 2018; Ott et al., 2019). However, the interaction effects can depend on corpus size and morphological richness (Haddow et al., 2018). Recent multilingual models leverage shared vocabularies to promote cross-lingual transfer while controlling drift via smoothing (Conneau et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020). Despite these benefits, overly aggressive smoothing may obscure rare-word learning in low-resource settings (Shen et al., 2016). Prior analyses caution that smoothing interacts with label noise and loss geometry in nontrivial ways (Ghosh et al., 2017; Meister et al., 2020). We unify these threads by comparing smoothing strengths under tied and untied vocabularies across diverse translation directions. Our review highlights open questions on principled schedules, adaptive schemes, and their synergy with tokenization choices.

Format.document:
Sparse attention mechanism The full attention mechanism has a quadratic memory cost. Prior research works have proposed different sparse attention mechanisms to reduce the memory cost. Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020) uses a dilated sliding window of blocks and global attention patterns. BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) employs sliding window and random blocks. Reformer (Kitaev et al., 2020) uses the locality-sensitive hashing. In addition to optimizing the encoder self-attention, Huang et al. (2021) propose head-wise positional strides to reduce the cost of the encoder-decoder attention. However, sparse attention diminishes the benefits of pretraining and sacrifices parts of the receptive field.

Extract-then-generate method The model first extracts salient text snippets from the input, followed by generating a concise overall summary. Most two-stage summarization approaches (Zhang et al., 2019;Lebanoff et al., 2019;Xu and Durrett, 2019;Bajaj et al., 2021) are trained separately, which suffer from information loss due to the cascaded errors. Some approaches attempt to reduce that loss by bridging the two stages. Chen and Bansal (2018) adopt reinforcement learning with a sentence-level policy gradient method. Bae et al. (2019) propose summary-level policy gradient. In addition to the drawbacks explained in Section 2.3, our model is different as we jointly train an extractthen-generate model for summarization using latent variables.

Divide-and-conquer approach A common approach in long input summarization is divide-andconquer (Gidiotis and Tsoumakas, 2020;Grail et al., 2021). This approach breaks a long input into multiple parts, which are summarized separately and combined to produce a final complete summary. However, these models do not capture the contextual dependencies across parts and assume a certain structure of the input (such as paper sections).

Hierarchical models Various hierarchical models have been proposed to handle the longer inputs. Cohan et al. (2018) model the document discourse structure with a hierarchical encoder and a discourse-aware decoder to generate the summary. HAT-Bart (Rohde et al., 2021) proposes a new Hierarchical Attention Transformer-based architecture that attempts to capture sentence and paragraphlevel information. HMNet (Zhu et al., 2020) builds a hierarchical structure that includes discourselevel information and speaker roles. However, these models focus mainly on model performance and not on reducing the memory and computational cost.

Memory-efficient training techniques such as gradient checkpointing and reversible layers further complement sparse attention without altering model semantics. Recent work explores retrieval-augmented summarization to bypass long-sequence encoding by conditioning on retrieved passages (Lewis et al., 2020;Borgeaud et al., 2022). A complementary perspective is offered by Zhong and Durrett, 2019) who analyze error propagation in cascaded models. However, retrieval can introduce topical drift when the index is noisy and may fail for domain-specific corpora. Another line of research investigates planner-based generation, where a high-level content plan is predicted before surface realization (Narayan et al., 2021). Our setting also relates to multi-document summarization, in which cross-document discourse and redundancy must be addressed (Fabbri et al., 2019). We differ from prior extract-then-abstract pipelines by integrating selection and compression through a shared latent representation trained end-to-end.

Format.document:
Semantic parsing seeks to map natural language to executable representations grounded in a schema or environment. Foundational work established grammar-based approaches and learning from denotations (Zelle and Mooney, 1996; Zettlemoyer and Collins, 2005; Pasupat and Liang, 2015). Recent neural models leverage sequence-to-sequence architectures and structured decoders to handle compositionality (Dong and Lapata, 2018; Yin and Neubig, 2017). This line of research emphasizes correctness of programs under a predefined grammar and type system (Krishnamurthy et al., 2017). Related advances in program synthesis similarly target mapping specifications to programs with formal semantics (Gulwani, 2011; Desai et al., 2016). A complementary thread uses weak supervision via answer supervision rather than full logical forms (Clarke et al., 2010; Berant et al., 2013). Despite progress, reliance on a fixed domain or API can limit generalization to open settings (Gupta et al., 2020). Our framing instead studies agents that communicate in free-form language to coordinate problem solving without assuming a hand designed DSL.

Multi-hop question answering evaluates the ability to integrate information across multiple sources. Benchmarks such as HotpotQA, QAngaroo, and StrategyQA operationalize multi-step reasoning across documents or facts (Yang et al., 2018; Welbl et al., 2018; Geva et al., 2021). However, numerous studies have revealed annotation artifacts and single-hop shortcuts that confound evaluation (Min et al., 2019a; Chen and Durrett, 2019). As a result, systems may achieve high scores without demonstrating robust compositional reasoning (Gardner et al., 2020; Trivedi et al., 2020). Dataset construction techniques such as adversarial filtering and perturbation aim to reduce these shortcuts (Nie et al., 2019; Bartolo et al., 2020). Modeling innovations include retrieval-augmented readers and graph-based reasoning over evidence chains (Clark and Gardner, 2018; Tu et al., 2020). Yet many approaches still struggle when intermediate steps are implicit, ambiguous, or require collaboration among distinct agents (Khot et al., 2021).

Question decomposition has emerged as a practical strategy to enforce intermediate structure in multi-hop QA. Pipelined methods decompose a question into sub-questions executed by a single model or toolset (Talmor and Berant, 2018; Perez et al., 2020). Other works learn latent decompositions using supervision only from final answers (Min et al., 2019b; Perez et al., 2020). While effective, these systems are often tailored to specific datasets and supervision regimes (Furrer et al., 2020). Moreover, evaluations rarely capture the dynamics of multi-agent collaboration that arise in realistic problem solving (Schick et al., 2023). Our study broadens this scope by involving multiple specialized agents that must exchange information through language to complete tasks. We further encourage models to learn decompositions through interaction rather than pre-specified schemes or gold step annotations.

Synthetic reasoning benchmarks offer controlled settings to probe systematic generalization. Classic datasets emphasize compositional rules and out-of-distribution splits that stress test neural models (Lake and Baroni, 2018; Keysers et al., 2020). More recent proposals introduce rich vocabularies, noise, and longer reasoning chains to close the gap with naturalistic tasks (Sinha et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021). Nevertheless, many synthetic setups lack interactive elements that reflect conversational coordination among agents (Hermann et al., 2017). We build on these insights to design environments where agents must request, provide, and verify partial information before committing to an answer. This design better isolates reasoning from spurious lexical correlations and shallow retrieval cues (Sagawa et al., 2020). It also facilitates transparent error analysis by tracing messages and intermediate commitments produced during collaboration.

Informed by the above literature, we structure our challenge around three dataset types and four cooperating agents. The agents include a retriever, a reader, a planner, and a verifier, each with distinct capabilities and partial observability. Interactions are governed by lightweight protocols that allow flexible turn taking while remaining agnostic to any particular ontology. To situate our work, we also draw methodological parallels with Lake and Baroni (2018 and subsequent analyses of systematicity in pretrained models (Nye et al., 2021). Unlike single-agent decomposers, our setting requires negotiation of subgoals and verification of evidence across turns. We provide evaluation protocols that measure both final accuracy and intermediate collaboration quality, including faithfulness of rationales and message utility. Together, these design choices aim to catalyze research on robust, interactive, and compositional reasoning beyond narrow dataset-specific heuristics.

Format.document: Sentence rewriting IUR can be considered to be similar to the sentence rewriting task (Xu and Veeramachaneni, 2021; Lin et al., 2021; Chen and Bansal, 2018; Cao et al., 2018). Recent studies have addressed the IUR task with various sophisticated methods. Text generation IUR can be formulated as text generation by using the seq2seq model (Pan et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2021). For the generation, several well-known pre-trained models have been applied (Lewis et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2020; Raffel et al., 2020) with promising results. We employ the T5 model (Raffel et al., 2020) as the main component to rewrite utterances. To address the problem of missing important tokens in the model's rewriting, we enhance T5 by introducing a Picker and two labeling methods (Section 3.2). The learning of Θ is carried out either by using utterance generation alone (the generator) or by combining two tasks: important token identification (the picker) and utterance generation (the generator). Incomplete utterance rewriting aims to recover elided or context-dependent information in multi-turn dialogues. Prior work has explored pointer-generator networks and copy mechanisms to preserve salient entities across turns (See et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2016). Context modeling is crucial, with hierarchical encoders and discourse-level attention improving fidelity in rewritten outputs (Serban et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2019). External knowledge bases have been integrated to resolve underspecified references such as times and locations (Zhou et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022). Data scarcity remains a bottleneck, motivating weak supervision and distant supervision from large conversational corpora (Henderson et al., 2019; Mehri et al., 2020). Evaluation protocols typically combine exact match, BLEU, and slot-level accuracy to balance surface form and semantic adequacy (Papineni et al., 2002; Sulem et al., 2018) and recommend significance analysis following (Dror et al., 2018. However, these metrics can mask pragmatic errors in entity grounding, which are better captured by task-based success measures (Budzianowski et al., 2018; Eric et al., 2019). Transfer learning from summarization and paraphrasing has proven beneficial due to shared compression and rephrasing skills (Zhang et al., 2020; Prakash et al., 2016). Pretraining on synthetic deletions of context tokens further improves robustness to ambiguous pronouns and ellipses (Kale and Rastogi, 2020; Pan et al., 2020). Recent conversational datasets introduce more challenging phenomena such as anaphora chains and cross-turn negation (Quan et al., 2020; Elgohary et al., 2021). Reinforcement learning has been employed to optimize end-to-end task completion after rewriting, reducing exposure bias from maximum likelihood training (Ranzato et al., 2016; Paulus et al., 2018). Despite these advances, model hallucination persists when contextual cues are sparse or contradictory (Maynez et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2018). Constrained decoding and edit-based generation help limit unsupported insertions while retaining fluency (Stahlberg and Byrne, 2019; Mallinson et al., 2020). Our approach differs by explicitly separating the identification of pivotal tokens from the generation module to encourage faithful copying under tight budgets. We additionally incorporate curriculum learning over context window sizes to mitigate overfitting to truncated histories (Bengio et al., 2009). To ensure fair comparison, we adhere to prior preprocessing pipelines and report statistical significance under paired bootstrap resampling (Koehn, 2004). Finally, we position IUR within broader controllable text rewriting, noting conceptual links to style transfer and simplification (Jin et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2016).

Going from audio recordings to fully annotated transcripts implies two successive segmentation steps: the first segments words and happens during the production of phonemic or orthographic transcripts; the second further splits words into morphs, which are then annotated with syntactic information and glosses. We mostly focus on the former task, assuming a two-step process: first, the computation of a phonemic transcript, that we assume are given; then the segmentation into words for which we consider two settings: batch and online learning. The word and morpheme segmentation tasks are closely related and rely on similar tools: using the Japhug corpus, which contains both levels of segmentations, we also study the implications of using lists of words vs. morphemes as weak supervision.

In its baseline form, the word segmentation process is fully unsupervised, and the only training material is a set of transcribed sentences (see Fig. ).

We rely on Bayesian non-parametric approaches to word segmentation (see (Cohen D. et al. (2016)) for a thorough exposition), and our baselines are the unigram version of the dpseg model (Goldwater et al., 2009) and a variant where the underlying Dirichlet Process is replaced by a Pitman-Yor Process as in (Neubig, 2014). We selected unigram models for their simplicity, which (a) makes them amenable to the processing of very small sets of sentences; (b) makes the online learning setting tractable. While using higher order models or more sophisticated models of the same family (Teh, 2006b;Mochihashi et al., 2009) may improve the performance (see for an experimental comparison), we believe that in our low-resource conditions these variations would be small, 2 and would not change our main conclusions.

Word segmentation models fundamentally rely on probabilistic models for word sequences defining P (w = w 1 . . . w T ); word sequences can also be viewed as segmented sequences of characters y = y 1 . . . y L , so that the same model can be used for the joint probability of (y, b), with b = b 1 . . . b L representing the vector of boundary locations where value b t = 1 (resp. b t = 0) denotes a boundary (resp. no boundary) after symbol y t . In an unsupervised setting, these boundaries are hidden and are latent variables in the model. Such models lend themselves well to Gibbs sampling, which repeatedly produces samples of each boundary given all the other boundaries in the corpus.

In dpseg, the underlying sequence model is a unigram model: P (w 1 . . . w T ) = T t=1 P (w t ). Format.document:
Due to the challenge of learning phonemes, early works on unsupervised speech representation learning (Park and Glass, 2005;Lee and Glass, 2012;Ondel et al., 2016) focus on learning speech segments sharing similar acoustic properties, or phones, without taking into account the meaning of the speech they are part of. There are two main approaches in this direction. One approach is to learn discrete phone-like units without any textual labels by modeling phone labels of the speech segments as latent variables. In particular, (Park and Glass, 2005;Jansen et al., 2010) first detect segments with recurring patterns in the speech corpus followed by graph clustering using the similarity graph formed by the segments. (Lee and Glass, 2012;Ondel et al., 2016;Kamper et al., 2016) develop probabilistic graphical models to jointly segment and cluster speech into phone-like segments. An extension to the latent variable approach is to introduce additional latent variables such as speaker identity (Ondel et al., 2019) or language identity (Yusuf et al., 2020) and develop mechanisms to disentangle these variables.

With the advance of deep learning, neural network models have also been proposed to learn unsupervised phone-level representation either by first learning a continuous representation (Chung et al., 2019;Feng et al., 2019;Nguyen et al., 2020) followed by off-line clustering, or by learning a discrete representation end-to-end with Gumbel softmax (Eloff et al., 2019b;Baevski et al., 2020) or vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) (van den Oord et al., 2017;Chorowski et al., 2019). However, codebooks learned by the neural approaches tend to be much larger than the number of phonemes (Baevski et al., 2020), leading to low scores in standard phoneme discovery metrics. The second approach utilizes weak supervision such as noisy phone labels predicted by a supervised, multilingual ASR system trained on other languages (Yeh et al., 2019; Baevski et al., 2021. Along this direction, (Żelasko et al., 2020;Feng et al., 2021a) systematically study the performance of zero-shot crosslingual ASR on 13 languages trained with international phonetic alphabet (IPA) tokens and found that the system tends to perform poorly on unseen languages. Instead, (Feng et al., 2021b) is able to discover phone-like units by clustering bottleneck features (BNF) from a factorized time-delay neural network (TDNN-f) trained with phone labels predicted by a crosslingual ASR (Feng et al., 2021a).

Several works have since shifted focus toward the more challenging phoneme discovery problem by formulating it as a self-supervised learning problem where the semantics of the speech are known, such as from translation, phonemelevel language models or other sensory modalities such as vision. (Jansen, 2013) has studied the use of pairwise word identity labels for training phoneme discovery models based on Gaussian mixture models (GMM); (Harwath and Glass, 2019) analyzes the hidden layers of a two-branch neural network trained to retrieve spoken captions with semantically related images and finds strong correlation between segment representation and phoneme boundaries. (Harwath et al., 2020) adds hierarchical vector quantization (VQ) layers in the same retrieval network and is able to find a much smaller codebook than the unsupervised neural approach (Baevski et al., 2020), and achieve high correlation with the phoneme inventory. (Godard et al., 2018;Boito et al., 2019) has studied the possibility of learning semantic units using an attention-based speech-to-text translation system, though the units appear to correlate more with words. Works on unsupervised speech recognition attempt to learn to recognize phonemes by leveraging the semantic information from a phoneme language model unpaired with the speech, typically by matching the empirical prior and posterior distributions of phonemes either using cross entropy (Yeh et al., 2019) or adversarial loss (Baevski et al., 2021). Throughout the paper, we use P{•} to denote probability. We use capital letters to denote random variables and lower-case letters to represent samples of random variables. We use P X := P{X = x} to denote both probability mass and density functions of random variable X, depending on whether it is continuous or discrete. Further, denote P Y |X (y|x) := P{Y = y|X = x} as the true conditional probability distribution of random variable Y = y given random variable X = x. The probability simplex in R d is denoted as ∆ d. This notation allows us to succinctly state objectives that couple acoustic evidence with discrete phonemic structure. In the remainder of this paper, we synthesize insights from these strands to motivate a compact codebook that better matches phonemic inventories. We also highlight open challenges in crosslingual transfer, data scarcity, and evaluation that frame our subsequent methodology and experiments.

Format.document: This section provides background and motivation for task and domain adaptability applied to concern detection in the 2017 French Election domain ( §2.1, §2.2), including concern values induced from Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) ( §2.3). Concern detection seeks to identify expressed moral or policy issues within text drawn from political discourse. Prior work on stance, sentiment, and toxicity provides related signals but lacks fine-grained moral categories (Mohammad et al., 2018; Johnson and Goldwasser, 2018). Moral Foundations Theory posits a small set of cross-cultural moral dimensions that can be operationalized for annotation (Haidt, 2012; Graham et al., 2013). Adapting models across tasks aims to leverage auxiliary supervision, such as emotion or stance labels, to improve concern classifiers under data scarcity (Ruder, 2019; Caruana, 1997). Domain adaptation is essential because lexical choices, hashtags, and rhetorical styles in French electoral Twitter differ from general corpora (Ben-David et al., 2010; Ramponi and Plank, 2020). Multilingual and cross-lingual transfer have improved political text analytics by sharing representations across languages (Conneau et al., 2020; Pires et al., 2019). However, domain-shifted moral language often exhibits sarcasm, coded references, and campaign-specific entities that degrade zero-shot performance (Garg et al., 2022). We therefore examine strategies combining task transfer and domain adaptation, including parameter-efficient tuning and adversarial alignment (Houlsby et al., 2019; Ganin and Lempitsky, 2015). For sequence labeling and classification, pretrained transformers provide robust baselines Raffel et al., 2019) in low-resource domains. Yet naïve fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting of moral nuances learned from auxiliary tasks (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Howard and Ruder, 2018). Recent work on multi-task learning with label taxonomies suggests hierarchical objectives can preserve shared structure while isolating domain-specific features (Sanh et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2019). In electoral contexts, issue frames and moral concerns are temporally coupled with campaign events, necessitating time-aware adaptation (Roberts et al., 2014; Eisenstein et al., 2014). We also consider weak supervision from distant signals such as party mentions and manifesto alignments to expand labeled coverage (Mintz et al., 2009; Barberá, 2015). Altogether, this study situates concern detection at the intersection of moral semantics, task transfer, and domain adaptation, with a focus on the 2017 French Election as a challenging yet representative testbed.

Format.document: Discrete Prompts The release of GPT-3 Brown et al. 2020) has led to interest in prompting, a new way to leverage pretrained language models (PLM). Brown et al. (2020) proposes an intuitive in-context learning paradigm by concatenating a few input and output examples and feeding them to the language model and let the model autoregressively generate answers for new examples. Recent works (Petroni et al., 2019; Davison et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2020) design prompts to probe the factual and commonsense knowledge encoded within a PLM. Recent works (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b; Gao et al., 2021) demonstrate that even smaller PLMs have similar few-shot learning capacity. Le Scao and Rush (2021) analyzes the effect of prompting and concludes that a single prompt may be worth 100 training examples in fine-tuning. Instead of manually designing prompts (i.e., prompt engineering), some recent studies also explore automatic prompt generation. PETAL (Schick et al., 2020) augments Pattern Exploiting Training (PET, Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b) with automatically identified label words; Gao et al., 2021 uses re-ranking to find the best label words by fine-tuning a RoBERTa model on the candidates searched by RoBERTa, and using an external generation model for data augmentation of prompt templates; AutoPrompt (Shin et al., 2020) uses a gradient-based search to determine both prompts and label words. However, these methods require parameter updates with gradient descent, which is infeasible without access to the model weights (e.g., GPT-3). PET and its variants also require a large unlabeled set and need to be fine-tuned multiple times. AutoPrompt uses discretization techniques to approximately map a continuous vector back to tokens in the vocabulary (i.e., "vocablization"). These searched prompts and labels are often uninterpretable by humans, and, different from these prior studies, our proposed AMuLaP is a simple and interpretable method for few-shot prompting that can work well with and without access to model weights, while concurrently to our work others propose a method that exploits an external knowledge base to find label mapping.

Format.document: Many idiom detection models build on insights about unconventional meaning in metaphor. A number of approaches use distributional models, such as Kintsch (2000), Utsumi (2011), Sa-Pereira (2016), and Shutova et al. (2012), the latter of which was one of the first to implement a fully unsupervised approach for encoding relationships between words, their contexts, and their dependencies. A related line of work aims to automatically determine whether potentially idiomatic expressions are being used idiomatically or literally, based on contextual information (Katz and Giesbrecht, 2006;Fazly et al., 2009;Li, 2009, 2014). Our measure of conventionality is inspired by the insights of these models; as described in Section 3.2, our measure uses differences in embeddings across contexts. Meanwhile, approaches to collocation detection have taken a probabilistic or information-theoretic approach that seeks to identify collocations using word combination probabilities. PMI is a frequently-used quantity for measuring cooccurrence probabilities (Fano, 1961;Church and Hanks, 1990), and related normalizations have been explored (Smith et al., 2017. Other implementations include selectional association (Resnik, 1996), symmetric conditional probability (Ferreira and Pereira Lopes, 1999), and log-likelihood (Dunning, 1993;Daille, 1996). While much of the literature in NLP recognizes that idioms share a cluster of properties, including semantic idiosyncrasy, syntactic inflexibility, and institutionalization (e.g., Sag et al., 2002;Fazly and Stevenson, 2006;Fazly et al., 2009), our approach is novel in attempting to characterize idioms along two orthogonal dimensions that correspond to specific proposals from the cognitive science literature. Our measures may offer a new avenue for tackling the problem of automatic idiom detection. Prior work also distinguishes between idiom token and idiom type identification, emphasizing corpus-level variability across genres and registers (Cook et al., 2008;Schneider et al., 2014). From a cognitive perspective, conventionalization interacts with familiarity and decomposability, factors that modulate processing cost in reading studies (Cacciari and Tabossi, 1988;Titone and Connine, 1999). Recent neural methods incorporate contextualized embeddings to capture such gradients, often combining sequence tagging with attention over candidate expressions (Salton et al., 2016;Hashempour and Villavicencio, 2020). Nevertheless, most evaluations remain limited to English newswire and social media, which raises questions about cross-linguistic generalization and domain shift (Muzny and Zettlemoyer, 2013;Peng et al., 2014). To address these gaps, we integrate corpus-informed priors with a calibration layer that downweights unreliable context cues, as suggested by Jones, 2020), while maintaining sensitivity to compositional signals in nearby syntax. We conclude by outlining how our framework can interface with lexicographic resources and active learning for improved coverage and interpretability in future work.

Format.document: The state of NLP in South Asia remains uneven across languages and tasks. Initiatives aimed at language technology have tended to prioritize officially recognized and standardized languages. Prominent resources include the EMILLE corpus (McEnery et al., 2000), IndicNLP Suite (Kakwani et al., 2020), and iNLTK (Arora, 2020). Community-building has been catalyzed by workshops such as DravidianLangTech (Chakravarthi et al., 2021) and WILDRE (Jha et al., 2020). Nevertheless, as survey tables consistently show, only a minority of regional languages benefit from sustained NLP research or consumer-facing tools. Computational historical linguistics intersects with core NLP activities including corpus construction, POS tagging, morphological analysis, and dependency parsing. For high-resource languages like Hindi, large hand-annotated treebanks support state-of-the-art neural modeling. Recent transformer models and pretraining pipelines have delivered strong performance for Hindi across semantics and transfer (Jain et al., 2020; Khanuja et al., 2021). Parallel resources and systems further enable robust English–Hindi translation and transliteration (Saini and Sahula, 2018). Yet sizable gaps persist for what Joshi et al. term the “Left-Behinds,” especially among minority and endangered languages (Joshi et al., 2020). Linguists have compiled small treebanks for languages such as Palula and Toda that await digitization and conversion to Universal Dependencies (Liljegren and Haider, 2015; Emeneau, 1984). New UD releases have begun to appear for Kangri, Mandeali, Bhojpuri, and Magahi (Ojha and Zeman, 2020). Historical and comparative linguistics in South Asia traces back to grammatical traditions associated with Pāṇini and Hemacandra. Following the recognition of the Indo‑European family, systematic comparative studies took root in the region. Influential grammars survey the Dravidian family (Caldwell, 1856; Andronov, 2003; Krishnamurti, 2003) and the Indo‑Aryan family (Beames, 1872; Hoernlé, 1880; Bloch, 1934; Masica, 1993). Emeneau introduced the notion of a South Asian linguistic area that cuts across genealogical boundaries (Emeneau, 1956). Subsequent micro‑areal work sheds light on contact and convergence dynamics (Peterson, 2017; Liljegren et al., 2021; Toulmin, 2006). The Linguistic Survey of India remains the only subcontinent‑wide undertaking of its scope (Grierson, 1903–1928). No comparably comprehensive, centralized repository covering lexicon, typology, and sociolinguistics has emerged since. Early comparativists often drew data from prestige standards like Delhi Hindi, with localized lects documented in a piecemeal fashion. Major reference works include the Comparative Dictionary of the Indo‑Aryan Languages (Turner, 1962–1966) and the Dravidian Etymological Dictionary (Burrow and Emeneau, 1984). Documentation of Austroasiatic languages has grown, though secondary analyses sometimes overgeneralize from limited primary data (Anderson, 2008). In NLP, corpus development and annotation workflows remain the main bottlenecks for many under-resourced languages. Multilingual pretraining has helped transfer representations across related scripts and families, as shown in (Conneau et al., 2020). However, domain mismatch, orthographic variation, and data scarcity still hamper downstream robustness. Progress also depends on open licensing, ethical data governance, and sustained community partnerships. For cross-lingual modeling, tokenization and script normalization require careful adaptation to Brahmic orthographies. Shared tasks have begun to benchmark morphological inflection, segmentation, and parsing for smaller languages. Nevertheless, many benchmarks underrepresent colloquial registers, code-mixing, and non‑standard spellings. Resource catalogs that integrate metadata on scripts, dialects, and domains can guide investment and reuse. As demonstrated in Kakwani et al. (2020), cross‑lingual toolchains can reduce duplication of effort when extended thoughtfully. This survey synthesizes the current landscape, emphasizing opportunities where modest curation could yield large gains. We conclude by outlining evaluation practices and reproducible baselines tailored to South Asian languages.

There is a long tradition of grounding language understanding on single images, in the form of visual question answering (Goyal et al., 2017; Hudson and Manning, 2019), visual dialogue (de Vries et al., 2017; Das et al., 2017), or visual entailment (Xie et al., 2019). Recently, more and more focus has been directed to settings where the visual context consists of multiple images, either conventional static pictures (Vedantam et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2019; Suhr et al., 2019; Forbes et al., 2019; Hendricks and Nematzadeh, 2021; Yan et al., 2021; Hosseinzadeh and Wang, 2021; Bogin et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021), or video frames (Jhamtani and Berg-Kirkpatrick, 2018a; Bansal et al., 2020). While many of these benchmarks involve just two images, COVR (Bogin et al., 2021) and ISVQA (Bansal et al., 2020) provide more images, similar to our sets of 10 images.

ISVQA and Spot-the-diff (Jhamtani and Berg-Kirkpatrick, 2018a) are most similar to our dataset, IMAGECODE. ISVQA is based on several video frames that are synthetic and cover a restricted domain, with short questions for Visual Question Answering. Spot-the-diff provides two frames from surveillance video cameras and descriptions of all their differences. IMAGECODE is unique as a) we cover a wider range of domains; b) we construct image sets that are maximally similar while being distinguishable through natural language (Section 3) and c) we limit descriptions to relevant differences. This results in (a) diverse, (b) complex and (c) pragmatically informative descriptions.

IMAGECODE elicits pragmatic reasoning (Andreas and Klein, 2016; Cohn-Gordon et al., 2018) as a listener has to consider the context and resolve ambiguities resulting from nuanced differences to solve the task. Our goal in this paper is to formalize multi-image description as a pragmatic reference game where utterances must discriminate among near-duplicate scenes. We position our work at the intersection of vision and language datasets and computational pragmatics. Prior image description corpora typically emphasize coverage of salient objects or events, whereas we emphasize contrastive detail that becomes meaningful only in context. As a result, conventional captioning metrics that reward n-gram overlap can undervalue truly informative differences. We therefore adopt evaluation protocols that balance surface similarity with referential success. In particular, we measure whether human or model listeners can identify the target image set from the provided description. This formulation connects our task to classic referential expression generation, but extends it from within-image localization to across-image disambiguation. It also relates to work on visual commonsense inference, since many differences require implicit world knowledge to articulate concisely. A persistent challenge in multi-image understanding is the combinatorial explosion of potential contrasts even for small sets. To cope with this challenge, we design sampling procedures that produce hard, but solvable, distractor sets without resorting to heavy annotation. Our construction pipeline selects candidate images with similar global embeddings and then filters them using lexical constraints derived from preliminary descriptions. The final dataset contains domains such as street scenes, tabletop settings, and natural landscapes with controlled visual entropy. We provide train, validation, and test splits that preserve domain diversity and minimize leakage across nearly identical scenes. We benchmark a suite of baselines spanning text-only, image-only, and multimodal encoders under both discriminative and generative objectives. For multimodal models, we compare late-fusion and cross-attention architectures that differ in how they align phrases to images. We also examine prompting strategies for large vision-language models when given a sorted grid of candidate images. Our experiments reveal that purely lexical cues are insufficient and that models benefit from explicit reasoning about attribute contrasts. Human performance remains high but not perfect, indicating that some sets demand fine-grained inference beyond trivial object counting. Error analysis shows that models often overfit to spurious color or texture cues rather than relational structure. We further analyze the role of negative sampling and find that models trained with adversarial distractors generalize better. To situate our contributions within prior art, we compare against multi-image VQA and visual dialogue settings that permit cross-image grounding (Hu, Suhr, and Forbes 2019). Several of those tasks permit success by attending to only one frame, which our design explicitly discourages. In contrast, our annotation guidelines require writers to include the minimal set of attributes that jointly rule out all distractors. We additionally report listener accuracy under time pressure to approximate realistic cognitive load. This perspective echoes findings from pragmatic modeling in language games, but highlights the added complexity introduced by visual variation. Our dataset thus complements existing resources and can serve as a stress test for multimodal reasoning across closely related scenes. Finally, we release code, data, and evaluation scripts to encourage reproducible research and standardized comparisons.

Format.document: Template-based data generation has been widely used for augmentation to inject numerical skills (Geva et al., 2020), improve consistency (Asai and Hajishirzi, 2020), and boost zero-shot accuracy (Zhao et al., 2019). Beyond augmentation, templates have supported dataset construction (Talmor and Berant, 2018; Thorne et al., 2021) and analysis of model generalization (Rozen et al., 2019). We build on this line of work by automatically generating examples through instantiation of templates with structured inputs. Because our approach operates solely over tables, it scales efficiently, exhibits rich lexical diversity, and transfers easily to new skills and domains. Recently, Thorne et al. (2021) introduced the WIKINLDB dataset to probe reasoning over sets of textual facts. Their queries are created from a knowledge graph, and the supporting facts are synthesized by a language model. Unlike WIKINLDB, which targets evaluation, our method uses generated examples to endow pretrained models with previously unseen reasoning skills. We also emphasize that tables are easier to collect at scale than knowledge graphs, which often have limited coverage. Prior work has intensively studied data augmentation for reading comprehension, question answering, and dialogue (Khashabi et al., 2020; Alberti et al., 2019; Puri et al., 2020; Bartolo et al., 2021). In contrast, we treat tables as primary sources for controllable generation rather than as targets of reasoning. Our pipeline converts schema-constrained rows into natural language statements suitable for pre-training. The resulting corpus complements existing supervision by focusing on compositional operations grounded in tabular values. Pre-training on tables has typically focused on reasoning directly over tables and knowledge bases (Yin et al., 2020; Herzig et al., 2020; Müller et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021; Neeraja et al., 2021b). Here, we instead leverage table-derived text to improve reasoning over unstructured passages. We evaluate the method on extractive and multi-hop benchmarks to assess transfer beyond the pre-training distribution. Our results indicate consistent gains in sample efficiency when fine-tuning on limited supervision. To further improve coverage, we adopt error-driven sampling that prioritizes templates yielding high model loss. Related strategies have been explored in active learning (Sharma et al., 2018) and reinforcement learning (Graves et al., 2017; Glover and Hokamp, 2019; Xu et al., 2019). Connections also exist to transfer learning (Pilault et al., 2021, and distributionally robust optimization (Oren et al., 2019; Sagawa et al., 2020). Similar to Gottumukkala et al. (2020), we construct heterogeneous batches based on estimated error profiles. This batching scheme reduces computational overhead while preserving diversity across skills and domains. We further analyze failure modes to guide iterative refinement of templates and sampling policies. Finally, we discuss ethical considerations of large-scale synthetic data creation and its potential biases. Together, these elements position our approach as a practical route to acquiring new reasoning skills with minimal manual annotation.

Format.document: This section reviews resources and recent advances in grammatical error correction for English and Chinese. We first summarize prominent English GEC datasets that shaped current benchmarks. The FCE corpus offers error-coded annotations aligned with learner essays (Yannakoudakis et al., 2011). Similarly, the NU-CLE dataset adopts an error-coded paradigm that captures fine-grained edits (Dahlmeier et al., 2013). In contrast, JFLEG emphasizes fluency by providing multiple human rewrites of learner sentences (Napoles et al., 2017). The W&I corpus extends this design and adds writer proficiency labels to support stratified evaluation (Bryant et al., 2019). Collectively, these corpora have enabled robust evaluation under both minimal edits and fluency-targeted rewrites. Additional English resources address specific domains such as academic writing and web text. The AESW shared task introduced annotated scientific writing to probe domain transfer (Daudaravicius et al., 2016). LOCNESS provides native and non-native essays for contrastive analysis (Bryant et al., 2019). GMEG aggregates edits across sources to enlarge the pool of supervised pairs (Napoles et al., 2019). CWEB contributes web-sourced sentences that reflect informal usage patterns (Flachs et al., 2020). These English datasets together support training and testing across diverse error distributions. Turning to Chinese GEC, publicly available resources remain comparatively scarce. The NLPCC-2018 shared task released parallel data and a standardized evaluation protocol (Zhao et al., 2018). The CGED series similarly focuses on detection and correction in educational settings (Rao et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2020). Beyond evaluation sets, widely used Chinese training corpora include Lang8 and HSK (Zhao et al., 2018; Xun, 2018). Despite these efforts, scale and coverage still lag behind their English counterparts. On the modeling side, sequence-to-sequence approaches established strong baselines for CGEC (Zhao et al., 2018. Subsequent systems increasingly adopted Transformer-based encoders and decoders for improved capacity (Zhao and Wang, 2020; Tang et al., 2021). Seq2Edit formulations reduce search complexity by predicting edit tags instead of tokens (Hinson et al., 2020). Off-the-shelf implementations such as GECToR have been readily applied to Chinese benchmarks (Liang et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2020). Non-autoregressive translation has also been explored to accelerate inference without large quality loss (Li and Shi, 2021). Alongside architectures, data augmentation and ensembling further improve robustness (Zhao and Wang, 2020; Tang et al., 2021; Hinson et al., 2020). Nevertheless, several open problems persist in cross-domain generalization and error type coverage. For English, fluency rewrites reduce exposure bias but complicate objective definitions for training. For Chinese, character-level edits interact with word segmentation, which challenges alignment and evaluation. Low-resource domains, such as specialized professional writing, remain underrepresented in both languages. Recent work has begun to curate native-speaker corpora to reduce confounds from interlanguage effects (Bryant et al., 2019). Cross-lingual transfer is a promising direction given shared error phenomena like article omission and preposition misuse. Multitask setups that combine detection and correction show gains in precision for high-stakes applications. Pretraining on heterogeneous edit signals, including paraphrase and style transfer, may further enrich representations. However, reliable measurement still depends on consistent annotation schemes and clear task definitions. Community-shared metrics and error taxonomies are critical to compare systems fairly across datasets. In this survey, we synthesize trends across datasets, models, and evaluation to highlight practical guidelines. We conclude that sustained progress requires larger Chinese corpora, better domain balance, and broader error coverage.
