Format.document: Code-switching in NLP has seen a rise of interest in recent years, including a dedicated workshop starting in 2014 (Diab et al., 2014) and still ongoing (Solorio et al., 2021). Within machine translation, code-switching has a long history of study (Le Féal, 1990; Climent et al., 2003; Sinha and Thakur, 2005; Johnson et al., 2017; Elmadany et al., 2021; Xu and Yvon, 2021). The advent of large multilingual sequence-to-sequence models such as mBART and mT5 has further catalyzed research on mixed-language generation (Liu et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2020; Gautam et al., 2021; Jawahar et al., 2021). Because naturally occurring CS data are scarce and annotation is costly, many MT works synthesize CS sentences by translating subsets of tokens within monolingual inputs (Song et al., 2019; Nakayama et al., 2019; Xu and Yvon, 2021). We depart from these strands by emphasizing naturally occurring CS data that better reflect authentic distributions and sociolinguistic patterns. In speech technologies, creating realistic synthetic CS audio is even more challenging due to prosodic cues, phonetic adaptation, and speaker variability. Nevertheless, dedicated ASR corpora containing natural CS exist, including the Bangor Miami corpus (Deuchar et al., 2014) and SEAME (Zeng et al., 2018). Furthermore, community evaluations such as the ASRU 2019 task have highlighted persistent difficulties in recognition under CS conditions. These ASR corpora rarely include translations aligned to the transcriptions because they were built primarily for recognition rather than translation. Two exceptions with parallel content allow deriving CS data for speech translation, which we leverage to construct our evaluation set in Section 3. Prior modeling work on CS ASR covers lexicon adaptation, phone merging, and acoustic modeling with multilingual features (Lyu et al., 2006; Ahmed and Tan, 2012; Seki et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2020; Du et al., 2021). However, recently introduced self-supervised speech encoders such as Wav2Vec, Wav2Vec 2.0, and HuBERT remain underexplored for CS phenomena (Schneider et al., 2019; Baevski et al., 2020; Hsu et al., 2021). Mixed-language input also requires robust language identification at the utterance or token level to guide downstream modules. Systems therefore incorporate explicit LID components or induce implicit LID through multitask training, often using auxiliary objectives during pretraining or finetuning (Mabokela et al., 2014; Watanabe et al., 2017; Hou et al., 2020; Xu and Yvon, 2021). A related line examines intra-word mixing, in which morphemes from different languages co-occur within a token, though we do not target this phenomenon here (Yılmaz et al., 2018; Mager et al., 2019). Beyond data and modeling, evaluation protocols for CS systems are still evolving, with debates about appropriate segmentations, references, and normalization. For MT, several studies including (Song et al., 2019 show that simple lexical substitution may exaggerate gains by aligning with subword vocabularies rather than capturing real bilingual alternation. In contrast, evaluations on conversational CS exhibit error patterns tied to discourse and pragmatics that are not observed on synthetic mixtures. In ASR, error analyses consistently report spikes in substitutions around switch points, named entities, and borrowed function words. Moreover, acoustic confusability between phonotactically similar segments across languages can inflate cross-language substitutions even with strong language models. Multilingual pretraining partially mitigates these issues by providing shared representations that align languages in embedding space. Yet, the extent to which these representations encode switch dynamics remains unclear, motivating targeted probing studies. Recent work explores control tokens, adapters, and routing mechanisms to steer generation in mixed-language contexts (Fan et al., 2021; Pfeiffer et al., 2020). Complementary strategies regularize decoders to reduce spurious switches while preserving legitimate alternations triggered by named entities and quotations. Data augmentation at the discourse level has also been proposed, composing switches according to conversational templates or topic shifts. However, augmentation methods can entrench unrealistic patterns if they ignore sociolinguistic constraints documented in field studies. Balanced sampling across domains and speakers is therefore necessary to prevent models from overfitting to idiosyncratic switch styles. Cross-task transfer between ASR and ST further raises questions about when to share encoders and when to specialize decoders for CS behaviors. Prior ST studies suggest that language tags and speech-text alignment cues can help the model anticipate switch boundaries during decoding. Our work situates itself within this landscape by assembling natural CS resources for both MT-style text and ST-style speech. We compare synthetic and natural CS settings under matched training budgets to isolate the contribution of data realism. We also analyze whether utterance-level LID supervision improves robustness relative to purely end-to-end training. For completeness, we report results with strong multilingual baselines and ablations on tokenization, language tags, and sampling. As a point of reference, we contrast our findings with prior synthetic CS studies to clarify differences in data generation and evaluation. Altogether, this related work motivates our methodology and frames our contributions within ongoing research on multilingual and code-switched modeling.

Format.document: Text Question Answering has become a central topic in natural language processing over the past decade. Researchers have investigated machine reading comprehension as a core paradigm for text QA, leveraging large-scale datasets and powerful neural architectures. Early benchmarks such as SQuAD established extractive formulations that spurred rapid progress in span prediction (Rajpurkar et al., 2016). Subsequent conversational datasets highlighted the need for modeling multi-turn context and dialog phenomena (Reddy et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2018). At the same time, pre-trained language models transformed the field by enabling strong generalization with limited task-specific supervision (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019). Generative architectures further broadened the design space by framing QA as conditional text generation rather than pure extraction (Raffel et al., 2020). Despite these advances, most studies assume clean written inputs and overlook modality-specific challenges present in speech. This gap has motivated growing interest in Spoken Question Answering, which requires reasoning over acoustically realized content and error-prone transcripts. SQA inherits difficulties from both automatic speech recognition and textual QA, including disfluencies, prosodic cues, and ambiguity introduced by recognition errors. Empirical analyses show that compounding errors from a cascaded ASR-plus-reader pipeline can substantially degrade end-task accuracy (Serdyuk et al., 2018; Su and Fung, 2020). To address error propagation, several works explore joint or end-to-end models that integrate acoustic and textual representations within a unified framework (Chuang et al., 2019). Others investigate robust training strategies and data augmentation schemes to better align ASR outputs with the expectations of downstream readers (Huang et al., 2018b; Hu et al., 2018). Benchmarking efforts have also expanded to include spoken variants of established datasets, enabling systematic evaluation across noise regimes and conversational settings (You et al., 2021; Palogiannidi et al., 2020). Nevertheless, many SQA datasets remain single-turn and fail to capture the dependencies that arise across extended dialog. Multi-turn settings introduce coreference, ellipsis, and context carryover, all of which increase the burden on modeling discourse structure. Conversational QA in speech additionally demands mechanisms for tracking who said what and when, especially in the presence of overlapping speech and channel variability. Prior work on spoken dialog comprehension suggests that exploiting dialog state and response structure can mitigate some of these issues (Tseng et al., 2016; Kim and Rush, 2016). Evidence from speech retrieval and understanding further indicates that careful conditioning on acoustic confidence and timing information improves robustness, see (Haghani et al., 2018 for early evidence) and related studies (Lugosch et al., 2019). Beyond modeling choices, evaluation protocols must account for ASR uncertainty, for example through n-best hypotheses or lattice-aware readers (Zhu et al., 2020). Recent work on confidence calibration and selective prediction further enables deployable SQA systems that abstain when uncertainty is high (Hahn and Choi, 2019). Despite progress, cross-domain generalization in SQA remains brittle, particularly when the acoustic environment or speaker population shifts. This limitation motivates techniques that transfer inductive biases from strong teachers to compact students through Knowledge Distillation. KD learns from soft targets or intermediate representations produced by a teacher, smoothing decision boundaries and improving data efficiency (Hinton et al., 2015). In NLP, sequence-level and token-level distillation have yielded competitive small models for generation and extraction tasks (Kim and Rush, 2016; Sanh et al., 2019). In speech, distillation has improved ASR, keyword spotting, and speaker recognition by leveraging ensembles or larger acoustic encoders (Hu et al., 2018). Extending KD to SQA allows the student to exploit both textual and acoustic cues distilled from multi-turn contexts. A promising strategy is to distill dialog flow signals such as answerability, turn salience, and coreference links learned by a teacher trained on clean transcripts. The student can then use these signals to resist noise and maintain coherence across turns while reasoning over imperfect ASR hypotheses. Complementary objectives, including consistency regularization across perturbed transcripts, can further stabilize training in low-resource settings. We hypothesize that multi-task distillation with auxiliary dialog-state prediction yields the most pronounced gains for multi-turn SQA. To test this hypothesis, we construct spoken counterparts of established conversational datasets and measure robustness across noise levels. Our experiments compare cascaded, joint, and end-to-end architectures to isolate the contributions of representation sharing and decoding strategy. Results indicate that distilling dialog flow improves both exact match and F1 under realistic word error rates, with the largest benefits on context-dependent questions. Analysis shows that the student better preserves entity chains and resolves ellipsis, even when the ASR omits key content words. These findings suggest a path toward compact, reliable SQA systems that can operate effectively in conversational human–machine interactions.

spans.span: Ribeiro et al.

Format.document: Current self-explaining models often enforce shortest yet sufficient rationales, with the assumption that short rationales are more intuitive to humans (Lei et al., 2016; Bastings et al., 2019). Paranjape et al. (2020) propose an information bottleneck approach to enable rationale length control. However, current studies have only assessed the methods with automatic metrics and have not evaluated human understanding across different rationale lengths. On the other hand, a line of studies measures the "human rationales alignment" (Paranjape et al., 2020), which compares how well model-generated rationales agree with human-grounded annotations (DeYoung et al., 2019). There are also studies involving humans-in-the-loop to evaluate explanations, such as asking humans to choose a better model (Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al., 2021). However, there is a lack of human evaluations on validating the effect of rationale length on human understanding. Prior work has debated whether shorter rationales truly aid comprehension or merely compress evidence at the cost of completeness (Hase and Bansal, 2020). User studies suggest that faithfulness and sufficiency are distinct constructs, and overly terse highlights can mislead judgments of model correctness (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020; Lamm et al., 2021). In explainable AI for healthcare and law, guidelines emphasize transparency that supports task performance rather than minimality per se (Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017; Lage et al., 2019). Datasets with human rationales, such as ERASER, have enabled standardized evaluation but still leave open how length interacts with cognitive load (DeYoung et al., 2019). We argue that rationale length should be treated as a controllable variable with measurable effects on reading time, answer accuracy, and calibration. Building on Ribeiro et al., we design a within-subjects protocol that isolates length from content and presentation factors. Our experiments compare extractive rationales, free-form natural-language rationales, and chain-of-thought style explanations under matched evidence coverage. We further examine whether length preferences differ across expertise levels and task types, extending analyses beyond sentiment and natural language inference to reading comprehension and fact verification. Finally, we synthesize implications for model training objectives that balance brevity with completeness, recommending evaluation designs that combine behavioral measures with post-task interviews (Carton et al., 2020; Narayanan et al., 2018).

spans.span: (Dev et al., 2021

Format.document: Measuring bias in NLP remains an urgent research priority. Several studies have investigated the prevalence of bias in NLP models (Caliskan et al., 2017; May et al., 2019; Bordia and Bowman, 2019; Davidson et al., 2019; Magee et al., 2021). Many of these works focus on cases of models exhibiting stereotyping behavior. Though Blodgett et al. (2020) note heterogeneity in definitions, empirical concerns are consistent. The finding that models encode associations tied to social stereotypes is well replicated. We adopt representational harms as our guiding conception of bias following Crawford (2017). This conception emphasizes how systems reinforce the subordination of identity groups. Our focus is therefore on outcomes that disparately affect socially salient categories. Measurement requires datasets that contrast groups rather than decontextualized attributes (Dev et al., 2021. Group-based evaluation highlights disparities that might be obscured by aggregate metrics. However, measuring bias reliably remains technically and conceptually challenging. Spurious correlations in training data can confound attempts to isolate harmful associations. Moreover, model calibration interacts with bias estimates in subtle, task-dependent ways. Prior work explores word embeddings as a locus of measurable stereotypes (Caliskan et al., 2017). Subsequent research extends analysis to contextual encoders and task-specific predictors. Bias in toxicity classification has been documented across multiple demographic groups (Davidson et al., 2019). Similar effects arise in language generation, question answering, and summarization settings. Dataset collection practices shape both the prevalence and detectability of stereotypes (Bender and Friedman, 2018). Annotation guidelines can inadvertently encode normative assumptions about language use. Crowdworker demographics further influence labeling consistency and perceived offensiveness. Beyond data, training objectives and architectures modulate bias propagation. Debiasing via counterfactual data augmentation shows promise but exhibits trade-offs (Maudslay et al., 2019). Constraints on utility, fairness, and robustness often conflict in deployment contexts. Auditing frameworks increasingly recommend transparent reporting of subgroup performance (Mitchell et al., 2019). We build on this guidance to propose a standardized evaluation protocol. Our protocol combines controlled templates with naturally occurring sentences from multiple domains. We align measurement with social categories most implicated in documented harms. For intersectional analysis, we include curated pairs spanning multiple identity dimensions. We also assess sensitivity to demographic terms, paraphrases, and implicit referents. The evaluation includes metrics for both average and worst-group performance (Hashimoto et al., 2018). We report confidence intervals to contextualize small but persistent disparities. Our experiments use pretrained transformers fine-tuned under matched data regimes. To reduce variance, we control for random seeds and training epochs across runs. We complement quantitative results with qualitative error analysis of failure cases. Finally, we discuss implications for governance, documentation, and future dataset design. Taken together, our contributions frame bias measurement as a cumulative, community-wide effort.

spans.span: Levitan et al. 2018

Format.document: The game of Mafia is particularly well-suited for the goal of determining whether the deceptive participants in a conversation can be identified from the contents of their utterances. As a social deduction game, Mafia elicits strategic lying and nuanced truth-telling under time pressure. This environment provides repeated, high-stakes interactions that approximate real-world deception while remaining ethically tractable. Unlike laboratory lie-detection protocols that isolate single statements, Mafia sessions produce long, interactive dialogues rich in pragmatic cues. These dialogues combine persuasion, accusation, and coalition formation, offering a natural testbed for computational models. In this paper we introduce a corpus of transcribed Mafia games annotated for speaker role and deception episodes. We study whether lexical, semantic, and discourse features are sufficient to identify deceptive speech without access to prosody or facial signals. Our approach treats deception detection as a supervised classification problem over utterance-level segments. We compare traditional bag-of-words baselines with pretrained transformer encoders adapted to conversational structure. To control for topical confounds, we design adversarial splits that prevent trivial memorization of player-specific idiolects. We further analyze feature importance and error patterns to understand when models succeed and fail. We position our work within the broader literature on deception in text and dialogue. Prior studies have examined stylistic markers such as function word rates, hedging, negation, and sentiment polarity. Other work explores discourse phenomena including contradiction, stance shifts, and turn-taking asymmetries in deceptive exchanges. Prosodic analyses of deception in laboratory dialogues report complementary cues, as in Levitan et al. 2018, though our focus is strictly lexical. Games and gamified protocols have also been proposed to simulate motivated reasoning and strategic communication. Compared with interview-style datasets, Mafia conversations offer contested claims, public evidence, and adversarial questioning at scale. From a methodological perspective, our study contributes a new multimodal alignment of utterances, timestamps, and player states. We release clear annotation guidelines that distinguish performative role-playing from intentional concealment of private information. We also quantify the extent to which deception correlates with role, pressure, and network centrality across sessions. Our baseline features include n-grams, dependency fragments, discourse markers, and conversation-level aggregation statistics. For neural models, we fine-tune a dialogue-aware encoder with segment embeddings, speaker tags, and relative turn indices. We evaluate accuracy, macro F1, and area under the precision–recall curve across multiple cross-validation folds. Robustness is assessed via counterfactual data augmentation that flips role labels while preserving lexical content where possible. We conduct ablation studies to measure the contribution of context window size, speaker history, and training-set balance. Human subject experiments provide upper bounds by asking annotators to identify deceptive utterances using text only. Qualitative analysis surfaces recurrent strategies such as vague quantification, evidential distancing, and selective agreement. Finally, we discuss ethical considerations, dataset licensing, and guidelines for responsible deployment in applied settings.

Format.document: Relation Extraction. Relation extraction aims to predict semantic relations between entities within a sentence or across sentences. Early supervised approaches relied on features derived from parse trees, lexical cues, and distant knowledge sources. Kernel methods and feature-rich linear classifiers achieved competitive results before the deep learning era (Qian et al., 2008; Hendrickx et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2016). With the advent of neural networks, convolutional and recurrent architectures reduced the need for manual feature engineering while improving robustness (Zeng et al., 2014; Zhang and Wang, 2015; Xiao and Liu, 2016). Attention mechanisms further enhanced the modeling of entity contexts and relation arguments (Shen and Huang, 2016; Zhou et al., 2016). Despite these advances, generalization remained limited by the scarcity of labeled data in specialized domains. Distant supervision attempted to scale annotation by aligning text with knowledge base facts, albeit at the cost of significant noise (Mintz et al., 2009; Riedel et al., 2010; Hoffmann et al., 2011). Multi-instance learning and noise-aware objectives were proposed to attenuate label sparsity and misalignment issues (Zeng et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2016). More recently, pretrained language models have become the de facto backbone for relation extraction due to their strong contextual representations (Devlin et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019). R-BERT augments BERT with entity markers to better capture pair-specific information for classification (Wu and He, 2019). Span-aware pooling and pairwise attention have also been explored to construct richer relation representations (Soares et al., 2019; Baldini Soares et al., 2019; Peters et al., 2019). Prompt-based tuning reframes relation extraction as masked language modeling to reduce task-specific parameters and improve data efficiency (Petroni et al., 2019; Schick and Schütze, 2021; Gao et al., 2021). In low-resource scenarios, meta-learning and calibration strategies have been shown to stabilize few-shot performance (Gao et al., 2019; Han et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2020). Domain adaptation remains challenging because entity distributions, relation inventories, and writing styles vary widely across corpora. Cross-sentence and document-level relation extraction adds discourse reasoning, coreference, and aggregation over multiple mentions to the modeling burden (Quirk and Poon, 2017; Yao et al., 2019; Nan et al., 2020). Graph neural networks and heterogeneous information fusion help integrate sentence-level cues with document structure (Zhang et al., 2018; Christopoulou et al., 2019; Nan et al., 2020). Joint modeling with entity linking or coreference resolution can further reduce error propagation across pipelines (Durrett and Klein, 2014; Miwa and Bansal, 2016; Luan et al., 2018). Evaluation protocols often rely on TACRED, SemEval, and biomedical benchmarks, which differ in label granularity and negative class prevalence (Hendrickx et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2017; Alt et al., 2020). Careful train and dev splits, along with robust negative sampling, are necessary to avoid inflation of scores due to lexical memorization (Levy et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018). As shown in (Li et al., 2020), careful entity typing can act as an auxiliary signal that improves classification margins. Nevertheless, improvements from type features are inconsistent when pretrained encoders already capture fine-grained semantics. In contrast to closed-world settings, open information extraction emphasizes relation discovery without schema constraints (Stanovsky et al., 2018; Saha et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2017). Clustering-based unsupervised methods group argument pairs by distributional similarity or pattern templates and then induce labels (Yao et al., 2011; Marcheggiani and Titov, 2016; Elsahar et al., 2017). Bootstrapping techniques iteratively expand seed patterns but risk semantic drift without confidence controls (Brin, 1998; Agichtein and Gravano, 2000; Etzioni et al., 2008). Recent work explores contrastive objectives for relation clustering as a way to align instance representations without annotated relations (Chopra et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Paperno et al., 2022). Another line of research leverages knowledge graphs to regularize predictions through constraints or representation alignment (Bordes et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2021; Xiong et al., 2017). Joint extraction of entities and relations mitigates exposure bias from pipeline errors and enables mutual reinforcement between tasks (Miwa and Sasaki, 2014; Miwa and Bansal, 2016; Zheng et al., 2017). Span-based decoders and sequence tagging reformulations reduce search complexity and unify modeling across tasks (Wadden et al., 2019; Dai et al., 2019; Zhong and Chen, 2021). Calibration and selective prediction have been advocated to handle long-tail relations and uncertain inputs in deployment (Guo et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2021; Kamath et al., 2020). For multilingual relation extraction, shared subword vocabularies and alignment objectives can exploit cross-lingual transfer (Conneau and Lample, 2019; Lauscher et al., 2020; Wu and Dredze, 2019). Data augmentation using paraphrasing, back-translation, and entity swaps has shown mixed success depending on label semantics and context sensitivity (Fadaee et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2020). Finally, rigorous error analysis reveals that many systems still struggle with compositional triggers, negation, and rare syntactic constructions. Addressing these shortcomings likely requires combining structured inductive biases with the data efficiency of pretrained encoders. Our review suggests that progress will come from integrating noise-robust learning, discourse-level reasoning, and principled evaluation practices.

Format.document:
Our work is in the research line of recommender systems widely studied because of their practical value in industry. For example, previous work explores users' chatting history to recommend conversations (Zeng et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2020b) and hashtags (Li et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2021), browsing history to recommend news (Wu et al., 2019; Qi et al., 2021), and purchase history to recommend products (Guo et al., 2020). In contrast to most recommendation studies focusing on exploiting target users' personal interest modeling from their historical behaviors, our work largely relies on the wording of a short query to figure out what is needed by a target user because they are anonymous for privacy concerns.

Within several branches of recommendation research, our task is by concept similar to expert recommendation for question answering Nikzad-Khasmakhi et al., 2019). In this field, many previous studies encode expertise knowledge in diverse streams, such as software engineering (Bhat et al., 2018), social activities (Bok et al., 2021), and community forums (Zhang and Wang, 2020). Nevertheless, few of them attempt to model expertise with modern NLP methods beyond keyword matching. On the contrary, language representations play an important role here to tackle our task: we substantially explore how semantic features help characterize doctor expertise, which has not been studied before.

Our work is also related to previous language understanding research over doctor‑patient dialogues on online health forums (Zeng et al., 2020a), where various compelling applications are explored, such as information extraction (Ramponi et al., 2020; Du et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020c), question answering (Pampari et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019), and medical report generation (Enarvi et al., 2020). In comparison with these studies, we focus on doctor expertise and characterize it from both profile metadata and past patient–doctor dialogues, which fills a gap in prior research. Methodologically, we build on pretrained language models to encode short queries and match them to domain expertise signals in a unified representation space (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019). This design allows us to transfer supervision from existing dialogue datasets and reduces dependence on user history that may be sparse or unavailable (Kang and McAuley, 2018). At the same time, we contrast our approach with topic or tag recommendation methods that primarily use co‑occurrence statistics (Mikolov et al., 2013; Levy and Goldberg, 2014). For evaluation, we adopt standard ranking metrics and simulate cold‑start scenarios to reflect realistic deployment settings, while acknowledging domain shift between sources and targets (Zhao et al., 2020). We further compare against expert routing systems in community QA, which often rely on handcrafted features and network centrality measures (Zhang et al., 2017; Pal et al., 2012) despite their limited portability across domains. Finally, we situate our contribution within ongoing efforts on retrieval‑augmented recommendation, where semantic retrievers are paired with task‑specific scorers to improve precision (Fisch et al., 2019; Karpukhin et al., 2020), and note that prior cross‑domain QA adaptation remains challenging in terms of both annotation and robustness (Fisch et al., 2019; Khashabi et al., 2020b.

spans.span: Cucerzan (2007)

Format.document: Entity linking aims to resolve ambiguous mentions in text to entries in a knowledge base. It has been widely studied with approaches ranging from graph-based heuristics to supervised learning (Milne and Witten, 2008; Cucerzan, 2007; Lazic et al., 2015b; Gupta et al., 2017; Raiman and Raiman, 2018). End-to-end neural models that jointly perform mention detection and disambiguation have boosted accuracy in realistic settings (Kolitsas et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2021). Complementary to within-document reasoning, cross-document coreference provides valuable signals for entity disambiguation (Bagga and Baldwin, 1998; Gooi and Allan, 2004; Singh et al., 2011; Barhom et al., 2019). Dutta and Weikum (2015) combine clustering-based decisions with sparse bag-of-words features, which are not well suited to modern embedding-based pipelines. The literature on heuristic candidate generation remains influential (Milne and Witten, 2008; Cucerzan (2007); Lazic et al., 2015b). However, candidate generation alone is insufficient without robust context modeling that accounts for fine-grained semantics and document structure (Cattan et al., 2020; Caciularu et al., 2021; Ravenscroft et al., 2021). Cross-encoders that jointly score mention–entity pairs with full attention deliver strong performance but are computationally heavy at inference time (Raiman and Raiman, 2018). Our work investigates how clustering signals can be exploited to train dual-encoders that preserve efficiency while approaching cross-encoder quality. In particular, we study training curricula that alternate between within-document and cross-document clusters to shape the representation geometry. If prediction efficiency is the only concern, model distillation can compress cross-encoders into lightweight students (Hinton et al., 2015; Izacard and Grave, 2021). We also consider alternatives such as poly-encoders that capture limited interactions at manageable cost (Humeau et al., 2020). Beyond supervised training, semi-automatic mining of hard negatives from large corpora further improves retrieval-oriented linking (Gupta et al., 2017). We evaluate our approach under both standard disambiguation and open-domain entity discovery settings, emphasizing recall at scale. Overall, our results suggest that clustering-based training is a practical route to scalable entity linking without sacrificing much accuracy on strong benchmarks.

Format.document: Entity-based modeling has been the prevailing approach to model coherence in pre-neural models. The entity grid is its most well-known implementa-tion (Barzilay and Lapata, 2008). It represents entities in a two-dimensional array to track their transitions between sentences. Many variations have been proposed to improve this model, e.g., projecting the grid into a graph representation (Guinaudeau and Strube, 2013) or converting the grid to a neural model (Tien Nguyen and Joty, 2017). However, the neural version of the entity grid (Tien Nguyen and Joty, 2017) has two limitations. First, Lai and Tetreault (2018) state that entity grids applied to downstream tasks are often extremely sparse. In their evaluation, it is difficult to find meaningful entity transitions between sentences in the grids. Accordingly, this model performs worse than other neural models. More importantly, this neural model cannot provide any clues of how this model works since Tien Nguyen and Joty (2017) apply a convolutional layer on the entity grid. The feature map of the convolutional layer is not interpretable. They cannot examine which entity is assigned more importantly than others by their model. In contrast, we constrain our model to capture focus on entities using noun phrases. Then our model tracks the changes of focus. Hence, it provides us with an interpretable focus (Section 5). More recently, Moon et al. (2019) propose a neural coherence model to exploit both local and structural aspects. They evaluate their model on an artificial task only, the shuffle test, which determines whether sentences in a document are shuffled or not. However, recent studies (Pishdad et al., 2020) claim that this artificial task is not suitable to evaluate coherence models. Lai and Tetreault (2018) show that the neural coherence models, which achieve the best performance on this task, do not outperform non-neural models on downstream tasks. More recently, Mohiuddin et al. (2021) find a weak correlation between the model performance in artificial tasks and downstream tasks. In our evaluation, we compare Moon et al. (2019) with ours in an artificial task as well as in three downstream tasks. Moon et al. (2019) perform the best in the artificial task, but do not outperform our model in three downstream tasks (Section 4). Despite these concerns, entity-centric models remain competitive due to their transparency and ease of integration with feature-based pipelines. Recent neural architectures attempt to encode discourse structures by modeling sentence ordering and topical continuity with hierarchical encoders (Li and Hovy, 2014; Ji and Smith, 2017). Nevertheless, hierarchical encoders often conflate topic shifts with coherence breaks, leading to unstable behavior across domains (Lai and Tetreault, 2018). A complementary line of work leverages coreference resolution to align mentions across sentences and construct discourse-aware representations (Clark and Manning, 2016; Joshi et al., 2019). While these approaches improve local consistency, they may overlook entity prominence and syntactic roles noted in classic accounts (Barzilay and Lapata, 2008; Guinaudeau and Strube, 2013. Building on these insights, several studies propose attention mechanisms to weight entities according to discourse salience (Liu and Lapata, 2018; Sukhbaatar et al., 2015). Others incorporate syntactic supervision via dependency paths to discern subject continuity from object rementioning (Kobayashi et al., 2020). Beyond modeling, evaluation practice has shifted toward task-oriented benchmarks including essay scoring, summary coherence, and factuality assessment (Novikova et al., 2017; Marie et al., 2021). However, benchmarks differ widely in annotation protocol and difficulty, complicating cross-study comparison (Bhandari et al., 2020). Masked language modeling (MLM; Devlin et al. 2019) is typically used to learn cross-lingual encoders such as multilingual BERT (mBERT; Devlin et al. 2019) and XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020). Format.document: Here we first review the related work of DA for NLP, then expound the differences between our method and the major existing ones. According to the methodology of data generation, existing methods can be categorized into three types: rule-based, interpolation-based, and model-based, respectively. Rule-based approaches manipulate tokens or structures using deterministic transformations such as synonyms substitution, template rewriting, or noise injection. These methods are simple and controllable, but they may distort label semantics if applied without constraints. Interpolation-based methods synthesize new samples by mixing features or examples in the embedding or input space. Such strategies can regularize models and smooth decision boundaries, yet they often require careful calibration to avoid unnatural artifacts. Model-based methods rely on learned generators, translating, paraphrasing, or sampling from language models to expand the training distribution. A comprehensive taxonomy of augmentation motivations has been discussed in (Johnson et al., 2020 and it highlights trade-offs among fidelity, diversity, and cost. Compared to prior taxonomies, our work emphasizes task-specific risk controls that preserve causal features while perturbing spurious cues. We frame augmentation as a constrained transformation problem with explicit invariances and equivariances. This perspective clarifies when augmentations should be label-preserving versus label-shifting, a distinction often glossed over in earlier surveys. We also revisit evaluation protocols, arguing that intrinsic similarity metrics are insufficient proxies for downstream generalization. Instead, we propose diagnostic splits that separate robustness gains from mere memorization of synthetic patterns. Finally, we discuss practical considerations such as compute budgets, data governance, and failure analysis to guide deployment in sensitive applications. Together, these points delineate the scope of our approach and situate it within the broader landscape of DA research.

In addition to HMMs and the CRF autoencoder (CRF-AE), a number of approaches have been explored. (2012) learn context-free embeddings by optimizing substitutional similarity derived from n-gram language models. Yuret et al. (2014) extend this idea to produce context-sensitive embeddings that better capture local dependencies. Gupta et al. (2020) introduce a deep clustering objective that projects mBERT features into a lower-dimensional, clustering-friendly space with a reconstruction term. Despite steady improvements on multilingual UD benchmarks, code releases for these systems remain scarce. A complementary line of work maximizes mutual information between word- and context-based predictors of tags. Building on classical distributional objectives, Stratos (2019) formalizes agreement constraints that can be optimized without labeled data. Recent studies investigate whether pretrained language models can serve as sources of inductive bias for unsupervised tagging and parsing. Beyond the Gupta et al. approach, few efforts leverage PLMs directly for POS induction. For unsupervised parsing, Wu et al. (2020) estimate interword correlations via perturbed masking and recover tree structure from those signals. Inspired by structural probes, Kim et al. (2020) infer constituency by measuring proximity between adjacent token representations. Cao et al. (2020) further combine PLMs with classical constituency tests to attain competitive performance without treebank supervision. Parallel to these trends, the CRF-AE has been applied broadly to unsupervised sequence labeling. Ammar et al. (2014) introduce the encoder–decoder formulation, and Cai et al. (2017) adapt it to dependency induction with reconstruction from predicted trees. While originally devised for fully unsupervised learning, subsequent work shows that semi-supervised variants of the CRF-AE can be effective for POS tagging and semantic parsing. For example, Zhang et al. (2017) and Jia et al. (2020) report gains when combining small labeled datasets with unlabeled corpora.

Format.document: Many pieces of previous work aim to measure knowledge stored in pretrained language models. Early studies explored whether masked language models encode factual associations that can be surfaced by cloze prompts. Petroni et al. (2019) propose to retrieve factual knowledge in BERT using cloze-style queries. Their experiments show that BERT can recall many relations without any task-specific finetuning. Subsequent work refined prompt design to mitigate sensitivity to surface forms. Jiang et al. (2020b) improve cloze queries using mining and paraphrasing strategies to increase coverage. Concurrently, template-free approaches examined the capacity of sequence-to-sequence models to answer factual questions directly from parameters. Roberts et al. (2020) introduce closed-book question answering as a probe of parametric knowledge. This line of research emphasizes what models know but less about where and how that knowledge is represented. Interpretability studies attempt to localize knowledge to neurons, heads, layers, or subspaces in the network. Elazar et al. (2021) measure and improve the consistency of factual predictions across paraphrases. Other analyses track how training objectives and data mixtures shape the emergence of factual competence. For example, scaling studies suggest that larger models memorize more facts but also generalize better with appropriate regularization. Recent work investigates causal interventions that edit individual facts without broad regressions. Meng et al. (2022) propose rank-one model editing to target specific associations in transformer layers. De Cao et al. (2021) develop Knowledge Editing via Language Models to insert or correct facts post hoc. Despite progress, it remains challenging to disentangle memorized patterns from genuinely compositional reasoning. Probing methods often conflate representational availability with linear extractability. Control experiments with counterfactual prompts and calibrated baselines help reduce misinterpretation. Beyond English, multilingual studies reveal uneven coverage across languages and scripts. Domain adaptation further complicates evaluation when facts shift over time or across corpora. Temporal robustness benchmarks test whether models update beliefs when new evidence appears. Knowledge-intensive tasks such as slot filling, open-domain QA, and entity linking provide complementary signals. Retrieval-augmented models separate storage from reasoning by consulting external sources at inference. Karpukhin et al. (2020) and Lewis et al. (2020) demonstrate strong gains from dense retrieval coupled with generation. Nevertheless, purely parametric probes remain valuable for auditing pretrained checkpoints. In this paper, we focus on opening the black box to identify neurons and pathways most responsible for factual responses. We adopt intervention-based analyses that quantify the causal effect of targeted component perturbations. Our approach complements prompt-based probing by revealing internal structure rather than only output behavior. We evaluate on established factual benchmarks to compare against cloze and closed-book baselines. For cloze probing, we follow prior templates and report calibrated accuracy under prompt paraphrases. For closed-book QA, we reproduce prior settings described in (Roberts et al., 2020 and analyze sensitivity to editing. Overall, our findings connect interpretability insights with practical guidance for responsible model deployment.

Table gives a summary of these narrative comprehension tasks, associated with their required skills of comprehension. We also reviewed studies on character-centered tasks over non-narrative texts like synopses and chit-chat (i.e., not story-related) conversations. Detailed rationales of the required skills for each task are discussed in Appendix A. Early benchmarks emphasized plot-level understanding with simple multiple-choice questions and cloze tests that probe surface coherence rather than deep role reasoning. More recent datasets seek to evaluate temporal and causal reasoning across long contexts, but they often omit explicit modeling of characters and their evolving attributes (Gonzalez et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019. In contrast, character-centered tasks focus on identity resolution, trait inference, intentions, and interactions, requiring persistent memory across scenes. Methods for these tasks range from rule-based pipelines to pretraining with narrative-specific objectives, yet evaluation remains fragmented across domains. Cross-genre comparisons reveal that models trained on short fables or movie synopses tend to overfit stylistic cues and fail to generalize to long-form literary fiction. For instance, approaches targeting persona consistency in conversations often struggle when transferred to literary novels with nested focalization. Building on these observations, we advocate for reporting skill-specific diagnostics and for separating character-level predictions from global story understanding to ensure clearer attribution of model capabilities.

Format.document: Extractive Related Work Generation. Early related work generation systems employed the extractive summarization approach. Hoang and Kan (2010) pioneered the task, developing rules to select sentences following a topic hierarchy tree that was assumed to be given as input. Hu and Wan (2014) grouped sentences into topic-biased clusters with PLSA, modeled sentence importance with SVR and applied a global optimization framework to select sentences. Chen and Zhuge (2019) se-lected sentences from papers that co-cited the same cited papers as the target paper in order to cover a minimum Steiner tree constructed from a paper's keywords. Wang et al. (2019) extracted Cited Text Spans (CTS), the matched text spans in the cited paper that are most related to a given citation. However, these extractive approaches aim to maximally cover the citation texts with the extracted sentences, thus mostly ignoring the reference type citations that are concise and abstractive ( §3.1.3). Abstractive Related Work Generation. Recently, Xing et al. (2020) extend the pointergenerator (See et al., 2017) to take two text inputs, allowing them to recover a masked citation sentence given its neighboring context sentences. Ge et al. (2021) encode the citation context, cited paper's abstract, and citation network and train their model with multiple objectives: sentence salience score regression of the cited paper's abstract, functional role classification of the citation sentence, and citation sentence generation. Chen et al. (2021) propose a relation-aware, multi-document encoder to generate a related work paragraph given a set of cited papers. Luu et al. (2021) fine-tune GPT2 (Radford et al., 2019) on scientific texts and explore several techniques for representing documents, such as using extracted named entities. All of the works described above focus on the generation aspect, while neglecting dataset collection; their datasets are mostly extracted automatically. Moreover, the datasets are not reused, though they are publicly available, because these works all use slightly different problem definitions, and thus the models are not directly comparable (Li and Ouyang, 2022). In this work, we focus on collecting a dataset that is widely applicable to various related work generation settings, rather than proposing another incomparable approach. A key challenge lies in modeling discourse structure so that models avoid redundantly quoting boilerplate phrases from source articles. Graph-based encoders have been explored to link citations and topical threads across documents (Yasunaga et al., 2019). Citation intent classification has likewise been integrated to condition generation on rhetorical roles such as background, method, or comparison (Jurgens et al., 2018;Cohan et al., 2019). Dataset quality remains a bottleneck because noisy alignments between citing and cited spans introduce spurious supervision signals (Fujii and Ishikawa, 2007;Cohan and Goharian, 2017). To mitigate such noise, some works adopt distant supervision with confidence reweighting and curriculum schedules (Zhou and Chen, 2021). However, domain shift across venues and subfields still degrades performance when training on one corpus and evaluating on another (Beltagy et al., 2019). Pre-training on large scientific corpora partly closes this gap by providing field-specific terminology and stylistic priors (Lo et al., 2020;Gururangan et al., 2020). Beyond sentence extraction, controllable generation aims to steer outputs by specifying target venues, novelty levels, or citation density (Keskar et al., 2019;Dathathri et al., 2020). While control signals improve faithfulness to user preferences, they also risk amplifying exposure bias when trained with teacher forcing alone (Holtzman et al., 2020). Recent reinforcement learning approaches optimize evaluation proxies such as coverage, coherence, and factual consistency with respect to a small set of human preferences (Stiennon et al., 2020;Bai et al., 2022). Nevertheless, automatic metrics for related work remain underdeveloped compared with summarization, with limited agreement to expert judgments (Fabbri et al., 2021). Consequently, reproducible benchmarks that standardize input construction, citation grounding, and evaluation protocols are urgently needed, as argued by Li 2022. We therefore release a curated dataset with explicit alignment between citation contexts and cited abstracts, along with strong extractive and abstractive baselines. Our benchmark is designed to encourage modular comparisons across retrieval, planning, and generation components, enabling clearer progress on related work generation.

Format.document: Vision-language few-shot learning. Leveraging aligned image–text corpora, vision–language models trained with contrastive objectives have shown strong zero-shot classification and retrieval performance (Jia et al., 2021; Radford et al., 2021). Beyond purely discriminative alignment, generative strategies that condition language models on visual tokens have emerged as a complementary paradigm (Tsimpoukelli et al., 2021; Alayrac et al., 2022). Different from the discriminative manner, Menick et al. (2021) prompt a large language model with a vision prefix in a generative way to enable few-shot transfer. While these systems excel with broad pre-training, their sample efficiency and robustness under distribution shift remain active research challenges Bommasani et al., 2021). This paper focuses on how prompt design, adaptation, and calibration influence few-shot generalization in multimodal settings. Language model prompting. Prompting reframes tasks as text infilling or conditional generation, thereby eliciting knowledge from frozen language models with minimal task-specific supervision (Petroni et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020). Following the taxonomy of prompt-based learning, methods span discrete templates, soft prompt vectors, and instruction tuning (Liu et al., 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Sanh et al., 2022). Early approaches relied on manual cloze prompts with verbalizers, later extended by automatic template mining and calibration techniques (Gao et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021). Semi-supervised variants such as PET and iPET demonstrate strong few-shot gains by iteratively relabeling unlabeled corpora with ensemble-produced pseudo-labels (Schick and Schütze, 2021a; Schick and Schütze, 2021b). In multimodal scenarios, prompts can target either the language backbone, the visual encoder, or the cross-modal fusion module, trading off flexibility and stability (Li et al., 2022; Jia et al., 2022). Recent work integrates contrastive pre-training with promptable decoders to better exploit weak supervision from captions and alt-text at web scale (Radford et al., 2021; Alayrac et al., 2022). Nevertheless, naively porting unimodal prompt heuristics to multimodal pipelines often underperforms due to modality mismatch, tokenization drift, and label space granularity (Tsimpoukelli et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022). We therefore analyze prompt transfer through the lens of distributional alignment, calibration, and retrieval-augmented conditioning, grounding claims in controlled few-shot benchmarks. Our study also examines the interaction between prompt length, visual prefix capacity, and in-context example selection strategies (Liu et al., 2021; Rubin et al., 2022). For completeness, we contrast parametric adaptation via soft prompts with lightweight fine-tuning of adapter layers on the same budget to isolate data efficiency effects (Lester et al., 2021; Pfeiffer et al., 2021). Finally, we relate our findings to the broader literature on instruction following and emergent abilities in large language models (Wei et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2022). Together, these threads situate our contributions within the evolving practice of prompt-driven, vision–language few-shot learning.

Format.document: Continuous prompts. There is a line of work focused on tuning continuous prompts (Li and Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Zhong et al., 2021; Qin and Eisner, 2021; Zhou et al., 2021). A recurring theme in this line of work is the strength of continuous prompt tuning, which results in strong yet compact models compared to conventional architecture fine-tuning approaches. Motivated by the success of continuous prompt tuning, this paper investigates the feasibility of interpreting a learned continuous prompt and its connection to discrete prompts. Discrete prompts. The release of GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) sparked a lot of excitement about the emergent ability of LMs in following discrete natural language prompts. Consequently, countless follow-up studies have used manually designed discrete prompts for probing LMs (Petroni et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2020), improving LMs few-shot ability (Schick and Schütze, 2021; Gao et al., 2021; Le Scao and Rush, 2021), and their zero-shot ability as well as transferability (Mishra et al., 2021a; Reynolds and McDonell, 2021). While discrete prompts have clear advantages, in addition to being human-readable and thus easily interpretable, we do not have efficient and algorithmic ways of reconstructing them. For example, Shin et al. (2020)'s algorithm discovers discrete prompts, yet the results are not human readable. Prior work also finds that model performance is highly sensitive to small changes in wordings (Mishra et al., 2021a) and that optimization over the discrete prompt space is nontrivial and often highly unstable. Our findings here about the disconnect between continuous prompts and their discrete interpretation provides another perspective on the difficulty of discovering discrete prompts via continuous optimization algorithms that directly or indirectly leverage the continuous space. Despite progress, the mechanisms by which soft prompts encode task information remain poorly understood. Recent studies analyze embedding trajectories and token salience to infer latent structure in learned prompts (Liu et al., 2022; Vu et al., 2022). However, most analyses rely on post hoc probing that may not faithfully capture the causal role of specific prompt dimensions. In contrast, we propose an intervention-based framework that perturbs subspaces of the prompt to test functional hypotheses. Our approach complements concurrent efforts on prompt initialization, regularization, and sparsity (Hambardzumyan et al., 2021; Mahabadi et al., 2022). It also clarifies when and why continuous prompts can approximate the behavior of handcrafted templates used in few-shot prompting. As demonstrated by Li and Liang, continuous tuning can achieve competitive performance with far fewer trainable parameters. Yet, semantic alignment between learned vectors and human-interpretable tokens is neither guaranteed nor necessary for generalization. Several works investigate transfer across tasks and domains by reusing or composing prompts (Vu et al., 2021; Asai et al., 2022). These studies suggest that modular prompt components can capture reusable inductive biases across related problems. Nevertheless, direct transplantation of a prompt often suffers from distribution shift and spurious correlations. Building on these insights, we evaluate whether interpretation-guided constraints can improve robustness without sacrificing accuracy. We compare against representative baselines in both encoder-only and encoder–decoder architectures, including BERT and T5 (Devlin et al., 2019; Raffel et al., 2020). To situate our contributions, we next review complementary lines of research on discrete templates and automated prompt discovery. Template mining approaches infer surface patterns from corpora or gradients and then validate candidates with held-out data (Shin et al., 2020; Wallace et al., 2019). While effective in some settings, these methods are sensitive to lexical artifacts and may not scale to complex compositional tasks. Meta-learning formulations treat prompts as fast parameters that adapt rapidly from small support sets (Finn et al., 2017; Bansal et al., 2020). Reinforcement learning has also been applied to optimize discrete prompts with non-differentiable objectives such as calibration or safety (Deng et al., 2022). Our work is orthogonal to these directions and instead examines the interpretability and controllability of already-trained soft prompts. From an evaluation perspective, we adopt diverse metrics beyond accuracy, including faithfulness tests and counterfactual sensitivity. We further analyze failure modes by correlating prompt subspace activations with error typologies on controlled benchmarks. Taken together, the results illuminate how prompt geometry mediates task heuristics learned during fine-tuning. This understanding enables principled design choices for practitioners who must balance efficiency, interpretability, and stability. We conclude by outlining open challenges for bridging continuous and discrete prompting, and by discussing implications for safe deployment in high-stakes applications.

Format.document: Pretrained Language Models. Owing to the great achievements Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) has made, the paradigm of pretrained language models (PLMs) is thriving (Radford et al., 2019; Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019b; Lewis et al., 2020; Raffel et al., 2020). It is widely recognized that PLMs can learn massive knowledge from large corpora, leading to significant progress in various language tasks. Given such results across extensive NLP tasks, it is timely to systematically evaluate the abilities of PLMs to deepen understanding and facilitate broader application. Language Model Evaluation. Many efforts have studied the evaluation of language model performance and generalization. Liu et al. (2019a) evaluate BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), GPT (Radford et al., 2018), and ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) on a variety of linguistic tasks. Their results suggest that features generated by PLMs are sufficient for high performance on a broad set of tasks but fail on tasks requiring fine-grained linguistic knowledge. Tenney et al. (2019) evaluate similar models on a suite of sub-sentence linguistic analysis tasks, showing that PLMs encode both syntax and semantics in their parameters. Zhou et al. (2020) reach a similar conclusion that PLMs can learn rich knowledge while focusing on evaluating commonsense. However, these studies focus on one dimension of PLM ability evaluation. Benchmark collections such as GLUE (Wang et al., 2019b) and CLUE (Xu et al., 2020) consider mixtures of tasks but lack comprehensive ability-centric coverage. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically evaluate PLMs by defining diverse abilities and performing extensive comparisons. We survey evaluation dimensions spanning linguistic competence, factuality, reasoning, robustness, and efficiency. Prior work on probing examines what linguistic features are linearly recoverable from hidden states (Adi et al., 2017; Hewitt and Manning, 2019; May et al., 2019). Challenge sets target specific phenomena to reduce superficial correlations in training data (McCoy et al., 2019; Warstadt et al., 2020). Adversarial evaluation reveals brittleness under meaning-preserving perturbations (Jia and Liang, 2017; Ribeiro et al., 2020). Calibration metrics assess whether a model’s confidence aligns with empirical accuracy (Guo et al., 2017; Desai and Durrett, 2020). Efficiency-oriented studies analyze trade-offs between parameter count, latency, and accuracy (Sanh et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020). Multilingual evaluation highlights cross-lingual transfer and typological challenges (Pires et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2020). Domain adaptation benchmarks test robustness under distribution shift from news to biomedical or legal text (Gururangan et al., 2020; Chalkidis et al., 2020). In-context learning and instruction tuning redefine evaluation protocols by changing how supervision is presented to the model (Brown et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022). The Transformer architecture remains foundational (see also Vaswani et al., 2017. Yet parameter scaling alone does not guarantee stronger reasoning without careful dataset design (Srivastava et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2022). Recent works argue for ability-specific evaluation suites that control confounders and use targeted diagnostics (Sakaguchi et al., 2021; Khashabi et al., 2020). Our framework unifies dataset selection, prompting strategies, and metric design to enable apples-to-apples comparisons. We adopt standardized pre-processing, consistent evaluation scripts, and public leaderboards to foster reproducibility (Pineau et al., 2021). In addition to accuracy, we track calibration, abstention quality, and cost-aware metrics to reflect real-world deployment needs (Dietterich, 2017; Kamath et al., 2020). For factuality, we incorporate knowledge-intensive tasks and automated verification pipelines (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019; Petroni et al., 2019). For robustness, we include noise-injection, paraphrase, and counterfactual evaluation to probe reliance on spurious cues (Kaushik et al., 2020; Gardner et al., 2020). For safety and ethics, we use toxicity, bias, and privacy assessments to characterize potential harms (Bender et al., 2021; Solaiman et al., 2019). We report per-ability scorecards and aggregated indices to surface trade-offs among capabilities. Finally, we release code, datasets, and evaluation logs to catalyze standardized, transparent assessment for future PLMs.

Format.document: Older methods for text-based stimulus representation include co-occurrence counts from large corpora and topic distributions learned from text. Early work linked distributional statistics to neural activity using simple semantic features derived from text (Mitchell et al., 2008). Subsequent studies extended these approaches with corpus-driven semantic spaces and models that captured narrative context (Pereira et al., 2013; Huth et al., 2016). Syntactic and discourse features were also leveraged to improve predictions of time-resolved brain responses during reading (Wehbe et al., 2014). Despite these advances, purely text-derived features often failed to account for multimodal aspects of meaning encountered in naturalistic settings. This limitation motivated the exploration of richer semantic and experiential representations that better approximate human conceptual knowledge. Semantic representation models based on distributed word embeddings became prevalent with the availability of large corpora and neural training methods (Pereira et al., 2016; Hollenstein et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020). Sentence-level encoders further captured compositional semantics and discourse structure relevant for narrative processing (Sun et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2020). Recurrent networks and early Transformer-based language models offered additional gains by modeling sequential dependencies at multiple scales (Jain and Huth, 2018; Gauthier and Levy, 2019; Schwartz et al., 2019). Linguistic studies have long observed the distinct properties of translationese from text originally authored in the same language (Toury, 1980;Gellerstam, 1986;Baker, 1993;Toury, 1995). Recent work in MT identifies the translationese-tooriginal portion of test sets (i.e., sets unaligned with the model direction) as statistically significantly easier (Graham et al., 2020), echoing many previous observations (Toral et al., 2018;Lembersky et al., 2012;Läubli et al., 2018), and thus some suggest excluding this portion from future test sets (Toral et al., 2018;Zhang and Toral, 2019;Graham et al., 2020;Barrault et al., 2019).

Based on this speculated inflation of MT performance due to the translationese in the test set, further work inspects what previous conclusions about the effectiveness of MT models should be recalibrated. Some discover that models with BT mostly improve on the inflated test set but not the other more challenging portion (Toral et al., 2018;Freitag et al., 2019;Edunov et al., 2020; Appendix A, Table 1) and raise concerns that BT is not as effective as expected. Others argue that BT can still improve on both test sets (Edunov et al., 2020).

Our work differs from all previous work in that we bring in two new important factors when considering how translationese affects MT performance, namely the train-test alignment, and data-model alignment. Moreover, beyond the correlation-based analysis in previous papers (Graham et al., 2020;Edunov et al., 2020), we conduct causal inference (Pearl, 2009;Peters et al., 2017) to contribute causal insights on how translationese affects MT.

Translationese has been attributed to interference from source syntax, normalization toward frequent target forms, and cautious lexical choices typical of novice translators (Baker, 1993;Toury, 1995). In MT evaluation, such distributional shifts can inflate scores for certain directions while obscuring generalization in realistic deployment (Graham et al., 2020). Back-translation (BT) interacts with these shifts because synthetic target-like text differs from human-produced originals, potentially aligning more closely with translationese segments (Sennrich et al., 2016;Edunov et al., 2020). Prior datasets often mixed original and translated content without explicit labels, limiting fine-grained analysis (Barrault et al., 2019). Recent corpora annotate text origin, enabling stratified reporting across translationese strata and model directions, building on Zhang and Toral (2019 and related tools (Toral et al., 2018). Nevertheless, practice lags behind recommendations, and leaderboard protocols rarely require origin-aware splits (Graham et al., 2020). We posit that two alignment concepts are essential: train–test alignment, capturing whether training distribution matches the evaluated direction, and data–model alignment, capturing inductive biases that favor particular distributions. The first determines whether improvements stem from genuine robustness or from fortunate overlap with translationese statistics (Peters et al., 2017). The second addresses architecture and objective choices that might privilege fluency over adequacy under distribution shift (Edunov et al., 2020). To empirically study these factors, we construct matched subsets controlling for source–target direction and for origin labels across multiple language pairs (Barrault et al., 2019;Läubli et al., 2018). We then estimate causal effects using adjustment sets identified from a domain graph and validate sensitivity to unobserved confounding (Pearl, 2009). Our findings suggest that improvements attributed to BT are partially mediated by alignment with translationese-heavy test conditions, but that causal gains remain for robust models trained with origin-aware objectives, consistent with Zhang and Toral (2019).

Format.document: In this section, we analyze the literature on the two main evaluation problems tackled in this paper: multi-labeling and class hierarchies, keeping the focus on extreme scenarios (numerous and unbalanced classes). Evaluating multi-label predictions with hundreds or thousands of categories requires metrics that remain informative under severe class imbalance. Early work emphasized micro and macro averaging to reconcile per-instance and per-class perspectives in multilabel classification. However, these aggregates often mask systematic errors against rare labels, which are precisely those of greatest interest in extreme regimes. Hierarchical taxonomies further complicate evaluation because misclassifications may be semantically close or distant depending on tree depth. Consequently, recent research seeks measures that incorporate both label frequency and structural proximity to reflect practical utility. Conventional accuracy is ill-suited when instances may bear multiple labels that interact through exclusivity, subsumption, or mutual reinforcement. Precision and recall defined at the instance level provide partial insight, yet they ignore correlations among labels that arise from ontology constraints. Label ranking approaches reformulate evaluation around ordering quality, using metrics such as average precision and normalized discounted cumulative gain. In extreme multi-label settings, researchers have argued for propensity-scored variants that downweight frequent head labels to counter long-tail bias. These adjustments aim to align model selection with downstream retrieval and recommendation tasks where recall over rare concepts is paramount. Still, standardized reporting remains fragmented, hindering cross-paper comparisons and meta-analyses. Hierarchical evaluation introduces a distinct set of challenges because distance in the taxonomy should modulate penalty severity. Path based losses, lowest common ancestor similarity, and information content weighting are common strategies to operationalize semantic distance. There is also debate regarding whether evaluation should be local to each internal node or global over the entire hierarchy. Local measures facilitate interpretability for error remediation in particular branches, whereas global measures encourage consistent depth-aware behavior. A further complication arises when hierarchies are directed acyclic graphs rather than trees, creating multiple ancestor paths. Robust metrics for such structures must avoid double-counting while preserving the intuition that nearby misclassifications are less harmful. Dataset scale and label sparsity interact to produce high variance estimates unless evaluation is carefully stratified. Bootstrapping over instances and labels, as well as hierarchical block resampling, has been proposed to quantify uncertainty on reported metrics. Cross-dataset benchmarking further stresses the need for protocol-level controls, including fixed candidate label spaces and identical preprocessing, Lopez et al. 2019; Kim and Park 2021. Without such controls, gains may reflect easier distributions, different negative sampling, or annotation guidelines rather than genuine model improvements. Public leaderboards have accelerated progress but occasionally reinforce metric gaming, motivating broader suites of criteria that capture calibration and fairness. Cost-sensitive analysis is especially relevant when false positives on certain branches carry disproportionate operational impact. Representation learning has progressed from bag-of-words and one-vs-rest linear models to architectures that exploit label semantics and hierarchy topology. Joint embedding methods posit a shared space for inputs and labels, enabling similarity based inference that scales sublinearly with the number of classes. Graph neural networks and hyperbolic embeddings explicitly encode tree or DAG geometry to improve both classification and evaluation robustness. Calibration techniques, including temperature scaling and focal losses, have been adapted to multi-label outputs to mitigate overconfidence on tail classes. Weak supervision and semi-supervised learning address annotation scarcity by propagating constraints from the hierarchy and leveraging unlabeled corpora. Recent work also explores counterfactual data augmentation to balance rare labels without distorting the underlying taxonomy. Despite these advances, a consensus on best practices for evaluation across extreme multi-label and hierarchical settings has not fully emerged. Community efforts now advocate theory-backed reporting templates, ablations on imbalance levels, and release of code for metric computation. Emerging application domains such as biomedical ontologies and product catalogs underscore the stakes of principled evaluation at scale. As we synthesize prior findings, we emphasize the complementarity of ranking-based and hierarchy-aware measures under realistic operational constraints. We identify open questions around calibration under taxonomic shifts, uncertainty quantification for rare paths, and reproducible benchmarking protocols. These gaps motivate our experimental design and the recommendations we articulate for future work.

Format.document: Fake news detection has emerged as a pressing research topic in natural language processing and computational social science. Early studies framed the task as document classification using stylistic cues, source metadata, and lexical features. Representative datasets and feature-based baselines appeared in the mid-2010s (Rubin et al., 2016; Wang, 2017; Rashkin et al., 2017; Pérez-Rosas et al., 2018). These works established the problem setting but offered limited generalization across outlets and topics (Sarkar et al., 2018; Atanasova et al., 2019). With the rise of deep learning, researchers shifted to neural encoders that learn representations directly from text. Recurrent neural networks and their gated variants were among the first successful models for this task (Karimi et al., 2018; Nasir et al., 2021). Transformer-based language models have since delivered state-of-the-art performance on several benchmarks (Zellers et al., 2019). Nevertheless, single-document encoders often overlook cross-article signals that are crucial for robust detection. One promising direction is to model relations among contemporaneous articles that report on the same events. Prior work explored aligning news content with external knowledge bases to check for inconsistencies (Karimi and Tang, 2019). However, KB coverage gaps and temporal lag can weaken such signals in fast-evolving news cycles. In contrast, cross-document inference can exploit redundancy and contradiction directly among related articles. Beyond textual content, auxiliary signals from user engagements and propagation patterns have proved informative (Shu et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2020). Multimodal approaches further integrate images and metadata to capture stylistic and semantic mismatches (Khattar et al., 2019; Tan, 2020. Yet many systems still treat articles independently and miss discourse-level consistency cues across sources. Building structured representations of entities and events can bridge this gap by enabling aggregation and reasoning. Fine-grained detection targets specific claims, entities, or event mentions within documents rather than entire articles. Such formulations are attractive because they surface the precise loci of misinformation for downstream interventions. However, extracting reliable claim graphs and aligning them across documents remains technically challenging. Existing studies on claim-level detection typically operate on per-article extractions without cross-document consolidation. Closely related is the fact verification task, which assesses the veracity of short statements against retrieved evidence. Large-scale resources have advanced this setting in the general domain (Thorne et al., 2018) and in specialized areas such as climate science and public health (Diggelmann et al., 2020; Wadden et al., 2020; Saakyan et al., 2021). Despite progress, verification systems optimized for short claims struggle to model the internal discourse structure of long-form news. Consequently, methods for document-level misinformation detection and claim-level verification should be seen as complementary. Dataset construction poses a persistent bottleneck because high-quality labels are expensive and time-consuming to obtain. Some corpora derive labels from source reliability, which risks confounding outlet style with truthfulness (Rashkin et al., 2017; Rubin et al., 2016). Others rely on annotations from professional fact-checking sites, yielding higher precision but limited coverage; see Shu et al. 2020 for a survey, and Pérez-Rosas et al. (2018) for a crowd-sourced corpus. Synthetic datasets generated via controllable text generation provide scale while introducing potential distributional artifacts (Zellers et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2020). To harness cross-document signals, we propose constructing within-document graphs that link entities and events extracted by information extraction pipelines. These graphs can then be merged into a cross-document knowledge graph that clusters event mentions and links articles to their constituent elements. Graph neural networks offer a unified framework to encode such structures and to propagate evidence across related articles. In a pipeline architecture, event-level predictions can regularize document-level decisions by reinforcing consistent signals. Our review highlights three open challenges for future work on misinformation detection. First, we need principled evaluation protocols that test generalization across outlets, topics, and time. Second, we must clarify the interplay among content features, propagation signals, and cross-document consistency when designing models (Khattar et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2020). Third, curated benchmarks should report both article-level and claim-level metrics while documenting annotation provenance and potential biases.
