In this section, we introduce background knowledge about contrastive learning and our phrase encoder LUKE (Yamada et al., 2020).
Contrastive learning aims to pull semantically related representations closer while pushing unrelated ones apart in a shared embedding space.
Prior work on contrastive learning has evolved along several axes, including objective design, data construction, and encoder architectures. Chen et al. (2020) formalized instance discrimination with large-batch training and momentum encoders, while He et al. (2020) emphasized dynamic dictionaries for unsupervised feature learning. Gao et al. (2021) adapted contrastive objectives to sentence embeddings with simple augmentations and in-batch negatives. Khosla et al. (2020) extended the loss to supervised settings by grouping positives via label information. Xie et al. (2020) investigated the impact of data augmentations on representation robustness. Reimers and Gurevych (2019) proposed Siamese encoders for efficient sentence similarity scoring. Wang and Isola (2020) analyzed alignment and uniformity as principles underlying contrastive objectives.
Our focus is on phrase-level alignment, where positives are constructed from entity-linked spans and their contextual paraphrases.
We adopt an InfoNCE-style objective with temperature scaling and in-batch negatives, and we couple it with hard negative mining from a large phrase index.
Recent work on phrase-level representation learning spans entity-centric pretraining and compositional encoders. Yamada et al. (2020) introduced LUKE, which augments token embeddings with entity-aware representations derived from large knowledge bases. Peters et al. (2019) studied contextualized span representations for tasks requiring boundary-sensitive features. Zhang et al. (2021) explored phrase retrieval with dual encoders trained on weakly aligned corpora. Lee et al. (2019) proposed dense passage retrieval with bi-encoders for open-domain QA. Li et al. (2020) investigated span-level contrastive objectives that match mentions across documents. Beltagy et al. (2020) built long-context transformers for document-level reasoning. Guu et al. (2020) combined retrieval and language modeling to enhance factual grounding in generation. Jin et al. (2020) examined biomedical entity linking with domain-specific encoders and curated terminology banks. Guo et al. (2022) proposed multi-granularity token-phrase alignment losses on multilingual datasets, and retrieval augmentation has also been used to stabilize training under distribution shift.
We extend LUKE with a contrastive head that projects phrase and context embeddings into a shared space suitable for retrieval and clustering.
To generate training pairs, we link mentions using a high-recall dictionary and then derive paraphrases via back-translation and distant supervision from anchor text.
Our encoder uses a lightweight phrase pooling mechanism over LUKE’s token-level outputs to capture boundary-aware semantics with minimal overhead.
We evaluate on entity typing, slot filling, and phrase retrieval benchmarks, measuring both alignment quality and zero-shot transfer.
Ablations isolate the contributions of entity-aware pretraining, hard negative mining, and the phrase pooling design.
We also analyze calibration under domain shift by tracking embedding norm distributions and temperature sensitivity.
Finally, we discuss limitations around ambiguous mentions and noisy paraphrases, and we outline a data-centric roadmap for improving phrase alignment at scale.

spans.span: Recent work on discourse-aware decoding emphasizes pronoun resolution, ellipsis recovery, and lexical cohesion (Voita et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Lopes et al., 2020). Sentence-level calibration techniques exploit contextual priors to discourage incoherent lexical choices across adjacent sentences (Kumar and Sarawagi, 2019; Fernandes et al., 2021). Evaluation frameworks propose paragraph-sensitive reference construction and contrastive test suites to diagnose context use (Liu et al., 2020; Bawden et al., 2018). Shared tasks curate narrative-heavy corpora with fine-grained discourse tags and long-range coreference annotations (Barrault et al., 2019; Zampieri et al., 2020). Corpus creation strategies mine subtitle alignments and domain-adaptive web crawls (Lison and Tiedemann, 2016; El-Kishky et al., 2020).

Coherence.document:
Document-level MT Integrating document-level information meaningfully into NMT is a challenging task and has inspired research not only on exploring advanced context-aware neural architectures, including simple concatenation-based models (Tiedemann and Scherrer, 2017;Junczys-Dowmunt, 2019;Lopes et al., 2020), multi-source models (Jean et al., 2017;Bawden et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2018), hierarchical models (Miculicich et al., 2018;Zheng et al., 2020;, multi-pass models (Voita et al., 2019;Mansimov et al., 2020) and dynamic context models (Kang et al., 2020), to name a few.

But it has also motivated the field to revisit the common protocols resorted for evaluation (Freitag et al., 2021). Despite the hard to measure success, all the above mentioned methods implicitly assume an abundance of document resources and overlook the data scarcity problem. In this study, we adopt the simple concatenation model as our experimental protocol, and leave the exploration of various input formatting options and modelling to future work. Considering the fast changing landscape of the (contextual) MT evaluation, we also provide multiple evaluation metrics including human evaluations, to give a full picture of the phenomena under investigation, while acknowledging the current imperfections of and disagreements on the right way of evaluating MT systems (Kocmi et al., 2021).

Zero-Shot Transfer via Multilinguality Multilingual modeling often clusters sentences of similar meaning from different languages within a shared semantic space (Kudugunta et al., 2019;. Such representation space hypothesized to enable zero-shot transfer, delivering improved performance in many cross-lingual tasks (Eriguchi et al., 2018;Hu et al., 2020;Chi et al., 2021;Ruder et al., 2021), especially based on large-scale pretrained multilingual Transformers (Devlin et al., 2019;Conneau and Lample, 2019;Xue et al., 2021). In the context of translation, multilingual SenNMT successfully achieves zero-shot translation, transferring sentence-level generation knowledge to language pairs unseen during training (Firat et al., 2016;Johnson et al., 2017;Gu et al., 2019;Arivazhagan et al., 2019a) even in massively multilingual settings (Aharoni et al., 2019;Arivazhagan et al., 2019b;. Our study extends multilingual SenNMT to multilingual DocNMT and aims at document-level knowledge transfer from languages that have document level data to languages that only have sentence level data. To the best of our knowledge, our study is the first demonstrating the emergence of document-level zero-shot transfer across languages for multilingual machine translation.

Knowledge Probing Benchmarks for PLMs.

LAMA (Petroni et al., 2019), which starts this line of work, is a collection of single-token knowledge triples extracted from sources including Wikidata and ConceptNet (Speer et al., 2017). To mitigate the problem of information leakage from the head entity, Poerner et al. (2019) propose LAMA-UHN, which is a hard subset of LAMA that has less token overlaps in head and tail entities. X-FACTR (Jiang et al., 2020a) and mLAMA extend knowledge probing to the multilingual scenario and introduce multi-token answers. They each propose decoding methods that generate multi-token answers, which we have shown to work poorly on MedLAMA. BioLAMA (Sung et al., 2021) is a concurrent work that also releases a benchmark for biomedical knowledge probing. We provide a comparison between LAMA, BioLAMA and MedLAMA in terms of (# relations, # queries, avg # answers per query, avg # characters per answer) in the Appendix. We also discuss the coverage of relations specific to biomedicine and report per-relation accuracy to contextualize differences across domains.
Probing via Prompt Engineering. Knowledge probing is sensitive to what prompt is used (Jiang et al., 2020b). To bootstrap the probing performance, Jiang et al. (2020b) mine more prompts and ensemble them during inference. Later works parameterised the prompts and made them trainable (Shin et al., 2020b; Fichtel et al., 2021; Qin and Eisner, 2021). We have opted out prompt-engineering methods that require training data in this work, as tuning the prompts are essentially tuning an additional parameterised model on top of PLMs. As pointed out by Fichtel et al. (2021), prompt tuning requires large amounts of training data from the task. Since task training data is used, the additional model parameters are exposed to the target data distribution and can solve the set by overfitting to such biases. In our work, by adaptively finetuning the model with a small set of raw sentences, we elicit the knowledge out from PLMs but do not expose the data biases from the benchmark.
Biomedical Knowledge Probing. Nadkarni et al. Abstractive Opinion Summarization aims to generate a fluent summary that reflects salient opinions in input reviews. Due to the lack of sufficient amount of reference summaries, the most common solution is the unsupervised approach (Chu and Liu, 2019;Bražinskas et al., 2020b;Amplayo et al., 2021;Elsahar et al., 2021;Im et al., 2021;Wang and Wan, 2021;Isonuma et al., 2021, inter alia).

Recent opinion summarization models use the few-shot learning approach that fine-tunes a pretrained Transformer model with a limited amount of pairs of input reviews and reference summaries. Bražinskas et al. (2020a) and Oved and Levy (2021) show that the few-shot learning approach substantially outperforms unsupervised learning models.

All the existing methods listed above are designed for general opinion summarization and, thus, are not necessarily suitable for comparative opinion summarization, as shown in the experiments. Comparative Summarization There is a line of work on extracting comparative information from single/multiple documents. Lerman and McDonald (2009) defined the contrastive summarization problem and presented early work on the problem. Their method selects sentences so that two sets of summaries can highlight differences. Wang et al. (2013) developed an extractive summarization method for a problem of Comparative Document Summarization, which is to select the most discriminative sentences from a given set of documents. Bista et al. (2019) tackled a similar problem by selecting documents that represent in-cluster documents while they are useful to distinguish from other clusters.

Other studies (Kim and Zhai, 2009;Huang et al., 2011;Sipos and Joachims, 2013;Ren et al., 2017) tackled similar tasks by developing extracting sentences/phrases from given sets of documents for comparative document analysis. Topic models have been also used to capture comparative topics for better understanding text corpora, but they do not generate textual summaries (Ren and de Rijke, 2015;He et al., 2016;Ibeke et al., 2017).

Our work differs from the existing work in two points. First, none of them focuses on generating common summaries. Second, all of the previous studies for contrastive summary generation use the extractive approach. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to develop an opinion summarization model and a benchmark for the abstractive contrastive and common summary generation tasks.

The LMs typically use a softmax layer to predict P S (x|c t ), the probability of the next word x given the context at the tth position c t:

where h ct is the tth hidden state in the context c, and w x is the output word embedding for the word x (i.e., the linear weights that project the hidden state to the logit of the word x).

Yang et al. (2018) point out that the log probability distribution over all the words in the vocabulary V is log (P S (x|c t)).

The distribution is a linear projection from the hidden state h ct with dimension D, so the degree of freedom in the distribution is only D (i.e., there cannot be more than D linearly independent log distributions), and we call this restriction the softmax bottleneck theory.

During training, the ideal output word embedding w x should be close to the hidden states of the contexts h ct that co-occur with the word x while far away from the other hidden states, which connects learning dynamics to geometric structure in the representation space.

A key finding in previous studies in discourse analysis is that most sentences have an independent well-formed sub-tree in the full document-level discourse tree (Joty et al., 2012). Researchers have taken advantage of this finding to build parsers that utilize different granularity levels of the document to achieve the state-of-the-art results (Kobayashi et al., 2020). This design has been empirically verified to be a generally advantageous framework, improving not only works using traditional feature engineering (Joty et al., 2013;Wang et al., 2017), but also deep learning models (Jia et al., 2018b;Kobayashi et al., 2020). We, therefore, introduce this design to our dependency parsing framework. Specifically, sub-trees for each sentence in a discourse are first built separately, then assembled to form a complete discourse tree. However, our model differs from prior works in that we make a clear distinction to derive better contextualized representations of EDUs from fine-tuning BERT separately for intra-and intersentential levels to dynamically capture different information needed for discourse analysis at different levels. We are also the first to design stacked sequence labeling models for discourse relation identification so that its hierarchical structure can explicitly capture both intra-sentential and intersentential writing patterns.

In the case of implicit relations between EDUs without clear connectives, it is crucial to introduce sequential information from the context to resolve ambiguity. Feng and Hirst (2014) rely on linearchain CRF with traditional feature engineering to make use of the sequential characteristics of the context for discourse constituent parsing. However, they greedily build up the discourse structure and relations from bottom up. At each timestep, they apply the CRF to obtain the locally optimized structure and relation. In this way, the model assigns relation gradually along with the construction of the parsing tree from bottom up, but only limited contextual information from the top level of the partially constructed tree can be used to predict relations. Besides, at each time-step, they sequentially assign relations to top nodes of the partial tree, without being aware that those nodes might represent different levels of discourse units (e.g. EDUs, sentences, or even paragraphs). In contrast, we explicitly train our sequence labeling models on both intra-and inter-sentential levels after a complete discourse tree is constructed so that we can infer from the whole context with a clear intention of capturing different writing patterns occurring at intra-and inter-sentential levels. Coherence.document: Text Knowledge enhanced methods. Recently, huge efforts on integrating knowledge into PTLMs have been made. One typical form of knowledge is a knowledge graph. There have been efforts of using knowledge graph to inject entity and relation representations, which are pre-computed from external source, into PTLMs (Zhang et al., 2019;Peters et al., 2019;He et al., 2020). Some other works try to retrieve or generate the sub-graph from the graph to solve the problem (Lin et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2020). Another existing form of knowledge is extra large-scale corpus. Works that use such corpus present knowledge-related pre-training objectives such as concept order recovering (Zhou et al., 2021), entity category prediction (Yu et al., 2020) and source of knowledge prediction (Wang et al., 2021). They are mostly focused on injecting world knowledge presented in text, rather than physical and visual commonsense knowledge that can be found in images. Recent studies on multi-modal transformers investigate cross-attention fusion between textual and visual streams (Chen et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022) without clarifying the dependency on prior textual pre-training. To situate our work, we review methods that augment PTLMs with structured and unstructured knowledge. Early approaches relied on fixed knowledge graph embeddings that were concatenated or gated into encoder layers. Subsequent methods developed retrieval components that identify task-relevant subgraphs at inference time. A parallel line of research introduced continual pretraining on domain corpora with entity-aware masking and span objectives. These strategies improved factual recall and entity disambiguation in information extraction and question answering. Nevertheless, they often neglect perceptual or procedural knowledge that is not well captured by text alone. Our study targets this gap by aligning textual representations with signals grounded in images and physical interactions. We consider knowledge graphs that encode affordances and spatial relations derived from annotated visual datasets. We also examine corpora that describe manipulation steps and outcomes in instructional narratives. By combining discrete relational structure with sequence-level descriptions, we aim to enhance reasoning about actions and object states. We prioritize approaches that remain parameter-efficient and compatible with standard PTLM checkpoints. Concretely, we extend a retrieval-augmented encoder with a lightweight adapter for multi-source evidence. The adapter conditions token representations on graph neighborhoods and visual descriptors. We then train with a curriculum that alternates between factual queries and commonsense action queries. This design encourages the model to unify symbolic links with perceptual cues. For evaluation, we adopt tasks that require grounded inference, including procedural QA and visual commonsense QA. We report metrics on answer accuracy, calibration, and retrieval faithfulness. In ablations, we isolate the contribution of graph structure, visual features, and corpus pretraining. Results indicate that joint conditioning yields consistent gains over text-only baselines. Error analysis shows improvements in object state transitions and tool-usage predictions. We also observe better robustness to distractor entities during retrieval. Finally, we discuss implications for scalable knowledge integration without exhaustive end-to-end finetuning. We release code, resources, and templates for reproducible experiments. Our contributions include a unified adapter, a mixed-source curriculum, and a benchmark protocol for grounded knowledge assessment. We anticipate broader impact in applications that require safe and reliable reasoning about the physical world. Future work will explore automatic curation of affordance graphs from weakly labeled images. We also plan to investigate continual updating mechanisms that preserve alignment across modalities. By advancing coherence between structured knowledge and perceptual signals, our approach moves PTLMs toward richer commonsense understanding.

Cross-lingual/Multilingual Machine Reading Comprehension Hsu et al. (2019) investigate cross-lingual transfer capability of multilingual BERT (mBERT) on MRC tasks and find that zeroshot learning based on PLM is feasible, even between distant languages, such as English and Chinese. Various approaches have been proposed on top of multilingual MRC based on PLMs. Cui et al. (2019) propose a method that combines multilingual BERT and back-translation for cross-lingual MRC. In order to effectively leverage translation Different from the above studies, we mainly consider the impact of syntactic divergences between the source and target language in zero-shot crosslingual transfer based on multilingual PLMs, and attempt to disassociate semantics from syntax and only transfer semantic to the target language.

Disentangled Representation Learning Recently, there has been a growing amount of work on learning disentangled latent representations in NLP tasks (Zhang et al., 2019;Hu et al., 2017;Yin et al., 2018). In this aspect, the most related work to our syntax-semantics decoupling method is the vMF-Gaussian Variational Autoencoder (VGVAE) model proposed by Chen et al. (2019). It is a generative model using two latent variables to represent semantics and syntax of the sentence, developed for monolingual setting and trained with paraphrases. It uses paraphrase reconstruction loss and a discriminative paraphrase loss to learn semantic representations and word order information for syntactic representations. We adapt this model to multilingual syntax-semantics disentanglement. We use bilingual sentence pairs to train our model with a cross-lingual reconstruction loss and semantic discrimination loss. To better disentangle semantics from complex and diverse syntax in multilingual PLMs, we introduce two additional syntax-related losses for incorporating POS tags and syntax trees. Recent advances in question answering under multilingual settings emphasize that pretrained encoders capture cross-lingual signals that can be surfaced with probing tasks (Artetxe et al., 2020; Pires et al., 2019; Conneau and Lample, 2019). Large-scale parallel corpora have been curated for evaluation in machine reading comprehension, often contrasting extractive and generative answer formats (Lewis et al., 2020; Clark et al., 2020). Tokenization granularity has also been examined as a factor in transfer efficiency, with subword regularization reported to increase robustness across scripts (Kudo, 2018). We position our work at the intersection of cross-lingual MRC and disentangled representation learning. Our primary goal is to assess whether separating syntactic and semantic factors improves zero-shot transfer on extractive MRC benchmarks. We contribute a training framework that jointly optimizes cross-lingual reconstruction and semantic discrimination while regularizing syntax via POS and dependency cues. We further analyze the role of syntactic distance between language pairs in modulating transfer gains. Our experiments span typologically diverse languages to stress-test the decoupling assumptions. We report detailed ablations over loss components, bilingual data sources, and alignment strategies. The results indicate that explicit syntax-guided disentanglement yields consistent improvements over strong mBERT and XLM-R baselines. We also find that the approach remains robust when parallel data is noisy or partially misaligned. Error analysis suggests that improvements are concentrated on questions involving long-distance dependencies and head-final structures. We release code, pretrained checkpoints, and training scripts to facilitate reproducibility. We additionally provide a multilingual diagnostic set targeting syntactic phenomena relevant to MRC. The diagnostic probes include control for answer length and clause embedding depth. We discuss limitations related to reliance on external taggers and parsers in low-resource settings. Future work may reduce supervision by leveraging unsupervised or weakly supervised syntax induction. This line of research could help unify cross-lingual transfer with structure-aware pretraining. Ultimately, our findings underscore the value of decoupling syntax from semantics for robust multilingual comprehension. By clarifying the contribution of structure, we aim to inform the design of next-generation multilingual PLMs. We conclude with open questions on scaling disentanglement to generative MRC and dialogue-oriented reading tasks.

Multiple efforts have looked into defining, measuring, and mitigating biases in NLP models (Sun et al., 2019;Mehrabi et al., 2019a;Sheng et al., 2021). Dwork et al. (2012) provide foundational definitions of fairness that have informed subsequent metric design in machine learning. Multiple recent works also focus on developing new dataset and associated metrics to capture various types of biases. For example,  and Nangia et al. (2020) propose dataset and metrics to measure social biases and stereotypes in language model generations, Bolukbasi et al. (2016); Caliskan et al. (2017); Manzini et al. (2019) define metrics to access gender and race biases in word vector representations, and  define metrics to quantify and mitigate biases in visual recognition task. Ethayarajh (2020) propose Bernstein bounds to represent uncertainty about the bias. Majority of these bias metrics are automatically computed, for example, using a regard classifier (Sheng et al., 2019), sentiment classifier , toxicity classifier (Dixon et al., 2018) or true positive rate difference between privileged and underprivileged groups (De-Arteaga et al., 2019b). A few works additionally validate the alignment of these automatically computed bias metrics with human understanding of biases by collecting annotations of biases on a subset of test data from crowdworkers (Sheng et al., 2019;. Blodgett et al. (2021Blodgett et al. ( , 2020 discuss the limitations of several of these bias datasets and measurements.

Recent work examines bias in pretrained language models via counterfactual data augmentation (Zmigrod et al., 2019), intrinsic association tests (May et al., 2019), and causal probing frameworks (Vig et al., 2020). Hovy and Spruit (2016) discuss social impacts of NLP technology and dataset documentation practices. Bender and Friedman (2018) introduce a data statement protocol for transparency, and Buolamwini and Gebru (2018) study demographic disparities in face recognition performance.

However, the majority of existing bias metrics are specific to the model type and the application domain used, they may not be tested for correlation with human judgement of biases, and their relationship to existing definitions of fairness has not been explored. Additionally, metrics such as true positive or error difference between groups requires ground truth labels, thereby making their computation in real-time systems difficult. Speicher et al. (2018) have attempted to present unified approach to measuring group and individual fairness via inequality indices, however we note that such metrics are non-trivial to extend to unstructured data such as text. For example, gender information in a text may be subtle (e.g. mention of softball) and it is unclear whether presence of this word should be considered to impact the genderness of the text. Accumulated prediction sensitivity metric, presented in this paper, attempts to address all the above limitations of existing bias metrics. We acknowledge that the proposed metric is yet to be associated with other notions of fairness (e.g. preference based notion of fairness (Zafar et al., 2017)).

Several approaches to zero-shot cross-lingual transfer exist and can broadly be divided into: a) Databased Transfer, which focuses on training data transformation and b) Model-based Transfer that centres around modifying models' training routine.

Data-based Transfer Translating utterances for the intent classification task is relatively straightforward so previous works focused on projecting and/or aligning the entity labels between translated utterances (Dou and Neubig, 2021). This technique is followed by standard supervised training with those pseudo-labels and is commonly known as a translate-train method. One of the earliest works still being used for this purpose is fastalign (Dyer et al., 2013). It's an unsupervised word aligner trained on a parallel corpus to map each word (thus its entity label) in the source utterance to the word(s) in the target user utterance. Projecting the entity labels can also be done with word-by-word translation and source label copying (Yi and Cheng, 2021). A teacher model then weakly labels the target data, which is used to train the final student model. Sometimes, this type of label projection is complemented with an additional entity alignment step (Li et al., 2021a). Better performance can be achieved by using machine translation with entity matching and distributional statistics (Jain et al., 2019) though this can be a costly process for each language. A category of 'word substitution' methods such as code-switching (Qin et al., 2020;Kuwanto et al., 2021) or dictionary-enhanced pretraining have also been shown to improve cross-lingual transfer.

Model-based Transfer Prior to the adoption of multilingual transformers (Lample and Conneau, 2019), task-oriented XNLU methods employed a BiLSTM encoder combined with different multilingual embeddings (Schuster et al., 2019). Newer approaches usually involve a pretrained XLM and the addition of some new training component with the inference routine remaining mostly unchanged. Xu et al. (2020) learn to jointly align and predict entity labels by fusing the source and target language embeddings with attention and using the resulting cross-lingual representation for entity prediction. Qi and Du (2020) include an adversarial language detector in training whose loss encourages the model to generate language-agnostic sentence representations for improved zero-shot trans-fer. Pan et al. (2020) and Chi et al. (2020) added a contrastive loss to pretraining that treats translated sentences as positive examples and unrelated sentences as negative samples. This training step helps the XLM produce similar embeddings in different languages. However, these methods require large annotated datasets and expensive model pretraining (Chi et al., 2020). Our proposed methods only use the English task data (which is relatively limited) and its translations for each language.

The most related prior works are Arivazhagan et al. (2019) for machine translation and XeroAlign for task-oriented XNLU. Both of these are cross-lingual alignment methods that use translated training data to zero-shot transfer the source language model to the target language. We focus on the latter work, called XeroAlign, which reported the most recent SOTA scores on our evaluation datasets. XeroAlign works by generating a sentence embedding of the user utterance for each language, e.g. English (source) and Thai (target) using the CLS token of the XLM. A Mean Squared Error loss function minimises the difference between the multilingual sentence embeddings and is backpropagated along with the main task loss. XeroAlign aims to bring sentence embeddings in different languages closer together with a bias towards intent classification due to the CLS embedding, which is the standard input to the intent classifier. We reproduce this method for analysis and comparisons but add a small post-processing step that distinctly improves the reported scores.

(2015) introduced cloze-style queries over news, Rajpurkar et al. (2016) framed extractive QA on Wikipedia, and Kwiatkowski et al. (2019) scaled open-domain answering with heterogeneous sources. Hill et al. (2016) collected the bAbI tasks to test reasoning with synthetic stories. Most narrative QA settings instead require modeling long-range dependencies across events and characters in realistic texts. The BookTest corpus (Bajgar et al., 2016) extended cloze queries to novels. NarrativeQA (Kocisky et al., 2018) paired plot summaries and full books/films with abstractive questions and answers. DREAM (Sun et al., 2019) targeted multi-turn dialogue comprehension in exams. SQuAD-style adversarial sets have also probed robustness. Educational question generation has investigated didactic scaffolding and item difficulty. TextbookQA (Kembhavi et al., 2017) aligned multimodal textbook content with questions. RACE (Lai et al., 2017) aggregated English examination questions from Chinese middle and high schools. DuoRC (Saha et al., 2018) introduced paraphrase-heavy movie synopses requiring inference.

Narrative datasets often evaluate cross-sentence reasoning, coreference, and character modeling across long contexts. Educational QA corpora, by contrast, foreground curricular alignment, cognitive skill coverage, and item difficulty calibration. Prior work has cataloged these dimensions to clarify where datasets stress comprehension versus retrieval. DREAM (Sun et al., 2019) targeted multi-turn dialogue comprehension in exams. SQuAD-style adversarial sets have also probed robustness. Educational question generation has investigated didactic scaffolding and item difficulty. TextbookQA (Kembhavi et al., 2017) aligned multimodal textbook content with questions. RACE (Lai et al., 2017) aggregated English examination questions from Chinese middle and high schools. DuoRC (Saha et al., 2018) introduced paraphrase-heavy movie synopses requiring inference. To ground the survey, we first group datasets by narrative source: literary fiction, film synopses, dialogues, and news-derived cloze narratives. We then articulate educational orientation along three axes: assessment context, annotation policy, and cognitive taxonomy. For literary fiction, NarrativeQA stands out for its dual setting (summary versus full text) that separates surface recall from deep narrative understanding. For film materials, MovieQA (Tapaswi et al., 2016) integrates plots, subtitles, and videos, enabling multimodal narrative reasoning. DuoRC focuses on paraphrastic divergence between documents and questions, intentionally reducing lexical overlaps. For dialogues, DREAM tests pragmatic inference and speaker attribution in multi-turn contexts. For news-style narratives, CNN/DailyMail variants remain useful for cloze-based sequence modeling. Turning to education-focused corpora, RACE provides multiple-choice items spanning literal, inferential, and summarization skills. TextbookQA layers diagrams and figures with explanatory passages to reflect classroom resources. ARC (Clark et al., 2018) contrasts easy versus challenge science questions to probe knowledge integration. SciQ (Welbl et al., 2017) offers crowdsourced science items with distractors designed to mimic classroom exams. MCTest (Richardson et al., 2013) supplies small, carefully controlled stories for elementary-level comprehension. TOEFL Listening Comprehension sets introduce authentic academic discourse for non-native learners. Several datasets bridge both aims: QuAC (Choi et al., 2018) and CoQA (Reddy et al., 2019) model conversational comprehension while retaining educational relevance. TREC-style QA remains a reference point for taxonomy and evaluation protocol design. MultiRC (Khashabi et al., 2018) emphasizes multi-sentence reasoning with calibrated distractors. As evaluation practices evolve, leaderboard saturation has motivated adversarial splits and length-controlled partitions. We synthesize these developments by highlighting implications for modeling architectures, annotation design, and curricular validity. The survey concludes with recommendations for dataset selection aligned to narrative complexity and instructional goals.

2.1 Pre-trained language model (PLM)

Most modern language models are based on the transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) architecture. The PLMs generally use only the encoder block of the transformer, which consists of two sublayers, a self-attention layer, and a feed-forward layer. BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) is the most widely used PLM, which consists of several layers of transformer encoders. The BERT was pre-trained for 4 days with a large amount of text data, which consists of 3.3 billion words, using masked language modeling and the next sentence prediction task in an unsupervised manner. This pre-trained parameter can be easily used in various downstream tasks by fine-tuning the model using the labeled dataset. Since the success of BERT, a variety of similar PLMs have emerged.

Coherence.document: There has been the argument revolving deep learning models that they are black-box and hard to offer explainable and interpretable predictions, which has led to a considerable amount of research work regarding their interpretability (Linardatos et al., 2021). The pre-trained BERT language model has been extensively analyzed since its launch, in particular, feature-based probes have been proposed to show how a particular layer, head, or neuron of BERT works on a downstream NLP task. Usually with a small set of additional parameters, a probe is trained in a supervised manner using feature representations from the pre-trained BERT, e.g. contextualized embeddings, to solve a particular task (Wu et al., 2020). Attention and structural probes have been invented to investigate different aspects of BERT and linguistics (Lin et al., 2019;Jawahar et al., 2019;Clark et al., 2019;Hewitt and Manning, 2019;Manning et al., 2020;Tenney et al., 2019a,b;Pruksachatkun et al., 2020). Latent ontology of contextual embeddings has also been investigated via cluster analysis (Michael et al., 2020). For works that emphasize probing contextualized representations for lexico-semantic relations, previous studies have investigated BERT for lexical relation classification via a neural network probe on type-level embeddings (Vulić et al., 2020). Researchers have also examined multilingual adaptations of BERT, domain-specific pretraining for biomedical and legal text, and prompt-based steering of masked language models to elicit latent relational knowledge (Devlin et al., 2019; Beltagy et al., 2019; Chalkidis et al., 2020; Petroni et al., 2019); knowledge graph completion methods compare structured inference against distributional cues, and few-shot prompting can expose parametric facts without fine-tuning (Bosselut et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2020). In this work, we differ from previous works by a goal to explicitly investigate how much BERT understands the IS-A relations and more importantly, transitivity. That is, we aim to find if and how often BERT makes logically consistent predictions for transitive relations. Moreover, we are devoted to investigating sense-aware IS-A relations, where IS-A relations are extracted from explicit word senses with associated contexts, so contextualized embeddings can be clearly mapped to senses.

Introduction

Pretrained LM in Open-domain dialogue has received sustained attention as models have scaled and datasets diversified for multi-turn interaction research. Many prior works tried to pretrain the models on large-scale social comment chains data like Reddit to model conversational behavior (Zhang et al., 2020; Adiwardana et al., 2020), followed by finetuning on the diverse target dialogue dataset to improve engagingness and humanness. Prior work emphasizes large-scale pretraining on conversational corpora to endow models with discourse competence and pragmatic flexibility (Roller et al., 2021). Smith et al. (2019) introduced a multi-turn response selection benchmark focusing on context coherence and persona consistency. Zhang et al. (2018) proposed PersonalDialog to capture speaker traits and long-range dependencies across sessions. While these efforts improved surface-level fluency, recent studies highlight shortcomings in factual grounding and safety in open-domain settings (Shuster et al., 2021; Dinan et al., 2021). Retrieval-augmented dialogue aims to mitigate hallucination by conditioning generation on retrieved passages from web or curated knowledge sources (Lewis et al., 2020; Komeili et al., 2022). Safety-aware data construction further introduces refusal behaviors and sensitive-topic handling to reduce harmful outputs during both pretraining and finetuning (Baheti et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2022). Instruction tuning with preference optimization has emerged to better align chat models with conversational goals while maintaining factuality and politeness (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022). To avoid undesired behaviors of the models including toxicity and bias from the human-human conversation, they merely exclude some parts of training data using automatic filtering by predefined criteria. Despite measurable gains, our work argues that filtering alone is insufficient without explicit safety objectives and grounding signals integrated throughout the training pipeline.

Quality Estimation Current SOTA models in sentence-level QE, which is typically framed as a regression task, mainly use multilingual representations from pre-trained transformers (Devlin et al., 2018), notably XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2019). The input to a sentence-level QE model is a concatenation of the source and translated sentences, separated by the [SEP] token. The sequence is encoded by the pre-trained Transformer model, and the [CLS] token is passed through a multilayer perceptron (MLP) layer to obtain a sentence-level score. During fine-tuning both the parameters of the pre-trained model and the parameters corresponding to the MLP layer are updated.

Word-level QE is typically addressed as a binary classification task, where the QE model needs to predict a binary label indicating whether a word is correct or wrong for each word in the MT output (Lee, 2020). As illustrated in Figure  (left), some supervised approaches use both sentence-level and word-level objectives in a multi-task setting, which results in superior performance (Kim et al., 2017;Lee, 2020). Methods that do not require word-level training data either need access to the MT model (Rikters and Fishel, 2017;Fomicheva et al., 2020b), or still treat the problem as a supervised task but use synthetically generated data for supervision (Tuan et al., 2021).

Rationale Extraction for NLP SOTA NLP models based on deep neural networks achieve high performance in a variety of tasks, often at the cost of interpretability (Lipton, 2016). Recent work aims to address this issue by focusing on two different goals. On the one hand, the aim is to produce justifications for model predictions that are plausible to the users, in order to increase users' trust (Ribeiro et al., 2016). On the other hand, the aim is to reveal the inner workings of the model and faithfully explain its predictions, so the explanation can be useful to model developers (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020).

Typically, explainability methods operate by selecting a portion of the input that justifies model prediction for a single data point. This can be done either by modifying the model architecture, or by trying to explain the predictions of a given model. The first type of approaches (a.k.a. rationalization by construction) involves imposing restrictions on the generated rationales to satisfy certain constraints, e.g. compactness (Yu et al., 2019;Chalkidis et al., 2021). Note that such restrictions often result in lower performance and indeed are not guaranteed to explain the behaviour of an unconstrained model (Jain et al., 2020). The second type of approaches (the so called post hoc) usually rely on feature attribution methods, which assign an importance value to each input feature of a network (Sundararajan et al., 2017;Schulz et al., 2020). These methods do not allow for introducing useful biases during training, but focus on faithfully explaining model behaviour.

Feature attribution has a long tradition in image recognition tasks (Simonyan et al., 2013) and only recently have been applied to some NLP tasks, most commonly text classification (DeYoung et al., 2019). QE is fundamentally different from text classification where clues are typically separate words or phrases (Zaidan et al., 2007) which often can be considered independently of the rest of the text. This independence assumption does not hold for the task of evaluating translation quality where a word cannot be identified as a clue (e.g. translation error) without considering the surrounding context. Furthermore, SOTA NLP models based on contextualized representations for input words make rationale extraction especially challenging, as the representation for a given word can encode not only the word identity but also its interactions with other words in the text. Recent work has revealed various interesting properties that characterize the information flow through hidden layers in deep transformer models (Voita et al., 2019;De Cao et al., 2020;Yun et al., 2021). We provide additional insights on this topic in Section 5.2.

Coherence.document: Introduction Synthetic translations are widely leveraged in neural machine translation to expand training signals when genuine bitext is scarce. Early efforts explored monolingual exploitation through forward translation of source-side corpora (Zhang and Zong, 2016) and through backtranslation of target-side texts (Sennrich et al., 2016a; Marie et al., 2020). These strategies increased domain coverage and lexical diversity without costly human annotation. Subsequent work refined sampling, decoding, and filtering to control noise in generated pairs. Backtranslation quality has been tied to iterative retraining cycles and domain-adaptive language modeling. Data curation pipelines now routinely balance synthetic and human-authored segments for stability. Synthetic augmentation has also been used to target low-resource transfer by pivoting through related languages. Researchers study how noise temperature and sampling affect rare token recall. Some approaches interleave synthetic and authentic batches to mitigate distribution drift. Adaptive schedules adjust the ratio of synthetic sentences across training epochs. Nguyen et al. (2020) diversify the parallel data via translating both sides using multiple models and then merge them with the original to train a final NMT model; Jiao et al. (2020) employ a similar approach to rejuvenate inactive examples that contribute the least to the model performance. Sequence-level knowledge distillation (Kim and Rush, 2016) can also be viewed as replacing original bitext with synthetic translations. Distillation reframes the objective by training on model-generated hypotheses that smooth the target distribution. This perspective aligns with findings that simpler targets can reduce exposure bias during decoding. Non-autoregressive systems are a prominent case where distilled corpora stabilize optimization. Gu et al. (2017) report substantial speedups with competitive accuracy under distilled supervision. Later studies integrate iterative refinement and latent alignment to close quality gaps. Researchers analyze how teacher decoding strategies shape student generalization. Empirical evidence indicates that beam size and length penalties modulate calibration. Studies also examine the interaction between backtranslation and distillation in joint curricula. Mixed regimes alternate synthetic targets from different teachers for robustness. While its original goal was to guide the training of a student model of small capacity with the output of a teacher of high capacity, distillation is also necessary to effectively train some categories of MT architectures such as non-autoregressive models (Gu et al., 2017). While it is not entirely clear why synthetic distilled samples are superior to original bitext in this case, recent studies suggest that the synthetic samples are simpler and thus easier to learn from (Zhou et al., 2019a;Xu et al., 2021). Despite gains, concerns remain about domain narrowing and stylistic homogenization. Recent work proposes round-trip filtering to retain only meaning-preserving synthetic pairs. Others advocate uncertainty-aware selection to downweight brittle hypotheses. Evaluation protocols now emphasize robustness across domains and noise profiles. Our study situates these threads by comparing curriculum schedules that interleave backtranslation and distillation under fixed compute budgets. We focus on practical settings where monolingual data are abundant but parallel data are limited. The proposed analysis isolates the effect of teacher diversity, decoding temperature, and synthetic ratio. We report results on standard benchmarks spanning high- and low-resource pairs. Findings highlight when additional synthetic volume saturates and when diversity continues to help. We release code and preprocessing scripts to support reproducibility. Finally, we discuss open questions around measuring semantic adequacy in heavily distilled corpora.

Conversational question answering. In recent years, several conversational question answering datasets have emerged, such as QuAC (Choi et al., 2018), CoQA (Reddy et al., 2019), andDoQA (Campos et al., 2020). Different from singleturn QA datasets (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), CQA requires the model to understand the question in the context of conversational history. There have been many methods proposed to improve CQA performance (Ohsugi et al., 2019;Chen et al., 2020;Qu et al., 2019;Kim et al., 2021) and significant improvement has been made on CQA benchmarks.

Besides text-based CQA tasks, there also exist CQA benchmarks that require other forms of modeling ability, such as combining textual evidence with background knowledge (Saeidi et al., 2018), utilizing structured knowledge base (Saha et al., 2018;Guo et al., 2018), as well as CQA in other modalities (Das et al., 2017).

Evaluation with predicted history. Only recently has it been noticed that the current method of evaluating CQA models is flawed. Mandya et al. (2020); Siblini et al. (2021) point out that using gold answers in history is not consistent with the realworld scenario and propose to use predicted history for evaluation. Chen et al. (2020) analyze pretraining strategies for CQA encoders, and Qu et al. (2019) investigate dialog-level attention mechanisms for context tracking, while Kim et al. (2021) explore turn-level reformulation for error robustness. Different from prior work, in this paper, we conduct a large scale human evaluation to support our claims, identify the issues with predicted history, and propose rewriting questions to further mitigate the gap to human evaluation.

Coherence.document:
Introduction

Natural language inference has catalyzed renewed interest in interpretability methods that connect model decisions to human-understandable evidence. Early studies argue that interpretability should be grounded in faithful attribution rather than post hoc plausibility (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Lipton, 2018). Subsequent work formalizes desiderata such as stability, sufficiency, and minimality for explanations tied to prediction changes (Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola, 2018; DeYoung et al., 2020). The community has converged on three major families of interpretability outputs relevant to inference tasks. Feature-based interpretation links internal activations to inputs through saliency, gradient-based scores, or perturbation analysis (Simonyan et al., 2013; Sundararajan et al., 2017; Jain and Wallace, 2019). Token-level interpretation highlights spans that are deemed crucial for the model decision, often trading off faithfulness and readability (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Thorne et al., 2019). Sentence-level interpretation aims for human-readable rationales that summarize multi-sentence evidence into coherent justifications (Camburu et al., 2018; Narang et al., 2020). Despite progress, most approaches optimize only one objective—either prediction accuracy or explanation quality—without explicitly modeling their mutual reinforcement.

[Prior work on natural language inference often presupposes that extracted rationales directly support model predictions without clarifying how complementary evidence is reconciled across heterogeneous sources (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018). Camburu et al. (2018) study natural language explanations accompanying decisions. Talmor et al. (2018) examine multi-hop question answering over knowledge, and Kumar and Talukdar (2020) investigate graph-structured supervision for explainability.]

Within feature-based methods, attention maps are frequently used as surrogate explanations, yet their faithfulness remains contested due to weak correlation with gradient-based measures (Jain and Wallace, 2019; Serrano and Smith, 2019). Heatmap-style visualizations aggregate token importances but can obscure interactions across sentences, challenging their utility for multi-hop inference (Samek et al., 2017; Chefer et al., 2021). Gradient and integrated-gradient techniques offer sensitivity guarantees but may still highlight spurious correlations induced by dataset artifacts (Sundararajan et al., 2017; McCoy et al., 2019). Perturbation-based attribution improves faithfulness estimates at the cost of computational expense and potential distribution shift (Fong and Vedaldi, 2017; Hooker et al., 2019). These observations motivate modeling strategies that jointly calibrate predictions and explanations.

Token-level rationales have been operationalized through extractive selectors trained to preserve label fidelity while minimizing text length (Lei et al., 2016; Bastings et al., 2019). Selector–predictor frameworks disentangle rationale extraction from classification to improve faithfulness, but they risk overfitting to annotation heuristics (Chang et al., 2020). Human-annotated rationales provide supervision signals for selector quality, yet agreement varies across domains and tasks (DeYoung et al., 2020). Recent benchmarks in fact verification and question answering further highlight the gap between faithful span selection and end-task performance (Thorne et al., 2019; Lamm et al., 2021). Bridging this gap requires architectures that use rationales as intermediate computation rather than mere outputs.

Sentence-level explanations offer higher readability and can summarize dispersed evidence across documents (Camburu et al., 2018; Narang et al., 2020). Retrieval-augmented generators produce natural language justifications conditioned on external corpora, but separating factual grounding from stylistic fluency remains difficult (Lewis et al., 2020; Rashkin et al., 2021). Controllability mechanisms regulate explanation specificity and stance, yet explicit coupling with verifier modules is often absent (Kumar and Talukdar, 2020; Lampinen et al., 2022). Work on causal mediation suggests that explanations should serve as mediators aligning intermediate representations with downstream entailment (Feder et al., 2021). This perspective encourages training setups in which justifications actively influence the predictor’s internal reasoning trajectory.

From a learning-theoretic viewpoint, multi-task objectives can encourage shared representations that benefit both accuracy and explanation quality when tasks are related but not redundant (Ruder, 2017). Joint training with agreement constraints aligns selector salience with generator content, while calibration losses regularize uncertainty in both predictions and explanations (Desai and Durrett, 2020; Kamath et al., 2020). Curriculum strategies can stage learning from token-level to sentence-level rationales to progressively structure evidence (Bengio et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2020). Such designs suggest a path for mutual promotion wherein better explanations produce better features and vice versa.

Our work formalizes mutual promotion as a closed-loop interaction between an inference module and a sentence-level explanation module. Concretely, the inference module proposes candidate evidence, the explanation module composes a justification, and a verifier adjudicates consistency between justification content and the predicted label. The resulting signals update both modules, rewarding alignments that improve task performance and penalizing unsupported claims. We also introduce a retrieval interface to supply verifiable facts that ground the generated explanations.

We evaluate on natural language inference and fact verification datasets where both labels and human-written justifications are available. Metrics include label accuracy, faithfulness via sufficiency and comprehensiveness tests, and explanation quality via factuality and entailment checks. Experimental results indicate that mutual promotion consistently improves both predictive performance and explanation grounding across domains. Ablations show that removing the verifier degrades faithfulness even when label accuracy remains competitive, underscoring the importance of closed-loop consistency. Qualitative analyses further illustrate how explanations evolve to cite more specific evidence as training progresses.

In summary, we position mutual promotion as a general strategy for coupling interpretability with predictive modeling in language understanding. By aligning the objectives of inference and explanation, our approach narrows the gap between plausibility and faithfulness. The framework is modular, data-efficient, and compatible with retrieval-augmented architectures. We release code and annotations to facilitate future work on controllable, verifiable explanations that improve decision quality.

2.1 Security and Privacy Concern of Pre-trained Models

Pre-trained models like BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) and GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) rely heavily on the use of plain text data to get human-like performance. Despite the remarkable achievements of pre-trained models, these state-of-the-art models can not directly answer some sensitive use cases, including the medical record (Christoph et al., 2015), search history (Shen et al., 2007) and other personally identifiable information (PII).

To avoid the direct computation on plain-text data, recent works like TextHide (Huang et al., 2020) and DP-finetuning (Kerrigan et al., 2020) introduce the classical federated learning and differential privacy (DP) to protect the sensitive data. However, TextHide (Huang et al., 2020) can only be applied to sentence-level tasks. Due to the mixup operation, TextHide fails to model token-level tasks like named entity recognition or semantic role labelling. DP-finetuning would greatly sacrifice the performance of fine-tuned model by 20% perplexity for a generation model like GPT-2. Recent studies explore privacy-preserving objectives for pre-training such as PATE-style aggregation for language tasks (Papernot et al., 2018), cryptographic approaches for secure aggregation in federated optimization (Bonawitz et al., 2017), and model auditing via membership inference risk estimators that quantify exposure in generative models (Carlini et al., 2022). We focus on practical configurations that maintain utility while offering quantifiable privacy guarantees. Our analysis considers the trade-off between privacy budgets and downstream accuracy under realistic fine-tuning regimes. We compare task families that stress token-level labeling against sequence-level generation. Prior work highlights that token-level gradients tend to leak more information than sequence-level gradients. We examine privacy amplification effects arising from subsampling in large-batch training. Our setting includes common pre-training corpora with PII redaction strategies. We evaluate attack surfaces for text reconstruction during inference. We study the interaction between clipping norms and optimizer dynamics in DP-SGD. Our experiments include ablations on gradient noise schedules across epochs. We additionally report robustness under distribution shift in the presence of privacy noise. We provide guidance on choosing hyperparameters that balance utility and risk. Our findings suggest that moderate noise can preserve NER performance. We also observe task-dependent sensitivity to μ and σ in privacy accounting. These observations inform deployment recommendations for sensitive domains. We release reproducible pipelines for DP-aware fine-tuning. We further discuss compliance implications for healthcare and finance. Overall, our work clarifies practical privacy baselines for pre-trained models.

Coherence.document: Pretrained Language Models Contextual representations such as ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) and BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) are not just useful for monolingual representations. Multilingual BERT (Devlin et al., 2019, mBERT), XLM (Lample and Conneau, 2019), and XLM-RoBERTa (Conneau et al., 2020, XLM-R) have surprisingly high cross-lingual transfer performance compared to the previous best practice: static cross-lingual word embeddings (Pires et al., 2019;Wu and Dredze, 2019). Multilingual models are also practicalwhy have hundreds of separate models for each language when you could do better with just one? However, there's a catch. Conneau et al. (2020) reports the "curse of multilinguality": as the number of pretraining languages increases, the better the cross-lingual transfer is up to some point, after which the performance in zero-shot transfer starts to decrease. Our work complements Conneau et al. (2020) by explicitly dividing up between seen and unseen languages during pretraining and testing whether the "curse of multilinguality" is also an issue for unseen languages too. To ground our investigation, we consider standardized benchmarks in cross-lingual natural language understanding and structured prediction. We emphasize evaluation protocols that separate zero-shot transfer from in-language fine-tuning to avoid conflating adaptation with generalization. We further analyze scaling trends with respect to corpus size, language coverage, and tokenization granularity. Recent prompting-based alignment methods focus on steering model behavior without modifying parameters (Lester et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023). Adapter-based transfer introduces lightweight modules to specialize shared backbones (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020). Task-balanced sampling and vocabulary sharing have been examined for data efficiency in multilingual pretraining (Chi et al., 2022). We build on these observations by isolating the impact of language exposure during pretraining while holding architecture and optimization constant. Our design contrasts a family of models with identical capacity but varying partitions of seen and unseen languages. We measure transfer both to typologically related and distant languages to probe whether overlap in subword statistics mediates the effect. We also ablate data temperature, per-language mixing ratios, and domain diversity to assess sensitivity to distributional skew. For robustness, we report results across multiple random seeds and training lengths to mitigate instability in low-resource regimes. We complement accuracy with calibration and consistency metrics to capture overconfidence and representational drift. To interpret transfer pathways, we analyze layer-wise probing results and lexical alignment scores derived from bilingual dictionaries. We include controlled ablations on tokenizer vocab size and share rate to disentangle segmentation from representation learning. We additionally evaluate catastrophic forgetting by fine-tuning on a subset of high-resource languages and re-testing zero-shot performance. Finally, we discuss practical implications for multilingual deployment, including model selection under compute budgets and the trade-off between language coverage and per-language performance.

Our goal is to enable end-to-end training of goaldirected dialogue agents. In these settings, an agent aims to complete a particular task with its utterances (Smith and Hipp, 1994). Goal-directed agents have been explored in contexts such as personal assistants (McTear, 2002;Budzianowski et al., 2018;Williams et al., 2014), recommendation systems (Liu et al., 2010;Kang et al., 2019), education (Yuan et al., 2008), and negotiation (He et al., 2018;Lewis et al., 2017). While there are multiple approaches to constructing dialogue agents, in this work we frame the problem of generating dialogue as a sequential decision making problem within a (partially observed) Markov Decision Process (MDP) (Singh et al., 1999;Young et al., 2013). Prior works that utilize such an MDP formulation typically aim to train a dialogue management system (Singh et al., 2002), in which the agent reasons about higher-level abstractions of the state of the conversation, and language generation is performed using a downstream procedure. Dialogue management systems have been trained using techniques such as online reinforcement learning via policy gradients (Gašić et al., 2011;He et al., 2018), off-policy reinforcement learning (Pietquin et al., 2011;Yu et al., 2016) or actor-critic methods (Su et al., 2017). Our method differs from dialogue management systems in that CALM is an end-to-end system optimized for successful task completion, and performs both high-level decision making and language generation.

Recent advancements in language models, such as recurrent neural networks (Sundermeyer et al., 2012;Asri et al., 2016;Su et al., 2016;Zhao et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2020a;Zhang et al., 2020) and attention-based architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017;Liu et al., 2019;Devlin et al., 2018;Brown et al., 2020), have spurred increasing interest in such endto-end dialogue systems (Hosseini-Asl et al., 2020;Peng et al., 2020;Adiwardana et al., 2020). Modelbased approaches, in which a learned agent is substituted for a human, allow learning to be done entirely within simulation without human intervention (Li et al., 2016;He et al., 2018;Kang et al., 2019;Lewis et al., 2017;Liu et al., 2018). In contrast to these approaches, CALM augments the traditional language modeling objective with taskspecific rewards in order to finetune a model that is more aware of task goals, which significantly improves performance over a naïve language model without the need for simulating human responses in an interactive training loop. Jaques et al. (2019) recently proposed a model-free, offline approach to undirected dialogue, or dialogue without a specific task goal. Our method differs in that we aim to solve goal-oriented dialogue which allows us to optimize task-specific objectives, and that we take a model-based RL approach which enables us to leverage fine-tuned language models.

Automatic evaluation of open-domain dialogue systems has a multifaceted nature with many finegrained quality aspects (Mehri and Eskénazi, 2020). Turn-level aspects show the quality of the system's utterance given a dialogue context from different perspectives including appropriateness, relevance, engaging, and etc (Lowe et al., 2017;Tao et al., 2018;Ghazarian et al., 2020). Whereas, conversation-level facets such as coherence, diversity, informative take into account the whole conversation and dialog flow (Vakulenko et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2021;Mehri and Eskénazi, 2020). Dialogue coherence evaluation is pertinent to the discourse coherence as a dialogue is counted as a multi-party discourse. Similar to discourse coherence, many original coherence evaluation metrics derived from Centering Model for monitoring the local focus of utterances and the entities distribution over utterances (Grosz and Sidner, 1986;Miltsakaki and Kukich, 2004;Lapata and Barzilay, 2005). A group of studies assess the coherence of dialogues with respect to entities and dialogue acts (Cervone and Riccardi, 2020;Mesgar et al., 2020). Another inspected approach for dialogue coherence evaluation is to represent dialogue in a structured graph format where contextually dependent neighbor utterances or concepts are connected nodes in the graph (Vakulenko et al., 2018;Mesgar et al., 2020;Huang et al., 2020). Graph convolutional networks are used to complete this task.

High quality training dataset is identified as one of the momentous and indelible components in automatic coherence evaluation. Some previous works construct such datasets by collecting human judgments (Higashinaka et al., 2014;Cervone and Riccardi, 2020). While many recent works rely on a more timely and costly affordable approach by automatically generating negative samples. The utterances of the coherent conversations from humanhuman interactions are manipulated by shuffling  their order, inserting or replacing irrelevant utterances (Vakulenko et al., 2018;Mesgar et al., 2020;Huang et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2021). In this work, we show that such changes can not truly represent machine generated incoherent conversations.

Early work on simplification relied on rules, e.g., to split or shorten long sentences (Chandrasekar and Srinivas, 1997;Carroll et al., 1998;Vickrey and Koller, 2008). Later work treated simplification as a monolingual phrase-based machine translation (MT) task (Coster and Kauchak, 2011;Wubben et al., 2012), with syntactic information added, such as constituency trees (Zhu et al., 2010). Recent work, reviewed below, leverages neural models in a generative and revision-based manner.

Supervised Generative Methods employ Seq2Seq (Sutskever et al., 2014) models to implicitly learn simplification operations from aligned complex-simple sentence pairs. Inspired by the success of Seq2Seq neural MT models, Nisioi et al. (2017) applied a Seq2Seq model for text simplification. Zhang and Lapata (2017) used reinforcement learning to optimize a reward based on simplicity, fluency and relevance, building on a Seq2Seq model. Recent methods build on transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) models, by integrating external databases containing simplification rules (Zhao et al., 2018), using an additional loss function to generate diverse outputs (Kriz et al., 2019), combining syntactic rules (Maddela et al., 2021), and conditioning on length and syntactic and lexical complexity features (Martin et al., 2020a).

Unsupervised Generative Methods rely on non-aligned complex and simple corpora instead of aligned complex-simple sentence pairs. Zhao et al. (2020) adopted a back-translation framework, whereas Surya et al. (2019) used an unsupervised style transfer paradigm. Martin et al. (2020b) used a pre-trained BART model fine-tuned on a paraphrased sentence pairs.

Controllable Generative Methods produce outputs at specified grade levels (Scarton and Specia, 2018;Nishihara et al., 2019), or apply syntactic or lexical constraints on the generated sentences (Martin et al., 2020a,b). However, these models do not provide any insights into how the simplification process is done and thus lack interpretability.

Supervised Revision-Based Methods use complex-simple sentence pairs to learn where to apply edit operations iteratively. Alva-Manchego et al. (2017) proposed a model using keep, replace, and delete operations. Some recent work used iterative non-autoregressive models to edit sentences by either predicting token-level editoperations (Omelianchuk et al., 2021) or using a fixed pipeline of edit operations (Agrawal et al., 2021). Dong et al. (2019) proposed a hybrid method with explicit edit operations in an endto-end generative model. Though these methods are more interpretable and controllable than generative methods, they still require complex-simple sentence pairs for training.

Unsupervised Revision-Based Methods such as Narayan and Gardent (2016) may apply a pipeline of edit operations in a fixed order. Kumar et al. (2020) then presented a general unsupervised revision-based approach by modelling text simplification as an unsupervised search problem. Prior controllable decoding methods for lexical simplification were explored by Zhang et al. (2022) with frequency-aware constraints. Xu et al. (2016) introduced evaluation metrics emphasizing simplicity and adequacy for system comparison. Pretrained masked LMs have also been applied to lexical substitution (Zhou et al., 2019). These strands have examined curriculum-based fine-tuning for readability (Laban et al., 2021). While GRS also relies on a revision-based framework and an unsupervised search strategy, we integrate a generative paraphrasing model into the framework to leverage the strengths of both text generation and text revision approaches.

The pretraining-finetuning paradigm (Howard and Ruder, 2018) shows tremendous success in fewshot NLU tasks. Various methods have been developed such as [CLS] classification (Devlin et al., 2018), prompting-based methods with discrete prompts (Schick and Schütze, 2021b;Gao et al., 2020) or continuous prompts (Liu et al., 2021b;Shin et al., 2020;Li and Liang, 2021;Lester et al., 2021), and methods that calibrate the output distribution (Yang et al., 2021;Zhao et al., 2021).

The fact that few-shot learning is sensitive to many factors and thus is extremely unstable (Liu et al., 2021a;Lu et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2020;Dodge et al., 2020) increases the difficulty of fewshot evaluation. Several works address evaluation protocols to mitigate the effects of instability: Gao et al. (2020) and Liu et al. (2021b) adopt a held-out set to select models. Perez et al. (2021) proposed K-fold cross-validation and minimum description length evaluation strategies. Bragg et al. (2021) andYe et al. (2021) proposed few-shot NLP benchmarks FLEX and Cross-Fit respectively. Our work differs from these works on few-shot evaluation in several aspects: (1) we propose three metrics to evaluate data split strategies; (2) while most prior work proposed evaluation protocols without justification, we conduct comprehensive experiments to support our key design choice; (3) we formulate a general evaluation framework; (4) our re-evaluation under the proposed framework leads to several key findings. Both FLEX and CrossFit study principles of designing tasks, datasets, and metrics, while we focus on addressing inherent problems of the evaluation procedure.

Coherence.document: In this section, we summarize existing works on syntactically and lexically CPG. Syntactically CPG generates a paraphrase constrained by a prespecified sentence of a certain syntax structure namely exemplar. However, the exemplar is only available during inference, resulting in a key challenge: obtaining manual exemplars for existing paraphrasing training datasets is prohibitively expensive. To address this, some of the previous works construct syntactical features from target sentences during training, such as POS Tagging, Constituent Tree, mask template as illustrated in Table . For instance, SCPN (Iyyer et al., 2018) makes the first attempt to introduce Linearised Constituent Tree (LCT) of target sentence into paraphrasing, where LCT is predicted based on predefined parse templates. Similarly, GuiG (Li et al., 2020) proposes two models to expand a partial template LCT and generate paraphrasing, respectively. Different from using LCT, SGCP (Kumar et al., 2020) introduces a graph encoder to encode the Constituent Tree of exemplar as the condition. Besides, masked template replaces several words of the exemplar with a special token to form a template as the condition. For example, BCPG (Liu et al., 2020b) follows BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) to randomly mask exemplar words, ParafraGPT (Bui  2019) make the first attempt to integrate keywords with copy mechanism. Despite their progress, existing works only focus on a special condition under either lexically or syntactically CPG. In comparison, GCPG jointly includes lexically and syntactically CPG, flexibly combining conditions in a unified circumstance.

Lifelong Learning for PLMs. Lifelong learning aims at incrementally acquiring new knowledge, and in the meantime, mitigating the catastrophic forgetting issue. Numerous efforts have been spent towards this goal, including (1) memory-based methods (Rebuffi et al., 2017;Rolnick et al., 2019), which perform experience replay with authentic data (de Masson d'Autume et al., 2019), automatically generated data (Sun et al., 2020), or previously computed gradients (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017) conserved in the memory, (2) consolidationbased methods (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017;Aljundi et al., 2018), which introduce additional regularization terms to consolidate the model parameters that are important to previous tasks, and (3) dynamic architecture methods (Rusu et al., 2016;Yoon et al., 2018), which fix trained network architectures in old tasks and dynamically grow branches for new tasks. Lifelong learning is also a hot topic for PLMs. Some target at domain adaptation through continual pre-training (Gururangan et al., 2020), parameter-efficient adapters (He et al., 2021) and sparse expert models (Gururangan et al., 2021). Others focus on the incremental acquisition of factual knowledge that changes over time (Dhingra et al., 2021;Jang et al., 2021). Recent work also explores retrieval-augmented language modeling for continual adaptation (Lewis et al., 2020), curriculum scheduling for domain drift (Xie et al., 2021), and evaluation protocols for evolving knowledge graphs (Kassner et al., 2021). Lee et al. (2020) study prompt-based continual tuning for task streams. Sun et al. (2021) propose gradient orthogonalization for sequence of tasks. Kumar et al. (2022) benchmark adapter fusion for evolving domains. Nguyen et al. (2019) examine uncertainty estimation in lifelong classifiers. However, the existing works seldom consider our lifelong learning setting where streaming data from multiple sources is sequentially gathered. A concurrent work  conducts empirical studies on conventional continual learning algorithms for PLM adaptation. However, they do not focus on PLM's training efficiency, which is different from our setting. More detailed comparisons are left in appendix F.

Efficient Pre-training in NLP. Many attempts have been made towards improving the efficiency of pre-training, such as designing novel pretraining tasks (Clark et al., 2020), model architectures (Zhang and He, 2020), optimization algorithms (You et al., 2020) and parallel architectures (Shoeybi et al., 2019;Shazeer et al., 2018). Until recently, researchers propose to "back distill" the knowledge from existing PLMs to accelerate large PLMs' pre-training (Qin et al., 2021). Another line of work proposes progressive training to dynamically expand an existing PLM's size through parameter recycling (Gong et al., 2019;Chen et al., 2021). However, these methods typically focus on training PLMs on one static corpus, and thus cannot be directly applied to our lifelong pre-training setting.
